units.label: Data, Features, and the ML Problem

lessons.label: The Shape of a Dataset: Rows, Features, Labels

sections.heading: The design matrix X and the label vector y
sections.body: In supervised machine learning, a dataset is organized as two linked objects: a design matrix X with n rows and p columns, and a label vector y with n entries, one per row. Each row of X is an instance, example, or observation — one measured thing (a flower, a patient, a game). Each column is a feature or attribute — one measured property recorded for every instance. The label vector y holds the target you want to predict and is kept structurally separate from X so no algorithm can peek at the answer while learning patterns in the features. A statistician's "predictor variables" and "response variable" name the same objects as an ML engineer's "features" and "label." The shape n x p is the first fact worth extracting about any dataset, because it bounds what is statistically possible: a p close to or larger than n invites overfitting before any algorithm is even chosen.

sections.heading: Fisher's iris set as the canonical shape
sections.body: The clearest historical example is Ronald Fisher's iris dataset, introduced in his 1936 paper "The Use of Multiple Measurements in Taxonomic Problems" in the Annals of Eugenics, using measurements collected by botanist Edgar Anderson. It has n = 150 rows (50 flowers each of Iris setosa, I. versicolor, and I. virginica) and p = 4 numeric features — sepal length, sepal width, petal length, petal width, all in centimeters — giving a 150 x 4 matrix X paired with a 150-entry y holding the species. Hadley Wickham's 2014 "Tidy Data" paper in the Journal of Statistical Software formalized the layout this table already follows: one row per observation, one column per variable, one value per cell. Data that breaks this rule — two measurements crammed into one cell, or a variable spread across several column headers — must be reshaped before X can even be defined.

sections.heading: Four feature types, and turning categories into numbers
sections.body: Features come in at least four flavors: numeric (petal length, continuous), ordinal (a 1-5 severity rating, ordered but not evenly spaced), categorical or nominal (species, unordered classes), and free text (a review sentence, needing its own vectorization step). Most learning algorithms expect numbers, so a nominal column with k categories is typically one-hot encoded: it is replaced by k binary (0/1) columns, one per category, with exactly one 1 per row. Applying this to Fisher's species column would turn a single 150 x 1 categorical column into a 150 x 3 indicator block, one binary column per species, if species were ever used as a feature rather than the target.

lessons.workedExample: Building X and y for the iris data: X is 150 x 4, with row 1 = [5.1, 3.5, 1.4, 0.2] (an I. setosa flower's sepal length, sepal width, petal length, petal width in cm), and y is a 150-entry vector whose first entry is "setosa." Now suppose a researcher wants to add the collection site (three greenhouses: A, B, C) as a feature. Site is nominal, so one-hot encoding replaces the single "site" column with three binary columns site_A, site_B, site_C; a flower from greenhouse B gets the row [0, 1, 0]. X grows from 150 x 4 to 150 x 7, while y is untouched — encoding only ever transforms features, never the label, which is exactly why keeping X and y separate objects matters from the start.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks "how many rows and columns are in your dataset, and which column is the label?" is testing whether you actually built a design matrix or just have a loose spreadsheet. Students commonly answer with the label column still folded into X's column count, or cannot state p without recounting features by hand. A confident, immediate answer — "n = 240 trials, p = 6 features, the label is a separate 240-entry vector" — signals the data was structured deliberately, not stumbled into, and it sets up every later question about splitting, leakage, and metrics, all of which assume this X/y separation already exists.

questions.prompt: In Fisher's 1936 iris dataset, what are n and p?

options.text: n = 4 features, p = 150 flowers
n = 150 flowers (rows), p = 4 features (columns)
n = 3 species, p = 150 flowers
n = 150, p = 3, one column per species

explanations.a: This reverses the convention: n always counts rows (instances), p always counts columns (features), not the other way around.
explanations.b: Correct — 150 flowers are the rows (instances) and the 4 cm measurements (sepal/petal length and width) are the columns (features).
explanations.c: Species is the label y, not a count of rows or columns of X, and there are 150 flowers, not 3.
explanations.d: The species label is a single target column, not spread across 3 one-hot columns in the raw dataset as given.

questions.prompt: A dataset has a single "blood pressure reading" column that sometimes contains two numbers separated by a slash (e.g., "120/80"). Which tidy-data rule from Wickham (2014) does this violate?

options.text: One row per observation
One column per variable, one value per cell
Labels must be numeric
Features must be one-hot encoded

explanations.a: The row-per-observation rule is about instances, not about how many values are packed into one cell.
explanations.b: Correct — systolic and diastolic are two separate variables crammed into one cell and one column, which Wickham's tidy-data standard forbids; they need two columns.
explanations.c: Tidy data does not require labels to be numeric; it requires consistent cell and column structure.
explanations.d: One-hot encoding is a technique for nominal features, unrelated to whether a cell holds a compound value.

questions.prompt: Match each feature to its correct type.

right.text: Numeric
Ordinal
Categorical / nominal
Free text

questions.explanation: Petal length is a continuous measurement (numeric); a 1-5 rating is ordered but not evenly spaced (ordinal); species names have no inherent order (categorical/nominal); a full review sentence requires text vectorization before it can enter X (free text).

questions.prompt: Put these steps in order for turning a raw "collection site" column (values: GreenhouseA, GreenhouseB, GreenhouseC) into model-ready features via one-hot encoding.

items.text: Identify that site is a nominal categorical feature with k=3 unique values
Create k=3 new binary columns, one per category
For each row, set a 1 in the column matching that row's category and 0 elsewhere
Drop the original text-valued site column from X

questions.explanation: One-hot encoding first identifies the number of categories k, then creates k binary columns, then fills each row with a single 1 in the matching column, then removes the original non-numeric column since the model needs numeric input.

lessons.label: Framing the Prediction Problem

sections.heading: Supervised versus unsupervised: what a label buys you
sections.body: Machine learning problems split first on whether a label vector y exists. Supervised learning has one: classification predicts a discrete category (spam or not-spam, which of three iris species), and regression predicts a continuous number (a test score, a house price). Unsupervised learning has no y at all — clustering groups instances by similarity without being told the right groups (k-means partitioning customers into segments), and dimensionality reduction compresses many correlated features into fewer components (principal component analysis collapsing dozens of gene-expression measurements into a handful of axes). The distinction matters because it determines which metrics can even be computed: accuracy and precision require a known correct answer to check against, so they are unavailable in clustering, where success is instead judged by internal measures like silhouette score or by whether the clusters later prove useful for a downstream supervised task.

sections.heading: The framing decision: unit, target, and what is knowable in time
sections.body: Choosing a framing means answering three questions before touching an algorithm. First, the unit of analysis: is one row a student, a single quiz attempt, or a student-week? Each choice changes n and what a feature even means. Second, the target: predicting "will this student pass" is a different problem from predicting "what score will this student get," even from identical raw data, because one collapses a number into a threshold and discards how far above or below it a student lands. Third, and most often violated, is information availability at prediction time — a feature is only legitimate if it would actually be known at the moment the prediction is needed, not derived from events that happen afterward. A model framed to run at the start of a unit cannot legitimately use that unit's final quiz score as an input feature, even though it lives in the same historical dataset.

sections.heading: One dataset, three framings, three different metrics
sections.body: Take a table of student study hours, prior GPA, and end-of-unit scores. Framing A predicts pass/fail (score >= 70): a binary classification problem scored with accuracy, precision, recall, or F1. Framing B predicts the raw score (0-100): a regression problem scored with mean absolute error or R-squared, and it preserves information framing A destroys — a 69 and a 40 both count as "fail," but only regression distinguishes them. Framing C predicts the score change from a prior baseline test: also regression, but now the target itself is a difference, so a model that is excellent at framing B can still be poor at framing C if it merely predicts "students who start high end high" without capturing growth. The algorithm can stay identical (say, a linear model) across all three; what changes the entire evaluation, including which metrics are meaningful, is the framing choice made before any modeling starts.

lessons.workedExample: A school wants to flag at-risk students. Framing 1 predicts pass/fail using accuracy — but if 90% of students pass, a model that always predicts "pass" scores 90% accuracy while catching zero at-risk students, so accuracy is misleading here. Framing 2 predicts the numeric final score with mean absolute error, letting a teacher see "predicted 63, actual 58" instead of a bare fail flag, which supports triage by degree of risk. Framing 3 predicts score change from the midterm, which surfaces students who are declining even if their absolute score is still passing — a signal framings 1 and 2 both miss entirely, even though all three framings start from the exact same rows of raw data.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks "why did you frame this as classification instead of regression?" is checking whether the framing was a deliberate design decision or an accident of whatever the modeling library defaulted to. A weak answer treats classification and regression as interchangeable technical choices; a strong answer explains what information the chosen framing preserves or discards — for instance, that a pass/fail framing throws away exactly the magnitude information a teacher would need to triage interventions, and that this was a conscious tradeoff, not an oversight. This question also exposes leakage-prone framings, since students who define their target loosely often let it depend on information from after the prediction moment.

questions.prompt: Match each ML task to its correct category.

left.text: Grouping customers by purchase similarity, no known groups

right.text: Supervised: classification
Supervised: regression
Unsupervised: clustering
Unsupervised: dimensionality reduction

questions.explanation: Spam detection predicts a discrete category (classification); house price is a continuous number (regression); grouping without known labels is clustering; compressing correlated features into fewer components is dimensionality reduction.

questions.prompt: Why is accuracy unavailable as a metric for a pure clustering task like k-means customer segmentation?

options.text: Accuracy only works for regression problems
There is no known correct label to compare cluster assignments against
Clustering algorithms are too slow to compute accuracy
Accuracy requires at least 4 features

explanations.a: Accuracy is actually a classification metric, not a regression one — the issue is the absence of a label, not the wrong metric family.
explanations.b: Correct — accuracy requires a ground-truth label to check predictions against; unsupervised clustering has no such label, so success is judged by internal measures like silhouette score or downstream usefulness instead.
explanations.c: Speed has nothing to do with whether accuracy is a valid metric.
explanations.d: The number of features is unrelated to whether a correct label exists to score against.

questions.prompt: A model framed to predict pass/fail at the start of a semester uses the student's final-exam score as a feature. What is the core framing problem here?

options.text: Pass/fail should have been framed as regression instead
The feature would not actually be known at the moment the prediction is needed
Classification models cannot use numeric features
The unit of analysis is undefined

explanations.a: The classification-vs-regression choice is a separate decision; the problem described here is about feature timing, not target type.
explanations.b: Correct — the final-exam score does not exist yet at the start of the semester, so using it as an input feature violates the third framing question: what is legitimately available at prediction time.
explanations.c: Classification models routinely use numeric features; that is not the issue.
explanations.d: The unit of analysis (a student) is clearly defined here; the problem is strictly about information timing.

questions.prompt: Order these three questions in the sequence they should be settled when framing a prediction problem, before any algorithm is chosen.

items.text: Decide the unit of analysis (e.g., one row = one student, or one student-week)
Decide exactly what the target is (e.g., pass/fail vs. raw score vs. score change)
Check which features are legitimately known at prediction time

questions.explanation: You must first fix what a row represents (unit of analysis), then define precisely what you are predicting for that unit (target), and only then audit whether each candidate feature would actually be available at the moment that prediction is needed.

lessons.label: Where Labels Come From: Ground Truth Is Manufactured

sections.heading: "Ground truth" is a human or instrument judgment, not a fact of nature
sections.body: The label vector y is treated as fixed truth during training, but it was produced by something fallible: a radiologist marking a tumor, a crowdworker tagging a tweet as toxic, or a sensor with its own calibration error. Whenever labels come from people, different annotators often disagree, so datasets are commonly labeled by multiple raters and reconciled. Naive percent agreement (the fraction of items two raters marked the same way) is the obvious first metric, but it is inflated by chance: if 90% of emails are not spam, two careless raters who both mostly guess "not spam" will agree roughly 80-90% of the time by luck alone, making the labeling look far more reliable than it is.

sections.heading: Cohen's kappa corrects for chance agreement
sections.body: Jacob Cohen introduced kappa in a 1960 Educational and Psychological Measurement paper specifically to fix this. Kappa is computed as (p_o - p_e) / (1 - p_e), where p_o is the observed percent agreement and p_e is the agreement expected purely from each rater's marginal tendencies if they were labeling independently at random. A kappa of 0 means the raters do no better than chance; 1 means perfect agreement. Landis and Koch's widely cited 1977 scale calls 0.41-0.60 "moderate," 0.61-0.80 "substantial," and above 0.80 "almost perfect" agreement. A dataset built from two annotators with kappa = 0.55 is telling you, quantitatively, that a meaningful fraction of its labels are essentially a coin flip on the boundary cases — and that noise becomes a hard ceiling: no algorithm trained on those labels can be more accurate than the labels themselves are consistent.

sections.heading: Proxy labels: measuring what you can get, not what you want
sections.body: Often the real construct cannot be measured directly, so a proxy stands in. Predictive policing systems have used arrest records as a proxy for crime, but arrests reflect where police already patrol at least as much as where crime occurs, so a model trained on arrests can learn patrol patterns rather than crime itself. Obermeyer et al.'s 2019 Science paper found a widely used U.S. healthcare algorithm used prior healthcare spending as a proxy for patient sickness, and because Black patients historically had less spending for the same level of need, the proxy systematically underestimated their risk. Billing/diagnosis codes used as a proxy for true illness carry the same gap: a code reflects what was billed, not necessarily what was present. In every case the model can only ever be as correct as the proxy is faithful to the real construct — however well the model fits, it fits the label it was given, not the truth.

lessons.workedExample: Two annotators label 100 movie reviews as positive/negative. They agree on 86, so raw percent agreement is 86%. But rater A marked 90 reviews positive and rater B marked 88 positive; if their markings were independent given these marginals, chance alone predicts agreement of about p_e = (0.90)(0.88) + (0.10)(0.12) = 0.804. Applying Cohen's formula, kappa = (0.86 - 0.804) / (1 - 0.804) ≈ 0.286 — only "fair" agreement by the Landis-Koch scale, despite 86% raw agreement looking reassuring. This gap exists because both raters overwhelmingly chose "positive," so much of their apparent agreement was two people making the same easy, common guess rather than genuinely concurring on hard cases.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks "how were your labels created, and how do you know they're reliable?" is probing whether you treated ground truth as given or interrogated it. A weak project reports raw percent agreement or, worse, never mentions who produced the labels at all. A strong project reports inter-rater kappa, acknowledges the label noise ceiling this implies for achievable accuracy, and — if using a proxy like billing codes or arrest data — explicitly names the gap between the proxy and the real-world construct it stands in for. This is one of the fastest ways a judge distinguishes a project that understands measurement from one that only understands algorithms.

questions.prompt: Why does raw percent agreement between two annotators overstate labeling reliability?

options.text: It does not account for agreement that would occur by chance given each rater's marginal tendencies
Percent agreement can never be computed for binary labels
It only applies to regression targets, not classification labels
It requires exactly three annotators to be valid

explanations.a: Correct — if both raters lean heavily toward one category, they will often agree just by both making the same common guess, inflating agreement beyond genuine consensus; Cohen's kappa subtracts out this chance component.
explanations.b: Percent agreement is trivially computable for binary labels; that is not the problem with it.
explanations.c: Percent agreement is used for categorical/classification labels, not regression targets — the framing is backwards.
explanations.d: Kappa and percent agreement can be computed with two or more raters; three is not a requirement.

questions.prompt: Per Landis and Koch's 1977 scale, a Cohen's kappa of 0.55 is generally described as what level of agreement?

options.text: Almost perfect
Substantial
Moderate
No better than chance

explanations.a: Almost perfect corresponds to kappa above roughly 0.80, well above 0.55.
explanations.b: Substantial corresponds to roughly 0.61-0.80; 0.55 falls just below that range.
explanations.c: Correct — 0.55 falls in the 0.41-0.60 band Landis and Koch label "moderate" agreement.
explanations.d: A kappa of 0 indicates chance-level agreement; 0.55 is well above zero and indicates real, if imperfect, agreement.

questions.prompt: Match each proxy label to the real-world construct it imperfectly stands in for.

right.text: Actual criminal activity
Actual patient sickness/need
Actual illness present

questions.explanation: Arrests are shaped by where police patrol, not just where crime occurs; healthcare spending (per Obermeyer et al., 2019, Science) reflects access and historical inequities as much as actual need; billing codes reflect what was documented and reimbursed, not necessarily the true clinical picture.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of building and validating a human-annotated label set, from first to last.

items.text: Define the labeling instructions/construct annotators should apply
Have multiple independent annotators label the same items
Compute Cohen's kappa to check agreement beyond chance
Reconcile disagreements (e.g., adjudication) before finalizing labels

questions.explanation: You must first define what annotators are judging, then collect independent labels from more than one rater, then quantify their agreement beyond chance with kappa, and only then reconcile disagreements to produce the final label set.

lessons.label: Splitting Data: Train, Validation, Test

sections.heading: Why held-out data exists: memorization versus generalization
sections.body: A model with enough parameters can memorize its training rows perfectly — fitting every quirk and coincidence in that specific sample — without learning any pattern that transfers to new data. Measuring performance only on the data used to fit the model therefore tells you almost nothing about how it will behave on the next case it sees; this is why every rigorous evaluation reserves data the model never touched during fitting. The whole point of a held-out set is to simulate, honestly, the future: data the model could not have memorized because it was hidden from training entirely.

sections.heading: Three splits, three separate jobs
sections.body: The training set fits model parameters. The validation set tunes choices the training process itself cannot decide — hyperparameters, which features to include, when to stop training — and because you look at validation performance repeatedly while making these choices, you are implicitly fitting to it too, just more weakly. The test set is examined exactly once, at the very end, to report a final, honest number; touching it more than once (to "improve" the model based on what it shows) turns it into a second validation set and invalidates the honesty the split was built to guarantee. Common conventions split roughly 60/20/20 (train/validation/test) for a single fixed split, or 80/20 (train/test) when validation is instead handled by k-fold cross-validation within the training portion.

sections.heading: Stratified splitting for small or imbalanced data
sections.body: A purely random split can, by bad luck, put nearly all of a rare class into one split — devastating for a dataset where only 5% of cases are positive, or where n is small enough that random variation swings class proportions noticeably. Stratified splitting fixes this by sampling within each class separately so every split preserves the overall class ratio; scikit-learn's train_test_split exposes this directly via its stratify argument.

sections.heading: When randomness itself is the wrong assumption
sections.body: Random splitting assumes every row is an independent, exchangeable unit, which two common data structures violate. Grouped data — repeated measurements from the same patient, subject, or school — must be split by group (e.g., scikit-learn's GroupKFold), keeping all of one patient's rows together on one side of the split; otherwise the model can effectively memorize that patient in training and then "predict" them again in test, inflating scores. Time-ordered data must split forward in time — training on the past and testing on a later window (e.g., TimeSeriesSplit) — because a model deployed in production will never see future data when predicting the past, so a random split that lets future rows leak into training answers a question no real deployment will ever face.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher has 500 patients, each with 10 visits (5,000 rows total), and wants to predict a diagnosis from visit features. A random 80/20 row-level split puts roughly 4,000 rows in train and 1,000 in test, but since each patient appears ~10 times, most test patients also have visits in train — the model can partly recognize the patient rather than generalize the diagnostic pattern, and reported accuracy comes in well above what a new, unseen patient would get. Switching to a group split by patient ID (e.g., 400 patients' ~4,000 visits in train, 100 different patients' ~1,000 visits in test) removes this shortcut entirely, and the test score typically drops — revealing the honest generalization performance the row-level split had been overstating.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks "how did you split your data, and why that way?" is checking whether the split was chosen to fit the data's actual structure or copied by default from a tutorial. A student who says "80/20 random split" for a dataset with repeated subjects or a time axis has, often unknowingly, built in a form of leakage that inflates every reported metric. A strong answer names the structure explicitly — "grouped by student ID because each student has multiple attempts" or "split forward in time because we're forecasting" — showing the split decision was reasoned from the data-generating process, not from habit.

questions.prompt: Why is the test set examined only once, at the very end?

options.text: Because test sets are always smaller than validation sets
Because repeatedly checking it and adjusting the model turns it into a second validation set, invalidating its honesty
Because test sets cannot be stratified
Because the test set is used to fit model parameters

explanations.a: Relative size is not the reason; the reason is about what repeated peeking does to the guarantee the split provides.
explanations.b: Correct — every time you look at test performance and adjust the model in response, you are implicitly fitting to the test set, which destroys its ability to give an honest, unbiased final estimate.
explanations.c: Stratification can be applied to any split, including test; that is unrelated to why it's checked only once.
explanations.d: The training set, not the test set, is used to fit model parameters.

questions.prompt: A dataset of 5,000 patient visits comes from only 500 unique patients (10 visits each). What is the correct way to split this for evaluating a model meant to work on new patients?

options.text: A random 80/20 split at the row (visit) level
A stratified split on the diagnosis label only
A group-based split that keeps all visits from one patient entirely in one split
A time-ordered split, since visits are recorded over time

explanations.a: A row-level random split lets the same patient's visits appear in both train and test, letting the model partly recognize patients instead of generalizing.
explanations.b: Stratifying by label alone does not prevent the same patient from appearing in both splits; it only balances class proportions.
explanations.c: Correct — grouping by patient ID ensures no patient's data leaks across the split boundary, so test performance reflects generalization to genuinely new patients.
explanations.d: Nothing in the scenario indicates the task is forecasting future visits from past ones; the core issue described is repeated measurements per patient, which calls for group splitting.

questions.prompt: Match each split-type scenario to the correct splitting strategy.

left.text: Only 5% of a small dataset belongs to the positive class
Same 200 students each contribute 5 quiz attempts
Predicting next month's sales from prior months' sales

right.text: Stratified split
Group-based split
Forward-in-time split

questions.explanation: Rare classes need stratified splitting to preserve class proportions across splits; repeated-subject data needs group splitting so one subject never spans both train and test; forecasting problems need a forward-in-time split so training only ever uses the past relative to test.

questions.prompt: Order these stages of a standard train/validation/test workflow by when each set is used.

items.text: Fit model parameters on the training set
Tune hyperparameters and feature choices using validation performance
Report final performance on the untouched test set, exactly once

questions.explanation: Training fits the parameters first, validation guides iterative tuning decisions next, and the test set is reserved until the very end to produce one honest, final performance number.

lessons.label: Data Leakage: The Bug That Fakes Success

sections.heading: Three kinds of leakage, one shared symptom
sections.body: Data leakage is any way that information the model should not have gets into training or evaluation, making performance look far better than it will be in real deployment. It comes in three main forms: target leakage, where a feature itself encodes the answer; train-test contamination, where information from the test set influences training; and temporal leakage, using future information to predict the past. All three share the same tell-tale symptom: implausibly high accuracy, an F1 or R-squared that looks too good relative to how hard the problem should be, is the single strongest warning sign that leakage, not genuine skill, produced the result. Published hospital-readmission models, for comparison, typically land around 65-75% accuracy on honest evaluation, so a science-fair project reporting 97% on the same kind of task should immediately trigger suspicion rather than celebration.

sections.heading: Target leakage: a feature that already contains the answer
sections.body: Target leakage happens when a feature is, in effect, a restatement of the label using information that would only exist because the outcome already happened. The classic medical example is predicting whether a patient has a bacterial infection using "antibiotic prescribed" as a feature — doctors mostly prescribe antibiotics because they already suspect infection, so the feature is downstream of the diagnosis, not a genuine predictor available beforehand. A model trained on it appears to nail the diagnosis while actually just detecting the doctor's own prior decision.

sections.heading: Train-test contamination and temporal leakage
sections.body: Train-test contamination occurs whenever any step touches the full dataset before the train/test split: fitting a scaler, imputer, or feature-selection procedure on all the data lets statistics from test rows (means, variances, correlations) quietly influence what the model sees during training. Duplicate rows split across train and test, or the same subject appearing in both, cause the identical problem discussed for grouped data. Temporal leakage is the time-ordered version: using a feature that was only computed or observed after the prediction moment — for instance, a stock-price feature averaged over a window that includes days after the date being predicted.

sections.heading: How common leakage actually is
sections.body: Kapoor and Narayanan's 2023 Patterns paper systematically surveyed the machine-learning-based science literature and found leakage affecting results across 294 papers spanning 17 scientific fields, from medicine to political science to computer security, showing that leakage is not a rare beginner's mistake but a pervasive failure mode even in published, peer-reviewed research. For a science-fair project, leakage is the single most common reason a reported result is simply wrong: it produces a model that looks excellent on paper and fails the moment it meets genuinely new data, because the "skill" it demonstrated during evaluation was never available at prediction time.

lessons.workedExample: A student builds a model to predict hospital readmission using a dataset where a "discharge summary contains follow-up appointment" feature turns out to be filled in only for patients who were, in fact, not readmitted (because a completed follow-up plan is written after discharge is deemed successful). The model hits 97% accuracy, which the student initially reports as a strong result. A more careful audit reveals the feature is filled in after the outcome is already known — pure target leakage. After removing it and any other post-discharge fields, accuracy drops to a much more modest 71%, which is the number that actually reflects what could be predicted using only information available at the moment of discharge.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees a science-fair model reporting 95%+ accuracy on a genuinely hard problem will almost always ask "what features are you using, and could any of them only exist after the outcome was known?" This question is the single fastest leakage detector a judge has, and being unable to answer it — or worse, discovering the answer live at the fair — undermines the entire project. A strong presenter preempts this by naming which features they audited for leakage, showing the pipeline was fit only on training data, and reporting a result they can defend as achievable at real prediction time, not one inflated by a hidden shortcut.

questions.prompt: A model predicting bacterial infection uses "antibiotic prescribed" as a feature and scores 97% accuracy. What kind of leakage is this?

options.text: Temporal leakage
Target leakage
Train-test contamination
No leakage — this is a legitimate feature

explanations.a: Temporal leakage specifically refers to using information from the future relative to a time-ordered prediction point, not a feature that directly encodes the outcome.
explanations.b: Correct — the antibiotic-prescribed feature is essentially a restatement of the diagnosis, since doctors prescribe antibiotics because they already suspect infection, making it target leakage.
explanations.c: Train-test contamination refers to test-set information influencing training (e.g., scaling before splitting), not a single feature encoding the answer.
explanations.d: This is a textbook case of leakage: the feature is downstream of the outcome, not a genuine predictor available before diagnosis.

questions.prompt: Why does fitting a StandardScaler on the entire dataset before splitting into train and test cause leakage?

options.text: It makes the model run slower
It lets statistics computed from test rows (mean, variance) influence the values the model trains on
Scalers can only be fit on labels, not features
It changes the number of features in X

explanations.a: Speed is unrelated; the issue is information flow between splits, not runtime.
explanations.b: Correct — the scaler's mean and variance are computed using test rows too, so information about the test set's distribution leaks into how training data gets transformed, inflating apparent performance.
explanations.c: Scalers are fit on features (X), not labels; this option describes something scalers don't even do.
explanations.d: Scaling transforms values within existing columns; it does not add or remove features.

questions.prompt: According to Kapoor and Narayanan's 2023 Patterns survey, roughly how many papers across how many scientific fields were found to be affected by data leakage?

options.text: 294 papers across 17 fields
12 papers across 2 fields
294 papers, all in computer science only
17 papers across 294 fields

explanations.a: Correct — their survey found leakage affecting 294 papers spanning 17 scientific fields, showing leakage is widespread even in peer-reviewed, published research.
explanations.b: This understates the scale the survey actually found by more than an order of magnitude.
explanations.c: The affected papers spanned 17 different scientific fields, not just computer science.
explanations.d: This reverses the two figures — it was 294 papers across 17 fields, not the other way around.

questions.prompt: Order these steps for correctly auditing a pipeline to avoid train-test contamination.

items.text: Split the raw data into train and test sets first
Fit the scaler/imputer/feature-selector only on the training set
Use the already-fit transformer to transform the test set (without refitting it)
Evaluate the trained model on the transformed test set

questions.explanation: The split must happen before any transformer is fit, the transformer is fit only on training rows, then that same fitted transformer is applied (not refit) to the test rows, and only then is the model evaluated — this order ensures no test-set statistics ever influence training.

lessons.label: Preprocessing Without Cheating: The Pipeline Discipline

sections.heading: Two scaling recipes: z-score standardization and min-max scaling
sections.body: Many algorithms (k-nearest neighbors, gradient descent-based models, anything using distances) are sensitive to features living on wildly different scales, so numeric features are typically rescaled. Z-score standardization subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation, (x - mean) / std, producing a feature centered at 0 with unit variance and no fixed bounds. Min-max scaling instead subtracts the minimum and divides by the range, (x - min) / (max - min), squashing every value into a fixed [0, 1] interval. Standardization is the more common default because it is less distorted by a single extreme outlier than min-max, whose bounds are defined by exactly the smallest and largest observed values; min-max is still preferred for neural networks and image pixel values, where a bounded [0, 1] input range is often assumed. Tree-based models (decision trees, random forests) are a notable exception — they split on thresholds rather than distances, so neither scaling method changes their predictions at all.

sections.heading: Missingness has a type, and the type should guide the fix
sections.body: Donald Rubin's 1976 Biometrika paper "Inference and Missing Data" classified missingness into three mechanisms. MCAR (missing completely at random): missingness is unrelated to any value, observed or not, e.g., a sensor randomly drops readings. MAR (missing at random): missingness depends on other observed features but not on the missing value itself, e.g., older patients skip a survey question more often, but conditional on age it's random. MNAR (missing not at random): missingness depends on the unobserved value itself, e.g., patients with the most severe symptoms are too sick to complete the survey. Mean or median imputation fills every gap with one summary value, which is simple but can distort variance and silently assumes something close to MCAR; adding a binary missingness indicator column alongside the imputed value preserves the signal that a value was missing at all, which matters most under MAR or MNAR, where missingness itself carries information.

sections.heading: Fit on train only: the rule and its structural fix
sections.body: Every transformer — scaler, imputer, or encoder — must be fit exclusively on the training set, then merely applied (transform, never refit) to validation and test. Fitting a scaler's mean and standard deviation on the whole dataset before splitting leaks test-set statistics into the values training sees, the same contamination mechanism covered for leakage generally. Scikit-learn's Pipeline class enforces this structurally: it chains preprocessing steps and a final estimator into one object, and calling pipeline.fit(X_train, y_train) fits every step using only training rows, while pipeline.predict(X_test) applies each fitted step's transform without ever refitting on test data, making the correct discipline the path of least resistance rather than something to remember by hand. This same Pipeline object plugs directly into cross_val_score or GridSearchCV, which refit every step fresh within each cross-validation fold, so no fold's validation rows ever influence that fold's preprocessing.

lessons.workedExample: A student has 1,000 rows with one numeric feature and fits a StandardScaler on all 1,000 rows before splitting 80/20, then trains a k-NN classifier, getting 89% test accuracy. Redone correctly — split first into 800 train / 200 test, fit the scaler on only the 800 training rows, then transform both splits with that fitted scaler — the same k-NN model scores 81% on test. The 8-point gap is entirely attributable to the leaked test-set mean and standard deviation subtly shifting where training-set points landed relative to the true (unknown, at training time) distribution boundary the test rows actually come from; 81% is the number that reflects real generalization.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks "where exactly in your code do you fit your scaler or imputer?" is checking for the single most common silent bug in student ML projects: preprocessing fit on the full dataset before splitting. A hesitant answer, or one that describes fitting the scaler once at the top of a script before any split happens, reveals inflated numbers the student may not even realize are wrong. Naming the scikit-learn Pipeline object specifically, and explaining that fit() only ever touches training rows, is a fast, concrete way to show the discipline was built into the code's structure rather than left to memory.

questions.prompt: Match each missingness mechanism (Rubin, 1976) to its example.

right.text: A sensor randomly drops readings unrelated to any value
Older patients skip a question more often, but it's random given age
The sickest patients are too ill to complete the survey

questions.explanation: MCAR means missingness is unrelated to any value at all (random sensor dropout); MAR means missingness depends on other observed features (age) but not the missing value itself; MNAR means missingness depends on the unobserved value itself (severity causing survey non-completion).

questions.prompt: Why does min-max scaling tend to be more distorted by outliers than z-score standardization?

options.text: Min-max scaling cannot be applied to numeric features
Min-max scaling's bounds are set exactly by the observed minimum and maximum, so one extreme value stretches the whole scale
Z-score standardization ignores the mean entirely
Min-max scaling always produces negative values

explanations.a: Min-max scaling is specifically designed for numeric features; that's not the issue.
explanations.b: Correct — because min-max scaling maps the observed min to 0 and observed max to 1, a single extreme outlier compresses every other value into a narrow band near the middle of the range.
explanations.c: Z-score standardization is centered on the mean; it does not ignore it.
explanations.d: Min-max scaling by construction bounds values to [0, 1], which are non-negative.

questions.prompt: A StandardScaler is fit on all 1,000 rows of a dataset, and only afterward is the data split 80/20 into train and test. What is the effect on reported test accuracy?

options.text: No effect — scaling never touches accuracy
Test accuracy is deflated because the scaler removes useful variance
Test accuracy is inflated because test-set mean and standard deviation leaked into how training data was scaled
The model can no longer be trained at all

explanations.a: Scaling changes the numeric values the model learns from, which does affect downstream accuracy, especially for distance-based models.
explanations.b: The effect runs the other way — fitting on the full dataset inflates rather than deflates the reported score.
explanations.c: Correct — the scaler's parameters are computed using test rows too, so test-set information leaks into the transformation applied to training data, producing an optimistic, unrealistic accuracy figure.
explanations.d: Fitting a scaler on the full dataset is a leakage bug, not something that prevents training from running.

questions.prompt: Order these steps for using a scikit-learn Pipeline correctly to avoid preprocessing leakage.

items.text: Split data into train and test sets
Build a Pipeline chaining a scaler/imputer and a final estimator
Call pipeline.fit(X_train, y_train), fitting every step on training rows only
Call pipeline.predict(X_test), applying each fitted step's transform without refitting

questions.explanation: The split happens first, then the Pipeline object is constructed, then fit() is called only on training data (fitting every preprocessing step and the estimator together), and finally predict() applies those already-fitted transforms to test data without ever refitting on it.

units.label: Models and the Training Loop

lessons.label: What 'Fitting a Model' Actually Means

sections.heading: A model is a family, not a formula
sections.body: Every supervised model is a parameterized family of functions f(x; theta), and 'training' means searching that family for the specific theta that minimizes a loss function L computed over the training set. For ordinary least squares (OLS) linear regression, the family is f(x) = theta_0 + theta_1*x_1 + ... + theta_p*x_p, and the loss is the sum of squared residuals. Before any data is seen, theta is unset — fitting is the optimization step that converts an untrained family into a specific, usable function. This framing generalizes: a decision tree's family is every possible tree of split thresholds up to some depth; a neural net's family is every weight matrix of a fixed architecture. What changes across model types is the shape of the family and the loss surface, not the basic loop of 'define family, define loss, search for the minimizer.'

sections.heading: Parameters the optimizer learns vs. hyperparameters you choose
sections.body: Keep two vocabularies strictly separate. PARAMETERS are the numbers the fitting algorithm sets by looking at data — the coefficients theta in OLS, the weights and biases in a neural net, the split thresholds inside a fitted tree. HYPERPARAMETERS are choices made before fitting starts, fixed externally by the practitioner or by a separate tuning loop such as grid search — the maximum depth of a tree, the learning rate and number of epochs for gradient descent, the k in k-nearest-neighbors, the regularization strength lambda. Confusing the two is a common vocabulary error: a tree's split thresholds are parameters because data decides them, but the tree's max_depth is a hyperparameter because you decide it, typically via cross-validation on a held-out fold, never by looking at test-set performance.

sections.heading: Closed-form vs. iterative fitting: OLS as the minimal case
sections.body: OLS is the cleanest illustration because it can be solved two ways. The closed-form route solves the normal equations theta = (X^T X)^(-1) X^T y directly — one matrix inversion, exact in one shot, a method Gauss and Legendre both worked out around 1805-1809 while fitting planetary and comet orbits. The iterative route instead starts from a guess and nudges theta downhill via gradient descent until convergence — slower per problem, but the only option once the loss lacks a clean closed form, as with logistic regression or neural nets. Both routes reach the same minimizer for OLS because squared-error loss on a linear model is convex with one global minimum. In code this loop compresses to two calls: model.fit(X_train, y_train) performs the search for theta, and model.predict(X_new) evaluates the resulting f(x; theta) on unseen inputs.

lessons.workedExample: A team fits OLS to predict a plant's height in cm from days-since-germination and fertilizer dose, getting f(x) = 2.1 + 0.85*days + 1.3*dose. Before fitting, the family was any f(x) = theta0 + theta1*days + theta2*dose — infinitely many candidate planes. Calling .fit() on 40 training rows solved the normal equations, producing exactly those three numbers as the minimizer of summed squared residuals on that data. Now .predict() on a new plant with days=10, dose=2 returns 2.1 + 8.5 + 2.6 = 13.2 cm without touching the training rows again. If the team later swaps in a neural net on the same inputs, the family becomes far larger and fitting must switch from the closed-form normal equations to iterative gradient descent, but the fit/predict contract stays identical.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'what exactly did your model learn?' is testing whether the student can name the actual fitted numbers rather than describe the model in the abstract. Judges also frequently probe the parameter/hyperparameter line directly — 'how did you choose k?' or 'how did you choose the tree depth?' — because a fair project that tuned a hyperparameter using the test set has leaked information, invalidating its reported accuracy. Stating precisely which numbers came from the data versus which numbers the team chose, ideally justified by a validation curve rather than trial and error on test data, signals real methodological control rather than a merely working notebook.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes parameters from hyperparameters?

options.text: Parameters are set before training begins; hyperparameters are learned from data
Parameters are learned by the fitting algorithm from data; hyperparameters are chosen by the practitioner before fitting
Hyperparameters only exist for neural networks, not for trees or linear models
Parameters and hyperparameters are two names for the same underlying quantity

explanations.a: This reverses the definitions — parameters are the learned quantities, not the pre-set ones.
explanations.b: Correct — theta in OLS or weights in a net are found by the optimizer from data; k, learning rate, max depth, and lambda are fixed by the practitioner beforehand.
explanations.c: Trees have hyperparameters too (max depth, min samples per leaf), and linear models have at least the choice of regularization strength.
explanations.d: They are distinct: one is discovered by optimization, the other is chosen and typically validated via cross-validation.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of iterative (gradient-descent) fitting in the order they occur within one training loop.

items.text: Initialize theta (e.g., zeros or small random values)
Compute predictions f(x; theta) on the training batch
Compute the gradient of the loss with respect to theta
Update theta := theta - eta * gradient
Check for convergence; repeat the loop if not converged

questions.explanation: Training starts from an initial guess, computes current predictions, differentiates the loss to find the descent direction, takes a step in that direction scaled by the learning rate, then checks whether to stop or loop again.

questions.prompt: The closed-form OLS solution theta = (X^T X)^(-1) X^T y requires which condition to exist as written?

options.text: X^T X must be invertible (non-singular)
At least one feature in X must be categorical
The loss must be cross-entropy rather than squared error
Gradient descent must be run first to provide a starting theta

explanations.a: Correct — if X^T X is singular (e.g., from perfectly collinear features), the matrix inverse does not exist and the normal equations cannot be solved directly.
explanations.b: Categorical features are irrelevant to invertibility; the condition concerns linear independence of the columns of X.
explanations.c: The normal equations are specific to squared-error loss; cross-entropy has no equivalent closed form.
explanations.d: The closed-form route is an alternative to gradient descent, not a follow-up to it — it requires no starting guess.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its role in the fit/predict framing of a model.

right.text: The parameters the search discovers
The objective the search minimizes
The step that performs the search over theta
The step that evaluates f(x; theta) on new data

questions.explanation: theta is what gets learned, the loss is what defines 'best' during that learning, .fit() runs the optimization that sets theta, and .predict() simply plugs new inputs into the now-fixed function.

lessons.label: Loss Functions: What the Model Is Actually Optimizing

sections.heading: Regression losses: MSE vs. MAE
sections.body: Mean squared error, MSE = (1/n) * sum (y_i - yhat_i)^2, is the default regression loss because squaring makes it differentiable everywhere, including exactly at zero error, which is what gradient-based optimizers need — the derivative with respect to a prediction is a smooth signal that vanishes only at the optimum. Squaring also means a single large residual dominates the sum: one residual of 10 contributes 100, ten times more than ten residuals of 1 combined (10*1=10), so MSE is highly sensitive to outliers. Mean absolute error, MAE = (1/n) * sum |y_i - yhat_i|, grows linearly instead, so a large residual contributes proportionally rather than quadratically, making MAE more robust to outliers — but its derivative is undefined at zero and constant elsewhere, which slows gradient-based fitting near the optimum, one reason MSE remains the more common default despite its outlier sensitivity. A middle path, Huber loss, proposed by statistician Peter Huber in a 1964 paper on robust estimation, behaves like MSE for small residuals and like MAE for large ones, switching at a threshold delta chosen by the practitioner.

sections.heading: Classification losses: cross-entropy and hinge loss
sections.body: Classification losses cannot use residuals directly because labels are categorical. Binary cross-entropy (log loss) is -[y*log(p) + (1-y)*log(1-p)], where p is the model's predicted probability of the positive class; it penalizes confident wrong predictions extremely harshly, since -log(p) approaches infinity as p approaches 0 for a true positive. Multiclass cross-entropy generalizes this to -sum_k y_k*log(p_k) across classes. Hinge loss, used by support vector machines, is max(0, 1 - y*f(x)) for labels y in {-1, +1}; it is exactly zero once a point is classified correctly with a margin of at least 1, so it does not keep rewarding an already-confident correct prediction the way cross-entropy does. This margin-only structure is why an SVM's decision boundary is defined entirely by its support vectors rather than by every training point, a formulation Corinna Cortes and Vladimir Vapnik popularized in their 1995 soft-margin SVM paper.

sections.heading: The loss you optimize is not the metric you report
sections.body: The distinction students most often blur is between the LOSS an optimizer minimizes during training and the METRIC used to report performance afterward. Accuracy — the fraction of predictions exactly correct — is a step function of the model's output: it does not change smoothly as parameters shift by a small amount, so its gradient is zero almost everywhere and undefined at the decision boundary. A gradient-based optimizer given zero gradient everywhere has no signal to follow, so accuracy cannot be optimized directly. Cross-entropy exists as a smooth, differentiable surrogate that correlates well with accuracy — minimizing it tends to improve accuracy — even though the two numbers are not the same quantity and can diverge, particularly under severe class imbalance.

lessons.workedExample: A regression model predicts exam scores with residuals [1, 1, 1, 1, 10] on five test points. MSE = (1+1+1+1+100)/5 = 20.8, dominated by the single outlier; MAE = (1+1+1+1+10)/5 = 2.8, barely moved by it. A classifier trained with cross-entropy that assigns a true positive a probability of only p=0.01 incurs -log(0.01) approx 4.6 nats of loss on that single example, versus -log(0.5) approx 0.69 for an uncertain-but-correct prediction — the loss punishes confident wrongness far more than uncertainty. An SVM given that same point with margin y*f(x)=1.5 incurs hinge loss max(0, 1-1.5)=0: past margin 1, hinge loss stops caring how confident the prediction becomes.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'why didn't you just train on accuracy directly?' is checking whether the student understands the loss/metric split, not merely that they memorized 'cross-entropy for classification.' The strong answer names the mechanism: accuracy is a non-differentiable step function with zero gradient almost everywhere, so it gives an optimizer nothing to follow, while cross-entropy is a smooth surrogate chosen because minimizing it tends to also raise accuracy. A judge may also probe MSE vs. MAE choice on a project with known outliers — the right answer ties the choice to squared vs. linear growth of the penalty, not a vague 'MAE is more robust.'

questions.prompt: Why can accuracy not be used as the loss that a gradient-based optimizer minimizes?

options.text: Accuracy is always lower than cross-entropy, so it is a worse number to report
Accuracy is a step function of the model output, so its gradient is zero almost everywhere and undefined at the boundary
Accuracy can only be computed after training finishes, never during it
Accuracy requires labeled test data, which optimizers are not allowed to see

explanations.a: Accuracy and cross-entropy are not even on the same scale, and this isn't why accuracy fails as a loss.
explanations.b: Correct — because tiny parameter changes almost never flip a prediction from correct to incorrect, the gradient of accuracy is zero nearly everywhere, giving gradient descent no usable signal.
explanations.c: Accuracy can be computed at any point during training on a batch of predictions; the issue is that it does not provide a usable gradient, not timing.
explanations.d: Accuracy is computed from predictions and true labels, the same labels the loss itself uses — the problem is differentiability, not label access.

questions.prompt: A dataset has one severe outlier among otherwise well-fit regression points. Which loss is more robust to that outlier, and why?

options.text: MSE, because squaring always reduces the effect of large errors
MAE, because the penalty grows linearly with residual size rather than quadratically
Both are equally robust since they are computed on the same residuals
Neither — robustness to outliers is only a property of cross-entropy

explanations.a: Squaring amplifies large errors rather than reducing them — a residual of 10 contributes 100, not a shrunken value.
explanations.b: Correct — MAE's penalty scales proportionally to |residual|, so one large residual cannot dominate the sum the way it does under squaring.
explanations.c: They use the same residuals but transform them differently (square vs. absolute value), giving very different sensitivity to outliers.
explanations.d: Cross-entropy is a classification loss and is not the relevant comparison for outlier-robustness in regression.

questions.prompt: Match each loss function to the setting it is designed for.

right.text: Regression, smooth everywhere, sensitive to outliers
Regression, robust to outliers, non-smooth at zero
Classification, penalizes confident wrong probabilities harshly
Margin-based classification (SVM), zero once margin exceeds 1

questions.explanation: MSE squares residuals (smooth, outlier-sensitive); MAE takes absolute value (robust, kinked at zero); cross-entropy uses -log(p) (blows up on confident errors); hinge loss is flat at zero past margin 1, caring only whether a point clears the margin.

questions.prompt: Order these four residuals from smallest to largest contribution to MEAN SQUARED ERROR.

items.text: Residual of 1
Residual of 2
Residual of 5
Residual of 10

questions.explanation: MSE squares each residual before averaging (1, 4, 25, 100), so the ordering matches the residual ordering directly — but the gaps between contributions grow much faster than the gaps between the residuals themselves, illustrating MSE's outlier sensitivity.

lessons.label: Gradient Descent, Epochs, Batches, and the Learning Rate

sections.heading: The update rule: theta := theta - eta * gradient
sections.body: The gradient of the loss with respect to theta, written grad_theta L, is a vector pointing in the direction of steepest INCREASE of the loss at the current theta. Since the goal is to minimize loss, gradient descent moves in the opposite direction: theta := theta - eta * grad_theta L, where eta, the learning rate, scales how large a step to take. Each such update is one ITERATION. An EPOCH is one full pass through the entire training set — a single epoch can contain many iterations if the data is processed in batches rather than all at once, so epoch and iteration are not interchangeable: epoch count times batches-per-epoch equals total iterations completed. The stochastic version of this update traces back to Herbert Robbins and Sutton Monro's 1951 paper on stochastic approximation, decades before it became the default way to train neural networks.

sections.heading: Full-batch, mini-batch, and stochastic gradient descent
sections.body: Three variants differ only in how much data each iteration's gradient is computed from. FULL-BATCH gradient descent computes the gradient over the entire training set before taking one step — accurate but slow per step and memory-heavy for large datasets. STOCHASTIC gradient descent (SGD) computes the gradient from a single random example per step — fast and noisy, with noise that can actually help the optimizer escape shallow local minima. MINI-BATCH gradient descent, the practical default, computes the gradient over a small random subset, commonly 32 to 256 examples, per step, trading the stability of full-batch against the speed of stochastic; it is what a batch_size argument controls in PyTorch or TensorFlow training loops.

sections.heading: The learning rate, and convex vs. non-convex loss surfaces
sections.body: The learning rate eta is arguably the single most consequential hyperparameter in the training loop. Too small, and descent crawls: loss decreases correctly but training may need thousands of extra epochs to converge, wasting compute. Too large, and updates overshoot the minimum — the loss oscillates, fails to settle, or in the worst case diverges outright, with weights growing until they overflow to NaN. Practitioners diagnose this from the loss curve and commonly use a decaying learning-rate schedule or an adaptive optimizer such as Adam, introduced by Diederik Kingma and Jimmy Ba in 2014, which rescales eta per-parameter automatically using running estimates of the gradient's mean and variance (default decay rates beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999). The loss surface itself also matters: linear and logistic regression have CONVEX loss surfaces, so gradient descent with a suitable eta is guaranteed to reach the global minimum loss value. The parameter vector that achieves it is unique only when the input features are linearly independent (full rank); when they are not, a flat set of parameter vectors all achieve that same minimal loss, and gradient descent simply settles somewhere on that set. Neural networks have NON-CONVEX surfaces riddled with local minima and saddle points, so gradient descent finds a good minimum with no guarantee it is the global one.

lessons.workedExample: A student trains a logistic regression classifier and plots training loss against iteration. With eta=0.001, loss drops smoothly but is still falling after 500 iterations — too small a step, wasting time. With eta=10, loss swings between 0.2 and 40 every few iterations and eventually reports NaN — the updates are overshooting so badly that weights blow up. Setting eta=0.05 makes loss fall smoothly to a stable plateau within 80 iterations across 16 epochs of a 400-row, batch-size-80 dataset (80 rows/batch x 5 batches = 400 rows = 1 epoch, so each epoch is 5 iterations, and 80 iterations span 16 epochs total).
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'what learning rate did you use, and how did you pick it?' is testing whether the student treated eta as a real hyperparameter tuned by watching the loss curve, rather than an untouched library default. A judge may also ask the epoch-vs-iteration question directly, since students frequently use the words interchangeably in write-ups; the correct answer ties epoch to 'one full pass over the data' and iteration to 'one gradient update,' with the batch size as the bridge between them. For neural-net projects, a judge probing 'how do you know you found the best possible weights?' is checking whether the student understands that non-convex surfaces offer no such guarantee.

questions.prompt: What typically happens to training when the learning rate is set far too large?

options.text: Training converges faster than optimal but still reaches the correct minimum
The loss oscillates, fails to settle, or diverges outright, sometimes producing NaN
The model ignores the learning rate entirely once it exceeds 1.0
Training slows down because each step takes longer to compute

explanations.a: A too-large learning rate overshoots the minimum rather than converging faster to it correctly.
explanations.b: Correct — oversized steps repeatedly overshoot the minimum, and in severe cases weight values grow without bound until they overflow to NaN.
explanations.c: There is no such cutoff behavior; learning rates above 1.0 are sometimes fine and sometimes catastrophic depending on the loss surface's curvature.
explanations.d: The learning rate does not change how long a step takes to compute, only how large a step is taken.

questions.prompt: Which gradient descent variant computes its gradient from a single randomly chosen training example per update?

options.text: Full-batch gradient descent
Mini-batch gradient descent
Stochastic gradient descent (SGD)
None of these — all variants require the full dataset per update

explanations.a: Full-batch uses the entire training set for every gradient computation, the opposite of a single example.
explanations.b: Mini-batch uses a small subset, typically 32-256 examples, not just one.
explanations.c: Correct — SGD's defining trait is computing the gradient from one random example per step, which is fast but noisy.
explanations.d: Full-batch is a real variant that does use the entire dataset per update, so this option is false on its face.

questions.prompt: Match each model's loss surface to its correct description.

right.text: Convex — a suitable learning rate guarantees reaching the global minimum loss value (the minimizing parameters are unique only if the features are linearly independent)
Non-convex — riddled with local minima and saddle points, no global guarantee

questions.explanation: Linear and logistic regression both have convex loss surfaces, so gradient descent always reaches the global minimum loss value (the minimizing parameters themselves are unique only when the features are linearly independent); deep networks have non-convex surfaces where gradient descent finds only a good, not guaranteed globally optimal, minimum.

questions.prompt: Order these gradient descent variants from LEAST noisy per-step gradient estimate to MOST noisy.

items.text: Full-batch gradient descent
Mini-batch gradient descent
Stochastic gradient descent

questions.explanation: Full-batch averages over the entire dataset, giving the smoothest gradient estimate; mini-batch averages over a small subset, adding moderate noise; stochastic uses just one example, giving the noisiest but cheapest per-step estimate.

lessons.label: Reading a Loss Curve

sections.heading: The diagnostic plot: training vs. validation loss by epoch
sections.body: The single most informative plot in the training loop is training loss and validation loss plotted on the same axes against epoch number. Early in training, both curves fall together as the model learns genuine signal shared between the two splits. At some point the validation curve flattens and then turns upward while the training curve keeps falling — this divergence marks the onset of OVERFITTING: the model has begun memorizing training-set idiosyncrasies, noise and quirks of specific rows, that do not generalize. The epoch at which validation loss is minimized, just before this upturn, is the natural stopping point; EARLY STOPPING formalizes this by saving the model's weights at that epoch and halting training once validation loss fails to improve for a set number of epochs, a 'patience' window, rather than training for a fixed, arbitrarily large epoch count. Lutz Prechelt's 1998 study of early-stopping criteria across neural-network benchmarks found that stopping the first time validation error fails to improve is often too eager, which is why a patience window of several epochs, rather than stopping at the very first uptick, tends to perform better in practice.

sections.heading: Failure signatures: flat, noisy, and exploding curves
sections.body: Several loss-curve shapes signal specific bugs rather than normal learning. A FLAT curve that never drops from its initial value usually means one of three things: the learning rate is far too small or far too large, the input features carry no real signal for the target, or there is a bug such as gradients not flowing, for example a frozen layer or labels mismatched to features by an indexing error. A NOISY, jagged curve that trends down but jumps wildly step to step points to too small a batch size, too high a learning rate, or both. An EXPLODING curve — loss rising sharply, then to infinity or NaN — signals a learning rate far too high or, in deep networks, unstable gradients propagating through many layers, addressed by gradient clipping or a smaller learning rate.

sections.heading: When validation loss looks BETTER than training loss
sections.body: A validation curve sitting below the training curve for a meaningful stretch is a red flag, not good news, because a model should rarely generalize better than it fits its own training data. The two common causes are DATA LEAKAGE — information from validation or test rows has leaked into training, via duplicated rows across splits or a feature that encodes the target — and a REGULARIZATION ARTIFACT, where techniques like dropout are active only during training, making training loss look artificially worse, but are turned off at evaluation time. This distinction matters for debugging: leakage falsely inflates apparent performance and must be hunted down via split hygiene, whereas the dropout artifact is expected and harmless.

lessons.workedExample: A student plots 60 epochs of training on a spam classifier. Both curves fall together through epoch 18, training loss reaching 0.15 and validation loss 0.19. Training loss keeps dropping from epoch 19 onward, reaching 0.03 by epoch 60, while validation loss keeps falling slightly further to its minimum of 0.18 at epoch 20, then turns upward, rising back to 0.31 by epoch 60. The minimum validation loss, 0.18, occurred at epoch 20 — that is the checkpoint an early-stopping callback with patience=5 would have saved, since validation loss failed to improve for 5 consecutive epochs by epoch 25 and training would halt there, avoiding 35 wasted epochs of pure memorization.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks a student to sketch their loss curve from memory is testing whether early stopping was a deliberate, monitored decision or just 'training for 100 epochs because that's what the tutorial did.' The strongest answers name the actual epoch where validation loss bottomed out and explain what happened after — rising validation loss with falling training loss is the textbook overfitting signature, and a student who can point to it on their own curve has clearly looked at the data rather than trusted a final printed accuracy number. A judge may also probe an unusual curve shape directly, since a flat or noisy curve in the appendix often reveals an unresolved bug the student glossed over.

questions.prompt: What does it mean when validation loss turns upward while training loss keeps falling?

options.text: The model has finished learning and further training is harmless
The onset of overfitting — the model is memorizing training-set noise that does not generalize
The learning rate is too small and needs to be increased
The validation set is too large and should be shrunk

explanations.a: Continued training past this point actively hurts generalization rather than being harmless.
explanations.b: Correct — this divergence is the textbook overfitting signature: genuine shared signal has been exhausted and the model is now fitting idiosyncrasies of the training rows.
explanations.c: Learning rate size affects how fast or unstable descent is, not this specific divergence pattern between two curves.
explanations.d: Validation set size affects how noisy the validation curve looks, not the fundamental divergence caused by overfitting.

questions.prompt: Order these stages of a typical training/validation loss curve as epochs progress.

items.text: Training and validation loss fall together
Validation loss reaches its minimum (the early-stopping point)
Validation loss rises while training loss keeps falling (overfitting)

questions.explanation: Training begins with both losses falling as shared signal is learned, reaches a point where validation loss bottoms out, and continued training beyond that point drives training loss lower purely by memorizing noise while validation loss worsens.

questions.prompt: Match each loss-curve failure signature to its most likely cause.

left.text: Validation curve sits below training curve

right.text: Learning rate wrong in either direction, no real signal in features, or a bug
Batch size too small, learning rate too high, or both
Learning rate far too high, or unstable gradients in a deep network
Data leakage between splits, or a regularization artifact like dropout

questions.explanation: A flat curve points to a broken signal path or badly set learning rate; jagged descent points to noisy small-batch or too-aggressive updates; an exploding curve points to instability from a too-high learning rate or unstable deep gradients; a validation curve below training points to leakage or a training-only regularizer like dropout.

questions.prompt: In an early-stopping callback, what does the 'patience' parameter control?

options.text: The number of epochs validation loss may fail to improve before training halts
The learning rate used during the final epoch
The number of training examples per batch
The total number of epochs the model is allowed to train, fixed in advance

explanations.a: Correct — patience sets how many consecutive epochs without validation-loss improvement are tolerated before training stops and the best checkpoint is restored.
explanations.b: Patience has nothing to do with the learning rate's value; it governs a stopping condition.
explanations.c: Batch size is a separate hyperparameter controlling how much data each gradient update uses.
explanations.d: Early stopping is precisely the alternative to a fixed epoch count — it stops adaptively based on validation performance.

lessons.label: Over- and Underfitting and the Bias-Variance Trade-off

sections.heading: Decomposing expected error into bias, variance, and noise
sections.body: Any model's expected squared error on a new point decomposes cleanly into three additive terms: E[(y - fhat(x))^2] = Bias(fhat(x))^2 + Var(fhat(x)) + sigma^2, where sigma^2 is IRREDUCIBLE NOISE inherent to the data-generating process, unfixable by any model. BIAS is the systematic gap between the average prediction, averaged over many resamples of the training set, and the true function — a model too simple for the underlying pattern has high bias no matter how much data it sees. VARIANCE is how much the prediction would change if the model were retrained on a different sample drawn from the same distribution — a model that fits every quirk of its particular training sample has high variance. The two terms trade off against each other as model capacity changes, which is why the decomposition is usually drawn as an intersecting pair of curves against increasing model complexity.

sections.heading: Polynomial degree 1 vs. 4 vs. 15 on the same points
sections.body: Polynomial regression on one scatter of points makes the trade-off concrete. A DEGREE-1 fit, a straight line, through data generated by a genuinely curved relationship underfits: it has high bias because a line cannot represent the curve, and it performs poorly on both training and validation points since it is wrong by roughly the same systematic amount everywhere. A DEGREE-4 fit can bend enough to track the true curve reasonably well, achieving low bias and moderate variance — often the best generalization in this family. A DEGREE-15 fit, with enough coefficients to snake through every training point, near-zero training error, overfits: variance explodes, because a small change in which points were sampled would send the wiggly curve through wildly different places between the fitted points, and performance on unseen x-values degrades sharply even though training error looks best of the three.

sections.heading: Model capacity and the double-descent wrinkle
sections.body: MODEL CAPACITY is the informal name for how large and flexible a model's function family is — polynomial degree, tree depth, and neural-network parameter count all serve as capacity knobs. The classical story is a U-shaped validation-error curve: error falls as capacity rises from zero (underfitting) then rises again once capacity is high enough to overfit. Mikhail Belkin, Daniel Hsu, Siyuan Ma, and Soumik Mandal complicated this picture in a 2019 PNAS paper, 'Reconciling modern machine learning practice and the classical bias-variance trade-off,' showing that pushing capacity further still, past the INTERPOLATION THRESHOLD where the model has just enough parameters to fit training data exactly, test error can fall again — a second descent they named DOUBLE DESCENT. This helps explain why enormous, heavily overparameterized neural networks often generalize well despite having far more parameters than training examples, a fact the classical U-curve alone could not account for.

lessons.workedExample: Fitting the same 20 noisy points from y = sin(x) + noise: a degree-1 line gets training MSE 0.41 and validation MSE 0.44 — both bad, the signature of high bias. A degree-4 polynomial gets training MSE 0.06 and validation MSE 0.09 — both low, the sweet spot. A degree-15 polynomial gets training MSE 0.001, essentially interpolating every point, but validation MSE jumps to 0.51, worse than the straight line, because the curve swings wildly between the training x-values wherever a new point falls. Only the middle model, degree 4, generalizes well; the other two fail in bias and variance directions respectively.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'how do you know your model isn't just memorizing?' wants to hear the bias-variance vocabulary applied to the student's actual train/validation numbers, not a definition recited from a textbook. The strongest answers name where on the capacity spectrum their chosen model sits and what evidence, specifically the gap between training and validation error, supports that placement. A sharp judge working with a student using a very large neural network may raise double descent directly, since 'more parameters than data points should overfit badly' is the classical intuition and a student aware of Belkin et al.'s 2019 finding can explain why an overparameterized net can still generalize well past the interpolation threshold.
