sections.body: R-squared is defined as 1 minus SS_res over SS_tot, where SS_res = Sigma (yi - yhat_i)^2 is the residual sum of squares your model leaves unexplained, and SS_tot = Sigma (yi - ybar)^2 is the sum of squares you would get by instead predicting every point as the training mean ybar. R-squared is not an absolute quality score - it is a ratio measuring how much better your model does than that trivial baseline. R-squared = 1 means zero residual error; R-squared = 0 means your model does exactly as well as guessing the mean every time; and, critically, R-squared can go negative. On the training data with ordinary least squares this cannot happen, because the fitted coefficients are chosen specifically to minimize SS_res. But on a held-out test set nothing guarantees SS_res is smaller than SS_tot - a model that overfit its training data, or that extrapolates into a region it never saw, can produce residuals larger than simply predicting the training mean, driving R-squared below zero.

sections.heading: Why R-squared never falls when you add a feature - and why adjusted R-squared exists
sections.body: A separate, often-missed fact: in ordinary least squares, R-squared can never decrease when you add another regressor to the training fit, however irrelevant that regressor is. This follows from the mechanics of minimization - OLS with p+1 parameters searches a strictly larger space than OLS with p parameters, since setting the new coefficient to zero recovers the old model, so the minimum SS_res it finds can only stay the same or shrink. Adjusted R-squared corrects for this inflation: adjusted R-squared = 1 minus (1 - R-squared) times (n-1)/(n-p-1), where n is sample size and p is the number of predictors. The (n-1)/(n-p-1) term grows as p grows, imposing a real penalty per added parameter - adjusted R-squared can fall even as raw R-squared rises, flagging a feature that is not earning its place in the model.

sections.heading: What a high R-squared does not certify
sections.body: Even a high R-squared certifies neither the right functional form nor a causal claim. A quadratic relationship squeezed through a straight-line fit can still produce R-squared above 0.9 if the curvature is mild over the observed range - the number says nothing about whether a line was the correct shape to fit in the first place. R-squared measures association, not mechanism: Tyler Vigen's Spurious Correlations project catalogs pairs like per-capita margarine consumption tracking Maine's divorce rate with R-squared above 0.9, driven purely by both variables trending over the same years. A high variance-explained figure is fully compatible with a confound, a coincidence, or reversed causation.

lessons.workedExample: A model predicting exam scores from study hours yields SS_res = 200 against SS_tot = 1000, with n=30 and p=1: R-squared = 1 - 200/1000 = 0.80, and adjusted R-squared = 1 - (0.20)(29/28), about 0.793. Add a second predictor - students' shoe size, plainly irrelevant - and OLS's larger search space finds a marginally better fit: SS_res drops to 198, so R-squared ticks up to 0.802. But recomputing adjusted R-squared with p=2 gives 1 - (0.198)(29/27), about 0.787 - it fell, even though raw R-squared rose. The rise in R-squared is the mathematical guarantee at work; the fall in adjusted R-squared is the penalty correctly flagging that shoe size bought a trivial fit improvement at the cost of a wasted degree of freedom.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'your R-squared is 0.95 - why don't you trust the model more?' is testing whether you understand what R-squared actually certifies. The strong answer distinguishes three claims R-squared does not make: that the functional form is correct, that any predictor is causal, and that the fit will generalize, since a negative test-set R-squared is possible and worth checking for. Naming adjusted R-squared unprompted, and explaining that raw R-squared mechanically cannot fall when regressors are added - so a fair comparison across models with different predictor counts requires the adjusted version - signals real statistical fluency rather than pattern-matched vocabulary.

questions.prompt: What does R-squared equal to 0 mean about a model?

options.text: The model has zero residual error
The model performs exactly as well as always predicting the training mean
The model's predictions are perfectly anti-correlated with the truth
The model has too many predictors

explanations.a: That describes R-squared = 1, where SS_res is zero.
explanations.b: Correct - R-squared = 0 occurs exactly when SS_res equals SS_tot, meaning the model does no better than the mean-prediction baseline.
explanations.c: Perfect anti-correlation would typically drive R-squared negative on a fixed-form fit, not to exactly zero.
explanations.d: R-squared = 0 says nothing directly about how many predictors are in the model.

questions.prompt: Under what circumstance can R-squared be negative?

options.text: Never - R-squared is mathematically bounded between 0 and 1
Only when the sample size is smaller than the number of predictors
When evaluated on data (such as a held-out test set) where the model's SS_res exceeds SS_tot
Only when using adjusted R-squared instead of raw R-squared

explanations.a: R-squared is not bounded below by 0 outside of the training-fit special case; it can go negative on new data.
explanations.b: Sample size relative to predictor count affects adjusted R-squared's penalty, not this negativity condition directly.
explanations.c: Correct - if the model's residual sum of squares on some dataset is larger than that dataset's total sum of squares, R-squared is negative, meaning the model underperforms the mean baseline there.
explanations.d: Both raw and adjusted R-squared can go negative; this isn't unique to the adjusted version.

questions.prompt: Match each R-squared value to what it indicates about model performance.

right.text: Model achieves zero residual error - a perfect fit
Model performs exactly as well as predicting the mean for every point
Model performs worse than predicting the training mean, typically seen on held-out data

questions.explanation: R-squared measures improvement over the mean-prediction baseline: 1 is a perfect fit, 0 ties the baseline exactly, and negative values mean the model is worse than that trivial baseline, which can only happen outside the training fit itself.

questions.prompt: Put these consequences of adding an irrelevant predictor to an OLS model in the order they logically follow from one another.

items.text: An irrelevant predictor is added to the OLS model
SS_res on the training data weakly decreases (or stays the same)
Raw R-squared weakly increases (or stays the same)
Adjusted R-squared may decrease if the fit improvement doesn't offset its added-parameter penalty

questions.explanation: Adding a predictor enlarges OLS's search space, so SS_res can only fall or stay flat, which mechanically pushes raw R-squared up or flat - but adjusted R-squared applies a penalty per parameter that can outweigh a tiny SS_res improvement, causing it to drop.

lessons.label: Residual Plots: The Most Informative Plot in Regression

sections.heading: The plot and the ideal pattern
sections.body: A residual is the leftover: ei = yi - yhat_i, the vertical distance between an observed value and the model's prediction for that point. Plotting residuals against the fitted values yhat_i - not against yi, which mechanically correlates with the residual - is, in statistician John Tukey's framing from his 1977 book Exploratory Data Analysis, one of the single most informative diagnostics in regression, often more revealing than any single summary number, because a scatter of hundreds of points collapses into one visual read. The ideal residual plot is a structureless horizontal band, centered on zero, with roughly constant spread across the full range of fitted values. That pattern says the model has extracted every systematic signal available in the predictors, and what's left is unpredictable noise - there is nothing left to model.

sections.heading: Three signatures of trouble
sections.body: Three deviations from that ideal band each diagnose a specific failure. Curvature - residuals arcing up then down, or down then up, as fitted values increase - means you fit a straight line to a relationship that bends; the fix is a transformation or a polynomial or spline term, not more data. A funnel shape - residual spread narrow at one end of the fitted range and wide at the other - is heteroscedasticity, non-constant error variance, common when y spans orders of magnitude, so absolute error grows with the size of the prediction; the Breusch-Pagan test, formalized in 1979, turns this pattern into a p-value, but the funnel is visible before any test runs, and the fix (log-transforming y, or weighted least squares) follows directly from seeing it. Outliers or clusters - a handful of points sitting far from the band, or two distinct residual bands - usually reveal a subgroup the model doesn't know about, such as a different regime or a data-entry error, rather than a global functional-form problem.

sections.heading: Localizing the problem: residual vs. feature and residual vs. time
sections.body: A residual-vs-fitted plot tells you something is wrong but not which predictor is responsible. Plotting residuals against each individual feature, one at a time, localizes the problem: curvature that appears only against one predictor points directly at that variable needing a transformation, while curvature against several predictors suggests a missing interaction or an omitted variable. For any data with a time index, a residual-vs-time plot is equally essential - a drift or trend in residuals over time signals autocorrelation or a process that changed, such as seasonality, sensor drift, or a policy shift, a failure mode invisible in a residual-vs-fitted plot alone.

lessons.workedExample: A model predicts house price from square footage. The residual-vs-fitted plot shows a clear funnel: for fitted prices under $200k, residuals cluster within plus or minus $10k, but for fitted prices above $800k, residuals swing plus or minus $150k. This is heteroscedasticity - error scales with price, not a constant amount. A Breusch-Pagan test confirms it with p less than 0.001. Re-fitting on log(price) instead of raw price and re-plotting residuals against the new fitted values shows the funnel has flattened into a roughly constant band, because the log transform converts multiplicative, percentage-sized errors into additive ones of comparable size across the price range.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges know a headline R-squared can hide problems a plot exposes immediately, so a project that reports metrics without a residual plot invites the question 'did you actually look at your errors, or just compute them?' A strong answer states what shape you'd expect if the model were adequate - a flat, structureless band - names which specific shape you actually found, and ties that shape to the concrete fix you applied: curvature to a transformation, a funnel to weighted least squares or a log transform. That causal chain from plot shape to diagnosis to fix is what separates a metrics-reporting project from a genuinely diagnosed one.

questions.prompt: What does an ideal residual-vs-fitted plot look like?

options.text: A structureless horizontal band centered on zero with constant spread
A perfectly straight diagonal line
A tight cluster of points in the upper-right corner
A U-shaped curve

explanations.a: Correct - a flat, structureless band means the model has captured all systematic signal and only noise remains.
explanations.b: A diagonal line would appear on a predicted-vs-actual parity plot, not a residual-vs-fitted plot, and residuals shouldn't trend with fitted values at all.
explanations.c: A cluster in one corner would indicate the fitted-value range is uneven or restricted, not an ideal residual pattern.
explanations.d: A U-shape is a curvature signature, indicating a missed nonlinear relationship, not the ideal pattern.

questions.prompt: A residual plot funnels outward - narrow spread at low fitted values, wide spread at high fitted values. What does this indicate, and what is a typical fix?

options.text: Heteroscedasticity; fix with a log transform of y or weighted least squares
A missing quadratic term; fix by adding a squared predictor
A single data-entry error; fix by deleting that one row
Perfect model fit; no fix needed

explanations.a: Correct - a funnel is the visual signature of non-constant error variance, addressed by transforming the target or reweighting the loss.
explanations.b: A missing quadratic term produces curvature (an arc), not a widening funnel.
explanations.c: A single bad row produces an isolated outlier point, not a systematic widening trend across the whole range.
explanations.d: A funnel is a clear deviation from the ideal structureless band, not a sign of a good fit.

questions.prompt: Match each residual plot pattern to its diagnosis.

left.text: Isolated outliers or two distinct clusters

right.text: Model has captured the systematic signal; nothing left to model
Wrong functional form - a line was fit to a bending relationship
Heteroscedasticity - error variance is not constant across fitted values
A subgroup or data issue the model doesn't account for

questions.explanation: Each residual pattern maps to a distinct root cause: a flat band means the model is adequate, curvature means the wrong shape was fit, a funnel means variance grows with the prediction, and outliers or clusters point to an unmodeled subgroup or data problem.

questions.prompt: Put the diagnostic workflow for using residual plots in the correct order.

items.text: Fit the regression model
Compute residuals (y minus fitted values)
Plot residuals against fitted values (and against each feature or time)
Identify which signature pattern appears (band, curve, funnel, or cluster)
Apply the targeted fix implied by that pattern

questions.explanation: The workflow proceeds from fitting the model, to computing residuals, to plotting them against fitted values or features, to reading which signature is present, to applying the fix that signature implies.

lessons.label: Predicted-vs-Actual Parity Plots

sections.heading: Constructing the parity plot
sections.body: A parity plot puts actual y on the x-axis and predicted yhat on the y-axis, with a 45-degree reference line y = x drawn through the origin. A perfect model puts every point exactly on that line; scatter around it is residual error in visual form, but unlike a residual-vs-fitted plot, the parity plot preserves the original scale of y on both axes, so ceiling, floor, and range problems are visible at a glance in a way percentage or standardized-residual plots hide. Points sitting consistently above the line mean the model overpredicts in that region; points below mean underprediction. Because both axes share the same variable, a parity plot also invites eyeballing where the model compresses its guesses - whether the cloud of points hugs the diagonal or instead flattens toward horizontal, in which case predictions barely vary even as the true value swings widely.

sections.heading: Classic pathologies: shrinkage, ceilings and floors, offsets
sections.body: Three pathologies recur. Shrinkage - points squeezed toward a horizontal line rather than following the diagonal - means the model hedges: it overpredicts at low true values and underpredicts at high true values, pulling every guess toward the middle of the training distribution. This is regression to the mean in the statistical sense Francis Galton first documented in 1886 comparing parents' and children's heights, finding tall parents' children trend shorter while short parents' children trend taller; regularized models (ridge, lasso) and averaging ensembles produce the same shrinkage by construction. Ceiling and floor effects appear as a flattening at the top or bottom of the plot - the model refuses to predict beyond some bound, common in tree-based models that cannot extrapolate past the training label range, since a tree's leaf output is always some training-set average. A systematic offset, where the point cloud runs parallel to y = x but shifted up or down, signals an additive bias, often from a missing intercept or an unmodeled confound shifting every prediction the same direction.

sections.heading: Slope as a quantitative statement of shrinkage
sections.body: Shrinkage can be stated as a number, not just a shape: fit a simple regression of yhat on y from the parity plot and read its slope. A slope of 1 with intercept 0 says predictions track truth one-to-one; a slope well below 1, say 0.6, quantifies exactly how much the model compresses its guesses toward the mean. R-squared alone cannot reveal this, because R-squared depends on the correlation between y and yhat, and correlation is invariant to the linear rescaling that produces the compression - a model can show a strong, nearly linear relationship between predicted and actual values, a high R-squared, while that relationship's slope sits far below 1, hedging every extreme prediction toward the average.

lessons.workedExample: A model predicts standardized test scores (range 0-100) for a diverse student population. On the parity plot, students with true scores near 95 show predictions clustering around 80, and students with true scores near 20 show predictions clustering around 38 - the point cloud visibly leans toward the middle rather than tracking the diagonal. Fitting yhat = a + b times y on the plotted points returns slope b of about 0.55 and intercept a of about 27: a quantitative shrinkage factor. Yet the model's R-squared is 0.82, since predicted and actual remain strongly, near-linearly correlated - a judge looking at R-squared alone would call this a strong model, missing that it systematically under-serves the highest performers and over-flags the lowest ones, exactly the students a placement decision most needs to get right.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge staring at a headline R-squared of 0.82 may assume the model is trustworthy across its whole range; the parity plot is how you show them it isn't. Presenting the plot alongside its fitted slope - 'my model's R-squared is 0.82, but the predicted-vs-actual slope is only 0.55, meaning it compresses extreme cases toward the average' - demonstrates you checked exactly the failure mode a single summary statistic cannot surface. This matters most whenever the extremes are the decision-relevant cases, such as screening for the highest-risk or highest-need students, and naming Galton's regression-to-the-mean phenomenon shows the shrinkage isn't a bug specific to your model but a known tendency of any noisy-fit averaging process.

questions.prompt: What does the reference line drawn on a predicted-vs-actual parity plot represent?

options.text: The line y = x, representing perfect prediction
The regression line fit only to the residuals
The mean of the predicted values
The 95% confidence interval boundary

explanations.a: Correct - the 45-degree line y = x marks where predicted equals actual, so any point exactly on it is a perfect prediction.
explanations.b: The reference line is fixed at y = x; it is not fit to the data at all.
explanations.c: The mean of predicted values is a single point, not a reference line across the whole plot.
explanations.d: A confidence interval boundary would be a separate, data-dependent band, not the fixed diagonal reference line.

questions.prompt: Why can't R-squared alone reveal that a model's predictions are shrunk toward the mean (slope well below 1 on the parity plot)?

options.text: R-squared depends on correlation, which is invariant to the linear rescaling that produces the shrinkage
R-squared can only be computed on training data, never on predictions
R-squared is undefined whenever shrinkage is present
R-squared and slope always move together, so this situation cannot occur

explanations.a: Correct - correlation, and therefore R-squared, measures how tightly points track a linear relationship, not what that relationship's slope is, so a strongly correlated but heavily compressed set of predictions still yields a high R-squared.
explanations.b: R-squared can be computed on any predicted-actual pair, including a held-out test set.
explanations.c: R-squared remains well defined even when shrinkage is present; it just doesn't detect it.
explanations.d: This is exactly the situation the lesson describes as occurring: high R-squared coexisting with a slope far below 1.

questions.prompt: Match each parity-plot pathology to its description.

right.text: Points compress toward horizontal; model hedges extremes toward the average
Predictions flatten at a bound and cannot go higher or lower, regardless of true value
Point cloud runs parallel to y = x but shifted, indicating an additive bias

questions.explanation: Shrinkage compresses predictions toward the center, ceiling/floor effects cap predictions at a bound regardless of the true value, and a systematic offset shifts the whole prediction cloud without changing its shape.

questions.prompt: Put the steps for quantifying shrinkage from a parity plot in the correct order.

items.text: Plot predicted values against actual values
Draw the y = x reference line
Visually check whether the cloud compresses toward horizontal
Fit a regression of predicted on actual to obtain a slope
Compare the fitted slope to 1 to quantify the shrinkage

questions.explanation: You first build the plot and its reference line, visually notice compression, then formalize that visual impression into a number by fitting a slope and comparing it to the ideal value of 1.

lessons.label: Anscombe's Quartet: Why Metrics Need Plots

sections.heading: Four datasets, one set of statistics
sections.body: In 1973, statistician Francis Anscombe published four small datasets (eleven points each) in the American Statistician that share, to two or three decimal places, the same mean x of 9.0, mean y of 7.50, variance of x of 11.0, variance of y near 4.13, correlation coefficient of 0.816, and best-fit regression line yhat = 3.00 + 0.500x with R-squared near 0.67. Any table of summary statistics would report these four datasets as identical. Plotted, they are nothing alike. Dataset I is a genuinely linear relationship with ordinary scatter around the line - the case the regression line actually describes well. Dataset II is a smooth, deterministic curve, a near-perfect downward-opening parabola; a straight line is the wrong shape, and its R-squared is an artifact of the summary math, not evidence of linearity. Dataset III is a perfectly linear relationship with one point displaced far off the line, dragging the fitted slope away from what the other ten points alone would produce. Dataset IV holds x constant at 8 for ten of eleven points and places one point at x = 19 with a large y - a single high-leverage observation manufacturing the entire correlation.

sections.heading: The Datasaurus Dozen extends the point
sections.body: Anscombe's four-dataset trick was extended dramatically by Justin Matejka and George Fitzmaurice of Autodesk Research in their 2017 CHI paper, Same Stats, Different Graphs. Using simulated annealing to nudge points while preserving summary statistics, they generated twelve new datasets to accompany the original dinosaur shape, for thirteen datasets total in the Datasaurus Dozen, sharing the same mean, standard deviation, and Pearson correlation to two decimal places. The other twelve include a circle, a star, parallel slanted lines, and an X shape - visually about as different from each other as datasets can be, yet numerically indistinguishable on every summary statistic a report table would normally show. Where Anscombe made the point with four small hand-built examples, Matejka and Fitzmaurice made it an interactive, almost playful demonstration that any finite set of summary numbers, however many you compute, can be satisfied by wildly different underlying shapes.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: The shared lesson across both is a rule, not a suggestion: never report a fit you have not plotted. Summary statistics - mean, variance, correlation, R-squared, a regression equation - are lossy compressions of the data, and the compression can discard exactly the information, such as curvature, an outlier, a leverage point, or a non-relationship, that determines whether the fit is trustworthy. A plot costs one line of code and catches what no additional decimal place of precision on a correlation coefficient ever will.

lessons.workedExample: A student is handed only a correlation coefficient (r = 0.816) and a regression equation (yhat = 3.00 + 0.500x) for an unlabeled dataset and asked to judge the fit's quality. Based on the numbers alone, they'd reasonably guess a solid linear relationship with R-squared near 0.67. Told the data is actually Anscombe's dataset II, they plot it and see a clean parabola - the 'good' correlation is measuring how well a straight line approximates a curve over a limited x-range, not evidence of a linear process. If instead it's dataset III, the plot reveals ten points sitting exactly on a different, steeper line, with one clear outlier solely responsible for the reported slope and correlation - dropping that single point would change the fitted equation entirely.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks to see the actual scatterplot behind a reported R-squared or regression line is running the Anscombe test, whether or not they'd name it that. Handing over only summary statistics and correlation, without ever having plotted the raw data, is exactly the failure mode Anscombe manufactured to make a point in 1973 - and the Datasaurus Dozen shows it hasn't gone away in the decades since. The strong response is to have the plot ready before it's asked for, and to be able to say what you were checking for: linearity, a single dominant outlier, or a leverage point standing in for real correlation.

questions.prompt: What do all four of Anscombe's 1973 datasets share, despite looking completely different when plotted?

options.text: The same underlying data-generating process
The same mean, variance, correlation, and fitted regression line, to two or three decimal places
The same number of outliers
The same sample size and nothing else

explanations.a: The datasets clearly come from different generating processes - one is linear-with-noise, one is a deterministic curve, and two involve outliers or leverage points.
explanations.b: Correct - mean x, mean y, variance of x, variance of y, correlation, and the fitted line all match closely across all four datasets.
explanations.c: Only two of the four datasets (III and IV) rely on a single unusual point; the other two do not.
explanations.d: They do share the same sample size (eleven points), but far more than that matches - the whole point is that the full battery of summary statistics matches.

questions.prompt: In Anscombe's dataset IV, what produces the reported correlation and regression line?

options.text: A genuinely linear relationship across the full range of x
A single high-leverage point at x = 19, while the other ten points sit at a constant x = 8
A smooth curved relationship
Random noise with no real pattern at all

explanations.a: There is no real linear trend across x in dataset IV, since x barely varies across ten of the eleven points.
explanations.b: Correct - with x fixed at 8 for ten points, the single point at x = 19 alone determines the appearance of a slope and correlation.
explanations.c: That describes dataset II's smooth parabola, not dataset IV.
explanations.d: Dataset IV does produce a reported non-zero correlation and slope; it just comes entirely from one leverage point rather than a genuine trend.

questions.prompt: Match each Anscombe dataset to what its scatterplot actually reveals.

right.text: A genuinely linear relationship with ordinary scatter
A smooth, deterministic curve poorly approximated by a line
A clean linear relationship with one outlier dragging the fitted slope
A constant x for all but one point, whose leverage manufactures the correlation

questions.explanation: Dataset I is the case the linear fit genuinely describes; dataset II is a curve masquerading as linear; dataset III is linear data corrupted by one outlier; dataset IV is a near-constant x variable with one leverage point creating the entire apparent relationship.

questions.prompt: Put these milestones in chronological order.

items.text: Francis Anscombe publishes the four-dataset quartet in the American Statistician
Alberto Cairo creates the original Datasaurus shape
Matejka and Fitzmaurice publish the Datasaurus Dozen at CHI using simulated annealing

questions.explanation: Anscombe's quartet appeared in 1973; Alberto Cairo created the original Datasaurus shape afterward; Matejka and Fitzmaurice built on that shape to publish the full Datasaurus Dozen at CHI in 2017.

lessons.label: Is My RMSE Good? Error in Context and Baselines

sections.heading: The first anchor: a naive baseline
sections.body: An RMSE of 0.3 is meaningless stated alone - it depends entirely on what you're predicting and what beating it would even mean. The first anchor is a trivial baseline: what RMSE would you get by always predicting the training mean of y for independent data, or the previous observed value for a time series? Meteorologists formalized this comparison decades ago as the skill score: skill = 1 minus RMSE_model divided by RMSE_baseline, where the baseline is typically climatology, the long-run average weather for that date, for seasonal forecasts, or persistence, tomorrow equals today, for short-horizon forecasts. A skill score of 0 means your model adds nothing over the naive baseline; negative skill means the model is actively worse. This is precisely the same ratio buried inside R-squared: R-squared = 1 minus SS_res over SS_tot is a skill score against the mean baseline, computed on variance instead of RMSE directly, so a judge's 'is your error good?' question and R-squared are really asking the same thing in different units.

sections.heading: Two more anchors: spread of y and the measurement noise floor
sections.body: The standard deviation of y, SD(y), tells you the error you'd expect from a model with zero information at all; RMSE divided by SD(y) below 1 means you've beaten pure noise, and this ratio is algebraically tied to R-squared, since for a model evaluated on its own training data, R-squared = 1 minus (RMSE/SD(y)) squared. The third anchor, and the one people most often skip, is the measurement noise floor: the error inherent in the instrument or process that produced y in the first place, independent of any model. A thermometer with plus-or-minus 0.5 degree precision cannot be predicted below an RMSE of 0.5 degrees by any model, however good, because that much scatter is baked into the labels. Reporting an RMSE without checking it against the label's own noise floor risks either declaring victory prematurely or chasing an improvement that is statistically impossible to achieve.

sections.heading: Normalized RMSE and MAPE's blow-up near zero
sections.body: Two common introductory transformations rescale RMSE for comparability. Normalized RMSE, typically RMSE divided by the range (max minus min) or the mean of y, expresses error as a fraction rather than a raw unit, letting you compare error across datasets with different scales. MAPE, mean absolute percentage error, the mean of |error| divided by |y|, does something similar but has one crucial failure: as any true value approaches zero, |error| divided by |y| approaches infinity, so a single near-zero label can make MAPE explode or become undefined - a well-known reason MAPE is unreliable for data that legitimately crosses or sits near zero, such as temperature in Celsius or net income, where normalized RMSE or a skill score is the safer choice.

lessons.workedExample: A judge asks: 'Your model's RMSE is 0.3 degrees - is that good?' First anchor: the baseline of always predicting yesterday's temperature (persistence) gives RMSE_baseline = 1.2, so skill = 1 minus 0.3/1.2 = 0.75 - the model removes 75% of the naive error. Second anchor: SD(y) across the season is 2.0 degrees, so RMSE/SD(y) = 0.15, consistent with R-squared near 1 minus 0.15 squared, about 0.977. Third anchor: the thermometer's stated precision is plus-or-minus 0.2 degrees, so an RMSE of 0.3 is only modestly above the physical noise floor, leaving little room to improve without a better instrument. All three anchors agree: 0.3 is good.
lessons.judgeFraming: 'Is 0.3 good?' is a trap for anyone who only memorized a single number, because the honest answer is always 'compared to what?' A prepared answer names at least one concrete anchor on the spot - the naive baseline's RMSE, the standard deviation of the target, or the instrument's known measurement noise - and turns the adjective into a ratio: 'we cut baseline error by 75%' or 'we're within 1.5 times the sensor's own noise floor' is a claim a judge can evaluate; 'pretty good' is not. Judges in quantitative fields are specifically listening for whether you reach for a ratio unprompted.

questions.prompt: What does a forecasting skill score of 0 mean?

options.text: The model's RMSE is exactly 0
The model performs exactly as well as the naive baseline (climatology or persistence)
The model is perfectly calibrated
The model has no measurement noise

explanations.a: A skill score of 0 says nothing about the raw RMSE value itself, only about how it compares to the baseline's RMSE.
explanations.b: Correct - skill = 1 minus RMSE_model/RMSE_baseline equals 0 exactly when the model's RMSE matches the baseline's RMSE.
explanations.c: Calibration is a separate property concerning whether predicted uncertainties match observed frequencies, not what the skill score measures.
explanations.d: Measurement noise is a property of the labeling process, not something the skill score reports.

questions.prompt: Why does MAPE (mean absolute percentage error) become unreliable or explode for data with values near zero?

options.text: Because MAPE requires the data to be normally distributed
Because MAPE divides each absolute error by the true value, so as the true value approaches zero the ratio approaches infinity
Because MAPE can only be computed on positive integers
MAPE does not have this problem; only RMSE does

explanations.a: MAPE makes no distributional assumption; its issue is purely arithmetic, from dividing by values near zero.
explanations.b: Correct - MAPE's formula is the mean of |error| divided by |y|, and dividing by a y approaching zero drives individual terms toward infinity.
explanations.c: MAPE can be computed on any real-valued data; the problem specifically arises when values sit near or cross zero.
explanations.d: RMSE has no such division-by-y term and does not blow up this way; the near-zero problem is specific to percentage-based metrics like MAPE.

questions.prompt: Match each anchor to what comparing your RMSE against it tells you.

left.text: Measurement noise floor of the instrument

right.text: How much better the model does than a trivial no-information guess (the skill score)
Whether the model has beaten pure variability, directly tied to R-squared
Whether further improvement is even physically possible given the label's own scatter

questions.explanation: The naive baseline anchors a skill score, the standard deviation of y ties directly to R-squared, and the measurement noise floor tells you the lowest RMSE that is even achievable given how the labels themselves were produced.

questions.prompt: Put the steps for answering 'is my RMSE good?' in the correct order.

items.text: State the raw RMSE
Compute the naive baseline's RMSE (mean prediction or persistence)
Compute the skill score: 1 minus RMSE/RMSE_baseline
Compare RMSE against SD(y) and the known measurement noise floor
Report the result as a ratio, not an adjective

questions.explanation: You start from the raw number, anchor it against a naive baseline to get a skill score, cross-check against the target's own variability and the instrument's noise floor, and finally communicate the result as a ratio rather than a vague adjective like 'good' or 'bad'.

units.label: Validation and Honest Evaluation

lessons.label: One Split Isn't Enough: Cross-Validation

sections.heading: The single-split lottery
sections.body: A team trains one gradient-boosted classifier on a 200-row science-fair dataset, splits it 80/20, and gets 86% accuracy. A labmate reruns the identical training code with a different random seed for the split and gets 78%. Nothing about the model changed - only which 40 rows landed in the test set. With only 40 test rows, each single prediction flipping right-to-wrong or wrong-to-right moves accuracy by 2.5 percentage points, so a handful of unlucky or lucky rows swings the reported number by eight points. This is not measurement error in the usual sense; it is sampling variance in the evaluation itself, and a single train/test split cannot distinguish "the model is good" from "this particular test set happened to be easy."

sections.heading: K-fold cross-validation and stratification
sections.body: K-fold cross-validation fixes this by using every row as test data exactly once. The data is partitioned into k roughly equal folds; the model trains on k-1 folds and is scored on the held-out fold, and this repeats k times so each fold serves as the test set once. The k scores are then combined rather than trusted individually. k=5 and k=10 are the standard choices: larger k means each training fold contains more data (closer to the full dataset, lower pessimistic bias) at the cost of k separate model fits and scores that are more correlated with each other. For classification with imbalanced classes, stratified k-fold enforces that each fold preserves the overall class proportions, so a fold does not accidentally land 90% negative examples by chance.

sections.heading: Leave-one-out and the reporting standard
sections.body: Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) pushes k to the extreme: k=n, so a single row is held out at a time and the model is refit n times. On a 200-row dataset that means 200 separate training runs. LOOCV is nearly unbiased for the true generalization error - each training set uses almost all the data - but it has surprisingly high variance across runs, because the n training sets overlap almost completely with each other, making the n error estimates highly correlated rather than independent evidence. Combined with its computational cost, LOOCV is now mostly reserved for very small datasets where every row is precious and k=5 or k=10 would otherwise waste too much training signal per fold. The reporting discipline that follows from all three variants: never quote a single fold's score as the result. Report the mean and standard deviation across folds - "82.1% ± 3.4% across 10 folds" - so a reader sees both the estimated performance and how much it might vary.

lessons.workedExample: A student runs 10-fold CV on the 200-row dataset instead of one split. Each fold holds out 20 rows; the model trains on the other 180 and is scored on the 20. The ten scores come back as 0.79, 0.83, 0.86, 0.81, 0.78, 0.85, 0.80, 0.84, 0.82, 0.87. The mean is 0.825 and the standard deviation is about 0.031. The student now reports "82.5% ± 3.1% (10-fold CV)" instead of either the lucky 86% or the unlucky 78% from a single split - the same two numbers that started this lesson turn out to be roughly a standard deviation and a half from the true 10-fold estimate in either direction - ordinary sampling noise, not two contradictory results.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees a single accuracy number with no fold structure will ask what happens on a different random split - and if the answer is "we didn't check," the result is unverified. Reporting a cross-validated mean and standard deviation preempts this: it shows the number is stable rather than a lucky draw, and the standard deviation itself is informative (a small one signals a robust model; a large one signals the dataset is too small or too noisy for the claimed precision). Judges specifically probe whether k=5/10 or LOOCV was used and why, since the choice trades off bias, variance, and compute cost.

questions.prompt: Why does a single 80/20 split on a 200-row dataset produce unstable accuracy estimates across different random seeds?

options.text: Because the model is necessarily overfitting to the training set
Because with only ~40 test rows, each prediction that flips right-to-wrong or wrong-to-right changes accuracy by about 2.5 points, so sampling variance dominates
Because accuracy is not a valid metric for any dataset under 1000 rows
Because 80/20 is mathematically the wrong ratio and 50/50 would remove the variance

explanations.a: Overfitting affects the gap between training and test performance, not the instability of the test score itself across different splits of the same size.
explanations.b: Correct - a small test set means accuracy moves in large discrete steps per flipped prediction, so which rows happen to land in the test fold matters a lot.
explanations.c: Accuracy remains a valid metric; the problem is evaluating it on too small and too variable a sample, not the metric's validity.
explanations.d: No split ratio eliminates sampling variance on a small test set; only aggregating over multiple splits (cross-validation) addresses it.

questions.prompt: What does stratified k-fold guarantee that plain k-fold does not?

options.text: Faster training because fewer folds are needed
Each fold preserves the overall class proportions of the full dataset
The hyperparameters are automatically tuned without a validation set
All folds are guaranteed to be exactly the same size

explanations.a: Stratification does not change the number of folds or training time; it changes how rows are assigned to folds.
explanations.b: Correct - stratified k-fold samples each fold so the minority/majority class ratio matches the full dataset, avoiding folds that are accidentally almost all one class.
explanations.c: Stratification is about fold composition, not hyperparameter search.
explanations.d: Plain k-fold already aims for equal-sized folds; near-equal sizing is not what stratification adds.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of standard k-fold cross-validation in the correct order.

items.text: Partition the dataset into k roughly equal folds
Train the model on k-1 folds and score it on the remaining held-out fold
Repeat training and scoring until every fold has served as the held-out test fold exactly once
Report the mean and standard deviation of the k scores

questions.explanation: K-fold first partitions the data, then rotates which fold is held out for training/scoring, repeats until every fold has been the test set once, and finally the k individual scores are summarized as a mean and standard deviation rather than reported individually.

questions.prompt: Match each cross-validation approach to its defining property.

right.text: Balances bias, variance, and compute cost for most moderate-size datasets
Nearly unbiased but high-variance, since n training sets almost entirely overlap; requires n model fits
Preserves the overall class proportions within each fold

questions.explanation: k=5/10 is the standard practical compromise; LOOCV (k=n) is nearly unbiased but its n highly overlapping training sets make the resulting error estimates high-variance and it is expensive to compute; stratified k-fold specifically fixes class-proportion imbalance across folds.

lessons.label: The Hyperparameter Selection Trap and Nested CV

sections.heading: How tuning contaminates the estimate
sections.body: Grid-searching hyperparameters against the same k-fold split you later report as "the model's cross-validation score" quietly contaminates the estimate. Trying twenty combinations of max_depth and learning_rate and keeping whichever one scored highest on that specific five-fold partition is a search over configurations, and the winning configuration is partly the one that fit the noise in those particular folds, not only the one that generalizes best. The more combinations tried, the larger this effect: with twenty candidates evaluated on the same five folds, at least one is likely to look a point or two better purely by chance, even if none of the twenty differ in any real way. The reported CV score for the "winning" hyperparameters is therefore optimistic - it has effectively been selected for looking good on that data, the same look-elsewhere problem that inflates significance in multiple-comparisons testing, just applied one level up, to model selection instead of model fitting.

sections.heading: Cawley and Talbot (2010) and the size of the optimism
sections.body: Gavin Cawley and Nicola Talbot formalized this in their 2010 Journal of Machine Learning Research paper, "On Over-fitting in Model Selection and Subsequent Selection Bias in Performance Evaluation" (JMLR 11:2079-2107). Their central point is that a model-selection criterion - cross-validation error evaluated across a grid of candidate hyperparameters - is itself a noisy statistic with its own variance, and minimizing over many candidates picks out whichever configuration got a lucky draw on that variance, not necessarily the configuration that is genuinely best. They argue low variance in the selection criterion matters as much as its being unbiased, and demonstrate that this selection bias can be surprisingly large - large enough, in some of their examples, to be comparable to or exceed the actual performance difference between the algorithms being compared. That is a direct warning against papers and projects that report "our tuned model beats the baseline by two points" using the same CV loop that did the tuning.

sections.heading: Nested cross-validation as the fix
sections.body: Nested cross-validation is the fix, sometimes called double cross-validation. An outer k-fold loop splits the data into outer-train and outer-test folds purely for the final performance estimate. Inside each outer-train fold, an entirely separate inner k-fold loop runs the hyperparameter search, selecting the best configuration using only that outer-train data - the outer-test fold is never touched during tuning. The model is refit with the winning hyperparameters on the full outer-train fold and scored once on the outer-test fold. Averaging these outer scores across all outer folds gives an honest estimate that has never seen its own test data during selection, at the cost of roughly outer-k times inner-k model fits - real compute, but the only way to report a tuned model's score without lying to yourself about it.

lessons.workedExample: A student grid-searches an SVM's C and gamma over 25 combinations using 5-fold CV, picks the combination scoring 91% mean accuracy, and reports "91% accuracy." A skeptical mentor reruns it with nested CV: an outer 5-fold loop for the estimate, an inner 5-fold loop (using only each outer-training fold) for the same 25-combination search. The nested outer-fold scores average to 85%. The six-point gap is the selection bias Cawley and Talbot describe - the 91% was the best of 25 noisy candidates on one fixed partition, not a property of the winning hyperparameters that would replicate on new data.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows this trap will ask a pointed question: "was this score from the same cross-validation loop that chose the hyperparameters?" A yes without nested CV is a red flag, because it means the reported number is inflated by exactly the mechanism Cawley and Talbot documented - search-induced optimism that grows with the number of configurations tried. A student who volunteers that they used nested CV, or at minimum a separate untouched validation set for tuning versus a final held-out test set for reporting, demonstrates they understand that model selection is itself a source of overfitting, not just model fitting.

questions.prompt: Why does selecting hyperparameters using the same k-fold CV score you later report as the final result produce an optimistic estimate?

options.text: Because k-fold CV always underestimates true performance regardless of tuning
Because the winning hyperparameter combination is partly chosen for fitting noise in that specific fold partition, and this selection effect grows with the number of combinations tried
Because hyperparameter tuning always causes the model to underfit
Because grid search is deterministic and cannot introduce any variance

explanations.a: K-fold CV is not systematically pessimistic; the bias introduced here is optimistic and comes from selection, not from CV itself.
explanations.b: Correct - this is the mechanism Cawley and Talbot describe: minimizing a noisy selection criterion over many candidates picks out lucky noise along with genuine improvement.
explanations.c: The problem is optimistic bias in the reported score, not underfitting of the trained model.
explanations.d: Grid search over many candidate configurations introduces exactly the kind of selection variance this lesson describes, even though each individual CV run is deterministic given a fixed data split.

questions.prompt: According to Cawley and Talbot's 2010 JMLR paper, what property of a model-selection criterion matters as much as it being unbiased?

options.text: Its computational speed
Its low variance
Its compatibility with deep learning frameworks
Its use of accuracy rather than any other metric

explanations.a: Speed is a practical concern but is not the property their paper identifies as comparably important to unbiasedness.
explanations.b: Correct - Cawley and Talbot argue that low variance in the selection criterion matters as much as unbiasedness, since high variance lets model selection overfit even when the criterion is unbiased on average.
explanations.c: The paper's argument is general to any model-selection procedure using cross-validation, not specific to deep learning.
explanations.d: The argument holds regardless of which metric the selection criterion is built from.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of nested cross-validation in the correct order for one outer fold.

items.text: Split off this outer fold as outer-test; the rest is outer-train
Run an inner k-fold hyperparameter search using only the outer-train data
Refit the model on the full outer-train data using the best hyperparameters found
Score the refit model once on the untouched outer-test fold

questions.explanation: Nested CV first isolates the outer-test fold from all tuning, searches hyperparameters only within the outer-train data via an inner loop, refits with the winning configuration on the full outer-train set, and only then scores on the outer-test fold that never influenced the search.

questions.prompt: Match each cross-validation setup to the role it plays.

left.text: Single CV loop used both to tune and to report the score

right.text: Produces an optimistic estimate contaminated by selection bias
Searches hyperparameters using only outer-train data
Produces the honest final performance estimate on data untouched by tuning

questions.explanation: Using one CV loop for both jobs conflates tuning and reporting and inflates the score; nested CV separates them, with the inner loop confined to tuning inside outer-train data and the outer loop providing the unbiased final estimate.

lessons.label: Cross-Validation When Rows Aren't Independent

sections.heading: The independence assumption k-fold quietly relies on
sections.body: Standard k-fold cross-validation silently assumes every row is an independent, interchangeable sample. That assumption breaks whenever rows are clustered - repeated measurements from the same patient, multiple plots within the same field trial, or several students from the same school. Random fold assignment then scatters rows from one cluster across both the training and test folds. The model can pick up on cluster-specific signal - a patient's particular anatomy, a plot's particular soil chemistry, a school's particular test-prep style - that has nothing to do with the pattern being studied, and it "cheats" by partially recognizing the cluster it has already seen elsewhere in training, rather than learning the underlying relationship being evaluated. The reported cross-validation score is then optimistic in a way that has nothing to do with the hyperparameter-tuning bias covered elsewhere - it comes purely from how rows were assigned to folds.

sections.heading: Grouped data: GroupKFold and LeaveOneGroupOut
sections.body: The concrete failure mode in medical imaging is well documented: a dataset of 20 patients contributing 50 scans each, split by scan rather than by patient, lets some of a given patient's scans land in training and others in the test fold. A model can then learn to recognize that particular patient's scanner artifacts or anatomical quirks and predict correctly on their held-out scans for reasons unrelated to disease status - the model is recognizing the patient, not detecting the disease - and reported accuracy is inflated relative to how the model will perform on a genuinely new, unseen patient. Scikit-learn's GroupKFold fixes this directly: it guarantees that no group (patient, plot, school) ever appears in both the training and test fold of any split. LeaveOneGroupOut takes the same idea to its extreme, holding out one entire group per fold - the group-level analogue of leave-one-out.

sections.heading: Time-ordered data: forward chaining
sections.body: Time-ordered data has the same disease in a different form: shuffling a time series into random folds lets future rows train a model that is then tested on the past, an advantage no deployed model will ever actually have in production. Forward-chaining validation fixes this by keeping every fold's training data strictly earlier in time than its test data - fold one trains on days 1-30 and tests on days 31-40, fold two trains on days 1-40 and tests on days 41-50, and so on, expanding the training window forward while the test window always sits just ahead of it. This lesson covers only the mechanism; deeper rolling-origin backtesting schemes purpose-built for time-series forecasting are covered separately in the Regression and Forecasting Evaluation branch.

lessons.workedExample: A student builds a skin-lesion classifier from a dataset of 30 patients, each with 15-20 photos, and reports 94% accuracy from random 5-fold CV. A reviewer points out the same patients appear across multiple folds. Rerunning with GroupKFold, keyed on patient ID, accuracy drops to 79%. The 15-point gap is the group-leakage effect: the original model had partially learned to recognize each patient's skin tone, lighting setup, and camera angle from their other photos already seen in training, and used that as a shortcut instead of the lesion features the classifier is actually supposed to detect.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge working with any dataset that has repeated subjects, sites, or time order will ask directly: "how were your folds constructed - by row, or by subject?" A project that split by row when the data has patients, students, or plots contributing multiple rows each has an inflated, unreliable headline number, and a judge who catches this will discount the result. For time-series projects, the equivalent question is whether any training fold ever contained data from after its test fold - an affirmative answer means the reported performance cannot be trusted for anything the team wants to actually forecast or diagnose going forward.

questions.prompt: In a medical imaging dataset where each patient contributes many scans, why does random row-level k-fold CV inflate the reported accuracy?

options.text: Because k-fold CV always overestimates accuracy on any imaging dataset
Because scans from the same patient can appear in both train and test folds, letting the model partially recognize the patient rather than detect the disease
Because medical images require larger batch sizes than the model was given
Because accuracy cannot be computed correctly on image data

explanations.a: The inflation here is specific to grouped data leaking across folds, not a general property of k-fold CV on all imaging tasks.
explanations.b: Correct - patient-specific artifacts (scanner signature, anatomy) leak between train and test when scans, not patients, are the unit of splitting.
explanations.c: Batch size is a training detail unrelated to this leakage mechanism.
explanations.d: Accuracy is computable; it is simply optimistic due to the leakage, not invalid as a metric.

questions.prompt: What does scikit-learn's GroupKFold guarantee that plain k-fold does not?

options.text: That the model will achieve higher accuracy
That no group (e.g. patient, plot, school) ever appears in both the train and test fold of the same split
That every fold has an equal number of groups regardless of dataset structure
That hyperparameters are tuned automatically for grouped data

explanations.a: GroupKFold typically lowers the reported score relative to leaky row-level splitting because it removes the artificial advantage of shared groups; it does not guarantee higher accuracy.
explanations.b: Correct - this is exactly the leakage GroupKFold prevents by keeping each group entirely within one side of every split.
explanations.c: GroupKFold balances fold sizes where possible but its defining guarantee is group separation, not perfectly equal counts.
explanations.d: GroupKFold controls fold assignment; it has no role in hyperparameter tuning.

questions.prompt: Put these forward-chaining validation folds in the order they would run, from earliest to latest test window.

items.text: Train on days 1-30, test on days 31-40
Train on days 1-40, test on days 41-50
Train on days 1-50, test on days 51-60
Train on days 1-60, test on days 61-70

questions.explanation: Forward chaining always expands the training window forward in time while the test window moves forward with it, so every fold trains only on data from before its own test period, matching the order the folds are listed here.

questions.prompt: Match each non-independent data situation to the validation scheme built to handle it.

left.text: Repeated measurements per patient, plot, or school
Wanting to hold out one entire group at a time
Time-ordered data where deployment only ever sees the future relative to training

right.text: GroupKFold
LeaveOneGroupOut
Forward-chaining validation

questions.explanation: GroupKFold keeps clusters intact across folds, LeaveOneGroupOut is its extreme one-group-out-at-a-time version, and forward-chaining keeps every training fold strictly earlier in time than the test data it is scored against.

lessons.label: Learning Curves: Would More Data Help?

sections.heading: What a learning curve plots
sections.body: A learning curve plots model score against the amount of training data used, with two lines on the same axes: the training score (computed on the data the model was fit to) and the validation score (computed via cross-validation on held-out data), at increasing training-set sizes - say 10%, 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100% of the available rows. The typical shape has the training score start near-perfect with very little data (a model can nearly memorize five rows) and decline as the training set grows and the model can no longer fit every point exactly; the validation score starts low and rises as more data lets the model learn genuine structure. Where the two curves end up, and how far apart they are, is the diagnostic signal - not the score at any one size in isolation. This gap is the practical, visual form of the bias-variance dilemma that Stuart Geman, Elie Bienenstock, and Rene Doursat formalized in their 1992 Neural Computation paper: error decomposes into bias (systematic underfitting) and variance (sensitivity to the particular training sample), and a learning curve is the cheapest way to see which one is dominating.

sections.heading: High bias: the converged plateau
sections.body: The high-bias archetype shows both curves converging quickly to a low plateau with only a small gap between them, often well before all available data has been used - for instance both curves flattening out around 65% accuracy by the time only half the available rows have been used. This means the model has already extracted essentially everything it is capable of extracting from the current features and hypothesis class - adding more rows of the same kind will not push either curve higher, because the ceiling is set by model capacity or feature quality, not by sample size. The fix is to change the model (add capacity, more flexible features, interaction terms) or engineer better inputs, not to spend a month collecting more of the same data.

sections.heading: High variance: the still-closing gap
sections.body: The high-variance archetype shows a wide, still-narrowing gap between a high training score and a lower validation score, with the validation curve still visibly rising at the largest training size tested. This means the model has enough capacity to fit the data well, but not enough data yet to constrain that capacity toward the true pattern rather than noise. Here, more data has real expected payoff, because the trend at the edge of the plot suggests the validation score has not yet leveled off.

sections.heading: The decision procedure
sections.body: The decision procedure that follows: before committing resources to collecting more data, plot the learning curve on what already exists. A converged, small-gap curve means redirect effort toward the model or features; a wide, still-closing gap means the data-collection investment is justified.

lessons.workedExample: A team's plant-disease classifier plateaus at 70% training accuracy and 68% validation accuracy using just 40% of their labeled images, with both curves flat from there to 100% of the data. Rather than spending three more weeks photographing leaves, they read the plateau correctly as high bias: the plain logistic regression on three hand-picked color features has hit its ceiling. Switching to a convolutional model with richer features, using the same image count, lifts validation accuracy to 88% - confirming the diagnosis that the bottleneck was model capacity, not sample size.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks "how do you know more data would help?" is testing whether the team ran this diagnostic before proposing a bigger data-collection effort as future work. A team that shows a learning curve and correctly reads whether the gap is converged or still closing demonstrates they understand the bias-variance distinction empirically, not just as a term to name-drop - and a team that proposes "collect more data" while their own curve shows a converged, small-gap plateau reveals they never actually looked.

questions.prompt: A learning curve shows the training and validation scores converging quickly to a low plateau with a small gap, well before all available data is used. What should the team do?

options.text: Collect substantially more data of the same kind, since the validation score is still low
Change the model or improve the features, since the plateau shows the current model has already extracted what it can
Nothing - a converged curve always means the project is finished
Switch to leave-one-out cross-validation to get a more accurate plateau

explanations.a: More data will not raise a plateau that has already converged with a small gap - the ceiling is set by model or feature capacity, not sample size.
explanations.b: Correct - a quickly converged, small-gap plateau is the high-bias signature, and the fix is a more expressive model or better features.
explanations.c: A low plateau means the model is systematically underperforming (high bias), not that the project has succeeded.
explanations.d: The choice of cross-validation scheme does not change the diagnosis; it does not resolve high bias.

questions.prompt: What does a wide gap between training and validation score that is still narrowing at the largest training size tested indicate?

options.text: High bias - the model needs more capacity
High variance - the model has enough capacity but not enough data yet to constrain it
The validation metric was computed incorrectly
The model is guaranteed to generalize perfectly with the current data

explanations.a: High bias produces a converged, small gap, not a wide still-closing one.
explanations.b: Correct - a wide, still-narrowing gap is the high-variance signature: the model can fit the training data well but is not yet constrained enough by sample size to generalize as well.
explanations.c: A wide, closing gap is a normal and expected learning-curve pattern, not evidence of a computation error.
explanations.d: A still-widening or still-closing gap is precisely evidence that generalization has not yet stabilized.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the learning-curve decision procedure in order.

items.text: Plot training and validation score against training-set size on the data already collected
Check whether the two curves have converged to a plateau with a small gap, or still show a wide gap
If converged with a small gap, change the model or features rather than collecting more data
If the gap is wide and still closing at the largest size tested, invest in collecting more data

questions.explanation: The procedure starts by producing the curve on existing data, then reads the shape of the gap, then branches: a converged small gap calls for changing the model or features, while a wide still-closing gap justifies collecting more data.

questions.prompt: Match each learning-curve pattern to its correct diagnosis and remedy.

left.text: Curves converge quickly to a low plateau, small gap
Wide gap between high training score and lower validation score, still closing at max data size
Training score near-perfect on a tiny training set

right.text: High bias - more data will not help; improve the model or features
High variance - more data is likely to help
Expected behavior of any flexible model when there are very few rows to fit

questions.explanation: A converged, small-gap plateau is high bias and calls for a model/feature change; a wide, still-closing gap is high variance and rewards more data; near-perfect training score on tiny data is simply what near-memorization looks like at the left edge of the curve, before it says anything about bias or variance.

lessons.label: Baselines You Must Beat

sections.heading: Why a bare metric means nothing
sections.body: A metric reported alone is uninterpretable. "My model got 92% accuracy" sounds impressive until someone asks what fraction of the data belongs to the majority class - if 95% of rows are the majority class, a classifier that always predicts that one class, learning nothing at all, already scores 95%, and the 92% "result" is actually worse than doing nothing. The number only becomes evidence of something once it is compared against a defined reference point that a domain expert or a naive rule could have hit without any modeling at all.

sections.heading: The baseline ladder
sections.body: A useful baseline ladder, roughly in order of sophistication: the majority-class baseline (always predict the single most frequent class, trivially scoring accuracy equal to that class's prevalence); the stratified-random baseline (predict each class randomly in proportion to its observed frequency, a fairer zero-skill reference for metrics like F1 or balanced accuracy that penalize majority-only prediction, since it does not automatically win on imbalanced data the way the majority baseline does); predict-the-mean for regression (always output the training set's average y, which is exactly the baseline that gives an R-squared of zero by definition) or predict-the-median as a variant robust to outliers (this does not generally yield an R-squared of zero - it yields R-squared at or below zero, equal to zero only when the median happens to equal the mean); a one-feature rule or domain heuristic (the simple threshold or rule of thumb a practitioner in the field would already use, such as "flag if temperature exceeds X"); and plain logistic or linear regression, which any more complex model - gradient boosting, a neural network - must beat by a meaningful margin to justify its added complexity and reduced interpretability.

sections.heading: DummyClassifier and DummyRegressor as the mechanical baseline
sections.body: Scikit-learn's DummyClassifier and DummyRegressor compute these mechanically, using the same fit/predict/score API as any real estimator, which makes an apples-to-apples comparison nearly free to produce. DummyClassifier's strategy argument takes "most_frequent", "stratified", "uniform", or "prior" to generate the classification baselines above; DummyRegressor's strategy argument takes "mean", "median", or "quantile" for the regression equivalents. Running the same cross-validation loop on both the dummy estimator and the real model, and reporting both numbers side by side, costs almost nothing computationally and answers the comparison question before anyone has to ask it.

sections.heading: The discipline
sections.body: The discipline this all supports is blunt: a metric reported without a baseline is not a result, it is a number with no way to judge whether it reflects skill or just the shape of the data. "My model got 92%" - full stop, no baseline in sight - is the single most common way an otherwise solid science-fair project fails at Q&A, because the very first question a competent judge asks is "92% compared to what?"

lessons.workedExample: A student reports 92% accuracy classifying whether a water sample is contaminated. Asked for the baseline, they run DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent") through the same 5-fold CV and get 95%, because only 5% of samples in their dataset are actually contaminated. Their 92% model, despite sounding strong, is worse than predicting "never contaminated" every time - and worse still, it likely means the model is missing most of the true contamination cases. Switching to F1 score against the stratified-random baseline reveals the model's real, more modest skill: an F1 of 0.41 versus a random baseline's 0.09, a genuine and defensible improvement the accuracy number alone had obscured.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask for the baseline before they ask for anything else about the model, because a headline metric with no reference point cannot be evaluated at all - it could reflect genuine skill or simply the base rate of the data. A team that proactively reports "92% vs. a 95% majority-class baseline, but F1 of 0.41 vs. 0.09 stratified-random" demonstrates they understand what their metric actually means, while a team caught flat-footed by "what's your baseline?" reveals they never checked whether their result was real.

questions.prompt: A model scores 92% accuracy on a dataset where 95% of rows belong to one class. What does this tell you?

options.text: The model is clearly better than chance, since 92% is a high number
The model performs worse than a trivial baseline that always predicts the majority class
Accuracy cannot be computed on imbalanced data
The model must be overfitting because 92% is suspiciously close to 95%

explanations.a: A high raw number is not evidence of skill by itself - it must be compared to what a trivial rule would achieve.
explanations.b: Correct - always predicting the majority class scores 95% here, so 92% is below that trivial baseline, meaning the model is doing worse than nothing.
explanations.c: Accuracy is computable on any classification dataset; the issue is that it is a poor stand-alone metric on imbalanced data, not that it can't be computed.
explanations.d: Closeness to the majority-class rate is expected on imbalanced data and is not by itself evidence of overfitting.

questions.prompt: Why is the stratified-random baseline often reported alongside the majority-class baseline, rather than relying on the majority-class baseline alone?

options.text: Because it is always numerically higher than the majority-class baseline
Because on metrics like F1 or balanced accuracy, the majority-class baseline does not automatically dominate, so a stratified-random reference gives a fairer zero-skill comparison
Because scikit-learn does not implement a majority-class baseline
Because stratified-random baselines are required by law for published results

explanations.a: It is not systematically higher; on plain accuracy it is usually lower than the majority-class baseline on imbalanced data.
explanations.b: Correct - F1 and balanced accuracy penalize ignoring the minority class, so the majority-class baseline scores poorly on them, and stratified-random gives a more informative zero-skill reference point for those metrics.
explanations.c: Scikit-learn's DummyClassifier implements both strategies ("most_frequent" and "stratified").
explanations.d: There is no such requirement; this is a methodological best practice, not a legal one.

questions.prompt: Put these baselines in order from least to most sophisticated.

items.text: Majority-class baseline (always predict the most frequent class)
Stratified-random baseline (predict classes in proportion to observed frequency)
One-feature rule or domain heuristic (a simple threshold a practitioner would already use)
Plain logistic or linear regression

questions.explanation: The ladder runs from the simplest possible rule (always predict the majority class), to a randomized but frequency-aware rule, to a single informative feature or expert heuristic, to a full but simple statistical model - each step incorporates more information than the last.

questions.prompt: Match each scikit-learn Dummy estimator strategy to what it computes.

right.text: Always predicts the single most common class label
Predicts classes randomly according to their observed frequency in training data
Always predicts the training set's average target value (the baseline that yields R-squared of zero)

questions.explanation: "most_frequent" gives the majority-class baseline, "stratified" gives the randomized frequency-weighted baseline, and DummyRegressor's "mean" strategy always outputs the training mean, which by construction achieves an R-squared of exactly zero.

lessons.label: Class Imbalance in Practice

sections.heading: What prevalence does to every metric
sections.body: Class imbalance distorts nearly every metric, not just accuracy. On a dataset where 2% of rows are the positive class, precision and recall both become numerically volatile with small denominators - a handful of false positives can crater precision even when the model is mostly right - while ROC-AUC can look deceptively strong (0.90 or higher) because the vast majority of true negatives are easy to rank correctly, inflating the curve even when the model barely distinguishes the rare positives that actually matter. The prevalence of the positive class is not a footnote; it changes what any given metric value means, which is why prevalence must be reported alongside the metric, not left implicit - an F1 of 0.4 means something very different at 50% prevalence than at 2%.

sections.heading: Four standard responses
sections.body: Four standard responses address imbalance. Class weighting reweights the loss function so misclassifying a minority-class row costs more than misclassifying a majority-class row, without touching the data itself - most scikit-learn classifiers accept a class_weight="balanced" argument that does this automatically, in inverse proportion to class frequency. Threshold shifting keeps the model's predicted probabilities untouched and instead moves the decision threshold away from the default 0.5 to trade precision for recall (or vice versa) based on the actual cost of each error type. Undersampling drops majority-class rows until classes are balanced, trading away data volume and potentially useful majority-class information for balance. SMOTE - Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique, introduced by Chawla, Bowyer, Hall, and Kegelmeyer in a 2002 Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research paper (volume 16, pages 321-357) - instead generates new synthetic minority-class points by interpolating along the line segment between a real minority point and one of its nearest minority-class neighbors, adding plausible variation rather than duplicating existing rows.

sections.heading: The risks, and two hard rules
sections.body: Each response carries a risk. Applying SMOTE before splitting into cross-validation folds is a leakage bug: synthetic points derived from a row that ends up in the test fold can share information with the same row's neighbors sitting in the training fold, inflating the validation score. SMOTE also distorts calibration, since it changes the effective class balance the model is trained on without changing the real-world prevalence the model will face at deployment, so predicted probabilities need recalibration afterward before they can be trusted as real probabilities. Two hard rules follow from all of this: never resample the validation or test set - only the training data may be reweighted, undersampled, or SMOTE-augmented - and always report the prevalence of each class alongside any performance metric.

lessons.workedExample: A team detecting a rare crop disease (3% prevalence) applies SMOTE to the entire dataset before running 5-fold CV, then reports 0.88 F1 and 0.95 ROC-AUC. A mentor points out the SMOTE step happened before the CV split, so synthetic points in the training folds were interpolated partly from real minority rows now sitting in the test fold. Rerunning with SMOTE applied only inside each training fold (never touching the untouched, still-imbalanced test fold) drops F1 to 0.61 - a large but honest number, alongside the disclosed 3% prevalence, that a judge can actually interpret.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge evaluating any classifier on real-world data will ask for the class prevalence before trusting any metric, since precision, recall, F1, and ROC-AUC all mean different things at different base rates. A team that resampled its test set, or ran SMOTE before splitting into folds, has an inflated number that will not survive a mentor's or judge's follow-up question about how the resampling was sequenced - stating the prevalence up front and explaining exactly which rows were resampled (training only) heads off the single most common integrity challenge to an imbalanced-data project.

questions.prompt: Why can ROC-AUC look deceptively strong on a severely imbalanced dataset even when the model barely distinguishes the rare positive class?

options.text: Because ROC-AUC cannot be computed on imbalanced data and defaults to a high value
Because the large majority of true negatives are easy to rank correctly, which inflates the curve even if the rare positives are poorly separated
Because ROC-AUC only considers the majority class by definition
Because ROC-AUC always equals 1 minus the prevalence of the minority class

explanations.a: ROC-AUC is well-defined and computable on imbalanced data; the issue is interpretation, not computability.
explanations.b: Correct - with many easy true negatives to rank against, the curve can look strong overall while doing a poor job separating the rare positive cases that matter most.
