Comparing their AUCs, he argues, is comparing numbers computed on different rulers, which is what he means by 'incoherent'. His proposed alternative, the H-measure, fixes a single, shared cost-weighting distribution across all classifiers being compared, restoring an apples-to-apples comparison at the price of the analyst having to specify that cost distribution up front rather than letting each model implicitly choose its own.

sections.heading: Field-specific and metric-specific challenges
sections.body: Lobo, Jimenez-Valverde, and Real's 2008 paper 'AUC: A Misleading Measure of the Performance of Predictive Distribution Models', from species distribution modeling in ecology, showed AUC can be insensitive to how well a model predicts the actual spatial shape of a species' range, and is sensitive to the extent of the study area in ways that make cross-study AUC comparisons unreliable. Separately, Chicco and Jurman's 2020 BMC Genomics paper argued for the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) over both F1 score and plain accuracy for binary classification, especially with imbalanced classes, because MCC is the only common metric of the three that uses all four confusion-matrix cells (true/false positives and negatives) symmetrically and produces a high score only when the classifier does well on BOTH classes, unlike F1 which ignores true negatives entirely and unlike raw accuracy which can look excellent on a 99%-negative dataset even while missing nearly every positive case.

sections.heading: The defense, and why the argument stays open
sections.body: AUC's defenders reply that its threshold-free ranking interpretation, established by Hanley and McNeil, is exactly the right tool when the deployment threshold genuinely isn't known yet, which is common early in model development. Hand's critique matters most once a real cost structure and threshold are being chosen for deployment; Lobo et al.'s critique matters most when comparing across differently-sized study regions; MCC's case is strongest under severe class imbalance. No single metric wins every scenario, which is why practitioners are increasingly advised to report several metrics side by side, AUC, MCC, and a calibrated cost-weighted score, rather than treat any one as a universal scoreboard that settles which model is 'better' on its own.

lessons.workedExample: Two disease-screening models both report AUC = 0.85. Following Hand's argument, this apparent tie can hide a real difference: if Model A's scores cluster tightly around the decision boundary while Model B's are spread widely, the two AUCs implicitly averaged over different effective cost-weightings, so the 0.85s are not directly comparable the way two accuracy percentages at a fixed, shared threshold would be. A team following Chicco and Jurman would instead also report MCC at the intended clinical threshold, and a team following Lobo et al. would flag that AUC comparisons only hold if both models were evaluated on datasets covering a similarly-sized population.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has read Hand's paper may press on whether the presented AUC of two models is truly comparable, since Hand's whole point is that it might not be; the strong response explains the implicit, classifier-dependent cost-averaging rather than just repeating 'AUC is threshold-free, so it's fair.' A judge could also ask why not just use accuracy or F1 instead, inviting the Chicco and Jurman case for MCC under imbalance. The honest, judge-satisfying answer is that this is a genuinely unresolved methodological debate, not a solved problem with one right metric, and naming multiple credible positions demonstrates real engagement rather than a memorized verdict.

questions.prompt: What is the core of David Hand's 2009 argument that AUC is 'incoherent'?

options.text: AUC cannot be computed for more than two classes
AUC implicitly averages over a misclassification-cost distribution that depends on the classifier being scored, so different classifiers are compared on different scales
AUC always equals accuracy at the optimal threshold
AUC requires a labeled validation set, which most classifiers lack

explanations.a: Hand's critique is about cost-weighting, not about class count limitations.
explanations.b: Correct — because the implicit cost distribution AUC averages over depends on each classifier's own score distribution, two AUCs are not on a shared scale.
explanations.c: AUC is explicitly threshold-independent; it is not equivalent to accuracy at any single threshold.
explanations.d: This is a general requirement for evaluating classifiers, not the specific flaw Hand identifies in AUC.

questions.prompt: Why do Chicco and Jurman (2020) argue for the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) over F1 score and accuracy?

options.text: MCC is easier to compute than accuracy
MCC uses all four confusion-matrix cells symmetrically and only scores high when both classes are predicted well
MCC does not require a confusion matrix at all
MCC is always numerically identical to accuracy

explanations.a: Computational ease is not their argument; the case is about what the metric actually rewards.
explanations.b: Correct — unlike F1 (which ignores true negatives) or accuracy (which can be misleading under imbalance), MCC incorporates all four cells and rewards balanced performance on both classes.
explanations.c: MCC is itself derived directly from the confusion matrix's four cells.
explanations.d: MCC and accuracy diverge sharply under class imbalance, which is precisely why Chicco and Jurman prefer MCC in that setting.

questions.prompt: Match each critique or defense to its source in the AUC metric debate.

left.text: AUC is incoherent; use the H-measure instead
AUC is misleading in species distribution modeling

right.text: David Hand, 2009, Machine Learning
Lobo, Jimenez-Valverde, and Real, 2008
Traced to Hanley and McNeil's ranking interpretation of AUC

questions.explanation: Hand's 2009 paper is the incoherence critique with the H-measure alternative; Lobo et al. 2008 raised the ecology-specific misleadingness concern; the defense of AUC rests on the ranking interpretation established by Hanley and McNeil.

lessons.label: Leakage and the Reproducibility Crisis in ML-Based Science

sections.heading: 294 papers, 17 fields, one recurring bug
sections.body: Sayash Kapoor and Arvind Narayanan's 2023 Patterns paper 'Leakage and Reproducibility Crisis in ML-Based Science' surveyed published research using machine learning across 17 scientific fields, from political science to medicine to genomics, and documented data leakage, where information from the test set improperly influences training or feature construction, in 294 papers, sorting the leaks into a taxonomy of concrete causes rather than treating them as one vague error. Their sharpest, most cited example is civil war prediction: several influential political-science papers claimed machine learning models substantially outperformed classical logistic regression at forecasting civil conflict onset. Kapoor and Narayanan traced the apparent advantage to leakage, test-period information bleeding into training features via how the country-year data was split and preprocessed, often because the split ignored time ordering entirely; once the leak was fixed with a properly temporal split, the machine learning models' claimed edge over plain logistic regression largely vanished, with the two approaches performing comparably on the corrected data, undercutting years of citations built on the original, leaky result.

sections.heading: A twenty-year-old warning made concrete
sections.body: The paper's explicit backdrop is John Ioannidis's widely cited 2005 PLoS Medicine paper 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False', which argued that small sample sizes, flexible analysis choices, and publication pressure toward positive results combine to make a large share of published findings statistically unreliable, independent of any particular method or field. Kapoor and Narayanan's contribution is showing a specific, mechanistic, and distinctly ML-flavored version of that same failure mode: leakage is not random noise but a systematic bias that inflates reported accuracy in a consistent direction, and it recurs independently across unrelated fields because the same handful of pipeline mistakes, improper train/test splitting, feature engineering that uses future or globally-computed information, get repeated by researchers applying ML methodology they weren't originally trained in.

sections.heading: Institutional fixes, and whether checklists are enough
sections.body: Responses include Joelle Pineau's ML Reproducibility Checklist, adopted by NeurIPS as a submission requirement starting in 2019, model info sheets and datasheets documenting a model's or dataset's intended use and known limitations, and the REFORMS reporting standard Kapoor co-authored, a checklist built specifically for ML-based science across scientific disciplines rather than for ML conference papers alone. Whether checklists alone can fix the underlying incentive structure driving leakage in the first place, the pressure to publish striking, headline-worthy results quickly, often in venues whose reviewers lack ML-specific methodological expertise, is the live, explicitly unresolved question the paper leaves open rather than answers.

lessons.workedExample: A political science paper splits a dataset of country-years into train and test sets randomly, ignoring time. Some training examples come from years AFTER some test examples. A feature like 'GDP growth over the following two years' (constructed using data that includes the outcome window) leaks future information into training. The model then 'predicts' civil war onset with high accuracy partly because it has implicitly seen outcome-adjacent information for similar time periods. Kapoor and Narayanan's fix, a strictly temporal split where all training data precedes all test data, and features built only from information available at prediction time, is exactly the kind of correction that erased the ML-over-logistic-regression advantage in the papers they re-examined.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge grading any project that reports 'our model beats a simple baseline by X%' should ask how the train/test split was constructed and whether any feature could have seen information from outside its own training window; this is precisely the leakage question Kapoor and Narayanan showed recurring across 294 papers. A stronger judge will also ask whether a checklist like Pineau's or REFORMS was followed, and whether the student can articulate why civil-war prediction's ML advantage disappeared under correction, rather than only reciting that leakage 'is bad' in the abstract.

questions.prompt: In Kapoor and Narayanan's civil war prediction example, what happened to machine learning's claimed advantage over logistic regression once leakage was corrected?

options.text: The ML advantage grew even larger
The claimed advantage largely vanished, with ML and logistic regression performing comparably
Logistic regression became completely unusable
The correction had no measurable effect on either model

explanations.a: The corrected comparison shrank the gap rather than widening it; leakage had been inflating ML's apparent edge.
explanations.b: Correct — once the leak (test-period information influencing training) was fixed, ML's reported superiority over logistic regression mostly disappeared.
explanations.c: Logistic regression remained a viable, usable baseline throughout; it was the ML models' inflated advantage that was undermined.
explanations.d: The correction was consequential precisely because it changed the comparative result, which is the paper's central finding.

questions.prompt: How does Kapoor and Narayanan's (2023) leakage finding relate to Ioannidis's 2005 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False'?

options.text: They are unrelated; Ioannidis's paper concerns only clinical trials
Kapoor and Narayanan document a specific, mechanistic, ML-particular version of the general unreliability Ioannidis warned about
Ioannidis's paper proves that leakage is impossible in properly randomized studies
Kapoor and Narayanan refute Ioannidis's claims using ML evidence

explanations.a: Ioannidis's argument was general across research fields, and Kapoor and Narayanan explicitly invoke it as backdrop for their ML-specific findings.
explanations.b: Correct — leakage is presented as a systematic, mechanistic instance of the broader publication-reliability problem Ioannidis described in 2005.
explanations.c: Ioannidis's paper is about statistical and structural causes of unreliable findings broadly, not a proof about randomization eliminating leakage.
explanations.d: Kapoor and Narayanan build on and extend Ioannidis's concerns rather than contradicting them.

questions.prompt: Put these ML-reproducibility milestones in chronological order.

items.text: Ioannidis publishes 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False'
Pineau's ML Reproducibility Checklist adopted at NeurIPS
Kapoor and Narayanan publish the leakage survey in Patterns
The REFORMS reporting standard is proposed

questions.explanation: Ioannidis's foundational critique came in 2005; Pineau's checklist was adopted at NeurIPS in the years following (starting 2019); Kapoor and Narayanan's leakage survey appeared in 2023; REFORMS followed as a cross-disciplinary reporting standard proposed around the same period.

units.label: Case Studies: When the Evaluation Decided the Outcome

lessons.label: Google Flu Trends: The Model That Died of Its Own Validation

sections.heading: A dazzling debut: nowcasting flu from search queries
sections.body: In 2008, Google launched Google Flu Trends (GFT), and in 2009 Ginsberg et al. published the method in Nature: correlate the frequency of roughly 50 million candidate search queries against CDC influenza-like-illness (ILI) surveillance data from 2003-2008, keep the ~45 queries whose regional correlation was highest, and sum them into a single index. The pitch was speed: CDC's ILINet data lags by one to two weeks because it is built from reports doctors' offices file after the fact, while Google could estimate today's flu prevalence from today's searches. GFT nailed the 2007-08 season in retrospective testing and was reported to track CDC data with r > 0.90 in validation regions. By 2009 the tool had expanded to cover more than 25 countries, and its early success made it the flagship example, cited in countless conference talks, of what real-time "big data" epidemiology could do without waiting on slow public-health reporting chains.

sections.heading: The collapse: 100 of 108 weeks wrong, and a pandemic missed entirely
sections.body: The failures accumulated quietly for years before Lazer, Kennedy, King, and Vespignani's 2014 Science paper, "The Parable of Google Flu: Traps in Big Data Analysis," made the pattern public: from August 2011 to September 2013, GFT overestimated ILI in 100 of 108 weeks, and at the widely cited January 2013 peak it predicted more than double the rate the CDC eventually confirmed. GFT had also completely missed the non-seasonal 2009 H1N1 pandemic, since its query set was tuned only on seasonal winter-flu correlations. Lazer's team named two causes: "big data hubris," the assumption that sample size and correlation substitute for a validated, mechanistic model, and "algorithm dynamics" — Google kept changing its own search engine (autocomplete, related-searches suggestions) in ways that shifted what people typed, silently moving the ground under features the model had frozen at launch.

sections.heading: The final indignity: a naive baseline won
sections.body: The most damning result was almost embarrassingly simple. Lazer's team built a bare-bones autoregressive model predicting the current week's ILI from nothing but the CDC's own ILI estimate from two or three weeks earlier plus a seasonal trend term — no search data, no machine learning. That lagged-CDC baseline outperformed GFT-alone on out-of-sample error, and a hybrid combining GFT with the lagged-CDC baseline beat both alone. Google quietly retired the public GFT dashboard in August 2015, folding the underlying estimates into a data-sharing API for outside researchers rather than continuing it as a standalone public tool. The recurring lesson: a model must be judged against a baseline evaluated the same way, out of sample, forward in time; GFT was never subjected to that test until outsiders imposed one years after launch.

lessons.workedExample: A public-health analyst in 2013 must explain to a hospital administrator why GFT's headline number can't be trusted this season. She pulls up Lazer et al.'s reanalysis and walks through the specific evaluation gap: GFT was validated once, in 2009, against 2003-2008 CDC data that had implicitly shaped which queries were chosen — never on a genuinely held-out future season. She plots GFT's weekly error against the two-week-lagged CDC baseline and shows the baseline's error band is tighter across most of the 108 weeks examined. Her conclusion: GFT's marketing claim of "nowcasting" was not the same claim as "validated forecasting," and the difference is a specific, missing evaluation protocol, not a philosophical nuance.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has read past the headlines will ask what exactly failed: the search-query signal, the statistical method, or the evaluation protocol. The precise answer is the evaluation protocol — GFT's ~45 queries were correlation-mined on historical data and never re-validated against a true forward-in-time holdout, so drift in Google's own algorithm silently broke the assumption that today's queries mean what 2008's queries meant. A student who can name Lazer et al. 2014, the 100-of-108-weeks figure, and the lagged-CDC baseline that beat it demonstrates real understanding of overfitting-to-history and non-stationarity, not just that "the model was wrong."

questions.prompt: What two root causes did Lazer et al.'s 2014 Science paper identify for Google Flu Trends' failure?

options.text: Big data hubris and algorithm dynamics
Overfitting and underfitting of the regression weights
Sample bias and p-hacking in query selection
Server latency and declining search volume

explanations.a: Correct — "big data hubris" (assuming correlation and scale substitute for validated methodology) and "algorithm dynamics" (Google's own search changes silently altering what queries meant) were the paper's named mechanisms.
explanations.b: The paper's critique was about evaluation and non-stationarity, not a bias-variance tradeoff in the regression itself.
explanations.c: Query selection was correlation-mined, but the paper's core argument was about validation and drift, not p-hacking specifically.
explanations.d: Latency and volume were never the issue; the queries were still available, they just no longer meant what they meant at training time.

questions.prompt: Put these events in the Google Flu Trends story in chronological order.

items.text: Google launches Google Flu Trends
Ginsberg et al. publish the method in Nature
GFT completely misses the non-seasonal H1N1 pandemic
GFT predicts more than double the CDC's confirmed ILI rate
Lazer et al. publish "The Parable of Google Flu" in Science

questions.explanation: GFT launched in 2008; the Nature paper describing the method appeared in early 2009; the H1N1 pandemic that GFT missed emerged later in 2009; the widely cited overestimate peak was January 2013; and Lazer, Kennedy, King, and Vespignani's public reckoning in Science followed in March 2014.

questions.prompt: Match each term from the Google Flu Trends case to its correct meaning.

right.text: The assumption that data volume and correlation substitute for validated, mechanistic modeling
The platform's own ongoing changes silently altering what the tracked features mean over time
A simple model using CDC's own recent numbers, which outperformed GFT alone

questions.explanation: Big data hubris is the overconfidence that scale replaces validation; algorithm dynamics is Google's own search-engine changes moving the ground under GFT's frozen query set; and the lagged-CDC baseline was the humble two-to-three-week-old CDC figure plus a seasonal term that beat GFT on out-of-sample error.

questions.prompt: Why did GFT completely miss the 2009 H1N1 pandemic?

options.text: H1N1 caused no detectable spike in flu-related search terms
Its query set was tuned only to seasonal winter-flu correlation patterns and did not generalize to a non-seasonal pandemic
Google suppressed flu-related searches during the outbreak
CDC surveillance data was unavailable that year

explanations.a: There was a real search response to H1N1; the problem was that GFT's fixed query weights were calibrated to a seasonal pattern H1N1 didn't follow.
explanations.b: Correct — the ~45 queries were selected to correlate with seasonal winter ILI, so a non-seasonal spring/summer pandemic fell outside what the frozen model was built to detect.
explanations.c: There is no evidence of suppression; the mismatch was a modeling and timing issue, not a data-availability one.
explanations.d: CDC continued reporting throughout 2009; GFT's failure was in its own query-correlation design, not missing ground truth.

lessons.label: The Epic Sepsis Model: Vendor AUC vs. External Validation

sections.heading: A proprietary model deployed before anyone outside the vendor could check it
sections.body: Epic Systems' proprietary Sepsis Prediction Model was embedded in the EHR software running at hundreds of U.S. hospitals by the late 2010s, silently scoring every admitted patient and firing best-practice-advisory alerts to nurses and physicians when a risk threshold was crossed. Epic and the University of Colorado Health jointly reported the model's discrimination as an AUC of 0.76 to 0.83, a figure hospital systems used to justify purchasing and deploying the tool, and one clinicians were told to trust when an alert fired at the bedside. That number, however, came from testing on data resembling the model's own development population, not from an independent hospital running its own patient mix, documentation habits, and lab-ordering conventions against the frozen model. By the time Wong et al. tested it, the Epic Sepsis Model was likely one of the most widely deployed proprietary clinical prediction tools in the country, running quietly in the background of ordinary hospital workflows across many health systems.

sections.heading: External validation cuts discrimination from 0.76-0.83 down to 0.63
sections.body: Wong et al. published the external test in JAMA Internal Medicine in June 2021: a retrospective cohort of 27,697 patients across 38,455 hospitalizations at Michigan Medicine, December 2018 to October 2019, scored by the live, unmodified Epic Sepsis Model. The AUC fell to 0.63 — barely above coin-flip discrimination and well short of the vendor-reported range. At Epic's own recommended alert threshold, sensitivity was only 33% (the model missed 67% of confirmed sepsis cases), specificity was 83%, positive predictive value was just 12%, and negative predictive value was 95% — meaning the model was far better at reassuring clinicians a patient was low-risk than at flagging a true case, the opposite of what a screening alert is supposed to do.

sections.heading: Alert fatigue is a precision problem, and 7% is the number that mattered
sections.body: The model generated alerts on 18% of all hospitalized patients, a volume nurses and physicians had to review on top of every other bedside task — the textbook mechanism of alert fatigue. Worse, among patients whose sepsis a clinician had already caught on their own, the model added almost nothing: at the recommended threshold it identified only 7% of sepsis cases that clinicians had missed. The gap between the vendor's internal AUC and Wong et al.'s external AUC compresses the whole lesson of this unit into two numbers: a metric computed on the population and pipeline it was built on is a claim about that population, not a portable fact about the model, and only an independent, differently sourced test converts the claim into a result. An accompanying JAMA Internal Medicine editorial titled "The Epic Sepsis Model Falls Short" made the broader point explicit: proprietary, vendor-validated-only models should not be trusted in clinical deployment until independently reproduced, exactly the standard this unit argues for everywhere else.

lessons.workedExample: A hospital data-science team considering the Epic Sepsis Model tries to reproduce Wong et al.'s approach before trusting the vendor's brochure. They pull their own 12 months of admissions, run the frozen, unmodified model against that held-out local cohort, and recompute AUC, sensitivity, specificity, and positive predictive value from scratch rather than citing Epic's number. When their local AUC lands at 0.65 and their PPV near 13%, closely matching Wong et al. rather than the vendor's 0.76-0.83, they present hospital leadership with a stark choice: keep the alert live and staff for a 1-in-8 true-positive rate, retrain on local data, or replace the tool.
lessons.judgeFraming: A sharp judge will ask what "validation" meant on the vendor's brochure versus in Wong et al.'s study, because the two numbers came from fundamentally different tests. Internal validation on a population resembling the training data measures how well a model fits data like what it has already seen; external validation on an unrelated hospital's patients, with that hospital's own documentation habits and lab-ordering patterns, measures whether the model generalizes at all. A student who can state both AUCs, the sensitivity and PPV figures, and frame alert fatigue as a precision problem measured in real nurse-hours shows they understand why internal metrics are a claim, not a result.

questions.prompt: What was the Epic Sepsis Model's AUC in Wong et al.'s 2021 external validation, compared with the vendor-reported figure?

options.text: 0.63 externally vs. 0.76-0.83 vendor-reported
0.91 externally vs. 0.76-0.83 vendor-reported
0.76 externally vs. 0.63 vendor-reported
Both figures were 0.83

explanations.a: Correct — Wong et al.'s independent test at Michigan Medicine found an AUC of 0.63, well below the 0.76-0.83 Epic and University of Colorado Health had jointly reported.
explanations.b: External validation lowered discrimination, it did not raise it above the vendor's figure.
explanations.c: This reverses the actual result; the external AUC was the lower number, not the higher one.
explanations.d: The two figures were different by a wide margin, which is the entire point of the case.

questions.prompt: What does a positive predictive value of 12% mean for alerts fired at the model's recommended threshold?

options.text: Only 12% of patients who received an alert actually had sepsis
The model was correct 88% of the time overall
12% of true sepsis cases were missed
The model's specificity was 12%

explanations.a: Correct — PPV is the share of positive predictions that are true positives, so 12% means roughly seven of every eight alerts fired on patients without sepsis.
explanations.b: Overall accuracy is a different, undefined figure here; PPV specifically describes alert precision, not overall correctness.
explanations.c: The share of missed true cases is captured by sensitivity (33% caught, 67% missed), not PPV.
explanations.d: Specificity was reported separately at 83%; PPV and specificity measure different things.

questions.prompt: Order the steps that separate a vendor's internal claim from an independently confirmed clinical result.

items.text: Vendor reports an AUC from internal testing on its own development-like population
Hospitals purchase and deploy the model based on the vendor's reported number
An independent team assembles an external cohort the model has never seen
The frozen, unmodified model is scored against that unseen cohort
AUC, sensitivity, and PPV are recomputed and compared against the vendor's figures

questions.explanation: The vendor's AUC came first and drove adoption; only afterward did Wong et al. build an independent external cohort, score the unmodified model against it, and recompute the metrics that revealed the gap.

questions.prompt: Match each metric from Wong et al.'s external validation to its value and meaning.

right.text: 0.63 — barely above chance discrimination
33% — the model caught only a third of confirmed sepsis cases
18% of all hospitalized patients received an alert
7% — the additional share of clinician-missed sepsis cases the model identified

questions.explanation: The external AUC of 0.63, sensitivity of 33%, an 18% overall alert rate, and only 7% added detection of clinician-missed cases together show a model that generated substantial alert volume while adding little real diagnostic value.

lessons.label: COVID-19 Prediction Models: Hundreds Built, Almost None Usable

sections.heading: Two independent reviews, the same verdict
sections.body: Two large reviews converged on the same conclusion during 2020-2021. Wynants et al.'s living systematic review, first published in the BMJ in April 2020 and updated repeatedly as the pandemic continued, eventually tracked more than 232 published diagnostic and prognostic COVID-19 prediction models and assessed each with PROBAST (the Prediction model Risk Of Bias ASsessment Tool); nearly all were rated high or unclear risk of bias. Separately, Roberts et al. published in Nature Machine Intelligence in 2021 after screening 2,212 papers on machine-learning models for detecting or prognosticating COVID-19 from chest X-rays and CT scans; only 62 passed initial screening for in-depth review, and of those 62 the authors found none of potential clinical use because of methodological flaws running through every one. Both reviews were assembled by consortium teams working through 2020 specifically because so many competing models were being built and, in some cases, pitched for real hospital deployment during a live public-health emergency, which raised the stakes of getting the evaluation right beyond an academic exercise.

sections.heading: Frankenstein datasets and the paediatric X-ray trap
sections.body: Roberts et al. coined "Frankenstein datasets" for a recurring construction flaw: multiple teams pulled COVID-positive images from one public repository and COVID-negative images from a different one, then recombined them without noticing that the same images had already been reused, and sometimes duplicated, across several of the supposedly independent public datasets other teams were also drawing from — collapsing the apparent diversity of training data into a much smaller, overlapping pool. The single most cited concrete failure was the paediatric-control trick: several models paired adult COVID-positive scans against a "normal" class built from paediatric chest X-rays used as healthy controls, simply because paediatric scans were the readily available non-COVID images at hand. Children's chests differ systematically from adults' on X-ray, so the models could hit high reported accuracy by learning to distinguish child from adult anatomy rather than COVID from no-COVID, a shortcut that evaporates on any real hospital population, which is overwhelmingly adult regardless of diagnosis.

sections.heading: The missing step: nobody validated externally
sections.body: Both reviews flagged the same structural absence: essentially none of the several hundred models screened were tested on an external dataset collected by a different team, at a different hospital, after the model was frozen. Performance was reported almost exclusively on internal train/test splits carved from the same Frankenstein pool, so an inflated accuracy figure and a genuine clinical signal were statistically indistinguishable from inside the paper itself. Wynants' team and Roberts' team both recommended the same fix that recurs through this whole unit: report an external, prospectively collected validation cohort, or the number is only a description of the training data, not evidence the model works.

lessons.workedExample: A student building a toy COVID chest-X-ray classifier for a science fair pulls positive images from one Kaggle set and negative images from a second, unrelated public pediatric-pneumonia dataset, and gets 96% test accuracy. Recognizing the paediatric-control trap from Roberts et al., she checks the negative class's age distribution and finds it is entirely under 12 — a Frankenstein dataset in miniature. She rebuilds the negative class from age-matched adult non-COVID chest X-rays instead, and accuracy drops to 78%, a far more honest number that reflects the disease signal rather than an age shortcut.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has read Roberts et al. or Wynants et al. will ask exactly one uncomfortable question about any imaging classifier: where did the negative (control) images come from, and are they matched to the positive images on everything except the disease? This single question exposes the paediatric-control trap and the Frankenstein-dataset problem in one move. A student who can preemptively describe how their control images were sourced and age/demographic-matched, and who can cite the 2,212-screened, 62-reviewed, zero-usable finding, demonstrates they understand that image classifiers routinely learn confounds rather than pathology.

questions.prompt: What did Roberts et al. mean by a "Frankenstein dataset"?

options.text: A dataset recombined from overlapping public sources, such that supposedly independent images and patients were duplicated across studies
A dataset stitched together from multiple hospitals' fully de-identified electronic health records
A dataset containing only synthetically generated, computer-drawn images
A dataset labeled by several disagreeing radiologists

explanations.a: Correct — teams unknowingly drew from the same small pool of public images repackaged across multiple repositories, so datasets that looked independent shared and duplicated content.
explanations.b: The problem was public image repositories, not EHR data, and it was about hidden overlap, not simple aggregation.
explanations.c: The images were real clinical scans, not synthetic; the flaw was in how real images were sourced and recombined.
explanations.d: Label disagreement among radiologists is a separate, real issue in medical imaging, but it is not what "Frankenstein dataset" refers to.

questions.prompt: Why did using paediatric chest X-rays as the "non-COVID" control class undermine several models?

options.text: Paediatric X-rays are always lower resolution than adult scans
The model could learn to distinguish child versus adult anatomy rather than COVID versus no-COVID, a shortcut that fails on real adult hospital populations
Children cannot contract COVID-19, so the negative label was factually wrong
Paediatric data-consent rules made the images legally unusable

explanations.a: Resolution differences were not the mechanism; systematic anatomical differences between child and adult chests were.
explanations.b: Correct — since positives were adults and negatives were children, the model could hit high accuracy by detecting age-related anatomy alone, a confound with zero connection to COVID pathology.
explanations.c: Children can and did contract COVID-19; the issue was a mismatched control group, not a false label.
explanations.d: The datasets were public research images already cleared for reuse; the flaw was scientific design, not a legal one.

questions.prompt: Put these events in the COVID-19 prediction-model review story in order.

items.text: Wynants et al.'s living systematic review is first published in the BMJ
Repeated updates grow the review to track more than 232 models
Roberts et al. screen 2,212 papers on imaging-based COVID models
62 of those papers are examined in depth
Zero of the 62 in-depth studies are judged of potential clinical use

questions.explanation: Wynants et al.'s BMJ review began in April 2020 and grew across living updates to more than 232 models; Roberts et al.'s Nature Machine Intelligence review then screened 2,212 papers, narrowed to 62 for in-depth review, and found none of those 62 clinically usable.

questions.prompt: Match each reviewer or finding to its correct figure.

right.text: Tracked more than 232 models across repeated updates
The risk-of-bias tool that rated nearly all models high or unclear risk
2,212 papers screened, narrowed to 62 examined in depth
Zero of the 62 in-depth studies judged of potential clinical use

questions.explanation: Wynants et al.'s review grew to over 232 tracked models, assessed with PROBAST, which flagged nearly all as high or unclear risk of bias; Roberts et al. separately screened 2,212 papers down to 62 in-depth reviews, none of which the authors judged clinically usable.

lessons.label: COMPAS: When a Fairness Fight Was Really a Metric Fight

sections.heading: ProPublica's 2016 analysis: unequal false-positive rates
sections.body: In May 2016, Julia Angwin, Jeff Larson, Surya Mattu, and Lauren Kirchner published "Machine Bias" in ProPublica, analyzing Northpointe's COMPAS recidivism risk score against roughly 7,000 defendants in Broward County, Florida. Their headline finding: among defendants who did NOT reoffend within two years, Black defendants were misclassified as high-risk at about 45%, versus about 23% for white defendants who also did not reoffend — a false-positive rate roughly double. Northpointe (later renamed Equivant) responded that COMPAS was well calibrated: within any given risk decile, Black and white defendants recidivated at statistically similar rates, meaning a score of 7 meant roughly the same real-world risk regardless of race. Checked against the same underlying data, both claims were true. COMPAS itself is not a machine-learning model in the modern sense but a weighted-questionnaire risk score built from 137 items covering criminal history, education, and social factors, feeding into a proprietary formula Northpointe never fully disclosed, which made independent scrutiny of its internals difficult and pushed both sides toward arguing over its outputs instead.

sections.heading: Why both sides were right: an impossibility result, not a data error
sections.body: Alexandra Chouldechova's 2017 paper "Fair Prediction with Disparate Impact" and Jon Kleinberg, Sendhil Mullainathan, and Manish Raghavan's 2016 paper "Inherent Trade-Offs in the Fair Determination of Risk Scores" independently proved the same result: when the base rate of the outcome (actual recidivism) differs between two groups, no score can simultaneously achieve calibration (equal predicted-risk-to-actual-risk mapping within each group) and equal false-positive/false-negative rates across groups, except in the trivial case of a perfect predictor. Because Black and white defendants in the COMPAS data had different underlying base rates of rearrest, ProPublica's fairness criterion (balanced error rates) and Northpointe's fairness criterion (calibration) were mathematically incompatible — satisfying one guarantees violating the other. This is not a limitation specific to COMPAS or to criminal justice: the same three-way tradeoff among calibration, equal false-positive rates, and equal false-negative rates applies to any risk score used on groups with different base rates, including credit scoring and medical risk models.

sections.heading: The metric everyone quoted hid the disagreement
sections.body: COMPAS's overall accuracy, roughly 65% and similar across race in the raw headline number, was the figure most press coverage led with, and it was compatible with both the ProPublica story and the Northpointe story, because aggregate accuracy averages over exactly the subgroup breakdown where the disagreement lived. The only way to see the conflict at all was to stop reporting one pooled number and audit error rates and calibration separately by subgroup — the method this Field Codex places in the Fairness, Bias, and Robustness branch. COMPAS shows why that separate branch exists: a model can look identical on one aggregate number while being simultaneously "fair" and "unfair" under two defensible, mutually exclusive definitions.

lessons.workedExample: A student re-analyzing a public COMPAS-style dataset for a project computes overall accuracy first and finds it nearly identical, about 65%, for Black and white defendants — the pooled number Northpointe and ProPublica both had access to. She then splits the confusion matrix by race and recomputes false-positive rate and calibration separately: false-positive rate is roughly double for Black defendants, while calibration curves nearly overlap. Because the two groups' base rates of actual reoffending differ in her data, she confirms with Chouldechova's formula that no threshold choice could have equalized both properties at once — the disagreement was mathematically forced, not a modeling mistake.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows the COMPAS story will not ask "was the model biased"; they will ask which fairness definition a student means, because ProPublica's and Northpointe's numbers were both correct under different, incompatible definitions. A strong answer names the impossibility result (Chouldechova 2017; Kleinberg, Mullainathan, and Raghavan 2016), explains that unequal base rates force a tradeoff between calibration and equal error rates, and states which definition the project's own evaluation prioritizes and why — showing that the choice of fairness metric is a policy decision, not a bug to be optimized away.

questions.prompt: What did ProPublica's 2016 "Machine Bias" analysis find about COMPAS's false-positive rates?

options.text: Black defendants who did not reoffend were flagged high-risk at about 45%, versus about 23% for white defendants
COMPAS was equally calibrated across race, with no disparity of any kind
White defendants were flagged high-risk more often overall than Black defendants
COMPAS showed no measurable racial disparity on any metric

explanations.a: Correct — this roughly 2-to-1 gap in false-positive rates among defendants who did not reoffend was the central finding of the ProPublica analysis.
explanations.b: Calibration was Northpointe's separate finding, using a different metric than the false-positive rate ProPublica reported.
explanations.c: The direction is reversed; Black defendants who did not reoffend were falsely flagged at a substantially higher rate.
explanations.d: There was a clear disparity on the false-positive-rate metric, even though calibration looked even across groups.

questions.prompt: Northpointe's rebuttal showed COMPAS was well calibrated across race. Is this compatible with ProPublica's false-positive-rate finding?

options.text: Yes — both can be simultaneously true when the two groups have different base rates of the outcome
No, one of the two studies must have used fabricated data
No, because calibration and false-positive rate always measure the same thing
Yes, but only because COMPAS scores were assigned at random

explanations.a: Correct — Chouldechova and Kleinberg-Mullainathan-Raghavan proved calibration and equalized error rates cannot both hold when base rates differ, so both findings being true is the mathematically expected outcome, not a contradiction.
explanations.b: Both studies used the same publicly released Broward County data; no fabrication was needed to produce this result.
explanations.c: Calibration and false-positive rate are distinct properties that coincide only under special conditions, such as equal base rates.
explanations.d: COMPAS scores were not random; the compatibility follows from the base-rate difference, not from noise in the scoring.

questions.prompt: Match each contribution to the researcher(s) or figure responsible for it.

left.text: "Inherent Trade-Offs in the Fair Determination of Risk Scores" (2016)

right.text: Found a roughly 45% vs. 23% false-positive-rate gap by race
Proved calibration and equal error rates cannot both hold when base rates differ
Independently proved the same impossibility result from a different angle
The headline number that hid the subgroup disagreement entirely

questions.explanation: Angwin, Larson, Mattu, and Kirchner's ProPublica piece found the false-positive-rate gap; Chouldechova and, independently, Kleinberg, Mullainathan, and Raghavan proved the underlying impossibility; and the pooled accuracy figure everyone quoted was compatible with both the ProPublica and Northpointe stories precisely because it averaged over the subgroup split where the conflict lived.

questions.prompt: Put these events in the COMPAS controversy in order.

items.text: Northpointe's COMPAS score is used in Broward County pretrial and sentencing decisions
ProPublica publishes "Machine Bias"
Northpointe rebuts, citing equal calibration across race
Chouldechova and Kleinberg, Mullainathan, and Raghavan publish impossibility proofs
The field adopts subgroup auditing of error rates and calibration as standard practice

questions.explanation: COMPAS was already in use before ProPublica's May 2016 exposé; Northpointe's calibration-based rebuttal followed shortly after; the formal impossibility proofs from Chouldechova and from Kleinberg, Mullainathan, and Raghavan appeared over the following year; and the practice of auditing subgroup error rates and calibration separately became standard afterward.

lessons.label: Building an Honest Evaluation: A Worked Science-Fair Case

sections.heading: The project, and the decision the metric must serve
sections.body: Consider a science-fair project predicting whether a hospital patient will be readmitted within 30 days from about 2,000 rows of tabular intake data. The first evaluation decision is not a metric — it is naming the real-world decision the model feeds: a nurse-staffing call-back list. That decision fixes which error costs are asymmetric (missing a true readmission is worse than one extra unnecessary call) and rules out plain accuracy, which would reward a model that just predicts "no readmission" for everyone. Real 30-day readmission rates typically run near 15-20%, so a trivial always-negative classifier already scores roughly 80-85% accuracy while catching zero true cases — that number is fixed as the majority-class baseline every later result must beat, before any modeling begins.

sections.heading: Split, pipeline, and cross-validation, in the order that avoids leakage
sections.body: Next comes the split, justified rather than default: if any patient appears with multiple admissions, splitting by row would leak that patient's history across train and test, so the split must be grouped by patient ID, or, if the readmission window matters, split temporally so the model is tested only on admissions after its training window ends. All preprocessing — imputing missing labs, scaling, one-hot encoding diagnosis codes — sits inside a single scikit-learn Pipeline fit only on the training fold, never on the full dataset first, so no information from held-out rows leaks into feature construction. The model then runs through 5-fold cross-validation on the training data, reporting the mean and standard deviation of the chosen metric across folds, since a mean alone hides whether performance is stable or one lucky fold, and a 95% confidence interval is computed from that fold-to-fold spread before the untouched test set is opened exactly once, at the very end.

sections.heading: What goes on the poster versus what stays in the notebook
sections.body: The poster shows the decision-relevant summary: the chosen metric, such as recall at a fixed precision or AUC, with its confidence interval next to the majority-class baseline, plus one confusion matrix from the held-out test fold — enough for a passerby to see the gap over baseline in ten seconds. The notebook keeps everything the poster cannot fit: the full per-fold metric table, the pipeline code, the group or temporal split logic, and residual or calibration plots for a judge who wants to dig in. When a judge asks "your accuracy is 0.94 — so what?", the rehearsed answer names the baseline (0.94 against an 85% majority-class baseline is a real but modest 9-point gain), states which error type the chosen metric actually protects against, and shows the confidence interval so the judge can see whether 0.94 is stable or a single lucky split.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose the project's 5 cross-validation folds give recall-at-90%-precision scores of 0.58, 0.61, 0.55, 0.63, and 0.59 — a mean of 0.592 and a standard deviation of about 0.030. The 95% confidence interval, computed as the mean plus or minus the t-distribution's critical value for 4 degrees of freedom (about 2.78 standard errors, not a flat 2, since only 5 folds are available) across 5 folds, spans about 0.55 to 0.63. On the poster, this appears as a single line: "Recall at 90% precision: 0.59 (95% CI 0.55-0.63), vs. 0.00 for the majority-class baseline at that precision level." The notebook underneath holds all five raw fold scores, the pipeline definition, and the group-split code that produced them, ready if a judge asks to see the work.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks "your accuracy is 0.94 — so what?" is testing whether a student can connect a number to a decision, not whether they can recite a number. The strong answer is layered: name the baseline the metric must beat, name the specific error type (false negative vs. false positive) the chosen metric was picked to control, and show the confidence interval so the judge can judge stability rather than take a single point estimate on faith. A student who instead just repeats "0.94 is high" has demonstrated they built a model but never designed an evaluation.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the evaluation workflow in the order this segment argues for.

items.text: Name the real-world decision and its asymmetric error costs
Establish the majority-class or naive baseline
Choose a grouped or temporal split to avoid leakage
Place preprocessing inside a pipeline fit only on the training fold
Run 5-fold cross-validation, reporting mean and standard deviation
Touch the held-out test set exactly once, at the end

questions.explanation: The decision and its costs must be named before any metric is chosen; the baseline is fixed next so later results have something honest to beat; the split and pipeline are designed to prevent leakage; cross-validation on the training data comes next; and the test set is opened only once, at the very end, so it stays a genuine held-out check.

questions.prompt: Why must preprocessing such as imputation, scaling, and encoding be fit only on the training fold, inside a pipeline?

options.text: It runs faster than fitting on the whole dataset
Fitting on the full dataset before splitting leaks information from held-out rows into the features, inflating apparent performance
scikit-learn requires pipelines syntactically for any preprocessing step
It reduces the total number of features in the model

explanations.a: Speed is not the reason; a pipeline can be just as fast, the issue is what data the preprocessing step is allowed to see.
explanations.b: Correct — if imputation or scaling statistics are computed using test-fold rows, information about the held-out data has already leaked into the features before evaluation, making the reported metric optimistic.
explanations.c: Pipelines are a convenience for correctness, not a hard syntactic requirement; the leakage risk exists whether or not a Pipeline object is used.
explanations.d: Feature count is unrelated; the concern is which rows the preprocessing statistics are computed from.

questions.prompt: Why is a grouped or temporal split necessary in this readmission project instead of a random row-level split?

options.text: Random row-level splitting is always statistically invalid in every project

If the same patient contributes multiple admissions, random splitting can leak that patient's history across train and test, and if the readmission window matters chronologically the model should be tested only on later admissions
Institutional review boards require temporal splits for all clinical data
Temporal splits always produce higher reported accuracy than random splits

explanations.a: Random splitting is fine in many settings; it becomes a problem specifically when rows are not independent, as with repeated patients.
explanations.b: Correct — repeated patients and time-dependent readmission windows both create leakage risks that a grouped or temporal split is designed to prevent.
explanations.c: No blanket IRB rule forces this; the requirement follows from the data's own structure, not an external policy.
explanations.d: Temporal splits typically produce lower, more honest accuracy by removing the leakage that inflates random-split results, not higher accuracy.

questions.prompt: A judge asks, "your accuracy is 0.94 — so what?" What is the strongest rehearsed answer?

options.text: Restate that 0.94 is a high number
Compare 0.94 against the majority-class baseline, name which error type the chosen metric protects against, and show the confidence interval
Explain that cross-validation was used to compute the number
Say accuracy is not an important metric

explanations.a: This restates the number without connecting it to the decision or the baseline, which is exactly what the question is probing for.
explanations.b: Correct — naming the baseline, the protected error type, and the confidence interval together show the number was designed around a decision, not just reported in isolation.
explanations.c: Mentioning cross-validation alone does not answer what the number means for the underlying decision.
explanations.d: Dismissing accuracy without explaining what should be used instead, and why, does not answer the judge's question.

questions.prompt: Match each project artifact to where it belongs.

left.text: Chosen metric plus confidence interval vs. baseline
One confusion matrix from the held-out test fold
Full per-fold metric table across all 5 folds
Preprocessing pipeline code and split logic

right.text: Belongs on the poster
Stays in the notebook

questions.explanation: The poster carries only the decision-relevant summary a passerby can absorb quickly: the metric with its confidence interval against baseline, and one confusion matrix. The full per-fold table and the pipeline and split code stay in the notebook for a judge who wants to verify the details.

units.label: Scores, Thresholds, and the Decision Rule

lessons.label: From Scores to Decisions: What a Classifier Actually Outputs

sections.heading: Three Layers Hiding Inside One Function Call
sections.body: Every classifier a judge sees actually computes three distinct things, but only one word, 'classifier,' describes all three. The first layer is the raw decision function: a logistic regression outputs a linear score w·x + b (the logit), an SVM outputs the signed distance w·x + b to the separating hyperplane, and a random forest outputs a vote fraction across trees. This raw score is unbounded (logistic, SVM) or bounded but uncalibrated (forest vote share) and by itself carries no probabilistic meaning. The second layer squashes that raw score into a bounded number: the sigmoid function sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^-z) maps any logit to (0,1) for binary problems, and softmax generalizes this to K classes by exponentiating each class's logit and normalizing so the K outputs sum to 1. The third layer is the hard label: a single decision rule, almost always 'threshold the squashed score at some cutoff t,' collapses the continuous score into a class assignment.

sections.heading: scikit-learn Hardwires t = 0.5 and Hides It
sections.body: scikit-learn's API design makes this three-layer structure easy to miss because most tutorials call only .predict(). Internally, .predict() on a LogisticRegression or RandomForestClassifier calls .predict_proba() and applies a fixed rule: label = 1 if P(y=1|x) >= 0.5, else 0. For an SVC, .predict() instead checks the sign of .decision_function(), a raw margin, threshold 0 rather than 0.5, but the same idea: one hardwired cutoff. .predict_proba() is the only method that returns the full squashed-score layer, and it is where a practitioner must go to apply any threshold other than 0.5. Critically, scikit-learn gives no built-in set_threshold() method on the base estimator; changing the operating point means calling predict_proba() (or decision_function()) yourself and comparing the output to your own chosen t. Treating .predict() as the classifier's real output silently accepts scikit-learn's default cutoff as your decision rule, whether or not it fits the problem.

sections.heading: Ranking Quality Is Not Decision Quality
sections.body: This split matters because two different families of metrics evaluate two different things. Rank-based metrics, AUC-ROC, AUC-PR, Spearman correlation between scores and outcomes, depend only on the relative order of scores across examples, and are mathematically invariant to any monotonic transform of the score, including recalibration. Decision-based metrics, accuracy, precision, recall, F1, the whole confusion matrix, depend on where a specific threshold t cuts that ordering, and change every time t moves even if the ranking is untouched. A model can have AUC = 0.95 (excellent discrimination between classes) yet post a terrible accuracy at t = 0.5 if its raw scores are poorly calibrated or the deployment prevalence differs sharply from training. Reporting only one metric family hides the other's story entirely.

lessons.workedExample: A student builds an SVC to flag defective solder joints from image features. clf.decision_function(x) returns -2.3 for a joint: negative, so clf.predict(x) returns 0 (good), using the hardwired threshold 0 on the margin. But CalibratedClassifierCV(clf).predict_proba(x) reports P(defective) = 0.41, still under 0.5, so the two hard-label paths agree here. Now suppose the factory's cost of missing a defect is 15x the cost of a false alarm; the student instead compares P(defective) to a custom cutoff of 0.06, computed from the cost ratio, and the same 0.41 score now clears the bar and gets flagged for manual inspection. Nothing about the model's ranking changed, only the decision layer moved.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'what does your model's output actually mean before you call .predict()?' is testing whether the student can name the three layers and knows which scikit-learn method exposes which one. Students who cite only accuracy, or only 'my model predicted correctly 94% of the time,' reveal they never left the hard-label layer, so they cannot answer follow-ups about how performance would change at a different operating point. A strong answer distinguishes the raw margin, the calibrated probability, and the thresholded label by name, and states explicitly that 0.5 is scikit-learn's default, not a law of classification.

questions.prompt: What does scikit-learn's .predict() do internally for a probabilistic classifier like LogisticRegression?

options.text: It re-fits the threshold via cross-validation on every call
It thresholds predict_proba's positive-class probability at 0.5
It always returns the raw decision_function value unchanged
It uses a Bayes-optimal threshold computed from class weights

explanations.a: There is no per-call refitting; the cutoff is a fixed constant, not learned or re-tuned.
explanations.b: Correct - LogisticRegression.predict() calls predict_proba() and labels an example positive when that probability is at least 0.5.
explanations.c: That describes decision_function() itself, which SVC's predict() thresholds at 0, not the probability-based predict() path.
explanations.d: scikit-learn has no built-in cost-aware threshold; 0.5 (or 0 for margins) is fixed regardless of class weights.

questions.prompt: Order the three layers of a classifier's computation from rawest to most processed.

items.text: Raw decision function / margin (e.g. logit, SVM distance)
Squashed score (sigmoid or softmax output)
Hard label after thresholding

questions.explanation: The raw margin or logit is computed first, then squashed into a bounded (0,1) score via sigmoid or softmax, and only then thresholded into a final hard class label.

questions.prompt: Match each metric to the quality it primarily measures.

right.text: Ranking quality (invariant to threshold and monotonic transforms)
Decision quality (depends on a specific chosen threshold)

questions.explanation: AUC-ROC and Spearman correlation depend only on score ordering, so they are ranking metrics unaffected by threshold choice. Accuracy and F1 are computed from a confusion matrix at one specific threshold, so they measure decision quality at that operating point.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would leave a model's AUC-ROC unchanged but could change its accuracy at t = 0.5?

options.text: Applying a monotonic recalibration transform to all scores
Retraining the model from scratch on entirely different data
Changing how the AUC formula is computed
Nothing; AUC and accuracy always move together

explanations.a: Correct - a monotonic transform preserves the rank order of scores (so AUC is unchanged) but can move many scores across the 0.5 cutoff (so accuracy changes).
explanations.b: Retraining on different data can change the underlying ranking itself, so it is not guaranteed to preserve AUC.
explanations.c: AUC is a well-defined quantity; changing how you compute it doesn't change the model's actual behavior.
explanations.d: They are independent properties precisely because one is threshold-invariant and the other is not.

lessons.label: Why 0.5 Is Almost Always the Wrong Threshold

sections.heading: The Three Conditions 0.5 Silently Assumes
sections.body: The 0.5 cutoff baked into scikit-learn's .predict() is optimal only when three separate conditions all hold at once, and real deployments routinely break at least one. First, CALIBRATION: the model's output must equal the true conditional probability, so that a bucket of examples scored 0.7 really does contain positives about 70% of the time. Many high-capacity models (gradient-boosted trees, deep nets, and SVMs run through Platt scaling) are excellent at ranking but systematically over- or under-confident, so their raw 0.7 might correspond to an empirical rate of 0.4 or 0.9. Second, EQUAL COSTS: 0.5 only makes sense if a false positive and a false negative cost the same amount, which is rare; missing a cancer case and ordering one extra biopsy are not equivalent harms. Third, MATCHING PREVALENCE: the threshold assumes the class balance seen at deployment equals the class balance seen during training; if a fraud model trained on a 50/50 curated sample is deployed on a 0.3%-fraud live stream, the implied prior is wrong by two orders of magnitude.

sections.heading: Deriving the Bayes-Optimal Threshold
sections.body: The correct cutoff falls out of decision theory directly. Suppose predicting positive when the true label is negative costs C_FP, and predicting negative when the true label is positive costs C_FN. For a case with estimated probability p = P(y=1|x), the expected cost of calling it positive is C_FP*(1-p), and the expected cost of calling it negative is C_FN*p. A rational rule predicts positive whenever the positive-call cost is lower: C_FP*(1-p) < C_FN*p. Rearranging, C_FP < p*(C_FP + C_FN), so predict positive when p > C_FP/(C_FP + C_FN). That ratio is the Bayes-optimal threshold t* = C_FP/(C_FP+C_FN). Notice t* = 0.5 only in the special case C_FP = C_FN; any asymmetry in cost pulls t* away from a half, and it does so independent of the calibration and prevalence issues above, which distort where p itself sits.

sections.heading: Fraud Example: Cost Ratio 1:20
sections.body: Consider a fraud-detection model where missing a fraudulent transaction (a false negative) costs roughly 20 times what a false alarm (a false positive: an annoyed customer and a manual review) costs, a 1:20 ratio, C_FP = 1, C_FN = 20. The Bayes-optimal threshold is t* = 1/(1+20) = 1/21, approximately 0.048. At the default t = 0.5, the model might catch only 31% of actual fraud (recall = 0.31), since most true fraud scores fall well under 0.5 given fraud's rarity. Lowering the cutoff to 0.048 accepts far more false alarms but pushes recall to roughly 0.86, nearly tripling the fraud caught, which is the economically rational trade given the 20x cost asymmetry.

lessons.workedExample: A hospital deploys a sepsis-risk model with predict_proba output p. A false negative (missed sepsis) risks death; a false positive (extra bloodwork and a nurse check) costs little, so the team sets C_FN = 25, C_FP = 1, giving t* = 1/26, approximately 0.038. At t = 0.5 the model flags only patients with p above half, missing most true sepsis cases because true positives are rare and often score p = 0.1-0.3. Re-running predict_proba and comparing to 0.038 instead of the hardwired 0.5 flags roughly three times as many at-risk patients for early antibiotics, accepting many more false alarms in exchange, exactly the trade the 25:1 cost ratio calls for.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'why did you pick threshold X instead of 0.5?' is checking whether the student treated 0.5 as a law of nature or as scikit-learn's arbitrary default. The strongest answers name the specific cost ratio for their domain, derive t* = C_FP/(C_FP+C_FN) rather than quoting it, and state which of the three assumptions (calibration, equal cost, matching prevalence) their project actually violates. A student who cannot say why their domain's false negatives and false positives are NOT equally costly has not thought past the library default, which is exactly the gap this question is designed to expose.

questions.prompt: A hospital assigns C_FP = 2 and C_FN = 18 for a diagnostic test. What is the Bayes-optimal threshold t*?

explanations.a: 0.5 is only correct when C_FP equals C_FN, which is not the case here (2 vs 18).
explanations.c: 0.9 would result from reversing the ratio (18/20), not from the correct C_FP/(C_FP+C_FN) formula.
explanations.d: 0.111 is C_FP/C_FN (2/18), not C_FP divided by the SUM C_FP+C_FN as the formula requires.

questions.prompt: Order the steps that derive the Bayes-optimal threshold from cost definitions.

items.text: Define C_FP and C_FN as the per-error costs
Write the expected cost of predicting positive as C_FP*(1-p)
Write the expected cost of predicting negative as C_FN*p
Set the two expected costs equal and solve for p
Obtain t* = C_FP/(C_FP+C_FN)

questions.explanation: You first name the two costs, write each decision's expected cost in terms of p, find the p where the two expected costs are equal (the switch point), and simplify that equality to the closed-form t*.

questions.prompt: Match each violated assumption to its consequence for the 0.5 threshold.

left.text: Prevalence shift between training and deployment

right.text: A score bucket of 0.7 does not actually contain 70% positives in reality
The optimal cutoff moves away from 0.5 even with perfectly calibrated probabilities
Training class balance no longer matches deployment, biasing the raw scores

questions.explanation: Miscalibration breaks the link between score and true probability; unequal costs pull the optimal cutoff away from 0.5 regardless of calibration; prevalence shift distorts the raw scores because the model learned a different class balance than the one it now faces.

questions.prompt: In the fraud example (C_FP = 1, C_FN = 20), what recall approximately results from moving the threshold from 0.5 to the Bayes-optimal 0.048?

options.text: Recall drops from 0.86 to 0.31
Recall rises from 0.31 to 0.86
Recall stays at 0.5 regardless of the threshold
Recall is undefined at any threshold other than 0.5

explanations.a: This reverses the direction; lowering the threshold to catch more fraud increases recall, it does not decrease it.
explanations.b: Correct - lowering the cutoff from 0.5 to roughly 0.048 catches far more true fraud cases, moving recall from about 0.31 to about 0.86.
explanations.c: Recall is a step function of threshold and changes substantially here; it does not stay fixed at 0.5.
explanations.d: Recall is well-defined at any threshold; it is simply the fraction of true positives caught at that cutoff.

lessons.label: The Threshold Sweep: Every Metric Is Really a Curve

sections.heading: Sweeping t Yields at Most n+1 Distinct Confusion Matrices
sections.body: Sort the n predicted scores from a validation set in ascending order. As you slide a threshold t continuously from below the smallest score to above the largest, the resulting hard labels, and therefore the entire confusion matrix (TP, FP, TN, FN), change only at the moments t crosses one of the n actual score values. Between any two consecutive sorted scores, every example keeps the same label regardless of where exactly t sits in that gap, so the confusion matrix is constant across the whole gap. With n examples there are n+1 such gaps (below the minimum, between each of the n-1 consecutive pairs, and above the maximum), so sweeping t across its entire range produces at most n+1 distinct confusion matrices. Every metric computed from a confusion matrix, true positive rate, false positive rate, precision, recall, F1, is therefore a step function of t with at most n+1 steps, not a smooth function and never a single scalar. This is exactly the discrete structure scikit-learn's roc_curve and precision_recall_curve functions exploit internally: rather than sampling t at arbitrary intervals, they enumerate only these n+1 breakpoints directly from the sorted scores, since evaluating anywhere else within a gap would be redundant.

sections.heading: Ties Collapse Operating Points into Diagonal Segments
sections.body: Real score distributions rarely have n distinct values; many examples land on identical or near-identical scores, especially from tree ensembles that output a vote fraction with only as many possible values as there are trees. When two or more examples share the exact same score, no single threshold can separate them, sliding t past that tied value flips all of them to the opposite label simultaneously. On an ROC curve, a run of tied scores of mixed true labels produces a diagonal segment (multiple points move together) rather than a sequence of clean single-example steps, because you cannot achieve any operating point strictly between them. Ties therefore reduce the number of achievable distinct operating points below the theoretical n+1 maximum and are the reason ROC curves drawn from coarse, low-cardinality scores look jagged or diagonal rather than smoothly stepped.

sections.heading: One Number Is One Point on a Curve
sections.body: 'My model is 94% accurate' names one point on a step function without naming which one. The same model, evaluated at a different threshold, might report 61% accuracy at t = 0.1 or 98% at t = 0.9, all true statements about the identical trained model. A complete claim states either the full curve (the ROC curve, the precision-recall curve, or a rank-based summary like AUC that aggregates every step) or names the specific operating threshold used alongside its full confusion matrix, so a reader can judge whether that particular point suits their costs.

lessons.workedExample: A student has 10 validation scores: 0.05, 0.12, 0.30, 0.31, 0.31, 0.45, 0.60, 0.72, 0.85, 0.91, with true labels [0,0,1,0,1,1,0,1,1,1]. Sorting gives 11 possible threshold gaps (n=10, n+1=11), but the tied pair at 0.31 (one true label 0, one true label 1) cannot be split by any single t, collapsing two of those gaps into one shared operating point, at most 10 distinct confusion matrices are actually achievable, not 11. Recomputing precision and recall at each of the 10 achievable thresholds and plotting them shows F1 peaking at t = 0.30 (F1 approximately 0.86), not at the default t = 0.5, where F1 drops to about 0.60.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'accurate compared to what threshold?' is testing whether the student understands that any single confusion-matrix metric is one sample from a step function, not a fixed property of the model. Students who cannot say how many distinct operating points their validation set even permits (at most n+1, fewer with ties) have likely reported the scikit-learn default without exploring the curve. The strongest answers bring the ROC or precision-recall curve itself, or at minimum state the chosen threshold explicitly alongside the full confusion matrix it produces.

questions.prompt: With n = 50 distinct validation scores and no ties, what is the maximum number of distinct confusion matrices obtainable by sweeping the threshold t?

explanations.a: 50 undercounts by one; the gaps below the minimum and above the maximum are also distinct achievable regions.
explanations.b: Correct - n distinct scores create n+1 threshold gaps (below min, between each consecutive pair, above max), giving 51 for n=50.
explanations.c: 49 would be the number of gaps strictly between consecutive scores, omitting the two end regions.
explanations.d: 100 has no basis in this construction; the count scales as n+1, not 2n.

questions.prompt: What effect do tied scores have on an ROC curve?

options.text: They have no effect on the curve's shape
They produce a diagonal segment, because tied points must move together
They always improve the reported AUC
They eliminate the need to choose a threshold at all

explanations.a: Ties reduce the number of achievable distinct operating points, which does change the curve's appearance.
explanations.b: Correct - since tied examples cannot be separated by any single threshold, sliding t past the tie flips them all at once, producing a diagonal jump rather than individual steps.
explanations.c: Ties do not systematically raise or lower AUC; they just make the empirical curve coarser.
explanations.d: A threshold is still required to produce hard labels; ties just limit which thresholds are distinguishable.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to build an empirical ROC curve from raw validation scores.

items.text: Sort the validation scores in ascending order
For each of the n+1 threshold gaps, compute the resulting confusion matrix
Compute TPR and FPR for each confusion matrix
Plot the (FPR, TPR) pairs and connect them in order of decreasing threshold

questions.explanation: You must first sort the scores to identify the distinct threshold gaps, compute a confusion matrix for each gap, derive TPR and FPR from each matrix, and finally plot and connect the resulting points to trace the curve.

questions.prompt: Match each claim to what it is missing or provides.

right.text: Incomplete decision claim: names a metric value with no stated threshold
Complete ranking claim: aggregates across all thresholds, no single t needed
Complete decision-point claim: names t and reports the resulting confusion-matrix metrics

questions.explanation: Reporting accuracy alone without a threshold is incomplete because accuracy is a step function of t. AUC is complete on its own because it aggregates over every threshold. Naming the threshold alongside its precision and recall is a complete decision-point claim.

lessons.label: Signal Detection Theory: Discriminability vs. Criterion

sections.heading: Green and Swets and the Equal-Variance Gaussian Model
sections.body: In 1966, psychophysicists David Green and John Swets published 'Signal Detection Theory and Psychophysics,' formalizing a model originally built for radar operators: on any trial, an observer sees a single internal evidence value drawn from one of two overlapping distributions. When only noise is present, the evidence is drawn from a 'noise' distribution; when a real signal is added to the noise, the evidence is drawn from a 'signal-plus-noise' distribution shifted to a higher mean. The simplest and most common version, the equal-variance Gaussian model, assumes both distributions are normal with the same variance (standardized to 1) but different means, noise centered at 0, signal-plus-noise centered at d'. The observer does not see which distribution generated a trial; they only see where the evidence value falls on this shared axis, and must decide 'yes, signal present' whenever it exceeds a criterion they set, called c. This is exactly the classifier-score-plus-threshold structure of any binary classifier, discovered and formalized decades before machine learning adopted it.

sections.heading: d' = z(TPR) - z(FPR): A Criterion-Free Separability Measure
sections.body: Because the two distributions are Gaussian with equal variance, the true positive rate (hit rate, the fraction of signal trials exceeding c) and the false positive rate (false-alarm rate, the fraction of noise trials exceeding c) are both determined by how far c sits from each distribution's mean, measured in standard deviations. Applying the inverse standard normal CDF, z(.), the probit function, to each rate converts these into z-scores on a common axis, and the algebra of the equal-variance model gives d' = z(TPR) - z(FPR) exactly, independent of where c was actually set. This is the key property: d' is a criterion-free measure of how separable the two distributions are, while c (or any classifier's threshold t) is a separate, freely chosen operating point. Two operators facing the identical d' can report wildly different TPR/FPR pairs simply by choosing different criteria.

sections.heading: d' and the Binormal ROC: Independent Knobs
sections.body: Each fixed value of d' traces exactly one binormal ROC curve, the set of all (FPR, TPR) pairs reachable by sliding c from negative infinity to positive infinity, and larger d' bows that curve further above the chance diagonal. Sliding the criterion moves you along a single curve without changing which curve you're on; only a genuine change in the underlying model (better features, more data, a different classifier) shifts to a different d' and a different curve entirely. This is the branch's central claim rendered in SDT's original vocabulary: a model's discriminative power (d', mirrored by AUC) and its chosen operating point (c, mirrored by threshold t) are independent knobs, and confusing them is a category error.

lessons.workedExample: A radiologist reviewing mammograms effectively performs an SDT task: noise trials are healthy scans, signal trials are cancerous ones, and their confidence rating is the evidence value. Suppose across a set of scans the radiologist achieves TPR = 0.90 and FPR = 0.20. Using a z-table (or norm.ppf in Python), z(0.90) is approximately 1.28 and z(0.20) is approximately -0.84, giving d' = 1.28 - (-0.84) = 2.12. A stricter radiologist who only flags scans they are very confident about might report TPR = 0.65, FPR = 0.02: z(0.65) is approximately 0.39, z(0.02) is approximately -2.05, giving d' = 0.39 - (-2.05) = 2.44, a similar separability, reached via a much more conservative criterion. Comparing raw TPR/FPR without computing d' would wrongly suggest the second radiologist is simply 'worse at catching cancer.'
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge familiar with psychology or signal processing may ask directly for d', or ask why two classifiers with different TPR/FPR pairs might have equal discriminability.
