Elkan also showed the optimal threshold on predicted probability p is t* = C_FP / (C_FP + C_FN): as C_FN grows relative to C_FP, the threshold for calling something positive drops, correctly making the classifier more trigger-happy about the more expensive error. Normalizing total expected cost by N (dividing by number of cases) turns it into a per-case expected cost, which is the version comparable across datasets of different sizes.

sections.heading: From theory to practice: MetaCost and the cost taxonomy
sections.body: Two companion results turned the cost matrix from theory into engineering practice. Pedro Domingos's MetaCost (KDD 1999, 'MetaCost: A General Method for Making Classifiers Cost-Sensitive') showed that ANY off-the-shelf classifier, treated as a black box, can be made cost-sensitive by relabeling training examples to their cost-minimizing class using bagged internal probability estimates, then retraining — no need to modify the base learner itself, and Domingos's benchmarks showed it beating cost-blind C4.5 and stratification-based resampling on cost reduction. Separately, Peter Turney's ICML-2000 workshop paper 'Types of Cost in Inductive Concept Learning' cataloged that misclassification cost is only one of roughly a dozen cost types practitioners conflate — including the cost of acquiring each feature (attribute cost), the cost of labeling more training data (instance cost), and computation cost — a reminder that C_FN/C_FP is a deliberately narrow slice of a much larger cost landscape.

lessons.workedExample: A hospital's sepsis-alert model runs on 10,000 patients; 200 actually develop sepsis (P=200, N=9800). At its current threshold: TPR=0.85 (170 caught, 30 missed), FPR=0.08 (784 false alarms). Clinicians estimate C_FN=100 (a missed sepsis case, in harm-adjusted units) and C_FP=1 (an unnecessary workup). Expected cost = 200×0.15×100 + 9800×0.08×1 = 3000 + 784 = 3784, or 0.378 per patient. Lowering the threshold to catch 3 more true positives at the cost of 200 more false alarms changes cost to 200×0.135×100+9800×~0.10×1 = 2700+980=3680 — a net improvement, because C_FN dominates. Note that an accuracy-optimized threshold would have moved the opposite direction, since 200 extra false alarms outnumber 3 extra true positives nearly 70-to-1 in raw count, even though the cost-optimized answer is correct once C_FN=100 is taken into account.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'why not just maximize accuracy?' is testing whether you understand that accuracy silently assumes equal costs. The strong answer names the actual cost matrix for your project's domain, states C_FN/C_FP explicitly, and cites Elkan's result that only the ratio — not the absolute dollar values — determines the optimal threshold. A student who can derive t* = C_FP/(C_FP+C_FN) on the spot, rather than reciting it, demonstrates they understand where the formula comes from, not just that it exists.

questions.prompt: According to Elkan's (2001) analysis, what determines the optimal classification threshold?

options.text: The absolute dollar value of C_FN and C_FP individually
Only the ratio between the misclassification costs
The total number of examples in the dataset
Whichever class is more prevalent, regardless of costs

explanations.a: Elkan showed adding a constant to a whole cost-matrix column leaves optimal decisions unchanged, so absolute values are not what matters.
explanations.b: Correct — only the difference/ratio of costs (C_FP/(C_FP+C_FN) for the threshold) determines optimal decisions, per Elkan's Foundations of Cost-Sensitive Learning (IJCAI 2001).
explanations.c: Dataset size affects the raw expected-cost total, not the optimal threshold itself.
explanations.d: Prevalence affects the raw counts P and N in the expected-cost formula, but the optimal threshold formula depends on cost ratio, not prevalence directly.

questions.prompt: A model has P=200 actual positives, N=9800 actual negatives, TPR=0.85, FPR=0.08, C_FN=100, C_FP=1. What is the expected cost?

explanations.a: Correct: 200×0.15×100 = 3000 (missed positives) plus 9800×0.08×1 = 784 (false alarms), total 3784.
explanations.b: 170 is the count of true positives caught, not the expected cost.
explanations.c: 984 omits the false-negative term entirely.
explanations.d: 17000 miscalculates by using 200×0.85×100 (true positives times cost) instead of the false-negative term 200×(1-TPR)×C_FN.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of building a cost-sensitive evaluation from scratch.

items.text: Write down C_FN and C_FP for the specific domain
Compute expected cost = P(1-TPR)C_FN + N·FPR·C_FP
Normalize by N for cross-dataset comparability
Derive/apply the optimal threshold t* = C_FP/(C_FP+C_FN)

questions.explanation: You must first elicit the costs, then compute raw expected cost from TPR/FPR, then normalize for comparability, and only then can the threshold formula (which is a function of those same costs) be applied to choose an operating point.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity to its role in the expected-cost framework.

right.text: Total cost contributed by false negatives
Total cost contributed by false positives
Optimal probability threshold t*

questions.explanation: P(1-TPR) is the count of missed positives, times their per-case cost C_FN, gives the FN cost term; N·FPR is the count of false alarms times C_FP gives the FP cost term; Elkan's threshold formula sets the boundary where marginal costs balance.

lessons.label: Cost Curves: The Dual View of ROC

sections.heading: Turning ROC points into lines: the point-line duality
sections.body: Chris Drummond and Robert Holte introduced the idea in their KDD 2000 paper 'Explicitly Representing Expected Cost: An Alternative to ROC Representation,' followed it with the argumentative 'What ROC Curves Can't Do (and Cost Curves Can),' and formalized the full technique in a 2006 Machine Learning journal paper, 'Cost Curves: An Improved Method for Visualizing Classifier Performance' (vol. 65, pp. 95-130). The core trick is a projective duality: every point (FPR, TPR) in ROC space becomes a LINE in cost-curve space, and every line in ROC space (like the chance diagonal) becomes a point. The cost-curve x-axis is 'probability-cost' PC(+), defined as PC(+) = p·C(FN) / (p·C(FN) + (1−p)·C(FP)), where p is the prior probability of the positive class — a single normalized skew term that folds together class prevalence and the cost ratio into one number between 0 and 1, so that PC(+)=0.5 represents a genuinely 'neutral' operating condition and any departure from 0.5 reflects either skewed prevalence, skewed cost, or both at once. The y-axis is normalized expected cost. A single classifier operating point, plotted across all possible values of PC(+), traces a straight line from (0, FPR) at PC(+)=0 to (1, 1−TPR) at PC(+)=1. This single line encodes that classifier's expected cost under every conceivable prevalence-and-cost regime at once, something one ROC point cannot show.

sections.heading: Why the lower envelope answers 'which model wins, and where'
sections.body: When you plot every classifier (or every threshold of one classifier, giving the full ROC curve as a family of lines) on the same cost-curve axes, the LOWER ENVELOPE of all those lines is the minimum achievable expected cost at each operating condition. This envelope is exactly the cost-curve transform of the ROC convex hull (ROCCH) — the set of ROC points that are Pareto-optimal at some cost/prevalence setting. Reading straight down at any x-position tells you which classifier wins there and by how much (the vertical gap between the winning line and the runner-up), which ROC space cannot show directly since ROC only ranks classifiers ordinally per point, not by cost magnitude. Because cost curves are literally lines fit from operating-point data, Drummond and Holte showed you can drop in binomial confidence intervals on TPR and FPR at each end, producing a confidence BAND around each line (widest at the ends, narrower with more test data) — letting you visually see whether one classifier's advantage over another is inside noise or a real, statistically significant win across a stated range of cost regimes.

lessons.workedExample: Two fraud classifiers, A (TPR=0.90, FPR=0.20) and B (TPR=0.70, FPR=0.05), look ambiguous on an ROC plot since neither dominates. As cost-curve lines: A runs from (0, 0.20) to (1, 0.10); B runs from (0, 0.05) to (1, 0.30). The lines cross around PC(+)≈0.43 (3/7). For PC(+) below that (rare fraud, or false alarms cheap relative to missed fraud), B's line is lower — B wins. Above it (fraud more prevalent, or missed fraud relatively cheaper), A wins. A team can now say 'deploy B in the low-fraud-rate region and A once fraud rate climbs above ~3-in-7 (~43%) weighted cases' instead of picking one model for all conditions.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has seen cost curves will ask what they show that ROC curves cannot: the answer is a directly readable expected-cost MAGNITUDE and a crossover point, not just an ordinal ranking. A weaker answer says 'cost curves are just another way to plot ROC'; a strong answer explains the point-line duality itself — why a single operating point becomes a full line across the PC(+) axis — and can locate the region where two crossing lines swap which classifier is preferable, with confidence bands showing whether that crossover is trustworthy given sample size.

questions.prompt: In the ROC-to-cost-curve duality, what does a single ROC point (FPR, TPR) become?

options.text: A single point at a fixed PC(+) value
A line spanning the full range of PC(+)
A confidence interval with no defined shape
The ROC convex hull itself

explanations.a: A fixed point would lose all information about how expected cost changes with prevalence/cost skew — the whole value of the transform is showing that variation.
explanations.b: Correct — one classifier operating point becomes a straight line from (0, FPR) to (1, 1-TPR) across probability-cost PC(+), per Drummond and Holte (2006).
explanations.c: Confidence bands are added around the line from binomial CIs on TPR/FPR, but the base object is a line, not an interval alone.
explanations.d: The ROCCH corresponds to the lower envelope of many lines, not to a single point's transform.

questions.prompt: What does the lower envelope of all classifiers' lines in cost-curve space represent?

options.text: The worst-performing classifier at every condition
The minimum achievable expected cost at each operating condition, i.e. the ROCCH transformed
A single fixed classifier chosen in advance
The average cost across all classifiers

explanations.a: The lower envelope is the BEST achievable cost, not the worst.
explanations.b: Correct — the lower envelope is exactly the cost-curve transform of the ROC convex hull, giving the minimum expected cost at every prevalence/cost skew.
explanations.c: The envelope can switch which classifier is optimal at different points, not fix one in advance.
explanations.d: It is a minimum (pointwise infimum), not an average.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to build and use a cost curve comparing two classifiers.

items.text: Compute each classifier's (FPR, TPR) operating point
Draw each as a line from (0,FPR) to (1,1-TPR) across PC(+)
Add confidence bands from binomial CIs on TPR/FPR
Read the crossover point(s) to see which classifier wins in which cost regime

questions.explanation: You need the raw operating point first, then the duality transform draws the line, then confidence bands quantify uncertainty, and only then does reading the plot tell you the winning regions.

questions.prompt: Match each cost-curve element to what it represents.

right.text: Normalized expected cost
Probability-cost, folding prevalence and cost ratio into one skew value
ROC convex hull, transformed

questions.explanation: PC(+) on the x-axis encodes both class prevalence and cost ratio as one number in [0,1]; the y-axis is normalized expected cost; and the lower envelope of all classifier lines is the cost-curve transform of the ROCCH.

lessons.label: Deriving a Threshold From Domain Costs

sections.heading: Three elicitations, one formula: t* = C_FP / (C_FP + C_FN)
sections.body: Turning Elkan's threshold formula into a number requires actually interviewing the domain, not guessing. Mammography screening: a missed cancer (false negative) delays treatment and can cost a life, commonly modeled as C_FN on the order of 20-100x a callback biopsy's cost, harm, and anxiety (C_FP≈1). At C_FN=50, t* = 1/51 ≈ 0.02 — flag almost anything even mildly suspicious, matching real radiology practice where recall rates run 8-12% against a ~0.3-0.5% cancer prevalence. Credit-card fraud: a missed fraud (C_FN) costs roughly the $200 chargeback plus processing overhead, while a false positive (C_FP) costs a declined legitimate purchase PLUS a churn risk — surveys of issuers put an angry customer's lifetime-value loss at $50-500. If C_FN=200 and C_FP=150, t*=150/350≈0.43 — a far more balanced threshold than mammography, because the false-positive cost isn't negligible here. Spam filtering: a missed spam (C_FN) is a minor annoyance (~$0.01-equivalent of attention), while a false positive that buries a job offer or a wire-transfer confirmation in junk can cost thousands. If C_FN=1 and C_FP=200, t*=200/201≈0.995 — filters should only act when extremely confident, explaining why spam folders under-flag rather than over-flag borderline mail. Each elicitation follows the same three-question script: what does missing a true positive actually cost downstream (in dollars, harm, or lost opportunity), what does a false alarm cost the person on the receiving end, and does either cost scale with volume (a single expensive false positive is different from many cheap ones).

sections.heading: Report an interval, not a false-precision point
sections.body: Nobody actually knows C_FN and C_FP to three significant figures — they're elicited from stakeholders who disagree, or estimated from noisy proxies like historical churn data. The scientifically honest move is sensitivity analysis: recompute t* across the PLAUSIBLE range of the cost ratio (say, C_FN/C_FP from 20 to 100 for mammography) and report the resulting threshold INTERVAL, e.g., 't* ∈ [0.0098, 0.048]', rather than a single number like 't*=0.02' that implies false confidence. Practically, this means plotting expected cost as a function of threshold for several cost-ratio scenarios and picking a threshold that stays near-optimal across the whole plausible range (a robust threshold) rather than one that's perfect for a single point estimate but catastrophic if the true ratio differs. This mirrors how clinical guidelines are actually built: the guideline names a RANGE of acceptable practice, not a single number, precisely because the underlying value judgment is contested. Health-economics practice calls this one-way or two-way sensitivity analysis, and the same logic applies outside medicine: a fraud team unsure whether churn cost is $50 or $500 should report how t* moves across that whole span before locking in a production threshold.

lessons.workedExample: A hospital wants a threshold for a mammography-adjunct model. Radiologists disagree: some treat a missed cancer as 30x worse than a callback, others say 80x. Computing t* at both ends: t*(30)=1/31≈0.032, t*(80)=1/81≈0.012. Rather than presenting 't*=0.02' as if it were settled, the team reports 'operating threshold should fall in [0.012, 0.032]; we recommend 0.015 as a compromise that stays within 15% of optimal expected cost across the whole disputed range' and shows the expected-cost-vs-threshold curve for both scenarios overlaid, so stakeholders can see how sensitive the recommendation actually is. This framing also lets the radiology group revisit the number later: if outcome data eventually pin the ratio closer to 80 than 30, the team can point back to the documented interval and justify tightening the threshold toward 0.012 without having to relitigate the whole elicitation from scratch.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge will probe whether you can DERIVE a threshold from a stated cost ratio, not just quote the formula. The stronger response walks through an actual elicitation — naming believable cost figures for the specific domain, computing t*, and sanity-checking that it matches known real-world practice (e.g., mammography's high recall rate at low prevalence). An expert-level answer volunteers the sensitivity analysis unprompted: 'since we're not certain of the ratio, here's the interval' — showing you understand that reporting a single threshold with unstated costs is a form of false precision.

questions.prompt: In the spam-filtering example, why is t* so close to 1 (≈0.995) rather than close to 0?

options.text: Because spam is rare in the training data
Because a false positive (burying an important email) is estimated far more costly than a false negative (missing spam)
Because t* only depends on class prevalence, not costs
Because the model's accuracy is very high

explanations.a: t* in this formula depends on the cost ratio C_FP/(C_FP+C_FN), not on prevalence directly.
explanations.b: Correct — when C_FP (losing an important email) vastly exceeds C_FN (a minor spam annoyance), t*=C_FP/(C_FP+C_FN) approaches 1, meaning the filter should only flag mail it's extremely confident about.
explanations.c: Elkan's threshold formula is a function of the cost ratio, not prevalence.
explanations.d: Accuracy is not part of the threshold derivation at all.

questions.prompt: For credit-card fraud with C_FN=200 and C_FP=150, what is t*?

explanations.a: Correct: t* = C_FP/(C_FP+C_FN) = 150/350 ≈ 0.43.
explanations.b: 0.57 would be C_FN/(C_FP+C_FN), i.e. inverting the formula's numerator.
explanations.c: 0.75 does not match the given cost figures under Elkan's formula.
explanations.d: 0.02 is the mammography-scenario answer, not this one — the ratios are very different.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a defensible cost-driven threshold derivation.

items.text: Elicit plausible ranges for C_FN and C_FP from domain stakeholders
Compute t* at the extremes of the plausible cost-ratio range
Report the resulting threshold interval, not a single false-precise number
Choose an operating threshold that stays near-optimal across the whole interval

questions.explanation: You must first get a plausible cost range from stakeholders, then propagate that range through t*'s formula, then report it honestly as an interval, and finally pick a robust operating point within it.

questions.prompt: Match each domain to its dominant cost asymmetry driving the threshold.

right.text: C_FN >> C_FP (missed cancer far worse than a callback), so t* is very low
C_FN and C_FP are comparable (chargeback vs. declined purchase plus churn), so t* is more balanced
C_FP >> C_FN (a buried important email far worse than a missed spam), so t* is very high

questions.explanation: Mammography's t*≈0.02 (recall-biased) comes from C_FN dominating; fraud's t*≈0.43 comes from comparable costs; spam's t*≈0.995 comes from C_FP dominating since a lost job offer is far costlier than a missed spam.

lessons.label: Metrics With Costs Baked In: F-beta, Youden's J, and Net Benefit

sections.heading: F-beta: a weight on recall disguised as a single number
sections.body: F_beta = (1+β²)·Precision·Recall / (β²·Precision + Recall) is often presented as a neutral 'balance' of precision and recall, but it is not neutral — it is a specific, tunable cost assumption. Setting β=1 (the ubiquitous F1) weights recall and precision equally in the harmonic mean, which implicitly treats a false negative and a false positive as equally costly RELATIVE to each class's base rate. Setting β=2 (F2) weights recall four times as heavily as precision (β² = 4), appropriate when missing a positive is far worse than a false alarm — the standard choice in medical screening triage and search-and-rescue detection. β=0.5 (F0.5) weights precision more, suited to spam-style domains where false positives are costlier. The point: choosing F1 over F2 IS choosing a cost ratio, whether or not the word 'cost' ever appears in the report. A student who writes 'we used F1 because it's standard' has silently picked C_FN=C_FP without saying so. The harmonic mean itself matters here too: unlike an arithmetic mean of precision and recall, the harmonic mean punishes a badly imbalanced pair severely — a model with precision=0.9 but recall=0.1 gets F1≈0.18, not 0.5 — which is why F-beta family metrics are preferred over simple averaging whenever one of the two components can collapse to near zero.

sections.heading: Youden's J and net benefit: same hidden assumption, different form
sections.body: Youden's J statistic (W.J. Youden, 1950, 'Index for Rating Diagnostic Tests', Cancer) is J = TPR + TNR − 1 = TPR − FPR, geometrically the vertical distance from the ROC chance diagonal to a given operating point. Maximizing J picks the point on the ROC curve farthest above the diagonal. This is mathematically equivalent to assuming a cost ratio C_FN/C_FP equal to the ratio of negative-to-positive prevalence (N/P) — it is NOT cost-neutral, it just hides the assumption inside a geometric-looking statistic. That means the 'optimal' Youden point shifts as prevalence shifts even if the true clinical costs never change, which is a common source of confusion when Youden's J is applied across populations with different disease rates. The house rule for both F-beta and Youden's J is the same: state the implied cost assumption OUT LOUD in the report — 'we chose F2, implying we weight recall about 4x precision' — rather than inheriting the default from a tutorial or a library's default scoring function without examining what it assumes. Youden originally developed J to compare two competing diagnostic tests on the same patients, and the 'Youden index' is still routinely reported in diagnostic-accuracy papers as if it were a cost-free, purely geometric optimum — a misconception this lesson explicitly corrects.

lessons.workedExample: A team building a rare-disease screening classifier defaults to reporting F1 because 'that's what sklearn shows by default.' Prevalence is 1%. Their model gets F1=0.40 (Precision=0.30, Recall=0.62). Recomputing as F2 = 5×0.30×0.62/(4×0.30+0.62) = 0.93/1.82 ≈ 0.51, a jump that better reflects the domain's true priority on catching cases. Separately, Youden's J = 0.62 − FPR; if FPR=0.05, J=0.57 — but since prevalence is only 1%, the point that maximizes J is calibrated to a 99:1 cost ratio the clinicians never actually endorsed, so the team documents this mismatch explicitly rather than presenting J's threshold as 'the' optimal cutoff.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing this topic wants to see whether you can name the cost assumption BEHIND a metric you didn't invent — most students can recite the F1 formula but freeze when asked 'what cost ratio does F1 assume?' The strong answer states plainly that F1 assumes equal costs for FN and FP relative to their base rates, that F2 quadruples recall's weight, and that Youden's J implicitly ties the assumed cost ratio to class prevalence via N/P — then says which one, if any, matches their actual domain, rather than defending whichever metric happened to be the library default.

questions.prompt: In F_beta, how much more heavily does F2 weight recall relative to precision compared to F1?

options.text: F2 weights recall 2 times as heavily as precision
F2 weights recall 4 times as heavily as precision (since β²=4)
F2 weights precision and recall identically, same as F1
F2 ignores precision entirely

explanations.a: The weight comes from β² in the formula, and β=2 gives β²=4, not 2.
explanations.b: Correct — F_beta = (1+β²)PR/(β²P+R), and with β=2 the β² term is 4, quadrupling recall's weight relative to F1's equal weighting.
explanations.c: F1 (β=1) is the equal-weighting case; F2 deliberately departs from that.
explanations.d: Precision still appears in both numerator and denominator; it's downweighted, not eliminated.

questions.prompt: What does maximizing Youden's J = TPR − FPR correspond to geometrically on an ROC plot?

options.text: The point closest to the top-left corner (0,1) in Euclidean distance
The point with the highest vertical distance above the chance diagonal
The point where precision equals recall
The area under the entire ROC curve

explanations.a: Euclidean distance to (0,1) is a different, related but distinct criterion from Youden's J.
explanations.b: Correct — J = TPR − FPR is exactly the vertical distance from a given operating point up to the chance diagonal (where TPR=FPR).
explanations.c: That describes a different balance point unrelated to J's definition.
explanations.d: AUC is the full-curve integral; J is a single-point statistic.

questions.prompt: Why is choosing F1 over F2 described as 'choosing a cost model'?

options.text: Because F1 and F2 always give identical scores in practice
Because each fixes a specific relative weight on recall vs. precision, which is equivalent to asserting a false-negative-to-false-positive cost ratio
Because F-beta scores have nothing to do with classifier errors
Because only F2, not F1, involves any cost assumption

explanations.a: They differ substantially whenever precision and recall diverge, as the worked example shows (0.40 vs 0.51).
explanations.b: Correct — the β parameter fixes how much more a missed positive counts versus a false alarm, which is precisely a cost-ratio assumption, whether stated or not.
explanations.c: F-beta is built directly from precision and recall, which are themselves built from FP/FN/TP counts.
explanations.d: F1 also encodes a cost assumption — equal weighting — it is just the specific, easy-to-miss case of β=1.

questions.prompt: Match each metric or statistic to the cost assumption it silently encodes.

right.text: Equal weight on precision and recall (implicit C_FN = C_FP relative weighting)
Recall weighted 4x precision, appropriate when missed positives are far costlier
Implicit cost ratio tied to the prevalence ratio N/P

questions.explanation: F1's β=1 gives equal weighting; F2's β=2 gives β²=4x weight on recall; Youden's J maximization is mathematically equivalent to assuming a cost ratio equal to the class prevalence ratio.

lessons.label: Decision Curve Analysis

sections.heading: Net benefit: folding a clinician's cost ratio into one threshold probability
sections.body: Andrew Vickers and Elena Elkin introduced decision curve analysis (DCA) in a 2006 Medical Decision Making paper, 'Decision Curve Analysis: A Novel Method for Evaluating Prediction Models.' The core formula is net benefit = TP/n − (FP/n)·(p_t/(1−p_t)), where n is the total sample size and p_t is the threshold probability at which a clinician is indifferent between treating and not treating. The trick is that p_t itself encodes the clinician's implicit cost ratio: if a doctor says 'I'd biopsy a patient if their cancer risk is above 10%,' that IS a statement that a missed cancer is roughly 9 times worse than an unnecessary biopsy, because p_t=0.10 corresponds to odds of C_FP:C_FN = p_t:(1−p_t) = 1:9. So instead of asking a clinician to name dollar costs directly (which they resist and can't do reliably), DCA asks the question they answer naturally every day — 'at what predicted risk would you act?' — and back-derives the cost ratio from that. This sidesteps the Elkan-style cost-elicitation problem from a different angle: rather than eliciting C_FN and C_FP in abstract units, DCA elicits a probability that clinicians already reason in daily practice, then lets the algebra of net benefit recover the equivalent cost ratio automatically.

sections.heading: Why DCA is now expected, and how it can contradict AUC
sections.body: Net benefit is plotted against p_t across a clinically plausible range, alongside two reference lines: 'treat all' (assume everyone is positive) and 'treat none' (net benefit fixed at zero). A model is only useful over the range of p_t where its curve lies ABOVE both reference lines — this directly answers 'is this model worth using at all, and over what risk range,' a question AUC cannot answer because AUC averages performance over threshold regions that may never be clinically relevant. This is precisely why DCA is now expected in clinical prediction-model papers (increasingly required by journals like Annals of Internal Medicine and endorsed in the TRIPOD reporting guideline): a model can have higher AUC than a competitor yet LOWER net benefit at every plausible p_t, if its extra discrimination comes from threshold regions nobody would clinically use — for instance, a model that's better at ranking very-low-risk patients apart from each other but no better at the 10-20% risk range clinicians actually act on. AUC being threshold-agnostic is exactly its blind spot here; DCA is threshold-explicit by design. Net benefit can also go negative, meaning a model actively harms decisions relative to doing nothing at that threshold — a possibility accuracy, sensitivity, and AUC have no mechanism to express at all, since none of them are denominated in the same units as clinical consequences.

lessons.workedExample: A new biomarker-based model for predicting complications gets AUC=0.82 versus AUC=0.78 for the old clinical model — seemingly better. Plotting DCA from p_t=0.05 to 0.30 (the clinically relevant risk range doctors actually use to decide on intervention), the new model's net-benefit curve sits BELOW the old model's for most of that range, only pulling ahead above p_t=0.35, a threshold no clinician would ever use for this condition. The AUC comparison would have wrongly favored the new, more expensive biomarker test; the DCA plot correctly shows it isn't worth adopting for actual decision-making.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge in a clinical-adjacent project should expect a DCA plot, not just AUC/accuracy, and will ask what net benefit means in plain language. The strong answer explains p_t as 'the risk level at which a doctor would act' and shows the formula linking p_t to an implicit cost ratio, then points to the treat-all/treat-none reference lines and states the p_t range over which the model actually helps. Naming a scenario where higher AUC coexists with lower net benefit across the clinically relevant range demonstrates you understand DCA is answering a genuinely different question than discrimination metrics.

questions.prompt: In decision curve analysis, what does the threshold probability p_t represent?

options.text: The model's predicted probability output for a random single patient
The risk level at which a clinician is indifferent between treating and not treating, implicitly encoding their cost ratio
The classifier's overall accuracy
The AUC of the ROC curve

explanations.a: p_t is a decision-policy parameter set by the clinician's preferences, not a single prediction.
explanations.b: Correct — Vickers and Elkin (2006) define p_t as the probability at which the expected benefit of treating equals the expected benefit of not treating, and this directly encodes an implicit cost ratio p_t/(1-p_t).
explanations.c: Accuracy is a separate, threshold-summarizing metric unrelated to p_t's clinical-preference meaning.
explanations.d: AUC is threshold-agnostic; p_t is specifically about picking one threshold from clinical preference.

questions.prompt: If a clinician sets p_t = 0.10, what implicit cost ratio does that represent?

options.text: A false positive is roughly 9 times worse than a false negative
A false negative is roughly 9 times worse than a false positive
False positives and false negatives are equally costly
The cost ratio cannot be derived from p_t alone

explanations.a: This inverts the ratio — a low p_t means the clinician acts even at low risk, implying missing a case (FN) is the far worse outcome.
explanations.b: Correct — odds of C_FP:C_FN = p_t:(1-p_t) = 0.10:0.90 = 1:9, so a missed positive is judged about 9x costlier than an unnecessary intervention.
explanations.c: Equal cost would correspond to p_t=0.5, not 0.10.
explanations.d: p_t/(1-p_t) directly gives the cost odds; this is the central mechanic of DCA.

questions.prompt: Why can a model with higher AUC have lower net benefit across the clinically relevant p_t range?

options.text: AUC and net benefit are mathematically identical, so this cannot happen
AUC averages discrimination over all thresholds, including ones far outside the range clinicians actually use, while net benefit is evaluated only at clinically relevant thresholds
Net benefit is always higher when AUC is higher, by definition
AUC only measures calibration, not discrimination

explanations.a: They measure different things and routinely disagree, which is the entire motivation for DCA.
explanations.b: Correct — a model can gain AUC from better ranking at irrelevant risk levels while performing no better, or worse, in the actual decision-relevant p_t range that DCA isolates.
explanations.c: This is exactly the false assumption DCA is designed to expose as wrong.
explanations.d: AUC measures discrimination (ranking ability), not calibration.

questions.prompt: Match each DCA element to its meaning.

right.text: Assumes net benefit fixed at zero
Assumes every patient is treated/positive
The core DCA formula weighting false positives by the odds implied by p_t

questions.explanation: Treat-all assumes everyone is intervened on; treat-none is the zero-benefit baseline; the net-benefit formula penalizes false positives by the cost-odds p_t/(1-p_t) implied by the clinician's stated threshold.

lessons.label: When You Cannot Name a Cost: Abstention and Deferral

sections.heading: Chow's rule: the optimum error-reject tradeoff
sections.body: Sometimes costs genuinely cannot be pinned down — stakeholders disagree, or the deployer (not the model builder) is the only one positioned to know the true cost. The honest response is to refuse to pick a single threshold and instead report the full performance curve, OR give the classifier a formal REJECT option: a third output meaning 'I decline to classify this case, refer it to a human.' C.K. Chow's 1970 paper 'On Optimum Recognition Error and Reject Tradeoff' (IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, vol. IT-16, pp. 41-46) proved the foundational result here: for a fixed reject cost, the optimal rule is to reject exactly when the maximum class posterior probability falls below a threshold, and this produces a strictly decreasing relationship between the reject rate and the error rate on the remaining, accepted cases — you can always trade coverage for accuracy, and Chow characterized the OPTIMAL exchange rate between them rather than an ad hoc one. Chow's original motivation was optical character recognition, where a human transcriber re-keys any character the machine won't commit to — the same architecture underlies modern content-moderation and radiology triage pipelines decades later.

sections.heading: Selective prediction and risk-coverage curves
sections.body: Modern 'selective prediction' research generalizes Chow's rule beyond simple posterior thresholding to any confidence score, including deep network softmax outputs or calibrated uncertainty estimates. The standard visualization is the RISK-COVERAGE CURVE: coverage on the x-axis is the fraction of cases the model chooses to answer (1.0 = answers everything, like a normal classifier; lower values mean it refers more cases to a human), and risk (error rate) on the y-axis is measured only on the cases it DID answer. A good selective classifier's curve drops steeply as coverage decreases — a small sacrifice in coverage buys a large accuracy gain, meaning its confidence scores are well-correlated with its actual correctness. This reframes triage as a genuine ENGINEERING CHOICE, not a failure to build a fully automated system: a human-in-the-loop system that answers 80% of cases at 99.5% accuracy and defers the hard 20% to an expert can be strictly better, in expected total cost including the expert's time, than a fully automated system forced to guess on every case. Choosing the coverage level is itself an operating-point decision, exactly analogous to choosing a classification threshold, just on a different axis. A common summary statistic, the area under the risk-coverage curve (AURC), lets teams compare two models' selective-prediction quality with a single number, analogous to how AUC summarizes an ROC curve — a lower AURC means a model's confidence scores more reliably separate its correct predictions from its mistakes across all possible abstention rates.

lessons.workedExample: A pathology-slide triage model can classify 100% of slides at 90% accuracy, or abstain on the 15% of cases where its confidence is lowest and hit 97% accuracy on the remaining 85%. Using Chow's rule, the team sets the reject threshold on posterior confidence to match the pathologists' stated tolerance for review workload (they can manually handle at most 20% of slides). The risk-coverage curve shows accuracy climbs sharply as coverage drops below ~90%, then plateaus — telling the team that abstaining on the worst 15% captures nearly all the achievable benefit, and abstaining further (say to 80% coverage, right at the pathologists' 20%-manual-review cap) would waste pathologist time on cases the model was already handling well.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge will ask what a team should do when nobody can agree on C_FN and C_FP. The weak answer picks a threshold arbitrarily anyway. The strong answer names Chow's 1970 optimal reject rule, explains that abstention converts an unanswerable cost question into a coverage-versus-risk tradeoff that a risk-coverage curve makes visible, and frames the choice of coverage level as a deliberate design decision made jointly with whoever bears the cost of the deferred cases — not an admission that the model failed.

questions.prompt: According to Chow's (1970) rule, when should a classifier reject (abstain on) a case?

options.text: Whenever the input is out-of-distribution, regardless of the model's confidence
When the maximum class posterior probability falls below a threshold set by the reject cost
Randomly, to keep coverage exactly at 50%
Only when the true label is already known

explanations.a: Chow's rule is defined purely in terms of the posterior probability threshold, not an explicit out-of-distribution detector.
explanations.b: Correct — Chow proved the optimal reject rule rejects exactly when the top posterior probability is below a threshold determined by the cost of rejecting versus the cost of an error.
explanations.c: The rule is a deterministic threshold rule tied to cost, not a random policy.
explanations.d: This would make abstention meaningless; the whole point is to abstain before the label is known.

questions.prompt: On a risk-coverage curve, what does 'coverage' measure?

options.text: The fraction of the feature space the training data spans
The fraction of cases the model chooses to answer rather than defer
The model's AUC
The total number of classes the model can predict

explanations.a: Coverage is about the model's decision to answer or abstain on individual cases, not about training-data feature coverage.
explanations.b: Correct — coverage = 1.0 means the model answers every case; lower coverage means it refers more cases to a human, with risk (error rate) measured only on the answered subset.
explanations.c: AUC is a separate, threshold-independent discrimination metric.
explanations.d: Coverage is unrelated to the number of output classes.

questions.prompt: Why is choosing to abstain on 15% of cases described as a legitimate engineering choice rather than a failure?

options.text: Because abstaining always improves accuracy on the abstained cases themselves
Because it can strictly lower expected total cost by combining automated accuracy on easy cases with expert judgment on hard ones, versus forcing a guess on everything
Because a model that abstains is legally required in most domains
Because abstention removes the need for any threshold at all

explanations.a: Abstained cases are never scored by the model at all, so there's no accuracy 'on' them to speak of.
explanations.b: Correct — the risk-coverage tradeoff shows that ceding the hardest cases to a human, while the model handles the confident majority, can be lower total expected cost than one system forced to answer everything.
explanations.c: This is a design/engineering argument, not a legal requirement in most domains.
explanations.d: Abstention itself is implemented via a threshold (Chow's rule) — it introduces a second threshold (the coverage level), not zero thresholds.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of building and using a selective-prediction system with a risk-coverage curve.

items.text: Obtain a confidence score (posterior probability or calibrated uncertainty) per case
Apply Chow's rule: reject cases below a confidence threshold
Plot the risk-coverage curve across possible thresholds
Jointly choose a coverage level with whoever bears the cost of deferred cases

questions.explanation: Selective prediction starts from a confidence score, applies a reject threshold per Chow's rule, characterizes the full tradeoff via the risk-coverage curve, and finally settles on an operating coverage level as a deliberate joint decision, not a default.

units.label: Imbalance and What the Summary Numbers Hide

lessons.label: The Accuracy Paradox and the Baseline You Must Report

sections.heading: The 99.9%-accurate model that catches nothing
sections.body: Consider a bank building a fraud classifier on real transaction data. The ULB Machine Learning Group's 2013 credit-card fraud dataset, released with Worldline and still the standard teaching set for this problem, contains 284,807 European card transactions with only 492 labeled fraudulent -- a positive rate of about 0.17%. A classifier that outputs "not fraud" for every single transaction, consulting zero features, scores roughly 99.83% accuracy. Push the imbalance further, to a 0.1% fraud rate typical of some production payment systems, and the identical do-nothing rule clears 99.9%. Nothing was learned, no feature was read, and the rule would miss every one of the fraudulent transactions that ever occurred -- yet the number reads like a triumph on a slide, especially to a non-technical audience that hears "99.9%" and stops listening.

sections.heading: Accuracy's floor is the majority-class rate
sections.body: This is not a quirk of fraud data; it is a property of the accuracy formula itself. For any binary problem with positive prevalence p, the constant rule that always predicts the majority label achieves accuracy equal to max(p, 1-p) -- the majority-class rate. Accuracy can never fall below this floor no matter how the classifier is trained, so a model only demonstrates real learning once its accuracy clears the floor by a meaningful margin, not merely matches or edges past it. At 50/50 balance the floor is a trivial 0.5, which is why accuracy behaves fine on textbook-balanced problems like digit recognition or coin-flip simulations. The floor rises toward 1.0 exactly as a problem becomes rare-event -- fraud, disease screening, rare machine failure, manufacturing defect detection -- so accuracy is least informative precisely where the stakes, and the cost of a missed positive, are highest.

sections.heading: The fix: never report a metric without a baseline
sections.body: The discipline that prevents this trap is procedural: state at least three baselines beside every headline number. The majority-class baseline (always predict the more common label) gives the accuracy floor directly. A stratified-random baseline (predict positive with probability equal to training prevalence, ignoring features) gives the chance floor for precision and F1. A simple single-feature or one-variable logistic-regression rule (e.g., flag any transaction over a dollar threshold) gives the floor for "an analyst using one obvious signal." A reported metric that fails to clear all three is not a result -- it is a number with no claim attached, and this discipline mirrors what careful clinical-prediction reporting and rigorous competition write-ups expect in spirit: a model is only newsworthy in proportion to how far past the cheapest available alternative it lands, not in proportion to its raw score.

lessons.workedExample: A team submits a churn-prediction model boasting 97% accuracy on a customer base where only 3% of customers churn monthly. Before celebrating, a reviewer asks for the three baselines. The majority-class baseline (predict "stays") also scores 97% -- identical to the model. The stratified-random baseline, flipping a coin weighted at 3% churn probability, scores about 94.2%. A single-feature rule -- flag anyone who canceled an add-on subscription last month -- scores 96.1% on its own. Once baselines are on the table, the model's 97% is revealed to be statistically indistinguishable from predicting nothing, and the team goes back to check whether any real signal was learned at all.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has seen a hundred fair projects has also seen a hundred inflated accuracy numbers, so the first question on any classification project with a rare positive class is almost always "what's the base rate, and what does the naive baseline score?" A team that cannot answer immediately signals they never checked whether their model beats doing nothing. A team that volunteers the majority-class rate, the stratified-random rate, and a one-feature rule before being asked -- and shows their real metric clears all three by a real margin -- has pre-empted the single most common way rare-event classification projects fool themselves and their judges.

questions.prompt: A classifier trained on a dataset with 0.5% positive prevalence predicts the negative class for every input. What accuracy does it achieve?

options.text: Cannot be determined without more information

explanations.a: 0.5% is the positive rate, not the accuracy of a rule that always predicts negative.
explanations.b: 50% would only be the floor if the classes were perfectly balanced.
explanations.c: Correct -- the majority-class floor is max(p, 1-p) = 1 - 0.005 = 99.5%.
explanations.d: It can be determined directly: the floor equals 1 minus the positive prevalence.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly explains why the majority-class baseline matters when reporting accuracy on an imbalanced dataset?

options.text: It shows the highest accuracy any classifier, real or trivial, could ever achieve
It sets a floor that a trivial always-predict-majority rule reaches, so a real model must clear it by a meaningful margin to demonstrate learning
It is only relevant when the dataset is exactly balanced
It replaces the need for precision and recall entirely

explanations.a: Accuracy has no fixed ceiling from the majority-class rule; a real model can and should exceed it.
explanations.b: Correct -- the majority-class baseline is the floor a trivial rule reaches, so clearing it is the minimum bar for a claim of learning.
explanations.c: It matters most when the dataset is imbalanced, not when it is balanced.
explanations.d: Baselines complement precision/recall; they don't substitute for reporting them.

questions.prompt: Order these four evaluation points from least sophisticated (uses no real features) to most sophisticated (uses all available features).

items.text: Majority-class baseline
Stratified-random baseline
Single-feature / one-variable rule
Fully trained model

questions.explanation: The majority-class and stratified-random baselines use zero real features, differing only in whether they are deterministic or randomized; the single-feature rule adds exactly one real predictor; the full model uses everything available.

questions.prompt: Match each baseline (or its absence) to what it reveals.

left.text: A metric reported with no baseline

right.text: The accuracy floor
The chance floor for precision/F1
What one obvious signal alone achieves
A claim with no demonstrated information value

questions.explanation: Each baseline exposes a different floor a real model must clear; reporting a metric with none of them attached leaves the reader unable to tell if anything was actually learned.

lessons.label: Why ROC Looks Deceptively Good on Rare-Positive Problems

sections.heading: FPR's denominator hides the damage
sections.body: An ROC curve plots true positive rate against false positive rate, and FPR = FP / (FP + TN) -- its denominator is the entire negative class. Under 1:1000 imbalance (say 100 real positives against 100,000 negatives), a classifier that fires 1,000 false alarms moves FPR to only 1,000 / 100,000 = 0.01, a shift too small to see on a 0-to-1 axis, let alone to distinguish visually from a threshold that produced only 100 false alarms. Because ROC space is normalized by the negative-class count, and negatives vastly outnumber positives under imbalance, an enormous absolute number of false positives compresses into a negligible FPR movement. That is precisely why ROC curves for rare-event classifiers -- fraud, intrusion detection, rare-disease screening -- routinely hug the top-left corner and look excellent even when the false-alarm volume behind them would overwhelm any team acting on the alerts.

sections.heading: The same 1,000 false positives crush precision
sections.body: Run the identical confusion-matrix cell counts through precision instead. With 100 true positives caught and 1,000 false positives, precision = TP / (TP + FP) = 100 / 1,100, about 0.09. Only roughly 9% of everything the model flags is real; an analyst acting on every alert is wrong about 91% of the time, a genuinely unusable rate for a fraud or intrusion team -- even though those same predictions produced an FPR of just 0.01. Davis and Goadrich's 2006 ICML paper, "The Relationship Between Precision-Recall and ROC Curves," formalized this exact gap: a curve that dominates in ROC space is not guaranteed to dominate in PR space, and the gap widens as class imbalance grows.

sections.heading: AUC of 0.95, unusable in production
sections.body: Because ROC-AUC integrates over the entire FPR range, including operating points no deployed system would ever choose (accepting FPR = 0.3 to catch a few more positives), a model can post AUC = 0.95 -- a headline number -- while its confusion matrix at any realistic operating threshold, like the 0.01-FPR point above, is dominated by false positives once translated into precision. Saito and Rehmsmeier's 2015 PLOS ONE paper made the same argument with real genomics and simulated data: ROC plots can visually mislead on imbalanced problems in a way PR plots do not, because PR plots directly show the fraction of positive predictions that are correct. The lesson generalizes beyond fraud: report a precision-recall curve, or precision at a fixed, realistic threshold, alongside ROC-AUC on any dataset where positives are rare, because ROC-AUC alone systematically overstates how useful the system will be once deployed.

lessons.workedExample: A fraud model, tested at a threshold that flags 1,100 of 100,100 transactions (100 real frauds, 100,000 legitimate), correctly catches all 100 frauds (recall = 1.0) while misflagging 1,000 legitimate transactions. Its ROC point sits at (FPR = 0.01, TPR = 1.0) -- essentially the top-left corner, visually indistinguishable from a near-perfect classifier, and the full curve integrates to roughly AUC = 0.95. Its PR point, from the identical predictions, sits at (recall = 1.0, precision = 0.09). Plotted on a PR curve, that point sags far below any usable operating region: nine of every ten flagged transactions are false alarms. Same predictions, same confusion matrix, opposite verdict depending on which curve a reviewer glances at first.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges who only ask for "AUC" are asking the wrong question on a rare-positive dataset, and a strong team says so before being asked: state the class prevalence, then show a PR curve or a precision-at-realistic-threshold number alongside any ROC-AUC claim. A judge with quantitative training may deliberately probe this by asking "what's your precision at the threshold you'd actually deploy?" specifically to check whether the team understands that a rare positive class inflates ROC-AUC through its FPR denominator. Volunteering the PR-space number pre-empts the trap and demonstrates the team understands why the two curves can disagree so sharply on the same model.

questions.prompt: With 100 real positives and 100,000 negatives, a classifier produces 1,000 false positives while catching all 100 true positives. What is its FPR?

explanations.b: 0.91 is close to 1 minus precision (1 - 0.09), not the FPR.
explanations.c: 0.10 misplaces the decimal; the true value is a tenth of that.
explanations.d: 1.0 is the recall/TPR in this example, not the FPR.

questions.prompt: In that same scenario, what is the precision?

explanations.a: 0.99 would require far fewer false positives relative to true positives than this scenario has.
explanations.b: Correct -- precision = TP / (TP + FP) = 100 / 1,100, about 0.09.
explanations.c: 0.50 would require FP to roughly equal TP, but here FP is ten times TP.
explanations.d: 1.00 precision would mean zero false positives, which contradicts the 1,000 false alarms given.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order that explains the ROC-vs-precision mismatch under imbalance.

items.text: Identify that FPR's denominator is the full negative-class count
Note that negatives vastly outnumber positives under imbalance
A large absolute false-positive count moves FPR only slightly
That same false-positive count, relative to the few true positives, crushes precision

questions.explanation: The mismatch starts with FPR's denominator being the whole negative class; because negatives dominate under imbalance, a huge false-positive count barely moves FPR, while that same count devastates precision, whose denominator is the much smaller set of predicted positives.

questions.prompt: Match each metric to the set of cases its denominator depends on.

right.text: All actual negatives (FP + TN)
All predicted positives (TP + FP)
All actual positives (TP + FN)
The overall positive prevalence

questions.explanation: FPR is normalized by all actual negatives, precision by all predicted positives, recall by all actual positives, and a random classifier's average precision equals the overall positive prevalence -- which is why these metrics respond so differently to the same confusion matrix under imbalance.

lessons.label: PR-AUC and Its Prevalence-Dependent Baseline

sections.heading: The random baseline for PR-AUC is the prevalence itself
sections.body: Unlike ROC, where an uninformative classifier always traces the diagonal and scores AUC = 0.5 regardless of class balance, the precision-recall curve's random baseline shifts with prevalence. For a classifier whose scores carry no real information -- ranking instances randomly with respect to the true label -- the expected average precision (the area summarized as PR-AUC) equals the positive rate p. This falls directly out of the definition of precision: with no informative ranking, the expected fraction of true positives among any slice of predicted positives is just the base rate. At 1% prevalence, the useless-classifier baseline is 0.01; at 50% prevalence it is 0.5. This single fact means a raw PR-AUC number carries no information by itself: "PR-AUC = 0.35" is spectacular on a 1%-positive fraud problem, roughly 35 times better than doing nothing, and unimpressive on a 50%-positive problem, barely better than a coin flip.

sections.heading: PR-AUC is not comparable across datasets
sections.body: Because the baseline moves with prevalence, PR-AUC values cannot be stacked side by side across different datasets, or even across different constructions of a test set from the same underlying data, unless prevalence is held fixed and reported alongside the number. Two published models each claiming "PR-AUC = 0.4" on two different rare-disease screening tasks are not making the same claim if one test set carries 2% prevalence and the other carries 10% -- the second number is much closer to chance, since its floor sits five times higher. Treating PR-AUC as a portable, dataset-independent score, the way people often (incorrectly) treat ROC-AUC, is one of the most common misreadings of this metric in student and even published work, and it routinely leads to a "better" model on paper that is actually just evaluated on an easier, more balanced slice of data.

sections.heading: The reporting fix, and the subsampling trap
sections.body: The fix is simple: always print prevalence next to PR-AUC, e.g., "PR-AUC = 0.35 at 1% prevalence (chance = 0.01)." A common and often silent violation of this discipline: a team subsamples the negative class in its test set, say to speed up evaluation or to make a plot look cleaner, which raises the effective positive rate on that test set and mechanically inflates PR-AUC even though nothing about the underlying classifier changed. Saito and Rehmsmeier's 2015 PLOS ONE paper, "The Precision-Recall Plot Is More Informative than the ROC Plot When Evaluating Binary Classifiers on Imbalanced Datasets," makes exactly this prevalence-sensitivity point and recommends evaluating on a test set whose prevalence matches deployment reality, not a rebalanced convenience sample.

lessons.workedExample: A screening model for a rare condition (true prevalence 2%) reports PR-AUC = 0.40 on its full test set. A second team, wanting a "cleaner" plot, keeps every positive but randomly drops 80% of the negatives, raising the test set's effective prevalence to roughly 9%. Re-running the identical model on this subsampled set produces PR-AUC = 0.58 -- an apparent 45% improvement from a change that touched nothing about the model itself. Reporting the second number without the prevalence shift would misrepresent the classifier as meaningfully better than it is; reporting both PR-AUC and the test-set prevalence together makes the inflation immediately visible to a careful reader.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows PR-AUC will ask for the test-set prevalence before accepting the number at all, because 0.35 means something completely different at 1% prevalence than at 40% prevalence. A team that states its prevalence unprompted, and can explain that a random classifier's expected PR-AUC equals that prevalence, demonstrates it understands the metric rather than having copied it from a library's output. The sharpest version of this question is procedural: "was your test set's class balance the same as your training set's, or did you rebalance it for any reason?" -- because rebalancing the test set is the single most common way PR-AUC gets silently inflated.

questions.prompt: A completely uninformative (random) classifier's expected average precision equals what?

options.text: 0.5, always
The positive class prevalence
The negative class prevalence
The classifier's ROC-AUC value

explanations.a: 0.5 is the ROC-AUC baseline for a random classifier, not the PR-AUC baseline.
explanations.b: Correct -- a random ranking's expected average precision equals the positive rate p.
explanations.c: It equals the positive rate, the complement of the negative prevalence, not the negative prevalence itself.
explanations.d: ROC-AUC and PR-AUC are different curves with different random baselines; they are not the same value.

questions.prompt: PR-AUC = 0.35 is reported on Dataset A (1% prevalence) and Dataset B (30% prevalence). What can you conclude?

options.text: The classifier performs identically well on both
You cannot compare the two directly without the prevalence baseline, but 0.35 is far more impressive on A than on B
PR-AUC is always directly comparable regardless of prevalence
B's result is more impressive because higher prevalence is inherently a harder problem

explanations.a: Identical PR-AUC numbers do not mean identical performance once the chance baseline differs so much between datasets.
explanations.b: Correct -- 0.35 is roughly 35x chance at 1% prevalence but close to chance at 30%, so the same number reflects very different performance.
explanations.c: This is exactly the mistake this lesson warns against; PR-AUC is prevalence-dependent and not portable across datasets.
explanations.d: Higher prevalence is not inherently harder; it simply raises the random baseline that PR-AUC must be compared against.

questions.prompt: Order the correct procedure for reporting and sanity-checking a PR-AUC number.

items.text: Note and record the test set's positive prevalence
Compute the chance baseline, equal to that prevalence
Compute the model's actual PR-AUC on the same test set
Report PR-AUC alongside the chance baseline before making any comparability claim

questions.explanation: Prevalence must be established first, since it defines the chance baseline (step 2); only then does the computed PR-AUC (step 3) mean anything, and it should never be reported or compared across datasets without that baseline attached (step 4).

questions.prompt: Match each action to its effect on PR-AUC's trustworthiness.

left.text: Subsampling negatives in the test set before evaluating
Comparing PR-AUC across datasets with different prevalence, with no adjustment
Holding test-set prevalence equal to deployment prevalence

right.text: Inflates PR-AUC without improving the model
Makes the PR-AUC number interpretable
Produces an invalid, misleading comparison
Ensures PR-AUC reflects real deployment performance

questions.explanation: Subsampling negatives inflates PR-AUC by raising effective prevalence; reporting prevalence makes the number readable; comparing across datasets without adjustment is invalid; and matching test-set prevalence to deployment is what makes PR-AUC trustworthy in the first place.

lessons.label: Matthews Correlation Coefficient: The Imbalance-Robust Summary

sections.heading: MCC as a correlation coefficient
sections.body: The Matthews correlation coefficient is defined as MCC = (TP*TN - FP*FN) / sqrt((TP+FP)(TP+FN)(TN+FP)(TN+FN)). This is not an arbitrary formula: it is exactly the Pearson correlation coefficient computed between the predicted binary vector and the true binary vector, better known in the 2x2-table literature as the phi coefficient. A useful identity ties it to a familiar statistical test: MCC squared equals the chi-squared test statistic for independence divided by the sample size (MCC^2 = chi^2 / n). MCC ranges from -1 to +1: +1 means perfect prediction, -1 means the classifier systematically inverts the true label, and 0 means the predictions are statistically uncorrelated with the truth -- chance level, not simply "no errors." Because it is a correlation, MCC treats over-predicting and under-predicting a class symmetrically, unlike metrics built only from one row or column of the confusion matrix.

sections.heading: Why all four confusion-matrix cells must be good
sections.body: Unlike accuracy or F1, MCC's denominator multiplies four separate marginal sums together: predicted positives (TP+FP), actual positives (TP+FN), actual negatives (FP+TN), and predicted negatives (FN+TN). If any one of these four sums is zero -- for instance, no actual negatives exist in the test data, or the classifier never once predicts the negative class -- the denominator is zero and MCC is defined by convention as 0, correctly flagging a degenerate case rather than throwing an arbitrary error. Because every marginal must be non-trivial and the numerator itself requires TP*TN to outweigh FP*FN, MCC only rewards a classifier that gets real signal from both the positive side and the negative side of the problem at once, simultaneously.

sections.heading: Chicco and Jurman (2020): where accuracy and F1 mislead
sections.body: Chicco and Jurman's 2020 BMC Genomics paper, "The Advantages of the Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) over F1 Score and Accuracy in Binary Classification Evaluation," builds six synthetic confusion-matrix cases plus a real genomics dataset to make this point concrete, and argues MCC should be adopted as the default single-number summary for binary classification in bioinformatics and beyond. Consider a case in their spirit: 100 test cases, 95 truly positive and 5 truly negative, and a classifier that predicts "positive" for all 100, never once examining the input. Accuracy is 95%, precision is 95%, recall is 100%, and F1 is about 0.974 -- every headline number looks outstanding, the kind of result that would headline a poster. But TN = 0 and FN = 0, so the MCC numerator TP*TN - FP*FN collapses to exactly 0 -- and the denominator's (TN+FN) term is also 0, so this is exactly the by-convention MCC = 0 case described above (not an ordinary division): MCC correctly reports chance-level performance, because the classifier never once demonstrated it could recognize the negative class at all, however good it looks on the positive side alone.

lessons.workedExample: A spam filter tested on 1,000 emails (50 spam, 950 legitimate) yields TP=40, FN=10, FP=5, TN=945. Plugging into the formula: numerator = 40*945 - 5*10 = 37,800 - 50 = 37,750; denominator = sqrt(45 * 50 * 950 * 955), approximately 45,180; MCC is about 37,750 / 45,180, roughly 0.84 -- a strong, believable score consistent with catching 80% of spam (recall = 40/50) while keeping false alarms low (precision = 40/45, about 0.89), because the filter handled both classes well. Contrast this with the all-positive classifier from the lesson: on this same 1,000-email set, calling every email spam would give recall 1.0 but precision only 0.05, and MCC would correctly collapse toward zero.
lessons.judgeFraming: MCC is not yet universally known outside ML-heavy fields, so a judge who asks about it is testing depth, not reciting folklore. Stating that MCC's denominator forces all four confusion-matrix cells to matter simultaneously -- which is exactly why it is the headline metric on an imbalanced problem -- shows real understanding, not memorized vocabulary. Anticipate the natural follow-up, "what does MCC = 0 actually mean?" (chance-level correlation, not merely "some errors"), and be ready to name the source: Chicco and Jurman's 2020 BMC Genomics paper is the standard citation for why MCC should be the default single-number summary over accuracy or F1 on imbalanced binary problems.

questions.prompt: What does an MCC value of exactly 0 indicate?

options.text: Perfect prediction
Prediction uncorrelated with the true labels -- chance level
The prediction is a total inversion of the truth
The classifier never predicts the positive class

explanations.a: Perfect prediction corresponds to MCC = +1, not 0.
explanations.b: Correct -- MCC = 0 means the predicted labels are statistically uncorrelated with the true labels, equivalent to chance performance.
explanations.c: Total inversion corresponds to MCC = -1, the opposite end of the scale.
explanations.d: Never predicting positive is one possible cause of a low MCC in some cases, but 0 specifically means zero correlation, not a statement about which class is predicted.

questions.prompt: MCC is mathematically equivalent to which classical statistic, computed on a 2x2 confusion matrix?

options.text: The Pearson (phi) correlation coefficient between predicted and true binary labels
The standard deviation of the classifier's residual errors
The Spearman rank correlation coefficient
The F1 score expressed in a different unit

explanations.a: Correct -- MCC is the phi coefficient, the Pearson correlation between the two binary vectors, and MCC^2 equals chi^2 / n.
explanations.b: Residual standard deviation is a regression concept and is not what MCC computes.
explanations.c: Spearman correlation is a rank-based statistic for ordinal or continuous data, not the identity MCC satisfies.
explanations.d: F1 and MCC are different formulas with different behavior, most notably F1's blindness to true negatives; they are not the same statistic.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to compute MCC from a raw confusion matrix.

items.text: Tally TP, FP, FN, and TN
Compute the numerator, TP*TN - FP*FN
Compute the denominator, the square root of the four marginal-sum products
Divide the numerator by the denominator

questions.explanation: You need the four raw counts before computing either the numerator or denominator, and the final MCC value is the numerator divided by the denominator, not the other way around.

questions.prompt: Match each confusion-matrix condition to what it does to MCC.

left.text: Classifier ignores the minority class entirely (e.g., predicts only the majority label)
Classifier performs well on both classes
One marginal sum (e.g., total actual negatives) is zero
TP*TN is much larger than FP*FN

right.text: MCC stays near zero despite high accuracy or F1
MCC correctly comes out high, reflecting genuine performance on both classes
MCC is undefined and set to 0 by convention
MCC's numerator is large and positive

questions.explanation: MCC is specifically constructed so that ignoring a class collapses the numerator toward zero, genuine both-class performance drives it high, a degenerate all-zero marginal makes it undefined by convention, and a numerator dominated by TP*TN over FP*FN pushes it toward a strong positive value.

lessons.label: F1's Blind Spot: It Never Looks at True Negatives

sections.heading: F1 has no TN term
sections.body: F1 = 2 * (precision * recall) / (precision + recall), where precision = TP / (TP+FP) and recall = TP / (TP+FN). Read the two ingredient formulas closely: true negatives never appear in either one, and therefore never appear anywhere in F1. Accuracy and MCC both use TN explicitly; F1 does not. Because of this, F1 measures only how the model performs on the union of "predicted positive" and "actually positive" instances -- it is structurally blind to how well the model recognizes the negative class, no matter how large or important that class is. That blindness is not a rare edge case: it is why F1 can reward a model that is simply aggressive about calling things positive, as long as its precision and recall on the positive side happen to look acceptable, even while it is quietly wrong about a large share of the negative class it never gets credit or blame for in the formula.

sections.heading: Swap the labels and F1 changes; accuracy and MCC don't
sections.body: A concrete diagnostic makes this vivid: relabel which class is called "positive" on the identical confusion matrix. Accuracy is unaffected, since it counts all correct predictions symmetrically regardless of label names. MCC is also invariant, because swapping TP with TN and FP with FN leaves both the numerator (TP*TN - FP*FN) and the four-term denominator unchanged -- multiplication commutes either way. F1, however, is built entirely from the "positive" side's precision and recall, so relabeling produces a genuinely different value: F1 computed treating the rare class as positive can diverge sharply from F1 computed treating the common class as positive. A paper or report that states "F1 = 0.9" without saying which class is positive is under-specified, since the reader cannot tell whether that number describes performance on the rare, high-stakes class or the common, low-stakes one.

sections.heading: Powers' (2011) alternatives, and when F1 is right
sections.body: David Powers' 2011 paper, "Evaluation: From Precision, Recall and F-Measure to ROC, Informedness, Markedness & Correlation," argues F1 inherits precision and recall's biases and proposes chance-corrected replacements: informedness = TPR + TNR - 1, equivalent to Youden's J statistic from 1950, and markedness = PPV + NPV - 1, with MCC recoverable as the signed geometric mean of the two. Both properly discount chance-level performance in a way F1 does not. Yet F1 remains the right default in information retrieval -- web search, document ranking -- where the negative class is every non-retrieved document on the internet, effectively unbounded and uncountable, so a metric that never needs a TN count is a feature, not a flaw.

lessons.workedExample: A rare-disease screen tests 10 sick patients and 990 healthy people. The model correctly flags 8 of the sick (TP=8, FN=2) and wrongly flags 20 healthy people as sick (FP=20, TN=970). Treating "sick" as positive: precision = 8/28, about 0.286, recall = 0.8, F1 is about 0.421. Now relabel "healthy" as positive: TP=970, FN=20, FP=2, TN=8. Precision = 970/972, about 0.998, recall = 970/990, about 0.980, F1 is about 0.989. Same predictions, same confusion matrix, and F1 swings from 0.42 to 0.99 depending only on which label is called positive. MCC, computed from the same four cells either way, stays fixed at one value, about 0.47, proving F1's number depends on a labeling convention that MCC does not.
lessons.judgeFraming: A quantitatively sharp judge may ask, "F1 with respect to which class?" precisely because F1 is not symmetric the way accuracy and MCC are, and a team that has only ever run a library's default F1 may not have noticed which class it was computed against. Being able to state that F1 structurally ignores true negatives, name Powers' informedness and markedness as the chance-corrected alternatives, and explain why F1 is nonetheless standard in information retrieval -- because "true negative" is an uncountable non-event there -- shows the team chose F1 deliberately for their problem rather than by accident of whatever their toolkit printed first.

questions.prompt: Which confusion-matrix quantity never appears anywhere in the F1 formula?

options.text: True positives (TP)
False positives (FP)
False negatives (FN)
True negatives (TN)

explanations.a: TP appears in both precision and recall, the two ingredients of F1.
explanations.b: FP appears in the precision denominator, so it does affect F1.
explanations.c: FN appears in the recall denominator, so it does affect F1.
explanations.d: Correct -- TN appears in neither precision's nor recall's formula, so it never enters F1 at all.

questions.prompt: If you swap which class is labeled "positive" on the exact same confusion matrix, what happens?

options.text: F1 stays the same, because it is a chance-corrected metric
F1 can change substantially, while accuracy and MCC stay the same
MCC changes but F1 and accuracy stay the same
All three metrics change identically

explanations.a: F1 is not chance-corrected, and it is exactly the metric that changes under this swap.
explanations.b: Correct -- F1 depends on which class is called positive, while accuracy counts symmetrically and MCC's formula is invariant under the swap.
explanations.c: MCC is invariant under this swap because its numerator and denominator are both symmetric in TP/TN and FP/FN.
explanations.d: The three metrics behave differently under relabeling; they do not all change together.

questions.prompt: Match each concept from Powers (2011) to its definition or context.

left.text: MCC's relation to the other two
The context where F1 is still the right choice

right.text: TPR + TNR - 1, equivalent to Youden's J
PPV + NPV - 1
The signed geometric mean of informedness and markedness
Information retrieval, where true negatives are unbounded and uncountable

questions.explanation: Powers defined informedness and markedness as chance-corrected counterparts to recall and precision respectively, showed MCC is their signed geometric mean, and still granted F1 a legitimate home in search and retrieval tasks where TN has no natural meaning.

questions.prompt: Order the diagnostic procedure for checking whether a reported F1 hides a labeling-dependence problem.

items.text: Compute F1 with the stated positive class
Swap which label is called positive on the same confusion matrix
Recompute F1 under the swapped labeling
Compare the two F1 values against MCC, which stays fixed either way

questions.explanation: The check only means something if you first fix the original F1, then deliberately relabel and recompute, and finally use MCC's label-invariance as the reference point for how much F1 moved purely from the relabeling.

lessons.label: Chance Correction: Cohen's Kappa and Balanced Accuracy

sections.heading: Two chance-corrected summaries, two different chances
sections.body: Cohen's kappa is defined as kappa = (p_o - p_e) / (1 - p_e), where p_o is the observed agreement -- accuracy, when a classifier's predictions are treated as a second rater alongside ground truth -- and p_e is the agreement expected purely by chance, computed from the marginal totals (row and column sums) of the 2x2 table. Balanced accuracy, by contrast, is (TPR + TNR) / 2, the sensitivity and specificity averaged, which reweights each class to contribute equally regardless of how many examples it has, making it invariant to prevalence in a way plain accuracy is not. Both are described as "chance-corrected," but they correct for chance through entirely different mechanisms -- kappa via the marginal totals of a two-rater table, balanced accuracy via a straight per-class average -- and they can disagree sharply on the same confusion matrix, sometimes moving in opposite directions as prevalence shifts.

sections.heading: Feinstein and Cicchetti's two paradoxes (1990)
sections.body: Feinstein and Cicchetti's two-part 1990 Journal of Clinical Epidemiology paper, "High Agreement but Low Kappa," documented two counterintuitive behaviors. Paradox 1: a high observed agreement p_o can be paradoxically pulled down to a low kappa when the table's marginal totals are heavily imbalanced, because skewed marginals raise p_e toward p_o, shrinking both the numerator and the denominator's headroom at once. Paradox 2: kappa can come out higher under an asymmetric imbalance in the marginals than under a symmetric one, even at identical p_o, because kappa also encodes rater bias -- systematic over- or under-calling of one label -- in a way invisible from raw agreement. Their companion paper derived separate bias and prevalence indices so the two effects could be reported apart from kappa itself, a recommendation later echoed by Byrt, Bishop, and Carlin's 1993 prevalence-adjusted bias-adjusted kappa (PABAK).

sections.heading: Balanced accuracy's silence, and a decision rule
sections.body: Balanced accuracy fixes accuracy's majority-class-floor problem but says nothing about precision: a screening model can post 95% sensitivity and 95% specificity and still generate mostly false alarms on a 0.1%-prevalent condition, because 5% of an enormous negative pool still dwarfs the true positives in raw count. Decision rule: lead with kappa when the project is genuinely an inter-rater agreement question, comparing a model's calls to a human annotator's, where both raters' marginal distributions matter; lead with balanced accuracy when the question is classifier quality across both classes regardless of prevalence and precision is not the deciding factor; and reach for MCC or an explicit precision-at-threshold number when the cost of acting on a false positive is what actually drives the decision, since neither kappa nor balanced accuracy speaks to that cost directly.

lessons.workedExample: A dermatology model's calls agree with a specialist on 950 of 1,000 lesions (p_o = 0.95, seemingly excellent). But 900 lesions are benign, and both the model and the specialist call "benign" on almost everything: predicted-benign totals 920, actual-benign totals 900.
