A model's outputs can even be shaped to look artificially calibrated at whatever bin edges an evaluator happens to use. Two fixes are standard. First, bin-free estimators, kernel-smoothed reliability curves or spline regressions of accuracy on confidence, eliminate the arbitrary edge choice entirely. Second, every reliability diagram should be paired with a histogram of the raw score distribution plotted directly beneath it, so a reader can see which bins rest on thousands of points versus which rest on a handful before trusting the reported gap.

lessons.workedExample: A team reports ECE = 0.02 for their model using M = 10 equal-width bins and calls it well calibrated. Re-running with M = 25 bins yields ECE = 0.09, because several of the finer bins near p = 0.95 now hold only 8-12 samples each, and their acc(B_m) swings wildly with sampling noise. Plotting the score histogram underneath reveals that 40% of all test cases fall in just two of the ten original bins, meaning the headline ECE = 0.02 was dominated by two well-populated, well-calibrated bins while sparse high-confidence bins were silently averaged away. A kernel-based reliability curve is fit instead, showing a real, bin-count-independent overconfidence gap in the 0.9-1.0 range.
lessons.judgeFraming: Any judge who knows to ask for a reliability diagram will often ask a second question: how many bins did you use, and does the number reported change if you use a different bin count? This directly tests whether the presenter understands that ECE and MCE are estimator choices, not ground truth. A strong answer shows the score histogram alongside the diagram, reports whether the result is stable across bin counts or binning schemes, and can name a bin-free alternative as evidence the team checked robustness rather than reporting whichever M made the number look smallest.

questions.prompt: On a reliability diagram, a bin whose point falls BELOW the 45-degree diagonal indicates what?

options.text: The model is overconfident in that bin: predicted probability exceeds observed frequency
The model is underconfident in that bin: observed frequency exceeds predicted probability
The bin has too few samples to be meaningful
The model's AUC is poor

explanations.a: Correct — below the diagonal means acc(B_m) is lower than conf(B_m), so the model claims more confidence than the observed outcomes support.
explanations.b: That describes a point ABOVE the diagonal, where observed frequency exceeds the stated confidence.
explanations.c: Sample size is a separate issue, visible only from the score histogram, not from a point's position relative to the diagonal.
explanations.d: The reliability diagram says nothing about rank-order discrimination or AUC.

questions.prompt: Why can increasing the number of bins M make ECE go up even for a model whose true calibration has not changed?

options.text: Because ECE is defined only for M = 10 bins and is undefined otherwise
Because finer bins hold fewer samples each, so acc(B_m) becomes noisier and the |acc-conf| gap inflates from sampling variance alone
Because more bins always force equal-width binning
Because MCE and ECE must always be equal

explanations.a: ECE's formula works for any M; there is no special status for M = 10.
explanations.b: Correct — this is exactly why ECE is a biased estimator: bin count is an analyst choice, and finer bins trade real signal for sampling noise.
explanations.c: Bin count and binning scheme (equal-width versus equal-frequency) are independent choices.
explanations.d: MCE reports only the single worst bin's gap; ECE is a sample-weighted average across all bins, and the two are rarely equal.

questions.prompt: Match each binned-calibration concept to its correct description.

right.text: Sample-weighted average of |acc(B_m) - conf(B_m)| across all bins
The single largest per-bin |acc(B_m) - conf(B_m)| gap
Chooses bin edges so each bin holds roughly n/M samples
Reveals which bins in the diagram above rest on too few points to trust

questions.explanation: ECE weights every bin's gap by its sample share and averages; MCE reports only the worst bin, which matters more for safety-critical use; equal-frequency binning stabilizes per-bin sample size by adjusting edge placement rather than width; and the score histogram is the standard companion plot that exposes which bins are too sparse to trust.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of constructing a reliability diagram and its ECE summary in the correct order.

items.text: Choose a binning scheme (equal-width or equal-frequency) and bin count M
Sort predictions into bins B_1 through B_M
Compute conf(B_m) and acc(B_m) for each bin
Plot (conf, acc) per bin against the diagonal, and the score histogram beneath it
Combine all bins into the single scalar ECE

questions.explanation: Binning scheme and count must be fixed first, since predictions cannot be sorted into bins that are not yet defined; per-bin confidence and accuracy are then computed from those bins; the diagram (with its histogram companion) is the visual product of those per-bin numbers; and ECE is the final sample-weighted collapse of the whole diagram into one scalar.

lessons.label: The Brier Score and Murphy's Decomposition

sections.heading: The Brier score: a scoring rule born in weather forecasting
sections.body: Glenn W. Brier introduced the Brier score in his 1950 Monthly Weather Review paper, "Verification of Forecasts Expressed in Terms of Probability," to grade weather forecasters who reported a probability of rain rather than a yes/no call. The formula is simply mean squared error applied to probabilities: BS = (1/n) * sum of (p_i - y_i)^2, where p_i is the predicted probability and y_i is the 0/1 outcome. BS = 0 is a perfect forecaster; for binary outcomes the worst possible score is 1, reached by confidently predicting the wrong class every time. Unlike accuracy at a single threshold, the Brier score rewards a forecaster for every fractional improvement in a probability estimate, not just for crossing a decision boundary, which is exactly why it became the standard for grading probabilistic forecasts rather than discrete predictions.

sections.heading: Murphy's three-term decomposition
sections.body: A single Brier score number conflates several distinct sources of error, a problem Allan H. Murphy solved in his 1973 Journal of Applied Meteorology paper, "A New Vector Partition of the Probability Score." Murphy's decomposition splits the Brier score into BS = reliability - resolution + uncertainty. Reliability, sometimes written as a positive penalty term, measures calibration directly: it is the sample-weighted squared gap between predicted probability and observed frequency within probability bins, structurally the same idea as ECE but in squared form. Resolution measures how much the model's bin-level outcome rates differ from the overall base rate; a model that separates genuinely different-risk groups earns high resolution, which subtracts from the score, so it rewards useful discrimination. Uncertainty, p-bar * (1 - p-bar) where p-bar is the overall base rate, is fixed by the data alone and represents irreducible difficulty no model can improve. This decomposition lets a team say precisely whether a mediocre Brier score comes from bad calibration, weak discrimination, or simply a hard, near-50/50 problem.

sections.heading: Log loss and the meaning of 'strictly proper'
sections.body: Log loss, -(1/n) * sum of [y_i * log(p_i) + (1-y_i) * log(1-p_i)], is the other workhorse probabilistic scoring rule, and it punishes overconfidence far more severely than the Brier score: a confident wrong prediction (p near 0 when y=1) sends the loss toward infinity, while a Brier-score error saturates at 1. Both Brier score and log loss are strictly proper scoring rules, a formal property meaning that if a forecaster genuinely believes the true probability is q, their expected score is uniquely optimized by reporting p = q exactly, not by hedging toward 0.5 or shading toward an extreme. This is what makes these two metrics untrickable, unlike accuracy, which a forecaster can sometimes improve by reporting a probability they do not actually believe.

lessons.workedExample: Two rare-disease models both score BS = 0.08 on the same test set, so a team assumes they are equally good. Running Murphy's decomposition reveals model A has reliability 0.01 and resolution 0.03 (uncertainty is 0.10 for both, fixed by the 10% prevalence), while model B has reliability 0.04 and resolution 0.06. Model B is worse calibrated but far better at separating true positives from true negatives; recalibrating model B with a post-hoc method (covered in the next lesson) would keep its superior resolution while driving reliability toward zero, producing a genuinely better model than A ever could become.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge comparing two models with nearly identical Brier scores may ask which one is actually better and why. Reporting only the aggregate BS cannot answer this; a strong presenter runs Murphy's decomposition and can say, concretely, that one model's error is calibration-driven (fixable by recalibration) while the other's is resolution-driven (a genuine discrimination limitation, fixable only by a better model or better features). A judge may also ask why log loss, not Brier score, is used when training a model directly, testing whether the presenter understands the infinite-penalty asymmetry between the two rules.

questions.prompt: In Murphy's (1973) decomposition, BS = reliability - resolution + uncertainty, which term is fixed by the data's base rate alone and cannot be improved by any model?

options.text: Reliability
Resolution
Uncertainty
The overall Brier score itself

explanations.a: Reliability measures calibration and is fixable by recalibration methods; it is not fixed by the base rate.
explanations.b: Resolution measures discrimination and depends on the model's ability to separate groups; it is not a fixed data property.
explanations.c: Correct — uncertainty equals p-bar * (1 - p-bar), the base rate's inherent variance, representing irreducible problem difficulty no model can change.
explanations.d: The overall Brier score is the sum of all three terms and is very much affected by model quality.

questions.prompt: Why does log loss send its penalty toward infinity for a confident wrong prediction, while the Brier score does not?

options.text: Log loss uses a logarithm of the predicted probability, which diverges as that probability approaches 0 for the true class; Brier score uses a bounded squared error
Log loss is not a proper scoring rule, so it behaves unpredictably
Brier score is undefined for confident predictions
They behave identically; this is a common misconception

explanations.a: Correct — log(p) approaches negative infinity as p approaches 0, so a confidently wrong forecast is penalized without bound, whereas squared error (p-y)^2 is capped at 1 for binary outcomes.
explanations.b: Log loss is in fact a strictly proper scoring rule, just one with a different, harsher penalty shape than the Brier score.
explanations.c: Brier score is well defined for any probability in [0,1], including confident ones; it simply does not diverge.
explanations.d: The two rules diverge sharply in behavior specifically at confident, wrong predictions.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for a scoring rule to be 'strictly proper'?

options.text: It can only be computed on binary classification problems
A forecaster who genuinely believes the true probability is q uniquely maximizes their expected score by reporting p = q, not any other value
The score is always between 0 and 1
It requires a held-out calibration set to compute

explanations.a: Strictly proper scoring rules exist for multiclass and continuous outcomes as well, not only binary problems.
explanations.b: Correct — this is the formal definition: the rule cannot be gamed, because honestly reporting your true belief is the unique score-optimizing strategy.
explanations.c: Boundedness is a separate property; log loss, for instance, is strictly proper but unbounded.
explanations.d: Strict propriety is a property of the scoring formula itself, evaluated on realized outcomes, not a data-splitting requirement.

questions.prompt: Match each term or rule to its correct description.

right.text: Mean squared error between predicted probability and binary outcome, introduced by Brier in 1950
Sample-weighted squared gap between predicted probability and observed frequency per bin
How much bin-level outcome rates differ from the overall base rate; rewards useful discrimination
Strictly proper rule whose penalty diverges to infinity for a confident wrong prediction

questions.explanation: The Brier score is Brier's 1950 mean-squared-error formulation; Murphy's 1973 decomposition splits it into a reliability term measuring calibration, a resolution term measuring discrimination relative to the base rate, plus a fixed uncertainty term; log loss is the other strictly proper rule, distinguished by its unbounded penalty for confident errors.

lessons.label: Fixing Calibration: Platt Scaling and Isotonic Regression

sections.heading: Platt scaling: fitting a sigmoid to SVM margins
sections.body: John Platt's 1999 paper, "Probabilistic Outputs for Support Vector Machines and Comparisons to Regularized Likelihood Methods," solved a specific problem: SVM decision margins are not probabilities at all, just signed distances from a hyperplane. Platt scaling fits a two-parameter sigmoid, P(y=1|f) = 1 / (1 + exp(A*f + B)), to the raw score f via maximum likelihood on a held-out set of (score, label) pairs, turning any monotone score into a probability. Platt also introduced a subtle but important trick: rather than fitting the sigmoid to the raw 0/1 labels, he fit it to smoothed target values, t+ = (N+ + 1)/(N+ + 2) for positives and t- = 1/(N- + 2) for negatives, derived from a Bayesian argument. This keeps the sigmoid from chasing exact 0s and 1s at the extremes, which would otherwise overfit the fitting set and push predictions toward useless certainty.

sections.heading: Isotonic regression and the pool-adjacent-violators algorithm
sections.body: Bianca Zadrozny and Charles Elkan proposed a shape-free alternative in two papers, ICML 2001's "Obtaining Calibrated Probability Estimates from Decision Trees and Naive Bayesian Classifiers" and KDD 2002's "Transforming Classifier Scores into Accurate Multiclass Probability Estimates." Isotonic regression fits the best-fitting free-form, non-decreasing step function mapping raw scores to calibrated probabilities, with no assumption that the distortion is sigmoid-shaped at all. It is solved by the pool-adjacent-violators (PAV) algorithm: sort points by score, then scan for any adjacent pair whose accuracy would decrease, pool that pair by averaging their outcomes into a single block, and repeat until the entire sequence is monotone non-decreasing. The result is a flexible step function that can track any monotone miscalibration pattern, not just an S-curve.

sections.heading: Practical rules: sample size, distortion shape, and calibration-set discipline
sections.body: The two methods trade flexibility for data hunger. Isotonic regression's step function has as many effective degrees of freedom as there are distinct score values, so it needs roughly 1,000 or more held-out calibration points before its estimate stabilizes; below that it overfits, producing a jagged, unreliable mapping. Platt scaling, with only two parameters, stays safe on small calibration sets, but it can only correct a genuinely sigmoid-shaped distortion; if the true miscalibration curve bends the other way, Platt scaling underfits and leaves error on the table. Both methods share one non-negotiable rule: the calibration set must be held out from both the original training data and the final test set. Fitting on training data leaks; fitting on test data invalidates every subsequent evaluation, since the recalibration function would have seen the very labels it is later judged against.

lessons.workedExample: A team trains an SVM on 50,000 labeled images and holds out 800 examples purely for calibration. With only 800 points, isotonic regression produces a visibly jagged step function that overfits noise in sparse score regions, so the team switches to Platt scaling, fitting A and B by maximum likelihood using Platt's smoothed targets instead of raw labels. Six months later, with 15,000 calibration examples now available, they refit with isotonic regression and it captures a non-sigmoidal dip in the mid-range scores that Platt scaling had been systematically unable to correct, lowering ECE further than Platt scaling ever could on this model.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows post-hoc calibration exists will often ask which method was used and why, specifically probing whether the choice matched the calibration set's size. Answering 'isotonic regression' when the calibration set has only 200 points, or 'Platt scaling' when the reliability diagram shows an obviously non-sigmoidal, wavy distortion, signals the method was picked by habit rather than by diagnosis. A strong answer also confirms the calibration set was disjoint from both training and test data, since a judge who catches a calibration set that overlaps the test set can invalidate every reported number that followed.

questions.prompt: Why did Platt (1999) fit his sigmoid to smoothed target values like t+ = (N+ + 1)/(N+ + 2) instead of the raw 0/1 labels?

options.text: Raw 0/1 labels are not compatible with the sigmoid function's output range
Fitting to exact 0s and 1s would push the sigmoid toward overconfident extremes and overfit the calibration set
It was required to make the SVM converge during original training
It removes the need for a held-out calibration set entirely

explanations.a: The sigmoid outputs values in (0,1) and is fully compatible with 0/1 labels; that is not the issue Platt's trick addresses.
explanations.b: Correct — Platt's smoothed targets, derived from a Bayesian argument, prevent the maximum-likelihood fit from chasing exact certainty and overfitting the small calibration sample.
explanations.c: Platt scaling is a post-hoc step applied after SVM training is complete; it does not affect the original SVM's convergence.
explanations.d: Platt scaling still requires a held-out set of (score, label) pairs to fit A and B; the smoothed-target trick only changes what those pairs are fit to.

questions.prompt: A team has only 300 calibration examples and a reliability diagram showing a clean, S-shaped distortion. Which method is the safer choice?

options.text: Isotonic regression, because it is strictly more flexible than any parametric method
Platt scaling, because its two-parameter sigmoid matches the observed S-shape and needs far less data
Neither method works with fewer than 10,000 examples
Isotonic regression, because the pool-adjacent-violators algorithm requires no minimum sample size

explanations.a: Isotonic's flexibility is a liability, not an asset, with only 300 points — it needs roughly 1,000 or more calibration points to stabilize and will overfit here.
explanations.b: Correct — a clean sigmoidal distortion is exactly what Platt scaling's two parameters are built to fix, and it remains stable on small calibration sets.
explanations.c: Platt scaling is commonly used successfully with calibration sets far smaller than 10,000 examples.
explanations.d: The PAV algorithm will run on any sample size, but the resulting step function overfits badly below roughly 1,000 points; 'runs without error' is not the same as 'produces a trustworthy calibration.'

questions.prompt: Match each calibration method or concept to its correct description.

right.text: Fits a two-parameter sigmoid to raw scores via maximum likelihood
Fits a free-form, non-decreasing step function with no assumed shape
Averages adjacent score-sorted points that violate monotonicity until the sequence is monotone
Must be held out from both the original training data and the final test set

questions.explanation: Platt scaling (1999) fits an assumed sigmoid shape; isotonic regression (Zadrozny and Elkan, 2001-2002) fits an unconstrained monotone step function; PAV is the algorithm that solves the isotonic fit by pooling monotonicity-violating pairs; and both methods require a calibration set disjoint from training and test data to avoid leakage or invalid evaluation.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the pool-adjacent-violators (PAV) algorithm in the correct order.

items.text: Sort all calibration points by their raw predicted score
Scan for any adjacent pair whose accuracy would decrease (a monotonicity violation)
Pool the violating pair by averaging their outcomes into one block
Repeat scanning and pooling until the full sequence is non-decreasing
Use the resulting step function as the calibration mapping

questions.explanation: PAV requires sorted scores before any violation can be detected; violations are found and pooled iteratively; the process repeats until monotonicity holds everywhere; only then is the resulting step function usable as the final calibration map.

lessons.label: Why Modern Models Are Miscalibrated

sections.heading: Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana (2005): a taxonomy of miscalibration by algorithm family
sections.body: Alexandru Niculescu-Mizil and Rich Caruana's ICML 2005 paper, "Predicting Good Probabilities with Supervised Learning," empirically mapped a distinctive miscalibration signature onto each learning algorithm family across a battery of benchmark datasets and ten learning methods. Maximum-margin methods, boosted decision trees and boosted stumps, push probability mass away from 0 and 1: boosting's objective keeps widening classification margin even after training accuracy saturates, so raw scores rarely approach the extremes even on easy cases, producing a characteristic sigmoid-shaped distortion where the reliability curve bows visibly inward toward the center. Naive Bayes shows the opposite failure: its conditional-independence assumption double-counts correlated evidence, multiplying redundant likelihoods together and driving predictions toward 0 and 1 far more aggressively than the data warrants, making it overconfident rather than underconfident. Support vector machines, also max-margin classifiers, output raw signed distances from the decision boundary with no probabilistic meaning at all, needing an explicit mapping before any probability can be reported. Well-regularized logistic regression, neural networks of that era, and bagged decision trees emerged nearly calibrated without any correction, since none of them optimize a margin objective at the expense of the likelihood.

sections.heading: Guo et al. (2017): deeper networks got less trustworthy while getting more accurate
sections.body: Chuan Guo, Geoff Pleiss, Yu Sun, and Kilian Weinberger's ICML 2017 paper, "On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks," showed that modern architectures such as deep ResNets are far more overconfident than 1990s-era networks like LeNet, even though test accuracy climbed substantially over the same period; ECE rose even as error fell. They isolated three independent architectural drivers of this overconfidence: increasing depth, increasing width, and decreasing weight decay each degrade calibration on their own, with batch normalization compounding the effect further. This decoupled a widely assumed link between accuracy and trustworthy probabilities, showing a network can become simultaneously more correct and less honest about its own uncertainty.

sections.heading: Temperature scaling: one parameter beats many
sections.body: Guo et al. compared several calibration fixes, histogram binning, isotonic regression, Bayesian Binning into Quantiles, Platt scaling, and Platt-style matrix and vector scaling, against temperature scaling, and found that temperature scaling outperformed every more complex alternative on nearly every architecture tested. Temperature scaling divides every logit by a single learned scalar T, fit by minimizing negative log-likelihood on a validation set (in practice T > 1 for the overconfident networks Guo et al. studied, softening confidence). Because dividing all logits by the same constant changes no relative ordering, it leaves accuracy and AUC completely untouched, only softening confidence. Its single parameter is precisely why it generalizes better than higher-capacity fixes like matrix scaling, which carry enough free parameters to overfit the modest validation set typically available for calibration.

lessons.workedExample: A team compares a boosted-tree model and a naive Bayes model on the same fraud-detection task, both with similar accuracy. The boosted tree's reliability diagram shows scores clustered between 0.3 and 0.7 even for cases that are almost certainly fraud or almost certainly not, the classic away-from-the-extremes sigmoid distortion Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana documented, so Platt scaling (built exactly for sigmoid-shaped distortion) corrects it well. The naive Bayes model instead reports 0.99 or 0.01 for nearly every case because its independence assumption compounds correlated fraud signals, a case of overconfidence needing the opposite correction, isotonic regression, since the naive Bayes distortion is not a clean sigmoid.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has read about deep learning overconfidence may ask why a presenter's neural network reports 99% confidence on a validation set where it is only right 85% of the time. The strongest answer names Guo et al. (2017) directly, explains that depth, width, and low weight decay are known drivers of exactly this gap, and reports having applied temperature scaling, a single learned scalar, rather than a more elaborate fix. A presenter using a boosted-tree or naive-Bayes model should likewise be able to name which of the two characteristic distortions from Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana (2005) applies to their model family and why.

questions.prompt: According to Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana (2005), how does naive Bayes typically miscalibrate compared to boosted decision trees?

options.text: Naive Bayes pushes predictions toward 0 and 1 (overconfident); boosted trees push predictions away from 0 and 1 (underconfident-looking, sigmoid-shaped)
Both push predictions toward 0 and 1 in identical ways
Naive Bayes is always perfectly calibrated; only boosted trees miscalibrate
Naive Bayes pushes predictions away from 0 and 1; boosted trees push predictions toward 0 and 1

explanations.a: Correct — naive Bayes' independence assumption double-counts correlated evidence and drives scores toward the extremes, while boosting's margin-maximizing objective keeps scores compressed away from 0 and 1, the opposite failure.
explanations.b: The two families showed opposite, not identical, miscalibration signatures in the study.
explanations.c: Naive Bayes was one of the more poorly calibrated methods in the study, not a well-calibrated one.
explanations.d: This reverses the actual finding: it is naive Bayes that pushes toward the extremes, and boosting that pushes away from them.

questions.prompt: Guo et al. (2017) found that increasing a neural network's depth and width, and decreasing its weight decay, tend to do what?

options.text: Improve both accuracy and calibration together
Improve accuracy while making the network more overconfident (worse calibration)
Leave both accuracy and calibration unchanged
Degrade accuracy while improving calibration

explanations.a: The paper's central finding is precisely that these two properties move in opposite directions, not together.
explanations.b: Correct — Guo et al. showed test accuracy improved across the era of deeper, wider networks with less weight decay, while ECE simultaneously rose, meaning confidence became decoupled from correctness.
explanations.c: Both accuracy and calibration changed substantially; neither stayed flat.
explanations.d: Accuracy generally improved alongside these architectural trends, not degraded; calibration is what worsened.

questions.prompt: Match each model family to the miscalibration signature Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana (2005) documented for it.

right.text: Scores pushed away from 0 and 1; sigmoid-shaped distortion from margin maximization
Scores pushed toward 0 and 1; overconfident due to compounding correlated evidence
Outputs raw signed distances with no inherent probabilistic meaning
Nearly calibrated without correction

questions.explanation: Boosting's margin objective compresses scores away from the extremes (sigmoid-shaped); naive Bayes' independence assumption drives scores toward the extremes (overconfident); SVMs output unscaled margins; and well-regularized logistic regression and bagged trees need little to no correction.

questions.prompt: Put these calibration-related papers in chronological order.

items.text: Platt's SVM probability scaling paper (1999)
Zadrozny and Elkan's isotonic regression calibration paper (2002)
Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana's algorithm-family miscalibration study (2005)
Guo et al.'s neural network calibration and temperature scaling paper (2017)

questions.explanation: The chronology runs Platt (1999), then Zadrozny and Elkan (2002), then Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana (2005), then Guo et al. (2017), spanning from early probability-calibration methods through the deep-learning-era overconfidence findings.

lessons.label: Calibration Under Shift, and the Limits of Recalibration

sections.heading: What recalibration cannot do: ranking is invariant under any monotone map
sections.body: Every post-hoc calibration method covered in this unit, Platt's sigmoid and isotonic's step function alike, is a monotone, non-decreasing function of the raw score. A monotone transformation can never change which of two examples has the higher score, only rescale the numeric gap between them, so a model's AUC and its full rank ordering are mathematically identical before and after recalibration. This means recalibration only ever repairs the printed decimal used for a threshold decision; it can never repair weak discrimination. If a model genuinely cannot separate positives from negatives, no calibration method fixes that, because the fix has to happen upstream, in the features or the model itself, not downstream in a recalibration layer. This is worth stating plainly because it is the single most common misunderstanding teams have about calibration tools: recalibrating a poor model produces a poor model with more honest-looking, but still poor, numbers.

sections.heading: Calibration achieved on one population breaks under shift at deployment
sections.body: A recalibration function fit on a derivation cohort assumes that cohort's label prevalence and feature distribution will hold at deployment, an assumption that regularly fails. Under prior shift, the disease prevalence or class balance itself differs between sites, say 5% in the training hospital versus 20% in a new one, and even a model with a perfectly valid likelihood ratio will report the wrong posterior probability unless explicitly adjusted for the new prior, a correction formalized in work such as Saerens, Latinne, and Decaestecker's 2002 EM-based prior-adaptation method. Under covariate shift, the feature distribution itself changes, a different patient mix or a different sensor population, and simple prior correction is not enough; the safer response is full refitting or importance-weighted recalibration on data representative of the new deployment population.

sections.heading: Sharpness subject to calibration, and conformal prediction as the distribution-free alternative
sections.body: Tilmann Gneiting, Fadoua Balabdaoui, and Adrian Raftery's 2007 Journal of the Royal Statistical Society paper, "Probabilistic Forecasts, Calibration and Sharpness," states the governing principle for this whole unit: the goal is to maximize sharpness subject to calibration. Calibration alone is a trivially gameable target, since a model that always predicts the overall base rate is perfectly calibrated in the aggregate yet useless for any individual decision; sharpness, how concentrated and confident predictions are, is what makes calibrated probabilities valuable. Conformal prediction, developed by Vladimir Vovk, Alexander Gammerman, and Glenn Shafer, offers a distribution-free route to this goal: rather than trusting a parametric or nonparametric recalibration curve to generalize, it uses the exchangeability of calibration and test data to construct prediction sets with a mathematically guaranteed coverage rate, at the cost of needing that exchangeability assumption to hold.

lessons.workedExample: A sepsis model is calibrated to perfection at Hospital A, where prevalence is 8%, using isotonic regression on a large validation set; its AUC there is 0.89. Deployed unchanged at Hospital B, where prevalence is 22% due to a sicker referral population, the same model keeps its 0.89 AUC exactly, since ranking never changed, but its calibration curve now sits well below the diagonal, systematically underestimating risk. The team applies a prior-correction adjustment using Hospital B's known 22% base rate rather than refitting isotonic regression from scratch, since the feature distribution (covariate shift) appears roughly stable between sites and only the prevalence shifted.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who understands recalibration may ask a pointed question: if your model performs worse at a new site, could recalibration alone fix it? The correct answer distinguishes two very different failures, ranking failure, which no recalibration method can touch, from calibration failure under prior or covariate shift, which prior-correction or refitting can address. A judge may also probe whether the presenter understands that a model which always predicts the base rate is technically calibrated but scientifically worthless, testing whether 'calibrated' is being used as an empty buzzword or as one half of the sharpness-subject-to-calibration standard the field actually holds models to.

questions.prompt: A model is passed through isotonic regression for recalibration. What happens to its AUC?

options.text: AUC stays exactly the same, because isotonic regression is a monotone transformation of the scores
AUC always improves after recalibration
AUC always gets worse after recalibration
AUC becomes undefined once scores are recalibrated

explanations.a: Correct — isotonic regression is monotone non-decreasing by construction, so it cannot change the rank order of scores, and AUC depends only on rank order.
explanations.b: Recalibration cannot repair discrimination; a model with poor ranking stays poor after recalibration.
explanations.c: AUC is unaffected, not degraded, by a purely monotone recalibration map.
explanations.d: AUC remains perfectly well defined; it is computed on the recalibrated scores exactly as it was on the raw scores, with an identical value.

questions.prompt: A model calibrated at Hospital A (8% disease prevalence) is deployed at Hospital B (22% prevalence), with a similar patient population otherwise. What is the most appropriate first fix?

options.text: Do nothing, since a monotone recalibration is invariant to deployment site
Apply a prior-correction adjustment using Hospital B's known base rate
Discard the model, since covariate shift makes it unusable
Recompute AUC, since prior shift changes the model's ranking ability

explanations.a: Recalibration being rank-invariant does not mean the model's reported probabilities stay valid across a prevalence change; the printed probabilities need adjusting.
explanations.b: Correct — a pure prevalence (prior) shift, with the feature distribution otherwise stable, calls for a prior-correction adjustment using the new site's known base rate rather than a full refit.
explanations.c: The scenario describes prior shift, not covariate shift, and prior shift is the more tractable, correctable case, not a reason to discard the model.
explanations.d: AUC depends on the model's feature-based ranking ability, which a pure prevalence shift does not directly change.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to its correct description.

right.text: How concentrated and confident predictions are, valuable only once calibration holds
The label prevalence differs between the training and deployment population
The feature distribution itself differs between the training and deployment population
A distribution-free method giving mathematically guaranteed coverage via exchangeability

questions.explanation: Gneiting, Balabdaoui, and Raftery (2007) define sharpness as concentration of predictions given calibration; prior shift is a change in label prevalence; covariate shift is a change in the feature distribution; and conformal prediction (Vovk, Gammerman, Shafer) supplies distribution-free guaranteed coverage using exchangeability rather than a fitted recalibration curve.

questions.prompt: Order these statements from most general principle to most specific implementation detail.

items.text: Maximize sharpness subject to calibration (Gneiting, Balabdaoui, and Raftery, 2007)
A model that always predicts the base rate is calibrated but not sharp, and therefore not useful
Under a pure prior shift, apply a prior-correction adjustment using the new base rate
The exact numeric multiplier used to adjust a specific model's posterior for Hospital B's 22% prevalence

questions.explanation: The general principle (maximize sharpness subject to calibration) motivates why trivial calibration is insufficient (the always-base-rate example), which motivates the general fix for one specific failure mode (prior-correction under prior shift), which is finally instantiated as one concrete numeric adjustment for one deployment site.

units.label: Multi-Class Evaluation and Reporting in the Field

lessons.label: Macro, Micro, and Weighted: Three Averages, Three Different Lies

sections.heading: Micro-averaging: pool the confusion matrix, then divide
sections.body: When a classifier has more than two classes, precision, recall, and F1 need a rule for combining per-class numbers into one score, and the rule you pick changes the answer more than the model does. MICRO-averaging pools every true positive, false positive, and false negative across all classes into one giant TP/FP/FN before computing precision, recall, or F1 a single time. In single-label multi-class classification, where each example gets exactly one predicted class, every misclassification is simultaneously an FP for the predicted class and an FN for the true class, so total FP always equals total FN across the whole matrix. That identity forces micro-precision, micro-recall, and micro-F1 to collapse to the exact same number, and that number equals overall accuracy. So a paper reporting "micro-F1 = 0.91" for a single-label multi-class task is, arithmetically, just reporting 91% accuracy under a fancier name.

sections.heading: Macro-averaging: one class, one vote, regardless of size
sections.body: MACRO-averaging computes precision, recall, and F1 separately for each class, then takes the unweighted mean across classes. A class with 10 examples counts exactly as much as a class with 9,000. This makes macro-F1 the metric of choice for exposing rare-class collapse, but it also means a single tiny, chronically-confused class can drag the whole average down by itself, or, if a rare class happens to be trivially separable, inflate it. WEIGHTED-averaging is macro-averaging's compromise: it computes the same per-class metrics but weights each class's contribution by its support (its share of the true examples), so the average tracks whichever classes are numerous. That is exactly its flaw for imbalance-monitoring purposes: a model that nails the 900-example majority class and completely misses a 10-example minority class still reports a high weighted-F1, because the minority class's near-zero score gets multiplied by a near-zero weight.

sections.heading: A concrete three-class split
sections.body: Consider three classes with supports 900, 90, and 10 (total 1,000). Suppose the model gets the majority class right almost every time, does moderately on the middle class, and essentially never identifies the 10-example class correctly. Micro-F1 (= accuracy) lands around 0.97 because 971 of 1,000 predictions are right. Weighted-F1 lands around 0.93, barely moved, because the 10-example class's near-zero F1 is scaled by weight 0.01. Macro-F1 lands around 0.62, because it averages in that class's failure at full, unweighted strength. The honest report leads with macro-F1 (and the per-class breakdown behind it) whenever any class's real-world cost is not proportional to its frequency — which is most diagnostic, safety, and fairness settings. scikit-learn's `classification_report` prints all three by default precisely because no single number is safe to read alone; a team that quotes one line from that table without saying which average it is has, whether intentionally or not, chosen the most flattering one.

lessons.workedExample: A tumor-subtype classifier is trained on 1,000 slides: 900 benign, 90 low-grade malignant, 10 high-grade malignant (rare but most lethal). The model predicts benign correctly 890 times, low-grade correctly 80 times, and high-grade correctly only 1 time out of 10. Confusion counts give micro-F1 (=accuracy) = 971/1000 ≈ 0.97. Weighted-F1 ≈ 0.93, since the high-grade class's poor F1 is scaled by its 1% weight and contributes little to the sum. Macro-F1, averaging the three per-class F1 scores unweighted, comes out near 0.62 — the number that actually reflects the model missing 9 of 10 high-grade cases.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has seen this trick will ask, immediately after any headline F1 number: "Micro, macro, or weighted — and what's the per-class breakdown?" A team that reports only micro-F1 on an imbalanced multi-class problem is, whether they know it or not, reporting accuracy and hiding exactly the rare-class failure a science-fair audience cares about (rare disease subtypes, rare defect types, rare species). Being able to state which classes drove the macro-F1 down, and why that is the number that matters for this problem's real costs, is what separates a team that understands its own model from one that picked the best-looking number.

questions.prompt: In single-label multi-class classification, why does micro-F1 always equal accuracy?

options.text: Because scikit-learn defines it that way by convention, with no underlying math reason
Because pooling FP and FN across all classes makes total FP equal total FN, forcing micro-precision, micro-recall, and micro-F1 to all equal (correct predictions) / (total predictions)
Because macro and micro averaging are mathematically identical for any dataset
Because micro-F1 ignores false negatives entirely

explanations.a: It is not an arbitrary convention; it follows directly from how single-label misclassifications are counted.
explanations.b: Correct — every misclassification is one FP (for the predicted class) and one FN (for the true class), so pooled FP = pooled FN, and precision = recall = F1 = accuracy.
explanations.c: Macro and micro diverge sharply on imbalanced data; only micro collapses to accuracy, not macro.
explanations.d: Micro-F1 still uses false negatives; the identity comes from FP and FN totals being equal, not from dropping either term.

questions.prompt: A model scores well on a 900-example class and near-zero on a 10-example class. Which averaging scheme will most clearly expose the rare-class failure?

options.text: Micro-averaging
Weighted-averaging
Macro-averaging
All three will show it equally

explanations.a: Micro-averaging equals overall accuracy here and is dominated by the 900-example class.
explanations.b: Weighted-averaging multiplies the rare class's poor score by its tiny support weight, nearly erasing its impact.
explanations.c: Correct — macro-averaging gives the 10-example class's F1 equal, unweighted standing alongside the 900-example class's F1, so a near-zero score there pulls the average down hard.
explanations.d: They diverge substantially in this scenario, as the worked example's 0.97 / 0.93 / 0.62 split shows.

questions.prompt: Match each averaging scheme to what it effectively equals or is dominated by in single-label multi-class classification.

right.text: Overall accuracy
Equal per-class vote regardless of frequency
Dominated by the most frequent classes

questions.explanation: Micro-F1 equals accuracy in single-label multi-class settings; macro-averaging gives every class equal weight regardless of support; weighted-averaging scales each class's contribution by its support, so frequent classes dominate.

questions.prompt: For the 900/90/10-support example in the lesson, order the three F1 scores from LOWEST to HIGHEST.

items.text: Macro-F1 (~0.62)
Weighted-F1 (~0.93)
Micro-F1 (~0.97)

questions.explanation: Macro-F1 (~0.62) is dragged down by the failing 10-example class counted at full weight; weighted-F1 (~0.93) nearly erases that failure via its tiny support weight; micro-F1 (~0.97), equal to accuracy, is dominated by the 900-example class.

questions.prompt: Which report is most honest for a rare, high-stakes class (e.g., a rare cancer subtype) inside an imbalanced multi-class problem?

options.text: Lead with micro-F1 only, since it is the single most common metric name
Lead with weighted-F1, since it accounts for class sizes
Lead with macro-F1 and the per-class breakdown
Report only overall accuracy

explanations.a: Micro-F1 equals accuracy and is silent on the rare class's near-total failure.
explanations.b: Weighted-F1 scales the rare class's failure down to near-invisibility by its tiny support weight.
explanations.c: Correct — macro-F1 weights every class equally regardless of frequency, and the per-class breakdown shows exactly which class is failing and how badly.
explanations.d: Accuracy is arithmetically identical to micro-F1 here and equally silent on the rare class.

lessons.label: Multi-Class ROC and AUC

sections.heading: One-vs-rest: k binary curves stapled together
sections.body: ROC curves and AUC are inherently binary constructs — one class is "positive," everything else is "negative." The most common multi-class extension, ONE-VS-REST (OvR), builds k separate binary ROC curves, one per class treated as positive against the pooled remainder, then averages the k AUCs. But each of those k problems has its own class prevalence (the target class's share versus everyone else's), and AUC is not fully prevalence-independent in the way people assume once you start averaging across classes with very different sizes. A MACRO average of the k AUCs treats every class equally regardless of size; a PREVALENCE-WEIGHTED average scales each class's AUC by its support, so the numerous classes dominate — the same macro-versus-weighted tension that infects F1 recurs here, and the two averages can rank two models differently. Because each OvR problem pools every other class into one 'negative' bucket, a class's OvR AUC can shift if the mix of the OTHER classes changes, even when that class's own scores never move — a distortion Tom Fawcett's widely cited 2006 tutorial 'An Introduction to ROC Analysis' (Pattern Recognition Letters) flags as a hazard of collapsing multiple classes into a single negative group.

sections.heading: One-vs-one and Hand & Till's M measure
sections.body: ONE-VS-ONE (OvO) instead builds a separate ROC/AUC for every pair of classes ((i, j)) using only the examples belonging to those two classes, giving k(k-1)/2 pairwise AUCs. David Hand and Robert Till's 2001 paper in Machine Learning, "A Simple Generalisation of the Area Under the ROC Curve for Multiple Class Classification Problems," proposed averaging these pairwise AUCs into the M measure: M = [2/(k(k-1))] × Σ A(i,j), summed over all unordered pairs. Hand and Till designed M specifically to be insensitive to the class distribution, because each pairwise A(i,j) is computed only from classes i and j's own examples — a class's overall prevalence in the full dataset never enters the calculation, unlike OvR's pooled-remainder approach.

sections.heading: Why nobody computes the true k-class surface, and the sklearn mapping
sections.body: The mathematically exact generalization of AUC to k classes is the VOLUME UNDER THE ROC SURFACE (VUS), integrating a full (k-1)-dimensional decision surface. It is well-defined for k=3 (a literal 3D surface, sometimes visualized) but the surface's dimensionality and the number of operating-point parameters grow so fast that it becomes computationally intractable and impossible to visualize beyond three or four classes — which is why OvR and OvO/M dominate practice instead. In scikit-learn's `roc_auc_score`, `multi_class='ovr'` combined with `average='macro'` gives unweighted OvR, `average='weighted'` gives prevalence-weighted OvR, and `multi_class='ovo'` with `average='macro'` computes the Hand-Till M measure.

lessons.workedExample: A 4-class plant-disease classifier has classes with wildly different prevalence: healthy (70%), blight (15%), rust (10%), and mosaic virus (5%). Computing OvR AUC per class and averaging with `average='weighted'` lets the healthy class's high AUC dominate the score, since it is 70% of the pooled 'rest' comparisons. Switching to `average='macro'` gives mosaic virus's AUC equal standing, which is far more informative since misdiagnosing a rare virus is the costlier error. Switching to `multi_class='ovo'` computes Hand and Till's M measure directly, and because it never pools by overall prevalence, it tends to agree with the macro-OvR ranking rather than the weighted-OvR one whenever prevalence is skewed.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has read past a single AUC number will ask which multi-class extension was used and why — because 'one-vs-rest weighted-macro' and 'one-vs-one M-measure' can rank the same two models in opposite order when classes are imbalanced. Naming Hand and Till (2001) and explaining that their M measure was explicitly engineered to be prevalence-insensitive shows you understand AUC is not automatically well-behaved once there are more than two classes, and that the choice of averaging scheme is itself a modeling decision, not a software default to leave untouched.

questions.prompt: What is the key design goal of Hand and Till's (2001) M measure?

options.text: To make AUC computation faster than one-vs-rest
To be insensitive to the overall class distribution, by averaging pairwise AUCs computed only from each pair's own examples
To replace ROC curves with precision-recall curves entirely
To compute the exact volume under the ROC surface for any number of classes

explanations.a: Speed was not the stated design goal; OvO actually requires more pairwise computations (k(k-1)/2) than OvR's k computations.
explanations.b: Correct — Hand and Till (2001) built M from pairwise AUCs A(i,j), each computed from only classes i and j, so no class's overall prevalence in the full dataset enters the score.
explanations.c: M is still an AUC-based (ROC-based) measure, not a precision-recall construct.
explanations.d: The exact volume under the ROC surface (VUS) is a separate, computationally intractable construct beyond three classes; M is a pairwise-averaging approximation, not VUS.

questions.prompt: Why is the true k-class generalization of AUC (volume under the ROC surface) rarely used beyond 3 classes?

options.text: It requires labeled data, unlike OvR and OvO
Its dimensionality and computation grow so fast with k that it becomes computationally and visually impractical
It only works for regression problems
scikit-learn does not support ROC curves at all

explanations.a: All these AUC-family methods require labeled data equally; that is not the limiting factor.
explanations.b: Correct — the surface's dimensionality scales with k, making both computation and visualization impractical past three or four classes, which is why OvR and OvO/M dominate practice.
explanations.c: ROC/AUC constructs are for classification, and VUS is specifically the multi-class classification generalization.
explanations.d: scikit-learn's `roc_auc_score` supports multi-class ROC/AUC via `multi_class='ovr'` and `'ovo'`.

questions.prompt: Match each scikit-learn `roc_auc_score` setting combination to what it computes.

right.text: Unweighted average of per-class one-vs-rest AUCs
Prevalence-weighted average of one-vs-rest AUCs
Hand and Till's M measure (pairwise, prevalence-insensitive)

questions.explanation: OvR with macro averaging gives every class's AUC equal weight; OvR with weighted averaging scales by class support; OvO with macro averaging computes the Hand-Till M measure, averaging pairwise AUCs that never reference overall class prevalence.

questions.prompt: Order these multi-class AUC approaches from FEWEST to MOST pairwise/per-class AUC computations required for a 4-class problem.

items.text: One-vs-rest (per class vs. pooled remainder)
One-vs-one / Hand-Till M (per class pair)
Volume under the ROC surface (full joint surface)

questions.explanation: One-vs-rest needs k=4 AUCs (one per class). One-vs-one needs k(k-1)/2=6 pairwise AUCs for 4 classes. The volume under the ROC surface integrates the full joint (k-1)-dimensional surface, which is the most complex of the three and impractical beyond a few classes.

lessons.label: Multi-Label and Hierarchical Evaluation

sections.heading: When one example needs several labels: exact match versus Hamming loss
sections.body: MULTI-LABEL classification allows each example to carry several correct labels simultaneously — a news article tagged both 'politics' and 'economy,' a gene annotated with several biological functions, a chest X-ray flagged for both 'cardiomegaly' and 'effusion,' as in the ChestX-ray14 and CheXpert datasets. The strictest scoring rule, EXACT-MATCH (subset) ACCURACY, counts a prediction correct only if its entire predicted label set equals the true set exactly — get four of five labels right and miss the fifth, and the example scores zero. This is brutally unforgiving on tasks with many possible labels, since the number of ways to be partially wrong grows combinatorially. HAMMING LOSS is the gentler complement: it scores each of the individual label decisions (present/absent) independently and averages the per-label error rate, so one wrong label out of twenty barely moves the score.

sections.heading: Example-based versus label-based F1, and ranking metrics
sections.body: F1 itself splits into two multi-label variants. EXAMPLE-BASED F1 computes precision/recall per EXAMPLE (across that example's predicted versus true label set) and averages over examples — it rewards getting each item's own labels mostly right. LABEL-BASED F1 (the macro/micro/weighted family from single-label classification) computes precision/recall per LABEL across all examples and averages over labels — it rewards getting each label class right across the dataset. The two can diverge sharply when label frequency is skewed. When the output is a ranked list rather than a set (rank candidate diagnoses, tag likely genres), RANKING LOSS counts how often an irrelevant label is ranked above a relevant one, COVERAGE measures how deep into the ranked list you must go to catch all true labels, and LABEL-BASED AVERAGE PRECISION scores ranking quality per label, mirroring precision-recall AUC.

sections.heading: Hierarchies punish flat metrics for treating all errors alike
sections.body: Many real label sets are HIERARCHICAL: ICD diagnostic codes, biological taxonomies, product catalogs. A flat metric treats confusing 'bacterial pneumonia' with 'viral pneumonia' (siblings under one parent) exactly the same as confusing it with 'fracture' (an unrelated branch), even though clinically and taxonomically the first error is far less severe. HIERARCHICAL evaluation instead weights an error by tree distance — how many edges separate the predicted and true node, or how much ancestor path they share — so sibling confusions cost little and cross-branch confusions cost a lot. Metrics built for this include hierarchical precision/recall (Kiritchenko, Matwin, Nock, and Famili, 2006, on hierarchical text categorization) and tree-distance-based loss functions that discount an error's cost by how much ancestor path the predicted and true nodes share; ignoring hierarchy and reporting flat accuracy on a taxonomic or diagnostic-code problem systematically overstates how 'wrong' a model's near-miss errors really are, and can make two models with very different failure patterns look identical.

lessons.workedExample: A radiology model tags chest X-rays with any of 14 possible findings (as in CheXpert). On one X-ray the true labels are {cardiomegaly, effusion} and the model predicts {cardiomegaly, effusion, edema}. Exact-match accuracy scores this example as a flat 0 — one extra label ruins it. Hamming loss instead scores 13 of 14 label-decisions correct (only 'edema' was a false positive), giving a much more informative near-miss error rate of about 0.07. If 'edema' and 'effusion' sit under the same hierarchical parent category ('fluid-related finding') while an unrelated miss like predicting 'fracture' would not, a hierarchical metric would penalize the edema slip far less than a cross-category error — information exact-match and Hamming both discard.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge evaluating a multi-label or hierarchical-label project (medical imaging, taxonomic classification, diagnostic coding) will ask whether you reported exact-match accuracy alone, because on tasks with many possible label combinations that number is often near zero even for a good model, and reporting it without Hamming loss or label-based F1 makes a genuinely useful model look broken. For hierarchical problems specifically, a judge may ask whether your evaluation gives partial credit for 'close' errors (sibling-node confusions) — a flat accuracy number that treats every wrong label as equally wrong signals you have not thought about what your label space's structure actually means for error severity.

questions.prompt: A multi-label model gets 9 of 10 labels right on an example (missing one). What does exact-match (subset) accuracy score this example?

options.text: 0.9, proportional to the fraction of correct labels
0, because the predicted label set does not exactly equal the true set
1, because the majority of labels are correct
It cannot be scored without knowing Hamming loss first

explanations.a: That proportional scoring describes Hamming loss's per-label averaging, not exact-match accuracy.
explanations.b: Correct — exact-match accuracy requires the entire predicted set to equal the entire true set; any single missed or extra label scores the whole example as wrong.
explanations.c: Exact-match accuracy has no partial credit; a majority-correct set still scores 0 if it is not a perfect match.
explanations.d: Exact-match accuracy is computed independently and does not require Hamming loss as an input.

questions.prompt: Match each multi-label metric to what it actually measures.

right.text: Whether the entire predicted label set equals the entire true set
Average error rate across individual present/absent label decisions
Precision/recall computed per example, averaged over examples
Precision/recall computed per label class, averaged over labels

questions.explanation: Exact-match accuracy requires the whole set to match; Hamming loss averages per-label present/absent errors; example-based F1 computes precision/recall per example and averages over examples; label-based F1 computes precision/recall per label and averages over labels (with macro/micro/weighted variants).

questions.prompt: Why does a flat accuracy metric mis-score a hierarchical label problem, such as ICD diagnostic codes?

options.text: Flat accuracy cannot be computed at all when labels form a tree
It treats confusing two sibling classes (e.g., bacterial vs. viral pneumonia) the same as confusing two unrelated classes, ignoring that the first error is far less severe
It always overestimates model performance on hierarchical data
Hierarchical labels cannot have a true label at all

explanations.a: Flat accuracy can technically be computed on hierarchical labels; the issue is that doing so throws away structural information.
explanations.b: Correct — flat accuracy assigns identical cost to every wrong prediction regardless of tree distance, so a near-miss sibling confusion counts exactly as badly as a distant, unrelated error.
explanations.c: It does not systematically overestimate; it simply fails to distinguish severity of different errors, which can make a model with mostly near-miss errors look no better than one with severe errors.
explanations.d: Hierarchical labels have well-defined true labels; the hierarchy is a structure over the label space, not an obstacle to labeling.

questions.prompt: Order these multi-label metrics from STRICTEST (most likely to score a near-miss as fully wrong) to MOST FORGIVING of a near-miss.

items.text: Exact-match (subset) accuracy
Label-based F1
Hamming loss

questions.explanation: Exact-match accuracy scores any imperfect set as entirely wrong. Label-based F1 credits correct label-by-label decisions but is still sensitive to specific classes doing poorly. Hamming loss averages over every individual label decision, so a single miss among many labels barely moves the score.

lessons.label: Case Studies: Where Evaluation Choices Changed the Outcome

sections.heading: Gulshan et al. (2016, JAMA): one AUC, two operating points, because one threshold cannot serve two jobs
sections.body: Varun Gulshan and colleagues at Google published 'Development and Validation of a Deep Learning Algorithm for Detection of Diabetic Retinopathy in Retinal Fundus Photographs' in JAMA in 2016, validating a deep learning system against ophthalmologist panels on two datasets, EyePACS-1 (9,963 images) and Messidor-2 (1,748 images). For referable diabetic retinopathy the AUC was 0.991 (95% CI, 0.988-0.993) on EyePACS-1 and 0.990 (95% CI, 0.986-0.995) on Messidor-2 — about as high as a summary metric gets. But a single AUC hides the fact that a screening program has to pick a THRESHOLD, and no one threshold serves every use case. So the team reported two distinct operating points on each dataset. The high-SENSITIVITY point (97.5% sensitivity, 93.4% specificity on EyePACS-1; 96.1% sensitivity, 93.9% specificity on Messidor-2) is tuned for mass screening, where a missed case is the costlier error. The high-SPECIFICITY point (87.0% sensitivity, 98.5% specificity on Messidor-2) is tuned instead to match human-grader specificity, minimizing unnecessary referrals. Same model, same AUC, two very different clinics. Publishing the 0.99 alone would have concealed that deploying it requires choosing which error you would rather make.

sections.heading: Wong et al. (2021, JAMA Internal Medicine): vendor AUC versus reality
sections.body: Karandeep Singh's group, led by Andrew Wong, externally validated the widely deployed Epic Sepsis Model across 38,455 hospitalizations (27,697 patients) at Michigan Medicine, December 2018-October 2019. Epic reported an internal AUC of 0.76-0.83. The external validation found AUC 0.63 (95% CI, 0.62-0.64), sensitivity of only 33% at the vendor's alert threshold, specificity 83%, and — critically — the model fired alerts on 18% of all hospitalized patients while still missing 67% of confirmed sepsis cases. This is the canonical case for why an AUC alone, especially one reported only by a model's own vendor, is not deployment evidence. The operating threshold's real-world sensitivity, its alert burden, and the clinician alert-fatigue cost only surface once somebody independent runs the model on a population the vendor did not train or tune on.

sections.heading: Card fraud: when the metric has to move with the money
sections.body: Card-fraud detection typically runs at roughly a 1-in-1,000 fraud base rate. At that prevalence, AUC-ROC stays deceptively high for almost any reasonable model, because the vast non-fraud majority dominates the false-positive-rate axis and makes the curve look good even when precision at any usable threshold is poor. PR-AUC (precision-recall AUC) is far more diagnostic here because both of its axes are conditioned on the rare positive class, so it reflects how many false alarms accompany each caught fraud. But the metric that ultimately governs the business decision is EXPECTED COST: (false-negative rate x average fraud loss) + (false-positive rate x cost of a wrongly blocked legitimate transaction and the customer-service fallout), evaluated across candidate thresholds — the only number that moves in the same direction as real money lost or saved.

lessons.workedExample: Take the Epic Sepsis Model figures literally: at Michigan Medicine, 33% sensitivity at 83% specificity means that of every 100 patients who actually developed sepsis, the model's alert caught only 33 in advance and silently missed 67 — while still generating an alert on 18% of ALL hospitalized patients, most of whom never developed sepsis. A hospital that had deployed based on the vendor's reported AUC of 0.76-0.83 alone, without an independent external validation like Wong et al.'s, would have had no way to know its clinicians were drowning in alerts for a model that actually caught only one in three real cases — the gap between vendor-reported and externally validated performance was the entire story.
lessons.judgeFraming: These three cases are exactly what a judge probing 'is your evaluation honest' is testing for. Wong et al. shows that a vendor's own reported metric is not independent evidence, and that AUC alone can mask an unusable sensitivity/alert-burden combination in practice. Gulshan et al. shows that publishing one AUC without stating the deployment threshold and its trade-off is incomplete, even for a genuinely excellent model. The fraud case shows that at extreme imbalance, AUC-ROC can be a placid, confidence-inspiring rounding error while PR-AUC and expected cost tell the true story. A judge who asks 'why not just report accuracy or AUC' wants to see that you know exactly which of these three failure modes it would hide.

questions.prompt: Why did Gulshan et al. (2016, JAMA) report TWO operating points instead of one for their diabetic retinopathy model?

options.text: Because the model's AUC was too low to pick a single threshold
Because mass screening (favoring sensitivity) and matching human-grader specificity are two different use cases that no single threshold serves equally well
Because JAMA requires exactly two operating points for all diagnostic papers
Because the two datasets, EyePACS-1 and Messidor-2, could not be combined for technical reasons

explanations.a: The AUC was very high (0.991 on EyePACS-1, 0.990 on Messidor-2); the two operating points exist because of use-case trade-offs, not a low-quality model.
explanations.b: Correct — a high-sensitivity point serves mass screening where missed cases are costliest, while a high-specificity point avoids over-referral; one threshold cannot optimize both goals at once.
explanations.c: This is not a journal formatting requirement; it reflects a genuine clinical deployment trade-off.
explanations.d: The two datasets were validated separately for generalizability, not because they were incompatible; the two operating points reflect a threshold trade-off, not a data-combination issue.

questions.prompt: In Wong et al.'s (2021) external validation of the Epic Sepsis Model, what was the key finding that the vendor's reported AUC had not revealed?

options.text: The model had a much higher AUC (0.95+) in real-world use than the vendor claimed
The model achieved only 33% sensitivity while generating alerts on 18% of all hospitalized patients, and its AUC dropped to 0.63 versus the vendor's claimed 0.76-0.83
The model had perfect specificity but no sensitivity at all
The vendor's AUC of 0.76-0.83 was confirmed exactly in external validation

explanations.a: The externally validated AUC (0.63) was substantially LOWER than the vendor's claim, not higher.
explanations.b: Correct — Wong et al. found AUC 0.63 (95% CI 0.62-0.64), sensitivity 33%, specificity 83%, and alerts on 18% of hospitalized patients while missing 67% of true sepsis cases.
explanations.c: Specificity was 83%, not perfect, and sensitivity was 33%, not zero — both were degraded, not one perfect and one absent.
explanations.d: The externally validated AUC of 0.63 fell well below the vendor's reported 0.76-0.83 range, exposing the internal-versus-external validation gap.

questions.prompt: In a card-fraud system with roughly a 1-in-1,000 fraud rate, why is PR-AUC preferred over AUC-ROC for evaluating the model?

options.text: PR-AUC is always mathematically larger than AUC-ROC

AUC-ROC's false-positive-rate axis is dominated by the huge non-fraud majority, so it stays high even when precision at usable thresholds is poor; PR-AUC's axes are conditioned on the rare positive class
AUC-ROC cannot be computed when the base rate is below 1%
PR-AUC and AUC-ROC always give identical rankings, so the choice does not matter

explanations.a: There is no such general mathematical relationship; PR-AUC is often numerically lower under heavy imbalance.
explanations.b: Correct — with a huge majority class, the false-positive rate denominator is dominated by non-fraud cases, keeping AUC-ROC deceptively high, while PR-AUC's precision axis directly reflects how many false alarms accompany each caught fraud.
explanations.c: AUC-ROC is computable at any base rate; the issue is that it becomes a poor discriminator of model quality, not that it becomes uncomputable.
explanations.d: The two can and do diverge sharply under extreme imbalance, which is exactly why the choice matters here.

questions.prompt: Each case study in this lesson taught one deployment lesson. Match them up by dragging the case studies into the order of the lessons below: (1) an internal, vendor-reported metric is not independent evidence; (2) one summary AUC can hide that different thresholds serve different real-world goals; (3) at extreme class imbalance, the metric must track real financial cost, not just discrimination.

items.text: Gulshan et al., diabetic retinopathy (two operating points)
Wong et al., Epic Sepsis Model (external validation)
Card fraud (1:1000 base rate)

questions.explanation: Lesson (1) — a vendor-reported metric is not independent evidence — is Wong et al.: Epic's own internally reported AUC of 0.76-0.83 collapsed to 0.63 the moment an independent team validated it at Michigan Medicine. Lesson (2) — one summary AUC hides that different thresholds serve different goals — is Gulshan et al.: an AUC of ~0.99 said nothing about whether to deploy the high-sensitivity screening threshold or the high-specificity referral-matching threshold, which is why the paper reported both. Lesson (3) — the metric must track real financial cost — is the card-fraud case: at a 1-in-1,000 base rate, AUC-ROC stays flatteringly high, and only PR-AUC and expected cost move with the money. So the order is Wong, then Gulshan, then fraud.

lessons.label: Reporting a Classifier Honestly at the Fair

sections.heading: The checklist: what a complete report actually contains
sections.body: Every case study in this segment traces back to a report that omitted something. A complete classifier report states CLASS PREVALENCE AND n for every class (so a reader can judge whether 91% accuracy means anything), a NAMED BASELINE (majority-class prediction, a simple logistic regression, or the prior clinical standard — never just 'better than chance' asserted without a number), BOTH ROC and PR curves (ROC alone hides precision collapse under imbalance, as the fraud case showed), an AUC reported WITH A CONFIDENCE INTERVAL (Wong et al. reported 0.63 with 95% CI 0.62-0.64 — the interval is what tells you whether 0.63 versus 0.76 is a real gap or noise), the CHOSEN THRESHOLD with its COST JUSTIFICATION (why this point on the curve, not another), a CHANCE-CORRECTED SUMMARY such as Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) or Cohen's kappa (both penalize a model for being right by luck on an imbalanced majority), and a RELIABILITY DIAGRAM showing whether a predicted 0.8 probability corresponds to an actual 80% event rate.

sections.heading: The standards that codify this: TRIPOD+AI and STARD
sections.body: This is not an invented checklist; it mirrors published reporting standards. TRIPOD+AI (2024 update to the original TRIPOD statement) sets reporting requirements specifically for AI/ML-based prediction models, including calibration, subgroup performance, and intended-use context. STARD (Standards for Reporting of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies), first published in 2003 and updated in STARD 2015, governs diagnostic-accuracy reporting broadly and requires sensitivity, specificity, and the 2x2 confusion table with confidence intervals, not a single summary statistic. Both exist because the biomedical literature accumulated exactly the failures these case studies describe — models reported with one flattering number and no way for an outside reader to check whether it would hold up. STARD 2015 alone lists 30 checklist items, and neither standard treats a single AUC or accuracy figure as sufficient on its own.

sections.heading: Four questions a judge will ask
sections.body: Distilled to the questions a judge actually asks at the table: What's your baseline — does beating 'always predict the majority class' actually mean anything here? Why that threshold — what cost trade-off, stated in real units (missed cases versus false alarms), justifies this specific point on the ROC/PR curve rather than another? What's your error bar — is your reported AUC or F1 a single point estimate, or does it come with a confidence interval or bootstrap spread that tells you whether a competing model's slightly higher number is a real difference? And is your 0.8 really an 80% — does a reliability diagram confirm the model's stated confidence matches its actual hit rate, or is it silently overconfident?

lessons.workedExample: A team reports 'our tumor-type classifier achieves 94% accuracy.' A judge asks the four questions in turn. Baseline: the majority tumor type is 88% of the dataset, so 'always predict majority' already scores 88% — the model's real lift is only 6 points, not 94. Threshold: the team used the scikit-learn default of 0.5 with no cost analysis, even though a missed malignant case is far costlier than a false alarm. Error bar: the 94% has no confidence interval, so a competing 95% claim from another team is statistically indistinguishable. Calibration: a reliability diagram shows predictions of 0.8 confidence are only right 60% of the time — the model is overconfident. All four gaps would have been caught by the checklist before the fair, not at the judging table.
lessons.judgeFraming: This lesson IS the judge's perspective: TRIPOD+AI and STARD exist because reviewers got tired of single flattering numbers with no way to check them, and a science-fair judge trained on or aware of these standards will run exactly this checklist mentally while you present. A team that pre-empts it — stating prevalence, naming a real baseline, showing both curves, giving a confidence interval, justifying the threshold in real costs, reporting a chance-corrected score, and showing a calibration plot — demonstrates it understands evaluation is not a formality tacked onto a finished model, but part of the scientific claim itself.

questions.prompt: Why does a complete classifier report need a NAMED baseline (e.g., majority-class prediction) rather than just the model's own accuracy number?

options.text: Because baselines are required by scikit-learn's API
Because a headline accuracy is meaningless without knowing what a trivial rule would already score on the same class distribution
Because baselines always outperform trained models
Because judges only care about the baseline, not the model

explanations.a: This is a reporting-standards and scientific-reasoning issue, not an API requirement.
explanations.b: Correct — as the worked example shows, 94% accuracy against an 88%-majority-class baseline is only a 6-point real lift, information invisible without the named baseline.
explanations.c: Baselines do not always outperform trained models; a good model should and often does beat them, but the comparison is what makes the number meaningful either way.
explanations.d: Judges care about both; the baseline is context that makes the model's own number interpretable.

questions.prompt: What does a reliability (calibration) diagram check that AUC and F1 do not?

options.text: Whether the model's predicted probabilities match observed event rates (e.g., predictions of 0.8 confidence are right about 80% of the time)
Whether the model runs fast enough for deployment
Whether the training data was collected ethically
Whether the model's ranking of examples by predicted risk is correct

explanations.a: Correct — AUC and F1 are insensitive to whether stated confidence values are accurate; a model can rank examples perfectly (high AUC) while still being badly overconfident or underconfident in its stated probabilities.
explanations.b: Calibration is about probability accuracy, not runtime performance.
explanations.c: Calibration is a statistical property of predicted probabilities, not a data-ethics audit.
explanations.d: Ranking correctness is closer to what AUC itself measures; calibration specifically checks whether the numeric probability values are trustworthy, which AUC does not require.

questions.prompt: Match each reporting standard or metric to what it specifically addresses.

right.text: Reporting standards for AI/ML-based prediction models, incl. calibration and subgroup performance
Reporting standards for diagnostic accuracy studies, incl. full 2x2 tables with confidence intervals
A chance-corrected summary that penalizes a model for being right by luck on an imbalanced majority

questions.explanation: TRIPOD+AI (a 2024 update to TRIPOD) governs AI/ML prediction-model reporting; STARD (2003, updated 2015) governs diagnostic-accuracy study reporting; MCC and Cohen's kappa are chance-corrected metrics that discount the inflation a model gets just from predicting the majority class often.

questions.prompt: A team is assembling their report. Order these checklist items in the sequence they logically depend on one another: (1) state class prevalence and n, (2) name a baseline using that prevalence, (3) justify the chosen threshold's real-world cost trade-off, (4) report a reliability diagram for that threshold's underlying probabilities.

items.text: State class prevalence and n
Name a baseline using that prevalence
Justify the chosen threshold's cost trade-off
Report a reliability diagram

questions.explanation: Prevalence and n must be known before a majority-class baseline can even be computed; the baseline gives context for judging any accuracy number; the threshold choice (and its cost justification) is where the model's probabilities become a decision; the reliability diagram then checks whether those underlying probabilities were trustworthy in the first place.

units.label: Foundations: What a Continuous Forecast Actually Claims

lessons.label: Regression, Forecasting, and Why Time Changes Everything

sections.heading: Cross-sectional assumptions break in time
