sections.body: Ordinary least-squares regression, and the train/test splitting used to evaluate it, both lean on one assumption: rows are exchangeable - shuffle them and nothing about the joint distribution changes. That assumption is exactly why standard k-fold cross-validation picks folds at random with no regard for row order. A forecasting problem breaks it in two specific ways. First, serial dependence: today's temperature, sales figure, or stock price is correlated with yesterday's, so adjacent rows carry shared information that i.i.d. sampling assumes away. Second, nonstationarity: the mean, variance, or seasonal pattern of a series can drift over the sample - a retailer's baseline demand in year three is not the same process as year one. Shuffle a time series into a random train/test split and test rows sit with their immediate temporal neighbors inside the training set; because of serial dependence, the model effectively gets to peek at values correlated with the answer, producing a validation score that looks strong and then collapses in production. Hyndman and Athanasopoulos's Forecasting: Principles and Practice (FPP3) treats this as a first-principles rule: time-series cross-validation must always respect order, evaluating on a rolling or expanding origin rather than random folds.

sections.heading: The vocabulary of forecasting problems
sections.body: The forecast origin, T, is the last time period with known data - the point the model stands at. The horizon, h, counts steps ahead from that origin: a forecast for y_{T+h} is an h-step-ahead forecast, and reported error must always specify which h it belongs to, since error typically grows with h. Lead time, borrowed from operations and supply-chain forecasting, is related but distinct: it is the delay between making a decision (ordering stock) and that decision taking effect, and it can exceed or fall short of the modeling horizon depending on production and shipping constraints. A one-step forecast predicts only y_{T+1}; multi-step forecasting predicts a whole path y_{T+1}, ..., y_{T+H}. Two strategies build that path. The recursive (iterated) strategy fits one one-step-ahead model and feeds each forecast back in as if it were observed data to produce the next: forecast y_{T+1}, then use it to forecast y_{T+2}, and so on, so errors compound and typically widen across the horizon. The direct strategy instead fits H separate models, each mapped straight from data available at T to a specific y_{T+h}, avoiding error propagation but needing H models whose forecasts across h need not even agree with each other - what FPP3 calls a lack of forecast coherence.

lessons.workedExample: A grocery chain's model stands at forecast origin T = 'end of Sunday' and needs a 7-day horizon for the coming week's staffing. Using the recursive strategy, it forecasts Monday's sales from Sunday's actuals, then plugs that Monday forecast in as if it were real data to forecast Tuesday, and so on through next Sunday - one model, but a bad Monday forecast drags every later day off too. Using the direct strategy, the chain instead trains seven separate models: one mapping Sunday's data straight to Monday, another straight to Tuesday, up through a model mapping Sunday's data straight to next Sunday. The seven direct forecasts never compound each other's errors, but nothing forces Tuesday's forecast to stay consistent with Monday's.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'how did you validate this' is testing whether the team understands why forecasting cannot borrow classification's random train/test split. Answering 'we did k-fold cross-validation' for a time series is a tell that the team never registered serial dependence or nonstationarity, and a sharp judge will immediately ask whether folds respected time order. The stronger answer names the forecast origin and horizon explicitly, states whether the model is recursive or direct, and explains that a recursive model's error typically grows with h precisely because early mistakes feed forward. That vocabulary signals the team read forecasting as its own discipline, not regression with a date column attached.

questions.prompt: Why is shuffling rows into a random train/test split invalid for a time series model?

options.text: Because time series data sets are always too small for k-fold cross-validation
Because serial dependence means neighboring rows share information, so a random split leaks correlated future data into training
Because regression models cannot process date-time columns
Because shuffling would change the units of the target variable

explanations.a: Sample size is not the issue - even a large time series still violates the exchangeability assumption a random split relies on.
explanations.b: Correct - adjacent rows are correlated through serial dependence, so a random split hands the model test-adjacent information during training, inflating validation scores.
explanations.c: Date-time columns are not the mechanism; the problem is the statistical dependence between neighboring observations, not a data-type limitation.
explanations.d: Shuffling never changes units - it changes which rows are visible to training, which is the actual problem.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of the recursive (iterated) multi-step forecasting strategy in the order they occur.

items.text: Forecast y_{T+1} using only actual data available at origin T
Treat the y_{T+1} forecast as if it were observed data
Forecast y_{T+2} using the origin's actual data plus the y_{T+1} forecast
Repeat the feed-forward step through y_{T+H}, so early errors propagate into every later forecast

questions.explanation: Recursive forecasting fits a single one-step model, then feeds each forecast back in as if it were real data to generate the next step, which is exactly why early errors compound across the horizon.

questions.prompt: Match each forecasting term to its definition.

right.text: The last time period for which actual data is known
The number of steps ahead from the origin being predicted
The delay between making a decision and that decision taking effect, which need not equal the horizon
Fitting a separate model per horizon step, mapped straight from origin data, avoiding compounding error but risking incoherent forecasts across h

questions.explanation: The origin is the last known data point, the horizon counts steps ahead from it, lead time is the decision-to-effect delay that can differ from the horizon, and the direct strategy trades away error compounding for a lack of guaranteed coherence across horizons.

questions.prompt: What is the primary disadvantage of the recursive (iterated) multi-step forecasting strategy compared to the direct strategy?

options.text: It requires training a separate model for every horizon step
Errors from early-horizon forecasts feed forward and compound into later-horizon forecasts
It cannot be used to produce a one-step-ahead forecast
It always requires more training data than the direct strategy

explanations.a: That describes the direct strategy, which fits one model per horizon - the recursive strategy fits only a single one-step model.
explanations.b: Correct - because each forecast is fed back in as pseudo-data, an early mistake is baked into every subsequent step's input.
explanations.c: A one-step forecast is exactly what the recursive strategy's single model produces at h=1; the issue only appears at longer horizons.
explanations.d: Data requirements are not the distinguishing factor between the two strategies; error propagation is.

lessons.label: The Loss Function Picks the Target: Mean, Median, or Quantile

sections.heading: Every loss function silently names a target
sections.body: Squared error loss, (y - yhat)^2, has an expectation that is minimized precisely when yhat equals the conditional mean of y - take the derivative with respect to yhat and set it to zero, and the mean falls out. Absolute error loss, |y - yhat|, is minimized instead by the conditional median, a classical result behind L1 regression: the median is the point that splits absolute deviations evenly on either side. Pinball (quantile) loss at level tau, defined as tau times (y - yhat) when y is at or above yhat and (1 - tau) times (yhat - y) otherwise, is minimized by the tau-quantile of the conditional distribution - the loss underlying the quantile regression Roger Koenker and Gilbert Bassett introduced in 1978. A parallel derivation shows why: differentiating pinball loss's expectation with respect to yhat and setting the result to zero shows the tau-quantile is exactly the value where tau equals the probability mass at or below it, which is why Koenker and Bassett's method could specify tau anywhere in (0,1) and recover the corresponding quantile directly, without fitting a full distributional model. Three different loss functions, three completely different target numbers. The loss function is not a scorekeeping detail added after modeling - it defines the estimand the model is being asked to produce.

sections.heading: Elicitability and consistent scoring functions
sections.body: Tilmann Gneiting formalized this relationship in 'Making and Evaluating Point Forecasts' (Journal of the American Statistical Association, 2011, vol. 106, pp. 746-762). A statistical functional T, such as the mean, median, or a given quantile, is elicitable if some scoring function makes T the unique minimizer of expected score - squared error, absolute error, and pinball loss are exactly the 'consistent' scoring functions for the mean, median, and tau-quantile respectively. Gneiting also showed some functionals resist elicitation entirely: the variance and expected shortfall cannot be uniquely elicited alone by any single scoring function. Fissler and Ziegel's 2016 follow-up in the Annals of Statistics ('Higher order elicitability and Osband's principle') proved that value-at-risk, already known to be elicitable as a quantile, and expected shortfall, which is not elicitable alone, ARE jointly elicitable together. Newey and Powell's 1987 paper on asymmetric least squares introduced a further elicitable family, expectiles, a hybrid between the mean and a quantile used in some risk-management and electricity-demand pipelines precisely because they stay jointly elicitable alongside the mean. Practically: on a right-skewed demand series, the mean sits above the median. A model trained to minimize RMSE chases the mean, pulled upward by rare spikes; judged instead by MAE, which rewards hitting the median, it loses to a model tuned for MAE from the start - not because anything broke, but because it was answering a different question.

lessons.workedExample: A logistics company models daily parcel counts, a right-skewed series: most days sit near 800 parcels, but roughly one day in twenty spikes past 3,000 during promotions. Team A tunes its model on RMSE and its forecasts cluster around 950, pulled upward by the rare spikes it is trying not to miss badly. Team B tunes on MAE and its forecasts cluster around 810, close to the typical day. Graded on MAE, Team B wins by construction - its loss targeted the median, the value MAE itself rewards. Graded on RMSE, Team A wins instead - not because it is the better model, but because each team's training loss matched the functional their grading metric elicits.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who hears 'our model achieves lower MAE' after being told the team optimized RMSE should ask what loss function the model was actually trained on - if the answer is squared error, the comparison pits a model tuned for one target against a metric rewarding a different one. Citing Gneiting's elicitability framework by name shows the team understands that mean, median, and quantile are three different numbers a model can output, and that fairly judging a model means training and grading with the SAME consistent scoring function, not switching the metric after training and calling it evaluation.

questions.prompt: Which functional does squared error loss elicit - that is, which value uniquely minimizes its expectation?

options.text: The conditional mean
The conditional median
The conditional mode
The 90th percentile of the conditional distribution

explanations.a: Correct - setting the derivative of expected squared error to zero yields the conditional mean as the unique minimizer.
explanations.b: The median minimizes expected absolute error, not squared error.
explanations.c: The mode is not the target of any of the three standard loss functions covered here.
explanations.d: A specific high percentile is elicited by pinball loss at that tau level, not by squared error.

questions.prompt: Match each loss function to the functional it elicits (the value that uniquely minimizes its expectation).

right.text: The conditional mean
The conditional median
The tau-quantile of the conditional distribution

questions.explanation: Squared error is minimized by the mean, absolute error by the median, and pinball loss at level tau by the tau-quantile - the basis of Koenker and Bassett's 1978 quantile regression.

questions.prompt: According to Gneiting's 2011 elicitability framework, what does it mean for a statistical functional (like the mean or a quantile) to be 'elicitable'?

options.text: It can be computed without any data
There exists a scoring function whose expected value is uniquely minimized by that functional
It is elicitable only when the underlying distribution is normal
It means the functional equals the sample size

explanations.a: Elicitability is a property tying a functional to a scoring function under a distribution, not a claim about needing no data.
explanations.b: Correct - this is Gneiting's definition: a consistent scoring function exists whose expected score is uniquely minimized at the true functional value.
explanations.c: Elicitability holds under general conditions and is not restricted to the normal distribution.
explanations.d: Sample size plays no role in the definition of elicitability.

questions.prompt: Put these developments in the loss-function and elicitability literature in chronological order.

items.text: Koenker and Bassett introduce quantile regression built on pinball loss (1978)
Gneiting formalizes elicitability and consistent scoring functions for point forecasts (2011)
Fissler and Ziegel prove value-at-risk and expected shortfall are jointly elicitable (2016)

questions.explanation: Quantile regression predates the formal elicitability framework by decades; Gneiting's 2011 paper named and systematized elicitability, and Fissler and Ziegel extended it in 2016 to jointly elicited pairs like value-at-risk and expected shortfall.

questions.prompt: On a right-skewed demand series, why does a model trained to minimize RMSE tend to forecast higher values than a model trained to minimize MAE?

options.text: RMSE-trained models always add a fixed constant to every prediction
RMSE targets the conditional mean, which right skew pulls upward, while MAE targets the conditional median, which sits closer to the typical value
MAE-trained models systematically underfit compared to RMSE-trained models
There is no real difference; the two models converge to the same forecast on any skewed series

explanations.a: No such constant adjustment exists - the difference comes from which functional each loss targets.
explanations.b: Correct - in a right-skewed distribution the mean exceeds the median, and each loss function pulls its model toward the functional it elicits.
explanations.c: This is not an underfitting effect - it is a difference in which target each loss defines.
explanations.d: The two models target different functionals and will diverge whenever the distribution is skewed, not converge.

lessons.label: Point Forecast vs. Predictive Distribution

sections.heading: A point forecast collapses a distribution into one number
sections.body: A forecasting model, properly understood, produces a full predictive distribution over possible future values - not a single number. The point forecast usually reported ('42 units next month') is one functional squeezed out of that distribution: the mean, the median, or some other quantile, per the elicitability framework covered in the prior lesson. Reporting only the point throws away everything the model knows about its own confidence. '42 units' with an implicit spread of 38 to 46 is a wildly different claim from '42 units' with a spread of 5 to 200, even though the headline number is identical - only the distribution underneath can tell the two apart.

sections.heading: Why a bare point forecast is unfalsifiable
sections.body: The claim '42 units next month,' stated alone, cannot be checked for calibration - only for a single realized point error, once. You cannot ask whether a forecast was well-calibrated without a stated uncertainty in the first place. Gneiting, Balabdaoui, and Raftery's 'Probabilistic Forecasts, Calibration and Sharpness' (Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 2007, vol. 69, pp. 243-268) formalizes the goal a good probabilistic forecast should chase: maximize sharpness (keep the distribution as narrow as possible) subject to calibration (the stated intervals must contain the true outcome the stated fraction of the time). A bare point number cannot even be evaluated against that principle - it has no calibration to check in the first place, only a single error after the fact. This is why weather services report 'a 70% chance of rain' rather than a bare 'it will rain': the percentage is a calibratable claim, checkable across many days, while a bare yes-or-no forecast is not.

sections.heading: The hierarchy of forecast objects
sections.body: Forecasts form a hierarchy of increasing informativeness. A point forecast is a single number. A prediction interval adds a lower and upper bound at a stated confidence level, such as an 80% interval. A quantile set reports several quantiles at once, sketching a coarse shape of the distribution - the 2020 M5 Uncertainty competition, run alongside the main M5 accuracy competition, required exactly this: nine quantile levels (0.005, 0.025, 0.165, 0.250, 0.500, 0.750, 0.835, 0.975, 0.995) forecast for each of 42,840 Walmart series, over 385,000 forecasts in total. A full predictive distribution reports the entire CDF or density. Each step up is scored by progressively richer tools this segment builds toward: prediction intervals by coverage and width, quantile sets by pinball loss averaged across levels, and full distributions by proper scoring rules such as the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), which integrates squared distance between the forecast CDF and the true outcome's step function across every threshold at once.

lessons.workedExample: A demand planner receives two forecasts for next month's orders, both reporting a point value of 42 units. Model A also reports an 80% prediction interval of [38, 46]; Model B reports an 80% interval of [5, 120]. The point forecasts are identical, so a report listing only '42 units' cannot distinguish them - yet Model A is telling the planner to stock tightly around 42, while Model B is really saying 'anywhere from 5 to 120, we have almost no idea.' Only by demanding the interval, not just the point, can the planner see that Model B's point forecast is nearly worthless despite matching Model A's number exactly.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who hears '42 units next month' should immediately ask 'what's the interval around that' or 'how confident are you.' A team that cannot answer is implicitly claiming false precision - a single number dressed up as a forecast when no uncertainty was ever quantified. The strongest answer distinguishes the point forecast from the underlying predictive distribution by name, states which functional (mean, median, or a given quantile) that point represents, and names which tool - interval, quantile set, or full density - will score the model's actual distributional claim rather than just today's single lucky or unlucky point error.

questions.prompt: What is a point forecast, precisely?

options.text: The full predictive distribution over future outcomes
A single functional (such as the mean, median, or a quantile) extracted from the full predictive distribution
A raw, unprocessed data point from the training set
The forecast origin, T

explanations.a: The full predictive distribution is the richer object a point forecast is extracted from, not the point forecast itself.
explanations.b: Correct - a point forecast is exactly one functional (mean, median, or a given quantile) squeezed out of the predictive distribution.
explanations.c: A point forecast is a model output about the future, not a raw observed training row.
explanations.d: The forecast origin is the last known time period, a separate concept from the forecast's output value.

questions.prompt: Order these forecast objects from least informative to most informative.

items.text: Point forecast (a single number)
Prediction interval (lower and upper bound at a stated confidence level)
Quantile set (several quantiles reported at once)
Full predictive distribution (entire CDF or density)

questions.explanation: Each step adds information: a bound around the point, several quantiles sketching a coarse shape, and finally the complete distribution over every possible outcome.

questions.prompt: According to Gneiting, Balabdaoui, and Raftery's 'sharpness subject to calibration' principle, what makes a probabilistic forecast good?

options.text: It should be as narrow as possible, with no requirement that its intervals actually contain the true outcome
It should be as sharp (narrow) as possible while remaining calibrated - its stated intervals contain the outcome the stated fraction of the time
It should always report the widest possible interval to avoid ever being wrong
Sharpness and calibration are the same property under different names

explanations.a: Sharpness without calibration is meaningless - a narrow interval that never contains the truth is useless, which is exactly why calibration is the constraint.
explanations.b: Correct - the principle is to maximize sharpness subject to the constraint that calibration holds, not to sacrifice one for the other.
explanations.c: Maximizing width alone trivially achieves calibration but destroys sharpness, which the principle explicitly does not want.
explanations.d: They are distinct properties: calibration concerns coverage accuracy, sharpness concerns how narrow the forecast is.

questions.prompt: Match each forecast object to the tool later used to score it.

right.text: A single realized error, such as MAE or RMSE
Coverage rate and interval width
Pinball loss averaged across multiple quantile levels
The continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), integrating error across every threshold at once

questions.explanation: Point forecasts get a single realized error metric, intervals are scored by coverage and width, quantile sets by pinball loss across levels, and full distributions by proper scoring rules like CRPS.

lessons.label: The Baselines You Must Beat: Naive, Seasonal Naive, Drift, and Mean

sections.heading: Four baseline formulas
sections.body: Naive: yhat_{T+h} = y_T for every h - carry the last observed value forward unchanged. Seasonal naive: yhat_{T+h} = y_{T+h-m}, where m is the seasonal period (m = 7 for daily data with weekly seasonality, m = 12 for monthly data with yearly seasonality) - carry forward the value from the same point in the last full cycle. Drift: yhat_{T+h} = y_T + h times (y_T - y_1)/(T - 1) - draws a straight line through the first and last observed points and extrapolates that average per-period change forward. Historical mean: yhat_{T+h} = the average of all observed y_1 through y_T for every h - ignores time structure entirely, forecasting the long-run average regardless of horizon. When the horizon extends beyond one full seasonal cycle, seasonal naive wraps around, referencing the same point in the most recently completed cycle rather than failing outright. None of these four requires fitting anything beyond arithmetic on the series itself, which is exactly why FPP3 calls them 'benchmark methods' and why they set the floor any real model must clear.

sections.heading: Why naive is hard to beat: the random-walk result
sections.body: Financial asset prices and many day-to-day weather series behave close to a random walk, y_t = y_{t-1} + epsilon_t, where epsilon is unpredictable noise. Under a true random walk, the theoretically optimal (minimum expected squared error) forecast for any horizon is exactly the naive forecast, since E[y_{T+h} | data] = y_T. This is the forecasting-side implication of Eugene Fama's efficient-market hypothesis (1970): if all available information is already priced in, the best predictor of tomorrow's price is today's price, and no model beats naive on average, only sometimes by luck. Meteorologists observe a parallel pattern at very short lead times - persistence forecasting, guessing tomorrow's temperature as today's - though modern numerical weather prediction overtakes persistence at longer horizons once more information becomes usable. The same logic explains why decades of technical-analysis backtests on daily closing prices of major indices have struggled to beat a simple buy-and-hold, naive-adjacent strategy after accounting for transaction costs.

sections.heading: Hyndman's baseline rule
sections.body: Rob Hyndman, co-author with George Athanasopoulos of Forecasting: Principles and Practice (FPP3), insists a reported error metric is meaningless in isolation: 'my model got RMSE 4.2' answers nothing until it sits beside the RMSE a naive or seasonal-naive baseline achieves on the identical held-out data. Beating naive by 5% might be a hard-won result on a near-random-walk series; the same 5% margin against an easy seasonal-naive baseline on a strongly seasonal series may mean the model barely tries. FPP3 builds the scaled errors covered later in this segment on exactly this discipline, but the underlying rule predates any specific metric: always print the baseline's number beside the model's number, on the same data, under the same loss.

lessons.workedExample: A retailer's daily sales series has weekly seasonality (m = 7) and a mild upward trend. Over the last 4 weeks of held-out data, naive (repeat yesterday) scores RMSE 38; seasonal naive (repeat the same weekday last week) scores RMSE 22; drift (extrapolate the trend from day 1 to day T) scores RMSE 29; and the historical mean scores RMSE 61. A gradient-boosted model trained on lagged features and calendar signals scores RMSE 19. Reported alone, 'RMSE 19' sounds solid. Placed beside seasonal naive's RMSE 22, the model is barely improving on a one-line rule that ignores every feature the model uses - a result that should make the team ask whether the extra complexity is earning its keep.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge should always ask 'compared to what baseline?' the moment a team reports a bare error number. A team that cannot immediately name their naive or seasonal-naive RMSE on the same test set has skipped the cheapest sanity check in forecasting - and on close-to-random-walk data like daily prices, failing to beat naive is not a minor miss, it is evidence the model is fitting noise. Citing Hyndman and Athanasopoulos's FPP3 baseline discipline by name, and reporting the baseline number alongside the model's number on identical data, signals the team understands that 'good' is always a relative, not absolute, claim in forecasting.

questions.prompt: Match each baseline method to its formula.

right.text: yhat_{T+h} = y_T
yhat_{T+h} = y_{T+h-m}
yhat_{T+h} = y_T + h times (y_T - y_1)/(T - 1)
yhat_{T+h} = the average of y_1 through y_T

questions.explanation: Naive repeats the last value, seasonal naive repeats the value from one full seasonal cycle back, drift extrapolates the average change between the first and last observed points, and the historical mean ignores time entirely.

questions.prompt: Under a true random-walk data-generating process, which forecast is the theoretically optimal (minimum expected squared error) forecast for any horizon h?

options.text: The historical mean
The naive forecast (last observed value)
The seasonal naive forecast
The drift forecast

explanations.a: The historical mean is optimal only if the series has no persistence at all, not under a random walk where the last value carries all the information.
explanations.b: Correct - for y_t = y_{t-1} + epsilon_t, E[y_{T+h} | data] = y_T exactly, making naive the optimal forecast.
explanations.c: Seasonal naive assumes a repeating seasonal structure a random walk does not have.
explanations.d: Drift assumes a fixed deterministic trend, which a pure random walk does not possess.

questions.prompt: According to the baseline discipline described in Hyndman and Athanasopoulos's FPP3, what is wrong with reporting 'my model achieved RMSE 4.2' with nothing else?

options.text: Nothing - RMSE alone is always sufficient to judge a forecasting model
RMSE is uninterpretable without a baseline RMSE, such as naive or seasonal naive, computed on the same held-out data
RMSE should never be used for time series, only scaled errors
4.2 is too small a number to be a realistic RMSE

explanations.a: A bare RMSE cannot be judged as good or bad without knowing what a trivial baseline scores on the same data.
explanations.b: Correct - this is the exact discipline FPP3 insists on: always place the model's error beside a baseline's error on identical data.
explanations.c: RMSE remains usable for time series; the issue is reporting it without any point of comparison, not the metric itself.
explanations.d: The magnitude of 4.2 depends entirely on the series' scale and units, which is precisely why a baseline comparison is needed.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of computing the drift forecast for a horizon h in the correct order.

items.text: Take the first observed value y_1 and the last observed value y_T
Compute the average per-period change: (y_T - y_1)/(T - 1)
Multiply the average per-period change by the horizon h
Add that product to the last observed value y_T to get yhat_{T+h}

questions.explanation: Drift first measures the average change per period between the first and last points, scales that rate by the horizon, and adds the result to the last observed value.

lessons.label: Where Forecast Error Comes From: Noise, Bias, Variance, and the Ceiling

sections.heading: The bias-variance-noise decomposition, applied to forecasting
sections.body: For a model fhat estimated from training data, expected squared forecast error at a given origin decomposes into three additive terms: E[(y - fhat)^2] = Var(epsilon) + (E[fhat] - f)^2 + Var(fhat) - irreducible noise, bias-squared, and estimation variance. This is the classic bias-variance tradeoff, formalized by Geman, Bienenstock, and Doursat in 'Neural Networks and the Bias/Variance Dilemma' (Neural Computation, 1992), applied here to a forecasting model whose input is the forecast origin and lookback window rather than an ordinary feature vector. The irreducible noise term, Var(epsilon), is a property of the series itself, not the model - it cannot be shrunk by more data, better features, or more compute, however sophisticated the fitting procedure.

sections.heading: The predictability ceiling: not all series are equally forecastable
sections.body: Some series carry strong deterministic structure - a trend, a repeating season; others sit close to pure noise. Mahmoud Kaboudan's 1999 measure in the Journal of Forecasting made this ceiling explicit before any model is even fit: a genetic-programming model's sum of squared errors on the real series is compared against its error on a randomly scrambled version of the same series, giving an index (Kaboudan's kappa) that runs from 0 (purely stochastic, scrambling changes nothing) to 100 (highly predictable, scrambling destroys performance). A related, more common approach uses spectral entropy - how spread out a series' power spectrum is across frequencies - as a forecastability feature, used in Hyndman, Wang, and Laptev's 2015 'Large-Scale Unusual Time Series Detection' and the accompanying tsfeatures toolkit to flag low-signal series automatically before committing modeling effort. Kang, Hyndman, and Smith-Miles extended this in a 2017 International Journal of Forecasting paper, plotting thousands of series by spectral entropy alongside trend and seasonal strength to map out an entire 'instance space' of forecastability before any single model is chosen.

sections.heading: Two conclusions students get backwards
sections.body: First, a 'bad-looking' RMSE can be the best achievable number on a genuinely noisy series - if Var(epsilon) dominates the decomposition, no modeling skill closes that gap, and comparing the raw number against a cleaner series compares two different ceilings, not two skill levels. Second, a 'great' R-squared on a strongly trending series can be nearly free: R-squared measures improvement over predicting the training mean, and a dominant trend means even a naive or drift baseline already captures most of that variance, so a high R-squared can reflect the series' own predictability ceiling rather than modeling skill. The fix is the same in both directions: check what a naive baseline and a forecastability measure say about the series before judging the model's number in isolation.

lessons.workedExample: Two teams forecast different series. Team A models airline ticket demand with strong weekly and holiday seasonality; their model achieves R-squared = 0.94. Team B models minute-by-minute foot traffic in an empty overnight parking garage, dominated by sensor noise; their best possible model achieves R-squared = 0.31. Team A's high R-squared mostly reflects the series' own strong seasonal ceiling - a seasonal-naive baseline alone would likely score close to 0.90. Team B's lower R-squared, once compared against a forecastability measure showing the series sits close to spectral white noise, may represent an excellent model already sitting near the irreducible-noise ceiling. Comparing 0.94 to 0.31 head-to-head, without checking each series' ceiling first, would wrongly declare Team A's model the better one.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who says 'your R-squared of 0.94 beats their 0.31, so your model is better' has skipped the ceiling check. The strong answer asks what a naive or seasonal-naive baseline would score on each series first, and separately reports each series' forecastability - spectral entropy or a Kaboudan-style scrambled-series comparison - before ever comparing model quality across series. Naming the bias-variance-noise decomposition explicitly, and pointing at the irreducible noise term as the reason a 'bad' RMSE can be un-improvable, signals the team understands that forecast quality is only ever measured relative to what that specific series allows, not against a universal bar.

questions.prompt: Expected squared forecast error decomposes into irreducible noise, bias-squared, and which third term?

options.text: Estimation variance - how much the fitted model's output would change across different training samples
Sample size
The forecast horizon h
The number of seasonal periods

explanations.a: Correct - Var(fhat), the estimation variance, is the third additive term alongside irreducible noise and bias-squared.
explanations.b: Sample size influences the size of the variance term but is not itself one of the three decomposition terms.
explanations.c: The horizon affects how large each term grows but is not one of the three additive components.
explanations.d: Seasonal periods are a property of a specific series, not a general term in the decomposition.

questions.prompt: Which term in the bias-variance-noise decomposition cannot be reduced by any amount of additional data, better features, or model tuning?

options.text: Bias
Estimation variance
Irreducible noise
All three terms are always reducible given enough data

explanations.a: Bias can shrink with a better-specified model or more relevant features.
explanations.b: Estimation variance can shrink with more training data or a lower-variance estimator.
explanations.c: Correct - irreducible noise, Var(epsilon), is a property of the series itself and stays fixed no matter how the model is improved.
explanations.d: Irreducible noise is, by definition, the one term that no modeling improvement can touch.

questions.prompt: Match each researcher or method to what it measures or describes.

right.text: Compares a genetic-programming model's error on the real series against its error on a randomly scrambled version of the same series
Measures how concentrated a series' power spectrum is in a few frequencies versus spread out like white noise
Splits expected squared forecast error into three additive sources of error

questions.explanation: Kaboudan's kappa index compares real-versus-scrambled prediction error, spectral entropy summarizes how noise-like a series' frequency spectrum is, and the bias-variance-noise decomposition splits forecast error into irreducible noise, bias-squared, and estimation variance.

questions.prompt: Put the reasoning steps in order for why a high R-squared on a strongly trending series can be a nearly free result rather than evidence of modeling skill.

items.text: Identify that the series has a strong deterministic trend or seasonal pattern
Compute what a naive or seasonal-naive baseline scores on that same series
Observe that the baseline alone already captures most of the variance around the training mean
Conclude that a model's true skill is only the R-squared it adds beyond that baseline ceiling, not the raw R-squared

questions.explanation: A high R-squared only reflects genuine modeling skill once it is checked against what a trivial baseline already achieves on that same trending or seasonal series.

lessons.label: Scale, Units, and the Problem of Comparing Errors Across Series

sections.heading: Why a bare RMSE cannot travel
sections.body: RMSE = 4.2 what - dollars, units sold, degrees Celsius? And relative to what typical magnitude? The number is scale-dependent: it inherits the units of y, so an RMSE of 4.2 against a series averaging 5 units a day is catastrophic, over 80% relative error, while the identical RMSE against a series averaging 5,000 units a day is noise-level, under a tenth of one percent. A raw error number can only be compared to another raw error number computed on a series with matching units and comparable magnitude - anything else is comparing numbers that happen to look alike.

sections.heading: Averaging RMSE across series is arithmetic nonsense
sections.body: Suppose a method is evaluated across many series at once - a retail chain's thousands of SKUs, or a macro model spanning many countries. Naively averaging each series' RMSE lets the few high-magnitude series dominate the average completely, drowning out how the method performs on low-magnitude series, even when the method is proportionally worse there. This is exactly the problem the Makridakis (M) competitions had to solve to rank dozens of forecasting methods on one leaderboard: the M3-Competition (Makridakis and Hibon, 2000) spanned 3,003 heterogeneous series; M4 (2018) scaled to 100,000 series and 61 methods; M5 (2020), run on Kaggle using Walmart data, spanned roughly 42,000 hierarchical series with wildly different daily volumes. M5 compounded the problem further by requiring forecasts at multiple aggregation levels of the same hierarchy at once - individual SKU, store, and total company demand - so a scale mismatch existed even within a single retailer's own series, not just across different retailers. None of these competitions could be ranked on raw, unscaled error without letting the largest-volume series silently decide the winner.

sections.heading: Three escape routes, previewed
sections.body: Percentage errors divide each error by the actual value, converting to a unit-free percentage - but blow up when y is zero or near zero, a routine occurrence in intermittent demand data. Relative errors compare the model's error against a baseline model's error, such as naive, computed on the SAME series, producing a ratio that cancels units and magnitude together since both numerator and denominator share them. Scaled errors divide by a fixed, series-specific denominator computed once from the training data's own historical variability - this segment's mean absolute scaled error (MASE), introduced by Hyndman and Koehler in a 2006 International Journal of Forecasting paper, divides MAE by the in-sample MAE of the naive one-step forecast, staying well-behaved even at zero - a MASE below 1 means the model beat naive, above 1 means it did not, regardless of the series' original units. Percentage, relative, and scaled are the entire menu Unit 2 works through, because the M-competitions proved no single one is flawless everywhere.

lessons.workedExample: A regional retail chain evaluates one forecasting method across two stores: a rural outlet selling an average of 5 units a day of a slow-moving item, and a flagship store selling an average of 5,000 units a day of a bestseller. The method scores RMSE 4.2 at both. At the rural store, RMSE 4.2 against a mean of 5 is enormous - the model is often off by close to its entire average sales volume. At the flagship store, RMSE 4.2 against a mean of 5,000 is negligible, under a tenth of a percent. Averaging the two RMSE values would report the method as performing identically at both stores, hiding that it is nearly useless at one and excellent at the other.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge should treat any RMSE reported without its series' typical magnitude or units as incomplete. If a team evaluates across multiple series - several stores, sensors, or countries - and reports one averaged RMSE, the sharp follow-up is whether the high-magnitude series are silently dominating that average. The strongest teams name which of the three escape routes - percentage, relative-to-baseline, or scaled - they used to make errors comparable across series, and can explain why they picked it, such as avoiding a percentage metric's blow-up near zero sales. Naming the M-competitions as the reason this problem is well studied signals real familiarity, not an improvised fix.

questions.prompt: Why can an RMSE of 4.2 not be judged as 'good' or 'bad' on its own?

options.text: Because RMSE is only defined for classification problems
Because RMSE inherits the units of y, so its meaning depends on the series' typical magnitude and units
Because RMSE can only be computed once a model has been deployed
Because 4.2 is not a valid RMSE value

explanations.a: RMSE is a standard regression and forecasting metric, not something specific to classification.
explanations.b: Correct - the same RMSE value can represent a huge relative error on a small-magnitude series or a trivial one on a large-magnitude series.
explanations.c: RMSE is computed on any held-out data, deployed or not; timing is not the issue.
explanations.d: 4.2 is a perfectly ordinary RMSE value; the problem is interpreting it without context, not its validity.

questions.prompt: Why is naively averaging RMSE across many heterogeneous series (different products, stores, or countries) misleading?

options.text: Because RMSE cannot be averaged mathematically at all
Because the few high-magnitude series dominate the average, hiding how the method performs on low-magnitude series
Because averaging requires every series to have the exact same length
Because RMSE is undefined whenever more than one series is involved

explanations.a: The arithmetic of averaging is fine; the problem is what the resulting number actually represents.
explanations.b: Correct - unscaled errors from large-volume series overwhelm the average, even when the method is proportionally worse elsewhere.
explanations.c: Series length is not the source of the problem; differing scale and magnitude are.
explanations.d: RMSE remains well defined per series; the issue is combining several of them into one misleading average.

questions.prompt: Match each escape route for cross-series comparison to its definition.

right.text: Divides each error by the actual value, producing a unit-free percentage that blows up near y = 0
Compares the model's error against a baseline model's error (such as naive) computed on the SAME series
Divides by a fixed denominator computed once from the series' own historical in-sample variability, such as MASE

questions.explanation: Percentage errors normalize by the actual value and fail near zero, relative errors normalize against a baseline's error on the same series, and scaled errors like MASE normalize against a fixed historical denominator that stays well-behaved at zero.

questions.prompt: Put these Makridakis (M) forecasting competitions in chronological order.

items.text: M1 competition (1982) - the original forecasting competition
M3 competition (2000) - expanded to 3,003 series
M4 competition (2018) - 100,000 series, 61 methods
M5 competition (2020) - Walmart hierarchical retail data, run on Kaggle

questions.explanation: The Makridakis competitions ran M1 in 1982, M3 in 2000 with 3,003 series, M4 in 2018 with 100,000 series, and M5 in 2020 on Kaggle using roughly 42,000 hierarchical Walmart series.

units.label: Error Measures and Where Each One Lies to You

lessons.label: MAE and RMSE: Definitions and What Their Gap Tells You

sections.heading: Two ways to average an error
sections.body: Mean Absolute Error and Root Mean Squared Error both summarize a set of prediction errors e_i = y_i - yhat_i into one number, but they aggregate differently. MAE = (1/n)Σ|e_i| takes the arithmetic mean of absolute errors -- every unit of error counts the same regardless of size. RMSE = sqrt((1/n)Σe_i^2) squares each error before averaging, then takes a square root to return to the original units -- a single large error contributes disproportionately because squaring amplifies it. Algebra fixes the relationship between the two: by the power-mean inequality, RMSE is always at least as large as MAE, with equality only when every |e_i| is identical. An upper bound also holds: because Σe_i^2 <= (Σ|e_i|)^2 for nonnegative terms, RMSE <= sqrt(n) x MAE. So the gap between the two isn't noise -- the ratio RMSE/MAE is itself a diagnostic. A ratio near 1 means errors are roughly uniform in size, a well-behaved model. A ratio climbing toward sqrt(n) means a small number of errors are dominating the sum -- the model is usually fine but occasionally very wrong.

sections.heading: The Willmott-Matsuura vs. Chai-Draxler fight
sections.body: This isn't a settled question in the literature. Cort Willmott and Kenji Matsuura's 2005 Climate Research paper, 'Advantages of the mean absolute error (MAE) over the root mean square error (RMSE) in assessing average model performance,' argued researchers should stop reporting RMSE at all: because RMSE's value depends on the distribution of error magnitudes and on sample size in ways MAE does not, two models with the same average error can produce different RMSE values, making RMSE an ambiguous summary of 'typical' error. The paper argued forcefully that RMSE should be abandoned in favor of MAE, and became the standard citation for that position in climate and hydrology work. Tianfeng Chai and Roland Draxler answered in 2014 in Geoscientific Model Development, 'Root mean square error (RMSE) or mean absolute error (MAE)? -- Arguments against avoiding RMSE in the literature.' They countered that RMSE is not ambiguous when the error distribution is known: if errors are approximately Gaussian, RMSE has a direct, well-defined relationship to the standard deviation of that distribution, which MAE lacks, making RMSE the theoretically correct measure under that assumption. Neither side won outright, and the debate is still cited on both sides more than a decade after Chai and Draxler's reply -- the practical lesson is that the choice encodes an assumption about the error distribution, and a report stating only one number hides information the other would reveal. A referee reading either paper in isolation would come away with a one-sided rule of thumb; reading both is what actually teaches when each measure is the honest one.

lessons.workedExample: A hydrology model produces 50 daily streamflow errors, 49 of them within +/-2% and one catastrophic 40% miss during a flash flood the model didn't anticipate. MAE stays small because 49 tiny errors dominate the average magnitude. RMSE spikes because that single 40% error gets squared before averaging, contributing far more to the sum than its raw size suggests. Reporting only MAE would let the team claim 'our model is accurate to within 2% on average' while quietly hiding the one day operators most needed a warning. Reporting only RMSE would make an otherwise excellent model look unreliable. Computing both and inspecting the RMSE/MAE ratio -- here well above 1 -- immediately flags that error magnitude is concentrated, not uniform, and tells the team exactly where to look next.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows both measures will ask why you reported one, the other, or both -- and 'RMSE is more sensitive to outliers' is only the textbook half of the answer. The stronger answer names the actual debate: state that Willmott and Matsuura pushed for MAE as the honest average, that Chai and Draxler defended RMSE under a Gaussian-error assumption, and that you checked which assumption fits your residuals before picking a headline number. Citing the RMSE/MAE ratio as a diagnostic -- rather than treating the two numbers as redundant -- shows you understand the gap between them carries information, not just noise.

questions.prompt: An RMSE/MAE ratio very close to 1 most directly indicates what about a model's errors?

options.text: Errors are roughly uniform in magnitude across observations
The model is unbiased on average
The sample size is too small to trust either metric
The model has systematically underestimated the target

explanations.a: Correct -- RMSE approaches MAE only when the individual |e_i| values are close to identical, since that is the equality case of the power-mean inequality.
explanations.b: Bias is about the sign and average of errors, not their spread; a ratio near 1 says nothing about bias.
explanations.c: The ratio is a property of the error distribution's shape, not a statement about whether n is adequate.
explanations.d: Systematic underestimation is a bias question; the RMSE/MAE ratio reflects concentration of error size, not direction.

questions.prompt: What is the core of Chai and Draxler's 2014 rebuttal to Willmott and Matsuura?

options.text: MAE is always mathematically undefined for real-valued data
RMSE is not ambiguous when errors are approximately Gaussian, since it relates directly to the error distribution's standard deviation
RMSE and MAE are always numerically identical in practice
Willmott and Matsuura's paper contained an arithmetic error in computing MAE
MAE should never be reported alongside RMSE

explanations.a: MAE is well-defined for any real-valued errors; this was never Chai and Draxler's claim.
explanations.b: Correct -- their central argument is that under a Gaussian error assumption RMSE ties directly to the standard deviation, giving it a precise theoretical meaning that MAE lacks.
explanations.c: The two are equal only when all absolute errors are identical, an unusual case, not the general rule.
explanations.d: Chai and Draxler disputed Willmott and Matsuura's reasoning and choice of examples, not their arithmetic.
explanations.e: Chai and Draxler did not argue MAE should be suppressed, only that RMSE should not be abandoned.

questions.prompt: For a fixed set of errors, order these three quantities from smallest to largest.

items.text: MAE
RMSE
sqrt(n) x MAE

questions.explanation: MAE <= RMSE always holds by the power-mean inequality, and RMSE <= sqrt(n) x MAE holds because Σe_i^2 <= (Σ|e_i|)^2 for nonnegative terms -- so MAE sits at the floor and sqrt(n) x MAE forms the ceiling.

questions.prompt: Match each paper to the position it argued in the MAE-vs-RMSE debate.

right.text: MAE is the honest, unambiguous average error; RMSE should be avoided in the literature
RMSE is correct and well-defined under a Gaussian error assumption; it should not be abandoned

questions.explanation: Willmott and Matsuura (2005, Climate Research) argued for MAE over RMSE as a more honest average; Chai and Draxler (2014, Geoscientific Model Development) rebutted that RMSE is theoretically justified when errors are approximately Gaussian.

lessons.label: RMSE's Outlier Sensitivity -- and When That's a Feature, Not a Bug

sections.heading: The arithmetic of one bad day
sections.body: Consider 100 forecast errors from a full year of daily demand: 99 days miss by exactly 1 unit, and one day -- a Black Friday nobody modeled -- misses by 20 units. MAE averages absolute error directly: (99x1 + 20)/100 = 119/100 = 1.19. RMSE squares before averaging: (99x1^2 + 20^2)/100 = (99+400)/100 = 4.99, and RMSE = sqrt(4.99) ~= 2.23. A single day out of 100 nearly doubles the reported error relative to MAE, and the RMSE-to-MAE ratio of about 1.87 sits well below its algebraic ceiling of sqrt(100) = 10 but far above the ~1.0 you'd see if all errors were equal in size -- squarely in the zone where the ratio signals a concentrated, not uniform, error profile. If a manager sees only RMSE, one anomalous day can make an otherwise reliable model look mediocre; if they see only MAE, that same day -- arguably the single most expensive miss of the year -- nearly disappears from the summary statistic.

sections.heading: When squaring the error is the honest choice
sections.body: Outlier sensitivity is a bug only if the true cost of an error is linear in its size. In several real domains it isn't. Grid balancing operators pay a cost that rises faster than linearly as an imbalance grows, because larger shortfalls require expensive fast-ramping reserve generation or risk cascading instability -- a quadratic loss like RMSE's squared term is a closer match to the true cost curve than MAE's linear one. Retail stockouts behave similarly: a demand-forecast miss of 20 units doesn't just cost 20 times the lost-sale cost of a miss of 1 unit -- it can trigger shelf gaps and customer churn that grow disproportionately with the size of the miss. Structural engineering has the same shape physically: stress and fatigue damage in materials scale nonlinearly with load deviation, so a metric that penalizes big misses more than proportionally reflects real physical risk. Peter Huber's 1964 robust-statistics work offers the explicit compromise: Huber loss is quadratic for small errors, behaving like squared error, and switches to linear for errors beyond a threshold delta, behaving like absolute error and resisting outlier domination. Choosing delta is choosing, explicitly, at what error size you stop believing a mistake this large should be punished quadratically -- the hedge the Willmott/Matsuura vs. Chai/Draxler debate forces you to make implicitly. Huber's own motivation in 1964 was robust location estimation under contaminated normal distributions, not forecasting, but the same shape now shows up throughout regression loss functions precisely because real cost curves are so rarely purely linear or purely quadratic across their whole range.

lessons.workedExample: A regional grid operator forecasts hourly demand and is deciding between two models. Model A has consistently small errors, mostly +/-1 MW, but one 20 MW miss during a heat-wave spike. Model B has uniformly moderate errors of +/-3 MW all day, every day. MAE alone might rank them close, but RMSE reveals Model A's tail risk: the 20 MW miss forces expensive last-minute reserve dispatch that costs far more than 20 times a routine 1 MW miss would, because reserve generators bill nonlinearly for last-minute ramping. An operator who only optimizes MAE would unknowingly favor a model that occasionally produces exactly the kind of large miss that is disproportionately expensive to correct in real time -- which is why an operator whose reserve costs scale faster than linearly should weight RMSE over MAE.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing this topic wants to see you resist the reflex that 'RMSE punishes outliers, so it's the wrong metric.' The stronger position names the cost structure of your specific domain: if the real-world consequence of an error grows faster than linearly -- grid reserve costs, stockout cascades, fatigue damage -- then RMSE's squaring isn't a flaw, it's the correct model of cost. Bringing up Huber loss as the deliberate middle ground, and being able to say what choosing a small vs. large delta threshold means for your project, shows you've thought about the shape of your loss function rather than picking a metric by default.

questions.prompt: In the example of 99 errors of 1 unit and one error of 20 units (n=100), what is the approximate RMSE?

explanations.a: 1.19 is the MAE for this set of errors, not the RMSE.
explanations.b: Correct -- mean squared error is (99x1 + 400)/100 = 4.99, and sqrt(4.99) is approximately 2.23.
explanations.c: 10.0 would be the algebraic ceiling sqrt(n) x MAE = sqrt(100) x 1.19, far above the actual RMSE.
explanations.d: 20 is the size of the single large error itself, not the aggregated RMSE across all 100 errors.

questions.prompt: Which reasoning correctly justifies preferring RMSE over MAE for grid-balancing evaluation?

options.text: Grid imbalance costs rise faster than linearly with imbalance size, so squaring the error better matches the true cost curve
RMSE is easier to compute than MAE for large datasets
RMSE and MAE always give identical rankings, so either works
Grid demand data never contains large errors, so RMSE and MAE behave the same way

explanations.a: Correct -- when the true cost of an error is quadratic rather than linear in its size, RMSE's squared term is a more faithful model of the cost than MAE's linear one.
explanations.b: Both are simple, comparably cheap computations; ease of computation is not the deciding factor here.
explanations.c: The two metrics only coincide when all errors are equal in magnitude; in general they can rank models differently.
explanations.d: Real grid demand data does contain occasional large deviations, such as heat-wave spikes, which is exactly why the choice of metric matters.

questions.prompt: Put these steps for choosing between MAE, RMSE, and Huber loss in the correct logical order.

items.text: Determine how the real-world cost scales with error size (linear, quadratic, or something else)
If cost is roughly linear, prefer MAE; if roughly quadratic, prefer RMSE
If cost is quadratic for small errors but linear for large ones, choose Huber loss instead
Set the Huber threshold delta at the error size where the cost stops accelerating

questions.explanation: You first diagnose how cost actually scales with error size, then pick MAE or RMSE if one regime applies cleanly; only if the cost transitions from quadratic to linear at some scale do you reach for Huber loss, at which point you must still set its delta threshold.

questions.prompt: Match each domain to the reason its cost structure favors a squared-error metric.

right.text: Large imbalances require disproportionately expensive fast-ramping reserve generation
Large misses trigger cascading shelf-gap and customer-churn effects beyond proportional lost-sales cost
Stress and fatigue damage scale nonlinearly with load deviation

questions.explanation: Each domain has a cost function that accelerates with error size: grid reserves, stockout cascades, and material fatigue all grow faster than linearly, making a quadratic loss like RMSE a better match than a linear one like MAE.

lessons.label: MAPE: The Most Popular Metric and Its Four Pathologies

sections.heading: A percentage that seems to solve everything
sections.body: Mean Absolute Percentage Error rescales each error into a percentage of the actual value before averaging: MAPE = (100/n) x Σ|Y_t - F_t| / |Y_t|. Because the result is a percentage rather than a unit-bound number, it appears to solve the problem MAE and RMSE both have -- a percentage should compare across products, currencies, and scales, making it the natural choice for a dashboard summarizing forecast quality across an entire catalog. That apparent universality is exactly why MAPE became the default metric on business dashboards long before its four structural pathologies were well understood outside the forecasting research community.

sections.heading: Pathology one and two: the denominator problem and the hidden bias
sections.body: The first two pathologies come from the denominator. Because MAPE divides by the actual value Y_t, it is undefined whenever Y_t = 0 and explosive as Y_t approaches zero: an actual of 0.1 against a forecast of 1.0 produces |0.1 - 1.0| / 0.1 = 9, a 900% error, even though the absolute miss is only 0.9 units. A single near-zero actual can dominate an entire MAPE average and make an otherwise strong forecast look catastrophic. The second pathology is a hidden asymmetry: for nonnegative forecasts, under-forecasting is capped -- the worst case is F = 0, giving exactly 100% error -- while over-forecasting is unbounded, since as F grows past Y the percentage error grows without limit. A model selected or trained to minimize MAPE is therefore penalized far harder for large over-forecasts than for large under-forecasts, so it systematically learns to forecast low: MAPE doesn't just measure bias, it manufactures it.

sections.heading: Pathology three and four, and why MAPE persists anyway
sections.body: The third failure is domain-dependent: MAPE is meaningless on any series that crosses or sits near zero, including interval-scale measurements like temperature in Celsius, where a true value of 1 degree turns a 2-degree forecast into a 100% error despite being a trivial physical miss. Fourth, intermittent-demand series -- spare parts, low-volume SKUs -- have long runs of zero actuals, which make MAPE either undefined or dominated by the handful of nonzero periods. Despite all four, MAPE persists on dashboards because it is the one metric a non-technical stakeholder can interpret without units or context -- 'off by 12%' means something to an executive in a way that an RMSE of 340 units does not, and that communicability keeps it in circulation even where it is measuring something skewed. Forecasting practitioners have proposed dozens of MAPE variants over the decades specifically to patch these four holes, but none has displaced MAPE's dashboard dominance, because none matches its one-sentence interpretability for a non-specialist audience.

lessons.workedExample: A retail chain reports MAPE across 200 SKUs. One slow-moving SKU sells 0.1 units per day on average; the model forecasts 1.0. That single SKU contributes a 900% error to the average, even though the absolute miss is under one unit. Meanwhile a high-volume SKU selling 10,000 units per day is off by 500 units -- a 5% error, arguably the more operationally important miss since it represents real warehouse and shelf impact. But averaged into an unweighted MAPE, the near-zero SKU's 900% swamps the high-volume SKU's 5%, and the reported blended MAPE looks alarming for reasons that have nothing to do with the model's actual business-relevant accuracy.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has seen MAPE misused will ask what happens to your metric near zero, and whether your model was implicitly trained to under-forecast. Naming all four pathologies unprompted -- the zero-division blowup, the over/under asymmetry, the meaninglessness on interval-scale or negative-valued series, and the failure on intermittent demand -- signals you didn't just adopt MAPE because it was already on the dashboard. The strongest answer also explains why it survives anyway: interpretability for non-technical stakeholders, not statistical merit.

questions.prompt: What is the MAPE contribution of a single point with actual = 0.1 and forecast = 1.0?

options.text: Undefined

explanations.a: 9% would result from dividing the absolute error by 10, not by the actual value of 0.1.
explanations.b: 90% understates it by a factor of 10; the correct denominator is the small actual value 0.1, not 1.0.
explanations.c: Correct -- |0.1 - 1.0| / 0.1 = 9, and 9 x 100% = 900%, driven entirely by the tiny actual value in the denominator.
explanations.d: The point is defined and computable since the actual value 0.1 is nonzero; it is merely explosive, not undefined.

questions.prompt: Why does minimizing MAPE tend to bias a model toward under-forecasting?

options.text: Under-forecast error is capped at 100% while over-forecast error is unbounded, so avoiding large penalties means forecasting low
MAPE ignores all errors where the forecast is below the actual value
MAPE always uses the forecast, not the actual, as its denominator
Under-forecasting is mathematically impossible to express in percentage terms

explanations.a: Correct -- with a nonnegative forecast, the worst under-forecast (F=0) gives exactly 100% error, while an over-forecast can grow arbitrarily large as F increases, so minimizing expected MAPE favors erring low.
explanations.b: MAPE includes under-forecast errors fully; it just bounds their maximum size rather than ignoring them.
explanations.c: The standard MAPE formula divides by the actual value Y_t, not the forecast.
explanations.d: Under-forecasting is expressed normally in MAPE; it is simply bounded above by 100% rather than unbounded.

questions.prompt: Order these actual/forecast pairs from smallest to largest resulting percentage error.

items.text: Actual 100, forecast 105
Actual 10, forecast 15
Actual 0.1, forecast 1.0

questions.explanation: The pairs give 5%, 50%, and 900% percentage error respectively -- the same absolute deviation pattern produces wildly different percentage errors depending on how small the actual value in the denominator is.

questions.prompt: Match each MAPE pathology to its description.

right.text: A tiny actual value like 0.1 can turn a sub-unit miss into a 900% error
A model trained to minimize MAPE implicitly learns to forecast low, since over-forecast penalties are unbounded
Temperature in Celsius makes trivial misses near zero degrees look like enormous percentage errors
Long runs of zero actuals leave the metric undefined or dominated by a handful of nonzero periods

questions.explanation: The four pathologies are distinct failure modes: explosive behavior near zero, a built-in bias toward under-forecasting, meaninglessness on interval or negative-valued scales, and breakdown on sparse intermittent-demand series.

lessons.label: sMAPE and the Attempted Fixes That Weren't

sections.heading: Symmetrizing the denominator
sections.body: Spyros Makridakis proposed symmetric MAPE in his 1993 International Journal of Forecasting paper, 'Accuracy measures: theoretical and practical concerns,' as a fix for MAPE's over/under asymmetry: instead of dividing by the actual value alone, sMAPE divides by the average of the actual and the forecast, sMAPE = (100/n) x Σ|Y_t - F_t| / ((|Y_t| + |F_t|)/2). The intent was to make an over-forecast and an under-forecast of the same absolute size score identically, since the denominator now reacts to both. Makridakis used the measure in the M3 forecasting competition he ran with Michele Hibon in the late 1990s, and it became the competition's headline accuracy metric, later carried into the M4 competition in 2018. Under this formula the nominal range is 0% to 200%, since |Y-F| can be at most twice the denominator average -- an odd ceiling by itself, since it means a forecast can be '200% wrong' in a metric that reads like a percentage. Signed variants of the formula, which preserve the direction of the error instead of taking its absolute value in the numerator, can extend the effective range down to -200% as well.

sections.heading: Still asymmetric, and M4's answer
sections.body: The symmetry Makridakis intended didn't survive contact with real numbers. Paul Goodwin and Richard Lawton's 1999 International Journal of Forecasting paper showed sMAPE is still asymmetric, just in a subtler way: for an actual of 100, an over-forecast of 150 gives sMAPE = 100x50/125 = 40%, but an under-forecast of 50 gives sMAPE = 100x50/75 ~= 66.7% -- the identical 50-unit miss scores nearly 1.7 times worse when the forecast falls below the actual than when it rises above it, because the denominator shrinks along with an under-forecast, inflating the ratio. Goodwin and Lawton concluded that sMAPE quietly rewards models that lean toward over-forecasting, the mirror image of MAPE's own bias toward under-forecasting -- so switching from one metric to the other doesn't remove asymmetry, it just flips which direction gets punished. By the time Makridakis, Spiliotis, and Assimakopoulos designed the M4 competition in 2018, this history had made the committee unwilling to crown a winner using either sMAPE or MASE alone. Their solution was the Overall Weighted Average: score each entry's sMAPE and MASE relative to a seasonal-naive benchmark's own scores on the same series, then average the two relative scores. A model has to perform well on both a percentage-based measure and a scale-based one to win -- a design that treats 'which metric is right' as unresolved rather than pretending one number settles it.

lessons.workedExample: Two demand forecasts for a product with actual sales of 100 units: Forecast A predicts 150, an over-forecast by 50; Forecast B predicts 50, an under-forecast by 50. Both misses are identical in absolute size. Under sMAPE, Forecast A scores 40% while Forecast B scores 66.7% -- the under-forecast is judged nearly twice as bad despite an identical-magnitude error, exactly the asymmetry Goodwin and Lawton documented in 1999. A forecasting team optimizing purely for low sMAPE would learn, over many such cases, to lean toward over-forecasting to avoid the harsher under-forecast penalty -- trading one metric-induced bias, MAPE's downward lean, for its mirror image, sMAPE's upward lean, rather than eliminating bias altogether.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge testing whether you actually understand sMAPE, rather than having memorized 'it fixes MAPE's asymmetry,' will ask you to compute it for a same-magnitude over- and under-forecast and show they differ. Being able to reproduce the 40% versus 66.7% split from Goodwin and Lawton's 1999 analysis -- and explain that it exists because the denominator itself moves with the forecast -- demonstrates real understanding. The strongest answer goes further and explains why M4 didn't just pick a better single metric: after two rounds of 'fixed' measures both turning out asymmetric, the committee's OWA blend is an admission that no single number is trustworthy alone.

questions.prompt: Who proposed symmetric MAPE, and in what year?

options.text: Hyndman and Koehler, 2006
Makridakis, 1993
Goodwin and Lawton, 1999
Chai and Draxler, 2014

explanations.a: Hyndman and Koehler's 2006 paper introduced MASE and a taxonomy of accuracy measures, not sMAPE.
explanations.b: Correct -- Spyros Makridakis introduced sMAPE in his 1993 International Journal of Forecasting paper on accuracy measures.
explanations.c: Goodwin and Lawton's 1999 paper analyzed and critiqued sMAPE's asymmetry; they did not originate it.
explanations.d: Chai and Draxler's 2014 paper is about the RMSE-versus-MAE debate, unrelated to sMAPE's origin.

questions.prompt: For an actual value of 100, what is the sMAPE for a forecast of 150 (an over-forecast by 50)?

explanations.b: 66.7% is the sMAPE for the under-forecast case (forecast of 50), not the over-forecast case.
explanations.c: 50% would be the plain MAPE relative to the actual value, not the symmetric version with the averaged denominator.
explanations.d: 100% is not the result of this calculation; it would require a far larger relative miss.

questions.prompt: What did Goodwin and Lawton's 1999 analysis demonstrate about sMAPE?

options.text: It is completely free of asymmetry, unlike MAPE
It penalizes under-forecasts more heavily than over-forecasts of the same absolute size, because the denominator shrinks with under-forecasting
It is undefined whenever the forecast is nonzero
It produces identical scores for over- and under-forecasts only when actual sales exceed 1000 units

explanations.a: This was precisely the claim Goodwin and Lawton refuted -- sMAPE remains asymmetric.
explanations.b: Correct -- because the denominator averages the actual and forecast, an under-forecast shrinks the denominator and inflates the ratio, giving under-forecasts a harsher score than equal-sized over-forecasts.
explanations.c: sMAPE is defined for nonzero forecasts and actuals; this option misstates its domain of definition.
explanations.d: The asymmetry Goodwin and Lawton found holds generally and does not depend on crossing a 1000-unit threshold.

questions.prompt: Place these developments in chronological order.

items.text: Makridakis introduces sMAPE
Goodwin and Lawton show sMAPE is still asymmetric
Hyndman and Koehler propose MASE and a full accuracy-measure taxonomy
M4 competition scores entries using OWA, a blend of relative sMAPE and relative MASE

questions.explanation: Makridakis introduced sMAPE in 1993; Goodwin and Lawton demonstrated its asymmetry in 1999; Hyndman and Koehler proposed MASE and the taxonomy in 2006; the M4 competition combined sMAPE and MASE into OWA in 2018.

lessons.label: MASE and Scaled Errors: Hyndman & Koehler 2006

sections.heading: Scaling by the naive forecast's own history
sections.body: Rob Hyndman and Anne Koehler's 2006 International Journal of Forecasting paper, 'Another look at measures of forecast accuracy,' surveyed the entire family of accuracy metrics -- scale-dependent (MAE, RMSE), percentage-based (MAPE, sMAPE), and relative (Theil's U, relative MAE) -- and showed each category fails somewhere: percentage errors blow up near zero, relative errors blow up when the benchmark's own error is near zero, and scale-dependent errors can't be compared across series in different units. Their fix was the Mean Absolute Scaled Error: instead of scaling by the actual value or a single benchmark forecast, scale by the in-sample mean absolute error of the naive one-step-ahead forecast on the same series. For a non-seasonal series, that in-sample scale is (1/(n-1)) x Σ|Y_t - Y_(t-1)| -- literally, how well a 'predict tomorrow equals today' forecaster would have done on the training history. MASE = MAE_model / (that in-sample scale). Because the denominator is only zero when the training series is perfectly constant, MASE is finite for essentially any real series, works identically whether the units are units sold, degrees, or dollars, and needs no special handling for zero actuals.

sections.heading: Interpreting the ratio, and its descendants
sections.body: The payoff is direct interpretability against a concrete baseline: MASE below 1 means the model beat the naive forecast on average; MASE equal to 1 means it tied naive; MASE of 1.4 means the model's average error was 40% worse than simply repeating the last observed value. For seasonal data, Hyndman and Koehler swap in the seasonal-naive forecast, comparing to the value one full season ago, so a model is judged against the best trivial baseline for that series' structure. The idea generalizes cleanly to squared error: RMSSE replaces the absolute-error terms with squared-error versions, keeping RMSE's sensitivity to large misses while remaining comparable across series. The M5 competition, run on Walmart retail data in 2020, adopted a weighted variant, WRMSSE, that scales each series' RMSSE contribution by its dollar sales -- so a large error on a high-revenue SKU counts for more of the final score than the same relative error on a slow-moving item, tying the statistical measure to the business quantity actually at stake. Despite this, MASE and its relatives remain mostly an academic and competition standard: research papers and competitions like M4 and M5 score on scaled measures almost by default now, while most industry dashboards still report MAPE, because MASE requires access to training history and doesn't translate into one intuitive sentence for a non-technical stakeholder.

lessons.workedExample: A retailer builds a demand model for a seasonal product line and reports MASE = 0.75 on a held-out test period. The in-sample scale -- the mean absolute error a naive seasonal forecast, last year's same week, would have produced on the training data -- was 40 units. A MASE of 0.75 means the model's average test error was 0.75 x 40 = 30 units, 25% better than simply repeating last year's numbers. Compare that to a second model that looks great on MAPE for high-volume weeks but has MASE = 1.3, 30% worse than the seasonal-naive baseline -- the scaled measure reveals the MAPE-favored model is actually losing to the simplest possible forecast once judged against the right yardstick.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows forecasting competitions will ask what your model is being compared against, not just what its raw error is. Citing Hyndman and Koehler's 2006 argument that scale-dependent, percentage, and relative measures each fail somewhere, and that MASE's fix is to scale by the naive forecast's own in-sample error, shows you understand why the measure exists rather than treating it as an arbitrary formula. Being able to state that MASE of 1.4 means '40% worse than naive' in one sentence, and naming M5's dollar-weighted WRMSSE as the natural extension when errors matter unequally, signals real fluency with the scaled-error family.

questions.prompt: A model reports MASE = 1.4 on a test series. What does this mean?

options.text: The model's average error was 40% better than the naive forecast
The model's average error was 40% worse than the naive forecast
The model's RMSE is 1.4 times its MAE
The result is undefined because MASE cannot exceed 1

explanations.a: A MASE below 1 would indicate beating naive; 1.4 is above 1, indicating the model performed worse than naive.
explanations.b: Correct -- MASE is the ratio of the model's MAE to the naive forecast's in-sample MAE, so 1.4 means 40% worse than naive.
explanations.c: MASE compares a model's error to a naive baseline's error, not RMSE to MAE within the same model.
explanations.d: MASE can exceed 1 whenever a model performs worse than the naive baseline; there is no upper bound of 1.

questions.prompt: Why is MASE's denominator, the in-sample naive MAE, rarely zero in practice?

options.text: Because naive forecasts are always perfectly accurate
Because it is only zero when the training series is a perfectly constant value
Because MASE has no denominator
Because it is always scaled by dollar sales

explanations.a: Naive forecasts are rarely perfectly accurate; if they were, the in-sample MAE would be zero, which is the exception, not the rule.
explanations.b: Correct -- the in-sample naive MAE sums consecutive absolute differences, which is zero only if every consecutive value in the training series is identical.
explanations.c: MASE is explicitly defined as a ratio with the in-sample naive MAE as its denominator.
explanations.d: Dollar-sales weighting is a feature of WRMSSE in the M5 competition, not of the base MASE denominator.
