questions.prompt: Match each scaled-error measure to its description.

right.text: Hyndman and Koehler's 2006 measure, scaled by the in-sample naive MAE
The squared-error analog of MASE
M5 competition's dollar-sales-weighted version used to score entries

questions.explanation: MASE is the original absolute-error scaled measure from Hyndman and Koehler (2006); RMSSE is its squared-error counterpart; WRMSSE weights RMSSE by each series' dollar sales, as used in the M5 competition.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for computing and interpreting a MASE score.

items.text: Compute the in-sample MAE of the naive (or seasonal-naive) forecast on the training data
Compute the model's MAE on the forecast period
Divide the model's MAE by the naive in-sample MAE
Interpret the ratio against 1: below 1 beats naive, above 1 loses to naive

questions.explanation: The naive in-sample scale must be established first, then the model's own error is computed, then the ratio is formed, and only then is it interpreted relative to the baseline of 1.

lessons.label: Relative Measures: Theil's U, Relative MAE, and Geometric Means

sections.heading: Two statistics, one confusing name
sections.body: Henri Theil introduced an inequality coefficient in his 1966 book Applied Economic Forecasting to compare a forecast against a naive alternative, but the literature that followed produced two distinct statistics both commonly called 'Theil's U,' and confusing them is a real and persistent error. U1 is bounded between 0 and 1: U1 = sqrt(Σ(F-A)^2/n) / (sqrt(ΣF^2/n) + sqrt(ΣA^2/n)). It only compares a model's errors to the raw magnitudes of its own forecasts and actuals -- it says nothing about a benchmark, and a U1 near 0 just means the model fits closely in absolute terms. U2 is a genuinely different quantity: it compares the model's period-to-period forecast errors to the errors a naive random-walk forecast would have made, U2 = sqrt(Σ((F_(t+1)-A_(t+1))/A_t)^2) / sqrt(Σ((A_(t+1)-A_t)/A_t)^2). U2 is unbounded above, and its interpretation matches MASE's: U2 below 1 beats naive, U2 equal to 1 ties naive, U2 above 1 loses to naive. Because both share Theil's name and a superficially similar square-root shape, papers frequently cite 'Theil's U' without specifying which one, and a reader has to infer from context -- bounded numbers near 0-1 suggest U1; numbers hovering around 1 that can exceed it suggest U2.

sections.heading: When relative errors blow up, and how geometric means resist it
sections.body: Relative MAE takes the same benchmark-comparison idea and simplifies it: RelMAE = MAE_model / MAE_benchmark, aggregating whole-series errors rather than Theil's period-by-period ratios. A per-period version, the relative absolute error RAE_t = |e_t| / |e*_t|, model error over naive error at time t, inherits a sharper version of the same problem Theil's U2 and MASE both try to dodge -- if the naive benchmark happens to nail a single period exactly, e*_t = 0 and RAE_t becomes infinite, and one lucky naive prediction can make an otherwise reasonable model's average relative error blow up to infinity. J. Scott Armstrong and Fred Collopy's 1992 paper, 'Error Measures for Generalizing about Forecasting Methods,' proposed the Geometric Mean Relative Absolute Error, GMRAE, as the resistant alternative: instead of arithmetically averaging the RAE_t values, take their geometric mean, equivalent to averaging log(RAE_t). A handful of extreme ratios still pull the geometric mean upward, but because the aggregation happens in log space, one moderately large outlier contributes far less distortion than it would to a plain arithmetic mean, where a single very large term can dominate the entire sum outright. In Hyndman and Koehler's 2006 taxonomy, Theil's U2, relative MAE, and GMRAE all sit in the same 'relative measures' category -- defined by comparison to a specific benchmark forecast -- distinct from percentage measures like MAPE and sMAPE, and from the scaled-error family MASE that Hyndman and Koehler argued should replace all three.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher compares two competing sales models against a naive random-walk benchmark across 52 weekly periods. In one week, the naive forecast happens to exactly match actual sales, making that week's naive error zero. Reporting mean relative absolute error, the arithmetic average of RAE_t, makes that single week's ratio infinite, and the whole 52-week average becomes infinite too -- a technically correct but practically useless result that erases 51 weeks of real signal. Switching to GMRAE, the researcher instead averages in log space; if only one or two weeks have extreme ratios while the rest cluster near 0.8 to 1.2, the geometric mean stays finite and close to that cluster, giving a usable summary the arithmetic mean could not.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge testing rigor here will ask you to state, precisely, which Theil's U you mean -- bounded U1 or naive-relative U2 -- since conflating them is the single most common error in citing this statistic. The stronger answer also explains why a geometric, not arithmetic, mean is used for GMRAE: because relative-error ratios can blow up when a benchmark's error is near zero, and log-space averaging resists a handful of huge ratios far better than a raw average does. Placing all three measures in Hyndman and Koehler's 'relative' category, distinct from percentage and scaled measures, shows the whole taxonomy, not just one formula.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between Theil's U1 and U2?

options.text: U1 is bounded between 0 and 1 and compares a model to its own forecast/actual magnitudes; U2 compares to a naive benchmark and is unbounded above
U1 and U2 are simply two names for the exact same formula
U1 is used only for classification problems, and U2 only for regression
U2 is always smaller than U1 for any dataset

explanations.a: Correct -- U1 is an inequality coefficient bounded in [0,1] with no benchmark, while U2 compares model errors to naive-forecast errors and can exceed 1.
explanations.b: They are structurally different formulas that happen to share Theil's name, which is exactly the source of the common confusion.
explanations.c: Both are regression-style forecast accuracy statistics; neither is a classification metric.
explanations.d: There is no general ordering between U1 and U2 since they measure fundamentally different things.

questions.prompt: Why can the per-period relative absolute error RAE_t become infinite?

options.text: Whenever the actual value at that period is zero
Whenever the naive benchmark's error at that period is exactly zero
Whenever the model's error exceeds 100 units
Only when a geometric mean is used to aggregate it

explanations.a: RAE_t divides the model's error by the naive benchmark's error, not by the actual value directly, so a zero actual does not by itself cause the blowup.
explanations.b: Correct -- RAE_t = |e_t| / |e*_t|, so if the naive forecast happens to be exact at time t, the denominator e*_t is zero and RAE_t is undefined or infinite.
explanations.c: The size of the model's own error does not by itself create a division-by-zero problem.
explanations.d: The geometric mean is the aggregation method that resists this blowup; it is not the cause of it.

questions.prompt: Match each accuracy measure to its category in Hyndman and Koehler's 2006 taxonomy.

right.text: Percentage measure
Scaled measure
Relative measure
Scale-dependent measure

questions.explanation: Hyndman and Koehler grouped MAPE among percentage measures, MASE among scaled measures, Theil's U2 among relative measures compared to a benchmark, and RMSE among the original scale-dependent measures.

questions.prompt: Place these publications in chronological order.

items.text: Theil publishes the U statistic
Armstrong and Collopy propose GMRAE
Makridakis introduces sMAPE
Hyndman and Koehler propose MASE and the full accuracy-measure taxonomy

questions.explanation: Theil's U dates to 1966, Armstrong and Collopy's GMRAE paper to 1992, Makridakis's sMAPE paper to 1993, and Hyndman and Koehler's MASE and taxonomy paper to 2006.

lessons.label: Choosing the Metric Before You See the Ranking

sections.heading: The same forecasts, three different winners
sections.body: Take two candidate demand-forecast models evaluated on the same five held-out points. Model A misses by 1, 1, 1, 1, and 10 units; Model B misses by 3, 3, 3, 3, and 3 units, perfectly uniform. MAE treats them by simple average: MAE_A = (1+1+1+1+10)/5 = 2.8, MAE_B = (3+3+3+3+3)/5 = 3.0. By MAE, Model A wins. RMSE squares first: RMSE_A = sqrt((1+1+1+1+100)/5) = sqrt(20.8) ~= 4.56, RMSE_B = sqrt((9x5)/5) = 3.0. By RMSE, Model B wins -- the single 10-unit miss in Model A's fifth point costs it the ranking outright once squared. Nothing about the underlying forecasts changed between the two evaluations; only the aggregation rule did. Add MAPE into the same comparison and a third possible ranking appears, because MAPE rescales each of those raw misses by whatever actual value happened to occur at that point -- if Model A's one large miss lands on a data point with a large actual value, its percentage error there is small and MAPE may still favor A; if it lands on a small-actual point, the same 10-unit miss can dominate MAPE the way it dominated RMSE. The ranking of 'better model' is not a fact about the models -- it is a fact about which formula and which data point you asked.

sections.heading: Aggregation is a second, compounding choice
sections.body: The choice doesn't stop at picking MAE versus RMSE versus MAPE -- how you aggregate across many series compounds the same ambiguity. Averaging per-series error scores treats every series equally regardless of its business weight; taking the median instead of the mean changes which series can drag the summary number, since a mean is pulled by a handful of badly-forecast series while a median ignores them entirely past the midpoint. Scoring per-horizon, day-1 error separate from day-7 error, versus pooling all horizons into one number answers a different question again -- a model that's excellent one day out and poor a week out looks mediocre when pooled, hiding which use case actually failed. Forecasting competitions treat this as a design problem, not an afterthought. The M4 competition, run by Makridakis, Spiliotis, and Assimakopoulos in 2018, built its Overall Weighted Average from two different metric families specifically so no single formula's blind spot could crown a winner. The M5 competition in 2020 went further, weighting each series' RMSSE contribution by its dollar sales into WRMSSE, so the aggregation itself encodes which errors the business actually cares about, not just which are statistically largest. Both committees fixed their metric and their aggregation rule before a single forecast was scored. The lesson generalizes: pre-register the metric and the aggregation method before you see any candidate model's results, or the temptation to pick whichever number flatters your preferred model after the fact becomes almost impossible to resist.

lessons.workedExample: A team building a demand-forecasting system for 500 SKUs runs three candidate models and computes MAE, RMSE, and MAPE for each, pooled across all SKUs. Model 1 wins on MAE, Model 2 wins on RMSE, and Model 3 wins on MAPE -- each metric picked a different champion from the identical set of forecasts. Rather than choosing whichever ranking favors the model the team already prefers, they return to their charter: the business cares about total dollar stockout cost, which scales roughly with squared error on high-revenue SKUs, so they had pre-committed to a dollar-weighted RMSSE-style score before evaluation began. That pre-registered choice, made before any model's numbers were visible, is what keeps the metric selection from becoming a post-hoc rationalization for a preferred result.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has seen many science-fair projects quietly pick 'whichever metric made our model look best' will ask when you chose your evaluation metric relative to when you saw your results. The right answer is before -- and being able to say so, backed by a concrete demonstration that MAE, RMSE, and MAPE can rank the same candidate models differently, shows you understand metric choice is a scientific decision with consequences, not a reporting formality. Citing M4's OWA and M5's WRMSSE as examples of committees who fixed both metric and aggregation in advance strengthens the point with real precedent.

questions.prompt: In the example where Model A's errors are 1,1,1,1,10 and Model B's are 3,3,3,3,3, which model does RMSE prefer, and why?

options.text: Model A, because RMSE ignores large individual errors
Model B, because squaring uniform errors keeps the sum smaller than squaring one dominant error
Model A, because MAE and RMSE always agree on ranking
Neither; RMSE gives them an identical score

explanations.a: RMSE does the opposite of ignoring large errors -- squaring amplifies them, which is exactly why Model A loses under RMSE.
explanations.b: Correct -- Model B's squared errors sum to 45 (9x5) versus Model A's 104 (4x1 + 100), giving RMSE_B = 3.0 versus RMSE_A ~= 4.56.
explanations.c: This example is specifically constructed to show MAE and RMSE can disagree: MAE favors Model A while RMSE favors Model B.
explanations.d: The computed RMSE values, 4.56 versus 3.0, are clearly different, not identical.

questions.prompt: What does pre-registering an evaluation metric and its aggregation rule before running any models protect against?

options.text: Higher computational cost of training
Post-hoc selection of whichever metric happens to favor a preferred model
Overfitting to the training set
Data leakage between training and test sets

explanations.a: Pre-registration is about the order of decisions, not about computational efficiency.
explanations.b: Correct -- if the metric is chosen after seeing results, it becomes easy to rationalize whichever formula favors the model you already prefer; fixing it in advance removes that temptation.
explanations.c: Overfitting is a modeling and validation-split issue, addressed by proper train/test separation, not by metric pre-registration.
explanations.d: Data leakage is a data-handling problem distinct from which accuracy formula and aggregation rule are used to score results.

questions.prompt: Match each competition to its composite aggregation design.

right.text: OWA -- blends relative sMAPE and relative MASE against a seasonal-naive benchmark
WRMSSE -- dollar-sales-weighted root mean squared scaled error

questions.explanation: M4 scored entries with the Overall Weighted Average, combining relative sMAPE and relative MASE; M5 scored entries with WRMSSE, which weights each series' contribution by its dollar sales.

questions.prompt: Order the decisions a team should settle, as introduced in this lesson, before evaluating any candidate model.

items.text: Choose the base error metric (e.g., MAE, RMSE, MAPE, or MASE)
Decide whether to aggregate across series using the mean or the median
Decide whether to score per-horizon or pool all horizons into one number
Decide whether to apply a business weighting, such as dollar sales

questions.explanation: The lesson introduces these in order: first the base metric, then the choice between mean and median aggregation, then per-horizon versus pooled scoring, then any business-driven weighting scheme layered on top.

units.label: Residual Diagnostics: Reading What the Model Left Behind

lessons.label: Residual vs. Error: The Distinction Judges Test

sections.heading: Two different quantities wearing the same word
sections.body: A residual is e_t = y_t - yhat_t, computed at a data point the model already saw during fitting -- the same point that pulled the coefficients toward it while the parameters were being estimated. A forecast error is computed at a point the model never touched: a held-out test row, or a future period that hadn't occurred when the parameters were estimated. Ordinary least squares literally minimizes the sum of squared residuals, so in-sample residuals are close to the smallest number that fitting procedure could produce for that data -- they look good almost by construction, not because the model generalizes well. Statisticians call this resubstitution bias: training error is a biased-low estimate of the error a model will make on new data, and the gap widens as model flexibility increases. A model with as many free parameters as data points can drive every in-sample residual to zero while forecasting terribly on anything new, which is why a poster reporting only training-set RMSE or R-squared invites an immediate credibility question. The fix is structural: hold out a test set, or use k-fold cross-validation (formalized by Mervyn Stone in 1974) or, for time-ordered data, rolling-origin evaluation, and report error computed only where the fitting process never looked. The size of the in-sample-versus-out-of-sample gap is itself diagnostic: a small gap suggests a model that was never flexible enough to overfit, while a large gap is a direct symptom of a model that memorized noise specific to the training rows.

sections.heading: Four assumptions, two different jobs
sections.body: Residual diagnostics conventionally check four properties: zero (conditional) mean, no autocorrelation, constant variance, and approximate normality. These do not carry equal weight. Zero mean and no autocorrelation are load-bearing for the point forecast alone: a nonzero mean residual means the model is systematically biased and a better forecast exists by simply subtracting that bias, and autocorrelated residuals mean predictable structure was left on the table -- both are point-estimate failures, independent of any interval. Constant variance and normality only matter once an uncertainty statement is attached to the forecast. A 95 percent Gaussian prediction interval assumes a constant residual standard deviation and a bell-shaped residual distribution; if variance actually grows with the fitted value, or the distribution has heavy tails, that interval's coverage claim is false even when the point forecast underneath it is fine. A team whose residuals fan out or whose Q-Q plot bends at the tails does not need to discard their point predictions, but they cannot honestly report a fixed-width 95 percent interval built on those residuals without first addressing the variance or normality problem.

lessons.workedExample: A team fits a regression predicting plant height from days of light exposure using all 60 of their lab's data points and reports RMSE = 0.8 cm computed on those same 60 points -- an in-sample residual. A judge asks how the model performs on plants it hasn't seen. The team re-runs the fit holding out 15 plants, fits on the remaining 45, and predicts the held-out 15: RMSE jumps to 2.3 cm. The gap shows the original 0.8 cm was optimistic because the fitting procedure had already seen and adjusted for every one of those 60 residuals. Reporting only the in-sample number would have overstated real predictive accuracy by nearly a factor of three.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'is that RMSE from data the model was trained on?' is testing whether a team understands that a fitting procedure is engineered to make in-sample residuals small, which makes in-sample error a poor stand-in for real predictive performance. A second common probe -- 'did you check if your residuals are correlated or if their spread changes?' -- tests whether the team knows only two of the four classic residual assumptions are needed to trust the forecast itself, while the other two are needed only if an interval is being claimed, a distinction many student posters blur.

questions.prompt: Why is an in-sample residual typically an optimistic estimate of a model's real predictive error?

options.text: The fitting procedure minimized error on that exact data, so the residual is close to the smallest value it could produce there
Out-of-sample data is inherently noisier than training data
In-sample residuals use a fundamentally different formula than forecast errors
Out-of-sample errors are always computed from a larger dataset

explanations.a: Correct -- least squares (or any fitting criterion) directly minimizes in-sample residuals, so they are optimistic by construction, not because the model generalizes well.
explanations.b: Noise level is a property of the data-generating process, not of whether a point was used for fitting; the bias comes from the fitting procedure, not extra noise.
explanations.c: Both use the same formula, y minus yhat -- the difference is only whether the model saw that point during fitting.
explanations.d: Dataset size is unrelated to the resubstitution bias; the bias appears even when train and test sets are the same size.

questions.prompt: Which two of the four classic residual assumptions must hold to trust a point forecast alone, with no interval attached?

options.text: Zero mean and no autocorrelation
Constant variance and normality
All four equally, with no distinction
None -- point forecasts require no residual assumptions

explanations.a: Correct -- a nonzero mean signals removable bias and autocorrelation signals unused structure; both are point-estimate failures independent of any interval.
explanations.b: Constant variance and normality only matter once you attach a probabilistic interval to the forecast; a biased or under-fit point forecast can still be flagged without them.
explanations.c: The four assumptions split into two point-forecast checks and two interval-only checks, not one undifferentiated group.
explanations.d: A model with nonzero-mean or autocorrelated residuals is demonstrably improvable, so point forecasts are not assumption-free.

questions.prompt: Match each residual property to what it guarantees when it holds.

left.text: Residual variance is constant across fitted values

right.text: The point forecast carries no systematic, removable bias
No predictable structure was left unmodeled
A fixed-width interval has correct width across the whole range
A Gaussian interval's tail coverage is accurate

questions.explanation: Zero mean and no autocorrelation protect the point forecast itself; constant variance and normality only protect claims about an interval built around that point forecast.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the correct order for honestly estimating out-of-sample forecast error.

items.text: Split the data into a training set and a held-out test set
Fit the model using only the training set
Generate predictions for the held-out test set
Compute error from test-set actuals minus test-set predictions

questions.explanation: The test set must be withheld before fitting, the model must never see it during estimation, predictions come after fitting, and only then is a legitimate out-of-sample error computed.

lessons.label: The Residual-vs-Fitted Plot: Funnel, Arc, and Band

sections.heading: One plot, a five-second read
sections.body: The residual-vs-fitted plot puts e_i = y_i - yhat_i on the vertical axis against yhat_i on the horizontal axis, and it appears on many science-fair regression posters because it compresses hundreds of numbers into one shape a judge can read in five seconds. There are exactly four shapes worth recognizing, and each maps to a different fix. The target shape is a structureless horizontal band: points scattered evenly above and below zero with no trend and no change in spread as fitted values increase. That band says the model extracted every systematic pattern the predictors could offer, leaving only noise -- there is nothing left to model, and the fix is: stop, the model is adequate on this axis. John Tukey pushed exactly this kind of plot-before-statistic habit in his 1977 book Exploratory Data Analysis, arguing that a shape a human can see often reveals a problem before any single summary number, like R-squared or RMSE, would flag it -- two datasets can share an identical R-squared while one has a clean band and the other a screaming funnel.

sections.heading: Funnel, arc, and stripes
sections.body: A funnel -- narrow spread at one end of the fitted range, widening toward the other -- is heteroscedasticity: error grows with the size of the prediction, common whenever y spans orders of magnitude (prices, populations, reaction counts). The fix is a variance-stabilizing transform, typically log(y) or a Box-Cox transform, or switching to weighted least squares. A U-shape or arc -- residuals dipping negative in the middle of the fitted range and rising positive at both ends, or the reverse -- means the model missed curvature: a straight line was fit to a bending relationship, and no amount of new data fixes it, only a polynomial term, spline, or transformed predictor will. Horizontal stripes or a hard floor -- residuals clustering onto a small number of discrete diagonal lines, or a visible lower boundary -- gives away a target that is actually rounded, censored, or count-valued (test scores rounded to the nearest point, a sensor that floors at zero, a count of insects per trap), which changes the appropriate model family entirely, often to Poisson or a censored-regression model rather than ordinary least squares. The Box-Cox family, introduced by George Box and David Cox in 1964, gives a one-parameter dial for the funnel fix: lambda = 0 recovers log(y), lambda = 0.5 recovers the square root, and lambda = 1 leaves the data untouched, with the value in between chosen to make residual spread as constant as possible.

lessons.workedExample: A team predicting reaction yield from catalyst concentration plots residuals against fitted yield and sees a clear arc: residuals run positive at low fitted yields, dip negative through the middle of the range, then swing positive again at high fitted yields. That arc is the signature of curvature, not heteroscedasticity -- the spread of the residuals stays roughly constant across the range, only the sign pattern changes. Adding a squared concentration term to the model and re-plotting flattens the arc into a structureless band, confirming the missing nonlinearity was concentration-squared, not an unstable variance that would have needed a log transform instead.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge glancing at a poster's residual-vs-fitted plot for five seconds is running exactly this four-way classification, and a team that cannot name which of the four shapes their own plot shows -- band, funnel, arc, or stripes -- has not actually looked at the diagnostic they printed. The stronger failure mode judges probe for is applying the wrong fix: reaching for a log transform when the real problem is a missing quadratic term (an arc, not a funnel), or vice versa. Naming the shape correctly and tying it to the matching fix is what turns a decorative plot into evidence of real diagnostic work.

questions.prompt: Match each residual-vs-fitted shape to its diagnosis.

left.text: Funnel widening as fitted values increase
U-shape or arc across the fitted range
Horizontal stripes or a hard floor

right.text: Model has captured the systematic signal; nothing left to fix
Heteroscedasticity: error variance grows with prediction size
Missing curvature: a line was fit to a bending relationship
Target is rounded, censored, or count-valued

questions.explanation: A band means the model is adequate, a funnel means variance scales with the fitted value, an arc means the functional form is wrong, and stripes or a floor mean the target itself is not continuous in the way ordinary least squares assumes.

questions.prompt: A residual-vs-fitted plot funnels outward at high fitted values. What is the most appropriate fix?

options.text: A log or Box-Cox transform of the target, or weighted least squares
Adding a squared predictor term
Switching the target to a Poisson count model
Collecting more data with the same design

explanations.a: Correct -- a funnel signals non-constant variance, which a variance-stabilizing transform or reweighted loss directly addresses.
explanations.b: A squared predictor fixes curvature (an arc pattern), which changes the sign trend of residuals, not their spreading width.
explanations.c: A Poisson model is the fix for stripe or floor patterns from a count-valued or censored target, not for a smoothly widening funnel.
explanations.d: More data with the same design will only make the funnel more visible; the underlying variance structure does not change with sample size.

questions.prompt: A residual plot shows points falling onto a small number of discrete diagonal stripes rather than a continuous scatter. What does this most likely indicate?

options.text: The target variable is rounded, censored, or count-valued rather than continuous
The model has too many predictors
The variance is growing with the fitted value
The model has perfectly captured the relationship

explanations.a: Correct -- stripes appear when many observations share the same rounded, censored, or integer-count target value, which ordinary least squares does not model correctly.
explanations.b: Too many predictors would tend to shrink residuals overall or cause instability, not produce discrete diagonal stripes.
explanations.c: Growing variance produces a funnel shape, a change in vertical spread, not discrete parallel stripes.
explanations.d: A perfect fit would show near-zero residuals everywhere, not a patterned discrete structure.

questions.prompt: Order the diagnostic process a student should follow when reading a residual-vs-fitted plot at a poster.

items.text: Locate zero on the vertical axis and check whether the band is centered there
Scan left to right for any trend in the sign of the residuals (arc)
Scan for any change in vertical spread across the fitted range (funnel)
Check for discrete stripes or a hard floor suggesting a non-continuous target
Apply the fix that matches whichever pattern was found

questions.explanation: The five-second read proceeds centering first, then curvature, then spread, then discreteness, and only then to the matched fix -- checking spread before curvature or vice versa works too, but skipping straight to a fix without identifying the shape risks applying the wrong one.

lessons.label: Predicted-vs-Actual Parity Plots and Regression to the Mean

sections.heading: The identity line versus the fitted line
sections.body: A parity plot puts predicted values on one axis and actual values on the other. Two lines matter, and they are easy to conflate. The identity line, y = x, is not fit to anything -- it is drawn once, always at 45 degrees, and represents the goal: a model whose predictions equal the truth everywhere. The fitted line is a separate least-squares regression of actual values on predicted values, estimated from the points actually plotted. A model is well-calibrated only when that second, fitted line sits on top of the first, fixed one -- intercept near 0, slope near 1. Students routinely eyeball a 'tight cloud of points' and call the model good without ever checking whether the cloud's own best-fit line has drifted away from the diagonal. This distinction is exactly why a parity plot is a separate diagnostic from a residual-vs-fitted plot: the residual plot checks whether error is structured across the range, while the parity plot checks the more specific claim of one-to-one agreement between what was predicted and what actually happened, a claim R-squared alone cannot verify.

sections.heading: Flattening: the classic slope-under-1 failure
sections.body: The most common miscalibration is flattening: the fitted line has a slope below 1, meaning the model over-predicts low actual values and under-predicts high ones, compressing its predictions toward the mean of the training targets -- a version of regression to the mean, the same phenomenon Francis Galton described in 1886 studying parents' and children's heights, where extreme parents produced less-extreme offspring. A shrinkage-heavy method (ridge regression, a small or heavily regularized tree ensemble, a model trained on a target with a narrow dynamic range) reproduces this same pull-toward-the-average pattern in its predictions. The formal check is to regress actual on predicted and jointly test intercept = 0 and slope = 1; failing that test while R-squared reads a healthy 0.9 is not a contradiction -- R-squared measures how tightly points cluster around whatever line best fits them, while the intercept-slope test asks whether that line is the correct one. A parity plot can show an R-squared of 0.9 with a fitted slope of 0.6, meaning predictions are precise but systematically wrong at both ends of the range, which is a calibration failure, not a success, however clean the scatter looks. The reverse pattern, a fitted slope above 1, is rarer but equally diagnosable -- it means the model over-reacts, exaggerating both low and high actuals, and the same intercept-slope test catches it just as directly.

lessons.workedExample: A team's model predicts exam scores and reports R-squared = 0.91 from the parity plot's tight scatter. A closer look at the fitted actual-on-predicted line shows intercept = 18 and slope = 0.62. For a predicted score of 40, the fitted line implies an actual average near 43 (18 + 0.62 times 40) -- the model under-predicted low scorers. For a predicted score of 95, the fitted line implies an actual average near 77 -- the model over-predicted high scorers. Testing intercept = 0 and slope = 1 jointly rejects at p less than 0.01. The R-squared was measuring tightness around the wrong line; the model needs recalibration, not just a higher R-squared to chase.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has seen this failure before will ask for the fitted line's intercept and slope, not just R-squared, precisely because R-squared cannot distinguish a well-calibrated model from a systematically flattened one. Naming regression to the mean by name, and connecting it to Galton's original height study, signals the team understands flattening as a known statistical phenomenon rather than a mysterious quirk of their specific model. The strongest answer states the intercept-slope test result explicitly and explains which end of the range -- high actuals, low actuals, or both -- the model is failing on.

questions.prompt: On a parity plot, what does the identity line (y = x) represent, and how does it differ from the fitted actual-on-predicted line?

options.text: The identity line is the fixed 45-degree goal; the fitted line is estimated from the plotted points and may deviate from it
They are the same line by definition and will always overlap
The identity line is estimated from the data; the fitted line is fixed at 45 degrees
The fitted line only exists when R-squared is above 0.9

explanations.a: Correct -- the identity line is drawn once as the calibration target, while the fitted line is a genuine regression of actual on predicted and can have any intercept or slope.
explanations.b: They coincide only for a perfectly calibrated model; miscalibration is exactly the gap between them.
explanations.c: This reverses the two lines -- the identity line is fixed, the fitted line is the one estimated from data.
explanations.d: The fitted line can be computed for any parity plot regardless of R-squared value.

questions.prompt: A parity plot's fitted line has slope 0.6. What does this indicate about the model's predictions?

options.text: The model over-predicts low actual values and under-predicts high actual values, compressing predictions toward the mean
The model is unbiased and simply noisier than an ideal model
The model under-predicts low values and over-predicts high values
A slope below 1 has no implication for calibration, only for R-squared

explanations.a: Correct -- a slope under 1 is the flattening signature: predictions are pulled toward the average, over-shooting at the low end and under-shooting at the high end.
explanations.b: Noise alone would not systematically shift the fitted line's slope away from 1; flattening is a bias pattern, not added noise.
explanations.c: This describes the opposite direction from flattening; flattening under-predicts the highs and over-predicts the lows, not the reverse.
explanations.d: Slope directly measures calibration -- a slope of 1 with intercept 0 is the definition of a calibrated parity plot.

questions.prompt: Match each parity-plot quantity to what it actually measures.

left.text: Slope of the fitted actual-on-predicted line
Intercept of the fitted actual-on-predicted line

right.text: How tightly points cluster around whichever line best fits them
Whether predictions are compressed toward the mean (flattening) or correctly scaled
Whether predictions are shifted up or down by a constant amount

questions.explanation: R-squared only measures scatter tightness around the best-fit line, not whether that line is the identity line; slope captures compression toward the mean, and intercept captures a constant additive offset.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the formal calibration check for a parity plot.

items.text: Generate predicted values for the held-out or test observations
Regress actual values on predicted values to get an intercept and slope
Test the joint hypothesis intercept = 0 and slope = 1
If the test rejects, diagnose flattening (or amplification) and recalibrate before trusting R-squared alone

questions.explanation: The check requires predictions first, then a fitted regression line from those predictions against actuals, then a formal test of that line against the identity line, and only then a calibration decision -- R-squared by itself skips every one of these steps.

lessons.label: Q-Q Plots and the Normality Question

sections.heading: Reading the shape against the diagonal
sections.body: A normal quantile-quantile (Q-Q) plot sorts the residuals and plots each one's quantile against the quantile a standard normal distribution would produce at that same rank. If residuals were exactly normal, every point would sit on the 45-degree reference line. Three deviations recur in practice. An S-curve -- points bowing below the line at the low end and above it at the high end, reversing curvature once in the middle -- means heavier tails than normal: more extreme values in both directions than a bell curve predicts, the signature of a distribution like the Student's t. A one-directional concave bend -- points consistently curving away from the line in the same rotational direction across the whole range -- means skew, typically right skew when the bend curves upward through the middle. Deviations confined to just the extreme few points at each end, with the bulk of the line straight, mean the body of the distribution is fine and only a handful of outlying residuals are non-normal, a much less consequential finding than a shape that deviates throughout. The Q-Q plot is worth pairing with a histogram of the same residuals: a histogram shows overall shape but hides exactly where along the distribution the mismatch occurs, while the Q-Q plot's axis is built specifically to stretch out the tails, which is where normality violations matter most for interval coverage.

sections.heading: Formal tests, and why they mislead at scale
sections.body: Two named tests formalize the eyeball check. Shapiro-Wilk, introduced by Samuel Shapiro and Martin Wilk in 1965, is generally the more powerful small-sample test. Jarque-Bera, from Carlos Jarque and Anil Bera around 1980, instead checks whether sample skewness and kurtosis match the normal values of 0 and 3 using a chi-squared statistic. Both share a scaling problem: statistical power grows with sample size, so at large n (hundreds or thousands of residuals) either test will reject normality for deviations too small to matter practically -- real data is essentially never exactly Gaussian, and a large enough sample has the power to prove it. The point students get wrong is the consequence: non-normal residuals do not invalidate the point forecast itself at all -- the mean or median prediction can be excellent regardless of residual shape. What non-normality invalidates is a Gaussian 95 percent prediction interval, which is calculated from a normal-distribution formula and becomes a false coverage claim the moment the true residual distribution has heavier or lighter tails than that formula assumes. A practical alternative when normality is genuinely violated is a bootstrap or empirical-quantile interval, which reads the interval bounds directly off the observed residual distribution instead of assuming a bell curve, sidestepping the normality question entirely rather than arguing about a p-value.

lessons.workedExample: A team's residual Q-Q plot shows a clean diagonal through the middle 90 percent of points but the two most extreme residuals -- one large positive, one large negative -- sit noticeably off the line. Shapiro-Wilk rejects normality at p = 0.02 because those two points pull the statistic. Because the deviation is confined to the extremes rather than an S-curve or a skewed bend through the whole plot, the team correctly concludes the bulk of their model's errors are well-approximated by a normal distribution, their point predictions remain trustworthy, and only a naive symmetric 95 percent interval computed from the full-sample standard deviation would understate risk in the tails.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this exactly because it is where students overreact: a Shapiro-Wilk p-value under 0.05 gets treated as 'my model failed,' when a shape confined to the tails, or a large n making any deviation significant, means the point forecast is untouched. The judge's real question is whether a rejected normality test changed anything about how the team reports uncertainty -- did they widen or reshape their interval, switch to a bootstrap or quantile-based interval, or did they just report the p-value and move on without acting on what it implies for the interval specifically.

questions.prompt: A residual Q-Q plot shows an S-curve: points bow below the reference line at the low end and above it at the high end. What does this indicate?

options.text: Heavier tails than a normal distribution -- more extreme values in both directions than expected
Right skew in the residual distribution
The residuals are perfectly normal
A single outlier is present

explanations.a: Correct -- an S-curve, with curvature reversing direction once, is the classic signature of heavy tails, common to distributions like Student's t.
explanations.b: Skew produces a one-directional concave bend across the whole range, not a curve that reverses direction in the middle.
explanations.c: Perfectly normal residuals would sit on the 45-degree line throughout, with no systematic bowing at either end.
explanations.d: A single outlier would show as one isolated point off the line, not a systematic S-shaped bow across the full range.

questions.prompt: Shapiro-Wilk rejects normality of a model's residuals with p = 0.001 on a dataset of 8,000 observations, but the Q-Q plot looks nearly straight throughout. What is the most defensible conclusion?

options.text: At large n, the test has power to detect trivial deviations from normality; the point forecast is likely still fine, but a Gaussian interval should be checked carefully
The point forecast is now invalid and the model must be discarded
The p-value is definitely a computational error since the plot looks straight
Normality tests are meaningless at any sample size and should never be run

explanations.a: Correct -- Shapiro-Wilk and similar tests grow more powerful with n, so at large samples they reject even negligible departures from normality; the plot's near-straight shape shows the departure is practically small.
explanations.b: Non-normal residuals do not invalidate a point forecast; they only threaten the validity of a Gaussian-based prediction interval.
explanations.c: A significant p-value on a large sample with a near-straight Q-Q plot is expected behavior, not an error -- the test is doing exactly what it is designed to do.
explanations.d: The tests remain informative at small to moderate n; the caveat is specifically about over-interpreting significance at large n.

questions.prompt: Match each Q-Q plot deviation pattern to its correct interpretation.

left.text: Deviation confined to the extreme few points only

right.text: Heavier or lighter tails than normal
Skewed residual distribution
Body of the distribution is fine; only a few outliers are non-normal

questions.explanation: An S-curve signals tail-weight mismatch, a one-directional bend signals skew, and deviation only at the extremes signals a handful of outliers rather than a globally wrong distribution.

questions.prompt: Order the correct response to a rejected normality test on model residuals.

items.text: Run Shapiro-Wilk or Jarque-Bera and note the p-value
Inspect the Q-Q plot to see where the deviation occurs (tails only, one-directional, or S-shaped)
Confirm the point forecast itself is unaffected by non-normality
Decide whether the Gaussian prediction interval needs replacing with a wider, skewed, or bootstrap-based interval

questions.explanation: The p-value alone does not say where the problem lies; the Q-Q shape localizes it, the point forecast is confirmed unaffected, and only then is the interval method reconsidered.

lessons.label: Autocorrelated Residuals: Information You Left on the Table

sections.heading: The residual ACF and its significance bands
sections.body: The residual autocorrelation function (ACF) plots the correlation between residuals separated by lag k -- e_t and e_{t-k} -- for k = 1, 2, 3, and so on. If a model has captured all predictable structure, residuals should behave like white noise: every lag's autocorrelation should hover near zero. The plot's significance bands, drawn at plus or minus 1.96 divided by the square root of T (the sample size), mark the range within which a white-noise process's sample autocorrelation would fall 95 percent of the time by chance alone. A bar crossing outside those bands at even one lag is a candidate signal, though with many lags plotted, a few crossings are expected by chance even for a genuinely white-noise series -- one isolated crossing at lag 7 is far weaker evidence than a cluster of crossings or a large spike at lag 1. A large spike specifically at lag 1 is the most common and most consequential finding in practice: it means yesterday's forecast error predicts today's, the clearest possible sign that a lagged term or an autoregressive component is missing from the model entirely.

sections.heading: Ljung-Box, Durbin-Watson, and Breusch-Godfrey
sections.body: The Ljung-Box test turns the whole ACF into a single portmanteau statistic, summing squared autocorrelations across multiple lags at once rather than testing one lag in isolation. The standard rule of thumb, used in Hyndman and Athanasopoulos's Forecasting: Principles and Practice, is h = 10 lags for non-seasonal data or h = 2m lags for seasonal data of period m (so h = 24 for monthly data). Because the residuals came from a fitted model, the test statistic's degrees of freedom must be reduced by the number of fitted parameters (K), giving h minus K degrees of freedom -- skipping this correction inflates the p-value and can hide real autocorrelation. Durbin-Watson, developed by James Durbin and Geoffrey Watson in 1950 and 1951, is older and narrower: it tests only lag-1 autocorrelation, and its statistic (ranging 0 to 4, with 2 indicating none) is invalid whenever a lagged dependent variable appears among the predictors. Breusch-Godfrey, from Trevor Breusch and Leslie Godfrey in 1978, generalizes to any number of lags and remains valid with lagged predictors, making it the more broadly applicable choice. The stakes of any of these tests rejecting are two-fold and both matter: a significant result proves a systematically better point forecast is achievable using information already in hand, and it typically means any prediction interval computed under an independence assumption is too narrow -- most often when the autocorrelation is positive (the common case in practice), since true variance under positively correlated errors is higher than the naive formula assumes; negative autocorrelation would instead push the naive interval too wide.

lessons.workedExample: A team forecasting daily lab temperature readings fits a linear trend model and checks the residual ACF: the bar at lag 1 spikes to 0.42, far outside the plus-or-minus-1.96-over-square-root-of-90 band (roughly 0.21 for T = 90). A Ljung-Box test at h = 10, with 1 degree of freedom subtracted for the one fitted slope parameter, rejects white noise at p less than 0.001. This means yesterday's over- or under-prediction predicts today's -- likely because the model missed a slow day-to-day drift, such as gradual equipment warm-up. Adding a lagged-residual (autoregressive) term to the model and re-checking the ACF brings every bar back inside the bands, confirming the missing structure has been captured.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees a forecasting project with no residual ACF or Ljung-Box result will ask directly whether the residuals were checked for leftover structure, because a significant autocorrelation is not a minor footnote -- it is proof a better forecast exists using only information the team already had, and it typically means any prediction interval reported is too narrow, since interval width formulas assume independent errors and the common case in practice is positive autocorrelation. The strongest answer names the specific lag or lags that triggered the rejection and explains, mechanically, why that lag makes sense given the process being forecast (a weekly cycle at lag 7, a daily carryover at lag 1).

questions.prompt: What do the significance bands on a residual ACF plot, drawn at roughly plus/minus 1.96 over the square root of T, represent?

options.text: The range within which a white-noise process's sample autocorrelation would fall about 95 percent of the time by chance
The exact threshold above which forecasts become unusable
The model's R-squared confidence interval
A fixed constant that never depends on sample size

explanations.a: Correct -- the bands are the 95 percent bounds for sample autocorrelation under the null hypothesis of white noise, scaled by 1 over the square root of the sample size.
explanations.b: Crossing the band flags a candidate signal for further testing, not an automatic verdict that forecasts are unusable.
explanations.c: The bands concern residual autocorrelation specifically, unrelated to R-squared.
explanations.d: The bands shrink as T grows, since the formula divides by the square root of T -- they are explicitly sample-size dependent.

questions.prompt: Why must Ljung-Box degrees of freedom be reduced by the number of fitted model parameters (K)?

options.text: Because the residuals came from a fitted model, and skipping the correction inflates the p-value, potentially hiding real autocorrelation
Because more parameters always increase autocorrelation
Because the correction is only cosmetic and does not change conclusions
Because Ljung-Box cannot be computed at all without this correction

explanations.a: Correct -- fitting parameters already removes some structure from the residuals, so the test's reference distribution must account for that, and omitting the correction understates evidence of true autocorrelation.
explanations.b: More parameters do not mechanically increase autocorrelation; the correction is about the test's reference distribution, not the residuals themselves.
explanations.c: The correction changes the degrees of freedom used to compute the p-value and can materially change the test's conclusion.
explanations.d: Ljung-Box can be computed without the correction; it will simply be a less accurate test.

questions.prompt: Match each autocorrelation test to its defining limitation or scope.

right.text: Tests only lag-1 autocorrelation; invalid with a lagged dependent variable as a predictor
Tests any number of lags and remains valid with lagged predictors
Portmanteau test summing squared autocorrelations across multiple lags at once

questions.explanation: Durbin-Watson is the oldest and narrowest, limited to lag 1 and invalid with lagged predictors; Breusch-Godfrey generalizes to any lag structure; Ljung-Box is the standard multi-lag portmanteau test used with forecasting models.

questions.prompt: Order the correct workflow for testing residual autocorrelation after fitting a forecasting model.

items.text: Compute residuals from the fitted model
Plot the residual ACF with 1.96/sqrt(T) significance bands
Run Ljung-Box at h = 10 (or 2m for seasonal data), adjusting degrees of freedom for fitted parameters
If significant, identify which lag(s) drive it and add the corresponding structure to the model

questions.explanation: Residuals must exist before any autocorrelation check, the ACF plot gives a first visual read, Ljung-Box formalizes it across multiple lags with the correct degrees-of-freedom adjustment, and a significant result should be traced to a specific lag and folded back into the model.

lessons.label: Heteroscedasticity: Detecting It and Fixing It

sections.heading: Formal tests behind the funnel
sections.body: Where the residual-vs-fitted funnel gives a visual read, Breusch-Pagan and White formalize it into a p-value. Breusch-Pagan, introduced by Trevor Breusch and Adrian Pagan in 1979, regresses the squared residuals on the original predictors and tests whether that auxiliary regression explains a significant share of variance -- if squared residuals rise with a predictor, variance is not constant. White's test, from Halbert White in 1980, generalizes this by also including squared predictors and cross-products in the auxiliary regression, catching heteroscedasticity driven by nonlinear or interaction effects that Breusch-Pagan's simpler linear version can miss, at the cost of needing more data to keep power reasonable. Both output a chi-squared statistic; a significant result confirms what the funnel shape already suggested, and both are considered a required companion to the visual check rather than a replacement for it, since a p-value alone cannot show which predictor or range is driving the effect. Inspecting the coefficients of the auxiliary regression itself, not just its overall p-value, tells you which predictor's variance-driving effect is strongest -- a useful step before choosing between a global transform of y and a predictor-specific weighting scheme.

sections.heading: The Box-Cox ladder and robust standard errors
sections.body: The Box-Cox transformation, from George Box and David Cox's 1964 paper, re-expresses the target along a one-parameter ladder indexed by lambda: lambda = 0 gives log(y), lambda = 0.5 gives the square root, and lambda = 1 leaves y unchanged, with lambda chosen (often by maximum likelihood) to make residual variance as constant as possible on the transformed scale. The consequence of skipping this step is concrete: a model reporting one constant-width prediction interval across its whole range, while the true error process is fanning wider at higher fitted values, systematically under-covers at the high end and over-covers at the low end, even though the average coverage across the whole dataset might look approximately correct. When the original scale must be preserved for interpretation -- a stakeholder needs dollars or grams, not log-dollars -- heteroscedasticity-robust standard errors, the White (1980) or Huber (1967) sandwich estimator, correct the standard errors used for hypothesis tests and confidence intervals without transforming y at all, trading a transformed scale for a more complex variance formula instead. Neither fix is universally superior: a transform changes what the model's coefficients mean (a slope becomes a percentage effect under a log transform), while robust standard errors leave coefficients interpretable in original units but do nothing to fix a fanning prediction interval, which is a separate problem the science-fair team must still address on its own.

lessons.workedExample: A team regressing household energy use on square footage sees a residual funnel and runs Breusch-Pagan: the auxiliary regression of squared residuals on square footage gives p = 0.003, confirming variance grows with home size. They try two fixes. First, log-transforming energy use and refitting: the residual funnel flattens, but predictions and intervals are now on a log scale needing back-transformation. Second, keeping energy use on its original scale but computing White standard errors for the coefficients: hypothesis tests on the slope are now valid, but the constant-width interval problem remains untouched, because robust standard errors fix inference on coefficients, not the shape of the prediction interval itself.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing this topic wants to see the connection between a formal test's p-value and an actual, stated consequence for intervals -- not just 'we ran Breusch-Pagan and it was significant.' The stronger answer explains which fix was chosen and why: a transform when the team could accept a changed scale, robust standard errors when the original units mattered for the science-fair conclusion but coefficient inference (not interval shape) was the concern. A team that names both options and picks deliberately signals they understand the tests diagnose the same problem but that the two fixes solve different halves of it.

questions.prompt: How does the White test for heteroscedasticity generalize beyond the Breusch-Pagan test?

options.text: It includes squared predictors and cross-products in the auxiliary regression, catching nonlinear or interaction-driven variance patterns
It uses a t-statistic instead of a chi-squared statistic
It requires no auxiliary regression at all
It only works when residuals are already known to be normal

explanations.a: Correct -- White's auxiliary regression adds squared terms and cross-products, so it can catch heteroscedasticity that depends on nonlinear or interaction effects Breusch-Pagan's linear-only version would miss.
explanations.b: Both Breusch-Pagan and White output a chi-squared statistic from their auxiliary regressions.
explanations.c: Both tests are built on an auxiliary regression of squared residuals on some set of regressors.
explanations.d: Neither test requires a normality assumption on the original residuals to be run.

questions.prompt: On the Box-Cox ladder, what value of lambda corresponds to a plain log transform of the target?

options.text: lambda = 0
lambda = 0.5
lambda = 1
lambda = 2

explanations.a: Correct -- the Box-Cox family is defined so that lambda = 0 is the limiting case that recovers log(y).
explanations.b: lambda = 0.5 corresponds to a square-root transform, a weaker variance-stabilizing transform than log.
explanations.c: lambda = 1 leaves the data on its original, untransformed scale.
explanations.d: lambda = 2 is not a standard point on the ladder used for variance stabilization; typical selected values fall between 0 and 1.

questions.prompt: A team wants to keep predictions in original dollar units but still get valid hypothesis tests on their model's coefficients despite heteroscedastic residuals. What should they use?

options.text: Heteroscedasticity-robust (White or Huber sandwich) standard errors
A Box-Cox log transform of the target
The Ljung-Box test
A Q-Q plot of the residuals

explanations.a: Correct -- robust standard errors correct coefficient inference for non-constant variance without changing the scale of the target variable.
explanations.b: A log transform changes the scale of y, which the team explicitly wants to avoid for interpretability.
explanations.c: Ljung-Box tests residual autocorrelation, a separate diagnostic unrelated to variance constancy.
explanations.d: A Q-Q plot checks residual normality, not variance constancy, and does not fix anything on its own.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for detecting and addressing heteroscedasticity while preserving the original scale of the target.

items.text: Notice a funnel shape in the residual-vs-fitted plot
Confirm it with a Breusch-Pagan or White test
Decide whether the target's original scale must be preserved for interpretation
If yes, recompute standard errors using a White or Huber sandwich estimator instead of transforming y

questions.explanation: The visual funnel comes first, a formal test confirms it, then the scale-preservation constraint determines whether a transform or a robust-standard-error correction is the appropriate fix.

lessons.label: Transformation Bias, Leverage, and Influential Points

sections.heading: Jensen's inequality and Duan's smearing estimator
sections.body: When a model is fit on log(y) and forecasts are un-logged by simply exponentiating, the result is systematically too low, on average, whenever the goal is the mean of y rather than its median. This follows from Jensen's inequality: exp is a convex function, so exp(E[log Y]) is less than or equal to E[Y], with equality only in degenerate cases. Exponentiating a mean forecast made on the log scale recovers an estimate of the median of y, not its mean, and the gap between median and mean grows with the residual variance on the log scale and with the skew of y's distribution. Naihua Duan's 1983 smearing estimator corrects this without assuming a normal error distribution: it re-scales the naive back-transformed forecast by the average of exp(residual) taken over the fitted model's own in-sample residuals, a nonparametric correction that works even when residuals are not Gaussian. Hyndman and Athanasopoulos's Forecasting: Principles and Practice documents an equivalent bias-adjustment formula for Box-Cox back-transformation that adds a variance-dependent correction term to the naive back-transformed point forecast, producing a mean forecast rather than a median one. Either correction is small when residual variance on the log scale is small, which is exactly why the bias is easy to miss in a clean-looking fit -- the gap only becomes visible, and consequential, once variance or skew is large enough to check explicitly rather than assumed away.

sections.heading: Leverage, Cook's distance, and the re-run rule
sections.body: Leverage measures how far a point sits in predictor (x) space, independent of its y-value, formalized as the diagonal of the hat matrix, h_ii, bounded between 0 and 1; a common flag threshold is leverage above 2p/n or 3p/n, where p is the number of fitted parameters. A high-leverage point is not automatically a problem -- it only becomes damaging when it also has a large residual. Cook's distance, introduced by R. Dennis Cook in 1977, combines both quantities into a single influence score measuring how much the entire fitted line would shift if that one point were deleted; a common flag threshold is a Cook's distance exceeding 4/n. A single influential point can swing a fitted slope enough to flip a conclusion about direction or significance. Because leverage, Cook's distance, residual shape, and variance are all computed from a specific fitted model on a specific scale, every one of these diagnostics must be re-run from scratch after any transformation of y or the predictors -- a point that was influential on the raw scale may not be on the log scale, and vice versa, so re-checking is not optional busywork but a genuine re-evaluation.

lessons.workedExample: A team fits log(sales) against advertising spend and forecasts a mean log-sales value of 4.0, exponentiating to get a point forecast of e^4.0 = 54.6 units. Because their in-sample residuals have a variance of 0.09 on the log scale, Duan's smearing factor -- the average of exp(residual) across their training residuals -- comes out to about 1.05, giving a corrected forecast of 54.6 times 1.05 = 57.3 units. The naive exponentiated forecast, 54.6, was a median-of-sales estimate and under-forecast the mean by roughly 5 percent; over many forecasts, that systematic gap compounds into a real under-prediction of total expected sales.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees a log-transformed model and a forecast obtained by simply exponentiating the fitted value is testing whether the team knows Jensen's inequality applies here, and that the naive back-transformation targets the median, not the mean -- a subtle but real bias that a team confident enough to log-transform their data should also be prepared to correct. A second probe is whether leverage and Cook's distance were re-examined after the transform, since a team that ran influence diagnostics only once, on the raw scale, may be carrying an unnoticed influential point on the scale their model actually fits.

questions.prompt: Why does simply exponentiating a mean forecast made on the log scale systematically under-forecast the mean of y?

options.text: By Jensen's inequality, exp is convex, so exp(E[log Y]) recovers an estimate of the median, not the mean, of Y
Exponentiation always introduces random noise into the forecast
Log transforms only work correctly when the target is already normally distributed
The bias only occurs when the model has more than one predictor

explanations.a: Correct -- Jensen's inequality for the convex exponential function means exponentiating a log-scale mean gives a median-of-Y estimate, which is less than or equal to the true mean of Y.
explanations.b: The gap is a deterministic, predictable bias from Jensen's inequality, not added randomness.
explanations.c: The bias arises specifically because of the nonlinearity of exp, regardless of whether y itself is normally distributed.
explanations.d: The bias is a property of the log-and-exponentiate transformation itself and occurs with any number of predictors, including just one.

questions.prompt: What does Duan's smearing estimator do differently from simply exponentiating a log-scale forecast?

options.text: It rescales the naive back-transformed forecast using the average of exp(residual) over the model's own residuals, without assuming normality
It assumes residuals are exactly Gaussian and applies a fixed formula based on that assumption
It discards the log transform entirely and refits on the raw scale
It only works for time series data, never for cross-sectional regression

explanations.a: Correct -- the smearing estimator is a nonparametric correction built directly from the empirical distribution of in-sample residuals, requiring no normality assumption.
explanations.b: The Gaussian-based bias-adjustment formula is a separate, parametric alternative; Duan's method is specifically nonparametric.
explanations.c: The smearing estimator still uses the log-scale fitted model; it corrects the back-transformation step, not the fitting step.
explanations.d: The estimator applies to any regression setting with a log-transformed target, not just time series.

questions.prompt: Match each influence-diagnostic concept to what it measures.

right.text: How far a point sits in predictor space, regardless of its y-value
How much the whole fitted line would shift if that point were deleted, combining leverage and residual size
How far that single point's y-value is from the model's prediction, alone

questions.explanation: Leverage is purely about predictor-space position, residual size alone is purely about fit at that point, and Cook's distance is the combined influence measure that determines whether a point actually swings the fitted model.

questions.prompt: Order the correct workflow when a target variable is log-transformed and later needs a point forecast in original units.

items.text: Fit the regression model on log(y)
Generate a mean forecast on the log scale
Apply a bias-adjustment (Duan's smearing or the fpp3 Box-Cox formula) rather than naively exponentiating
Re-run leverage, Cook's distance, and all other residual diagnostics on the transformed-scale model

questions.explanation: Fitting comes first, then a log-scale forecast, then the bias-corrected back-transformation rather than a naive exponentiation, and finally a full re-run of every influence and residual diagnostic, since none of them carry over unchanged from the raw scale to the transformed one.

units.label: R-squared, Fit Statistics, and the Interpretation Traps

lessons.label: What R-squared Actually Measures

sections.heading: The ratio 1 minus SSE over SST is a comparison, not a grade
sections.body: R-squared is defined as 1 minus the ratio of your model's sum of squared errors (SSE) to the total sum of squares (SST), where SST is the squared deviation of each observed y from the sample mean of y. That denominator is not an abstract normalizing constant — it is the SSE of a specific, concrete baseline model: one that ignores every predictor and always guesses the mean of y. R-squared is therefore a head-to-head scorecard against the single dumbest model you could build, a report card measured against a model with zero information. An R-squared of 0.80 says 'my model's errors are 20% of the size, in squared terms, of always guessing the average' — a meaningful claim, but a much weaker one than 'my model is accurate,' since the bar it clears is set on the floor.

sections.heading: Equal to squared correlation in simple OLS — and only there
sections.body: In simple linear regression with one predictor and an intercept, R-squared is not just related to Pearson's correlation coefficient r — it is exactly r squared, a direct algebraic identity from the normal equations of ordinary least squares. That identity is why researchers before regression software existed used r-squared informally as a fit measure. But the identity is narrow: it holds only for OLS with a single regressor and an intercept. Add a second predictor, drop the intercept, or switch to ridge regression, logistic regression, or any non-OLS estimator, and R-squared is no longer any squared correlation — it is just 1 minus SSE over SST, computed from whatever fit the estimator produced, and can even go negative outside OLS-with-intercept settings.

sections.heading: Why adding any column, including noise, can never hurt in-sample R-squared
sections.body: Ordinary least squares finds the coefficient vector that minimizes SSE over all vectors of that dimension. Adding a predictor column enlarges the search space without shrinking it — the old best-fit solution remains reachable by setting the new coefficient to exactly zero. So minimum SSE can only fall or stay flat, never rise, meaning in-sample R-squared can never decrease when you add a column, regardless of whether that column carries real signal or is pure random noise. Push this to its logical extreme: with 30 rows and 20 columns of independent random numbers with no relationship to y, ordinary least squares will fit the noise so well that R-squared climbs past 0.9 — not because the noise predicts anything, but because 20 free coefficients are being tuned against 30 data points, leaving almost no residual degrees of freedom to resist overfitting.

lessons.workedExample: Simulate 30 rows of an outcome y generated from one true predictor x plus random error, then generate 20 additional columns of pure np.random.normal() noise built with zero relationship to y. Fit OLS with only x: R-squared lands near the modest true value, say 0.25. Now fit OLS with all 21 predictors. Because 30 observations are being fit with 21 coefficients — only 9 residual degrees of freedom — the least-squares optimizer finds combinations of noise columns that happen to align with this sample's specific 30 residuals, and R-squared jumps past 0.90 even though every added column is independent random noise. Nothing about the true relationship improved; the model memorized sampling noise using nearly as many parameters as data points.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'what does your R-squared of 0.85 actually mean' is testing whether you know it is a comparison to a mean-only baseline, not an absolute accuracy grade. The sharper follow-up — 'did you check whether adding more variables just inflated that number' — probes the noise guarantee directly: because in-sample R-squared mechanically cannot fall when predictors are added, a high value reached by throwing many candidate variables at a small dataset is a red flag, not an achievement. A student who explains why R-squared rose without any real gain in predictive power, and who reaches for adjusted R-squared or a held-out test set instead, shows they understand the metric's construction rather than treating it as a black-box success signal.

questions.prompt: In simple linear regression with a single predictor and an intercept, R-squared equals which quantity exactly?

options.text: The slope coefficient of the regression line
The squared Pearson correlation coefficient, r-squared
1 minus the p-value of the slope
The standard error of the residuals

explanations.a: The slope has different units and is not bounded between 0 and 1 the way R-squared is; they are not the same quantity.
explanations.b: Correct — this is a direct algebraic identity from OLS's normal equations, but it holds only for simple regression with an intercept.
explanations.c: R-squared and the p-value are computed from different quantities and are not algebraically interchangeable.
explanations.d: The residual standard error is in the units of y and measures typical error size, not a proportion of variance explained.

questions.prompt: A dataset has 30 rows. A researcher adds 20 columns of pure random noise, entirely unrelated to y, to a regression that already included x. What happens to in-sample R-squared?

options.text: It is guaranteed to increase or, at worst, stay exactly the same
It decreases, because irrelevant columns add no information
It becomes undefined once noise columns are present
It only changes if the noise happens to correlate with x

explanations.a: Correct — OLS minimizes SSE, and the old solution stays reachable by zeroing the new coefficients, so SSE cannot rise and R-squared cannot fall.
explanations.b: This is the intuitive but wrong answer: R-squared is a mechanical, in-sample quantity that cannot fall when a column is added, regardless of relevance.
explanations.c: R-squared remains perfectly well-defined; it is simply computed from the new, larger fitted model.
explanations.d: The guarantee holds unconditionally for in-sample OLS R-squared, whether or not the added columns correlate with anything.

questions.prompt: In the formula R-squared = 1 - SSE/SST, what does SST represent?

options.text: The sum of squared errors from a mean-only baseline model
The sum of squared errors of your fitted model
The total number of predictors used in the model
The sample size multiplied by the residual variance

explanations.a: Correct — SST is the sum of squared deviations of y from its own mean, which is exactly the SSE you would get from always predicting the mean.
explanations.b: That quantity is SSE, the numerator of the ratio, not SST, the denominator.
explanations.c: SST has nothing to do with predictor count; it is purely a property of the outcome variable y.
explanations.d: That description does not match SST's definition as a sum of squared deviations from the mean.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of the noise-inflation demonstration in the order they were performed.

items.text: Fit OLS with just the true predictor x and record a baseline R-squared near 0.25
Generate 20 columns of independent random noise unrelated to y
Fit OLS again using x plus all 20 noise columns
Observe R-squared climb past 0.9 because 21 coefficients are fit to only 30 rows

questions.explanation: The baseline model is fit first to establish the true signal's modest R-squared; only then are noise columns generated and added, and the inflated R-squared is observed as the final consequence of near-zero residual degrees of freedom.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

right.text: 1 minus SSE divided by SST
Sum of squared deviations of y from its mean (the mean-only baseline's errors)
Sum of squared residuals from the fitted model
In simple OLS with an intercept, its square equals R-squared

questions.explanation: R-squared is the ratio 1 - SSE/SST; SST is the mean-only baseline's squared error; SSE is the fitted model's squared error; and Pearson's r, squared, equals R-squared only in simple OLS regression with an intercept.

lessons.label: Adjusted R-squared, AIC, BIC, and AICc — Fit With a Penalty

sections.heading: Adjusted R-squared: the one fit statistic that can fall
sections.body: Adjusted R-squared rescales ordinary R-squared by degrees of freedom: 1 - (1-R-squared) * (n-1)/(n-k-1), where n is sample size and k is the number of predictors. Because the penalty term grows with k, adding a predictor that barely reduces SSE can make adjusted R-squared drop even while raw R-squared rises by construction — the one statistic in this family that can send an honest signal that a variable is not earning its place. Concretely, with n = 50 and k = 5, the multiplier (n-1)/(n-k-1) is 49/44 ≈ 1.11; push k to 20 and it becomes 49/29 ≈ 1.69, so the same tiny drop in raw R-squared gets amplified far more once many parameters are already in play. It remains an in-sample quantity computed from the same fitted residuals as R-squared itself, just with bookkeeping for how many parameters purchased the fit.

sections.heading: Where AIC and BIC came from
sections.body: Hirotugu Akaike introduced AIC in 1973-1974 by connecting maximum-likelihood fit to the Kullback-Leibler divergence between a candidate model and the unknown true data-generating process, giving a principled information-theoretic penalty rather than an ad hoc one. Gideon Schwarz introduced the competing Bayesian Information Criterion, also called the Schwarz Criterion, in 1978, deriving it as a large-sample approximation to the Bayes factor between models under a specific prior — a fundamentally different justification from Akaike's, which is why the two criteria can rank the same candidate models differently.

sections.heading: AIC and BIC charge per parameter, but at different rates
sections.body: Akaike's Information Criterion is AIC = 2k - 2ln(L), where L is the model's maximized likelihood; the Bayesian Information Criterion is BIC = k*ln(n) - 2ln(L). Both are lower-is-better. AIC charges a flat 2 points per parameter; BIC charges ln(n) points per parameter, which exceeds 2 once n is larger than about 8 observations — so BIC penalizes complexity harder and systematically favors smaller models than AIC as sample size grows. When n/k drops below roughly 40, the standard AIC becomes biased toward overfit models in small samples, and the corrected AICc = AIC + 2k(k+1)/(n-k-1) is the recommended replacement.

sections.heading: What each is proven to approximate — and the hard boundary
sections.body: The two penalties are not arbitrary: Stone (1977) showed AIC is asymptotically equivalent to leave-one-out cross-validation error, meaning minimizing AIC approximates minimizing out-of-sample prediction error as sample size grows. Schwarz (1978) showed BIC is model-selection consistent — if the true data-generating model is among the candidates, BIC's probability of selecting it converges to 1 as n grows, a property plain AIC lacks. Despite these asymptotic guarantees, all four statistics — R-squared, adjusted R-squared, AIC, and BIC — are computed entirely from the training data used to fit the model.
