None of them is a substitute for evaluating forecast error on data the model never saw.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher compares three models for predicting lab scores from 45 observations: Model A with 3 predictors, Model B with 8, Model C with 15. Raw R-squared rises monotonically, A to B to C, as expected. Adjusted R-squared peaks at Model B and falls for Model C, flagging the extra 7 parameters as not worth their cost. AIC also favors Model B. BIC, with its harsher ln(45) ≈ 3.8-point-per-parameter charge versus AIC's flat 2, favors an even smaller model, Model A. Because n/k for Model C is 45/15 = 3, far below 40, the researcher recomputes AICc for all three and finds it agrees with BIC: Model A is safest given how few observations support each added parameter.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees you comparing models by raw R-squared alone will ask whether you controlled for the number of parameters — the expected fix is adjusted R-squared, AIC, or BIC, and a strong answer explains why BIC's log(n) penalty makes it choose more conservatively than AIC's flat 2k as the dataset grows. The harder follow-up is procedural: 'you picked the best model by AIC — how do you know it forecasts well?' The defensible answer is that AIC, BIC, and adjusted R-squared are all computed on the training fit, and none of them replaces measuring error on a genuine held-out sample, which is the only direct evidence of forecasting ability.

questions.prompt: Why can adjusted R-squared decrease when a new predictor is added, unlike raw R-squared, which never can?

options.text: Adjusted R-squared is computed on a held-out test set
Its formula includes a degrees-of-freedom penalty that grows with the number of predictors
It is always equal to AIC divided by sample size
It only uses half of the training data by convention

explanations.a: Adjusted R-squared is still computed entirely from in-sample residuals; it is not a cross-validated or held-out quantity.
explanations.b: Correct — the (n-1)/(n-k-1) term grows as k grows, so a predictor that barely reduces SSE can still lower the adjusted value.
explanations.c: Adjusted R-squared and AIC are different formulas built from different penalty structures; one is not a rescaling of the other.
explanations.d: There is no such data-splitting convention in the definition of adjusted R-squared.

questions.prompt: As sample size n grows, why does BIC tend to select smaller models than AIC?

options.text: BIC's penalty per parameter is ln(n), which exceeds AIC's flat 2 once n is larger than about 8
BIC only considers models with fewer than 5 predictors by definition
AIC's penalty grows faster than BIC's as n increases
BIC ignores the likelihood term entirely

explanations.a: Correct — BIC charges ln(n) per parameter versus AIC's constant 2, and ln(n) > 2 once n exceeds about 8, so BIC penalizes complexity increasingly harder as data grows.
explanations.b: BIC has no hard cap on predictor count; its selectivity comes purely from the size of the per-parameter penalty.
explanations.c: This has the comparison backwards — it is BIC's penalty that grows with n, while AIC's stays fixed at 2 per parameter.
explanations.d: Both AIC and BIC include the same -2ln(L) likelihood term; they differ only in the complexity penalty added to it.

questions.prompt: A model has n = 40 observations and k = 12 parameters, so n/k ≈ 3.3. Which statistic is recommended over plain AIC in this situation?

options.text: AICc, the small-sample-corrected version of AIC
Plain R-squared, since it needs no correction
The Pearson correlation coefficient
Adjusted R-squared, since it replaces AIC entirely

explanations.a: Correct — the standard rule of thumb is to prefer AICc once n/k falls below roughly 40, and here n/k is only about 3.3, well under that threshold.
explanations.b: Raw R-squared has no built-in parameter penalty at all and does not address the small-sample bias AICc corrects for.
explanations.c: The correlation coefficient measures a different thing entirely and is not a model-comparison criterion.
explanations.d: Adjusted R-squared is a separate statistic with its own penalty structure; it does not replace or correct AIC.

questions.prompt: Match each fit statistic or property to what it is proven or defined to do.

right.text: Asymptotically equivalent to leave-one-out cross-validation error (Stone, 1977)
Consistent for the true model if it is among the candidates (Schwarz, 1978)
k times ln(n), harsher than AIC's flat 2k for typical sample sizes
Recommended correction when n/k is below roughly 40

questions.explanation: AIC approximates leave-one-out CV error asymptotically; BIC is model-selection consistent when the true model is a candidate; BIC's penalty is k*ln(n), harsher than AIC's 2k; and AICc corrects AIC's small-sample bias when n/k drops below about 40.

questions.prompt: A researcher selects the model with the lowest AIC among several candidates. What is the one claim this selection does NOT support on its own?

options.text: That this model balances fit and complexity better than the others in the candidate set
That this model has been shown to forecast well on data it has never seen
That the model's likelihood, adjusted for parameter count, was most favorable among candidates
That simpler alternatives were penalized less harshly for their parameter count

explanations.a: This is exactly what a lowest-AIC selection does support — it is the intended in-sample balance between fit and complexity.
explanations.b: Correct — AIC, like R-squared, adjusted R-squared, and BIC, is computed entirely from training data; only an actual held-out or forecast test provides direct evidence of forecasting ability.
explanations.c: This is a correct description of what AIC compares across candidate models, so it is supported by the selection.
explanations.d: This is also a true description of how AIC's flat 2k penalty treats simpler models relative to more complex ones.

lessons.label: Out-of-Sample R-squared Can Be Negative — and Usually Should Scare You

sections.heading: The baseline quietly changes when you go out-of-sample
sections.body: In-sample R-squared compares your model's SSE against the SSE of a mean-only model fit on the SAME data. The out-of-sample version, R-squared_OOS = 1 - sum((y_test - yhat)^2) / sum((y_test - ybar_train)^2), used to score a model on a held-out test set, keeps the same 1-minus-ratio structure, but the denominator is now built from the TRAINING mean applied to test observations, since the true test mean is unknown at deployment time. If your model's test-set squared errors exceed what you would have gotten by just predicting the training mean for every test point, R-squared goes negative — a real, meaningful result, not a bug. This is exactly why scikit-learn's r2_score function routinely returns negative numbers on test data, and why students who have only ever seen the bounded 0-to-1 in-sample version assume their code is broken when it happens.

sections.heading: A field split over what counts as a failure
sections.body: Goyal and Welch's 2008 re-examination, 'A Comprehensive Look at the Empirical Performance of Equity Premium Prediction' (Review of Financial Studies), tested essentially every predictor proposed in the academic literature and found most produced negative historical out-of-sample R-squared against the trailing historical-average benchmark — a result read at the time as a broad indictment of return predictability. Campbell and Thompson's companion 2008 paper, 'Predicting Excess Stock Returns Out of Sample: Can Anything Beat the Historical Average?,' pushed back: once sensible sign and theory-based restrictions are imposed on the same predictors, out-of-sample R-squared of roughly 0.5% per month becomes achievable, and that is economically large, since compounded over years of asset-allocation decisions even that small an edge measurably shifts an investor's optimal portfolio and expected wealth. Whether a given out-of-sample R-squared counts as success or failure depends entirely on how much unpredictability the field expects, not a universal cutoff borrowed from in-sample OLS intuition.

sections.heading: What to do when the number comes back negative
sections.body: Outside finance, a negative out-of-sample R-squared on a student's own project — say, forecasting next semester's lab reagent costs from this semester's features — is a genuine warning sign, not automatically a dead end. The right response is diagnostic, not cosmetic: check whether the train-test split crosses a real regime change (new suppliers, new lab protocol) that the training period never saw, whether the model is overfit and needs regularization or fewer parameters, or whether a naive baseline genuinely is the right forecast for this variable. Reporting the negative value honestly, alongside the training-mean baseline it was compared against, is far more defensible in front of a judge than silently reporting only the in-sample R-squared and hoping the gap goes unnoticed.

lessons.workedExample: A student trains a regression on 2020-2023 data to predict next-month lab supply costs, then evaluates it on held-out 2024 data. The test SSE turns out larger than what a naive forecast of 'always predict the 2020-2023 training-period average cost' would have produced on that same 2024 data. Plugging into 1 - SSE_test/SST_test-vs-training-mean yields R-squared = -0.18. The student initially assumes a coding error, but the number is correct: the model's out-of-sample predictions were actually worse than ignoring the new features entirely and just repeating the historical average, likely because the cost relationship shifted between the training and test periods, a form of distribution drift the training-period R-squared could never have revealed.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who spots a negative R-squared on your test set may initially suspect a coding error, so a fast, confident explanation — that the test SST is computed from the training mean, not the test mean, and that this makes negative values both possible and diagnostic of real underperformance — signals genuine understanding of the metric's construction. The sharper test comes next: can you argue that a small positive out-of-sample R-squared is not automatically weak? Citing Campbell and Thompson's 0.5%-per-month result, and explaining why compounding and decision-relevance can make a tiny R-squared economically meaningful, shows you evaluate model performance against the right benchmark for the field rather than a memorized universal threshold.

questions.prompt: Why can out-of-sample R-squared be negative, unlike in-sample OLS R-squared, which is bounded between 0 and 1?

options.text: The test-set SST is built from the training-set mean, so a model can lose to that baseline on new data
R-squared is undefined outside of training data and negative values are a display artifact
Negative R-squared only occurs when the model uses regularization
Out-of-sample R-squared uses a different formula entirely, unrelated to SSE and SST

explanations.a: Correct — the baseline for the test-set comparison is the training mean applied to test data, not a mean fit on the test data itself, so the model can genuinely underperform that baseline.
explanations.b: The negative value is a real, meaningful computation, not a display bug or an undefined quantity.
explanations.c: Negative out-of-sample R-squared can occur with any estimator, regularized or not; it is about baseline comparison, not regularization.
explanations.d: The formula is the same 1 - SSE/SST structure; only which data built SST differs between the in-sample and out-of-sample cases.

questions.prompt: According to Campbell and Thompson (2008), an out-of-sample R-squared of about 0.5% per month for predicting equity returns is best described as:

options.text: Statistically meaningless and indistinguishable from zero
Economically large, because small monthly edges compound into meaningful effects on asset allocation
Evidence that the model is nearly as good as a perfect predictor
Proof that the historical average is a poor benchmark

explanations.a: Campbell and Thompson explicitly argue the opposite: a small out-of-sample R-squared in this setting is economically meaningful, not negligible.
explanations.b: Correct — this is the paper's core point: a tiny out-of-sample R-squared, in a domain where returns are famously hard to predict, can still shift optimal portfolio decisions meaningfully.
explanations.c: An R-squared of 0.5% is far from near-perfect prediction; the paper's point is about economic significance despite a small statistical value, not near-perfect accuracy.
explanations.d: The paper uses the historical average specifically because it is a strong, hard-to-beat benchmark in this domain, not a weak one.

questions.prompt: A student sees scikit-learn's r2_score() return -0.3 on their test set and assumes it is a bug. What is the correct response?

options.text: It is likely correct: the model's test predictions were worse than always guessing the training-period mean
r2_score() cannot return negative values, so this must be a version bug
Negative values only appear when the target variable is negative
The student should clip the result to 0 before reporting it

explanations.a: Correct — this is expected, documented behavior of r2_score() on test data and reflects genuine underperformance relative to the training-mean baseline.
explanations.b: r2_score() is explicitly documented to be capable of returning negative values on arbitrarily poor test-set predictions.
explanations.c: The sign of the target variable is irrelevant; negative R-squared depends on relative squared errors, not the sign of y.
explanations.d: Clipping to 0 would hide real information about the model underperforming the baseline; the honest move is to report and investigate the negative value.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to its correct description regarding out-of-sample R-squared.

right.text: Built using the TRAINING mean applied to test observations, not a test-set mean
Showed ~0.5%/month out-of-sample R-squared can be economically large for equity returns
Routinely returns negative values; this is documented, expected behavior
Means the model's test errors exceeded those of predicting the training mean

questions.explanation: Test-set SST uses the training mean as its baseline; Campbell and Thompson showed small out-of-sample R-squared can be economically meaningful; sklearn's r2_score documents negative outputs as expected; and a negative value directly means the model lost to the training-mean baseline on new data.

lessons.label: Anscombe, the Datasaurus, and Why a Number Is Not a Diagnostic

sections.heading: Four datasets, one set of statistics, four different stories
sections.body: In 1973, statistician Francis Anscombe published 'Graphs in Statistical Analysis' in The American Statistician, constructing four small datasets (11 points each) that share the same mean x of 9, mean y of 7.50, x-variance, y-variance, correlation of about 0.816, and OLS regression line y = 3.00 + 0.500x — and therefore the identical R-squared of about 0.667. Plotted, they are nothing alike: dataset I is a genuine linear relationship with normal scatter; dataset II is a clean curve that a straight line badly misrepresents; dataset III is a perfect line broken by a single outlier that drags the fitted slope away from the other ten points; dataset IV is nearly a vertical stack of identical x-values plus one extreme leverage point that alone generates the entire correlation. Anscombe built the quartet specifically to attack the practice of judging a fit from summary statistics without ever looking at a plot.

sections.heading: The Datasaurus Dozen: the same trick, automated and exaggerated
sections.body: In 2017, Justin Matejka and George Fitzmaurice published 'Same Stats, Different Graphs' at the ACM CHI conference, using a simulated-annealing algorithm to generate twelve additional datasets that match a thirteenth, seed dataset shaped like a cartoon dinosaur — all thirteen sharing the same mean x (about 54.3), mean y (about 47.8), standard deviations, and correlation (about -0.06) to two decimal places. The shapes range from a star to parallel lines to circles, none resembling a simple linear trend, yet every one of them would report a nearly identical, near-zero R-squared (roughly 0.06 squared, under 0.004) if a straight line were forced through it. Where Anscombe made his point with four hand-built cases, Matejka and Fitzmaurice showed the same failure mode scales to essentially arbitrary shapes via an automated, repeatable procedure.

sections.heading: Why R-squared specifically is the wrong lone judge
sections.body: Both demonstrations target R-squared precisely because it collapses an entire two-dimensional scatter into one number describing linear variance explained — any information about curvature, clustering, heteroscedasticity, or a single dominant point is thrown away in that collapse by construction, not by carelessness. A residual plot, by contrast, preserves exactly the information R-squared discards: it shows whether errors are patternless (supporting the linear fit) or systematically curved, fan-shaped, or dominated by one point (undermining it). The practical rule these two studies jointly establish is that R-squared and a residual or scatter plot are a single reporting unit — publishing one without the other is publishing half an analysis, whether the summary number looks flatteringly high, as in Anscombe's 0.667 across four shapes, or reassuringly near zero, as in the Datasaurus Dozen's shared near-zero correlation across thirteen wildly different scatters.

lessons.workedExample: A student fits a linear model to dataset III from Anscombe's quartet and reports R-squared = 0.667 with a straight face, treating it as evidence of a solid linear fit. A plot immediately reveals the truth: ten of the eleven points sit on a perfect line, and one severe outlier is single-handedly dragging the fitted slope and inflating the residual sum of squares in a way that happens to reproduce the same R-squared as the genuinely linear dataset I. The correct fix is not a better R-squared threshold — it is removing or separately investigating the outlier, refitting, and reporting both the revised fit and the fact that one point changed the conclusion, something no summary statistic alone would have surfaced.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge shown only an R-squared value and a regression equation, with no residual plot, should immediately ask 'can I see the scatterplot and residuals.' Anscombe's quartet is the canonical proof that identical R-squared, correlation, means, and even the fitted line can hide a linear relationship, a curve, an outlier-driven artifact, or a single-point leverage case — four completely different scientific conclusions. A student who volunteers the plot alongside the number, unprompted, signals they know R-squared is necessary but nowhere near sufficient; a student who offers only the number, especially a suspiciously clean one, invites exactly the follow-up question that exposes an unexamined fit.

questions.prompt: All four datasets in Anscombe's 1973 quartet share which of the following?

options.text: Identical means, variances, correlation, regression line, and R-squared, despite very different shapes
Identical raw data values, just plotted differently
The same R-squared but different correlation coefficients
No outliers in any of the four datasets

explanations.a: Correct — Anscombe deliberately constructed all four to match on mean, variance, correlation (~0.816), the fitted line (y = 3.00 + 0.500x), and R-squared (~0.667), while looking completely different when plotted.
explanations.b: The four datasets have different raw (x, y) pairs; only their summary statistics coincide, not the underlying values.
explanations.c: Since R-squared equals correlation squared in simple OLS, identical R-squared across the quartet implies identical correlation magnitude as well.
explanations.d: Dataset III specifically contains a single clear outlier, and dataset IV is built almost entirely around one leverage point.

questions.prompt: What did Matejka and Fitzmaurice's 2017 'Same Stats, Different Graphs' paper add beyond Anscombe's original point?

options.text: An algorithmic method generating many arbitrary shapes (a star, circles, a dinosaur) sharing summary statistics to two decimal places
A proof that R-squared cannot be computed for nonlinear data
A correction formula that fixes R-squared so it detects nonlinearity automatically
A replication showing Anscombe's original four datasets were mistaken

explanations.a: Correct — using simulated annealing, they generated thirteen datasets, including the 'Datasaurus' shape, that all match the same summary statistics to two decimal places, generalizing Anscombe's manual construction into an automated method.
explanations.b: R-squared is perfectly computable for any linear fit to any data, nonlinear or not; the issue is that the number alone does not reveal the shape.
explanations.c: No such corrective formula exists or was proposed; the paper's point is precisely that summary statistics, including R-squared, cannot be trusted alone.
explanations.d: The paper builds on and extends Anscombe's original insight; it does not challenge or overturn his 1973 result.

questions.prompt: What is the single strongest rule these two studies establish for reporting a regression fit?

options.text: R-squared and a residual or scatter plot should always be reported together, never the number alone
R-squared should be replaced entirely by the correlation coefficient
Only datasets with R-squared above 0.9 need to be plotted
Outliers should always be deleted before computing R-squared

explanations.a: Correct — this is the shared conclusion of both studies: an R-squared or correlation value in isolation cannot distinguish a genuine linear fit from a curve, an outlier artifact, or an arbitrary shape.
explanations.b: Correlation has the identical blind spot as R-squared in simple OLS, since one is just the square of the other; swapping one number for another does not fix the underlying problem.
explanations.c: The need to plot data applies regardless of how high or low R-squared is; a high R-squared is exactly the case that most tempts people to skip the plot, which is the failure mode both studies target.
explanations.d: Outliers should be investigated and reported, not automatically deleted; dataset III's point is that blind deletion without investigation is itself a bad practice.

questions.prompt: Match each Anscombe's-quartet dataset to what its scatterplot actually looks like.

right.text: A genuine linear relationship with normal scatter around the line
A clean curve poorly represented by a straight line
A near-perfect line broken by a single outlier
Nearly identical x-values plus one extreme leverage point driving the whole correlation

questions.explanation: Dataset I is genuinely linear, dataset II is a curve masquerading as linear, dataset III is a clean line wrecked by one outlier, and dataset IV is a vertical stack of x-values whose entire correlation comes from a single leverage point.

lessons.label: Pseudo-R-squared and Variants That Don't Mean What OLS R-squared Means

sections.heading: Why logistic and other GLM models needed their own R-squared
sections.body: Ordinary R-squared is built from sums of squared residuals, a quantity that only makes clean sense for models fit by minimizing squared error. Logistic regression, Poisson regression, and other generalized linear models are instead fit by maximizing likelihood, so several competing pseudo-R-squared statistics were built from log-likelihoods rather than residuals. McFadden's pseudo-R-squared, introduced by Daniel McFadden in his 1974 chapter 'Conditional Logit Analysis of Qualitative Choice Behavior,' is 1 - ln(L_model)/ln(L_null), comparing your fitted model's log-likelihood to that of an intercept-only null model — structurally parallel to OLS R-squared's 1 - SSE/SST, but built from likelihoods rather than variance, and bounded between 0 and a value just under 1. The 'pseudo' prefix is a deliberate warning label: unlike OLS R-squared, none of these is derived from a variance-decomposition identity, so none carries the 'proportion of variance explained' interpretation by construction, only an analogous direction (higher is better fit) and an analogous 0-to-nearly-1 scale.

sections.heading: Cox-Snell, Nagelkerke, and Efron: three more attempts at the same idea
sections.body: The Cox-Snell pseudo-R-squared, from David Cox and Joyce Snell's 1989 book 'Analysis of Binary Data,' is 1 - (L_null/L_model)^(2/n), but it cannot reach 1 even for a perfect-fitting model, a flaw Nico Nagelkerke's 1991 Biometrika note 'A Note on a General Definition of the Coefficient of Determination' fixes by dividing Cox-Snell's value by its own theoretical maximum, rescaling it to span 0 to 1. Bradley Efron's R-squared, from his 1978 paper 'Regression and ANOVA with Zero-One Data,' takes a different route entirely, applying the OLS-style 1 - SSE/SST formula directly to observed binary outcomes versus predicted probabilities, making it the pseudo-R-squared most directly comparable in spirit to the familiar linear version, though still not identical in what it certifies.

sections.heading: Different scales mean different judgments of 'good'
sections.body: McFadden himself noted that values between roughly 0.2 and 0.4 represent an excellent fit for his pseudo-R-squared, a range that would be a mediocre-to-weak result for OLS R-squared — because likelihood ratios compress far more aggressively than variance ratios do as fit improves, since a saturated binary-choice model's log-likelihood is rarely far from the null's in absolute terms. None of these four statistics is 'variance explained': each is an internally consistent measure of relative likelihood improvement or classification accuracy, useful for comparing nested models within the same family and estimator, but not for comparing a logistic model's 0.3 against an OLS model's 0.3 as though the numbers meant the same thing. This is also why a likelihood-ratio test, not a pseudo-R-squared comparison, is the standard way to formally decide whether adding a predictor to a logistic model improved the fit.

lessons.workedExample: A team fits a logistic regression predicting whether a lab team's project reaches the science fair, getting McFadden's pseudo-R-squared of 0.28. A teammate, used to OLS, worries 0.28 is a weak result. Checking McFadden's own guidance resolves it: 0.2 to 0.4 is his stated range for an excellent-fitting model, since the null log-likelihood for binary outcomes shrinks far less dramatically than SST does for continuous outcomes, so the same numeric improvement corresponds to a much stronger fit. The team also computes Nagelkerke's rescaled version, getting 0.41, and reports both figures alongside a classification accuracy number, since neither pseudo-R-squared alone certifies the model the way OLS R-squared would for a linear fit.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge trained on OLS intuition who sees 'R-squared = 0.35' on a logistic regression slide may assume the model is weak, since 0.35 is mediocre for linear regression. The prepared answer is not to apologize for the number but to reframe it: name which pseudo-R-squared was computed, explain that McFadden's own benchmark places 0.2-0.4 as excellent, and note that pseudo-R-squared values are not portable across model families the way OLS R-squared roughly is between similarly-specified linear models. A student who can also cite Nagelkerke's rescaling or Efron's alternative construction shows they understand these are a family of related-but-distinct constructions, not one universal metric wearing different names.

questions.prompt: Why couldn't ordinary OLS R-squared (1 - SSE/SST) be used directly for a logistic regression model?

options.text: Logistic regression is fit by maximizing likelihood, not minimizing squared error, so pseudo-R-squared measures were built from log-likelihoods instead
Logistic regression has no null model to compare against
SSE cannot be computed for any binary outcome under any circumstances
R-squared was banned from use with binary data by statistical convention

explanations.a: Correct — because logistic regression's fitting criterion is likelihood, not squared error, pseudo-R-squared measures like McFadden's substitute log-likelihood ratios for the SSE/SST structure.
explanations.b: An intercept-only null model exists for logistic regression exactly as it does for OLS; McFadden's measure is built by comparing against it.
explanations.c: Efron's R-squared specifically does compute an SSE/SST-style ratio using observed outcomes versus predicted probabilities; it is not banned, just not the standard approach.
explanations.d: There is no such formal prohibition; multiple pseudo-R-squared variants were developed precisely because none is a perfect drop-in replacement.

questions.prompt: According to McFadden's own guidance, a pseudo-R-squared value between roughly 0.2 and 0.4 represents:

options.text: A weak, barely-better-than-random fit
An excellent fit, despite being a range that would be mediocre for OLS R-squared
Evidence of overfitting requiring immediate regularization
A value only achievable with more than 1,000 observations

explanations.a: This is the intuitive OLS-trained misreading; McFadden's own benchmark places this exact range as excellent, not weak.
explanations.b: Correct — McFadden noted 0.2 to 0.4 indicates excellent fit for his pseudo-R-squared, since log-likelihood ratios compress much more than variance ratios as fit improves.
explanations.c: The value alone says nothing about overfitting; that requires comparing training and held-out performance, not reading the pseudo-R-squared in isolation.
explanations.d: McFadden's benchmark is about the value's interpretation, not a function of a minimum sample size threshold.

questions.prompt: What flaw in the Cox-Snell pseudo-R-squared does Nagelkerke's 1991 adjustment fix?

options.text: Cox-Snell cannot reach a value of 1 even for a perfectly fitting model; Nagelkerke rescales it by its theoretical maximum
Cox-Snell can be negative for any model, which Nagelkerke prevents
Cox-Snell requires continuous outcomes, which Nagelkerke extended to binary data
Cox-Snell ignores sample size entirely, which Nagelkerke's version corrects

explanations.a: Correct — Cox-Snell's ceiling is below 1 even for a perfect fit; Nagelkerke divides by that theoretical maximum so the rescaled version can reach 1.
explanations.b: Cox-Snell's range issue is its ceiling below 1, not a negativity problem; Nagelkerke's fix targets the upper bound specifically.
explanations.c: Cox-Snell was already designed for likelihood-based models including binary outcomes; the extension to binary data was not Nagelkerke's contribution.
explanations.d: Cox-Snell's formula does include sample size n in its exponent; Nagelkerke's adjustment is about the ceiling value, not sample-size sensitivity.

questions.prompt: Match each pseudo-R-squared to how it is constructed.

right.text: 1 minus the ratio of model log-likelihood to null-model log-likelihood
1 minus a likelihood ratio raised to the power 2/n, unable to reach 1
Cox-Snell's value divided by its own theoretical maximum, rescaled to reach 1
The OLS-style 1 - SSE/SST formula applied to observed outcomes versus predicted probabilities

questions.explanation: McFadden's compares log-likelihoods directly; Cox-Snell uses a likelihood ratio that caps below 1; Nagelkerke rescales Cox-Snell to reach 1; and Efron's applies the familiar SSE/SST structure to binary outcomes and predicted probabilities.

questions.prompt: A judge asks, 'your R-squared is only 0.35 — is that bad?' What is the strongest response?

options.text: Immediately agree and promise to add more predictors to raise the number
Identify which R-squared variant was computed and explain that its scale and benchmark differ from OLS R-squared, so 0.35 may indicate a strong fit depending on which measure it is
Explain that all R-squared values above 0 are automatically acceptable
Refuse to discuss the number since R-squared is never meaningful

explanations.a: Adding predictors without justification risks the noise-inflation problem covered elsewhere in this unit and does not address the actual question about interpretation.
explanations.b: Correct — naming the specific measure (McFadden's, Efron's, or OLS) and its appropriate benchmark directly answers whether 0.35 is strong or weak for that particular construction.
explanations.c: This overclaims; some R-squared variants and contexts do call for concern at low values, so a blanket 'always acceptable' answer is not defensible.
explanations.d: R-squared, in its various forms, is a legitimate and informative statistic; refusing to engage with the question avoids demonstrating exactly the understanding a judge is testing for.

lessons.label: Spurious Regression: Granger & Newbold 1974

sections.heading: The simulation that shook econometrics
sections.body: In their 1974 paper 'Spurious Regressions in Econometrics' (Journal of Econometrics), Clive Granger and Paul Newbold simulated pairs of completely independent random walks — series with no causal or statistical connection whatsoever, each just a running sum of independent random shocks — and regressed one on the other. If the two series were truly unrelated, textbook theory predicts a significant t-statistic (|t| > 2) on the slope only about 5% of the time, purely by chance. Instead, Granger and Newbold found significant t-statistics far more often than 5%, alongside R-squared averaging around 0.26 for a single independent random-walk regressor, even though by construction neither series could possibly explain the other. The culprit is that both series trend and wander over long stretches, and OLS mistakes shared wandering for a shared relationship. Granger and Newbold's paper is credited with coining the term 'spurious regression' itself, and it forced the entire econometrics profession to confront how often published time-series results built on levels data — GDP, prices, stock indices — might be capturing nothing more than two unrelated series drifting in the same rough direction.

sections.heading: A diagnostic rule of thumb, and the theory behind it
sections.body: From this work came a widely repeated rule of thumb: if a regression's R-squared exceeds its Durbin-Watson statistic, suspect a spurious result, since a DW statistic near zero signals strongly autocorrelated (trending) residuals, exactly the fingerprint left by two unrelated random walks. Peter Phillips supplied the rigorous asymptotic theory in his 1986 paper 'Understanding Spurious Regressions in Econometrics' (Journal of Econometrics), proving that as sample size grows, the t-statistics in a spurious regression do not converge to a stable distribution but instead diverge, so the false 'significance' actually gets worse, not better, with more data — the opposite of how t-statistics normally behave under a true null.

sections.heading: The fix: differencing and unit-root testing
sections.body: The standard remedy is to test each series for a unit root, most commonly with the Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test or the complementary KPSS test, before ever regressing one time series on another. If a series has a unit root — meaning it is non-stationary and behaves like a random walk — differencing it (working with period-to-period changes instead of levels) typically removes the trending behavior that manufactures spurious relationships. Any student regressing two time series that each drift upward or downward over time, from stock prices to population counts to cumulative lab measurements, is standing in exactly the setup Granger and Newbold's simulation was built to expose. Cointegration analysis, developed later by Granger himself, offers a more advanced middle ground for the rare cases where two genuinely non-stationary series do share a real long-run equilibrium relationship, but that is an exception requiring its own formal test, not a default assumption.

lessons.workedExample: A student regresses cumulative total pages read by their lab team against cumulative total experiments logged by an entirely unrelated lab across campus, both series simply trending upward over the semester. The regression returns R-squared = 0.81 and a t-statistic of 6.2 on the slope, looking like a strong, highly significant relationship. Checking the Durbin-Watson statistic reveals it is only 0.3 — far below the R-squared of 0.81, triggering the classic warning sign. Running an ADF test on both series confirms each has a unit root. Differencing both series (day-to-day changes rather than cumulative totals) and re-running the regression collapses R-squared to near 0 and the t-statistic to statistically insignificant, revealing the original 'relationship' was spurious: two unrelated series that both simply trended upward all semester.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees two trending time series regressed on each other with an impressively high R-squared should ask whether a unit-root test was run before the regression, and whether the Durbin-Watson statistic was checked against R-squared. Citing Granger and Newbold's 1974 finding that independent random walks routinely produce R-squared averaging around 0.26 (with 'significant' t-statistics), and Phillips's 1986 proof that this false significance worsens rather than improves with more data, shows the student understands that a high R-squared on trending series is not evidence of a relationship at all. The strongest answer names the actual remedy performed — ADF or KPSS testing followed by differencing — rather than simply asserting the result is trustworthy.

questions.prompt: In Granger and Newbold's 1974 simulation, two completely independent random walks were regressed on each other. What did they find?

options.text: Significant t-statistics appeared far more than the expected 5% of the time, with R-squared averaging around 0.26
R-squared was always exactly 0, confirming no relationship
Significant results appeared in exactly 5% of trials, matching theoretical expectations
The Durbin-Watson statistic was always higher than R-squared

explanations.a: Correct — this is the central, unsettling finding: elevated R-squared and frequent false 'significance' arise mechanically from two series that merely happen to both trend, with no real relationship.
explanations.b: R-squared was not near 0; the trending behavior common to both independent series produced R-squared averaging around 0.26, despite no real connection.
explanations.c: The whole point of the paper is that significant results appeared far more often than the 5% rate textbook theory would predict under true independence.
explanations.d: The classic spurious-regression signature is the opposite: a high R-squared paired with a LOW Durbin-Watson statistic, not a high one.

questions.prompt: What is the rule-of-thumb diagnostic for suspecting a spurious regression?

options.text: R-squared exceeding the Durbin-Watson statistic
R-squared falling below 0.1
The Durbin-Watson statistic exceeding 2.5
A sample size smaller than 30 observations

explanations.a: Correct — this is the classic rule of thumb from the spurious regression literature: R-squared greater than the Durbin-Watson statistic (which will be low near zero for trending, autocorrelated residuals) signals a likely spurious fit.
explanations.b: A low R-squared is not the warning sign here; spurious regressions are characterized by suspiciously HIGH R-squared, not low.
explanations.c: A Durbin-Watson statistic well above 2 generally suggests negative autocorrelation, not the positive-autocorrelation signature of a spurious trending regression.
explanations.d: Spurious regression is a large-sample phenomenon in Phillips's theory; small sample size alone is not the diagnostic criterion.

questions.prompt: According to Phillips (1986), as sample size increases in a spurious regression between independent random walks, the slope's t-statistic:

options.text: Diverges rather than converging to a stable distribution, so false significance worsens with more data
Converges to the standard normal distribution, as with typical regressions
Always converges to exactly zero
Becomes unbiased and reliable once the sample exceeds 1,000 observations

explanations.a: Correct — Phillips's asymptotic theory shows the t-statistic diverges as sample size grows in the spurious case, meaning the problem gets worse, not better, with more data.
explanations.b: This is precisely what Phillips showed does NOT happen in the spurious case, in contrast to standard well-specified regressions.
explanations.c: The t-statistic diverges rather than shrinking to zero; it tends toward larger, more 'significant-looking' magnitudes as sample size grows.
explanations.d: There is no sample size at which the spurious relationship becomes reliable; Phillips's result is specifically that more data does not fix the problem.

questions.prompt: Put the diagnostic-and-fix workflow for a suspicious high-R-squared time-series regression in the correct order.

items.text: Notice R-squared is high while the Durbin-Watson statistic is low
Run a unit-root test (ADF or KPSS) on each series
Difference each series found to have a unit root
Re-run the regression on the differenced series and check whether the relationship survives

questions.explanation: The R-squared-versus-Durbin-Watson comparison is the first warning sign; unit-root testing then confirms whether the series are non-stationary; differencing removes the trending behavior; and only then is the regression re-run to see if any genuine relationship remains.

questions.prompt: Match each contribution to the researcher(s) responsible.

left.text: Simulated independent random walks and found spurious R-squared and t-statistics
Provided the asymptotic theory explaining why t-statistics diverge
Standard test for a unit root in a time series
Standard remedy that removes trending behavior before regression

right.text: Granger and Newbold (1974)
Phillips (1986)
Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test
Differencing the series

questions.explanation: Granger and Newbold ran the founding simulation; Phillips supplied the asymptotic theory of divergence; the ADF test (alongside KPSS) checks for a unit root; and differencing the series is the standard fix once a unit root is found.

units.label: Landmark Work and Open Debates

lessons.label: Makridakis, M1, and M2: The Uncomfortable Finding

sections.heading: A contested paper starts a fight
sections.body: In 1979, Spyros Makridakis and Michele Hibon published 'Accuracy of Forecasting: An Empirical Investigation' in the Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series A, volume 142. Comparing forecasting methods across a set of real time series, they reported that simple methods — moving averages, single exponential smoothing — often matched or beat statistically sophisticated Box-Jenkins ARIMA models. Because the paper was a discussion paper, prominent statisticians attached formal rebuttals directly to the published text, arguing the series were unrepresentative, the horizons too short, and the accuracy measures (dominated by MAPE) biased toward whichever method happened to under-forecast. Rather than concede the point in a footnote, Makridakis responded the only way an empiricist can: by designing a far larger, openly documented competition and inviting the same critics to submit methods themselves.

sections.heading: M1 (1982): 1001 series, one uncomfortable answer
sections.body: The M-Competition (Makridakis et al., 1982, Journal of Forecasting, vol. 1) ran 1001 time series — micro-economic, macro-economic, industry, and demographic, at yearly, quarterly, and monthly frequencies — through 24 methods contributed by different research teams, scored on multiple accuracy measures across multiple forecast horizons. The result repeated the 1979 finding at far larger scale: simple methods such as single, Holt, and Brown exponential smoothing frequently outperformed full Box-Jenkins ARIMA models, which require manual identification, differencing, and multi-parameter estimation for every series. Critics again attacked the design — data selection, MAPE as the primary measure, aggregating results across wildly heterogeneous series — but subsequent reanalyses by outside researchers through the 1980s reproduced the core ranking rather than overturning it.

sections.heading: M2 (1993): removing the excuses
sections.body: The M2-Competition (Makridakis et al., 1993, International Journal of Forecasting) answered the fairness objection directly by trading scale for realism. Only 29 series were used — 23 from four collaborating companies plus 6 US macroeconomic series — but forecasters were given real-time access to the companies, could request additional domain information and data on demand, and submitted forecasts across several rounds with feedback between rounds, directly addressing the 'statisticians never get context' critique of M1. Simple and damped exponential smoothing still matched or beat the more complex, information-rich submissions. Two competitions built on opposite design philosophies — one huge and automated, one small and judgment-rich — converged on the same conclusion: added statistical sophistication was not reliably converting into forecast accuracy. This pairing became the empirical seed of the field's enduring 'complexity does not pay' orthodoxy, one later competitions would repeatedly re-test.

lessons.workedExample: A student forecasting a school's monthly enrollment fits a full seasonal ARIMA model — identifying orders via ACF/PACF, differencing for a unit root, estimating five parameters — and, separately, a damped exponential smoothing model with two parameters. On a rolling-origin backtest, the damped model's MAPE is 6.1% versus the ARIMA model's 7.4%. Rather than assume the ARIMA fit is wrong, the student recognizes this is exactly the M1/M2 pattern: a short, noisy real-world series often rewards a simple, stable model over a flexible one prone to overfitting its own identification step.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows forecasting will ask why a supposedly worse method keeps winning real competitions. The defensible answer is that M1 and M2 tested exactly this claim, with different designs addressing different objections, and both returned the same result — so 'more sophisticated' is an empirical claim to test, not an assumption to import. A student who cites Box-Jenkins ARIMA as automatically superior to exponential smoothing without mentioning M1/M2 is showing textbook knowledge without competition-tested knowledge.

questions.prompt: What core finding did the M1 (1982) and M2 (1993) competitions share, despite very different designs?

options.text: ARIMA models always outperformed exponential smoothing on longer horizons
Simple and damped exponential smoothing matched or beat more sophisticated methods like Box-Jenkins ARIMA
Accuracy measures could not be agreed upon, so no conclusion was possible
Judgmental forecasts from company staff were uniformly worse than any statistical method

explanations.a: The opposite pattern was observed — simple methods held their own or won even as forecasters expected sophistication to help most.
explanations.b: Correct — both competitions, despite M2's added domain information and revision rounds, reproduced the M1 result that simplicity did not cost accuracy.
explanations.c: Both competitions did use defined accuracy measures and did produce a clear directional finding, which is exactly what triggered the pushback.
explanations.d: M2 specifically incorporated judgmental input from company forecasters as part of its design; it was not tested as uniformly inferior.

questions.prompt: Why was M2 (1993) designed with only 29 series and real-time forecaster access, in contrast to M1's 1001 series?

options.text: To make the competition faster to run
To answer the specific critique that M1's forecasters lacked context and could not ask questions about the data
Because 29 series is the minimum needed for statistical significance
Because companies refused to share more than 29 series

explanations.a: Speed was not the design rationale; depth of engagement with fewer series was.
explanations.b: Correct — M2 traded scale for realism, giving forecasters domain information and iterative feedback to directly address the 'unfair to statisticians' objection to M1.
explanations.c: There is no such statistical threshold; the number reflects the practical scope of real-time collaboration with four companies.
explanations.d: The scope was a deliberate design choice for depth, not a data-availability constraint.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the Makridakis forecasting-accuracy controversy chronologically.

items.text: Makridakis & Hibon publish the contested 1979 JRSS paper
M1-Competition runs 1001 series across 24 methods
M2-Competition uses 29 series with real-time forecaster feedback

questions.explanation: The 1979 JRSS paper's contested finding (1979) prompted the larger M1-Competition (1982), whose result was then re-tested under a redesigned, feedback-driven protocol in M2 (1993).

questions.prompt: In the M1-Competition, what specifically outperformed full Box-Jenkins ARIMA models on many series?

options.text: Single, Holt, and Brown exponential smoothing
Neural network forecasts
Random walk with no parameters at all
Multivariate regression with external predictors

explanations.a: Correct — these low-parameter smoothing methods frequently matched or beat ARIMA's multi-step identification-and-estimation process.
explanations.b: Neural network methods were not part of the 1982 competition; that era predates their common use in forecasting comparisons.
explanations.c: A pure random walk was a baseline reference, not the method that was documented as beating ARIMA.
explanations.d: External-predictor regression was not the highlighted comparison method in the M1 result.

lessons.label: M3 (2000) and the Theta Method

sections.heading: A bigger, more careful test
sections.body: The M3-Competition (Makridakis & Hibon, 2000, International Journal of Forecasting, vol. 16) scaled the M1/M2 program up to 3003 time series drawn from micro, industry, macro, finance, and demographic domains at yearly, quarterly, monthly, and 'other' frequencies, and compared 24 methods spanning naive baselines, exponential smoothing variants, full Box-Jenkins ARIMA, neural networks, and expert-system approaches like Rule-Based Forecasting. The winner, judged across symmetric MAPE (sMAPE) and other error measures at multiple horizons, was the Theta method, submitted by Vassilis Assimakopoulos and Konstantinos Nikolopoulos. Theta decomposes a series into two or more 'theta lines' — modifications of the local curvature of the data via a coefficient theta applied to the series' second differences — forecasts each line separately (typically one with theta near 0, extrapolated linearly, and one with theta near 2, extrapolated by SES), then recombines them by simple averaging. In the original 2000 paper, this was presented as a genuinely new decomposition approach, and its win over 23 rival methods, including full ARIMA and neural nets, made it the headline result of the competition.

sections.heading: Unmasking Theta: Hyndman & Billah, 2003
sections.body: Rob Hyndman and Baki Billah's 2003 paper 'Unmasking the Theta method' (International Journal of Forecasting, vol. 19, pp. 287-290) showed that for the standard M3-winning case — theta = 0 and theta = 2, combined with equal weights — the Theta method's forecasts are mathematically identical to simple exponential smoothing with drift, where the drift term equals exactly half the slope of a linear trend fitted to the whole series. What Assimakopoulos and Nikolopoulos had presented as several pages of curvature-modifying algebra reduced, under Hyndman and Billah's derivation, to a two-parameter classic already in every forecasting textbook. The winner of the largest, most rigorous forecasting competition run to that date was, underneath its notation, one of the oldest methods in the field.

sections.heading: What M3 actually taught, once you set Theta aside
sections.body: Three conclusions from M3 outlasted the Theta episode. First, combinations of forecasts consistently beat individual methods across the 3003 series — averaging several imperfect forecasts reduced error more reliably than picking the single 'best' model for each series. Second, relative accuracy is horizon-dependent: a method ranked well at a one-step-ahead horizon could rank poorly at horizon twelve, so no single method dominated across all forecast lengths. Third, and echoing M1/M2's finding two decades apart, statistical sophistication again failed to buy accuracy — full ARIMA and neural network entries did not systematically outperform simple ones, and the strongest performers (Theta, damped smoothing, and combinations) were all structurally simple.

lessons.workedExample: A team building a five-year lab-supply-cost forecast finds a paper claiming Theta 'won the biggest forecasting competition ever run' and adopts it uncritically as their headline method. A sharper team reads Hyndman & Billah 2003 first, realizes Theta (with the standard parameters) is simple exponential smoothing with drift equal to half the fitted linear trend's slope, implements that two-line formula directly, and reports it honestly as 'SES with drift, empirically equivalent to the M3-winning Theta method' — same forecast, correct attribution, and a demonstration they understand the method rather than just the trophy.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge familiar with the M-competitions may ask what actually won M3 and why that matters. The strong answer is not just 'Theta' but the follow-up: Theta was later proven equivalent to SES with drift, so the real lesson is that a disguised classic beat dozens of more elaborate contenders — reinforcing, not contradicting, the M1/M2 pattern. A student who cites Theta as a mysterious advanced technique without knowing the 2003 unmasking result is repeating the myth rather than the finding.

questions.prompt: What did Hyndman & Billah (2003) demonstrate about the Theta method that won M3?

options.text: It was mathematically equivalent to simple exponential smoothing with drift, for the standard parameter choice
It was a computational error and should not have won M3
It only worked on macroeconomic series, not micro or industry series
It was equivalent to a full Box-Jenkins ARIMA model

explanations.a: Correct — for theta = 0 and theta = 2 combined equally, Theta's forecasts reduce to SES with a drift term of half the linear trend slope.
explanations.b: Hyndman and Billah did not challenge the competition result; they reinterpreted the method mathematically, not the win itself.
explanations.c: The equivalence result is about the method's mathematical structure, not a domain restriction found in the M3 data.
explanations.d: The equivalence shown was to simple exponential smoothing with drift, a much simpler model than ARIMA, not to ARIMA itself.

questions.prompt: Who submitted the Theta method to the M3-Competition?

options.text: Spyros Makridakis and Michele Hibon
Vassilis Assimakopoulos and Konstantinos Nikolopoulos
Rob Hyndman and Baki Billah
Slawek Smyl

explanations.a: Makridakis and Hibon organized and reported on the M3-Competition; they did not submit the Theta method itself.
explanations.b: Correct — Assimakopoulos and Nikolopoulos introduced the Theta method as a 2000 decomposition approach, and it won M3.
explanations.c: Hyndman and Billah authored the 2003 paper that reinterpreted Theta as SES with drift; they did not submit it to M3.
explanations.d: Smyl is associated with the later M4-Competition's ES-RNN, not the M3-era Theta method.

questions.prompt: Put these M3-related events in chronological order.

items.text: Assimakopoulos & Nikolopoulos introduce the Theta method
M3-Competition runs 3003 series and Theta wins
Hyndman & Billah publish 'Unmasking the Theta method'

questions.explanation: Theta was introduced in 2000, entered and won the M3-Competition (reported in 2000), and was mathematically reinterpreted as SES with drift by Hyndman & Billah in 2003.

questions.prompt: Match each durable M3 conclusion to its description.

right.text: Averaging several imperfect forecasts reduced error more reliably than picking one 'best' model
A method ranked well at one-step-ahead could rank poorly at twelve steps, so no method dominated every horizon
Complex methods, including neural networks and full ARIMA, did not systematically beat simple methods like Theta or damped smoothing

questions.explanation: M3's three durable takeaways were that forecast combinations outperformed single models, relative rankings shifted with the forecast horizon, and added statistical or computational complexity did not reliably translate into higher accuracy.

lessons.label: Tashman 2000 and the Standards for Out-of-Sample Testing

sections.heading: The paper that named the sample-size problem
sections.body: Leonard Tashman's 'Out-of-sample tests of forecasting accuracy: an analysis and review,' published in the International Journal of Forecasting in 2000 (vol. 16), surveyed decades of forecasting-evaluation studies and formalized a distinction the field had used loosely: fixed-origin versus rolling-origin evaluation. In fixed-origin evaluation, a model is trained once on data up to a single cutoff and tested on the remaining held-out period — producing exactly one forecast error per horizon for the entire exercise, no matter how long the series is. In rolling-origin evaluation (also called rolling-window or time-series cross-validation), the training cutoff advances repeatedly through the data, re-fitting or re-forecasting at each successive origin, so each horizon accumulates many independent error observations spread across many origins rather than a single one.

sections.heading: Why one holdout is a sample size of one
sections.body: Tashman's central methodological point is blunt: a fixed-origin test produces exactly one error value per forecast horizon. Whatever conclusion is drawn from it — 'Method A beats Method B by 3 MAPE points on this series' — rests on one draw from a noisy process, statistically indistinguishable from luck without repetition to check it against. Reviewing the empirical literature, Tashman found that studies relying only on fixed-origin testing were systematically more likely to report large, possibly spurious differences between competing methods, while rolling-origin designs produced more stable and more replicable rankings, because each reported error became an average over many origins rather than one realization of noise. He argued this was not a minor implementation detail but the difference between a genuine evaluation and a one-off anecdote mistaken for evidence.

sections.heading: The protocol the field now assumes
sections.body: Tashman's review helped cement rolling-origin evaluation as the default expectation in serious forecasting research, echoing the general statistical principle that a single data point cannot support a claim about an underlying distribution. The paper's legacy shows up every time a forecasting paper reports mean error across multiple origins rather than a lone number, and in the default expanding- or sliding-window cross-validation schemes built into modern forecasting libraries. Held-out data is still essential — training a model on data it will later be judged against remains invalid regardless of origin count — but Tashman's argument is that a single held-out period only answers 'what happened once,' never 'what should I expect on average, and how much should I trust that estimate.' Tashman also noted that rolling-origin results should be reported per horizon rather than pooled across horizons, since a method's relative ranking commonly shifts between short and long horizons, a point that dovetails directly with M3's own horizon-dependence finding.

lessons.workedExample: A student forecasting a lab's weekly reagent consumption splits 104 weeks of data: the first 83 weeks for training, the last 21 for a single holdout test, and reports 'my LSTM beat exponential smoothing by 2 MAPE points on the holdout.' A judge who has read Tashman asks how many origins that comparison is based on — the honest answer is one. Redone with a rolling-origin design — refitting both models at 15 successive weekly origins and averaging the resulting errors — the LSTM's advantage shrinks to 0.3 points and reverses at three of the fifteen origins, revealing the original single-split result was largely noise.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge evaluating any forecasting claim should ask exactly one Tashman-shaped question: how many origins was that error averaged over? 'I held out the last 20%' describes a fixed-origin test with an implicit sample size of one — a single number dressed up as evidence. A student who instead reports errors averaged across a rolling-origin scheme, and can state how many origins were used, is demonstrating they understand why the protocol exists rather than just following a convention they were told to follow.

questions.prompt: According to Tashman (2000), what is the key statistical weakness of fixed-origin evaluation?

options.text: It cannot be implemented in most forecasting software
It produces exactly one error per horizon, so a reported difference is a single noisy draw, not a stable estimate
It always overestimates the accuracy of simple methods
It requires more computation than rolling-origin evaluation

explanations.a: Fixed-origin testing is trivially easy to implement, which is part of why it remains common despite the weakness Tashman identified.
explanations.b: Correct — with one train/test split, each forecast horizon yields a single error value, offering no way to distinguish a real effect from chance.
explanations.c: Tashman's critique is about sample size and stability of the comparison, not a directional bias toward simple or complex methods.
explanations.d: Rolling-origin evaluation is more computationally expensive than fixed-origin, not less, since it re-fits or re-forecasts at every origin.

questions.prompt: In rolling-origin evaluation, what changes as the forecast origin advances through the data?

options.text: The accuracy measure itself is redefined at each origin
The training cutoff moves forward and the model is re-fit or re-forecast, accumulating multiple errors per horizon
The test set grows to include the entire series
Only the final origin's result is kept; earlier origins are discarded

explanations.a: The measure (e.g., MAPE, MASE) stays fixed; what changes is how many times it is computed and averaged.
explanations.b: Correct — each successive origin gives a fresh train/test split, and horizon-specific errors accumulate across all of them.
explanations.c: The test set at each origin is typically the next block of held-out points, not the whole remaining series at once.
explanations.d: The entire point of the design is to keep and average results from every origin, not just the last one.

questions.prompt: Match each evaluation term to its correct description per Tashman's framework.

right.text: A single train/test split producing exactly one error per horizon
The training cutoff advances repeatedly, producing many errors per horizon across origins
Tashman's argument that one holdout error cannot support a general accuracy claim

questions.explanation: Fixed-origin uses one split (one error per horizon); rolling-origin repeats the split across many advancing origins (many errors per horizon); and Tashman's 'sample size of one' point is the reason fixed-origin results should not be trusted as general accuracy claims.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a proper rolling-origin evaluation, as implied by Tashman's review.

items.text: Choose an initial training cutoff (origin)
Fit or forecast and record the error at each horizon
Advance the origin forward and repeat fitting/forecasting
Average the recorded errors across all origins per horizon

questions.explanation: A rolling-origin scheme starts from an initial cutoff, records errors, advances the cutoff and repeats, and only at the end averages across all the accumulated origins to get a stable per-horizon estimate.

lessons.label: Armstrong & Collopy 1992 vs. Hyndman & Koehler 2006: The Fight Over the Metric

sections.heading: Armstrong & Collopy (1992): testing the measures themselves
sections.body: J. Scott Armstrong and Fred Collopy's 'Error Measures for Generalizing about Forecasting Methods: Empirical Comparisons' (International Journal of Forecasting, 1992) did something unusual: instead of comparing forecasting methods, it compared the error measures used to judge them, testing reliability (does the ranking stay stable across similar datasets), protection against outliers (does one extreme series distort the whole comparison), and sensitivity to genuine accuracy differences. MAPE (Mean Absolute Percentage Error) failed badly on outlier protection, since it explodes whenever the actual value is near zero, and can silently favor methods that under-forecast. Armstrong and Collopy instead recommended relative measures built on the Relative Absolute Error (RAE) — especially the Geometric Mean RAE (GMRAE) for calibrating a model across a set of series, and the Median RAE (MdRAE) for selecting the most accurate method when few series are available — both of which compare a method's error against a naive random-walk benchmark and are more reliable for drawing general conclusions across many series with different scales and units. Their paper was among the first to treat accuracy-measure selection itself as an empirical question rather than a matter of convention.

sections.heading: Hyndman & Koehler (2006): cataloguing every measure's failure mode
sections.body: Rob Hyndman and Anne Koehler's 'Another look at measures of forecast accuracy' (International Journal of Forecasting, 2006) went further, systematically cataloguing how each common measure fails: MAPE is undefined or explodes near zero and is asymmetric in its penalty; symmetric MAPE (sMAPE), introduced to fix the asymmetry, can still produce negative or infinite values and penalizes over- and under-forecasts unequally in practice; relative-error measures like Theil's U break down whenever the naive benchmark itself has a near-zero error. Their proposed fix was the Mean Absolute Scaled Error (MASE) — scaling each forecast error by the mean absolute error of a naive in-sample forecast, giving a measure with no division-by-near-zero problem, that works for series with zeros, and that stays interpretable across completely different scales and units.

sections.heading: The unresolved sociology
sections.body: The field's actual response is the interesting part: despite two influential papers, fourteen years apart, methodically documenting that MAPE and sMAPE are broken, both measures remained the most commonly reported in industry practice and academic papers well past 2006. When the M4-Competition ran in 2018, its organizers hedged rather than picking a side outright, scoring accuracy with a composite of sMAPE and MASE together (OWA, the Overall Weighted Average) instead of committing fully to MASE alone. The metric fight was won on the evidence and lost on adoption — MAPE persists largely because it is easy to explain to non-technical stakeholders, a practical pressure neither paper's statistical argument could overcome.

lessons.workedExample: A team forecasting weekly lab-consumable orders reports 'our model achieves 8% MAPE' as their headline claim. A judge points out that several weeks in their data have near-zero baseline demand (holiday weeks), where MAPE mathematically explodes or becomes meaningless. Recomputing with MASE — scaling their model's mean absolute error against a naive one-step-ahead in-sample forecast — the team gets a stable value of 0.71, meaning their model is 29% better than naive, a claim that survives the near-zero weeks intact and that a statistically literate judge can actually interpret.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows this literature will not be impressed by a MAPE number alone — the sophisticated move is naming MASE (or at least Theil's U) and explaining why: MAPE is undefined near zero and penalizes over-forecasts and under-forecasts asymmetrically. Equally sophisticated is knowing that the field agreed on this in 1992 and again in 2006 and largely ignored it anyway, and that M4 itself hedged with a composite metric — showing the student understands both the technical argument and its messy real-world adoption.

questions.prompt: What specific weakness of MAPE did Armstrong & Collopy (1992) identify?

options.text: It is too computationally expensive for large datasets
It fails outlier protection because it explodes when actual values are near zero, and can favor under-forecasting
It cannot be computed for quarterly or monthly data
It only works for classification problems, not regression

explanations.a: MAPE is computationally trivial; the critique was about statistical reliability, not computational cost.
explanations.b: Correct — MAPE's denominator is the actual value, so near-zero actuals cause huge or undefined percentage errors, and it asymmetrically penalizes forecasts.
explanations.c: MAPE can be computed at any frequency; the flaw is about zero-crossing values, not data frequency.
explanations.d: MAPE is a regression-forecasting error measure; it has no relevance to classification at all.

questions.prompt: What accuracy measure did Hyndman & Koehler (2006) propose as a general-purpose default, and why?

options.text: sMAPE, because it fixes MAPE's asymmetry completely
MASE, because it scales error against a naive in-sample forecast and avoids division-by-near-zero problems
GMRAE, because it was already the field standard
Raw RMSE, because it is unit-free across series

explanations.a: Hyndman & Koehler specifically showed sMAPE still has failure modes, including negative or infinite values, so they did not endorse it as the fix.
explanations.b: Correct — MASE divides by the mean absolute error of a naive in-sample forecast, sidestepping near-zero actuals and staying comparable across series and scales.
explanations.c: GMRAE/MdRAE were Armstrong & Collopy's 1992 recommendations, not Hyndman & Koehler's 2006 proposal, and relative-error measures like these have their own near-zero benchmark issue.
explanations.d: RMSE is in the original units of the series, so it is not comparable across series with different scales — the opposite of what was needed.

questions.prompt: How did the M4-Competition (2018) organizers handle the choice between MASE and sMAPE for scoring accuracy?

options.text: They used only MASE, fully adopting Hyndman & Koehler's recommendation
They used only MAPE, ignoring both papers
They hedged with a composite measure (OWA) combining sMAPE and MASE rather than choosing one
They let each participant choose their own accuracy measure

explanations.a: M4 did not fully commit to MASE alone; it combined MASE with sMAPE rather than replacing sMAPE outright.
explanations.b: Plain MAPE was not the primary M4 accuracy score; sMAPE and MASE were both incorporated.
explanations.c: Correct — M4's Overall Weighted Average (OWA) combined sMAPE and MASE, a sociological compromise rather than a resolution of the 1992/2006 critiques.
explanations.d: M4 used a single defined scoring protocol (OWA) for all submissions, not participant-chosen measures.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the error-measure debate chronologically.

items.text: Armstrong & Collopy publish empirical comparisons of error measures, favoring relative measures over MAPE
Hyndman & Koehler catalogue every measure's failure mode and propose MASE
M4-Competition scores accuracy with a composite of sMAPE and MASE (OWA)

questions.explanation: Armstrong & Collopy's 1992 critique came first, Hyndman & Koehler's 2006 MASE proposal followed, and M4 in 2018 responded to both by adopting a hedged composite rather than fully committing to either side.

lessons.label: M4 (2018): 100,000 Series and Slava Smyl's Hybrid

sections.heading: Scaling up, and machine learning enters seriously
sections.body: The M4-Competition, organized by Spyros Makridakis, Evangelos Spiliotis, and Vassilis Assimakopoulos and reported in 2018-2020 in the International Journal of Forecasting, expanded the M-competition series to 100,000 time series across six data domains and multiple frequencies, and for the first time drew serious participation from machine-learning researchers alongside traditional statistical forecasters. Sixty-one methods were submitted in total, including six pure machine-learning entries — models with no explicit statistical time-series structure — competing against classical statistical benchmarks and hybrid approaches, scored primarily on the Overall Weighted Average (OWA) of sMAPE and MASE, the compromise metric the competition adopted rather than choosing one measure outright. The jump from M3's 3003 series to M4's 100,000 was itself a deliberate response to critics who had argued earlier competitions were too small to generalize.

sections.heading: Smyl's ES-RNN wins; FFORMA takes second
sections.body: Uber data scientist Slawek Smyl won outright with ES-RNN (Exponential Smoothing - Recurrent Neural Network), a hybrid architecture that fit a per-series exponential smoothing model to handle each series' individual level and seasonality, then fed the de-leveled, de-seasonalized residual into a single LSTM neural network trained jointly and globally across all series in a category. This let the model share learned patterns across thousands of series while still respecting each series' own scale and seasonal shape. Second place went to FFORMA (Feature-based Forecast Model Averaging), built by Pablo Montero-Manso, George Athanasopoulos, Rob Hyndman, and Thiyanga Talagala, which used gradient-boosted trees to learn, from statistical features of each series (trend strength, seasonality strength, entropy, and similar diagnostics), how to weight an ensemble of classical statistical forecasting methods per series rather than picking one method outright. Both winning entries thus used machine learning not to replace statistical forecasting but to route or reshape it.

sections.heading: The headline versus the actual lesson
sections.body: M4's most-quoted finding was that all six pure machine-learning submissions — models using no statistical time-series component at all — finished behind the simple statistical Comb benchmark (an equal-weighted combination of basic methods), reinforcing the 'complexity does not pay' reading from M1 through M3. But the more accurate reading of the actual winners complicates that headline: first place (ES-RNN) and second place (FFORMA) were both hybrids that fused machine learning with statistical forecasting rather than replacing it. The real M4 lesson was not 'ML loses to statistics' but 'ML fused with statistical structure beats either pure approach alone' — a distinction the popular retelling routinely drops.

lessons.workedExample: A team building a science-fair forecast for lab reagent orders reads only the popular summary — 'ML lost every M4 category to statistics' — and concludes they should scrap their gradient-boosted model entirely for plain exponential smoothing. A team that read the actual M4 results instead builds a hybrid: exponential smoothing handles each reagent's baseline level and weekly seasonality, and a small neural network is trained across all reagents jointly to capture shared demand patterns from the residuals, mirroring Smyl's ES-RNN design at a much smaller scale — and reports the honest distinction between the headline and the winning architecture.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has heard 'M4 proved ML doesn't work for forecasting' should be corrected carefully: the six pure-ML entries did lose to the Comb benchmark, but first and second place were both ML-statistics hybrids, not pure statistics. A student who can name Smyl's ES-RNN and Montero-Manso's FFORMA specifically, and explain why hybrids won while pure ML didn't, demonstrates they read past the popular one-line summary of the competition.

questions.prompt: What architecture did Slawek Smyl use to win the M4-Competition?

explanations.a: Smyl's winning entry was explicitly a hybrid, not a pure transformer or pure neural architecture.
explanations.b: Correct — ES-RNN handled each series' own level and seasonality with exponential smoothing, then a single LSTM trained globally across many series modeled the residual structure.
explanations.c: ARIMA was one of the classical statistical benchmarks M4 compared against, not Smyl's winning method.
explanations.d: That description matches FFORMA, the second-place entry, not Smyl's first-place ES-RNN.

options.text: Slawek Smyl; it combined exponential smoothing with an LSTM
Montero-Manso, Athanasopoulos, Hyndman, and Talagala; it used gradient-boosted trees to learn per-series weights for an ensemble of statistical methods
Makridakis and Hibon; it re-ran the Theta method at scale
Armstrong and Collopy; it selected the best single accuracy measure

explanations.a: That describes Smyl's first-place ES-RNN, a different team and different architecture from FFORMA.
explanations.b: Correct — FFORMA (Feature-based Forecast Model Averaging) used gradient boosting on statistical features of each series to weight a pool of classical forecasting methods.

explanations.d: Armstrong and Collopy's 1992 work concerned error-measure evaluation, unrelated to the M4 FFORMA submission.

questions.prompt: What is the more accurate reading of M4's outcome, beyond the popular headline that 'pure ML lost to statistics'?

The top two finishers were both hybrids fusing machine learning with statistical structure, not pure statistics
All 60 submitted methods performed identically within measurement error
