explanations.a: The winning and runner-up methods both used neural-network or tree-based machine learning components, contradicting a blanket dismissal of ML.
explanations.b: Correct — ES-RNN (1st) and FFORMA (2nd) both combined ML with statistical forecasting structure, meaning the real signal is about fusion, not ML's failure.
explanations.c: M4 reported clear, meaningfully different accuracy rankings across submissions, including the pure-ML entries trailing the Comb benchmark.
explanations.d: Pure ARIMA was a benchmark method, not among the top hybrid-driven finishers.

questions.prompt: Order these facts about M4 as the argument builds from the popular headline to the corrected lesson.

items.text: M4 scales to 100,000 series and draws serious ML participation for the first time
All six pure-ML submissions finish behind the simple statistical Comb benchmark
ES-RNN (hybrid) wins first place and FFORMA (hybrid) takes second
The corrected lesson: ML fused with statistical structure beat both pure ML and pure statistics

questions.explanation: M4's scale drew in ML methods, whose pure form underperformed the Comb benchmark; but the actual winners were hybrids, giving the corrected takeaway that fusion, not pure ML or pure statistics, is what won.

lessons.label: M5 (2020): Walmart, LightGBM, and the Turn

sections.heading: A different kind of dataset entirely
sections.body: The M5-Competition, run from March to June 2020 and reported by Makridakis, Spiliotis, and Assimakopoulos, broke from the M1-M4 lineage's mixed-domain series and instead used one real, richly structured dataset: 42,840 hierarchical daily sales series from Walmart, organized by item, store, department, category, and state, with ten stores across three US states and roughly five years of daily history. Unlike earlier competitions, M5 supplied exogenous variables directly — selling price, promotional and SNAP (food-assistance) calendar events, and day-of-week/holiday effects — turning it from a pure extrapolation problem into a problem with genuine external predictors. M5 ran two parallel tracks: an Accuracy track scored by WRMSSE (Weighted Root Mean Squared Scaled Error, aggregated across the full product-location hierarchy) and an Uncertainty track scored by the pinball (quantile) loss across nine probability levels.

sections.heading: Gradient boosting sweeps the accuracy track
sections.body: Essentially every top entry in the M5 Accuracy track used LightGBM, a gradient-boosted decision tree framework, trained globally across many series at once rather than fit series-by-series. The winning team (a South Korean undergraduate) combined an equal-weighted ensemble of multiple LightGBM models trained at different aggregation levels — per store, per store-category, and per store-department. Across the top 50 submissions, all beat the best statistical benchmark by more than 14%, and the top five beat it by over 20%, with the winning entry improving on it by 22.4%. This flatly reversed M4's headline: three years after 'ML lost every M4 category to statistics,' gradient boosting decisively won M5's accuracy track.

sections.heading: What actually changed, and where it didn't
sections.body: The turn was not simply 'ML got smarter.' Three concrete factors explain it: cross-series global learning let LightGBM models pool patterns across tens of thousands of related series rather than fitting each in isolation; genuine exogenous features (price changes, promotions, SNAP dates, calendar effects) gave tree models real predictive signal that pure extrapolation methods structurally cannot use; and the sheer sample size — 42,840 series with dense daily history — favored data-hungry, flexible models in a way M3's shorter series could not. The Uncertainty track told a different story: statistical and hybrid methods stayed far more competitive there, since well-calibrated quantile forecasts require different modeling assumptions than point-accuracy alone, showing the ML advantage was specific to the accuracy objective, not universal. This split matters methodologically: a single competition can produce opposite headlines depending on which loss function is being optimized, so 'ML beat statistics at M5' is only fully true for point forecasts, not for the full predictive distribution.

lessons.workedExample: A team forecasting daily attendance at a school science fair across multiple classrooms tries a single classical exponential smoothing model per classroom, ignoring that a school holiday and a same-week pep rally shift attendance for every classroom simultaneously. Following M5's lesson, they instead pool all classrooms' attendance history into one LightGBM model, adding holiday, day-of-week, and event-flag features as exogenous inputs. The pooled, feature-rich model captures the shared holiday effect that per-classroom smoothing could never see, mirroring exactly the combination of global learning and exogenous features that drove M5's LightGBM sweep.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows M4's headline may assume ML always loses to statistics in forecasting. The correct, more current answer is that M5 (2020) reversed this specifically in the accuracy track, and the reversal is explainable, not mysterious: global cross-series learning, real exogenous features, and a much larger dataset. A judge will also want to hear that the uncertainty track behaved differently, showing the student understands that 'ML wins' is conditional on the objective being optimized, not a blanket law of forecasting.

questions.prompt: What single method dominated the top entries in the M5 Accuracy track?

options.text: LightGBM, a gradient-boosted decision tree framework, trained globally across many series
The Theta method, as in M3
ES-RNN, as in M4
Full Box-Jenkins ARIMA fit per series

explanations.a: Correct — essentially every top M5 Accuracy submission used LightGBM, typically trained across many series jointly rather than one model per series.
explanations.b: Theta won the earlier M3-Competition, not M5, and was not the dominant M5 approach.
explanations.c: ES-RNN was Smyl's winning M4 architecture; M5's top methods were gradient-boosted trees, not that RNN hybrid.
explanations.d: Per-series ARIMA was one of the statistical benchmarks M5's LightGBM entries decisively beat, not the winning approach.

questions.prompt: By how much did the M5 winning team's forecast improve on the best statistical benchmark?

options.text: It performed worse than the benchmark

explanations.a: Correct — the winning entry improved on the top-performing statistical benchmark by 22.4%, part of a pattern where the top five all exceeded 20% improvement.
explanations.b: The actual margin was an order of magnitude larger than this figure.
explanations.c: 50% overstates the reported improvement; the documented figure for the winner was 22.4%.
explanations.d: The entire top-50 field beat the statistical benchmark by more than 14%, so the winner clearly outperformed it, not the reverse.

questions.prompt: Match each factor to how it specifically contributed to LightGBM's M5 accuracy-track dominance.

right.text: 42,840 series with dense daily history favored flexible, data-hungry models over per-series fits
Price, promotions, SNAP dates, and calendar effects gave real predictive signal that pure extrapolation cannot use
Pooling patterns across tens of thousands of related series instead of fitting each series in isolation

questions.explanation: LightGBM's M5 sweep is best explained by three concrete mechanisms: learning jointly across series, exploiting real external predictors, and having enough data volume to support a flexible, high-capacity model.

questions.prompt: Order these M-competition milestones on the statistics-versus-ML question.

items.text: M3 (2000): Theta, a disguised classical method, wins
M4 (2018): all pure-ML entries lose to the statistical Comb benchmark; hybrids ES-RNN and FFORMA win 1st/2nd
M5 (2020): LightGBM entries sweep the accuracy track, decisively beating statistical benchmarks

questions.explanation: The chronological arc runs from M3's classical-method win, through M4's hybrid-wins/pure-ML-losses split, to M5's clear reversal where gradient boosting decisively outperformed statistical benchmarks on the accuracy track.

lessons.label: The Live Argument: Do ML Forecasters Actually Beat Statistical Ones?

sections.heading: Makridakis, Spiliotis & Assimakopoulos 2018: a direct challenge
sections.body: In 'Statistical and Machine Learning forecasting methods: Concerns and ways forward' (PLOS ONE, 2018), Spyros Makridakis, Evangelos Spiliotis, and Vassilis Assimakopoulos tested ten popular machine-learning methods — including neural networks, support vector regression, and Gaussian processes — against eight traditional statistical benchmarks on the M3 dataset's 1045 monthly series. Every ML method performed worse than simple statistical methods across accuracy measures, and the paper argued this contradicted the enthusiasm for ML then building in the forecasting literature. The response was immediate and pointed: critics argued the ML models were undertuned relative to published best practice, that the comparison used a one-step-ahead framing unfavorable to some architectures, and that 1045 series is a modest sample for training data-hungry models. The exchange itself became as informative as the original finding — it forced the field to specify what a fair ML-vs-statistics comparison requires.

sections.heading: Diebold's warning about testing 'accuracy' at all
sections.body: Francis Diebold's 2015 retrospective 'Comparing Predictive Accuracy, Twenty Years Later: A Personal Perspective on the Use and Abuse of Diebold-Mariano Tests' (Journal of Business & Economic Statistics), revisiting his own 1995 Diebold-Mariano test with Roberto Mariano, warned that the test is routinely misapplied: it is designed to compare the accuracy of two sequences of forecasts, not to compare two underlying models' in-sample fit or to substitute for proper significance testing on model parameters. Diebold documented widespread misuse where researchers ran the DM test on nested models or nested forecasts, violating the test's assumptions and inflating apparent significance — a caution directly relevant to any forecasting comparison, ML included, that reports a p-value without checking whether the test's assumptions actually hold.

sections.heading: DLinear and the open questions
sections.body: Ailing Zeng, Muxi Chen, Lei Zhang, and Qiang Xu's 2023 AAAI paper 'Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?' delivered a fresh version of the same argument: a single-layer linear model, DLinear, which decomposes a series into trend and seasonal components before applying separate linear layers to each, matched or beat several complex transformer-based forecasters (including Informer, Autoformer, and FEDformer) on standard long-horizon benchmarks. The open questions this whole thread raises remain live: whether published benchmarks suffer from leakage or overfitting to a handful of popular datasets, whether ML architectures are tuned as carefully as their statistical competitors, and whether M-competition series — largely short, low-frequency business series — resemble the long, dense, feature-rich series a modern ML system is actually built for.

lessons.workedExample: A student reads a paper claiming 'our transformer beats all statistical baselines, p < 0.01 by the Diebold-Mariano test' and is ready to adopt the transformer for their science-fair forecasting project. Applying Diebold's 2015 warning, they check whether the compared models are nested and whether the test was run on genuine out-of-sample forecast errors rather than in-sample fit — and find the paper compared nested model variants, invalidating the reported significance. They then check Zeng et al. 2023's finding that a one-layer DLinear often matches transformers on standard benchmarks, and decide to benchmark a simple linear baseline before trusting any complex architecture's reported win.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing forecasting-method claims will want to see the student engage with the actual controversy, not just cite 'ML wins' or 'ML loses' as settled. The strong answer names Makridakis-Spiliotis-Assimakopoulos 2018, the tuning and framing critiques it drew, Diebold's warning about DM-test misuse, and Zeng et al.'s DLinear result — and concludes with the honest open question of whether standard benchmark series resemble the judge's own project data at all, rather than pretending the debate is resolved in either direction.

questions.prompt: What did Makridakis, Spiliotis & Assimakopoulos (2018, PLOS ONE) find when testing ten ML methods against eight statistical benchmarks on M3 data?

explanations.a: The paper's headline finding was the opposite — ML methods underperformed simple statistical benchmarks across the tested measures.
explanations.b: Correct — all ten ML methods tested, including neural networks and support vector regression, performed worse than the eight simple statistical benchmarks on M3 series.
explanations.c: The paper reported a clear directional gap favoring statistical methods, not a tie.
explanations.d: The study ran to completion with a clear result; it was contested on methodology (tuning, framing, sample size), not abandoned for missing data.

questions.prompt: What is Diebold's (2015) central warning about the Diebold-Mariano test?

options.text: It should never be used for any forecasting comparison
It is routinely misapplied to compare models' in-sample fit or nested forecasts, violating the test's assumptions

It requires machine-learning methods specifically to be excluded

explanations.a: Diebold defended the test's proper use; his concern was misuse, not the test's validity when applied correctly.
explanations.b: Correct — Diebold documented widespread misapplication comparing nested models or in-sample fit rather than genuine out-of-sample forecast sequences, inflating apparent significance.
explanations.c: The DM test was designed specifically for comparing predictive accuracy of forecasts, a forecasting-specific tool, not a classification metric.
explanations.d: The warning applies to any misuse regardless of whether ML or purely statistical models are being compared.

questions.prompt: What did Zeng et al. (2023) show with DLinear?

options.text: A one-layer linear model matched or beat several transformer-based forecasters on standard long-horizon benchmarks
Transformers always outperform linear models regardless of dataset

explanations.a: Correct — DLinear, decomposing a series into trend and seasonal components before applying simple linear layers, matched or beat models like Informer, Autoformer, and FEDformer.
explanations.b: The paper's whole point was the reverse: the simple linear model matched or beat several transformer architectures on the tested benchmarks.
explanations.c: DLinear is dramatically simpler and has far fewer parameters than the transformer architectures it was compared against.
explanations.d: DLinear is a time-series forecasting model, not a classification method.

questions.prompt: Order these contributions to the ML-versus-statistics forecasting debate chronologically.

items.text: Diebold & Mariano introduce their original predictive-accuracy test (1995)
Makridakis, Spiliotis & Assimakopoulos find ML methods losing to statistical ones on M3 data (2018)
Diebold publishes a retrospective warning about DM-test misuse (2015)

questions.explanation: The Diebold-Mariano test itself dates to 1995; Diebold's own retrospective warning about its misuse came in 2015; the Makridakis-Spiliotis-Assimakopoulos ML-versus-statistics study followed in 2018; and Zeng et al.'s DLinear challenge to transformer architectures came in 2023.

units.label: Backtesting and Rolling-Origin Validation

lessons.label: Why Random k-Fold Leaks the Future into the Past

sections.heading: The shuffle hides a direction
sections.body: Standard k-fold cross-validation assumes rows are exchangeable: shuffle them, split into k groups, and each fold is an equally valid stand-in for unseen data. That assumption underwrites everything from scikit-learn's default KFold to the vast majority of Kaggle notebooks. Time series break it, because rows are NOT exchangeable -- they are ordered, and a forecaster only ever gets to see the past, never a randomly sampled slice of the whole timeline. Bergmeir and Benitez (2012, Information Sciences, "On the use of cross-validation for time series predictor evaluation") formalized this: when the underlying process has serial dependence -- autocorrelated errors, trend, seasonality -- shuffled k-fold systematically overstates accuracy, because training folds end up containing observations from BOTH before and after each validation point, something a genuine forecast deployment could never provide.

sections.heading: Quantifying the leak: the 80% figure
sections.body: Take a validation row drawn from early in the series -- say the earliest fifth of the timeline, chronological quantile t = 0.2. In a random 5-fold split, the fraction of the total dataset dated after that row is (1 - t) = 0.8, and because fold membership is independent of time order, that same 80% ratio carries into the training set: roughly 80% of this row's training neighbors are dated AFTER it. The derivation is short: of the (1-t) fraction of rows dated after this point, about 4/5 land in the other four (training) folds and 1/5 lands in this row's own fold, so the training-set-after-this-point ratio simplifies back to (1-t) regardless of k. The model is therefore not forecasting -- it is interpolating between a known future and a known past neighbor, a task far easier than genuine extrapolation, which is exactly why the reported error looks so good.

sections.heading: The diagnostic and its extension to panel data
sections.body: The tell-tale symptom is a gap between the cross-validated score and live performance: a shuffled-CV RMSE of, say, 2.1 units next to a first-live-month RMSE of 4.5 units is not model drift, it is a measurement artifact from training on the future. Treat any large CV-to-live gap on a temporally ordered problem as a leakage alarm before blaming distribution shift. The rule generalizes: whenever a row's label or features depend on information that would not exist at decision time, random splitting leaks. This includes grouped or panel data -- patient visits, store-months, student quiz attempts -- where many rows share a subject; GroupKFold-style splitting by subject prevents a different leak (a model memorizing one patient's or store's idiosyncrasies) but does NOT by itself fix temporal leakage if time also matters within that subject's own history, so panel forecasting problems typically need both a subject-aware AND a time-aware split simultaneously.

lessons.workedExample: A retailer builds a demand model on three years of weekly sales and evaluates it with shuffled 5-fold CV, getting RMSE = 18 units. Deployed live, month-one RMSE is 41 units. Suspecting leakage, the team re-runs validation with the folds kept in chronological blocks (no shuffling): CV RMSE jumps to 39 units, matching the live number almost exactly. The shuffled version had let the model see next month's promotional spike sitting in the training fold while validating on the week before it -- the model had learned to read the answer key rather than forecast it.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has run any real forecasting project will immediately ask how you validated a time-ordered model, because shuffled CV inflating scores is one of the most common silent bugs in student ML projects. A strong answer names the mechanism precisely -- neighbors from both directions in time collapsing the task into interpolation -- rather than just saying 'CV can leak.' Being able to estimate the size of the leak (the 80%-style calculation) rather than just asserting its existence separates a team that understands the math from one that memorized a rule.

questions.prompt: Why does shuffled k-fold CV overstate accuracy on a serially dependent time series?

options.text: Shuffling reduces the total amount of training data available
Training folds end up containing rows from both before and after each validation point, turning forecasting into interpolation
Shuffled folds always have unequal class balance
k-fold CV cannot be computed on numeric time-indexed data at all

explanations.a: The total data volume is unchanged by shuffling -- only the ordering relationship between train and validation rows changes.
explanations.b: Correct -- this is the mechanism Bergmeir and Benitez (2012) identify: exchangeability fails for dependent series, so a shuffled split trains on future neighbors of the validation point.
explanations.c: Class balance is a separate concern (relevant mainly in classification) and is not the reason temporal leakage occurs.
explanations.d: k-fold CV can be computed on any numeric data; the problem is that the resulting score is a biased estimate of forecasting accuracy, not that computation fails.

questions.prompt: A validation row sits at chronological quantile t = 0.2 (early in the series) in a random 5-fold split. Roughly what fraction of its training-set neighbors are dated AFTER it?

options.text: About 20%
About 50%, since fold assignment is random
About 80%, since fold membership is independent of time and 1 - t = 0.8
0%, because training folds never contain future data

explanations.a: 20% would be the fraction of rows dated BEFORE this point, not after -- the after-fraction is 1 - t.
explanations.b: 50% would only hold on average across all rows in the series (t = 0.5), not for a specific early row at t = 0.2.
explanations.c: Correct -- since (1 - t) of all rows are dated after this point and fold membership does not depend on time, that same ratio, about 80%, appears in the training set.
explanations.d: This is exactly the failure mode being described: random-split training folds DO contain future data relative to an early validation row.

questions.prompt: Match each observed symptom or fix to what it indicates about validation design.

left.text: CV RMSE = 2.1 but first live-month RMSE = 4.5

right.text: Classic symptom of training-future-leaked cross-validation
Prevents subject-level memorization but not necessarily within-subject temporal leakage
Shuffled k-fold overstates accuracy when the series has serial dependence

questions.explanation: A large CV-to-live gap is the practical tell of leaked future data; grouping by subject stops one leak (memorizing a specific patient or store) but does not automatically respect time order within that subject's records; and Bergmeir & Benitez's core result is that exchangeability, the assumption underlying shuffled CV, fails for dependent series.

questions.prompt: Order the steps a team should take after noticing a suspicious gap between CV score and live performance on a time-ordered model.

items.text: Notice CV RMSE is much better than first-live-month RMSE
Check whether validation folds were built by random shuffling
Re-run validation using chronologically ordered (non-shuffled) folds
Compare the new CV score to the live score to confirm the leak explanation

questions.explanation: The investigation starts from the observed symptom (a gap), moves to inspecting the suspected cause (shuffled splitting), then tests the hypothesis by rebuilding folds respecting time order, and finally confirms by checking whether the corrected CV score now matches live performance.

lessons.label: Rolling-Origin (Walk-Forward) Evaluation, Step by Step

sections.heading: Tashman's protocol
sections.body: Leonard Tashman's widely cited review (2000, International Journal of Forecasting, "Out-of-sample tests of forecasting accuracy: an analysis and review") formalized what practitioners now call rolling-origin or walk-forward evaluation, the time-series analogue of cross-validation. The recipe: fix a minimum training window ending at some origin date, forecast h steps ahead from that origin, record the error at each horizon, then advance the origin forward by one step (or a larger stride, if refitting is expensive), refit or incrementally update the model, and repeat until the data runs out. Every forecast is made using only data that existed before its origin, so the resulting errors are honest estimates of live performance rather than interpolation. Tashman's review surveyed decades of prior forecasting-competition practice and argued that too many published comparisons relied on a single train/test split, which is really just one origin -- a sample size of one for judging a method.

sections.heading: How many origins is enough
sections.body: A single origin tells you almost nothing about a method's reliability, because that one split could happen to favor or disadvantage a given model by chance. Rolling the origin forward dozens or hundreds of times converts a single anecdote into a distribution of errors per horizon, which is what makes later statistical comparisons (such as a Diebold-Mariano test on the resulting loss differentials) meaningful in the first place. The number of usable origins is constrained by how much history exists after satisfying the minimum training window and the largest horizon needed -- a series of 120 months with a 24-month minimum window and a 12-month maximum horizon yields at most 120 - 24 - 12 = 84 possible origins, before any stride is applied to cut compute.

sections.heading: Expanding vs. sliding windows
sections.body: Two window policies exist. An EXPANDING window keeps every origin's training set starting from the same fixed start date, so the training window grows longer as the origin advances -- appropriate when the process is stationary and more history only helps. A SLIDING (rolling) window instead drops the oldest observations as new ones arrive, keeping a constant-length lookback -- this wins under regime change, because stale pre-shift data would otherwise pull the fit toward a relationship that no longer holds, such as a demand model trained across a supply shock. Choosing between them is a bias-variance tradeoff specific to the process: expanding lowers variance from more data, sliding lowers bias toward outdated regimes.

sections.heading: Report error PER horizon, not pooled
sections.body: Rolling-origin evaluation naturally produces an error matrix indexed by origin (rows) and horizon (columns, h = 1, 2, ... H). Reporting a single pooled RMSE across all cells hides two distinct claims: h=1 accuracy (next period, informed by the most recent observation) and h=12 accuracy (a year out, compounding uncertainty) are different tasks with different error magnitudes, and a model can be excellent at one and mediocre at the other. Averaging over origins WITHIN each horizon column, then reporting the resulting curve of error versus horizon, is the standard the forecasting literature expects and is what Tashman's review argues should replace single-number summaries.

lessons.workedExample: A team forecasting monthly electricity demand fixes a 24-month minimum training window, forecasts horizons h=1 through h=6, and slides the origin forward one month at a time across five and a half years of data, refitting each time. This produces 36 origins by 6 horizons, a 216-cell error matrix. Averaging within columns shows MAPE of 3.1% at h=1 rising to 9.4% at h=6 -- a genuine finding about how far ahead the model is reliable. Had they pooled all 216 cells into one MAPE of 6.2%, that number would answer no question a planner actually has, since planners need to know accuracy AT a specific lead time, not averaged across all of them.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge evaluating a forecasting project will look for whether error is reported as a function of horizon rather than a single number, because pooling horizons is a well-known way to make a mediocre long-horizon model look acceptable by blending in easy short-horizon accuracy. Asking 'what is your h=1 error versus your h=12 error, and why do they differ' probes whether the team actually ran a rolling-origin backtest or just fit once and reported an aggregate. Justifying the expanding-versus-sliding choice with a stated belief about regime stability shows real design intent rather than a default library setting.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of Tashman's rolling-origin evaluation protocol for a single pass through the data.

items.text: Fix a minimum training window ending at the current origin
Forecast h steps ahead from that origin
Record the error at each horizon
Advance the origin by one step or a stride, refit or update, and repeat

questions.explanation: Tashman's (2000) protocol fixes the training window at an origin, forecasts forward from it, logs the resulting error, then moves the origin ahead and repeats, building up an error matrix over many origins.

questions.prompt: Under a regime change (e.g., a structural break in the underlying process), which window policy tends to perform better, and why?

options.text: Expanding window, because more data always reduces error
Sliding window, because it drops stale pre-shift data that would otherwise bias the fit toward an outdated relationship
Neither differs, since both use the same model class
Expanding window, because it prevents the training set from ever shrinking

explanations.a: More data helps under stationarity, but under a regime change, old data reflects a relationship that no longer holds and actively hurts the fit.
explanations.b: Correct -- a sliding window's constant-length lookback discards observations from before the shift, keeping the model tuned to the current regime.
explanations.c: The window policy changes what data the SAME model class is fit on, which does affect performance under a structural break.
explanations.d: Preventing shrinkage is true of expanding windows but is not the reason it underperforms under regime change; the issue is stale data pulling the fit off target.

questions.prompt: Why is reporting a single pooled RMSE across all horizons in a rolling-origin error matrix misleading?

options.text: Pooling is mathematically invalid and cannot be computed
It collapses two different claims -- near-term accuracy and long-horizon accuracy -- into one number, hiding how error grows with horizon
RMSE cannot be averaged across different origins
Pooling always makes the reported error look worse than it truly is

explanations.a: Pooling is computable; the objection is about what the resulting number means, not whether it can be calculated.
explanations.b: Correct -- h=1 and h=12 are different forecasting tasks with different error magnitudes; a pooled number cannot tell a planner what accuracy to expect at a specific lead time.
explanations.c: RMSE can be averaged across origins; the concern is about pooling across horizon columns, which mixes tasks of different difficulty.
explanations.d: Pooling can make error look better OR worse depending on which horizons dominate the matrix; the core problem is loss of the per-horizon breakdown, not a directional bias.

questions.prompt: Match each rolling-origin design element to its description.

left.text: Error matrix from a rolling-origin backtest

right.text: Training set always starts at the same fixed date and grows with each origin
Training set keeps a constant length, dropping the oldest data as new data arrives
Indexed by origin and horizon, averaged within horizon columns for reporting

questions.explanation: An expanding window keeps a fixed start date so the training set only grows; a sliding window keeps a fixed length by dropping old data; and the rolling-origin process naturally yields an origin-by-horizon error matrix that should be summarized by horizon column, not pooled entirely.

lessons.label: Designing the Split: Horizons, Origins, Gaps, and Purging

sections.heading: Matching the horizon to the decision, and how many origins you need
sections.body: The evaluation horizon must equal the decision horizon: if a supply chain team commits to orders 8 weeks out, the model must be scored at h=8, not at whatever h happens to make the error curve look best. Choosing the horizon to flatter the metric rather than to match the real decision is a subtle form of overfitting the report, not the model. Separately, a single origin cannot support a claim that one model beats another -- an RMSE difference needs enough independent-ish origins for its standard error to shrink below the difference itself, and because adjacent origins in a rolling backtest overlap heavily in their training data, the effective sample size is far smaller than the raw origin count suggests; dozens of origins spread over multiple distinct episodes (not just adjacent weeks) are typically needed before a difference is trustworthy.

sections.heading: The embargo/gap: why rolling features straddle the boundary
sections.body: A feature like a 28-day moving average computed at the train/validation boundary uses data that stretches back 28 days AND, if computed carelessly on the full series before splitting, can stretch forward across the boundary too. Marcos Lopez de Prado's "Advances in Financial Machine Learning" (Wiley, 2018) names this precisely: labels and features near a split boundary read across it, because rolling windows, lagged targets, and the labeling horizon all overlap in time. His fix is PURGED cross-validation -- remove any training observation whose feature or label window overlaps the validation window -- combined with an EMBARGO, a further buffer immediately after the validation block during which training points are also dropped, because information can leak backward through the model's own serial correlation even after the direct overlap ends.

sections.heading: Blocked and hv-block CV for dependent data
sections.body: Outside finance, Jeffrey Racine's hv-block cross-validation (2000, Journal of Econometrics, "Consistent cross-validatory model-selection for dependent data: hv-block cross-validation") generalizes leave-one-out CV for dependent series by removing an h-width window around each left-out point (matching the data's dependence length) plus a further v-width buffer, proving this restores consistent model selection where naive leave-one-out fails under autocorrelation -- the ordinary leave-one-out estimator is inconsistent precisely because a single removed point still has near-neighbors, before and after, sitting in the training set. Blocked CV is the simpler cousin: split the series into contiguous chronological blocks rather than purging point-by-point, trading some statistical efficiency for implementation simplicity that is easier to explain and audit. All three approaches -- purged-and-embargoed, hv-block, and simple blocking -- solve the same underlying problem: dependence between adjacent-in-time observations means a bare boundary is not enough; some buffer zone, sized to how far the dependence actually reaches, is required before a held-out score can be trusted.

lessons.workedExample: A credit-risk model uses a feature that is a 28-day rolling default rate, and the label is 'defaults within the next 90 days.' Naively splitting at day 1000 lets a training row at day 990 have a label that resolves at day 1080 -- 80 days into the nominal validation period -- and lets a validation row at day 1005 have a rolling-average feature computed using days 977-1005, some of which came from the training side. Applying Lopez de Prado's purge removes training rows whose label windows extend past day 1000, and an embargo of 90 days after the split removes validation-adjacent training rows on the far side, leaving a clean gap on both edges of the boundary.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge with quantitative finance or econometrics exposure will ask specifically about boundary contamination, because it is invisible in a naive train/test split and only shows up as an unexplained live-versus-backtest gap months later. Being able to name WHY a gap is needed -- feature windows and label horizons both straddle the split -- rather than citing 'purging' as a buzzword demonstrates genuine understanding. A judge may also probe how many origins were tested before trusting an RMSE difference, since a single lucky split is a common way student projects arrive at an impressive-looking but statistically meaningless improvement.

questions.prompt: A team choosing which forecast horizon to report picks h=3 because it produces the lowest error, even though the business commits to decisions 8 weeks ahead. What is the problem?

options.text: There is no problem; lower error is always the better number to report
The evaluation horizon must match the decision horizon, so reporting h=3 misrepresents accuracy at the horizon that actually matters
h=3 is invalid because rolling-origin backtests cannot evaluate short horizons
The problem is only that h=3 requires more origins than h=8

explanations.a: Optimizing which number to report rather than reporting the horizon the decision actually needs is a form of overfitting the report, not genuine improvement.
explanations.b: Correct -- accuracy at h=3 says nothing about accuracy at h=8, and the business decision is made at h=8, so that is the horizon that must be scored.
explanations.c: Rolling-origin backtests can evaluate any horizon, including short ones; the issue here is horizon selection, not backtest capability.
explanations.d: The number of origins available does not depend on which horizon is reported after the fact; the issue is choosing the reported horizon to flatter the metric.

questions.prompt: Why does Lopez de Prado's purged CV also require an embargo AFTER the validation block, not just removal of overlapping training points?

options.text: Because embargoes are a regulatory requirement in financial machine learning
Because serial correlation can let information leak backward through the model even after direct feature/label overlap ends
Because embargoes reduce the total size of the validation set
Because purging alone always removes 100% of the leakage

explanations.a: This is not a regulatory concept; it is a statistical safeguard against residual dependence.
explanations.b: Correct -- even after removing points with direct feature/label overlap, autocorrelation in the series can still let training points close in time to the validation block carry leaked signal.
explanations.c: Embargo shrinks the training set near the boundary, not the validation set itself.
explanations.d: If purging alone removed all leakage, no embargo would be needed; the embargo exists precisely because purging is not sufficient by itself.

questions.prompt: Match each cross-validation variant for dependent data to its defining mechanism.

right.text: Removes training points whose feature/label windows overlap validation, plus a post-validation buffer
Removes an h-width window matched to dependence length around each left-out point, plus a v-width buffer, for consistent model selection
Splits the series into contiguous chronological segments rather than purging point-by-point

questions.explanation: Purged-and-embargoed CV targets financial-style overlapping feature/label windows with a buffer on both sides; Racine's hv-block CV generalizes leave-one-out with an h-window plus v-buffer sized to the data's dependence structure; and blocked CV takes the simpler route of contiguous chronological segments.

questions.prompt: Order the reasoning steps for diagnosing and fixing boundary contamination from a 28-day rolling-average feature at a train/validation split.

items.text: Notice the feature is a rolling window that spans dates on both sides of the split
Identify which training rows have feature or label windows overlapping the validation block
Purge those overlapping training rows from the training set
Apply an embargo buffer after the validation block to remove residual serially-correlated leakage

questions.explanation: The process starts by recognizing the rolling window straddles the boundary, then locates the specific overlapping rows, purges them, and finally adds an embargo buffer to catch leakage that survives purging due to serial correlation.

lessons.label: Time-Series Leakage in Feature Engineering

sections.heading: Global preprocessors: scalers, imputers, and target encodings fit on everything
sections.body: The most common leak has nothing to do with the model itself: fitting a StandardScaler, a mean-imputer, or a target-mean encoding on the FULL series before splitting means the scaler's mean and variance, the imputer's fill value, or the encoding's category-mean all incorporate future observations. A validation-period row then gets transformed using statistics that partly describe data from after it happened, so even a trivial linear model can look artificially sharp. The fix mirrors any leakage rule -- fit every preprocessor only on data available at or before the current training origin, then apply (never re-fit) it to validation and future data, refitting again only when the origin itself advances in a rolling backtest. In scikit-learn terms, this means the Pipeline's fit call must be scoped to each origin's training slice, never called once on the concatenated full dataset.

sections.heading: Centered windows peek forward
sections.body: A centered rolling mean at time t, by construction, averages observations from t-w through t+w -- it needs w future points to exist before it can be computed, which is fine for smoothing a historical chart but invalid as a real-time feature, since at the actual forecast origin those future points do not yet exist. The correct feature is a TRAILING (causal) rolling statistic, using only t-2w through t, or equivalently a centered window computed with a lag large enough that its rightmost edge never crosses the origin. Confusing 'smooths nicely in a plot' with 'usable at forecast time' is one of the most common and hardest-to-spot feature-engineering bugs in time series work.

sections.heading: Data revisions: using the vintage, not the final number
sections.body: Many economic and public-health series are revised after first release: initial U.S. GDP growth estimates and early case counts during an outbreak are routinely restated weeks or months later as more complete data arrives, sometimes by large margins -- the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis publishes GDP in three successive vintages (advance, second, third estimate) before later annual and comprehensive revisions can move it further still. A backtest that feeds a model the FINAL, revised GDP figure for March when forecasting from an origin in April uses information that would not have existed at that origin -- the original April analyst only had the preliminary advance estimate. The Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis's ALFRED (Archival Federal Reserve Economic Data) exists precisely to solve this: it serves the VINTAGE of each series as it was published on any given historical date, letting a backtest reconstruct exactly what was knowable at each origin, as opposed to FRED's standard interface, which by default only serves the latest revised values.

lessons.workedExample: A student building a recession-prediction model uses the current (2026-vintage) GDP growth series all the way back to 2008, including heavily revised early-pandemic figures, and gets a suspiciously strong backtest. Pulling the same dates from ALFRED's real-time vintages instead, they find the Q1 2020 advance GDP estimate released in late April 2020 was far rougher than the fully revised figure history now shows -- the model's apparent skill at flagging the 2020 downturn early partly reflects hindsight-corrected data, not real predictive power. Re-running the backtest on vintage data available at each origin drops the reported accuracy measurably, revealing the true, honest performance.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'could you have computed every one of your features using only data stamped before the forecast origin' is running the single audit question that catches nearly all time-series leakage at once -- global scalers, centered windows, and revised data all fail it for the same underlying reason. A team that can answer this cleanly for each feature, rather than asserting 'we split before modeling' as if that alone were sufficient, demonstrates they understand that leakage can enter through preprocessing and data vintage long before any model is fit.

questions.prompt: A StandardScaler is fit once on the entire time series before any train/validation split. What is the leak?

options.text: There is no leak, because scaling does not use the target variable
The scaler's mean and variance are computed using future observations, so validation rows are transformed using statistics that partly describe data from after they occurred
The leak only matters if the scaler is a MinMaxScaler, not a StandardScaler
Scalers cannot leak because they operate column-wise, not row-wise

explanations.a: Leakage is not limited to target-dependent transforms; any statistic computed over future feature values also leaks temporal information.
explanations.b: Correct -- fitting on the whole series means every summary statistic used to transform a validation-period row was partly derived from points that had not occurred yet at that row's time.
explanations.c: The mechanism applies to any global preprocessor -- mean/variance scalers, min-max scalers, imputers, and target encodings alike.
explanations.d: Operating column-wise does not prevent the leak; the statistics computed over that column still span the whole timeline, future included.

questions.prompt: Why is a centered rolling mean invalid as a real-time forecasting feature, even though it produces a smoother chart?

options.text: Centered means are never more accurate than trailing means
It requires observations from after time t, which do not exist yet at the actual forecast origin
Centered rolling means cannot be computed in most software libraries
Centered means are only invalid if the window size is even

explanations.a: The objection is not about accuracy at all -- it's about availability at forecast time.
explanations.b: Correct -- a centered window at time t needs points from t+1 through t+w, which have not happened yet when a real forecast is actually made at t.
explanations.c: Most libraries compute centered rolling means easily; the problem is purely one of information availability, not implementation.
explanations.d: Window parity is irrelevant to whether the feature looks ahead; any centered window, odd or even width, uses future points.

questions.prompt: Match each time-series feature-engineering leak to its correct description or fix.

right.text: Fit only on data available at or before the current training origin, then apply without re-fitting
Replace with a trailing (causal) window that only uses past observations
Use the real-time vintage of the series as published at that origin (e.g., via ALFRED), not the final revised figure

questions.explanation: Global preprocessors must be fit origin-by-origin using only past data; centered windows must become trailing windows to avoid needing future points; and revised series need real-time vintage data, which ALFRED provides, to reconstruct what was actually knowable at each origin.

questions.prompt: What is the single audit question that catches nearly all time-series feature leakage at once?

options.text: Did the model achieve a low training error?
Could I have computed this feature at the forecast origin, using only data stamped before it?
Is the feature numeric or categorical?
Did the feature improve the validation R-squared?

explanations.a: Low training error is unrelated to leakage and can occur with or without it.
explanations.b: Correct -- this single question applied to every feature catches global preprocessors, centered windows, and revised-data leaks all at once, because each fails it for a different concrete reason.
explanations.c: Feature type has no bearing on whether the value was actually knowable at the forecast origin.
explanations.d: Improving validation R-squared is actually a symptom leakage often PRODUCES, not a test that detects it -- a leaked feature typically raises this exact metric.

lessons.label: Is the Difference Real? Diebold-Mariano and Its Abuse

sections.heading: The test and its small-sample fix
sections.body: Diebold and Mariano's 1995 paper (Journal of Business & Economic Statistics, "Comparing Predictive Accuracy") proposed testing whether two forecasts' loss differential series -- e.g., squared error of model A minus squared error of model B, at each origin -- has mean zero, using a t-statistic built on a heteroskedasticity-and-autocorrelation-consistent (HAC, Newey-West style) variance estimator, because the loss differentials from overlapping-horizon forecasts are themselves autocorrelated: a forecast made at origin 50 for h=6 and one made at origin 51 for h=6 share almost all of their training data and much of their target period, so their errors move together. With few origins the asymptotic normal-reference test over-rejects the null of equal accuracy, so Harvey, Leybourne, and Newbold (1997, International Journal of Forecasting, "Testing the equality of prediction mean squared errors") proposed a small-sample correction that rescales the DM statistic downward and compares it to a Student-t distribution with (n-1) degrees of freedom rather than a standard normal.

sections.heading: Forecasts, not models, and the nested-model trap
sections.body: Diebold's 2015 retrospective (Journal of Business & Economic Statistics, "Comparing Predictive Accuracy, Twenty Years Later") stresses a point often lost in application: DM compares two FORECASTS as realized, not two data-generating models in the abstract, and it is invalid when one model NESTS the other -- e.g., comparing a restricted AR(1) against an AR(2) that contains it as a special case -- because under the null of equal accuracy the nested comparison's asymptotic variance degenerates. Clark and West (2007, Journal of Econometrics, "Approximately normal tests for equal predictive accuracy in nested models") built a corrected statistic specifically for this nested case, adjusting for the extra noise the larger model's estimated parameters introduce even when the added terms carry no true signal.

sections.heading: Many series, many comparisons: MCS and the M4 approach
sections.body: Testing one model against another across hundreds of series multiplies the chance of a spuriously significant win somewhere, the same multiple-comparison problem familiar from running many uncorrected t-tests. Hansen, Lunde, and Nason's Model Confidence Set (2011, Econometrica, "The Model Confidence Set") addresses this directly, returning a SET of models statistically indistinguishable from the best rather than declaring one lone winner, controlling the familywise error rate across the whole comparison rather than per pairwise test. The M4 forecasting competition's post-hoc analysis (Makridakis, Spiliotis, and Assimakopoulos, 2018-2020, International Journal of Forecasting) ranked methods across 100,000 series using a multiple-comparisons-with-the-best (MCB) test on sMAPE rankings, precisely because pairwise DM tests repeated at that scale would manufacture false positives by sheer volume; when even rank tests get too noisy to separate close competitors, reporting the full distribution of per-series differences, not a single winner, is the honest fallback.

lessons.workedExample: A team claims Model A beats Model B because DM gives p=0.03 across 15 rolling-origin forecasts. Checking assumptions: the loss differentials are strongly autocorrelated (adjacent origins share most of their training window), the sample is small, and Model A is actually Model B plus two extra lag terms -- a nested comparison. Applying the Harvey-Leybourne-Newbold correction for the small sample and switching to a Clark-West statistic for the nested case, the p-value rises to 0.29: the original claim was an artifact of using the wrong test for the actual comparison being made, not evidence of a real accuracy difference.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge with any statistics background will ask three things in sequence: was the variance estimator HAC-corrected for autocorrelated loss differentials, was a small-sample correction applied, and are the two models nested (in which case ordinary DM is simply the wrong tool, and Clark-West is needed instead). A team that ran DM across many series without any multiple-comparison control, and reports every marginally significant win as a discovery, reveals they have not internalized why methods like the Model Confidence Set exist. Naming these failure modes precisely, rather than treating a p-value as automatically conclusive, is what separates real statistical literacy from pattern-matched significance testing.

questions.prompt: Why does the Diebold-Mariano test require a HAC (Newey-West style) variance estimator rather than an ordinary variance estimate?

options.text: Because the loss differential series from overlapping-horizon forecasts is typically autocorrelated
Because HAC estimators always produce smaller p-values
Because the test statistic is otherwise undefined for negative loss differentials
Because ordinary least squares cannot be used with time-indexed data

explanations.a: Correct -- adjacent rolling-origin forecasts share overlapping data and horizons, so their loss differentials are autocorrelated, and an ordinary variance estimator would understate the true variance and over-reject.
explanations.b: HAC estimators do not systematically shrink p-values; they correct the variance estimate to reflect the true sampling uncertainty, which can move the p-value in either direction.
explanations.c: The test statistic is well defined regardless of the sign of individual loss differentials; sign is not the issue HAC addresses.
explanations.d: The test does not use OLS on the raw series; it computes a t-statistic on the mean of the loss-differential series.

questions.prompt: Why is an ordinary Diebold-Mariano test invalid for comparing a restricted model against a larger model that nests it (e.g., AR(1) vs. AR(2))?

options.text: Nested models can never be compared by any statistical test
Under the null of equal accuracy, the asymptotic variance of the loss differential degenerates for nested comparisons, invalidating the standard DM reference distribution
AR(2) models cannot produce a loss differential series
Nested models always have identical forecast errors by construction

explanations.a: Nested models CAN be compared, but with a different test -- Clark and West (2007) built exactly this corrected statistic.
explanations.b: Correct -- this degeneracy under the null is precisely why Diebold (2015) flags ordinary DM as invalid here and why Clark-West exists as the fix.
explanations.c: AR(2) models produce loss differentials like any other forecast; the problem is specific to the nested null, not to computing the series.
explanations.d: Nested models generally produce different forecasts and different errors; they are not identical, which is exactly why a valid test for comparing them is still needed.

questions.prompt: Match each named contribution to what it corrects or provides.

left.text: Hansen, Lunde & Nason's Model Confidence Set (2011)

right.text: Small-sample correction to the DM statistic using a Student-t reference distribution
Corrected test statistic valid for comparing nested models
Returns a set of statistically indistinguishable top models, controlling familywise error across many comparisons

questions.explanation: Harvey, Leybourne & Newbold fixed DM's small-sample over-rejection; Clark & West fixed its invalidity for nested-model comparisons; and the Model Confidence Set addresses the separate multiple-comparison problem of testing across many series or models at once.

questions.prompt: Order the diagnostic steps before trusting a Diebold-Mariano result comparing two forecasting models across many series.

items.text: Check whether the loss-differential series is autocorrelated and needs a HAC variance estimator
Check whether the sample of origins is small enough to need the Harvey-Leybourne-Newbold correction
Check whether the two models are nested, requiring a Clark-West statistic instead of ordinary DM
If testing across many series, apply a multiple-comparison control such as the Model Confidence Set rather than reading raw pairwise p-values

questions.explanation: The checks proceed from the basic variance-estimator assumption, to sample-size adequacy, to whether the specific model pair is nested, and finally to whether the comparison is being repeated across enough series that a multiple-comparison correction is needed.

lessons.label: Backtest Overfitting: When Your Backtest Stops Being Evidence

sections.heading: Bailey and Lopez de Prado: any Sharpe ratio, on demand
sections.body: Bailey, Borwein, Lopez de Prado, and Zhu's "The Probability of Backtest Overfitting" (Journal of Computational Finance, Vol. 20, No. 4, 2017, pp. 39-69; first circulated as an SSRN working paper in 2013-2014) and companion paper "Pseudo-Mathematics and Financial Charlatanism" (2014, Notices of the American Mathematical Society) make a sharp point with simulation: given roughly seven years of daily data and enough independent strategy variants to try -- a few thousand parameter combinations is plenty -- you can find a combination that produces essentially ANY target in-sample Sharpe ratio purely by chance, with no real skill involved. This is not a hypothetical: their simulations show the number of trials needed to hit an in-sample Sharpe above 1 or 2 by pure luck is small enough that ordinary parameter-sweep tuning, of the kind any student project runs routinely when grid-searching hyperparameters, crosses it without anyone intending to overfit. The paper's title choice, invoking "charlatanism," is deliberate: the authors argue that reporting an in-sample-optimized Sharpe without disclosing the trial count is functionally indistinguishable from fabricating the number.

sections.heading: Why more trials always help, mechanically
sections.body: The intuition scales like an extreme-value problem: the maximum of many noisy draws grows with the number of draws, even when every individual draw has expected value zero. Running 10 backtests and taking the best is materially different from running 10,000 and taking the best, even on identical underlying data with zero true edge, because the expected maximum of a larger sample of noise is mechanically larger. This is precisely why a trial count is not a footnote but a required input to interpreting any headline backtest number -- the number alone, without knowing how many candidates were searched to produce it, carries almost no information about whether real skill is present.

sections.heading: The deflated Sharpe ratio
sections.body: Bailey and Lopez de Prado's follow-up, "The Deflated Sharpe Ratio: Correcting for Selection Bias, Backtest Overfitting, and Non-Normality" (Journal of Portfolio Management, Vol. 40, No. 5, 2014, pp. 94-107), formalizes the fix: adjust the observed Sharpe ratio downward using the number of independent trials attempted, the variance of Sharpe ratios across those trials, and corrections for skewness and kurtosis in the returns, producing a probability that the observed Sharpe exceeds what pure luck across that many trials would produce. A headline Sharpe of 2.0 found after testing 500 variants deflates to something much closer to zero once the trial count is honestly accounted for -- the number is the same, but the evidentiary weight behind it collapses.

sections.heading: The visible public version and the discipline
sections.body: The same phenomenon plays out publicly on Kaggle: leaderboard shakeups, where a team's public-leaderboard rank collapses on the hidden private leaderboard, are the crowd-scale version of backtest overfitting -- thousands of competitors collectively trying enough submissions that some rise to the top of the public split by chance rather than genuine generalization. The M5 Accuracy competition (2020) saw a notably large shakeup, with several top public-leaderboard finishers dropping sharply once scored against the private holdout. The discipline both settings demand is the same: count and report the number of trials or submissions attempted, and preserve one truly untouched final holdout that is evaluated exactly once, since any holdout checked and re-checked during development stops functioning as a holdout at all.

lessons.workedExample: A student team backtests a trading rule, sweeping 800 combinations of moving-average lengths and stop-loss thresholds over seven years of daily prices, and reports the single best combination's Sharpe ratio of 1.8 as their result. Applying the deflated Sharpe ratio calculation with 800 trials, the adjusted probability that this Sharpe reflects genuine skill rather than the best-of-800 draw from noise comes out below 50% -- the headline number was likely the luckiest of many similarly-mediocre variants, not a discovery. The team had never set aside a final untouched holdout period, so there was no clean way to check the finding independently.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge versed in this literature will ask directly: how many parameter combinations, features, or model variants did you try before reporting this result, and did you hold out a final period you touched only once? A team that cannot answer the trial-count question, or that used the same historical window for both tuning and the final claim, is exhibiting exactly the pattern Bailey and Lopez de Prado warn about. Citing the deflated Sharpe ratio, or simply reporting the trial count honestly alongside the headline metric, shows the team understands that an impressive backtest number without that context is closer to charlatanism than evidence.

questions.prompt: According to Bailey and Lopez de Prado's backtest-overfitting work, why can testing enough strategy variants over about seven years of daily data produce almost any target Sharpe ratio?

options.text: Because seven years is too short a period for any Sharpe ratio to be statistically meaningful
Because with enough independent trials, pure chance alone is likely to produce a variant whose in-sample Sharpe reaches the target, with no real skill involved
Because Sharpe ratios are not well-defined for daily data
Because seven years always contains at least one market crash that inflates Sharpe ratios

explanations.a: The point is not that seven years is inherently too short in general -- it's that trying enough variants over ANY fixed window lets chance alone produce an appealing-looking result.
explanations.b: Correct -- this is the core simulation result: enough independent trials makes hitting a target Sharpe by luck highly likely, which is exactly what makes an unreported trial count so dangerous.
explanations.c: Sharpe ratios are well-defined for daily return data; the issue is statistical, about multiple testing, not about definition.
explanations.d: The result does not depend on any specific market event occurring in the window; it is a general statistical consequence of multiple testing.

questions.prompt: What does the deflated Sharpe ratio adjust for that a raw reported Sharpe ratio does not?

options.text: It only adjusts for transaction costs
It adjusts for the number of independent trials attempted, the variance across those trials, and non-normality (skewness/kurtosis) in returns
It replaces the Sharpe ratio with a completely different risk metric
It only adjusts for the length of the backtest window

explanations.a: Transaction costs are a separate concern from what the deflated Sharpe ratio specifically targets.
explanations.b: Correct -- Bailey and Lopez de Prado (Journal of Portfolio Management, 2014) built the deflation to account for selection bias from multiple trials plus return non-normality, producing a probability the true skill exceeds zero.
explanations.c: It is a correction applied to the Sharpe ratio framework, not a replacement metric.
explanations.d: Window length is one input to some related calculations, but the deflation's defining feature is its correction for trial count and distributional shape, not window length alone.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to its role in the backtest-overfitting discussion.

left.text: "The Probability of Backtest Overfitting" (Bailey, Borwein, Lopez de Prado & Zhu; Journal of Computational Finance, 2017)

right.text: Simulation showing enough trials can hit any target Sharpe by chance alone
Crowd-scale visible analogue: public-split rank collapsing once scored on the hidden private split
Must be evaluated exactly once, since repeated checking during development destroys its validity as a holdout

questions.explanation: Bailey, Borwein, Lopez de Prado, and Zhu's paper supplies the formal simulation result; Kaggle leaderboard shakeups like M5's are the same phenomenon playing out visibly across thousands of competitors; and a final holdout only serves its purpose if it is evaluated a single time, not iterated against.

questions.prompt: Order the disciplined workflow that avoids reporting an overfit backtest result as if it were evidence.

items.text: Set aside a final holdout period before any tuning begins, and do not look at it
Tune and sweep model variants only on the remaining (non-holdout) data, tracking the number of trials attempted
Deflate or contextualize the best in-sample result using the recorded trial count
Evaluate the single chosen final model on the untouched holdout exactly once and report that result

questions.explanation: The holdout must be reserved before tuning starts; tuning proceeds on the remaining data while trials are counted; the resulting best-in-sample number is then deflated or contextualized using that trial count; and only afterward is the untouched holdout used, a single time, to report a trustworthy final result.

units.label: Prediction Intervals, Probabilistic Forecasts, and Real Systems

lessons.label: Prediction Interval vs. Confidence Interval: The Distinction Almost Nobody Reports

sections.heading: A Confidence Interval Answers a Different Question Than a Prediction Interval
sections.body: Fit an OLS regression ŷ = b0 + b1x to n data points. At a given x0, two entirely different questions can be asked. The confidence interval (CI) answers: where does the true mean response E[Y|x0] fall — a fixed but unknown PARAMETER, the average score every student who studies x0 hours would get if you could observe infinitely many of them. The prediction interval (PI) answers: where does one NEW, unobserved Y fall — a random variable that still carries whatever noise term epsilon the population has, on top of not knowing the parameters exactly. A CI is a claim about a population average; a PI is a claim about a single future data point. Reporting a CI's tight band as if it bounds a specific new measurement — which is what most dashboards implicitly do — silently deletes an entire source of uncertainty from the reported number.

sections.heading: The OLS Algebra: Where the Extra Sigma-Squared Term Comes From
sections.body: Both intervals build on the same fitted value ŷ(x0) = b0 + b1x0 and the same residual variance estimate s². The mean-response (CI) variance is Var[ŷ(x0)] = s²[1/n + (x0 - x̄)²/Sxx], where Sxx = Σ(xi - x̄)². This only reflects uncertainty in ESTIMATING b0 and b1 — it shrinks toward zero as n grows because more data pins down the line more precisely. The new-observation (PI) variance adds one more term: Var[y0 - ŷ(x0)] = s²[1 + 1/n + (x0 - x̄)²/Sxx]. That leading '1' is the observation's own irreducible noise, epsilon ~ N(0, sigma²) — it does not shrink with n, because no amount of data about past students tells you what random deviation the NEXT student's score will have from the line. As n grows, the CI collapses toward a point; the PI floor stays at roughly ±1.96·sigma. A huge sample size can make a CI look deceptively precise while the honest PI stays wide.

sections.heading: The Blunt Finding: Nobody Reports Either
sections.body: In practice — student capstones and production dashboards alike — the number on the slide is usually a bare point estimate: 'predicted revenue: $4.2M,' no interval of either kind attached. When an interval does appear, it is frequently the CI, pulled straight from a stats package's default output, mislabeled and misused as if it bounded the next data point — understating the true uncertainty by exactly the missing sigma² term. The question 'how sure are you, and sure about what — the average, or this one case?' is the single question a rigorous judge can ask that ends most posters, because the presenter has never distinguished the two.

lessons.workedExample: A class of n=25 students: hours studied (x) predicts exam score (y) via ŷ = 62 + 3.1x, residual standard error s = 4.2, x̄ = 5 hours, Sxx = 180. At x0 = 8 hours: ŷ(8) = 86.8. The CI variance term is s²[1/25 + (8-5)²/180] = 17.64 × [0.04 + 0.05] = 1.59, giving a 95% CI of roughly 86.8 ± 1.96(1.26) ≈ [84.3, 89.3] — the average score of ALL students who study 8 hours. The PI variance adds the leading 1: 17.64 × [1 + 0.04 + 0.05] = 19.24, giving a 95% PI of 86.8 ± 1.96(4.39) ≈ [78.2, 95.4] — roughly 3.5x wider, because it must also cover one individual student's random deviation from that average.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has taken one regression course will ask exactly one clarifying question when they see an interval on a poster: 'is that interval for the average outcome, or for a new case?' If the presenter cannot answer instantly — or worse, used a CI to make a claim about a single future prediction — it signals the interval was copy-pasted from software output rather than understood. Distinguishing the two by name, and being able to say which term (the extra sigma²) makes the PI wider, is a two-sentence answer that separates a team that understands its own uncertainty from one that decorated a point estimate with an interval-shaped prop.

questions.prompt: A regression predicts exam score from study hours. Which statement correctly describes a 95% prediction interval at x0 = 8 hours?

options.text: It bounds the average score of all students who study exactly 8 hours, 95% of the time.
It bounds a single new student's score with 95% probability, and is wider than the corresponding confidence interval because it includes the noise term.
It equals the confidence interval exactly, since both come from the same fitted line.
It becomes zero-width as the sample size n grows to infinity.

explanations.a: That describes the confidence interval, which targets the mean response E[Y|x0], a parameter — not a single new observation.
explanations.b: Correct — the prediction interval covers one new Y, so its variance formula adds the leading '1' term for the observation's own irreducible noise, making it wider than the CI.
explanations.c: They differ by exactly the extra sigma² term in the PI's variance formula; they are equal only in the degenerate case where that term is zero, which never happens.
explanations.d: The PI's width approaches a nonzero floor (roughly ±1.96·sigma) as n grows; only the CI shrinks toward zero.

questions.prompt: As the sample size n grows toward infinity, holding x0 and sigma fixed, what happens to the confidence interval and prediction interval widths?

options.text: Both shrink to zero width.
The confidence interval shrinks toward zero width; the prediction interval shrinks toward a nonzero floor near ±1.96·sigma.
The prediction interval shrinks toward zero width; the confidence interval stays wide.
Neither changes; both widths are fixed entirely by x0.

explanations.a: The CI's 1/n and (x0-x̄)²/Sxx terms do vanish as n grows, but the PI keeps its leading '1' term, which never vanishes.
explanations.b: Correct — the CI only carries parameter-estimation uncertainty, which more data resolves; the PI also carries the new observation's own noise, which no amount of data can eliminate.
explanations.c: This reverses the correct relationship: it is the CI, not the PI, that collapses toward zero width as n grows.
explanations.d: Both widths also depend on n and s²; x0 only affects the (x0-x̄)²/Sxx term, not the whole formula.

questions.prompt: Put the steps for computing a 95% prediction interval at a new x0 in the correct order.

items.text: Fit OLS to the data to obtain b0, b1, and the residual variance estimate s²
Compute the fitted value ŷ(x0)
Compute the prediction variance s²[1 + 1/n + (x0-x̄)²/Sxx]
Multiply the square root of that variance by the appropriate t critical value
Add and subtract the result from ŷ(x0) to form the interval

questions.explanation: You must first estimate the model (s1), evaluate it at the point of interest (s2), compute the prediction-specific variance including the leading '1' term (s3), scale by the critical value to get the margin (s4), and finally apply that margin around the point estimate (s5).

questions.prompt: Match each term in the prediction-interval variance formula s²[1 + 1/n + (x0-x̄)²/Sxx] to what it represents.

right.text: Irreducible noise of a brand-new observation; present only in the PI formula, not the CI formula
Uncertainty in estimating the intercept from a finite sample, which shrinks as n grows
Extra uncertainty that grows when predicting far from the mean of the observed x values
The estimated residual variance that scales every other term in the formula

questions.explanation: The '1' is the only term unique to the PI and represents the new observation's own noise; 1/n and (x0-x̄)²/Sxx both come from parameter-estimation uncertainty and appear in the CI formula too; s² is the residual variance estimate that scales the whole expression.

lessons.label: Why Real Prediction Intervals Are Too Narrow

sections.heading: Three Sources of Uncertainty, One Textbook Formula Captures Only One
sections.body: The textbook prediction interval formula from the previous lesson — ŷ(x0) ± t·s·sqrt(1 + 1/n + (x0-x̄)²/Sxx) — is only correct if two assumptions hold exactly: the FUNCTIONAL FORM of the model is right (a straight line really does describe the relationship, an ARIMA(1,1,0) really is the data-generating process), and the estimated parameters b0, b1 are the TRUE parameters rather than estimates with their own sampling error. Real forecasting problems violate both. There is INNOVATION uncertainty (the noise term itself, which the formula does capture), PARAMETER uncertainty (the coefficients are estimated from finite data and are themselves random — the 1/n term is a crude patch for this, but only while assuming the model form is correct), and MODEL uncertainty (the true relationship might not be linear or ARIMA at all, and no term in the classical formula accounts for having picked the wrong specification). Only the first source is fully priced in; the other two are usually ignored or badly approximated.

sections.heading: The Empirical Verdict: Chatfield 1993 and the M-Competitions
sections.body: Chris Chatfield's 1993 Journal of Business & Economic Statistics paper 'Calculating Interval Forecasts' reviewed decades of applied forecasting and concluded that model misspecification, not sampling noise, is usually the dominant reason nominal intervals fail — intervals computed from an assumed-correct model are almost always too narrow in practice. The M-competitions supplied the numbers: Makridakis, Hibon, Lusk, Belhadjali & Targett (1987) checked nominal 95% intervals against the 1,001 M-competition series and found roughly 17.8% of actual observations fell OUTSIDE the interval overall — nearly four times the expected 5% — rising to about 33% for yearly series. The M4 competition (2018), which scaled the same test to 100,000 series across yearly, quarterly, monthly, weekly, daily, and hourly frequencies, had organizers explicitly hypothesize going in that '95% PIs will underestimate reality considerably, and this underestimation will increase as the forecasting horizon lengthens,' and the submissions confirmed it: standard methods systematically failed to price in enough uncertainty, especially several steps ahead.

sections.heading: Multi-Step Widening and the Constant-Width Tell
sections.body: A well-specified interval should WIDEN with the forecast horizon h, because errors compound: a random walk's h-step-ahead forecast variance grows as h·sigma², so its interval half-width grows as sqrt(h) rather than staying flat. A dashboard that draws the same ±X band around every day of a 30-day forecast is a visible tell that no real per-horizon interval was computed — it was likely copied from the one-step-ahead residual standard error and stretched across the whole chart. Honest multi-step intervals fan outward, often visibly, from the last observed point.

lessons.workedExample: A retailer fits a random-walk model to weekly demand and reports a flat ±50-unit band on every one of the next 12 weekly forecasts. Checking the math: if the one-step innovation standard deviation is sigma=20 units, an honest h-step-ahead interval for a random walk widens as sigma·sqrt(h) — at h=1 that's ±39 units (1.96×20), but at h=12 it should be ±136 units (1.96×20×sqrt(12)=1.96×69.3), not ±50. The flat band under-covers badly by week 12: a true 95% interval is over 2.7x wider than what was drawn. Back-testing the reported band against 40 realized weeks would very likely show empirical coverage well under 95%, especially at longer horizons — precisely the Chatfield/M-competition finding.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who plots a team's forecast band against realized held-out values doesn't need statistics jargon to catch this failure — a flat band that the actual series keeps poking outside of, more often at long horizons than short ones, is visible on the chart itself. The sharper follow-up is: 'did you compute this interval's width per-horizon, or reuse the one-step residual SD for the whole chart?' A team that cites Chatfield (1993) or the M-competition's empirical-coverage numbers, and can show their own interval's MEASURED coverage on a backtest, has done the work the formula alone cannot.

questions.prompt: What did Makridakis, Hibon, Lusk, Belhadjali & Targett (1987) find when they checked nominal 95% intervals against the M-competition's 1,001 series?

options.text: About 5% of observations fell outside the interval, matching the nominal rate closely
About 17.8% of observations fell outside overall, rising to about 33% for yearly series
Every series showed intervals that were too WIDE rather than too narrow
Coverage was perfect during fitting and during forecasting alike

explanations.a: This is the nominal expectation, not what was observed; the actual miss rate was far higher than 5%.
explanations.b: Correct — roughly 17.8% of observations fell outside the nominal 95% interval overall, and about 33% for yearly series, nearly four to seven times the expected 5%.
explanations.c: The finding was the opposite: intervals were too NARROW, undercovering the true outcomes.
explanations.d: Coverage was close to nominal during in-sample fitting but much worse when the model was used for genuine out-of-sample forecasting.

questions.prompt: Why do textbook prediction interval formulas typically understate real-world forecast uncertainty?

options.text: They correctly capture innovation, parameter, and model uncertainty, so the understatement must come from bad luck alone
