Repeating this for all 500 trees and averaging the increases gives annual_income a permutation importance of roughly 0.07, meaning the forest's actual predictions lose about 7 percentage points of accuracy when this feature's information is destroyed — a direct behavioral measurement rather than an in-sample impurity count.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks how permutation importance is actually computed, row by row, is testing whether the student can distinguish it from a vague 'shuffle a column and see what happens' folk description. The precise answer, score each tree's own out-of-bag rows before and after permuting one column within those same rows, then average the error increase across trees, shows real command of Breiman 2001's algorithm. A sharper judge will also ask why this measures something MDI cannot: because it is evaluated out-of-sample and captures the trained model's actual behavioral reliance on a feature, not the split search's in-sample bookkeeping.

questions.prompt: Roughly what fraction of training rows are, on average, out-of-bag for any single bootstrap-sampled tree?

options.text: About 10%
About 25%
About 36.8%
About 50%

explanations.a: This underestimates how much bootstrap sampling with replacement leaves unused; the correct limit is close to 37%, not 10%.
explanations.b: This is closer than 10% but still below the actual limiting fraction of about 36.8%.
explanations.c: Correct — as n grows, (1 - 1/n)^n converges to e^-1, approximately 0.368, so about 36.8% of rows are left out-of-bag on average per tree.
explanations.d: This overestimates the fraction; roughly a third, not half, of rows are typically left out-of-bag.

questions.prompt: In Breiman's permutation importance algorithm, which rows are used to compute the baseline and permuted error for a given tree?

options.text: The tree's own training (in-bag) rows
The tree's out-of-bag rows only
The entire dataset regardless of bag membership
A freshly held-out test set created just for this calculation

explanations.a: Scoring on in-bag rows would evaluate the tree on data it memorized, not a fair estimate of its reliance on the feature.
explanations.b: Correct — Breiman's algorithm scores each tree only on its own out-of-bag rows, both before and after permuting the feature, reusing the OOB bookkeeping the forest already produces.
explanations.c: Using the entire dataset would include in-bag rows the tree has already seen, contaminating the error estimate with memorization.
explanations.d: No separate held-out set is created; the OOB rows already serve that purpose for free.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for computing permutation importance for one feature across a random forest.

items.text: For each tree, score its own OOB rows to get a baseline error
Within those same OOB rows, randomly permute the values of the feature being tested
Re-score the tree on the OOB rows with the permuted feature and record the increase in error
Average the error increase for that feature across all trees in the forest

questions.explanation: Baseline OOB error is computed first, then the feature is permuted within those same rows, then the tree is re-scored to measure the error increase, and finally that increase is averaged across every tree in the forest to yield the feature's permutation importance.

questions.prompt: Match each importance measure to its defining property.

right.text: Computed in-sample on training data at no extra cost during tree growth
Computed out-of-sample on OOB rows, measuring the fitted model's reliance on a feature

questions.explanation: MDI is a byproduct of the greedy split search on training data, while permutation importance is measured out-of-sample by scrambling a feature within OOB rows and observing the resulting drop in the fitted model's accuracy.

lessons.label: Permutation Importance Fails Under Correlated Features

sections.heading: The duplicate-column demonstration
sections.body: The clearest demonstration of permutation importance's failure mode is deliberate: take a feature X that is genuinely and strongly predictive, create an exact duplicate column X' = X, and refit the random forest with both included. Both X and X' individually now score near-zero permutation importance, even though the underlying signal they jointly carry is essential to the model's accuracy. The mechanism is straightforward: at any split where the tree would have used X, it can equally well use X' instead, since they are identical, so the forest spreads its splits across both copies roughly evenly. When you then permute only X across the OOB rows, the tree can still recover the same information intact from the untouched X' at nearby or later splits, so predictions barely degrade — and the same argument applies symmetrically when only X' is permuted. A feature the model absolutely could not do without is reported as unimportant, purely because it has a redundant twin.

sections.heading: Beyond exact duplicates: correlated groups dilute importance
sections.body: This is not limited to literal duplicates. Any set of highly correlated features produces a diluted version of the same effect: the forest's splits get distributed across the correlated group rather than concentrated on whichever single feature is most directly causal, so permuting any one member only partially disrupts the information the model can still recover from its correlated partners. The more correlated partners a feature has, and the higher the correlation, the more its individual permutation importance is suppressed relative to its true contribution — a systematic understatement of importance for any feature that happens to travel with correlated company in the dataset.

sections.heading: The fix: conditional permutation importance
sections.body: Carolin Strobl, Anne-Laure Boulesteix, Thomas Kneib, Thomas Augustin, and Achim Zeileis addressed this directly in 'Conditional Variable Importance for Random Forests' (BMC Bioinformatics, 2008, volume 9, article 307). Their fix is conditional permutation importance: rather than permuting feature m's values freely across all OOB rows, the algorithm partitions the OOB rows into a grid defined by the values of m's correlated covariates, then permutes m's values only within each grid cell, shuffling among rows that already share similar values of the correlated partners. This keeps every permuted record inside the realistic joint distribution of the correlated group instead of breaking the correlation structure, so the resulting importance measures what m contributes beyond information already available from its correlated partners — restoring a sensible, non-collapsed importance to features like X and X' rather than splitting credit into two near-zero halves.

lessons.workedExample: A student models exam performance using 'hours_studied' and, by mistake, includes both hours_studied and an identical rescaled copy minutes_studied (minutes_studied = hours_studied times 60). Standard permutation importance reports both features near zero, because permuting hours_studied alone leaves minutes_studied intact for the forest to fall back on, and vice versa — the printed importance table wrongly suggests study time doesn't matter for the exam score. Recomputing with Strobl et al. 2008's conditional permutation importance, which permutes each feature only within grid cells matched on the other, both copies now correctly show high importance, because the conditional procedure can no longer borrow the untouched twin's information to reconstruct what was destroyed.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has seen a permutation importance table with two correlated features both scoring near zero will ask whether the student trusted that result or investigated it. The strong answer names the duplicate-column demonstration directly: permuting one correlated copy lets the model recover the same signal from its untouched partner, so both score as unimportant even though the pair is jointly essential. Citing Strobl et al. 2008's conditional permutation importance, which restricts shuffling to a grid partition of correlated covariates, shows the student knows a validated fix exists rather than simply discarding permutation importance as unreliable whenever correlation is present.

questions.prompt: If a genuinely predictive feature X is exactly duplicated as X', what does standard (unconditional) permutation importance report for X and X'?

options.text: Both near-zero, because the model can recover X's information from the untouched duplicate when either alone is permuted
Both very high, because duplicating a feature doubles its counted importance
X high and X' zero, because trees always prefer the first column in the dataset
An error, because most implementations reject exact duplicate columns

explanations.a: Correct — because the two copies are identical, the model can substitute the untouched duplicate for whichever copy was permuted, so predictions barely degrade and both score as unimportant.
explanations.b: The opposite occurs: importance is diluted toward zero, not doubled, because credit is spread across two redundant columns.
explanations.c: Trees have no inherent preference for column order; both copies are used interchangeably wherever either would help.
explanations.d: Random forest implementations do not reject duplicate columns; they simply treat them as two ordinary, redundant features.

questions.prompt: What does Strobl et al. 2008's conditional permutation importance change about the permutation step?

options.text: It permutes the feature across the entire dataset instead of just OOB rows
It permutes the feature only within a grid partition defined by its correlated covariates, instead of freely across all rows
It removes correlated features from the model entirely before scoring
It replaces permutation with mean decrease impurity

explanations.a: The scope of rows used (OOB) is unchanged; what changes is how the permutation is restricted within those rows.
explanations.b: Correct — permuting only within grid cells matched on correlated covariates keeps synthetic rows inside the realistic joint distribution, isolating the feature's own contribution.
explanations.c: No features are removed from the model; the fix changes how one feature is permuted, not the model's feature set.
explanations.d: Conditional permutation importance is still a permutation-based measure; it does not switch to the impurity-based MDI approach.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the duplicate-column demonstration.

items.text: Identify a feature X known to be genuinely predictive
Add an exact duplicate column X' = X to the feature set
Refit the random forest with both X and X' included
Compute standard permutation importance and observe both X and X' score near zero

questions.explanation: The demonstration starts by picking a truly predictive feature, duplicating it, refitting the model with both copies present, and finally observing that unconditional permutation importance collapses both copies' scores toward zero.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to its correct description.

right.text: Permutes a feature within grid cells matched on correlated covariates
Permutes a feature freely across all OOB rows, ignoring correlation structure
Shows a genuinely essential feature can score near-zero importance when a redundant correlated twin exists

questions.explanation: Unconditional permutation importance shuffles a feature across all OOB rows regardless of correlation; conditional permutation importance restricts shuffling to a grid partition of correlated covariates; and the duplicate-column demonstration shows the resulting failure mode when correlated (or identical) features are present.

lessons.label: Off-Manifold Permutation: 'Please Stop Permuting Features'

sections.heading: Permutation manufactures records that cannot exist
sections.body: Giles Hooker, Lucas Mentch, and Siyu Zhou's paper, circulated informally as 'Please Stop Permuting Features' before its 2021 publication in Statistics and Computing as 'Unrestricted permutation forces extrapolation: variable importance requires at least one more model, or there is no free variable importance,' names a problem baked into every permutation-based importance measure. Permuting a column independently of every other column preserves that column's own marginal distribution but destroys its joint relationship with the rest of the row. The resulting synthetic record can be a combination that never occurs in reality: permuting a pregnancy indicator independently of sex can label a male record as pregnant; permuting height independently of weight can produce a two-meter-tall, twenty-kilogram person. Every real row in the data respects the joint structure of the population it was drawn from; a permuted row typically does not, and the model is then asked to score an input it never could have seen during training.

sections.heading: Why off-manifold queries contaminate the score
sections.body: This matters because a model's prediction on a point far outside the training data's support, off the data manifold, is not really constrained by anything it learned about real relationships; it reflects however the model happens to extrapolate in a region with no training examples to anchor it, which can be close to arbitrary. Hooker, Mentch, and Zhou show this extrapolation behavior systematically contaminates the resulting importance score: part of the measured increase in error after permutation is really measuring the model's arbitrary behavior on impossible inputs, not its reliance on genuine, in-distribution signal. Two models with identical real-world reliance on a feature can report different permutation importances purely because they extrapolate differently off-manifold.

sections.heading: The honest alternatives, and their cost
sections.body: The honest fix requires giving up permutation's free-lunch property. Jing Lei, Max G'Sell, Alessandro Rinaldo, Ryan Tibshirani, and Larry Wasserman's 2018 Journal of the American Statistical Association paper 'Distribution-Free Predictive Inference for Regression' introduced LOCO (leave-one-covariate-out): refit the model with feature j removed entirely, and compare its error to the full model's error; the gap is j's importance, computed with zero synthetic rows because no row was ever corrupted. Conditional permutation (Strobl et al. 2008) and knockoff-based schemes, which construct synthetic 'fake' copies of a feature preserving its correlation structure with the rest of the data (model-X knockoffs, Candes et al.), offer intermediate fixes that stay closer to the real joint distribution without a full refit. All three routes share the same honest cost Hooker, Mentch, and Zhou's title states outright: computing trustworthy variable importance requires at least one more model, not a free byproduct of the one you already fit.

lessons.workedExample: A hospital readmission model includes both 'is_pregnant' and 'sex'. Standard permutation importance shuffles is_pregnant across all OOB rows independently of sex, producing records like 'male, is_pregnant = true' that cannot exist in the real population. The model, never trained on such combinations, extrapolates somewhat arbitrarily on them, and the resulting error increase partly reflects that arbitrary extrapolation rather than genuine reliance on pregnancy status. Switching to LOCO, refitting the model with is_pregnant dropped and comparing the new error to the original, avoids creating any impossible row, at the cost of one extra full model fit per feature checked — exactly the 'one more model' Hooker, Mentch, and Zhou's title insists is unavoidable for trustworthy importance.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has read 'Please Stop Permuting Features' may ask the student to name a concrete impossible record permutation can manufacture, a pregnant man, an impossibly light and tall person, testing whether the student understands the off-manifold problem mechanically rather than as an abstract caveat. The stronger follow-up asks what the student's project actually did about it: naming LOCO, conditional permutation, or knockoffs, and being honest that each costs at least one additional model fit, shows the student understands that trustworthy variable importance is not free, and that 'my forest already computes this for me' is not a defensible final answer.

questions.prompt: What problem do Hooker, Mentch & Zhou identify with unrestricted feature permutation?

options.text: It is too computationally expensive to run at scale
Permuting a feature independently of correlated features can create combinations that don't exist in reality, forcing the model to extrapolate off the data manifold
It only works for classification, not regression
It always underestimates every feature's importance by the same fixed amount

explanations.a: Their objection is about validity, not computational cost — unrestricted permutation is in fact cheap, which is part of the problem.
explanations.b: Correct — breaking a feature's joint relationship with correlated covariates can manufacture impossible records (e.g. a pregnant man), forcing the model to score inputs far outside its training distribution.
explanations.c: The off-manifold problem applies to both classification and regression models alike; it is not restricted to one task type.
explanations.d: The contamination is not a fixed, uniform underestimate; it depends on how each specific model happens to extrapolate off-manifold.

questions.prompt: According to Hooker, Mentch & Zhou, what does a trustworthy fix for variable importance require?

options.text: Nothing extra — permutation is already unbiased if enough trees are used
At least one additional model, such as a refit as in LOCO, rather than a free byproduct of the fitted model
Switching entirely to mean decrease impurity instead of permutation
Discarding any feature that can produce an off-manifold combination

explanations.a: Adding more trees does not fix the off-manifold contamination; the bias is structural, not a variance issue that averages away.
explanations.b: Correct — the paper's title states this outright: there is no free variable importance, and trustworthy measurement requires at least one more model, such as LOCO's refit.
explanations.c: MDI has its own separate, well-documented cardinality bias (Strobl et al. 2007) and does not solve the off-manifold problem, which is specific to permutation-based methods.
explanations.d: Discarding features is not the proposed remedy; the fix changes how importance is measured, not which features are kept.

questions.prompt: Match each approach to its correct description.

right.text: Permutes within a grid partition of correlated covariates to stay closer to the joint distribution
Refits the model with the feature removed and compares error to the full model
Constructs synthetic but realistic 'fake' copies preserving the feature's correlation structure

questions.explanation: LOCO refits the model without the feature and compares errors; conditional permutation restricts shuffling to a grid partition of correlated covariates; and knockoff schemes construct realistic synthetic copies that preserve the feature's correlation structure with the rest of the data.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of computing LOCO importance for feature j.

items.text: Fit the full model using all features including j
Refit the model with feature j removed entirely
Compute prediction error for both the full and the reduced model
Take the gap between the reduced model's error and the full model's error as feature j's importance

questions.explanation: LOCO first fits the full model, then refits it with feature j dropped, then computes both models' errors, and finally reports the error gap as feature j's importance — with no permuted or synthetic rows involved at any step.

units.label: Model-Agnostic Explanation: LIME and SHAP

lessons.label: LIME: Local Surrogates (Ribeiro, Singh & Guestrin 2016)

sections.heading: The Paper and the Core Idea
sections.body: Marco Ribeiro, Sameer Singh, and Carlos Guestrin introduced LIME — Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations — in "Why Should I Trust You? Explaining the Predictions of Any Classifier," presented at KDD 2016. The paper's premise: a model can be arbitrarily complex and opaque (a random forest, a deep net, a gradient-boosted ensemble) yet still be explained locally, one prediction at a time, by fitting a simple interpretable model g that mimics the black box f only in the immediate neighborhood of a single instance x. LIME never touches f's internals — it only queries f(z) for perturbed inputs z, which is what makes it model-agnostic: the same recipe explains an SVM, a CNN, or an XGBoost model without modification. The paper frames this as a trust problem, not just an accuracy problem: a practitioner deciding whether to deploy a model needs a reason for a SPECIFIC prediction, and global accuracy on a held-out set answers a different question than 'why did the model say this, for this row, right now.'

sections.heading: Building the Interpretable Representation and Sampling Perturbations
sections.body: Before perturbing anything, LIME maps the raw instance x to an interpretable binary representation x' in {0,1}^d'. For images, x' is one bit per superpixel (a contiguous patch from a segmentation algorithm such as quickshift); for text, one bit per word present in the document; for tabular data, one bit per discretized bin of each continuous feature. Perturbed samples z' are generated by randomly switching components off — graying out superpixels, deleting words, or replacing a bin's value with a value drawn from the training distribution — then mapped back to the original input space as z and passed through the real model to get the label f(z). This produces a synthetic local dataset of (z', f(z)) pairs entirely of LIME's own construction; the black box never sees x directly during this step.

sections.heading: The Objective: Weighted Local Fidelity Plus Sparsity
sections.body: Each perturbed sample is weighted by an exponential proximity kernel πx(z) = exp(−D(x,z)²/σ²), using cosine distance for text and L2 distance for images, so samples close to x dominate the fit and distant ones are nearly ignored. LIME then fits a sparse linear surrogate g by K-LASSO: a LASSO regularization path first selects the K most predictive interpretable features, and weighted least squares fits their coefficients on the remaining pairs. Formally, the explanation is ξ(x) = argmin_g L(f,g,πx) + Ω(g), minimizing a weighted squared-error local infidelity term L against a complexity penalty Ω(g) that caps g to K non-zero weights. The reported explanation — the signed coefficients of g — describes the surrogate's local behavior, not f's true mechanism; it is only trustworthy within the neighborhood πx actually weighted, and a different σ or a different perturbation sample can yield a different g.

lessons.workedExample: A hospital deploys a gradient-boosted model to flag pneumonia risk from patient records. For one patient flagged high-risk, LIME discretizes the tabular record into bins (age 60-70, white-cell count high, asthma-history yes/no, etc.), generates 5,000 perturbed rows by randomly resetting bins to background values, scores each with the real model, weights each row by proximity to the original patient via the exponential kernel, and fits a K-LASSO surrogate capped at K=6 features. The surrogate returns positive coefficients on 'age 60-70' and 'white-cell count high' and a negative coefficient on 'no asthma history' — meaning that, near this patient, having no asthma history locally pushed the score down. The clinician reads these six weights as the explanation, understanding they describe g's local fit, not a proof about the boosted model's global logic.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has read the paper will ask what, precisely, K-LASSO is doing and why the kernel is exponential rather than linear — vague answers like 'it approximates the model' collapse under a follow-up asking what is being approximated FOR, over WHAT neighborhood, and USING what loss. The strong answer names the two-term objective (weighted infidelity plus a sparsity penalty), states that σ and the sampling scheme are chosen by the practitioner rather than derived from theory, and is explicit that the coefficients belong to the surrogate g, not to f — conflating the two is the single most common and most damaging mistake presenters make with LIME.

questions.prompt: Which paper and venue introduced LIME?

options.text: Lundberg & Lee, NeurIPS 2017
Ribeiro, Singh & Guestrin, "Why Should I Trust You?", KDD 2016
Shapley, "A Value for n-Person Games," 1953
Wachter, Mittelstadt & Russell, 2017

explanations.a: That is the SHAP paper, published a year after LIME.
explanations.b: Correct — LIME comes from this 2016 KDD paper.
explanations.c: That is the founding game-theory paper behind Shapley values, decades earlier.
explanations.d: That paper introduces counterfactual explanations, a different explanation format.

questions.prompt: Put LIME's recipe steps in the order they actually happen.

items.text: Map the input to an interpretable binary representation
Sample perturbations by switching components off
Score each perturbed sample with the black-box model
Weight each sample by an exponential proximity kernel
Fit a sparse linear surrogate via K-LASSO

questions.explanation: LIME first builds the interpretable representation, then samples perturbations within it, scores each with the real model, weights them by proximity to x, and only then fits the K-LASSO surrogate on the weighted data.

questions.prompt: In the objective ξ(x) = argmin_g L(f,g,πx) + Ω(g), what does Ω(g) do?

options.text: Measures the weighted squared error between f and g
Penalizes complexity, capping g to K non-zero coefficients
Computes the exponential proximity kernel
Discretizes continuous features into bins

explanations.a: That role belongs to L(f,g,πx), the local infidelity term.
explanations.b: Correct — Ω(g) is the complexity penalty that keeps the surrogate sparse (K-LASSO).
explanations.c: The kernel πx is computed separately and used to weight samples inside L.
explanations.d: Discretization happens earlier, when building the interpretable representation.

questions.prompt: Match each data type to the interpretable unit LIME toggles when perturbing it.

right.text: Superpixel present/absent
Word present/absent
Discretized feature bin

questions.explanation: LIME's interpretable representation is domain-specific: superpixels for images, bag-of-words presence for text, and discretized bins for continuous tabular features.

questions.prompt: The coefficients LIME reports for an explanation are best described as:

options.text: Exact global feature importances of the black-box model f
Coefficients of the local surrogate g, valid only near x
Shapley values of the features
Gradients of f with respect to each input

explanations.a: LIME never claims global validity — the surrogate is fit only in a local neighborhood.
explanations.b: Correct — the explanation belongs to the fitted surrogate g, trustworthy only within the weighted local neighborhood used to build it.
explanations.c: Shapley values come from a different, game-theoretic construction (see the SHAP lessons in this unit).
explanations.d: LIME is gradient-free; it works via black-box queries on perturbed samples, not differentiation.

lessons.label: The Husky-vs-Wolf Experiment and SP-LIME

sections.heading: The Deliberately Broken Classifier
sections.body: To demonstrate that accuracy alone doesn't earn trust, Ribeiro, Singh, and Guestrin trained a logistic-regression classifier on a small set of wolf and husky photos, deliberately seeding the training data so that every wolf photo happened to have a snowy background and every husky photo did not. The resulting classifier scored well on held-out accuracy while actually keying on snow pixels rather than any feature of the animal itself — a caricature of how a spurious correlation can masquerade as competence. It was invented specifically as a stress test: could an explanation method expose a bad feature that an accuracy score alone would never reveal?

sections.heading: The 27-Subject User Study
sections.body: The authors recruited 27 subjects with some machine-learning background and, without disclosing the trick, asked two things: whether they trusted the classifier's predictions, and what features they believed it used. Before seeing any explanation, 10 of 27 said they trusted the classifier, and only 12 of 27 named snow as a possible cue — most assumed it was looking at the animal. Each subject was then shown LIME explanations that highlighted the snowy background as the pixels driving the wolf prediction. Afterward, trust in the classifier collapsed to just 3 of 27, and 25 of 27 correctly named snow as the feature it relied on. The explanation did not change the model; it changed what humans knew about it, and the swing — 10 to 3 trusting, 12 to 25 identifying snow — is the paper's headline evidence that local explanations surface failures accuracy alone cannot.

sections.heading: SP-LIME: Auditing a Model Globally From a Few Local Explanations
sections.body: A single LIME explanation only vouches for one instance. Submodular Pick (SP-LIME) selects a budget of B instances whose explanations, taken together, cover as much of the feature space as possible without redundancy — instances that all highlight the same feature contribute little once one of them has been shown, so SP-LIME favors a diverse, non-overlapping set. It builds an importance matrix across many explained instances, defines a coverage function over which features have been 'shown' by at least one instance in the picked set, and greedily adds whichever remaining instance increases coverage the most until the budget B is exhausted — an efficient approximation to the NP-hard submodular-maximization problem, justified because greedy selection is provably within a constant factor of the optimal set for submodular coverage functions. An auditor can then form a global judgment about the model from a small, engineered sample of local stories rather than reading every explanation.

lessons.workedExample: A curriculum committee vets an admissions-scoring model before a pilot. Rather than reading LIME explanations for all 3,000 applicant rows, they run SP-LIME with a budget of B=10. The algorithm builds a matrix of which interpretable features (GPA bucket, essay-word features, zip-code bin) each row's explanation would surface, then greedily selects the 10 rows whose combined explanations cover the widest set of distinct influential features instead of picking 10 rows that all highlight GPA. Reviewing just those 10 explanations, the committee discovers one row's high score was driven by a zip-code bin correlated with a wealthy district — a husky-vs-wolf-style shortcut — surfaced only because SP-LIME's coverage objective forced a feature-diverse sample instead of ten redundant, GPA-only stories.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges know accuracy scores can hide shortcut learning, so this experiment is the go-to probe for 'how do you know your model is right for the right reasons.' A judge may ask for the exact numbers (10/27 and 12/27 before, 3/27 and 25/27 after) to check the presenter actually read the paper rather than gesturing at 'a user study.' A second, sharper question is why SP-LIME picks a diverse set rather than the B most confident or highest-accuracy instances — the correct answer is that redundant explanations of the same feature waste the auditor's limited attention, so coverage, not confidence, is the optimization target.

questions.prompt: Why was the wolf/husky classifier deliberately broken?

options.text: It was trained on corrupted, low-resolution images
All wolf training photos had snowy backgrounds, so the model learned to key on snow instead of the animal
It used too few training examples to learn any pattern
It was a random baseline with no learned weights

explanations.a: Image quality was not the manipulation — the training set's snow/animal correlation was.
explanations.b: Correct — seeding every wolf photo with snow made snow, not the animal, the learned feature.
explanations.c: It had enough examples to fit a working (if wrong) decision rule and score well on held-out accuracy.
explanations.d: It was a real trained logistic-regression classifier, not a random baseline.

questions.prompt: How many of the 27 subjects said they trusted the classifier before seeing explanations, and how many after?

options.text: 10 before, 3 after
12 before, 25 after
3 before, 10 after
27 before, 0 after

explanations.a: Correct — trust dropped from 10 of 27 to 3 of 27 after seeing LIME's explanations.
explanations.b: 12 before and 25 after are the counts of subjects who named snow as a possible cue, not trust counts.
explanations.c: This reverses the direction — trust fell after explanations, it did not rise.
explanations.d: Neither extreme (unanimous trust or zero trust) matches the reported figures.

questions.prompt: What does SP-LIME optimize when selecting B instances to show a human auditor?

options.text: The highest-accuracy predictions in the dataset
The most confident predictions the model makes
A diverse, non-redundant set of instances that together cover the feature space
The instances with the largest LIME kernel width

explanations.a: SP-LIME has no access to ground-truth accuracy per instance for this purpose; it works from explanation coverage.
explanations.b: Confidence is not the objective — a set of confident but redundant explanations would still fail to surface unseen features.
explanations.c: Correct — the submodular pick maximizes non-redundant coverage of the feature space across the picked instances.
explanations.d: Kernel width is a LIME sampling parameter, not part of SP-LIME's selection criterion.

questions.prompt: Put the study's steps, and SP-LIME's role after it, in order.

items.text: Train a classifier on snow-confounded wolf/husky photos
Survey subjects on trust and suspected features, before explanations
Show subjects LIME explanations highlighting snow
Resurvey subjects and observe trust collapse
Apply SP-LIME to pick a diverse instance set for global auditing

questions.explanation: The classifier is trained first, subjects are surveyed before and after seeing LIME explanations, and SP-LIME is the separate, later technique for auditing a model globally using a handful of local explanations.

questions.prompt: Match each reported figure to what it measured in the 27-subject study.

right.text: Trusted the classifier, before explanations
Named snow as a possible cue, before explanations
Trusted the classifier, after explanations
Named snow as a possible cue, after explanations

questions.explanation: Trust fell from 10/27 to 3/27 while correct identification of snow as the driving feature rose from 12/27 to 25/27, once subjects saw LIME's explanations.

lessons.label: LIME's Knobs and Its Instability

sections.heading: Three Unprincipled Choices That Decide the Answer
sections.body: LIME has no theory that sets its kernel width σ — the reference implementation defaults to a formula (roughly 0.75 times the square root of the number of features for tabular data) but offers no guarantee it is correct for any specific model or dataset. Because σ controls how tightly 'local' the neighborhood is, changing it can move an attribution's SIGN, not just its magnitude: a feature that looks protective under a narrow kernel can look harmful under a wider one, because the two kernels are effectively fitting the surrogate to different regions of f's decision surface. On a real dataset, a practitioner might see a 'high blood pressure' coefficient flip from positive to negative just by doubling σ, with no change whatsoever to the underlying model. Kernel width is chosen by the analyst, not derived from f.

sections.heading: Sampling and Discretization Add More Variance
sections.body: The number and distribution of perturbation samples is the second unprincipled choice: LIME typically draws several thousand perturbed points, but running the exact same explanation twice on the identical row, with the identical model, produces different coefficients each time, because sampling is stochastic and the local region is often sparsely and unevenly covered near real data. The third choice is the discretization of continuous features into bins — the bin edges chosen (quartiles versus deciles versus domain-specific cutoffs) change which interpretable feature 'fires' for a given value of x, which can shift which coefficient absorbs the effect entirely. None of the three choices is dictated by the underlying black-box model; all three are analyst degrees of freedom that a differently-configured LIME run can flip.

sections.heading: Alvarez-Melis & Jaakkola 2018 and the Fidelity Discipline
sections.body: David Alvarez-Melis and Tommi Jaakkola's 2018 paper, 'On the Robustness of Interpretability Methods,' formalized this instability by treating an explanation method as a function from inputs to attribution vectors and measuring its local Lipschitz constant — the largest change in explanation divided by the smallest change in input, searched for empirically via local perturbation search. They found that LIME-style surrogates can have arbitrarily large Lipschitz constants: two inputs a human would call nearly identical can receive explanations that disagree on which features matter, even though the underlying black box's own predictions barely moved. Their prescribed discipline, now standard practice, is to never present a LIME plot without also reporting the surrogate's own local fidelity — the R² of g's fit to f on the weighted perturbed sample used to build it. A low R² means the linear surrogate barely tracks the black box in that neighborhood, so its coefficients describe noise the analyst happened to fit, not the model's actual local behavior.

lessons.workedExample: An analyst explains a loan-denial model's decision for one applicant using LIME with default settings (σ=0.75√d, 5,000 samples, quartile discretization) and gets a top negative coefficient on 'debt-to-income ratio, high bin.' Re-running with a wider kernel (σ doubled) and decile bins instead of quartiles, the top negative coefficient becomes 'credit inquiries, high bin' instead — same applicant, same denied loan, same black-box model, different story. Before presenting either version, the analyst checks R² for both surrogate fits: the quartile version fits at R²=0.81, the decile version at R²=0.44. Reporting only the well-fit version, with its R² stated alongside the coefficients, is the responsible choice; presenting the poorly-fit one as if it explained the decision would be reporting noise as insight.
lessons.judgeFraming: Any judge who has run LIME twice on the same row and gotten different answers will ask how you know your explanation reflects the model rather than your choice of σ, sample count, or bin edges. The disciplined answer is to report the surrogate's local R² alongside every plot and to show the explanation is stable across a few reruns and kernel widths before treating any single coefficient as meaningful — citing Alvarez-Melis and Jaakkola's 2018 robustness result signals you know this is a documented property of local surrogates, not a bug specific to your implementation.

questions.prompt: What does the kernel width σ control in LIME, and why is choosing it risky?

options.text: It sets the number of perturbation samples, and there is no risk
It defines how 'local' the neighborhood is, and changing it can flip an attribution's sign with no change to the underlying model
It discretizes continuous features into bins
It sets the LASSO complexity penalty Ω(g)

explanations.a: Sample count is a separate, also-unprincipled knob; σ is about neighborhood size, and the risk is real.
explanations.b: Correct — σ has no theory setting it, and different values can fit the surrogate to different regions of f's surface, flipping signs.
explanations.c: Discretization of bins is a distinct, third unprincipled choice.
explanations.d: The complexity penalty is set separately by the K in K-LASSO, not by σ.

questions.prompt: What did Alvarez-Melis & Jaakkola (2018) demonstrate about local explainers like LIME?

options.text: LIME explanations are always stable regardless of input perturbation
Local explainers can have high local Lipschitz constants — nearly identical inputs can receive very different explanations
SHAP is unstable but LIME is provably stable
Kernel width has no measurable effect on the resulting explanation

explanations.a: The opposite is true — this is precisely the instability they documented.
explanations.b: Correct — they measured large local Lipschitz constants empirically, showing explanations can diverge sharply for nearly identical inputs.
explanations.c: Their result is about local surrogate explainers generally, not a SHAP-versus-LIME comparison.
explanations.d: Kernel width strongly affects which region the surrogate fits, and thus the explanation.

questions.prompt: Why should a LIME plot always be reported alongside the surrogate's local R²?

options.text: R² automatically sets the correct kernel width
A low R² means the linear surrogate does not actually track the black box locally, so its coefficients may just be noise
R² determines how many perturbation samples to draw
R² is a required input to the K-LASSO algorithm before it can run

explanations.a: R² is a diagnostic computed AFTER fitting; it does not feed back into choosing σ automatically.
explanations.b: Correct — R² tells you whether the surrogate is a good local fit; without it, coefficients from a poorly-fit surrogate look just as authoritative as a well-fit one.
explanations.c: Sample count is chosen before fitting; R² is measured afterward.
explanations.d: K-LASSO runs regardless of R²; R² is reported as a diagnostic on the resulting fit.

questions.prompt: Put the responsible LIME diagnostic workflow in order.

items.text: Generate a LIME explanation for the instance
Check the surrogate's local R²
Rerun with a different kernel width, sample count, or bin edges
Compare stability of the explanation across reruns
Report the explanation together with its R² and a stability caveat

questions.explanation: Generate the explanation, check its fidelity, rerun under different settings to probe instability, compare the results, and only then report the finding with its fidelity and stability caveats attached.

questions.prompt: Match each unprincipled knob to why it destabilizes LIME's answer.

right.text: No theory sets it; changing it can flip an attribution's sign
Stochastic; two runs on the identical row can differ
Bin-edge choice changes which interpretable feature fires for a given value

questions.explanation: All three are analyst-chosen degrees of freedom with no grounding in the black-box model itself, and each destabilizes the explanation in a distinct way.

lessons.label: Shapley Values: The Game-Theoretic Import (Shapley 1953)

sections.heading: A Value for n-Person Games (Shapley, 1953)
sections.body: Lloyd Shapley's 1953 paper, 'A Value for n-Person Games,' asked a cooperative-game-theory question with no obvious answer: if a coalition of M players jointly produces some total payoff (a 'game' v that maps any subset, or coalition, S of players to a value v(S)), how should that payoff be fairly divided among the players? Shapley proposed answering by imagining every possible ORDER in which players could join the coalition one at a time, crediting each player with the marginal payoff their joining adds at that point in that order, then averaging that marginal contribution over all M! possible orderings. Feature-attribution methods later reuse this exact machinery by treating each input feature as a 'player' and the model's prediction as the payoff a coalition of present features produces.

sections.heading: The Uniqueness Theorem: Four Axioms, One Answer
sections.body: Shapley did not just propose a formula; he proved it was the ONLY value satisfying four reasonable fairness axioms simultaneously. Efficiency requires that the players' values sum exactly to v of the full coalition — nothing left over or double-counted. Symmetry requires that two players who contribute identically to every coalition receive identical values, regardless of their labels. Dummy (the null-player axiom) requires that a player who adds zero marginal value to every coalition it could join receives a value of exactly zero. Additivity requires that if two separate games are combined, a player's value in the combined game equals the sum of its values in the two games separately. Shapley proved exactly one value function satisfies all four at once — the averaged-marginal-contribution formula — which is what gives the Shapley value its authority in feature attribution: any deviation from it necessarily breaks one of these four properties.

sections.heading: From Cooperative Games to Feature Explanation
sections.body: Shapley's own motivation was economic — dividing gains from cooperation among firms or agents — and the result was recognized decades later: he shared the 2012 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences with Alvin Roth 'for the theory of stable allocations and the practice of market design,' with the Shapley value as one pillar of that body of work. Applying the framework to machine learning required reinterpreting 'players' as input features and v(S) as the model's expected output when only the features in S are known, with the rest marginalized out or replaced by background values. Erik Štrumbelj and Igor Kononenko did this explicitly years before SHAP existed, publishing a Monte-Carlo sampling approximation of Shapley values for explaining individual classifier predictions in 2010 and expanding it in a 2014 journal paper — establishing that Shapley-value feature attribution was a known, usable technique well before Lundberg and Lee's 2017 unification.

lessons.workedExample: Three features — age, blood pressure, cholesterol — jointly 'produce' a model's risk score. To find blood pressure's Shapley value, consider all 3! = 6 orderings in which the three features could be revealed to the model one at a time. In the ordering age→blood pressure→cholesterol, blood pressure's marginal contribution is [prediction with age and blood pressure known] minus [prediction with only age known]. Repeating this for all six orderings and averaging the six marginal contributions gives blood pressure's Shapley value. Because the calculation used every ordering, not just one, the axioms guarantee the three features' Shapley values sum exactly to the gap between the full prediction and the model's average output (efficiency) — a property that would not hold if the analyst had simply picked one convenient ordering and stopped there.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows game theory may ask why Shapley values, specifically, rather than some other way of splitting credit among features. The strong answer is not 'they're standard' but Shapley's 1953 uniqueness proof: efficiency, symmetry, dummy, and additivity together pin down exactly one formula, so any competing attribution scheme necessarily violates one of those four properties. A sharper follow-up — why should a judge care about an economics result from 1953 applied to machine learning — is answered by naming that Shapley shared the 2012 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for this line of work, and that Štrumbelj and Kononenko were already applying it to model explanation in 2010.

questions.prompt: In Shapley's construction, a player's value is computed as:

options.text: Its contribution measured in just one arbitrary ordering
Its marginal contribution averaged over all M! possible orderings of the players
Its raw coefficient from a linear regression
The impurity gain it produces at the root of a decision tree

explanations.a: A single ordering would not satisfy the fairness axioms Shapley required; averaging over all orderings is essential.
explanations.b: Correct — averaging marginal contributions over every possible joining order is exactly Shapley's construction.
explanations.c: Regression coefficients come from a different (and much later) attribution approach, not Shapley's original game-theoretic construction.
explanations.d: Impurity gain is a tree-specific heuristic, unrelated to Shapley's coalitional-game averaging.

questions.prompt: Match each of Shapley's four axioms to its statement.

right.text: Values sum exactly to the total coalition payoff
Players with identical marginal contributions to every coalition get identical values
A player contributing zero marginal value to every coalition gets a value of zero
A player's value in a combined game equals the sum of its values in the two separate games

questions.explanation: These four axioms, taken together, are exactly what Shapley proved pin down a single unique value function.

questions.prompt: Shapley shared the 2012 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences with whom?

options.text: Daniel Kahneman
Alvin Roth
Elinor Ostrom
Jean Tirole

explanations.a: Kahneman won an earlier Nobel (2002) for behavioral economics, unrelated to this prize.
explanations.b: Correct — Shapley shared the 2012 prize with Alvin Roth for the theory of stable allocations and market design.
explanations.c: Ostrom won in 2009 for economic governance, not the same prize.
explanations.d: Tirole won the 2014 prize for market power and regulation, a different year and topic.

questions.prompt: Who published a Monte-Carlo sampling approximation of Shapley values for explaining individual model predictions years before the SHAP paper?

options.text: Lundberg & Lee
Ribeiro, Singh & Guestrin
Štrumbelj & Kononenko
Alvarez-Melis & Jaakkola

explanations.a: Lundberg & Lee unified additive attribution methods as SHAP in 2017, after Štrumbelj & Kononenko's work.
explanations.b: Ribeiro, Singh & Guestrin authored LIME and Anchors, not the Monte-Carlo Shapley approximation.
explanations.c: Correct — their 2010 and 2014 papers applied Monte-Carlo Shapley-value approximation to model explanation before SHAP existed.
explanations.d: Alvarez-Melis & Jaakkola studied explanation robustness, not Shapley-value approximation.

questions.prompt: Put these events in chronological order.

items.text: Shapley's "A Value for n-Person Games" (1953)
Štrumbelj & Kononenko's Monte-Carlo Shapley approximation for model explanation (2010)
Shapley shares the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences (2012)
Lundberg & Lee unify additive attribution methods as SHAP (2017)

questions.explanation: The theory came first in 1953, its Monte-Carlo application to model explanation in 2010, Shapley's Nobel recognition in 2012, and SHAP's unification of attribution methods in 2017.

lessons.label: SHAP: A Unified Framework (Lundberg & Lee 2017)

sections.heading: Defining the Class: Additive Feature Attribution Methods
sections.body: Scott Lundberg and Su-In Lee's 2017 NIPS paper, 'A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions,' observed that several existing explanation methods, despite looking unrelated, are all special cases of one mathematical form: an explanation model g(z') = φ0 + Σ_{i=1}^{M} φi z'i, a linear function over a simplified binary input z' where each φi is the attribution assigned to feature i and φ0 is a base value. They named this class 'additive feature attribution methods' and showed LIME (whose K-LASSO surrogate is exactly this form, with weights fit by local regression), DeepLIFT (attributions computed by backpropagating differences from a reference activation), layer-wise relevance propagation (attributions computed by redistributing a network's output backward through its layers), and classic Shapley regression values (from earlier econometrics work) are all members of the same family, differing only in HOW they estimate the φi.

sections.heading: Three Properties and a Uniqueness Theorem
sections.body: Having unified the class, Lundberg and Lee asked which member, if any, is uniquely justified, and proposed three desirable properties. Local accuracy requires φ0 + Σφi to exactly equal f(x) for the specific instance being explained — attributions must fully account for the prediction, not merely approximate it. Missingness requires that a feature absent from the input (z'i = 0) receives φi = 0 — no credit for a feature that was never there. Consistency requires that if a model changes so a feature's marginal contribution increases or stays the same for every possible coalition, that feature's attribution cannot decrease. They proved only one member of the additive feature attribution class satisfies all three simultaneously: the Shapley values of a specific value function v(S), defined as the model's expected output conditioned on the features in S. This member is what the paper names SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations).

sections.heading: The Consistency Counterexample: Why Gain-Based Tree Importance Fails
sections.body: To show consistency is not automatic, the paper contrasts SHAP with the common gain-based (Saabas-style) tree feature-importance method, which credits a feature at each split proportional to how much that split reduces impurity, without reweighting for how often that path is actually taken across the whole ensemble. They construct a pair of tree models where feature B's marginal contribution is provably at least as large as feature A's in every coalition, yet gain-based importance still ranks A above B, because gain only counts local impurity reduction at splits and can overweight a feature appearing in an early, high-volume split without it truly driving the output more. SHAP's Shapley-value construction cannot make this mistake by the consistency theorem itself; a heuristic importance measure with no matching theorem can and does.

lessons.workedExample: A credit-scoring team compares two tree models fit on the same two features, income and zip code. In model 1, income drives most splits; in model 2, the team retrains so zip code contributes at least as much to every coalition's marginal value as it did in model 1, while income's role shrinks. A gain-based tree-importance report ranks income above zip code in BOTH models — even in model 2, where zip code provably matters at least as much everywhere. Recomputing with SHAP, zip code's φ rises from model 1 to model 2 and its ranking correctly overtakes income's, because SHAP's consistency property guarantees an attribution cannot fall when a feature's true marginal contribution rises — exactly the guarantee gain-based importance lacks.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge comparing two feature-importance charts from different model versions may notice a feature's rank moved the 'wrong' way and ask whether that is a bug. The strong answer distinguishes measures that carry Lundberg and Lee's consistency guarantee (SHAP) from ones that don't (gain-based tree importance), and states the guarantee precisely: if a feature's marginal contribution to every possible coalition rises or holds steady across models, its attribution cannot fall. Naming the paper's actual counterexample — where gain-based importance ranks a demonstrably more-relied-upon feature LOWER — shows the presenter understands why the property matters, not just that SHAP is 'more accurate.'

questions.prompt: In g(z') = φ0 + Σφi z'i, what does φ0 represent?

options.text: The Shapley kernel width used for sampling coalitions
The base/expected value the explanation starts from before any feature contributions are added
The number of non-zero coefficients in the explanation
The LASSO penalty term from K-LASSO

explanations.a: Kernel width is a KernelSHAP computation detail, not part of the additive attribution formula itself.
explanations.b: Correct — φ0 is the model's expected output before any feature-specific attribution is added.
explanations.c: That count is a sparsity property of LIME's surrogate specifically, not a general part of the additive form.
explanations.d: The LASSO penalty is a LIME-specific fitting detail, not φ0 in the unified additive form.

questions.prompt: Match each of Lundberg & Lee's three properties to its definition.

right.text: φ0 + Σφi must exactly equal f(x) for the explained instance
A feature absent from the input must receive zero attribution
If a feature's marginal contribution never decreases across models, its attribution cannot decrease

questions.explanation: These are the three properties Lundberg and Lee use to prove SHAP is the unique member of the additive feature attribution class satisfying all of them at once.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was NOT one of the pre-existing methods the 2017 paper identified as an additive feature attribution method?

options.text: LIME
DeepLIFT
Layer-wise relevance propagation
TreeSHAP

explanations.a: LIME's K-LASSO surrogate was explicitly shown to fit the additive attribution form.
explanations.b: DeepLIFT was one of the methods unified under the additive attribution class.
explanations.c: Layer-wise relevance propagation was also shown to be a member of the class.
explanations.d: Correct — TreeSHAP is a computation algorithm introduced by Lundberg and colleagues a year later (2018), not one of the pre-existing methods unified in the 2017 paper.

questions.prompt: What does the paper's consistency counterexample demonstrate?

options.text: SHAP values are sometimes negative
Gain-based tree importance can rank a feature lower even when the model provably relies on it more
LIME and SHAP always produce identical explanations
DeepLIFT violates the local accuracy property

explanations.a: Negative attributions are normal and expected; the counterexample is about ranking, not sign.
explanations.b: Correct — the counterexample shows gain-based importance can inconsistently under-rank a feature the model demonstrably relies on more.
explanations.c: The two methods can and do disagree; the paper unifies their FORM, not their numeric output.
explanations.d: DeepLIFT is presented as satisfying local accuracy; the counterexample targets gain-based tree importance specifically.

questions.prompt: Put the paper's argument in the order it is built.

items.text: Define the additive feature attribution class g(z') = φ0 + Σφi z'i
Show LIME, DeepLIFT, and LRP all fit the class
State the three properties: local accuracy, missingness, consistency
Prove Shapley values are the unique member satisfying all three
Contrast with gain-based tree importance via the consistency counterexample

questions.explanation: The paper first defines the class, shows existing methods belong to it, states the desired properties, proves SHAP is the unique member with all three, and then uses a counterexample to show a non-SHAP heuristic lacking the theorem can fail.

lessons.label: Computing SHAP: KernelSHAP, TreeSHAP, and DeepSHAP

sections.heading: Why Exact Shapley Values Are Intractable
sections.body: Computing an exact Shapley value for one feature requires evaluating the model on every possible coalition subset that does or doesn't include it — 2^(M-1) subsets per feature, or 2^M total coalitions across all M features — because the definition averages marginal contributions over every possible subset the other players could already occupy. For a modest 20-feature tabular model, that is over a million model evaluations; for a model with hundreds of engineered features, exact brute-force computation is simply impossible in any practical time budget. Every practical SHAP algorithm exists to approximate or short-circuit this exponential sum without abandoning the axioms that make Shapley values unique in the first place.

sections.heading: KernelSHAP: Model-Agnostic but Slow
sections.body: KernelSHAP, introduced alongside the original SHAP paper, treats Shapley value computation as a weighted linear regression: it samples a manageable number of coalitions z', evaluates the model with each coalition's features present and the rest replaced by background or reference values, and weights each sampled coalition by the Shapley kernel — a weighting function assigning very high weight to coalitions of size 1 or M-1 and lower weight to intermediate sizes, chosen so the weighted-least-squares solution of this regression equals the true Shapley values in the limit. It works on ANY model, since it only queries f, but that generality costs speed and exactness: with too few sampled coalitions its output remains an approximation, not the exact value.

sections.heading: TreeSHAP: Exact Values in Polynomial Time
sections.body: For tree-based models (random forests, gradient-boosted trees), Lundberg, Erion, and Lee's 2018 paper and its 2020 Nature Machine Intelligence extension introduced TreeSHAP, which exploits a tree's recursive structure to compute EXACT Shapley values — no sampling, no approximation — in O(TLD²) time, where T is the number of trees, L the maximum number of leaves, and D the maximum depth, instead of the O(2^M) exact brute force would require. It does this by tracking, for every possible subset size, how prediction paths through the tree would be reweighted if a feature were 'removed,' using a recursive algorithm over the tree's own branches rather than re-running the model on synthetic coalitions at all.

sections.heading: DeepSHAP and the Real Reason SHAP Won
sections.body: For neural networks, DeepSHAP combines DeepLIFT's efficient backward-pass attribution rule with Shapley values, treating each layer as a mini-game and composing per-layer attributions through the network via a chain rule; for linear models, LinearSHAP computes exact Shapley values directly from the model's coefficients and feature covariances, in closed form. The practical upshot across all three algorithms is the same: SHAP became the default explanation method for gradient-boosted trees not because its axioms are more compelling than LIME's, but because TreeSHAP made an exact, axiom-satisfying explanation computable fast enough to run on every row of a production dataset — tractability, not theory, is what put SHAP into everyday tooling like XGBoost and LightGBM.

lessons.workedExample: A risk team has an XGBoost model with 150 features trained on loan applications. Computing exact Shapley values by brute force would require evaluating roughly 2^150 coalitions per row — impossible. Because the model is tree-based, they run TreeSHAP instead, which walks each tree's decision paths once per row and returns exact Shapley values for all 150 features in a fraction of a second, at a cost scaling with the number of trees, leaves, and depth rather than the number of features combinatorially. For a small logistic-regression calibration layer, they use LinearSHAP instead, computing exact contributions in closed form from the fitted coefficients and feature covariance matrix. Only for a small black-box vendor model with no accessible structure do they fall back to slower, approximate KernelSHAP.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'why does everyone use SHAP for XGBoost specifically' is testing whether the presenter knows this is an engineering fact, not a theoretical one: TreeSHAP computes the exact, axiom-satisfying Shapley value in polynomial time only because tree structure permits it, while the same exactness for an arbitrary black box would still cost O(2^M). The strong answer names the complexity classes — O(2^M) exact brute force versus O(TLD²) TreeSHAP — and states that KernelSHAP remains the fallback for non-tree, non-neural models precisely because it is the only one of the three requiring no structural assumption about f.

questions.prompt: Why is exact Shapley value computation intractable for most real models?

options.text: The model must be retrained separately for each feature
It requires evaluating the model on up to 2^M coalitions across M features
It needs labeled ground-truth data that is usually unavailable
It only works for linear models

explanations.a: No retraining is required; the black box is only queried, not refit.
explanations.b: Correct — the exact Shapley definition sums over every coalition subset, giving exponential 2^M cost.
explanations.c: Shapley computation only needs the model's own outputs, not ground-truth labels.
explanations.d: Exact Shapley values are defined for any model class; the intractability is combinatorial, not model-type-specific.

questions.prompt: What makes KernelSHAP "model-agnostic"?

options.text: It only works on tree ensembles
It computes attributions via a weighted linear regression over sampled coalitions, querying only f's outputs
It requires access to the model's internal gradients
It is exact by construction, regardless of sample count

explanations.a: TreeSHAP, not KernelSHAP, is the tree-specific algorithm.
explanations.b: Correct — KernelSHAP treats the model as a black box, needing only its output on sampled coalitions.
explanations.c: Gradients are used by DeepSHAP, not KernelSHAP, which needs no internal access at all.
explanations.d: KernelSHAP is an approximation unless the number of sampled coalitions reaches the full exponential set.

questions.prompt: TreeSHAP's computational complexity is best described as:

options.text: O(2^M), the same as brute-force exact computation
O(TLD²), where T is trees, L is leaves, and D is depth
O(M!), scaling with the factorial of the feature count
O(M log M)

explanations.a: TreeSHAP's entire purpose is to avoid this exponential cost.
explanations.b: Correct — TreeSHAP computes exact values in polynomial time using tree structure, per Lundberg, Erion & Lee 2018.
explanations.c: Factorial cost would correspond to enumerating orderings directly; TreeSHAP avoids this via recursive path reweighting.
explanations.d: This complexity is not the one derived for TreeSHAP in the cited papers.

questions.prompt: Match each SHAP computation algorithm to its target and approach.

right.text: Any model, via weighted regression over sampled coalitions (slow, approximate)
Tree ensembles, exact values via recursive path-reweighting (fast, polynomial time)
Neural nets via DeepLIFT-style backward passes, or linear models in closed form

questions.explanation: Each algorithm trades generality for speed differently: KernelSHAP assumes nothing about the model, TreeSHAP exploits tree structure for exact polynomial-time values, and DeepSHAP/LinearSHAP exploit neural-net or linear-model structure respectively.

questions.prompt: Put this line of reasoning about SHAP computation in order.

items.text: Exact Shapley requires evaluating up to 2^M coalitions
KernelSHAP approximates via sampled, kernel-weighted regression
TreeSHAP exploits tree structure for exact values in polynomial time
DeepSHAP/LinearSHAP extend efficient computation to neural nets and linear models
TreeSHAP's speed, not superior theory, drives SHAP's adoption for gradient boosting

questions.explanation: The intractability of exact computation motivates KernelSHAP's model-agnostic approximation, TreeSHAP's exact polynomial-time algorithm for trees, and DeepSHAP/LinearSHAP's extensions — with TreeSHAP's tractability, specifically, explaining SHAP's dominance in gradient-boosted tree tooling.

lessons.label: What SHAP Actually Says — and What It Does Not

sections.heading: The Additivity Identity, Verified by Hand
sections.body: Every SHAP explanation satisfies φ0 + Σ_{i=1}^{M} φi = f(x) exactly, for the specific row x being explained — this is the local accuracy property from the Lundberg-Lee theorem, and it is directly checkable: sum the base value φ0 (the model's average output over the background dataset) and every feature's signed φi, and the total must equal the model's actual output for that row, to within numerical tolerance. If a practitioner's tally does not match f(x), the computation — background set, coalition sampling, or approximation method — is wrong, not the theorem; this hand-check is a cheap, reliable way to catch a buggy SHAP implementation before trusting anything it reports. This identity is also what SHAP explains: the DEVIATION of this one prediction from the average prediction, decomposed additively across features, in the model's own output units (log-odds, probability, dollars) — never a claim about the world outside the model.

sections.heading: Two Boundaries: Aggregation Is Not the Same Question, and Alternatives Exist
sections.body: Averaging |φi| across many rows produces a global importance ranking, but this is an AGGREGATION of local attributions, answering 'how much did this feature move predictions on average,' a different question from permutation importance's 'how much does shuffling this feature hurt overall accuracy.' The two can legitimately disagree on which feature ranks first without either being wrong, because a feature can swing individual predictions substantially in offsetting directions (large mean |SHAP|) while contributing little to aggregate accuracy (small permutation importance), or vice versa. SHAP is also not the only local-explanation format: Anchors, from Ribeiro, Singh, and Guestrin's 2018 AAAI paper, return high-precision IF-THEN rules with an explicit coverage statistic — what fraction of the input space the rule applies to — instead of signed weights, trading nuance for a guarantee-like statement a non-technical reader can act on directly.

sections.heading: Counterfactuals: A Different Question Entirely
sections.body: Sandra Wachter, Brent Mittelstadt, and Chris Russell's 2017 paper, 'Counterfactual Explanations without Opening the Black Box,' proposed a third format that answers neither 'what did each feature contribute' (SHAP) nor 'what rule covers this case' (Anchors) but 'what is the smallest change to x that would have flipped the outcome' — for example, the minimal income increase that would flip a loan denial to an approval. They argued this format is especially suited to contexts like GDPR's 'right to explanation,' because it tells the affected person an actionable path rather than a decomposition of a score they cannot act on directly. None of SHAP, Anchors, or counterfactuals is strictly superior; they answer different questions, and choosing among them means first asking which question the audience actually needs answered.

lessons.workedExample: For a single applicant, a model outputs f(x) = 0.72 probability of default. The background average is φ0 = 0.35. SHAP reports φ_income = −0.10, φ_late_payments = +0.30, φ_credit_age = +0.05, and six more features summing to φ_other = +0.12. Checking the identity by hand: 0.35 + (−0.10) + 0.30 + 0.05 + 0.12 = 0.72, matching f(x) exactly — additivity holds. Separately, the team runs permutation importance on the full validation set and finds credit_age ranks ABOVE late_payments in overall accuracy impact, even though late_payments had the larger mean |SHAP| across individual rows. Both rankings are computed correctly; they answer different questions — local attribution to this row's deviation versus global degradation of accuracy when shuffled — so the team reports both rather than picking one as 'the' importance ranking.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge may hand you a printout and ask you to prove the SHAP values are internally consistent — the correct response is to add up φ0 and every φi on the spot and show it equals f(x); failing to do this on demand suggests the presenter never checked their own numbers. A second, more searching question is why a mean-|SHAP| ranking and a permutation-importance ranking disagree on the same model — the strong answer distinguishes local aggregation from global perturbation and states plainly that SHAP explains this model's output for this row, not any real-world causal claim, avoiding the common overreach of treating φi as evidence about the world.

questions.prompt: The identity φ0 + Σφi = f(x) means:

options.text: SHAP values are only approximate and never sum exactly
The base value plus every feature's signed contribution exactly reconstructs the model's actual output for that row
φ0 must always equal zero
The identity only holds for tree-based models

explanations.a: Local accuracy is an exact identity, not an approximation, whenever the SHAP values are computed correctly.
explanations.b: Correct — this is the local accuracy property: the components sum exactly to f(x) for the explained row.
explanations.c: φ0 is the background/expected output and is generally nonzero.
explanations.d: The identity holds for SHAP values regardless of model class; how they are computed (KernelSHAP, TreeSHAP, DeepSHAP) differs, but the identity itself does not.

questions.prompt: Global mean|SHAP| importance and permutation importance can rank features differently because:

options.text: One of the two methods must have been computed incorrectly
They answer different questions — average local attribution to individual predictions versus impact on overall accuracy when shuffled — so disagreement doesn't mean either is wrong
Permutation importance is always more accurate than SHAP
Mean|SHAP| ignores feature interactions entirely

explanations.a: Both can be computed correctly and still legitimately disagree, since they measure different things.
explanations.b: Correct — one aggregates local attributions, the other measures accuracy degradation from shuffling; a feature can score high on one and low on the other without contradiction.
explanations.c: Neither method is universally 'more accurate'; they are answers to different questions.
explanations.d: SHAP values are computed from a model that can include interactions; mean|SHAP| does not ignore them, it just aggregates differently than permutation importance.

questions.prompt: What does an Anchors explanation (Ribeiro, Singh & Guestrin, 2018 AAAI) provide that a SHAP explanation does not?

options.text: Exact Shapley values
A high-precision IF-THEN rule with a coverage statistic describing what fraction of inputs it applies to
A base value φ0
Gradient information about the model

explanations.a: Anchors do not compute Shapley values at all; that is SHAP's construction, not theirs.
explanations.b: Correct — Anchors return a rule with an explicit coverage statistic instead of signed feature weights.
explanations.c: A base value is specific to the additive attribution form used by SHAP, not the Anchors format.
explanations.d: Anchors are model-agnostic and rule-based; they do not require or report gradients.

questions.prompt: Order these explanation formats by how much of the input space a single explanation instance is guaranteed to describe, from least to most.

items.text: A single SHAP explanation (one row's deviation from the base value)
A single Anchors rule (a region with an explicit coverage statistic)
Global mean|SHAP| importance (aggregated across every row in the dataset)

questions.explanation: A single SHAP explanation describes only one row's deviation; a single Anchors rule explicitly covers a stated region of the input space; and global mean|SHAP| aggregates local attributions across the entire dataset.

questions.prompt: Match each explanation format to the question it answers.

right.text: How much did each feature contribute to this row's deviation from the base value
What if-then rule, with what coverage, predicts this outcome with high precision
What is the smallest input change that would flip the outcome

questions.explanation: SHAP decomposes a prediction additively, Anchors states a covering rule with a precision/coverage guarantee, and counterfactuals identify the minimal actionable change that would have changed the outcome.

units.label: Reading Effects: PDP, ICE, ALE, and Interaction

lessons.label: Partial Dependence Plots (Friedman 2001)

sections.heading: Friedman's estimator, from gradient boosting's own paper
sections.body: Partial dependence plots (PDPs) were introduced almost as an aside inside Jerome Friedman's 2001 paper 'Greedy Function Approximation: A Gradient Boosting Machine' (Annals of Statistics, volume 29, issue 5, pages 1189-1232) — the same paper that gave the field gradient boosting itself. Friedman needed a way to visualize what the boosted ensembles he'd just built were actually doing, since a sum of hundreds of shallow trees has no coefficients to read off. His fix: split the feature vector into the subset S you care about (often one feature) and the complement C (everything else). Freeze S at a value s, then average the model's prediction f(s, x_C) over the empirical distribution of C observed in the training data. Sweep s across a grid and plot the resulting averages — that curve is the partial dependence function. Friedman originally worked this out for regression trees and boosted tree ensembles specifically because their piecewise-constant structure makes the averaging step cheap to compute exactly by tracking which leaves each training row falls into, rather than requiring a fresh full pass over the data for every grid point — an efficiency detail that mattered when he was demonstrating gradient boosting on datasets with thousands of rows and dozens of trees. The technique generalizes to any model that can be queried for a prediction, tree-based or not, which is why it became a standard model-agnostic tool rather than staying a gradient-boosting-specific trick.

sections.heading: Reading the axes correctly
sections.body: The y-axis is the model's raw output — a predicted price, a log-odds, a class probability for the average case — averaged across every other feature's real combinations. It is NOT a prediction for any specific row; no single house in the training set has 'all other features held at their marginal distribution.' That means the PLOT'S LEVEL is not the object of interest and is often arbitrary depending on centering convention; what carries the signal is the curve's SHAPE — is it monotonic, does it plateau, does it have a kink at some threshold. A flat PDP says the model's average response barely moves with that feature; a steep one says it does, on average. Because the y-axis conflates the model's actual behavior with an average, every PDP should ship next to a rug plot or histogram of the feature's real distribution — a PDP that curves dramatically over a region with almost no data (e.g., house sizes above 6,000 sq ft in a mostly-suburban dataset) is extrapolation dressed up as a trend, not evidence. A second axis convention worth naming: some implementations offer a centering option that shifts the curve so it reads zero at a reference point (scikit-learn's PartialDependenceDisplay added a `centered=True` flag in version 1.1, but does NOT center by default), purely so multiple curves can be compared on the same panel — when centering IS applied, that choice is cosmetic and must not be read as evidence the feature's baseline effect is zero.

lessons.workedExample: A student trains a gradient-boosted regressor on housing data and wants to show how predicted price responds to square footage. They pick 30 grid points spanning the observed range of square footage, and at each grid point s they replace every row's square-footage value with s (leaving bedrooms, location, and age at their real, original values for that row), run all rows through the model, and average the predictions. Plotting these 30 averages against s produces the PDP.
