They overlay a rug plot beneath it and notice the curve flattens sharply past 4,500 sq ft — exactly where the rug shows almost no training houses, a signal to distrust that region rather than report it as 'price plateaus for large homes.'
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has seen a PDP before will ask what exactly is being averaged over, and a student who can say 'the empirical marginal distribution of every OTHER feature, per Friedman 2001' rather than 'the model's typical behavior' has clearly read the source rather than a blog summary. The sharper follow-up — 'why is the rug plot mandatory, not decorative' — tests whether the student understands that a PDP without a density check invites reporting extrapolated fiction as a discovered pattern, which is exactly the failure the next lesson names directly.

questions.prompt: In Friedman's 2001 partial dependence estimator, what is averaged over when computing the value at a grid point s for feature S?

options.text: The model's predictions across the empirical marginal distribution of all other features, C
The training labels for rows near s
The feature importances of all other features
Only the rows whose value of S is closest to s

explanations.a: Correct — PDP fixes S at s, keeps each row's real values for the complement C, and averages the model's output over those real C combinations.
explanations.b: PDP averages model PREDICTIONS, not the raw training labels; it says nothing about ground truth, only about the fitted function.
explanations.c: Feature importance is a separate concept measuring reliance on a feature, not part of the PDP averaging step.
explanations.d: That description is closer to a binned conditional plot (an M-plot), not a PDP — PDP forces S to s for every row, not just nearby ones.

questions.prompt: Why must a PDP be shown alongside a rug plot or histogram of the feature?

options.text: Because the PDP's y-axis units are otherwise unreadable
Because regions of the curve over sparse or empty data are extrapolated, not observed, behavior
Because the rug plot corrects the PDP's averaging formula
Because journals require it as a formatting convention

explanations.a: The y-axis is readable as a model output on the original scale; the issue is not units but where the model was actually queried with real support.
explanations.b: Correct — the PDP grid sweeps the full range of S regardless of data density, so shape claims over sparse regions are unsupported extrapolation.
explanations.c: The rug plot is diagnostic only; it does not alter the underlying partial dependence computation.
explanations.d: It is a substantive statistical safeguard, not a stylistic norm.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of computing one point on a partial dependence curve for feature S at grid value s.

items.text: Choose a grid value s for feature S
Replace every row's S value with s, keeping each row's other features (C) at their real values
Run the modified dataset through the trained model to get one prediction per row
Average those predictions to get the PDP value at s

questions.explanation: Friedman's estimator fixes S at a chosen grid value, substitutes it into every observed row while leaving the complement features untouched, scores the model on the resulting synthetic rows, and averages the outputs — repeating across the grid traces the full curve.

questions.prompt: Match each PDP element to what it actually represents.

left.text: The y-axis value at a grid point

right.text: The model's average predicted output over the empirical distribution of other features
The primary evidence of how the model responds to the feature
A check on which regions of the curve reflect real data support

questions.explanation: The y-axis is an average model output, not a real prediction; the curve's shape (not its absolute level) is the signal worth reporting; and the rug plot tells you which parts of that shape are trustworthy versus extrapolated.

lessons.label: How PDPs Lie: Aggregation and Extrapolation

sections.heading: Failure mode one: aggregation erases pure interactions
sections.body: A PDP is an average, and averages can cancel real signal. Construct a model where a feature X raises the prediction by +10 for half the population and lowers it by -10 for the other half, with the sign determined entirely by a second feature (a pure interaction, no main effect). Averaging across the population at every grid value of X produces a flat line at roughly zero — the PDP reports 'this feature has no effect,' when in fact the model depends on it heavily, just conditionally. This is not a rare edge case: any XOR-like structure between two features, or a threshold effect that reverses direction depending on group membership, produces this exact flat-line illusion — the kind of structure a shallow decision tree or a boosted ensemble with depth-2+ trees can represent easily, since a single split on the second feature is enough to flip the sign of the first feature's leaf-level contribution. The PDP is mathematically doing what it claims (averaging predictions), but 'no average effect' and 'no effect' are different claims, and the plot cannot distinguish them without help from ICE curves (next lesson).

sections.heading: Failure mode two: extrapolation off the data manifold
sections.body: The second failure is independent of the first and comes from HOW the PDP holds other features fixed. Because it substitutes each grid value of S into every row while leaving that row's other features (C) untouched, it manufactures combinations that may never occur together. Sweep 'number of bedrooms' from 1 to 6 while a particular row's square footage stays at 400 m², and the model gets asked to score a 6-bedroom 400-m² house — a combination absent from (or physically impossible in) the training distribution. When features are correlated, as square footage and bedroom count nearly always are, this happens at every grid point away from each row's own value, not occasionally. The model's response to that impossible input is unconstrained: trees and neural nets alike will emit SOME number, but it reflects the model's behavior in a region it never learned, not a real relationship. This is the identical off-manifold pathology that unrestricted permutation importance suffers from — both procedures break real feature correlations by construction, and both should be read with that caveat attached rather than trusted at face value. Practitioners mitigate this two ways: restricting the PDP's plotted range to the convex hull (or a joint-density threshold) of the actual data, which is the direct fix but requires computing that joint density in the first place; or switching estimators entirely to Accumulated Local Effects (ALE), covered two lessons ahead, which avoids manufacturing off-manifold rows by construction rather than by post-hoc trimming.

lessons.workedExample: A student models house price from square footage and bedroom count, which correlate strongly (bigger houses have more bedrooms). The PDP for bedroom count rises smoothly from 1 to 6, and the student is tempted to report 'each extra bedroom adds about $18,000.' But checking which rows contribute to the grid point at '6 bedrooms' shows the model was evaluated on synthetic combinations like a 500-m² six-bedroom house that never appears in the data. The visible rise is partly the model extrapolating past its training support, not a clean marginal bedroom effect — the student instead reports the PDP only over the range where a joint histogram of the two features shows real density, and flags the rest as unsupported.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probing interpretability plots often ask the trap question 'so this feature doesn't matter?' the moment they see a flat PDP — the strong answer distinguishes 'no marginal effect on average' from 'no effect,' and names the interaction test that would resolve it. A second, sharper probe asks whether the features behind the plotted curve are correlated in the real data; a student who can point to where the PDP queries impossible feature combinations, rather than insisting the curve is simply 'the model's behavior,' demonstrates they understand extrapolation as a structural property of the method, not an occasional glitch.

questions.prompt: A model has a pure interaction: feature X raises the prediction for half the rows and lowers it by the same amount for the other half, with no main effect. What does the PDP for X show?

options.text: A curve that rises for half the grid and falls for the other half
Roughly a flat line near zero, falsely suggesting X has no effect
An error, since PDP cannot be computed for interacting features
The same shape as the interaction term itself

explanations.a: The PDP averages across the WHOLE population at each grid value, not per subgroup, so the opposite-signed effects cancel rather than showing as two branches.
explanations.b: Correct — averaging +10 and -10 responses across the population yields close to zero at every grid point, hiding a real, strong conditional effect.
explanations.c: PDP is always computable; it just produces a misleading answer here, not a computational failure.
explanations.d: The PDP shows the AVERAGE, which cancels the interaction's opposite signs rather than reproducing its shape.

questions.prompt: Why does the PDP for bedroom count risk extrapolation when bedroom count and square footage are correlated?

options.text: Because PDP requires features to be independent to compute at all
Because sweeping bedroom count while holding each row's real square footage fixed creates combinations absent from the training distribution
Because correlated features always produce identical PDP curves
Because the model rejects correlated inputs and returns null

explanations.a: PDP is computable regardless of correlation; the issue is the trustworthiness of the result, not whether it runs.
explanations.b: Correct — the grid-substitution step manufactures off-manifold rows whenever the swept feature correlates with features left at their real values.
explanations.c: Correlation causes extrapolation risk; it does not force the two features' PDPs to match each other.
explanations.d: Models score whatever numeric input they receive; they do not detect or reject implausible combinations.

questions.prompt: Match each PDP failure mode to its underlying cause.

left.text: Aggregation failure (flat line hides real effect)

right.text: Averaging opposite-signed conditional effects across the population cancels them
Sweeping one feature while holding correlated features fixed queries off-manifold combinations

questions.explanation: Aggregation failure comes from averaging over rows with cancelling conditional effects (a pure interaction); extrapolation failure comes from the grid-substitution mechanism itself creating unrealistic feature combinations under correlation.

questions.prompt: What other well-known interpretability method shares PDP's extrapolation pathology, and why?

options.text: Confusion matrices, because they also use grids
Unrestricted permutation importance, because it also breaks real feature correlations by shuffling one feature independently of the rest
ROC curves, because they also average over a range
Nothing else shares this problem; it is unique to PDP

explanations.a: Confusion matrices summarize classification outcomes and do not involve feature substitution or extrapolation.
explanations.b: Correct — permutation importance shuffles a feature's values across rows independently of the others, creating the same kind of off-manifold combinations when features are correlated.
explanations.c: ROC curves summarize classifier performance across thresholds; they don't substitute feature values into rows.
explanations.d: The off-manifold pathology is a known shared weakness across any method that breaks feature correlations by holding some features fixed while varying others independently.

lessons.label: ICE Curves: Peeking Inside the PDP (Goldstein et al. 2015)

sections.heading: One curve per observation instead of one average
sections.body: Alex Goldstein, Adam Kapelner, Justin Bleich, and Emil Pitkin's 2015 paper 'Peeking Inside the Black Box: Visualizing Statistical Learning with Plots of Individual Conditional Expectation' (Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics, volume 24, issue 1, pages 44-65) proposed the direct fix to the PDP's aggregation blindness described in the last lesson: stop averaging before plotting. For each individual row i, sweep feature S across the same grid while holding that row's OTHER features at their own observed values, and plot the resulting curve for that one row. Do this for every row (or a sample of them) and overlay all the curves on one axis — this is an ICE plot. The PDP is recoverable exactly as the POINTWISE MEAN of all the ICE curves at each grid value, so ICE is a strict refinement, never a replacement: everything the PDP shows is still there, just unaveraged. Goldstein et al. released their method alongside the R package ICEbox; the motivation is easiest to see through a Simpson's-paradox-like lens: an aggregate trend can point one direction while every meaningful subgroup points another, and a black-box model with enough capacity can and does encode exactly that structure without any warning sign in the PDP alone.

sections.heading: Reading the fan, and two named variants
sections.body: The diagnostic power is in the SHAPE of the bundle. If all curves rise and fall together, roughly parallel, the PDP faithfully summarizes every row and there's no hidden interaction. If curves cross, fan out, or split into groups moving in different directions under a PDP that looks flat or mild, that fan is the visual signature of an interaction the PDP averaged away — exactly the pure-interaction case from the prior lesson would show as two clean bundles of lines with opposite slopes. Goldstein et al. also propose CENTERED ICE (c-ICE): shift every curve so it passes through zero at one reference grid point (often the leftmost), which strips out level differences between rows and isolates differences in SLOPE, making heterogeneity easier to see when curves start at very different heights. DERIVATIVE ICE (d-ICE) plots each curve's numerical derivative with respect to S instead of its level, which pinpoints exactly which grid region the interaction activates in — flat derivative curves that suddenly diverge mark where the model's behavior starts depending on another feature. In practice, plotting hundreds of raw ICE curves overlaid on one axis produces visual clutter (overplotting), so implementations typically sample a few dozen rows, or thin the color/opacity of each line, to keep the fan bundle legible while still exposing crossing patterns.

lessons.workedExample: Returning to the earlier pure-interaction construction — feature X raises the prediction for half the rows and lowers it for the other half depending on a second feature Z — the PDP for X is a flat line near zero. Plotting ICE instead shows two clean families of parallel lines: one bundle sloping upward (the Z=1 rows) and one sloping downward (the Z=0 rows), crossing near the middle of the grid. A student who only ran the PDP would conclude X is irrelevant; overlaying ICE curves immediately reveals two subpopulations with opposite, strong responses to X, prompting the correct next step of coloring the ICE bundle by Z to confirm the interaction and reporting the conditional effect instead of the misleading average.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has just watched a student explain a flat PDP as 'no effect' will often ask 'how would you check that,' and the ICE plot is the direct, citable answer — Goldstein et al. 2015 built it for exactly this diagnostic purpose. The stronger follow-up asks the student to distinguish centered ICE from raw ICE: naming that c-ICE removes level differences to expose slope heterogeneity (rather than just saying 'it's a cleaner version') shows the student understands what each transformation is designed to isolate, not just that the tool exists.

questions.prompt: How is the PDP curve related to a set of ICE curves for the same feature?

options.text: The PDP is unrelated; it is computed from an entirely different formula
The PDP is the pointwise mean of all the individual ICE curves at each grid value
The PDP is the single ICE curve closest to the median row
The PDP is the derivative of the ICE curves

explanations.a: PDP and ICE use the same underlying grid-substitution mechanism; PDP is just the aggregated version.
explanations.b: Correct — Goldstein et al. show PDP is recovered exactly by averaging all ICE curves' values at each grid point.
explanations.c: PDP averages across ALL rows, not just one representative curve.
explanations.d: The derivative relationship describes d-ICE, a separate variant, not the PDP itself.

questions.prompt: A PDP looks nearly flat, but the ICE plot shows curves splitting into two bundles sloping in opposite directions. What does this indicate?

options.text: A computational error in the ICE algorithm
An interaction effect that the PDP's averaging hid
That the feature truly has no effect on any row
That the model is overfit and should be discarded

explanations.a: Crossing or diverging ICE curves are a real, expected pattern under interaction, not a bug.
explanations.b: Correct — this fan/crossing pattern under a flat PDP is precisely the visual signature of a hidden interaction, as described in Goldstein et al. 2015.
explanations.c: The opposite is true: strong per-row effects exist, they just cancel on average.
explanations.d: This pattern reflects a real interaction structure in the fitted function; it says nothing directly about overfitting.

questions.prompt: Match each ICE variant to what it does.

right.text: Plots each row's actual predicted level across the grid, unmodified
Shifts every curve to start at zero at a reference point, isolating slope differences
Plots each curve's numerical derivative to locate where interactions activate

questions.explanation: Raw ICE shows unmodified per-row prediction curves; c-ICE anchors every curve at a common reference value to strip out level and expose slope heterogeneity; d-ICE plots derivatives to pinpoint the grid region where an interaction begins to matter.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of building an ICE plot for feature S from a fitted model.

items.text: Pick one observation (row) from the dataset
Sweep S across a grid, substituting each grid value while keeping that row's other features at its own observed values
Record the model's prediction at each grid value to form one curve for that row
Repeat for many (or all) rows and overlay every resulting curve on one plot

questions.explanation: ICE repeats the PDP's grid-substitution mechanism per individual row instead of averaging immediately, producing one curve per observation; overlaying all of them (or their mean, which recovers the PDP) reveals heterogeneity the average alone would hide.

lessons.label: ALE Plots: Fixing the Extrapolation (Apley & Zhu 2020)

sections.heading: Bin, difference, then accumulate
sections.body: Daniel Apley and Jingyu Zhu's 'Visualizing the Effects of Predictor Variables in Black Box Supervised Learning Models' (Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, volume 82, issue 4, pages 1059-1086, 2020, first circulated as arXiv:1612.08468 in 2016) targets the PDP's extrapolation problem directly rather than patching around it. Accumulated Local Effects (ALE) first bins the feature S into intervals. Within each bin, ALE takes only the points whose OBSERVED value of S actually falls in that bin — no substitution into rows where it doesn't belong — and computes the DIFFERENCE in the model's prediction between the bin's upper edge and lower edge, holding every other feature at that row's own real values. Averaging these local differences within the bin gives a local effect estimate, and summing (accumulating) these local effects across bins from left to right builds the final ALE curve. Because ALE only ever evaluates the model at the bin edges using rows genuinely near those values, it never manufactures the impossible feature combinations that PDP's full-range substitution does. Apley circulated the method as arXiv:1612.08468 in 2016, and it took until 2020 for the peer-reviewed version to appear in JRSS-B — a four-year gap during which ALE was already being implemented in the R package ALEPlot and in Python's alibi and PyALE libraries, evidence that practitioners found the extrapolation fix compelling well before the formal statistical review concluded.

sections.heading: Three methods, three different compromises
sections.body: Apley and Zhu frame ALE against two existing alternatives to make the tradeoff explicit. M-PLOTS (Marginal plots) simply condition on the feature's bin — average the prediction for rows whose S actually falls in that bin — but because the other correlated features move together with S inside that bin, an M-plot's effect estimate is CONFOUNDED with those other features' effects and cannot isolate S's own contribution. PDPs marginalize over the full population regardless of local density, avoiding confounding but extrapolating, as covered earlier. ALE takes a third path — differencing within a bin using only genuinely local data, then accumulating — which avoids both confounding (each bin's difference uses real, locally-observed rows) and extrapolation (it never substitutes S far from where a row's neighbors actually sit). The cost is real: ALE's estimate is sensitive to bin width and count (too few bins blur real structure, too many make each bin's difference noisy from too little data), and its y-axis is a CENTERED accumulated effect relative to the feature's mean, which reads less intuitively than a PDP's direct average-prediction scale.

lessons.workedExample: Modeling house price from square footage and bedroom count, a student bins square footage into twenty intervals. Within the bin covering 1,400-1,500 sq ft, they take only the rows whose square footage actually lands there, and for each such row compute the model's predicted price at 1,500 minus its predicted price at 1,400, with bedroom count and every other feature left at that row's real value. Averaging these differences across the bin's rows gives the local effect for that interval; summing all such local effects from the smallest bin up to the current one produces the ALE value at 1,500 sq ft. Because no row's bedroom count was ever paired with a square footage far from its real neighborhood, the resulting curve reflects square footage's own contribution without inventing a 400-m² one-bedroom house.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge already primed by PDP's extrapolation weakness will ask 'so why not always use ALE,' and the strong answer names the concrete cost — bin-width sensitivity and a centered, less intuitive y-axis — rather than presenting ALE as a strict improvement with no downside. The sharper test is asking the student to place all three methods (M-plot, PDP, ALE) on the confounding-versus-extrapolation tradeoff in one sentence each; being able to state that M-plots confound, PDPs extrapolate, and ALE differences-then-accumulates to dodge both shows genuine comparative understanding, not memorized praise for the newest method.

questions.prompt: What operation does ALE perform within each bin of the feature, before accumulating?

options.text: It averages the raw prediction level for rows in that bin
It computes the difference in prediction between the bin's upper and lower edge, using only rows whose observed feature value falls in that bin
It substitutes the bin's midpoint into every row in the dataset
It counts how many rows fall in the bin

explanations.a: Averaging raw levels within a bin, without differencing, describes an M-plot, which confounds correlated features rather than isolating the local effect.
explanations.b: Correct — ALE's core step is a local DIFFERENCE at the bin's edges, computed only from rows genuinely observed in that bin, which is what avoids both confounding and extrapolation.
explanations.c: Substituting one value into every row regardless of that row's real feature values is the PDP's mechanism, the one ALE is designed to avoid.
explanations.d: Counting rows describes a histogram, not the local-effect computation ALE performs.

questions.prompt: Match each method to its central weakness, per Apley & Zhu's comparison.

right.text: Confounds the target feature's effect with correlated features' effects because it conditions on the bin
Extrapolates to impossible feature combinations because it marginalizes over the full population
Sensitive to bin width/count, and its centered y-axis is harder to read intuitively

questions.explanation: M-plots condition on the bin so correlated features move together with S, confounding the estimate; PDPs marginalize over all rows regardless of local density, producing extrapolation under correlation; ALE avoids both by differencing locally then accumulating, at the cost of bin-width sensitivity and a less intuitive centered scale.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of computing an ALE value at a given point on the feature grid.

items.text: Bin the feature into intervals
Within a bin, select only the rows whose observed feature value falls in that bin
Compute each selected row's prediction difference between the bin's upper and lower edge, and average these differences within the bin
Accumulate (sum) the local effects across bins up to the point of interest

questions.explanation: ALE bins the feature, restricts each bin's computation to rows genuinely observed there, computes and averages local prediction differences at the bin edges, then sums those local effects across bins to build the accumulated curve.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't ALE suffer from PDP's extrapolation problem when features are correlated?

options.text: Because ALE ignores correlated features entirely
Because ALE only evaluates the model near a bin's edges using rows that actually have values near that bin, never substituting the feature far from a row's real neighborhood
Because ALE uses a different, more powerful model than PDP
Because ALE only works when no features are correlated

explanations.a: ALE still holds other features at each row's real values; it does not ignore them, it simply avoids substituting the target feature into implausible combinations.
explanations.b: Correct — restricting each bin's difference computation to rows locally observed there means ALE never queries the model far outside a row's real neighborhood.
explanations.c: ALE and PDP are both post-hoc visualization techniques applied to the same fitted model; the difference is the estimator, not the underlying model.
explanations.d: ALE is specifically designed to remain valid under correlated features, which is its main advantage over PDP.

lessons.label: Two-Way Effects and Detecting Interactions

sections.heading: From lines to heatmaps: reading a diagonal ridge
sections.body: Both PDP and ALE extend to a pair of features S = {X, Z} by producing a 2D grid instead of a 1D one, visualized as a heatmap or contour plot rather than a curve. If X and Z affected the prediction independently (no interaction), the heatmap would look like a simple additive overlay — its rows and columns would each look like the 1D PDP for that feature, roughly reproduced everywhere regardless of the other feature's value. A genuine interaction shows up as a DIAGONAL RIDGE or twist: the effect of X changes shape depending on where you are in Z's range — a heatmap where high predictions cluster along a diagonal band (rather than a simple horizontal or vertical gradient) is the visual tell that the model combines the two features nonadditively, echoing the same crossing-ICE-curves signature from two lessons back, now shown as a full 2D surface instead of a bundle of 1D lines. ALE extends to two dimensions the same way PDP does — the second-order ALE surface differences the model at cell corners of a 2D bin grid rather than at 1D bin edges, and is preferred over a 2D PDP for the identical reason the 1D case favored it: it avoids querying the model at joint feature combinations that never occur together in the training data.

sections.heading: Naming the interaction: the H-statistic and SHAP interaction values
sections.body: Reading a heatmap is qualitative; Friedman and Popescu's 2008 paper 'Predictive Learning via Rule Ensembles' (Annals of Applied Statistics, volume 2, issue 3, pages 916-954) gives a quantitative instrument, the H-STATISTIC. It compares the 2D partial dependence of the pair (X, Z) against the sum of their individual 1D partial dependences; the squared difference, normalized by the variance of the joint effect, gives H² — roughly, the SHARE of the pair's joint variance NOT explained by adding their separate main effects. H² near 0 means the pair is additive; H² approaching 1 means the model relies almost entirely on their combination. The catch: computing it exactly requires evaluating the model over the full grid of BOTH features for every row, an O(n²) cost in the number of grid points (and expensive again per pair, so checking all pairs among many features scales quadratically in feature count too), and with small n the variance estimates in the denominator get unstable, producing noisy or inflated H² values. Lundberg, Erion, and Lee's 2018 paper 'Consistent Individualized Feature Attribution for Tree Ensembles' (arXiv:1802.03888) offers a per-row alternative: SHAP INTERACTION VALUES decompose each prediction's total SHAP attribution into a main-effect term per feature plus a pairwise interaction term per feature pair, using the Shapley interaction index from cooperative game theory, giving an interaction estimate for each individual prediction rather than one global number.

lessons.workedExample: A student suspects their gradient-boosted model uses square footage and neighborhood jointly rather than additively. They compute a 2D PDP heatmap over both features and see predicted price rising along a diagonal band — high only when both are simultaneously large — rather than a clean grid pattern. To quantify this, they compute the H-statistic for the pair and get H² = 0.34, meaning about a third of the pair's joint variance in predicted price is not explained by adding the two features' separate PDPs. Cross-checking with SHAP interaction values on a sample of rows, they find the interaction term is largest exactly for rows in the priciest neighborhood with above-median square footage, confirming the heatmap's diagonal ridge is a real, localized interaction rather than an artifact of the grid.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees a 2D heatmap will often ask 'is that interaction real or just how heatmaps look,' and the strong answer moves straight to a number — the H-statistic or a SHAP interaction value — rather than describing the picture again. The sharper probe is cost: asking why a student didn't run the H-statistic on every pair among twenty features tests whether they understand its O(n²) evaluation cost and its instability at small sample sizes, versus just asserting the statistic exists without appreciating why practitioners reach for SHAP interaction values on large feature sets instead.

questions.prompt: What visual pattern in a 2D PDP or ALE heatmap indicates a genuine interaction between the two features?

options.text: A simple horizontal or vertical gradient that matches each feature's own 1D curve
A diagonal ridge or twist where the effect of one feature changes shape depending on the other feature's value
Uniform color across the entire heatmap
Any heatmap with more than two colors

explanations.a: A gradient that simply reproduces each feature's own 1D effect everywhere is the signature of ADDITIVITY (no interaction), not the presence of one.
explanations.b: Correct — a diagonal band or twist means the combined effect can't be decomposed into the two features' separate contributions, the visual hallmark of a real interaction.
explanations.c: A uniform heatmap suggests neither feature has much effect at all, not an interaction.
explanations.d: Color count is not diagnostic; the SHAPE of the color pattern (diagonal versus grid-aligned) is what carries the signal.

questions.prompt: What does Friedman and Popescu's H-statistic (H²) measure?

options.text: The correlation between the two raw feature values
The share of the pair's joint partial-dependence variance not explained by summing their individual 1D partial dependences
The number of trees in the ensemble that use both features
The prediction accuracy lost when one of the two features is removed

explanations.a: H² measures interaction in the fitted model's response, not raw correlation between the two input features.
explanations.b: Correct — H² compares the 2D joint partial dependence against the sum of the two 1D partial dependences, with the unexplained share normalized into H².
explanations.c: H² is defined from partial dependence functions, not from counting tree structure internals.
explanations.d: That description matches a feature-removal importance measure, not the H-statistic's variance-decomposition definition.

questions.prompt: What is a known practical limitation of the H-statistic?

options.text: It cannot be computed for tree-based models
It is O(n²) to compute and its estimates become unstable at small sample sizes
It only works for classification models, never regression
It requires labeled interaction ground truth to calibrate

explanations.a: The H-statistic works with any model that supports partial dependence, tree-based or otherwise.
explanations.b: Correct — the joint-grid evaluation needed for the 2D partial dependence scales quadratically, and small n makes the variance terms in H² noisy or inflated.
explanations.c: The H-statistic is defined generally on partial dependence functions and applies to both regression and classification outputs.
explanations.d: It is computed directly from the model's own partial dependence functions and needs no external ground truth.

questions.prompt: Match each interaction-detection tool to its scope and cost.

right.text: One global number per feature pair, O(n²) evaluation cost, unstable at small n
A per-row decomposition of each prediction's attribution into main effect and pairwise interaction terms

questions.explanation: The H-statistic gives one aggregate global measure of a pair's interaction strength at quadratic evaluation cost; SHAP interaction values instead decompose each individual prediction's Shapley attribution into main-effect and pairwise-interaction terms, giving a row-level answer.

lessons.label: Reading SHAP's Standard Plots Without Overreading Them

sections.heading: Three plots, three different jobs
sections.body: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations, Lundberg & Lee) produces one attribution value per feature per row, and three standard plots present that same underlying number differently. The BEESWARM (summary) plot puts one dot per row per feature: the x-position is that row's SHAP value (how much the feature pushed the prediction up or down), the color encodes the feature's own raw value (commonly red = high, blue = low), and features are stacked top-to-bottom ordered by mean absolute SHAP value across all rows — a global importance ranking built from local numbers. The WATERFALL (or force) plot is the single-prediction view: starting from the model's base value (its average output over the training set), it stacks each feature's SHAP contribution as a step, walking left to right until it lands exactly on f(x), the model's actual output for that one row — a full accounting of one decision, not a summary. The DEPENDENCE PLOT is SHAP's answer to the PDP: x is the feature's raw value, y is that feature's SHAP value per row, plotted as a scatter (often colored by a second, interacting feature). All three plots are drawn from the same underlying Shapley-value computation that Lundberg and Su-In Lee formalized in their 2017 NeurIPS paper 'A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions,' which is why a beeswarm plot, a waterfall plot, and a dependence plot for the same model never contradict each other — they are three views of one consistent set of numbers, additive by construction so that every row's SHAP values sum to f(x) minus the base value exactly.

sections.heading: The interaction clue and three misreads
sections.body: In a SHAP dependence plot, VERTICAL SPREAD at a fixed x-value is itself evidence, not noise: if two rows share the same feature value but get different SHAP values, some OTHER feature must be responsible for the difference, which is exactly what an interaction is. Coloring the dots by a suspected second feature often reveals that spread as a clean split. Three misreads recur. First, treating mean absolute SHAP value (beeswarm ordering) as an EFFECT SIZE in real units — it ranks how much a feature moves predictions across the dataset, but says nothing about the sign, shape, or units of that movement, which is what the dependence plot is for. Second, dismissing vertical spread in a dependence plot as noise or measurement error, when it is frequently a legitimate interaction signal worth investigating rather than smoothing over. Third, narrating a dependence plot causally ('higher X causes higher predictions') when SHAP values describe the FITTED MODEL's attribution, not a causal effect in the world — the model may have learned a spurious or confounded association that a dependence plot will faithfully report.

lessons.workedExample: A student builds a beeswarm plot for a churn model and sees 'tenure' ranked highest by mean absolute SHAP value, with blue dots (low tenure) clustered at strongly positive SHAP values and red dots (high tenure) clustered negative — a clean, interpretable pattern. They then build tenure's dependence plot and notice, at a fixed low-tenure value, some rows have strongly positive SHAP values and others near zero. Coloring by 'contract type' shows the spread splits cleanly: month-to-month contracts sit high, annual contracts sit low at the same tenure value. The student reports tenure's importance from the beeswarm, its shape from the dependence plot, and the spread as a genuine tenure-by-contract-type interaction rather than folding it into a single 'tenure matters' headline.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees a beeswarm plot will often ask what the ranking actually measures, and the strong answer distinguishes mean absolute SHAP (a magnitude-only importance ranking) from a real-units effect size, deferring the direction-and-shape question to the dependence plot. The sharper test is pointing at vertical spread in a dependence plot and asking what it means: a student who says 'noise' misses the interaction signal entirely, while one who says 'evidence some other feature is modulating this one, worth coloring by a candidate' shows they understand SHAP's plots as a coordinated system, not three unrelated pictures.

questions.prompt: Match each SHAP plot to what it is built to show.

right.text: Global feature importance ranking with per-row SHAP values and feature-value coloring
A single prediction's full accounting from base value to f(x)
SHAP value versus raw feature value across rows, revealing shape and interaction via spread

questions.explanation: The beeswarm plot ranks features globally by mean absolute SHAP value while showing every row's signed contribution and feature-value color; the waterfall plot walks one specific prediction step by step from the base value to the final output; the dependence plot is SHAP's per-feature effect curve, where vertical scatter at fixed x signals an interaction with another feature.

questions.prompt: What does mean absolute SHAP value (used to order the beeswarm plot) actually measure?

options.text: The real-units effect size and direction of a feature's impact on the prediction
The magnitude of a feature's contribution to predictions across the dataset, without indicating direction or shape
The feature's correlation with the true label
The p-value of the feature in a hypothesis test

explanations.a: Mean absolute SHAP collapses sign and shape into a single magnitude number; it is not itself a real-units effect size with direction.
explanations.b: Correct — it ranks how much, on average, a feature moves predictions in magnitude, which is a different question from direction or functional shape.
explanations.c: SHAP values are attributions from the fitted model's predictions, not a correlation-with-label statistic.
explanations.d: SHAP values are not a hypothesis-testing output and carry no p-value.

questions.prompt: In a SHAP dependence plot, what does vertical spread of points at a fixed x-value most likely indicate?

options.text: Random measurement noise that should be smoothed away
An interaction with some other feature that differs between those rows
A coding error in the SHAP computation
That the feature has no effect on the model

explanations.a: Treating the spread as noise is one of the standard misreads; it usually reflects real structure rather than randomness.
explanations.b: Correct — if two rows share the same feature value but different SHAP values, something else in the row must explain the difference, which is the definition of an interaction.
explanations.c: Vertical spread is an expected, informative property of SHAP dependence plots for models with interactions, not a bug.
explanations.d: Substantial spread combined with visible trend indicates the feature does matter, and does so in a way that depends on other features.

questions.prompt: A student sees a rising SHAP dependence plot for 'ad spend' and says 'this proves more ad spend causes higher predicted sales.' What is wrong with this statement?

options.text: Nothing; SHAP dependence plots directly establish causation
SHAP values describe the fitted model's attribution pattern, not a causal effect in the real world, so the model may have learned a spurious or confounded association
The plot must be mislabeled since SHAP values cannot be positive for a feature
Dependence plots only apply to classification models, not sales prediction

explanations.a: SHAP explains what the MODEL does, which is a different claim from what causes what in the real world.
explanations.b: Correct — a rising dependence plot shows the model's learned association, which can reflect confounding or spurious correlation in training data rather than a true causal mechanism.
explanations.c: SHAP values can be positive or negative depending on whether a feature pushes the prediction up or down; a rising positive trend is unremarkable and not evidence of mislabeling.
explanations.d: SHAP dependence plots apply equally to regression outputs like predicted sales and to classification probabilities.

lessons.label: Importance vs Effect vs Relevance — Three Different Questions

sections.heading: Three words judges use interchangeably that answer different questions
sections.body: IMPORTANCE asks how much the model's overall performance relies on a feature: permutation importance (shuffle the feature, measure the drop in accuracy or error), mean decrease in impurity (MDI, built into tree ensembles), and mean absolute SHAP value all answer this, and all three are aggregate, dataset-level numbers with no sign or shape attached. EFFECT asks a different question: for a one-unit change in the feature, which direction and by how much does the model's OUTPUT move, holding the interpretive frame fixed — this is exactly what PDP, ALE, and ICE curves from the last four lessons are built to show, and unlike importance, effect curves can be flat, monotonic, U-shaped, or discontinuous. RELEVANCE asks a third, row-specific question: for THIS ONE decision, which features actually drove the outcome and by how much, which is what SHAP values, LIME's local linear approximations, and Anchors' if-then rule explanations are built to answer, and which can differ sharply row to row even when the global importance ranking is fixed. LIME, introduced by Ribeiro, Singh, and Guestrin in their 2016 KDD paper 'Why Should I Trust You?', fits a simple interpretable model (typically sparse linear regression) to perturbed samples in the local neighborhood of one row; Anchors, from the same group's 2018 AAAI paper, instead returns a minimal if-then rule (an 'anchor') that, when satisfied, fixes the prediction with high probability regardless of the other features' values — a different, rule-based notion of local relevance rather than a per-feature numeric weight.

sections.heading: The case where they visibly diverge
sections.body: The clearest way to see these three come apart is a feature ranked FIRST on permutation importance whose PDP is nearly flat across its observed range. This is not a contradiction: it means the model relies heavily on the feature, but only THROUGH INTERACTIONS with other features, not through an independent marginal response — permutation importance breaks and re-scrambles every other feature's correlation structure along with it, so the accuracy drop it measures captures the feature's full role including its interactions, while the PDP (or ALE) only shows the feature's isolated main effect, which can be small or zero even when the total contribution is large. Checking ICE curves or the H-statistic for that feature typically confirms the story: importance is high, the average shape is flat, but individual rows or subgroups swing strongly with an opposite sign. For a science-fair board, each concept earns its own panel: report importance to justify WHICH features to feature at all, an effect plot (PDP/ALE, with ICE to check for hidden interaction) to describe HOW the model responds, and a row-level SHAP or LIME explanation to justify any single decision the judges ask you to walk through by name.

lessons.workedExample: A student's admissions-risk model ranks 'first-generation status' first by permutation importance, but its PDP is almost flat, hovering near the base rate across both categories. Confused, they plot ICE curves for the feature and find two clean bundles: for students with low standardized test scores, first-generation status swings the prediction sharply upward; for students with high test scores, it barely moves the prediction at all. The H-statistic for the pair (first-generation status, test score) comes out high, confirming a strong interaction. The student now reports importance ('the model relies heavily on this feature'), effect ('but its average marginal effect is small'), and relevance for a specific flagged student ('for this individual, SHAP attributes +0.18 to first-generation status specifically because their test score is low') as three separate, correctly-scoped claims instead of one muddled sentence.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges frequently ask 'so how important is this feature' as a single catch-all question, and the strongest answer refuses to collapse it: naming which of the three questions is actually being asked, and which plot answers it, signals real fluency. The sharpest probe is the divergence case itself — a judge who has seen a high-importance, flat-PDP feature before will ask the student to explain it, and the correct move is naming interaction (with ICE or the H-statistic as the check) rather than treating the mismatch as a bug in the pipeline or picking whichever number sounds more impressive.

questions.prompt: Match each question to the method(s) built to answer it.

left.text: Importance: how much does overall performance rely on this feature?
Effect: which direction and magnitude does the output move per unit change?
Relevance: what drove this one specific decision?

right.text: Permutation importance, MDI, mean absolute SHAP value
PDP, ALE, ICE curves
Row-level SHAP values, LIME, Anchors

questions.explanation: Importance is answered by aggregate, sign-free measures like permutation importance, MDI, and mean absolute SHAP; effect is answered by shape-revealing curves like PDP, ALE, and ICE; relevance is answered by row-specific explanations like SHAP values for one prediction, LIME, and Anchors' rule-based explanations.

questions.prompt: A feature ranks first by permutation importance but has a nearly flat PDP across its observed range. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The permutation importance calculation is broken and should be re-run
The feature matters mainly through interactions with other features, not through an independent marginal effect
The PDP is broken and should be re-run
This combination is impossible and indicates a labeling error

explanations.a: Permutation importance is functioning correctly here; it captures the feature's total contribution including interactions, which a flat PDP alone would not reveal.
explanations.b: Correct — permutation importance reflects the feature's full role (including interaction effects), while the PDP shows only its isolated marginal effect, which can be small even when the total reliance is large.
explanations.c: A flat PDP is a valid, expected outcome when a feature's effect is conditional on other features rather than a stable main effect.
explanations.d: This exact divergence is a known, well-understood pattern rather than a sign of an error; ICE curves or the H-statistic typically confirm the interaction explanation.

questions.prompt: Which check would best confirm that a high-importance, flat-PDP feature's role is driven by interaction rather than measurement error?

options.text: Re-computing the PDP with a finer grid
Examining ICE curves for that feature, or computing the H-statistic against candidate partner features
Re-running permutation importance with a different random seed
Checking the feature's correlation with the training label

explanations.a: A finer PDP grid still averages over the population and would not reveal the subgroup-level effects that a flat PDP is hiding.
explanations.b: Correct — ICE curves reveal whether the flat PDP hides diverging per-row responses, and the H-statistic quantifies the joint variance not explained by additive main effects with a specific partner feature.
explanations.c: Permutation importance is already an aggregate measure; changing its random seed does not diagnose why the PDP looks flat despite high importance.
explanations.d: Correlation with the label describes a marginal statistical relationship in the raw data, not why the fitted model's PDP and permutation importance disagree.

questions.prompt: For a science-fair board, which single artifact would you use to answer a judge's question about why the model flagged one specific student's application?

options.text: The global permutation importance ranking
A row-level SHAP or LIME explanation for that specific prediction
The PDP for the top-ranked feature
The model's overall accuracy score

explanations.a: Global importance ranks features across the whole dataset; it cannot explain one individual's specific outcome.
explanations.b: Correct — relevance questions about a single decision are exactly what row-level SHAP values, LIME, or Anchors are designed to answer.
explanations.c: A PDP describes an average marginal effect across the population, not what happened for one specific row.
explanations.d: Overall accuracy describes aggregate model performance and says nothing about any individual prediction's reasoning.

units.label: Landmark Work & Open Debates

lessons.label: Breiman's Two Cultures (2001) and the Rashomon Effect

sections.heading: Two cultures analyzing the same data
sections.body: In 2001, Leo Breiman published "Statistical Modeling: The Two Cultures" in Statistical Science (16(3):199-231), arguing statisticians split into two cultures that rarely spoke to each other. The data-modeling culture assumes the data were generated by a stochastic model — linear regression, logistic regression, Cox proportional hazards — then reads scientific meaning directly off the fitted parameters: a coefficient IS the effect of a variable. The algorithmic-modeling culture, Breiman's own home turf as sole inventor of random forests and co-inventor of CART (with Friedman, Olshen, and Stone), treats the true data-generating mechanism as unknown, optimizing predictive accuracy on held-out data with trees, ensembles, or neural nets regardless of whether the model resembles nature's process. Breiman's provocation was a number: he estimated 98% of academic statisticians worked inside the data-modeling culture, leaving roughly 2% doing algorithmic modeling, and argued that near-total dominance had cost the field access to genomics, text, and image problems where no simple stochastic model plausibly holds.

sections.heading: The Rashomon effect: many equally good, disagreeing models
sections.body: Breiman named a second problem after Akira Kurosawa's 1950 film Rashomon, in which four witnesses describe the same crime with mutually incompatible stories. In modeling terms: for a single dataset there is often a large set — a "Rashomon set" — of models drawn from very different function classes (a pruned tree, a logistic regression, a random forest) that all achieve essentially the same held-out accuracy, yet disagree sharply about which variables matter and by how much. Discussant Hoadley illustrated this in the published exchange over Breiman's paper: many different subsets of predictor variables — anywhere from 27 to 36 characteristics — all achieved essentially the same test-set accuracy, yet pointed to different variables as important. (A similar instability shows up today in random forest variable-importance scores that shift noticeably across reseeded runs or when correlated predictors are dropped, even though test accuracy barely moves — a later illustration of the same phenomenon, not Breiman's own.) If two equally accurate models can rank the same variable as the top predictor and as noise, then "the" variable-importance ranking a practitioner reports is really one arbitrary draw from a population of equally valid, disagreeing rankings — a finding that anticipates later multiplicity work by Cynthia Rudin and others two decades on.

sections.heading: The discussion: Cox, Efron, and Parzen push back
sections.body: Statistical Science publishes major papers with invited discussion, and Breiman's discussants pushed back hard. David Cox and Bradley Efron both defended data modeling as indispensable for scientific understanding, not just prediction: Efron opened his comment by writing that, at first glance, Breiman's paper "looks like an argument against parsimony and scientific insight, and in favor of black boxes with lots of knobs to twiddle," adding that at second glance it still looked that way, and he argued the actual "prediction culture" was already far bigger than Breiman's 2% estimate, at least around Stanford. Emanuel Parzen argued Breiman's split was too narrow, proposing statistics actually contains many cultures beyond his two — maximum-entropy modeling, robust statistics, Bayesian inference, and quantile-based methods. Breiman's rejoinder held firm: prediction accuracy on new data is the only check nature gives you for free, and interpretability is not evidence a model is correct.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose two teams model the same 2,000-patient dataset to predict hospital readmission. Team A fits a pruned decision tree and reports that prior-admission count is by far the strongest predictor. Team B fits a random forest on the identical data and reports that lab-result variability, not prior admissions, dominates — while prior admissions barely register. Both models score 84% held-out accuracy; neither is wrong about accuracy. This is Breiman's Rashomon set in miniature: a family of equally predictive models telling incompatible stories about which variable to act on. An administrator who took Team A's ranking at face value and built an intervention around prior-admission counts would be building on one arbitrary draw from that set, not an established causal driver — exactly the trap Breiman flagged before "variable importance" was a term data scientists used daily.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has read Breiman will ask which culture your project belongs to — did you fit a stochastic model and interpret its coefficients, or did you optimize a black box for accuracy and only afterward extract importance scores? Either answer is defensible, but only if you can name it. The sharper follow-up is whether you checked for a Rashomon set: did you re-fit with a different seed, algorithm, or feature subset and see whether your top predictor survives? A team that reports one importance ranking with no such check has, unknowingly, reported one witness's account of a Kurosawa-style crime scene and called it the truth.

questions.prompt: According to Breiman's 2001 paper, approximately what percentage of academic statisticians worked inside the data-modeling culture?

explanations.a: Breiman's estimate was far more lopsided than an even split.
explanations.b: This understates how dominant Breiman claimed the data-modeling culture was.
explanations.c: Correct — Breiman estimated 98% of academic statisticians worked in the data-modeling culture, leaving about 2% doing algorithmic modeling.
explanations.d: This is closer to Breiman's estimate of the algorithmic-modeling culture's share, not the data-modeling culture's.

questions.prompt: As Breiman used the term, what is the "Rashomon effect"?

options.text: The fact that more complex models always fit training data better
A large set of models from different function classes achieving near-identical accuracy but conflicting variable-importance rankings
A statistical test for whether a coefficient is significantly different from zero
The tendency of algorithmic models to overfit small datasets

explanations.a: This describes overfitting generally, not the specific multiplicity problem Breiman named after Kurosawa's film.
explanations.b: Correct — the Rashomon effect is the existence of a "Rashomon set" of equally accurate but disagreeing models, so there is no single, unambiguous variable-importance ranking.
explanations.c: This describes a significance test, unrelated to the multiplicity phenomenon Breiman described.
explanations.d: Overfitting is a distinct concept; the Rashomon effect concerns disagreement among equally well-generalizing models, not poor generalization.

questions.prompt: Put these parts of the published exchange in the order they occurred.

items.text: Breiman publishes 'Statistical Modeling: The Two Cultures' in Statistical Science
Invited discussants (including Cox, Efron, and Parzen) publish responses
Breiman publishes a rejoinder defending prediction accuracy as the only free check nature gives you

questions.explanation: Statistical Science's format runs the main paper first, then invited discussants respond in the same issue, and the original author closes with a rejoinder — which is exactly how the Two Cultures exchange unfolded.

questions.prompt: Match each discussant to the argument they made against Breiman.

right.text: Argued explicit stochastic models are needed for genuine scientific inference, not just prediction
Wrote that the paper looked like an argument for black boxes with lots of knobs to twiddle, and that the real prediction culture was already bigger than Breiman's 2% estimate
Argued statistics contains many cultures beyond Breiman's two, citing maximum-entropy, robust, Bayesian, and quantile methods

questions.explanation: Cox emphasized that explicit models support scientific inference beyond mere prediction, Efron argued the paper read as an argument for black-box methods and that the prediction culture was already bigger than Breiman's 2% figure, and Parzen proposed that many cultures — not just two — describe how statisticians actually work.

lessons.label: Rudin 2019: Stop Explaining Black Boxes

sections.heading: An explanation is a second model, not a window into the first
sections.body: In 2019, Cynthia Rudin published "Stop explaining black box machine learning models for high stakes decisions and use interpretable models instead" in Nature Machine Intelligence (1:206-215). Her core logical argument: a post-hoc explanation method (LIME, SHAP, saliency maps) is, by construction, a SECOND, simpler model fit to approximate the first, complex one's behavior. If that second model were perfectly faithful everywhere, it would simply BE the first model — there would be no complexity left to hide. Since the whole point of the black box was that no simple model matched its accuracy, the explanation must be unfaithful somewhere, and because the true black box is inscrutable, you cannot know where. Rudin argues this makes post-hoc explanation dangerous specifically in high-stakes settings — parole, lending, diagnosis — where a confidently wrong explanation of a confidently wrong decision is worse than no explanation at all.

sections.heading: The evidence: interpretable models keep matching black boxes
sections.body: Rudin backs the argument with cases where fully interpretable models matched black-box accuracy on real high-stakes data. Angelino et al. (2018) built CORELS, an algorithm producing certifiably optimal, human-readable rule lists, and showed a list using just two or three conditions matched the accuracy of COMPAS, the proprietary recidivism-risk black box exposed by ProPublica's 2016 investigation. In the 2018 FICO Explainable Machine Learning Challenge, Rudin's Duke team did not submit an explanation of a black box at all — they submitted a fully transparent, globally interpretable model (a generalized additive model with pairwise interactions) and won the Recognition Award for it. From these and similar structured-data cases, Rudin argues the accuracy-interpretability trade-off is largely a myth once features are meaningfully engineered — the trade-off is real mainly for raw, unstructured inputs like pixels.

sections.heading: The policy conclusion
sections.body: Rudin's practical recommendation follows directly: for high-stakes decisions about people, build models that are interpretable from the start — sparse linear models, rule lists, or scoring systems a human can audit line by line — rather than deploying a black box and bolting on a post-hoc explainer afterward. She singles out COMPAS-style proprietary risk scores, first exposed by ProPublica's 2016 recidivism investigation, as a case where an interpretable alternative existed and was not adopted, arguing the choice to keep the black box was often about ownership, patent protection, and liability rather than any genuine accuracy requirement. She also distinguishes vocabulary carefully: she reserves "interpretable" for models that are transparent by construction and treats "explainable" as the (in her view, suspect) label attached to post-hoc approximations of an opaque model — a terminology split that later shaped how the DARPA XAI program and journal reviewers described competing approaches.

lessons.workedExample: A judge sentencing tool flags a defendant as high-risk using a black-box ensemble; a LIME explanation for that one case highlights "prior arrests" and "age" as the top two contributing factors. Rudin's argument says this explanation is a locally fit approximation, not a readout of the ensemble's actual computation — so it could easily be omitting that the model also leaned on a proxy correlated with zip code. Contrast this with Angelino et al.'s CORELS rule list: "IF priors > 3 AND age < 25 THEN high-risk," which matches COMPAS's accuracy while being the actual decision rule, not a guess at one. The second scenario has no fidelity gap because there is nothing hidden behind the explanation — the rule list IS the model.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows Rudin's paper will press on whether your project's "explanation" is a genuinely faithful account of the model or a separately fit approximation — ask what guarantee you have that the explanation matches the black box everywhere, not just on the examples you checked. The stronger answer, per Rudin, is to show the accuracy-interpretability trade-off didn't actually cost you anything on your (likely structured, engineered-feature) dataset, the way CORELS matched COMPAS and Rudin's own team won FICO's Recognition Award without sacrificing accuracy.

questions.prompt: Why does Rudin argue post-hoc explanations of black-box models are inherently unreliable?

options.text: Because explanation algorithms like LIME and SHAP have not been implemented in production software
Because an explanation is a second, simpler model approximating the first — if it were perfectly faithful everywhere it would just be the original model, so it must be wrong somewhere unknowable
Because regulators have banned the use of explanation methods in high-stakes settings
Because black-box models are always less accurate than interpretable ones

explanations.a: This is not Rudin's argument; the methods are widely implemented, which is precisely what concerns her.
explanations.b: Correct — this is the logical core of Rudin's 2019 paper: a faithful-everywhere approximation would collapse into being the original model, so any genuine simplification must diverge from the black box somewhere you cannot identify.
explanations.c: No such blanket regulatory ban existed at the time of Rudin's paper; her argument is conceptual, not regulatory.
explanations.d: Rudin argues the opposite — that on structured data, accuracy often is NOT sacrificed by using interpretable models.

questions.prompt: What did Rudin's Duke team submit to the 2018 FICO Explainable Machine Learning Challenge?

options.text: A LIME explanation of a gradient-boosted black box
A fully transparent, globally interpretable model, rather than an explanation of a black box
A SHAP-based feature-importance report
A neural network with attention visualizations

explanations.a: This is exactly what Rudin's team declined to do, in contrast to competitors who submitted explanations.
explanations.b: Correct — the Duke team submitted a globally interpretable model (a generalized additive model with pairwise interactions) instead of an explanation, and won the Recognition Award for it.
explanations.c: SHAP explains a separate black box; the Duke team's entry needed no such post-hoc explainer since it was interpretable by construction.
explanations.d: Attention visualizations are a deep-learning explanation technique, not what the interpretable-model entry used.

questions.prompt: Match each piece of evidence Rudin cites to what it demonstrates.

left.text: Angelino et al. 2018 CORELS rule lists

right.text: A two-or-three-condition interpretable rule list matched its accuracy on recidivism prediction
Won a Recognition Award by submitting an interpretable model instead of a black-box explanation
A black-box risk score whose interpretable rule-list alternative matched its accuracy

questions.explanation: CORELS produced the matching rule list itself; the Duke FICO entry was the interpretable-model submission that won recognition; COMPAS was the proprietary black box that CORELS's rule list matched in accuracy.

questions.prompt: According to Rudin, where does the accuracy-interpretability trade-off remain most real?

options.text: On structured, tabular data with meaningfully engineered features
On raw, unstructured inputs like pixels, where simple models struggle to match deep networks
Nowhere — Rudin claims the trade-off never exists in any setting
Only in criminal justice applications specifically

explanations.a: Rudin argues the trade-off is largely a myth precisely on this kind of structured, feature-engineered data.
explanations.b: Correct — Rudin concedes the trade-off is more genuine on raw, unstructured data such as images, where interpretable models have more trouble matching deep network accuracy.
explanations.c: Rudin does not make an absolute claim of zero trade-off everywhere; she distinguishes structured from unstructured data.
explanations.d: Her claim about structured data generalizes beyond criminal justice to any domain with meaningful engineered features.

lessons.label: The Counter-Case: Validated Black Boxes May Be Enough

sections.heading: London 2019: medicine already accepts unexplained mechanisms
sections.body: Alex John London's 2019 Hastings Center Report piece, "Artificial Intelligence and Black-Box Medical Decisions: Accuracy versus Explainability," makes the strongest direct reply to Rudin. His claim: medicine routinely approves interventions whose mechanism of action is unknown or was unknown for decades. Aspirin was used for pain relief for over 70 years before its mechanism — prostaglandin synthesis inhibition via COX enzymes — was worked out by John Vane in 1971, work that later won him a Nobel Prize. Lithium remains a first-line bipolar treatment today with its precise mechanism still not fully settled, decades after its 1949 introduction by John Cade. If physicians accept a pill that works without a mechanistic story, London argues, demanding one from an equally validated algorithm is a double standard — and insisting on it anyway trades away accuracy that could save patients, for interpretability that offers doctors comfort rather than better outcomes. What medicine actually demands of aspirin and lithium, London stresses, is not a mechanism but evidence: controlled trials showing the intervention reliably works and is safe.

sections.heading: Ghassemi, Oakden-Rayner & Beam 2021: the opposite fix
sections.body: Ghassemi, Oakden-Rayner, and Beam's 2021 Lancet Digital Health paper, "The false hope of current approaches to explainable AI in health care," agrees with Rudin's diagnosis but not her prescription. They agree that today's post-hoc explanation methods — saliency maps, SHAP, attention weights — are not trustworthy enough to justify an individual clinical decision, echoing Rudin's fidelity concern. But instead of concluding "use simpler models," they conclude the field needs what medicine already demands of drugs: rigorous prospective validation through clinical trials, external test sets, and post-deployment monitoring, regardless of whether the underlying model is a simple score or a deep network. For them, the fix is process, not model class.

sections.heading: Where all three camps actually agree
sections.body: Read together, Rudin, London, and Ghassemi et al. converge on more than their headlines suggest. All three agree current post-hoc explanations are not reliable enough to justify trusting an individual high-stakes prediction — none defends LIME or SHAP as sufficient safeguards. All three agree unvalidated deployment is dangerous, and all three reject the popular idea that bolting an explanation onto a black box makes it safe to trust. The dispute is narrower than it looks: Rudin wants the model itself to be transparent by construction; London and Ghassemi et al. want the validation PROCESS to be rigorous, and will accept an opaque model as long as it survives that process, the same way clinicians accept opaque drugs that survive controlled trials rather than a mechanistic explanation.

lessons.workedExample: A hospital is choosing between a sparse logistic-regression sepsis-risk score (auditable line by line, slightly lower AUC) and a deep neural network (higher AUC, validated in three independent prospective trials across different hospital systems). A Rudin-style critic asks the network team to show their model's decisions are transparent; a London-style reply points out clinicians already prescribe metformin without fully knowing its mechanism, so demanding mechanistic transparency from the network but not the drug is inconsistent. A Ghassemi-style compromise: approve the network not because a SHAP plot explains it, but because it cleared prospective validation across sites — while remaining just as skeptical of any single-patient SHAP explanation the vendor supplies alongside it.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge familiar with this debate will ask which standard your project is actually being held to: are you defending a black box because it was rigorously validated (the London/Ghassemi standard), or because a post-hoc explanation made it feel understood (the standard all three papers reject)? The strongest answer names the real disagreement precisely — model transparency versus validation rigor — rather than treating "explainable AI" as a single settled solution the literature agrees on.

questions.prompt: What is the core of Alex John London's 2019 argument against demanding mechanistic transparency from medical AI?

options.text: Medicine has never approved any treatment without a known mechanism
Medicine already accepts treatments like aspirin and lithium whose mechanisms were unknown or remain unsettled, so demanding mechanistic clarity only from algorithms is a double standard
Explainability methods are technically impossible to build
Black-box models are always more accurate than interpretable ones in every domain

explanations.a: This is the opposite of London's point — his examples (aspirin, lithium) are precisely treatments accepted without full mechanistic understanding.
explanations.b: Correct — London points to aspirin (mechanism unknown for decades before Vane's 1971 work) and lithium (still not fully settled) as accepted treatments lacking mechanistic transparency, making it inconsistent to require it only of algorithms.
explanations.c: London's argument is about a double standard in what is demanded, not about technical feasibility of explanation methods.
explanations.d: London does not make this blanket accuracy claim; his argument concerns consistency of standards, not universal accuracy superiority.

questions.prompt: Ghassemi, Oakden-Rayner, and Beam (2021) agree with Rudin that current XAI methods are untrustworthy for individual decisions. What do they propose instead of Rudin's solution?

options.text: Banning machine learning from clinical settings entirely
Rigorous prospective validation of models — the same standard medicine applies to drugs — rather than requiring simpler, inherently interpretable models
Requiring every model to publish its full source code
Relying more heavily on saliency maps and attention weights

explanations.a: Their paper is critical of unvalidated XAI claims, not of clinical AI use altogether.
explanations.b: Correct — they conclude the fix is rigorous prospective validation and monitoring, treating an opaque model as acceptable if it survives that process, unlike Rudin who insists on interpretable-by-design models.
explanations.c: Source-code publication does not address the fidelity concerns they raise about explanation methods.
explanations.d: They explicitly argue these current explanation approaches are not trustworthy for individual decisions — the opposite of relying on them more.

questions.prompt: Match each author or author group to their proposed solution to the black-box problem.

right.text: Build interpretable-by-design models instead of explaining black boxes
Accept validated black boxes, since medicine already accepts unexplained mechanisms
Demand rigorous prospective validation and monitoring regardless of model class

questions.explanation: Rudin insists on interpretable models from the start; London argues validated black boxes are acceptable by medicine's own precedent; Ghassemi, Oakden-Rayner, and Beam propose rigorous validation as the actual fix, independent of whether the model is transparent.

questions.prompt: Where do Rudin, London, and Ghassemi et al. actually agree, despite their differing prescriptions?

options.text: They all agree current post-hoc explanation methods like SHAP and saliency maps are not reliable enough to justify trusting a single high-stakes prediction
They all agree black-box models should never be used in medicine under any circumstances
They all agree explainability methods fully solve the trust problem in healthcare AI
They all agree unvalidated deployment of any model, interpretable or not, is acceptable if it is fast

explanations.a: Correct — all three sources converge on skepticism toward current post-hoc explanation methods as sufficient justification for trusting an individual prediction; they differ only on the remedy.
explanations.b: London explicitly argues validated black boxes can be acceptable, so this is not a shared position.
explanations.c: This contradicts Ghassemi et al.'s central claim that current XAI approaches offer 'false hope,' not a solved problem.
explanations.d: All three sources treat unvalidated deployment as dangerous, not acceptable regardless of speed.

lessons.label: Fooling LIME and SHAP (Slack et al. 2020)

sections.heading: The scaffolding attack
sections.body: Dylan Slack, Sophie Hilgard, Emily Jia, Sameer Singh, and Himabindu Lakkaraju's 2020 AIES paper, "Fooling LIME and SHAP: Adversarial Attacks on Post hoc Explanation Methods," exploits a structural weakness in how these explainers work. Both LIME and KernelSHAP generate their explanations by perturbing an input — masking or randomizing feature values — and querying the model on those synthetic, off-distribution perturbed points, then fitting a simple, weighted local model (a sparse linear model, in both cases) to the responses. Slack et al.'s "scaffolding" attack trains an out-of-distribution (OOD) detector, itself just a classifier trained to distinguish the explainer's perturbed samples from realistic data, that recognizes when a query looks like one of these synthetic perturbations rather than a real input. The adversary then builds a two-model system: perturbed, explainer-generated queries get routed to an innocuous, unbiased decision rule (often as simple as always predicting the base rate), while real inputs are quietly routed to the actual biased classifier making the deployed decisions. The explainer only ever samples the innocuous branch, so its fitted local approximation describes a model that is not the one actually in production.

sections.heading: The demonstration: race-driven decisions, race-free explanations
sections.body: Slack et al. built a classifier that used race directly to predict COMPAS-style recidivism risk — a blatantly discriminatory rule — then wrapped it in the scaffolding. When LIME or SHAP explained the model's real-world predictions, race never appeared as an important feature; the explanations pointed to innocuous variables instead, even though the deployed model's actual decisions were driven by race. The attack worked because the explainers only ever "saw" the innocuous branch's behavior on the perturbed samples they generated — the explanation was faithful to a model that was never actually making the real decisions.

sections.heading: Fairwashing spreads beyond one attack
sections.body: The vulnerability generalizes well beyond one attack on two tools. Aïvodji et al.'s 2019 ICML paper "Fairwashing: the risk of rationalization" showed an adversary can search, among many candidate interpretable surrogate models, for one that looks fair and is highly faithful to a biased black box's outputs on average, while still rationalizing unfair individual decisions — a distinct but related manipulation that needs no OOD detector at all.
