Dimanov, Bhatt, Jamnik, and Weller (2020) went further still, training models that simultaneously conceal an unfair feature's influence from several explanation methods at once — including saliency and gradient-based approaches, not just LIME and SHAP — showing the underlying problem is not a fixable quirk of any one explainer but a general property of post-hoc explanation as a strategy.

lessons.workedExample: A lending company wants its LIME explanations to look regulator-friendly. It builds an OOD detector that flags any input with unusual missing-value patterns or feature combinations unlikely to occur naturally — exactly what LIME's random perturbations produce. Perturbed queries get routed to a race-blind, income-and-credit-history-only decision function; real applications get routed to the true model, which weights zip code (a known race proxy) heavily. A regulator runs LIME on ten denied applications and sees "credit history" and "income" as the top features every time, with zip code never appearing — because LIME never queried the real model on a realistic, race-correlated input. The audit passes; the discrimination continues undetected.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows this paper will ask not just "did you generate a SHAP or LIME explanation?" but "could this explanation have been gamed by an adversary who knows LIME and SHAP query off-distribution?" The strongest defense is showing you tested the explanation against realistic, in-distribution perturbations or an adversarial audit, rather than trusting a single explanation report — because Slack et al. demonstrated that a blatantly biased model can produce a clean-looking explanation with no code changes to the explainer itself, only to the model being explained.

questions.prompt: What structural weakness does Slack et al.'s scaffolding attack exploit in LIME and KernelSHAP?

options.text: Both methods require access to the model's source code, which the attack denies them
Both methods generate explanations by querying the model on perturbed, off-distribution synthetic inputs, which an adversary can detect and route separately from real inputs
Both methods only work on linear models, so any nonlinear model automatically fools them
Both methods require labeled training data that the attack poisons

explanations.a: LIME and SHAP are typically model-agnostic and query-based, not requiring source-code access; this is not the exploited weakness.
explanations.b: Correct — the attack trains an out-of-distribution detector to recognize the explainer's synthetic perturbed queries and route them to a harmless surrogate, while real inputs reach the biased model.
explanations.c: LIME and SHAP are designed to be model-agnostic and work with nonlinear models; this is not the vulnerability described.
explanations.d: The attack manipulates the model being explained and query routing, not the explainer's training data.

questions.prompt: In Slack et al.'s demonstration, what happened when a race-driven COMPAS-style classifier was wrapped in the scaffolding attack?

options.text: LIME and SHAP correctly flagged race as the top predictor every time
The explanations pointed to innocuous features and never mentioned race, even though race actually drove the real decisions
The model's accuracy dropped to random chance
LIME and SHAP refused to produce any explanation at all

explanations.a: This is the opposite of the paper's finding — the whole point was that the explanations concealed race's role.
explanations.b: Correct — because the explainers only sampled the innocuous branch's behavior on perturbed queries, the explanations never surfaced race as important, despite race driving the real model's decisions.
explanations.c: The scaffolding attack does not require sacrificing the real model's accuracy on genuine inputs.
explanations.d: The explainers produced clean-looking, plausible explanations — that was precisely the danger, not a refusal to explain.

questions.prompt: Match each paper to the manipulation of post-hoc explanations it demonstrates.

right.text: Routes perturbed explainer queries to an innocuous surrogate while real inputs reach the biased model
Searches for an interpretable surrogate that looks fair and matches the black box's average outputs while rationalizing unfair individual decisions
Trains a model that conceals an unfair feature's influence from several different explanation methods simultaneously

questions.explanation: Slack et al.'s scaffolding attack routes queries by distribution; Aïvodji et al.'s fairwashing finds a fair-looking surrogate that still rationalizes unfairness; Dimanov et al. train a model that fools multiple explainers at once.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of Slack et al.'s scaffolding attack as it processes an incoming query.

items.text: An out-of-distribution detector examines the incoming query
The query is routed: perturbed/synthetic queries go to an innocuous surrogate, real inputs go to the biased model
A response is returned to whichever caller sent the query (explainer or real user)
The explainer fits a local model to the responses it received and reports feature importances

questions.explanation: The attack first classifies each incoming query as in-distribution or perturbed, then routes it accordingly, returns the appropriate response, and only then does the explainer build its (misleading) local approximation from the responses it happened to receive.

lessons.label: Do Explanations Track the Model? Sanity Checks and Impossibility Results

sections.heading: Two randomization tests, one embarrassing result
sections.body: Adebayo, Gilmer, Muelly, Goodfellow, Hardt, and Kim's 2018 NeurIPS paper, "Sanity Checks for Saliency Maps," proposed two blunt tests a saliency method should obviously pass. The model-parameter randomization test progressively re-initializes a trained network's weights, layer by layer, with random values and checks whether the saliency map changes; if a method still highlights the same pixels on a network whose weights are pure noise, it cannot be explaining what that network learned. The data randomization test retrains the same architecture on data with shuffled, meaningless labels and checks the same thing. The result: Gradients and Grad-CAM changed substantially under both tests, as a faithful method should, but Guided Backprop and Guided Grad-CAM — two of the most visually polished and widely used saliency methods at the time — produced maps nearly indistinguishable from the original, fully trained network's maps, even when most of the network's weights were randomized. They were functioning as edge detectors reacting to input structure, essentially independent of what the model had learned.

sections.heading: ROAR: saliency methods that don't beat random ranking
sections.body: Hooker, Erhan, Kindermans, and Kim's 2019 NeurIPS paper introduced ROAR (RemOve And Retrain), addressing a subtler flaw than Adebayo et al.'s randomization tests: even a saliency map that IS sensitive to the trained model's weights might still be ranking pixels in an order unrelated to what the model actually relies on for prediction. ROAR's fix is to stop merely inspecting the map and instead intervene: remove the top-ranked pixels it identifies, replace them with an uninformative fill value, retrain the model from scratch on the modified images, and measure how much accuracy drops. A genuinely important feature, removed, should hurt accuracy substantially — a model retrained without it has genuinely lost information. Several popular saliency methods, evaluated this way across standard image benchmarks, performed no better than a method that removed a purely random ranking of pixels, meaning the importance they visually assigned did not correspond to features the retrained model actually needed to reach its original accuracy.

sections.heading: Bilodeau et al. 2024: an impossibility theorem
sections.body: Bilodeau, Jaques, Koh, and Kim's 2024 PNAS paper, "Impossibility theorems for feature attribution," proved a stronger, non-empirical claim: for reasonably rich model classes (including ordinary neural networks), any attribution method that is both complete (attributions sum to the model's output) and linear — a property shared by Integrated Gradients and SHAP — can provably perform no better than random guessing on certain questions about model behavior, such as identifying spurious features or predicting recourse. This turns decades of empirical failures into a mathematical limit on what these popular attribution methods can ever guarantee.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher uses Guided Grad-CAM to argue their pneumonia-detection CNN "looks at" the lung opacities radiologists care about, producing a compelling heatmap overlay. Applying Adebayo et al.'s model-randomization test — re-initializing the network's convolutional layers to random weights — the heatmap barely changes: it still outlines the lung boundary, because Guided Grad-CAM is partly acting as an edge detector on the X-ray's anatomy, not a readout of the trained model's disease-detection logic. Running ROAR confirms the concern: removing the heatmap's top pixels and retraining barely hurts accuracy, meaning those pixels weren't load-bearing for the model's actual predictions. The heatmap looked clinically plausible and was largely unrelated to what the network had learned.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows this literature will not be satisfied by a saliency map that merely "looks right" to a human eye — outlining the tumor, the face, the object — because Adebayo et al. showed exactly that plausibility can survive complete randomization of the model. The strong response is to show you ran a sanity check: does the explanation change when the model's weights are randomized, or when top-ranked pixels are removed and the model is retrained (ROAR)? Citing Bilodeau et al.'s impossibility result also shows you understand this isn't a bug to patch — some questions are provably beyond what complete, linear attribution methods can answer.

questions.prompt: In Adebayo et al.'s model-parameter randomization test, what result would indicate a saliency method is NOT actually explaining the trained model?

options.text: The saliency map changes substantially when the network's weights are randomized
The saliency map remains nearly unchanged even when most of the network's weights are randomized
The saliency map becomes completely blank when weights are randomized
The saliency map only changes for the final layer's weights

explanations.a: This is the expected, healthy behavior of a faithful method like plain Gradients or Grad-CAM — it indicates sensitivity to the model's actual learned weights.
explanations.b: Correct — this is exactly what Adebayo et al. found for Guided Backprop and Guided Grad-CAM: maps stayed nearly identical to the trained model's maps even under substantial weight randomization, showing they weren't tracking what the network learned.
explanations.c: A blank map isn't what was observed; the failing methods still produced visually plausible, structured maps — that was the problem.
explanations.d: The test randomizes layers progressively (often from the top/output layer down), and the failure mode was insensitivity across most of this progression, not just the final layer.

questions.prompt: What does the ROAR (RemOve And Retrain) methodology from Hooker et al. 2019 actually measure?

options.text: Whether a human rater finds the saliency map visually convincing
Whether removing the pixels a saliency method ranks as most important, then retraining, actually hurts accuracy more than removing a random ranking would
The computational speed of different saliency algorithms
Whether the saliency map is smooth or noisy in appearance

explanations.a: ROAR is a quantitative, retraining-based test, not a subjective human-rating study.
explanations.b: Correct — ROAR removes the top-ranked features, retrains from scratch, and checks the accuracy drop against a random-ranking baseline; several popular methods performed no better than random by this measure.
explanations.c: Speed is not what ROAR evaluates; it evaluates whether ranked importance corresponds to features the retrained model actually needs.
explanations.d: Visual smoothness is unrelated to the accuracy-drop-on-retraining criterion ROAR uses.

questions.prompt: What did Bilodeau, Jaques, Koh, and Kim (2024, PNAS) prove about attribution methods that are both complete and linear, such as Integrated Gradients and SHAP?

options.text: They always achieve perfect accuracy on identifying spurious features
For sufficiently rich model classes, they can provably perform no better than random guessing on certain model-behavior questions
They are guaranteed to match human intuition about feature importance
They are the only attribution methods that pass Adebayo et al.'s sanity checks

explanations.a: This is the opposite of the paper's finding, which is a fundamental limitation, not a guarantee of success.
explanations.b: Correct — Bilodeau et al. proved a mathematical impossibility result: completeness plus linearity provably caps performance at no better than random guessing for certain questions, for rich enough model classes.
explanations.c: The paper makes no claim about matching human intuition; it is a formal result about what the methods can guarantee about model behavior.
explanations.d: The paper does not evaluate or claim these methods pass the empirical sanity checks from Adebayo et al.; it proves a separate, formal limitation.

questions.prompt: Order these findings from the earliest published to the most recent.

items.text: Adebayo et al.: Sanity Checks for Saliency Maps (NeurIPS)
Hooker et al.: ROAR shows several saliency methods no better than random ranking (NeurIPS)
Bilodeau et al.: Impossibility theorems for feature attribution (PNAS)

questions.explanation: Adebayo et al.'s sanity checks appeared in 2018, Hooker et al.'s ROAR benchmark followed in 2019, and Bilodeau et al.'s formal impossibility theorems were published in 2024 — each building a stronger case against trusting popular attribution methods.

lessons.label: The Shapley Wars: Which Shapley Value, and Is It Even the Right Question?

sections.heading: Not one Shapley value, but many
sections.body: SHAP's appeal rests on a clean pitch: Shapley values are the UNIQUE way to fairly split a prediction among features, guaranteed by four game-theoretic axioms from Lloyd Shapley's 1953 cooperative-game-theory work. Sundararajan and Najmi's 2020 ICML paper, "The Many Shapley Values for Model Explanation," punctures that uniqueness claim: the axioms only pin down the answer once you fix what happens when a feature is "removed," and there are several defensible, mutually incompatible choices. Baseline Shapley replaces a removed feature with a fixed reference value (like zero or a dataset mean); conditional-expectation Shapley instead averages the model's output over the feature's conditional distribution given the remaining features. These give genuinely different numeric answers to "how important is this feature" for the same model and the same input, and no axiom tells you which removal convention is the right one.

sections.heading: Interventional versus conditional: a causal fault line
sections.body: The removal-convention split has hardened into a methodological camp war. Janzing, Minorics, and Blöbaum's 2020 AISTATS paper, "Feature relevance quantification in explainable AI: A causal problem," argues that asking how important a feature is only makes sense as a causal, interventional question — you should break the feature's real-world statistical dependence on other features and see what happens, the way an experimenter intervenes on one variable. Chen, Janizek, Lundberg, and Lee's 2020 paper "True to the Model or True to the Data?" frames the same split differently: interventional (marginal) Shapley values are true to the model — they describe exactly what the trained function does, ignoring real feature correlations — while conditional (observational) Shapley values are true to the data, respecting real-world dependencies but attributing importance to features the model may never actually use, because a correlated proxy stood in for it.

sections.heading: Is Shapley even the right question?
sections.body: Kumar, Venkatasubramanian, Scheidegger, and Friedler's 2020 ICML paper, "Problems with Shapley-value-based explanations as feature importance measures," goes further still, arguing Shapley-based feature importance answers a well-defined game-theoretic question — how should a fixed total payoff be fairly divided among cooperating players — that no practitioner trying to debug or audit a model actually asked, since a feature is not a player voluntarily joining a coalition and a prediction is not a payoff to be split. Krishna et al.'s 2022 "disagreement problem" study surveyed working data scientists directly and found different explainers — including different Shapley variants, LIME, and gradient-based methods — routinely rank the same feature's importance differently on the same model and dataset, and that practitioners resolve the conflict largely by gut feel or by whichever method happened to be already installed, with no principled tie-breaking rule in common use across the field.

lessons.workedExample: A data scientist explains a loan-denial model with SHAP using its default background-data setting, which computes something close to a conditional-expectation value, and gets "debt-to-income ratio" as the top feature. A colleague reruns the same model with Baseline Shapley, replacing missing features with zeros, and gets "years of credit history" as the top feature instead — same model, same applicant, two disagreeing top-line answers, because the two runs disagree on what "removing" a feature means. Per Janzing et al., only the interventional version really asks "if we could causally change this applicant's credit history, holding everything else fixed, how would the prediction move"; the conditional version instead partly reflects that credit history correlates with income in the training data.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has followed the Shapley literature will not accept "we used SHAP" as a complete methodological description, because SHAP ships with several removal conventions that can disagree. The sharper question is which variant you used and why — interventional/marginal if you want an answer true to the model's actual computation, conditional/observational if you want an answer that respects real feature dependencies — and whether you checked if a different reasonable choice, or a different explainer altogether, would have named a different top feature, per Krishna et al.'s documented disagreement problem.

questions.prompt: According to Sundararajan and Najmi (2020), why isn't there a single, unique "the" Shapley value for a given model and input?

options.text: Because Shapley's original 1953 axioms are mathematically inconsistent and admit no solution

Because the axioms only fix the answer once you choose a convention for what happens when a feature is 'removed,' and multiple defensible conventions (like Baseline Shapley and conditional-expectation Shapley) give different numeric answers
Because Shapley values can only be computed for linear models
Because SHAP software has a bug that produces random output

explanations.a: Shapley's axioms are consistent and do pin down a unique value once the removal convention (the value function) is fixed; the issue is that convention itself is not fixed by the axioms.
explanations.b: Correct — Sundararajan and Najmi show the axioms alone don't specify how to model a 'removed' feature, and different reasonable choices (Baseline Shapley, conditional-expectation Shapley) yield different, mutually incompatible attributions.
explanations.c: Shapley-value methods are explicitly designed to be model-agnostic, applying to nonlinear models as well.
explanations.d: This is a conceptual multiplicity in the method's definition, not a software defect.

questions.prompt: In Chen, Janizek, Lundberg, and Lee's framing ("True to the Model or True to the Data?"), what does an interventional (marginal) Shapley value prioritize?

options.text: Faithfulness to real-world statistical dependencies between features, even if that means attributing importance to features the model doesn't use
Faithfulness to exactly what the trained function computes, ignoring real feature correlations
Matching a human's subjective intuition about which feature should matter most
Maximizing the model's held-out prediction accuracy

explanations.a: This describes the conditional (observational) approach, the paper's other pole, not the interventional one.
explanations.b: Correct — the interventional/marginal approach is 'true to the model': it describes what the function does when a feature changes, deliberately ignoring real-world correlations between features.
explanations.c: The interventional/conditional distinction is a technical modeling choice about the value function, not a measure of human intuition.
explanations.d: Shapley-value computation does not alter or optimize the underlying model's accuracy; it attributes importance for a fixed, already-trained model.

questions.prompt: What is the central objection Kumar, Venkatasubramanian, Scheidegger, and Friedler (2020) raise against Shapley-based feature importance?

options.text: That Shapley values are too computationally expensive to ever be practical
That Shapley values answer a well-defined game-theoretic fair-division question that no practitioner trying to diagnose model behavior actually asked
That Shapley values are only valid for cooperative games with fewer than three players
That Shapley values always agree with LIME's rankings

explanations.a: Computational cost is a separate, well-known concern about Shapley values, but it is not the central objection in this paper.
explanations.b: Correct — their argument is conceptual: Shapley values were designed to fairly split a cooperative payoff among players, and repurposing that answer as 'feature importance' answers a question practitioners were not actually posing.
explanations.c: Shapley's framework applies to games with any number of players; this is not a limitation the paper raises.
explanations.d: The paper (and the broader disagreement-problem literature) documents that Shapley-based rankings often disagree with LIME, not agree with it.

questions.prompt: Match each paper to its position in the Shapley debate.

right.text: Catalogues mutually incompatible Shapley variants (e.g., Baseline vs. conditional-expectation Shapley)
Argues feature relevance is fundamentally a causal, interventional question
Documents that different explainers rank the same feature's importance differently, and practitioners resolve it by gut feel

questions.explanation: Sundararajan and Najmi catalogue the many incompatible Shapley definitions; Janzing, Minorics, and Blöbaum argue for a causal/interventional framing of feature relevance; Krishna et al. empirically document the disagreement problem among practitioners using different explainers.

units.label: Advanced: Reliance, Causation, and Faithfulness

lessons.label: Importance to Whom? Model Reliance vs Model Class Reliance

sections.heading: One fit is an arbitrary draw, not a fact about the world
sections.body: Aaron Fisher, Cynthia Rudin, and Francesca Dominici's 2019 JMLR paper 'All Models are Wrong, but Many are Useful' starts from an uncomfortable observation: permutation importance, run on one fitted model, answers 'how much does THIS fit rely on X' rather than 'how important is X.' Refit the same data with a different random seed, a different hyperparameter grid, or a different algorithm entirely, and a variable's importance can swing wildly even though every fit achieves nearly identical accuracy. Fisher, Rudin, and Dominici call the score for a single model 'model reliance' (MR) — a formal permutation-based analog of the importance scores practitioners compute every day. MR is well-defined and useful, but it is a statement about one arbitrary member of a much larger set of equally defensible models.

sections.heading: Model class reliance and the Rashomon set
sections.body: The paper's real contribution is 'model class reliance' (MCR): instead of one number, compute the RANGE of MR across every model in a class whose accuracy is within some chosen tolerance epsilon of the best achievable empirical risk — the 'Rashomon set,' named by Leo Breiman for the film where witnesses give irreconcilable but equally plausible accounts of one event. MCR reports a [minimum, maximum] reliance interval over that whole set, not a point estimate from one fit, and the paper derives closed-form bounds for linear and related model classes so the interval can be computed without literally enumerating every model. Applied to a public dataset of Broward County, Florida criminal records (the ProPublica COMPAS data), Fisher, Rudin, and Dominici study reliance on both sex and race and show race's interval spans an enormous range — some near-optimal models barely use it, others lean on it heavily — while accuracy across the whole Rashomon set barely moves. A single model's importance score would have reported only one arbitrary point inside that band, hiding the real ambiguity about whether race is doing predictive work at all.

sections.heading: The consequence for reporting importance
sections.body: The takeaway is procedural: a bare importance number invites the question 'important according to which of the many equally-good models?' An MCR-style interval — or at minimum, importance recomputed across several retrained models with different seeds and architectures — is the honest version of the claim. If a variable's interval is narrow and high across the whole Rashomon set, the finding is robust to which near-optimal model happened to get fit; if it spans near zero up to a large value, the single-model number that a project reports was never a stable property of the problem, only an artifact of that one training run's random seed, feature-subsampling draw, or hyperparameter choice.

lessons.workedExample: A team fits a random forest to predict recidivism and reports that prior-arrest count is the top feature by permutation importance, with race a distant fifth at 0.02. Following Fisher, Rudin, and Dominici's approach, they instead retrain 200 models within 1% of the best observed accuracy (varying seed, depth, and feature subsampling) and compute each variable's reliance in every one. Prior-arrest count stays high across all 200 fits (MCR interval roughly [0.18, 0.24]), but race's interval turns out to be [0.01, 0.31] — some equally accurate models lean on it heavily. The single-model figure of 0.02 was one arbitrary draw from that band, not a fact about how much the data 'needs' race.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has seen one too many science-fair posters with a single importance bar chart will ask: 'if you retrained this with a different seed, would that bar move?' A student who can answer with an MCR-style range — or who at least ran the permutation importance across multiple retrained models and reports the spread — demonstrates they understand that importance is a property of a MODEL, not of the phenomenon, and that Rashomon-set thinking is the field's answer to that gap.

questions.prompt: What does Fisher, Rudin & Dominici's 'model class reliance' (MCR) report that a single model's permutation importance cannot?

options.text: A single, more precisely estimated importance value
The range of reliance across every model in the Rashomon set of near-optimal models
A p-value testing whether importance is exactly zero
The importance of the variable in the true data-generating process

explanations.a: MCR is deliberately an interval, not a sharper point estimate — the paper's argument is that a point estimate hides real ambiguity.
explanations.b: Correct — MCR is the [min, max] range of model reliance across all models achieving near-best accuracy, capturing how much importance varies among equally good fits.
explanations.c: MCR is a descriptive range over a model class, not a hypothesis test.
explanations.d: MCR still only describes what fitted models rely on, not any ground truth about the world — that gap is the subject of the next lesson.

questions.prompt: In the paper's application to the Broward County recidivism dataset, what did the race variable's MCR interval look like relative to accuracy across the Rashomon set?

options.text: Race's reliance interval was narrow and near zero across all near-optimal models
Race's reliance interval spanned a wide range while accuracy across the set stayed nearly flat
Race could not be included in any near-optimal model
Only one model in the Rashomon set used race at all

explanations.a: The interval was wide, not narrow — that breadth is the paper's central empirical point.
explanations.b: Correct — race's reliance ranged from very low to substantial across models that were all within a small tolerance of the best accuracy, showing reliance is underdetermined by predictive performance alone.
explanations.c: Many near-optimal models did use race; the point is variability in HOW MUCH, not exclusion.
explanations.d: Multiple models across the Rashomon set assigned race meaningfully high reliance, not just one.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its definition from Fisher, Rudin & Dominici (2019).

right.text: Permutation-based reliance score computed for one fitted model
The range of MR across every model achieving near-best accuracy
The set of all models whose accuracy is within a chosen tolerance of the best achievable

questions.explanation: MR is the single-model analog of permutation importance; the Rashomon set is the pool of near-equally-accurate models (named after the film depicting irreconcilable eyewitness accounts); MCR is the min-max range of MR computed across that entire pool.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of computing a model class reliance (MCR) interval for one variable.

items.text: Fit the best-performing model and record its accuracy
Set an accuracy tolerance and collect all models within it (the Rashomon set)
Compute permutation-based model reliance for the variable in every model in the set
Report the minimum and maximum reliance across the set as the MCR interval

questions.explanation: MCR requires first establishing the best achievable accuracy, then defining the Rashomon set relative to a tolerance around it, then computing single-model reliance for every member, and finally reporting the resulting range rather than any single value.

lessons.label: Why the Model's Importance Is Not the World's Effect

sections.heading: The proxy problem: the model uses whatever was cheapest
sections.body: An importance score or a partial dependence plot (PDP) can only report what the fitted function actually used — and a model has no way to distinguish a true cause from a correlate that happened to be cheaply available and predictive. ZIP code is the classic case: a lending or recidivism model that scores ZIP code as highly important is very likely using it as a proxy for race, given decades of documented residential segregation in the United States, not discovering that geography itself causes default or reoffending. In clinical models, Caruana-style pneumonia and readmission risk scores often find 'received supplemental oxygen' important for mortality not because oxygen delivery is dangerous, but because it proxies for overall treatment intensity and how sick the clinical team judged the patient at admission. In criminal-justice risk tools, prior-arrest count proxies for how heavily a neighborhood is policed rather than an individual's true propensity to offend — two people who committed the identical act have very different odds of an arrest record depending on how many patrols cover their block. A model trained on any of these datasets has no mechanism to prefer the true cause over the cheaper, more available correlate; it optimizes prediction, and correlates are frequently easier to exploit than causes. In every case, attribution answers only 'what did the fitted function use to predict,' never 'what does the world actually use to generate the outcome.'

sections.heading: The formal boundary: Zhao & Hastie's back-door result
sections.body: Qingyuan Zhao and Trevor Hastie's 2021 paper in the Journal of Business & Economic Statistics, 'Causal Interpretations of Black-Box Models' (a preprint circulating since 2016), makes the gap precise rather than just cautionary. They show that Jerome Friedman's partial dependence plot has EXACTLY the same formula as Judea Pearl's back-door adjustment from causal inference: averaging predictions over the observed distribution of the other covariates, holding the feature of interest fixed, is algebraically identical to a back-door-adjusted causal effect estimate. That equivalence means a PDP recovers a genuine causal effect — not just an association — under two conditions: the back-door criterion (the variables held fixed while averaging must block every back-door path from the feature to the outcome, i.e., no unmeasured confounding) and positivity (every combination of the confounders and the feature of interest must have a nonzero chance of occurring in the data, so the model is never silently extrapolating into regions it never observed). Neither condition is verifiable from the fitted model itself, no matter how accurate that model is — both come from a causal diagram (DAG) that the analyst must supply from domain knowledge, before the model is ever touched, and Zhao and Hastie are explicit that good predictive accuracy is necessary but nowhere near sufficient for the causal reading to hold.

lessons.workedExample: A team builds a PDP showing that a hospital readmission model's predicted risk drops sharply as 'number of specialist visits' increases, and they want to claim more specialist visits CAUSE lower readmission. Applying Zhao and Hastie's criterion, they draw a DAG: severity of underlying illness affects both how many specialists a patient sees and whether they get readmitted. Severity is a back-door path the model does not measure, so the back-door criterion fails, and the PDP's downward slope is confounded — sicker patients see more specialists AND get readmitted more, muting or reversing the effect. Only if the team could condition on full severity (e.g., from a randomized referral trial) would the same PDP formula support a causal reading.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge will often ask a project claiming 'X is important' whether they mean X causes the outcome or X merely correlates with it in this dataset. The strong answer names the proxy explicitly (ZIP code standing in for race, oxygen for treatment intensity, arrests for policing intensity) and states which causal assumption — back-door blocking, positivity — the project can and cannot verify, rather than conflating a model artifact with a discovery about the world.

questions.prompt: According to Zhao & Hastie (2021), a partial dependence plot has the same formula as which causal-inference tool?

options.text: Pearl's back-door adjustment
A randomized controlled trial's intention-to-treat estimate
Instrumental variable regression
Propensity score matching with caliper trimming

explanations.a: Correct — Zhao and Hastie show the PDP formula is algebraically identical to Pearl's back-door adjustment formula, which is why a PDP can recover a causal effect under the same assumptions that adjustment requires.
explanations.b: An RCT's ITT estimate doesn't require a back-door adjustment at all, since randomization removes confounding directly; that's not the connection Zhao and Hastie draw.
explanations.c: Instrumental variables solve confounding through a different mechanism (an exogenous instrument) and are not the formula Zhao and Hastie equate to the PDP.
explanations.d: Propensity score matching is a different causal-inference technique with its own estimator; the paper's specific equivalence is to back-door adjustment.

questions.prompt: A recidivism model scores ZIP code as highly important. What is the most likely explanation given the proxy problem?

options.text: Geography itself causes criminal behavior
ZIP code is a cheap, available correlate of race due to residential segregation
The model has discovered a novel causal mechanism worth publishing
Importance scores are meaningless for any spatial variable

explanations.a: This overinterprets an association as a causal claim about geography itself, exactly the error the proxy problem warns against.
explanations.b: Correct — ZIP code frequently proxies for race and socioeconomic history because of segregation, and a model has no way to tell 'proxy' from 'cause' — it only sees what predicts well.
explanations.c: High importance for a proxy variable is an artifact of correlated data, not a novel causal discovery.
explanations.d: Spatial variables can be genuinely important predictively; the issue is specifically about causal interpretation, not that importance scores are meaningless.

questions.prompt: Match each proxy variable to what it is most likely standing in for.

right.text: Race, via residential segregation
Overall treatment intensity / perceived severity
Local policing intensity, not individual behavior

questions.explanation: Each of these commonly-important features is importable as a proxy: ZIP code for race given segregation patterns, supplemental oxygen for how aggressively a patient was treated, and prior arrests for how heavily a neighborhood is policed rather than for the individual's true underlying behavior.

questions.prompt: Where do the back-door criterion and positivity assumptions needed for a causal PDP reading come from?

options.text: They are automatically verified by the model's cross-validated accuracy
They come from a causal diagram (DAG) the analyst supplies using domain knowledge, not from the fitting procedure
They are guaranteed whenever the model is a black box like a neural network
They follow automatically from having a large enough sample size

explanations.a: Predictive accuracy says nothing about whether confounders are measured or overlap holds; it cannot verify either assumption.
explanations.b: Correct — both conditions are causal assumptions about the data-generating process that the analyst must justify via a DAG built from domain knowledge; no amount of model fitting can supply or verify them.
explanations.c: Model complexity or opacity has no bearing on whether the causal assumptions hold — a black box and a linear model face the identical requirement.
explanations.d: Sample size affects estimation precision, not whether confounding is absent or every covariate combination is observed.

lessons.label: The Asthma Paradox (Caruana et al. 2015)

sections.heading: A rule that was true of the data and lethal as a policy
sections.body: Rich Caruana, Yin Lou, Johannes Gehrke, Paul Koch, Marc Sturm, and Noemie Elhadad's 2015 KDD paper 'Intelligible Models for HealthCare: Predicting Pneumonia Risk and Hospital 30-day Readmission' built models on real hospital records to predict which pneumonia patients were at high risk of dying, so hospitals could prioritize scarce ICU beds and staff attention. Their model learned that a documented history of asthma was associated with LOWER risk of dying from pneumonia — the opposite of medical intuition, since asthma is a well-established risk factor that should worsen a respiratory illness like pneumonia, not protect against it. The pattern was not a data bug or a coding error: in the training hospitals' actual clinical practice, asthmatic pneumonia patients were routinely triaged directly to the ICU and given aggressive, immediate care specifically BECAUSE clinicians already knew asthma made them high-risk. That aggressive, early care worked well enough that these patients' recorded 30-day outcomes ended up looking better on average than non-asthmatic pneumonia patients who received standard-priority care. The raw association between HasAsthma and lower mortality was genuinely, reproducibly present in the historical data — and it would have been a lethal rule to hard-code into a deployed triage system, since it would actively push a naive model to send future asthmatic patients toward lower-priority, standard care instead of the aggressive treatment that produced the good outcomes in the first place.

sections.heading: Why intelligibility, not accuracy, caught it
sections.body: The team could see this pattern only because they used GA2M models (generalized additive models with pairwise interactions) — an intelligible model class where each feature's contribution can be read off directly as a shape function, rather than buried inside millions of opaque weights. Choosing an intelligible model here cost nothing in accuracy: in the paper's own AUC comparison on the pneumonia task, GA2M scored highest of every model class tested — logistic regression, standard GAMs, random forests, and LogitBoost — not a runner-up the team tolerated for the sake of auditability. The asthma pattern was catchable specifically because intelligibility and accuracy were not in tension: a clinician could read the HasAsthma shape function directly and flag the counterintuitive downward slope before deployment, without paying any performance premium for that inspectability.

sections.heading: The general lesson: confounding by treatment inverts the causal arrow
sections.body: The asthma pattern generalizes to any setting where treatment intensity is itself a response to a variable, not independent of it: sicker-looking patients get more aggressive care, which improves their outcomes, which then makes the RISK FACTOR look protective in the raw association. Any model trained on observational treatment decisions risks learning this inversion — treatment-confounding is the mechanism, and intelligibility is what lets a human catch it before deployment rather than after.

lessons.workedExample: A hospital deploys a black-box gradient-boosted model to triage pneumonia patients, unaware it has learned the asthma-mortality inversion. The model assigns a diabetic-with-asthma patient a LOWER risk score than a similar patient without asthma, so the diabetic patient is routed to a general ward instead of the ICU. Had the hospital used a GA2M model like Caruana et al.'s, a clinician reviewing the shape function for HasAsthma would immediately see the counterintuitive downward slope, recognize it does not match medical knowledge, investigate, and discover the triage-confound before the rule ever reached a real patient — exactly the audit step the 2015 team performed.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows this literature will ask directly: 'how would you have caught a rule like the asthma one?' The strong answer is not 'we'd get more data' but 'we would use an intelligible model class specifically so a domain expert can inspect each feature's learned shape and flag anything that contradicts known mechanism' — and can note that in Caruana et al.'s own results this cost nothing: GA2M was the top-scoring model in their comparison, not a trade-off the team accepted.

questions.prompt: Why did Caruana et al.'s (2015) pneumonia model learn that a history of asthma was associated with LOWER mortality risk?

options.text: Asthma medication directly protects the lungs from pneumonia complications
Asthmatic patients were triaged directly to the ICU and received aggressive care, improving their recorded outcomes
The training data mislabeled asthma patients as pneumonia-free
Asthma is rare enough that the model treated it as statistical noise

explanations.a: There is no such protective medical mechanism; asthma is a genuine risk factor for worse pneumonia outcomes, not a protective one.
explanations.b: Correct — clinicians already knew asthma raised risk, so they routed these patients to the ICU for aggressive care, and that care improved outcomes enough to make the raw association look protective.
explanations.c: This was not a labeling error; the association reflected real treatment patterns in the data, not a data-quality bug.
explanations.d: Asthma was common enough in the pneumonia cohort to produce a clear, consistent, learnable pattern rather than being ignored as noise.

questions.prompt: What did Caruana et al.'s own AUC comparison show about GA2M relative to the other models they tested (logistic regression, standard GAMs, random forests, LogitBoost)?

options.text: GA2M scored noticeably lower, and the team accepted that cost for its interpretability
GA2M scored highest of every method compared, so its interpretability came at no accuracy cost
GA2M could not be scored with AUC because it is an intelligible model
GA2M was left out of the comparison because it took too long to train

explanations.a: The paper's own table shows the opposite: GA2M was not a lower-scoring model the team tolerated for auditability's sake.
explanations.b: Correct — GA2M had the highest AUC of any method in the paper's comparison table, so choosing it for its readable shape functions required no accuracy trade-off; that per-feature readability is exactly what let the team catch the asthma pattern before deployment.
explanations.c: AUC is a standard metric for any model producing a risk score, including GA2M; it was computed and reported for GA2M in the paper's own table.
explanations.d: GA2M was included and directly compared in the paper's results; it was not excluded.

questions.prompt: Order the causal chain that produced the counterintuitive asthma-mortality association in the training data.

items.text: Clinicians recognize asthma as a known pneumonia risk factor
Asthmatic pneumonia patients are triaged directly to the ICU for aggressive care
Aggressive care improves these patients' recorded outcomes relative to average
The raw data association makes asthma look protective rather than harmful

questions.explanation: The inversion arises because clinicians' correct prior belief (asthma is risky) drove a treatment response (ICU triage) that improved outcomes enough to flip the raw correlation, illustrating how treatment-confounding can invert a learned association relative to the true causal risk.

questions.prompt: What general mechanism does the asthma case illustrate about observational treatment data?

options.text: Models trained on observational data always underestimate true risk factors
When treatment intensity responds to a risk factor, the resulting improved outcomes can make that risk factor look protective in raw association
Intelligible models are always less accurate than black-box models
Pneumonia risk models cannot be built from electronic health record data

explanations.a: The case shows the opposite direction is possible too — the risk factor was actually made to look artificially protective, not underestimated.
explanations.b: Correct — this is the general treatment-confounding mechanism: because sicker-looking patients get more aggressive, effective care, the risk factor that triggered that care can appear protective in the raw observational association even though it remains a genuine risk factor causally.
explanations.c: GA2M scored highest of every model compared in this very paper; intelligible models are not universally less accurate, and here there was no accuracy cost at all.
explanations.d: EHR data is exactly what Caruana et al. used to build a working, deployed-grade model; the case is not an argument against EHR-based modeling.

lessons.label: Shortcut Learning: When Importance Is Telling the Truth About a Broken Dataset

sections.heading: Zech et al. 2018: metal tokens instead of lungs
sections.body: John Zech and colleagues' 2018 PLOS Medicine study, 'Variable generalization performance of a deep learning model to detect pneumonia in chest radiographs,' trained CNNs on 158,323 chest X-rays pooled from three institutions — the NIH Clinical Center (112,120 images from 30,805 patients), Mount Sinai Hospital (42,396 images from 12,904 patients), and the Indiana University Network for Patient Care (3,807 images from 3,683 patients) — and found that a model trained on one hospital's data lost substantial accuracy when tested on another hospital's images, even though the underlying disease was the same. The saliency maps explained why: radiology technicians place a small radiopaque metal token in the image's corner during portable, bedside scans, which are disproportionately ordered for sicker inpatients who cannot be moved to the main radiology suite. The CNN learned to detect that token — a marker of scanner type and patient acuity, not of any lung pathology — as a shortcut correlated with pneumonia prevalence at each individual site. The model was not lying about what it found important; the token really did predict pneumonia within each hospital's own data distribution. It simply was not lung disease, and that distinction only shows up the moment the model is tested somewhere else.

sections.heading: DeGrave, Janizek & Lee 2021: catching shortcuts with saliency plus a generative model
sections.body: Alex DeGrave, Joseph Janizek, and Su-In Lee's 2021 Nature Machine Intelligence paper, 'AI for radiographic COVID-19 detection selects shortcuts over signal,' pushed the diagnosis further. Saliency maps alone are often ambiguous, so the team paired saliency with a generative model that could synthesize and manipulate image regions, directly testing whether flagged regions causally drove the prediction. They confirmed several COVID-detection models were keying on laterality markers (L/R tags radiologists stamp onto films), image borders, and even stray arrows or text burned into scans during acquisition — artifacts that happened to differ systematically between COVID-positive and COVID-negative source datasets, producing high in-distribution accuracy that evaporated on new hospitals' data.

sections.heading: The taxonomy and the useful conclusion
sections.body: Robert Geirhos and colleagues' 2020 Nature Machine Intelligence paper 'Shortcut Learning in Deep Neural Networks' names this failure mode generally: a model finds the decision rule that is easiest to learn from the training distribution, and 'easiest' is frequently a spurious, dataset-specific artifact rather than the intended signal — with no way to tell from training accuracy alone. Put together, these cases argue that post-hoc explanation earns its keep far more reliably as a DATASET DEBUGGER — surfacing exactly which artifact a model is exploiting so it can be removed or controlled for — than as a tool for scientific discovery about disease itself.

lessons.workedExample: A team trains a CNN to classify COVID-19 from chest X-rays scraped from several public repositories, hitting 94% held-out accuracy. Before presenting it as a diagnostic discovery, they generate saliency maps and find the hottest pixels cluster at the image border and a corner text stamp, not the lungs. Following DeGrave, Janizek and Lee's approach, they use an image generator to insert and remove that corner stamp on identical lung images and watch the prediction flip — confirming the stamp, not any pathology, drives most of the accuracy. They report the finding as evidence the dataset conflates source repository with diagnosis, and treat the saliency map as a debugging tool that killed a false discovery rather than as proof the model 'understands' COVID-19.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge will press on generalization: 'did you test this model on data from a different source?' A student who cites Zech et al.'s cross-hospital collapse and DeGrave, Janizek and Lee's generative-model confirmation shows they know high accuracy on one dataset can be entirely explained by a shortcut, and that the right response to a saliency map showing something odd is to treat it as a signal the DATASET is broken, not as a report on the disease.

questions.prompt: In Zech et al.'s 2018 PLOS Medicine study, what artifact did the pneumonia-detection CNN learn to key on?

options.text: A radiopaque metal token placed during portable bedside scans, correlated with patient acuity
The patient's age printed in the image header
Variation in lung opacity that radiologists themselves use
The compression artifact from JPEG file format

explanations.a: Correct — the token marking a portable scan correlated with sicker inpatients and thus with pneumonia prevalence at each site, giving the model a shortcut that didn't transfer across hospitals.
explanations.b: The paper's central finding was the metal token artifact, not printed age text driving the shortcut.
explanations.c: Genuine lung-opacity signal is what the model was SUPPOSED to use; the problem is it relied on the token instead.
explanations.d: The finding was about a physical scanner marker, not a compression artifact.

questions.prompt: How did DeGrave, Janizek & Lee (2021) go beyond saliency maps alone to confirm a shortcut in COVID-19 detection models?

options.text: They collected a much larger labeled dataset from a single hospital
They paired saliency maps with a generative model to manipulate flagged regions and test whether predictions changed causally
They asked radiologists to manually re-label every image
They reduced the model to a linear classifier for easier interpretation

explanations.a: More data from one hospital would not test whether a specific flagged region was causally responsible for predictions.
explanations.b: Correct — combining saliency with a generative model let them directly manipulate suspected shortcut regions (laterality markers, borders, arrows) and observe the causal effect on predictions, moving beyond saliency's correlational ambiguity.
explanations.c: Manual relabeling was not the method used to isolate the shortcut mechanism.
explanations.d: The paper worked with the deep models directly rather than substituting a simpler linear model.

questions.prompt: Match each shortcut-learning study or concept to what it contributed.

right.text: General taxonomy naming shortcut learning as models favoring the easiest-to-learn spurious rule
Cross-hospital pneumonia CNN collapse traced to a metal-token scanner artifact
Confirmed COVID-detection shortcuts (laterality markers, borders, arrows) using saliency plus a generative model

questions.explanation: Zech et al. documented the cross-institutional generalization failure and its metal-token cause; DeGrave, Janizek and Lee causally confirmed COVID-detection shortcuts with a generative model; Geirhos et al. supplied the general taxonomy explaining why deep networks favor such artifacts.

questions.prompt: What is the useful conclusion these shortcut-learning cases support about post-hoc explanation methods like saliency maps?

options.text: They are unreliable and should never be used for any purpose
They earn their keep most reliably as a dataset debugger, surfacing artifacts to remove, rather than as a tool for scientific discovery about disease
They prove a model has learned true medical mechanism whenever they highlight anatomically plausible regions
They should replace held-out test accuracy as the primary evaluation metric

explanations.a: The cases show saliency maps were exactly what caught the shortcuts — the tool has clear value, just a specific, more modest role than 'scientific discovery.'
explanations.b: Correct — in every case here, saliency/explanation tools were valuable for exposing what a model actually keyed on so a bad dataset artifact could be identified and fixed, which is a debugging role rather than evidence of medical discovery.
explanations.c: Highlighting an anatomically plausible region is not sufficient proof of true mechanism; it can still be confounded with an artifact correlated with that region.
explanations.d: Saliency maps complement rather than replace held-out accuracy; they diagnose why accuracy might not generalize, not substitute for measuring it.

lessons.label: Testing Faithfulness: Deletion, Retraining, and Noise Baselines

sections.heading: ROAR: remove and retrain, not remove and reuse
sections.body: Sara Hooker, Dumitru Erhan, Pieter-Jan Kindermans, and Been Kim's 2019 NeurIPS paper 'A Benchmark for Interpretability Methods in Deep Neural Networks' introduced ROAR (RemOve And Retrain) precisely because the obvious, cheaper test is broken. That naive test — delete the top-ranked pixels or features according to some attribution method, then feed the mutilated input straight into the ORIGINAL, already-trained model — is misleading, because the original model was never trained on inputs with holes or gray boxes punched into them; a large performance drop can simply reflect distribution shift, the model being confused by an input shape it has never encountered, rather than reflecting the true importance of whatever was removed. ROAR's fix is to remove the flagged features and RETRAIN the model completely from scratch on the modified dataset every single time a different fraction of features is removed. A feature-attribution method is validated only if removing the features IT calls most important causes the largest accuracy drop after this full retraining step, which controls for the distribution-shift confound entirely by ensuring the model has genuinely adapted to the reduced input it now sees.

sections.heading: LOCO: the expensive gold standard
sections.body: Jing Lei, Max G'Sell, Alessandro Rinaldo, Ryan Tibshirani, and Larry Wasserman's 2018 JASA paper on distribution-free predictive inference introduced LOCO (leave-one-covariate-out): refit the model with one covariate entirely removed, and define that covariate's importance as the resulting change in held-out predictive loss. LOCO answers the causal-adjacent question 'how much does the model NEED this variable,' with formal distribution-free inference guarantees, but it requires one full retrain per candidate variable — computationally prohibitive at scale, which is exactly why cheaper proxies matter for a student project.

sections.heading: Cheap, decidable tests any project can run
sections.body: Three practical tools bring this rigor within reach. First, add a column of pure random noise to the feature set before fitting: any real feature that ranks BELOW the noise column in importance has not cleared the floor for being established as real, since noise has zero true relationship to the outcome by construction. Second, Miron Kursa and Witold Rudnicki's 2010 Boruta algorithm (Journal of Statistical Software) automates this idea for all-relevant feature selection: it creates 'shadow features' by randomly shuffling each real feature's values, fits the model on the combined real-plus-shadow set, and iteratively keeps only features that consistently beat the best shadow feature's importance across many runs. Third, André Altmann, Laura Toloşi, Oliver Sander, and Thomas Lengauer's 2010 Bioinformatics paper PIMP (permutation importance p-values) supplies actual p-values for permutation importance scores by comparing each observed score against a null distribution built from many permutations, converting a bare importance ranking into a statistically decidable claim.

lessons.workedExample: A student team ranks five features by permutation importance and finds 'zodiac sign' (added as a joke control) ranks fourth out of five — above two supposedly meaningful features. Rather than trusting the ranking as-is, they add a genuine random-noise column and rerun: two of their 'real' features now rank below the noise column, meaning those two have not cleared the floor for being real signal. They then run Boruta, which confirms the same two features never beat their shadow copies across 100 iterations and should be dropped, while running PIMP on the remaining three gives p-values below 0.01, letting them report those three as importance findings that are statistically distinguishable from chance.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'how do you know this feature's importance is real and not noise?' is testing whether a team ran ANY decidable check. Naming a random-noise column as the floor, Boruta's shadow-feature procedure, or PIMP's permutation p-values shows the team treated their importance ranking as a testable claim rather than a picture to admire — and understanding why ROAR retrains (to avoid confounding importance with distribution shift) versus why LOCO is the expensive gold standard shows genuine grasp of the trade-offs.

questions.prompt: Why does ROAR (Hooker et al. 2019) require RETRAINING the model after removing top-ranked features, rather than just feeding the modified input to the original model?

options.text: Retraining is faster than evaluating the original model
Feeding modified inputs to the original model confounds true feature importance with distribution shift, since the model never saw inputs missing those features during training
The original model's weights become invalid after any feature is removed
Retraining is required by the JMLR review process

explanations.a: Retraining is far more computationally expensive, not faster; the reason is methodological, not efficiency.
explanations.b: Correct — without retraining, a large accuracy drop could simply mean the model is confused by out-of-distribution blanked inputs, not that the removed feature was truly important; retraining isolates the actual value of the removed information.
explanations.c: Model weights remain numerically valid on modified inputs; the issue is that predictions become unreliable due to distribution shift, not invalidity.
explanations.d: This is a methodological requirement of the ROAR benchmark itself, unrelated to any journal's review process.

questions.prompt: What does LOCO (Lei, G'Sell, Rinaldo, Tibshirani & Wasserman 2018) define as a covariate's importance?

options.text: The covariate's raw correlation with the outcome
The change in held-out predictive loss when the model is refit with that covariate entirely removed
The covariate's coefficient magnitude in a linear regression
The number of times the covariate is selected across bootstrap samples

explanations.a: Raw correlation ignores the rest of the model and doesn't require any refitting; LOCO is specifically defined through a refitting comparison.
explanations.b: Correct — LOCO refits the model leaving one covariate out entirely and measures the resulting change in held-out loss, giving a model-free, distribution-free notion of importance with formal inference guarantees.
explanations.c: LOCO is model-agnostic and does not rely on coefficients, which would only apply to linear models.
explanations.d: Selection frequency across bootstraps describes a different kind of stability measure, not LOCO's defining quantity.

questions.prompt: Match each faithfulness tool to what it provides.

right.text: A floor: any real feature ranking below it has not cleared the bar for being established
Iterative shadow-feature comparison for all-relevant feature selection
P-values for permutation importance scores against a null distribution

questions.explanation: A single random-noise column gives a cheap floor for comparison; Boruta automates that idea with repeatedly-shuffled shadow copies of every real feature to decide all-relevant status; PIMP formalizes the comparison into an actual p-value for each importance score.

questions.prompt: Order these faithfulness checks from cheapest/quickest to most expensive/rigorous.

items.text: Add a single random-noise column as an importance floor
Run Boruta's iterative shadow-feature comparison across many runs
Run PIMP to get permutation-importance p-values from a null distribution
Run full LOCO retraining, refitting the model once per candidate covariate

questions.explanation: A single noise column is nearly free to add; Boruta requires many iterations of shuffling and refitting shadow features; PIMP requires building a null distribution via repeated permutations to compute p-values; full LOCO retraining, requiring one complete model refit per covariate, is the most computationally expensive but most rigorous option.

lessons.label: Humans in the Loop: Explanations Can Make People Worse

sections.heading: Transparency bought over-trust, not scrutiny
sections.body: Forough Poursabzi-Sangdeh, Daniel Goldstein, Jake Hofman, Jennifer Wortman Vaughan, and Hanna Wallach's 2021 CHI paper 'Manipulating and Measuring Model Interpretability' ran a sequence of pre-registered experiments totaling 3,800 participants on a task predicting apartment prices, varying only two factors long assumed to make a model more interpretable: the number of features it used (a small handful versus dozens) and how transparent its inner workings were shown to be (a fully visible linear formula versus an opaque model that only reveals its output). Every version of the model was functionally identical underneath — only the presentation changed. The uncomfortable result: participants shown a CLEAR, transparent two-feature model with visibly displayed weights were LESS able to detect when the model made an obvious mistake and correct their own final answer for it than participants shown a more opaque, harder-to-inspect model — and the transparent-model group also reported trusting it more and deferring to it more often. Making a model's reasoning visible did not make people better auditors of it; empirically, it made people more willing to simply defer to it instead of checking its work.

sections.heading: Even experts skip scrutiny when tools feel like assurance
sections.body: Harmanpreet Kaur, Harsha Nori, Samuel Jenkins, Rich Caruana, Hanna Wallach, and Jennifer Wortman Vaughan's 2020 CHI paper 'Interpreting Interpretability: Understanding Data Scientists' Use of Interpretability Tools for Machine Learning' found that trained data scientists using SHAP values and GAM outputs on models with deliberately injected data bugs frequently missed those bugs — the interpretability tools functioned as an assurance ritual, a box to check, rather than triggering genuine investigation. Participants over-trusted the outputs' correctness and under-questioned whether the underlying model or data pipeline itself was sound, even though the tools were, in principle, capable of surfacing exactly the injected problems.

sections.heading: Explanations can be engineered to manipulate, not just fail to help
sections.body: Himabindu Lakkaraju and Osbert Bastani's 2020 AIES paper 'How do I fool you? Manipulating User Trust via Misleading Black Box Explanations' showed the failure can be adversarial rather than accidental: they demonstrated explanations can be deliberately constructed to make a biased or unreliable model appear fair and trustworthy to human reviewers, hiding the model's true decision logic behind a plausible-looking but functionally disconnected justification, and that reviewers in their user study were reliably fooled by these engineered explanations. Together these three studies argue that an explanation's persuasive power and its diagnostic value are separate, independently-varying properties — a clear, satisfying-looking explanation can actively suppress the very scrutiny that would catch a real problem, whether the mismatch between appearance and substance is accidental, as in the first two studies, or deliberately engineered, as Lakkaraju and Bastani show is possible.

lessons.workedExample: A hospital gives clinicians a transparent two-feature triage model with visible weights, expecting the visibility to help clinicians catch errors. Following Poursabzi-Sangdeh et al.'s design, the researchers secretly test cases where the model gives an obviously wrong recommendation. Clinicians using the transparent model catch the error LESS often than a comparison group using an opaque version of the same model, because the visible weights create a false sense that 'the reasoning is right there, so it must be sound' — mirroring Kaur et al.'s finding that data scientists similarly stopped scrutinizing SHAP-explained models for injected bugs once the explanation output looked reasonable.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has read this literature will push back on the intuitive claim 'we made our model interpretable, so users can catch its mistakes.' The strong response cites Poursabzi-Sangdeh et al.'s finding that transparency measurably REDUCED mistake-detection and increased trust, plus Kaur et al.'s finding that even data scientists using SHAP missed injected bugs — showing the team understands that an explanation's clarity and its actual diagnostic value are not the same thing, and that this gap can even be exploited (Lakkaraju & Bastani).

questions.prompt: In Poursabzi-Sangdeh et al.'s 2021 CHI study (N=3,800), what happened when participants were shown a clear, transparent two-feature model with visible weights?

options.text: They detected and corrected the model's mistakes more often than with an opaque model
They were less able to detect and correct the model's mistakes, and trusted it more
They ignored the model's predictions entirely
Their performance was identical regardless of transparency

explanations.a: This is the intuitive expectation the study actually contradicts — transparency did not improve mistake detection.
explanations.b: Correct — transparency and few features increased trust while REDUCING participants' ability to catch the model's errors, the paper's central and counterintuitive finding.
explanations.c: Participants did not ignore the model; if anything they deferred to it more, the opposite of ignoring it.
explanations.d: The study specifically found a measurable difference, not equivalent performance across the transparency conditions.

questions.prompt: What did Kaur, Nori, Jenkins, Caruana, Wallach & Wortman Vaughan (2020) find about data scientists using SHAP and GAM outputs?

options.text: They correctly identified all deliberately injected data bugs
They frequently missed injected bugs, treating the interpretability tools as an assurance ritual rather than triggering deeper investigation
They refused to use SHAP or GAM outputs at all
They only used the tools correctly after months of additional training

explanations.a: The finding was the opposite — data scientists frequently missed the deliberately injected bugs despite having these tools available.
explanations.b: Correct — the tools' outputs functioned more as a box-checking ritual than as a genuine trigger for scrutiny, so even trained data scientists missed problems the tools could in principle have surfaced.
explanations.c: Participants did use the tools; the issue was how superficially they engaged with the output, not refusal to use them.
explanations.d: The study did not find that additional training was the resolution being tested or reported.

questions.prompt: Match each study to its central finding about human-in-the-loop explanation use.

right.text: Transparent, clear models reduced mistake detection and increased trust
Data scientists using SHAP/GAM tools missed deliberately injected bugs
Explanations can be deliberately engineered to make an untrustworthy model look fair

questions.explanation: Poursabzi-Sangdeh et al. showed transparency itself can suppress error detection; Kaur et al. showed even trained data scientists treat interpretability tool output as assurance rather than genuine scrutiny; Lakkaraju and Bastani showed the same gap can be exploited adversarially to manufacture false trust.

questions.prompt: What is the shared conclusion these three studies support about explanation and trust?

options.text: An explanation's persuasive clarity and its actual diagnostic value are separate properties, and a satisfying explanation can suppress scrutiny
More interpretable models are always safer to deploy without further testing
Human reviewers should never be involved in checking model outputs
SHAP and GAM outputs are provably incorrect and should be discontinued

explanations.a: Correct — across all three studies, a clear or satisfying-looking explanation reduced rather than increased genuine scrutiny, showing persuasiveness and diagnostic value are distinct and can even work against each other.
explanations.b: The Poursabzi-Sangdeh result directly contradicts this — more interpretable presentation correlated with worse error-catching, not automatic safety.
explanations.c: The studies argue for better-designed human oversight, not for removing humans from the loop entirely.
explanations.d: The tools themselves are not shown to be incorrect; the issue is how humans engage with their output, not the tools' technical validity.

units.label: Applications, Case Studies, and the Fair

lessons.label: The Reporting Standard for an Interpretability Claim

sections.heading: Name the method and its version, because they are not the same quantity
sections.body: A board that says "feature X is important" without naming the method is not reporting a result, it is reporting a vibe. Mean decrease in impurity (MDI, the default in scikit-learn's RandomForestClassifier.feature_importances_), permutation importance (Breiman 2001; Fisher, Rudin & Dominici's 2019 model-class-reliance generalization), and mean absolute SHAP value (Lundberg & Lee 2017) are three different quantities computed three different ways, and they can and do rank features differently on the same fitted model. MDI is biased toward high-cardinality and continuous features (Strobl et al. 2007 demonstrated this with simulated null features) and, worse, is computed on TRAINING data, so it reflects overfitting, not generalization. A defensible report states the method by name, the package and version that computed it, and whether it was measured on training or held-out data.

sections.heading: The three things a claim needs beyond a single number: baseline, uncertainty, correlation
sections.body: First, a noise-column baseline: inject one or more synthetic random columns (shuffled or drawn from noise) into the feature matrix, refit, and report their importance as the floor. Any real feature scoring at or below the noise column's importance is not distinguishable from chance. Second, an uncertainty band: permutation importance run once is a single realization of a random shuffle; repeating it across 20-50 seeds (or bootstrap-refitting the model on resampled training sets) turns a point estimate into a range, and overlapping ranges between two features means their RANK is not established. Third, a correlation matrix of the top features: permutation importance and SHAP both split credit unpredictably among correlated features (a well-documented failure mode — permuting one of two r=0.9-correlated features barely hurts accuracy because the model can lean on its partner), so a board reporting "X matters, Y doesn't" without disclosing r(X,Y) is hiding the one fact that would let a reader judge the claim.

sections.heading: If LIME was used, fidelity is not optional; and the sentence to never write
sections.body: A LIME explanation is a local linear surrogate's coefficients, not the model's own logic (Ribeiro, Singh & Guestrin 2016) — reporting the coefficients without the surrogate's local R^2 or infidelity score hides whether the "explanation" fits the black box at all in that neighborhood; a low local fidelity means the coefficients describe a surrogate that does not match the model there. Across all of this, one sentence should never appear in a board: "feature X causes Y." Importance, whether from MDI, permutation, or SHAP, measures association with the model's predictions, not causation in the world (see the causal-inference lessons in this track for why that gap cannot be closed by any importance method alone). The defensible replacement names the mechanism actually measured: "the model's held-out error rises N% when X is permuted; X is correlated r=... with Z, so we cannot separate their individual effects."

lessons.workedExample: A team's board claims "study hours is the most important predictor of exam score, importance = 0.31." A judge asks: which method? They used scikit-learn's default MDI on the training set, never checked a noise column, never checked correlation, and ran it once. Rewritten to standard: "Permutation importance (5 seeds, held-out fold): study_hours mean importance 0.14 (range 0.11-0.17), versus a synthetic noise column at 0.02, so the signal is real. study_hours is correlated r=0.62 with prior_gpa, so we cannot cleanly separate their individual contributions to the model's error. We do not claim study_hours causes higher scores." The second version survives a judge's follow-up; the first collapses on the first question.
lessons.judgeFraming: This is the single most common gap between a science-fair board and a defensible analysis, so judges probe it first: naming the exact method exposes whether the team understands that MDI, permutation, and SHAP measure different things, and asking for a noise-column baseline or an uncertainty range exposes whether a single run was mistaken for a stable finding. A team that pre-empts these questions by disclosing the method, the baseline, the range, and the top-feature correlation signals it understands what an importance number can and cannot support — which is exactly the discipline a fair rewards.

questions.prompt: Why is MDI (mean decrease in impurity) importance considered unreliable on its own?

options.text: It only works for regression models, never classifiers
It is biased toward high-cardinality/continuous features and is typically computed on training data, so it can reflect overfitting
It cannot be computed for tree-based models
It always agrees exactly with permutation importance

explanations.a: MDI is used for both; the concern is a bias/data-leakage issue, not a model-type restriction.
explanations.b: Correct — Strobl et al. 2007 showed the high-cardinality bias, and scikit-learn's default computes it on training data, conflating importance with overfitting.
explanations.c: MDI is specifically a tree-based-model quantity (impurity decrease at splits); it exists precisely because trees compute it natively.
explanations.d: They frequently disagree, which is exactly why the method must be named — they are different quantities.

questions.prompt: A noise-column baseline is used to:

options.text: Improve the model's held-out accuracy
Establish the importance floor below which a feature's signal is indistinguishable from chance
Replace the need for a train/test split
Compute SHAP values faster

explanations.a: Adding a random column does not improve accuracy; it is a diagnostic, not a modeling improvement.
explanations.b: Correct — a real feature scoring at or below a synthetic random column's importance has not demonstrated a real signal.
explanations.c: It is unrelated to train/test splitting, though the importance measurement itself should still use held-out data.
explanations.d: Runtime is unaffected; the noise column is simply one more column run through the same procedure.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of building a defensible importance claim in order.

items.text: Name the exact method and package/version used
Add a noise-column baseline and refit
Repeat across seeds/bootstraps to get an uncertainty range
Report the correlation matrix of top features
State the finding as an association claim, not a causal one
