questions.explanation: A defensible claim starts by naming the method (since MDI/permutation/SHAP differ), adds a noise baseline, repeats the measurement for an uncertainty range, discloses correlation among top features, and finally states the result as association-with-error, never causation.

questions.prompt: If a LIME explanation is reported without its local fidelity (local R^2 or infidelity score), what is missing?

options.text: Whether the surrogate model actually approximates the black box in that neighborhood
The p-value of the coefficients
The global accuracy of the black-box model
Nothing; fidelity is optional metadata

explanations.a: Correct — low local fidelity means the reported coefficients belong to a surrogate that does not actually track the black box near that instance, making the explanation untrustworthy.
explanations.b: LIME's K-LASSO fit does not report coefficient p-values in the standard formulation; fidelity is the relevant diagnostic instead.
explanations.c: Global accuracy is a separate, model-level statistic unrelated to a single local explanation's trustworthiness.
explanations.d: It is not optional — without it there is no way to know if the surrogate fit the neighborhood at all.

questions.prompt: Match each defensible sentence fragment to what it replaces or fixes.

left.text: "held-out error rises N% when X is permuted"

right.text: Replaces the unsupported causal claim "X causes Y"
Discloses a confounder that prevents separating individual effects
Establishes exactly which quantity and how much uncertainty is behind the number

questions.explanation: Each fragment fixes one specific gap: the error-rise phrasing avoids claiming causation, naming a correlated feature discloses a confound the analysis cannot separate, and naming the method plus seed count gives the number provenance and an uncertainty range.

lessons.label: Case: Prescience — SHAP at the Operating Table (Lundberg et al. 2018)

sections.heading: The problem: predicting hypoxaemia minute by minute during anaesthesia
sections.body: Scott Lundberg, Bala Nair, Monica Vavilala, and colleagues published "Explainable machine-learning predictions for the prevention of hypoxaemia during surgery" in Nature Biomedical Engineering in 2018. The team trained a gradient-boosted tree model, Prescience, on minute-by-minute intraoperative data (vitals, ventilator settings, drug doses) from over 50,000 surgeries at the University of Washington to predict a patient's risk of hypoxaemia (dangerously low blood oxygen) in the near future, both before surgery and continuously during it. A risk score alone is nearly useless to an anaesthesiologist mid-procedure: a number with no reason attached gives no lever to pull. So every prediction was paired with a real-time explanation, rendered as a force plot at the bedside monitor, showing WHICH factors were driving that patient's risk up or down at that moment and by how much.

sections.heading: The result: explanations measurably improved clinician anticipation
sections.body: The paper's own reported figures: with Prescience's aid, anaesthesiologists' discrimination ability (AUC) for anticipating hypoxaemia rose from 0.60 to 0.76 preoperatively and from 0.66 to 0.78 in real time during surgery (both P<0.0001), relative to unaided prediction. Separately, using only the real-time results, the paper reports that anaesthesiologists who currently anticipate roughly 15% of hypoxaemia events could anticipate roughly 30% with the system's aid — a doubling — and many of the newly anticipated events were tied to modifiable factors (a drug dose, a ventilator setting) an anaesthesiologist could actually act on in the moment. This is a rare instance where an interpretability system's benefit was measured as a downstream human-decision outcome — anticipation of a real clinical event by a real clinician — rather than merely as a property of the explanation itself, such as a fidelity score or a user-satisfaction survey.

sections.heading: The design constraint that produced TreeSHAP
sections.body: Explaining a single prediction with exact Shapley values is, in general, exponential in the number of features (2^M model evaluations for M features) — intractable to compute in the seconds available during live surgery, and far too slow to recompute every minute for every patient on a ward. Prescience's deployment requirement — local, per-patient, per-minute explanations computed fast enough to matter at the bedside — is exactly what motivated Lundberg, Erion & Lee's TreeSHAP algorithm (2018/2020), which exploits tree structure to compute EXACT Shapley values for tree ensembles in low-order polynomial time (roughly O(T L D^2), scaling with the number of trees T, leaves L, and max depth D) rather than exponential time. Without that speed constraint from a real clinical deployment, there would have been far less pressure to solve the exact-Shapley-for-trees problem efficiently; Prescience is the case where a deployment need directly shaped an interpretability algorithm's design, not the other way around.

lessons.workedExample: An anaesthesiologist is 40 minutes into a procedure when Prescience's risk score for the next 5 minutes jumps. The accompanying SHAP explanation shows the top three contributors for THIS patient at THIS minute: a recent propofol bolus, a falling tidal volume trend, and a below-baseline SpO2 reading, each with a signed local contribution to the score. Because the explanation is local and per-minute rather than a static global ranking, the anaesthesiologist can act on the modifiable ones immediately — adjusting the ventilator setting — rather than parsing a generic list of "factors associated with hypoxaemia" that may not apply to this patient right now.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge will ask what the reported AUC gain (0.60→0.76 preoperative, 0.66→0.78 real-time) is measured against and whether the explanation itself, not just the prediction, was shown to help — the strong answer names the paper's own comparison (aided vs. unaided AUC, pre-op and real-time, plus the separate 15%-to-30% real-time anticipation-rate reframing) rather than a vague "doctors liked it." A sharper judge will ask why a slower, exact global Shapley calculation would not have worked here; the answer is the real-time constraint of live surgery, which is precisely why this case is paired with TreeSHAP's polynomial-time algorithm rather than any generic explainer.

questions.prompt: What did Lundberg et al. 2018 report as Prescience's effect on anaesthesiologists' anticipation of hypoxaemia?

options.text: No measurable change
AUC rose from 0.60 to 0.76 preoperatively and 0.66 to 0.78 in real time (both P<0.0001)
A 50% reduction in surgery duration
Complete elimination of hypoxaemia events

explanations.a: The paper reports a specific, non-zero improvement in both settings.
explanations.b: Correct — the paper reports AUC improving from 0.60 to 0.76 preoperatively and from 0.66 to 0.78 in real time, aided versus unaided (both P<0.0001).
explanations.c: Surgery duration was not the measured outcome; anticipation of hypoxaemia risk was.
explanations.d: The claim is improved anticipation, framed (in the separate real-time-only extrapolation) as roughly doubling the fraction of events anticipated (about 15% to about 30%), not elimination.

questions.prompt: Why did Prescience's deployment setting specifically require an explanation method fast enough for real time?

options.text: Because exact Shapley value computation is exponential in the number of features, and clinicians needed answers within the operative timescale
Because hospitals do not allow any machine-learning models
Because SHAP values cannot be computed for tree models at all
Because the model needed to be retrained every minute

explanations.a: Correct — general exact Shapley computation scales exponentially with feature count, which is infeasible during live surgery, motivating a fast tree-specific algorithm.
explanations.b: The deployment happened; the constraint was computational speed, not a prohibition on ML.
explanations.c: SHAP values can be computed for trees, and TreeSHAP is exactly the fast algorithm developed for that purpose.
explanations.d: The model itself was trained once beforehand; only the explanation was computed per patient per minute, not the model retrained.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the causal chain from clinical need to algorithm.

items.text: Anaesthesiologists need per-patient, per-minute hypoxaemia risk explanations
Exact Shapley computation is too slow for real-time use
Lundberg, Erion & Lee develop TreeSHAP for polynomial-time exact attribution on trees
Prescience delivers real-time local explanations at the bedside

questions.explanation: The clinical need for real-time, local explanations exposed the computational bottleneck of exact Shapley values, which motivated TreeSHAP's development, which in turn enabled the deployed real-time explanations in Prescience.

questions.prompt: Match each element of the Prescience case to what it represents.

right.text: Training data scale for the gradient-boosted risk model
Reported preoperative / real-time AUC improvement
Polynomial-time exact Shapley algorithm for trees

questions.explanation: The 50,000+ surgeries were the training corpus, the AUC figures (0.60→0.76 preop, 0.66→0.78 real-time) are the paper's reported human-anticipation improvements, and TreeSHAP is the fast exact algorithm the deployment constraint motivated.

lessons.label: Case: Global Understanding Built From Local Explanations (Lundberg et al. 2020)

sections.heading: Stacking thousands of exact local attributions into a global picture
sections.body: Lundberg, Erion, Chen, DeGrave, Prutkin, Nair, Katz, Himmelfarb, Bansal & Lee published "From local explanations to global understanding with explainable AI for trees" in Nature Machine Intelligence in 2020, building directly on the TreeSHAP algorithm the same group had introduced for Prescience. The paper's structural move: instead of computing one global importance number per feature (as MDI or permutation importance does), compute an EXACT TreeSHAP attribution for every feature, for every single patient in the dataset, then stack thousands of these local vectors into three complementary views — a summary plot (each dot one patient-feature attribution, colored by feature value, showing the full distribution of effects rather than one average), a dependence plot (a feature's value on the x-axis against its SHAP value on the y-axis, revealing shape), and a supervised clustering of patients by their SHAP-value profiles rather than by raw feature values.

sections.heading: What this surfaced in chronic kidney disease and NHANES mortality data
sections.body: Applied to chronic kidney disease progression data and to NHANES (National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey) mortality data, this stacking approach surfaced NON-MONOTONE relationships — for example, a risk factor whose SHAP dependence plot rose, fell, then rose again across its range — that a single global MDI ranking necessarily flattens into one importance number with no shape information at all. The paper also introduced SHAP interaction values, a second-order extension that splits a feature's attribution into its main effect and its pairwise interaction effects with every other feature, surfacing interactions a plain dependence plot would blur together. The SHAP-based clustering also identified population subgroups sharing similar RISK MECHANISMS (similar patterns of which features drove their risk up or down) even when those subgroups did not share similar raw feature values, a distinction a conventional clustering on the raw features could not make. The paper also demonstrated using per-feature SHAP distributions over time to monitor a deployed hospital mortality model for performance degradation as the input data drifted.

sections.heading: The structural lesson: global SHAP is an aggregation, not a separate measurement
sections.body: The core teaching point for this track: SHAP's "global" plots are not a new, independently-computed quantity the way MDI or permutation importance are — they are literally the local, per-instance attributions summarized (e.g., averaged in absolute value, or plotted as a distribution). This is precisely why SHAP's global ranking can legitimately DISAGREE with permutation importance on the same model without either being "wrong": permutation importance measures a global quantity directly (how much held-out error rises when a feature is shuffled across the whole dataset), while SHAP's global picture is built bottom-up from local game-theoretic credit assignment at each instance. Two different constructions of "importance," both mathematically well-defined, can rank the same features differently.

lessons.workedExample: A team studying a diabetes-risk dataset computes SHAP values for every patient and plots a dependence plot for BMI. Instead of a straight upward line, it shows SHAP contribution rising sharply from BMI 20-30, flattening from 30-35, then rising again above 35 — a non-monotone, two-regime pattern invisible in a single MDI importance score of, say, 0.18. Separately, permutation importance ranks a different feature (fasting glucose) above BMI. Rather than treating this as a contradiction, the team reports both: "BMI shows a non-monotone SHAP dependence, most consequential above 35; permutation importance ranks fasting glucose higher because shuffling it does more damage to held-out accuracy — the two methods measure different constructions of importance and are not required to agree."
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows this paper will ask whether the student understands that SHAP's summary and dependence plots are built FROM the local explanations, not computed as an independent global statistic — a student who calls SHAP importance and permutation importance "the same thing measured two ways" has missed the structural point. The strongest answer explains why the two can disagree without either being an error, and cites the paper's demonstrated payoff (non-monotone relationships, mechanism-based subgroups, drift monitoring) as evidence that the local-to-global aggregation reveals structure a single global number cannot.

questions.prompt: What is the structural difference between SHAP's global summary/dependence plots and a permutation importance ranking?

options.text: SHAP's global view is an aggregation of exact per-instance local attributions; permutation importance is measured directly as a global quantity
They are mathematically identical formulas
Permutation importance is also built by summing local explanations
SHAP cannot produce any global view, only local ones

explanations.a: Correct — this is the paper's core structural point: SHAP's global picture is built bottom-up from thousands of exact local attributions, while permutation importance is computed directly at the global (whole-dataset, error-based) level.
explanations.b: They are different constructions and can disagree, which the paper explicitly demonstrates is not a contradiction.
explanations.c: Permutation importance shuffles a feature across the whole dataset and measures the resulting global error change directly, not by summing per-instance attributions.
explanations.d: The paper's entire contribution is showing how to build useful global views (summary, dependence, clustering) from stacked local TreeSHAP values.

questions.prompt: What kind of relationship did the SHAP dependence plots surface that a single global MDI ranking cannot show?

options.text: Non-monotone, shape-revealing relationships between a feature's value and its effect on the prediction
The exact training time of the model
The number of trees in the ensemble
Whether the dataset had missing values

explanations.a: Correct — a dependence plot shows the full shape of a feature's effect (e.g., rise-flatten-rise), while MDI collapses everything to one number with no shape information.
explanations.b: Training time is unrelated to what a dependence plot visualizes.
explanations.c: The number of trees is a hyperparameter of the model, not something a dependence plot reveals.
explanations.d: Missing-value structure is a separate data-quality question from the shape of a feature's effect.

questions.prompt: Match each of the paper's three global views to what it shows.

right.text: Distribution of every patient-feature attribution, colored by feature value
A single feature's value plotted against its SHAP contribution, revealing shape
Patient subgroups sharing similar risk MECHANISMS, not raw feature similarity

questions.explanation: The summary plot shows the full distribution of local attributions across patients, the dependence plot reveals a single feature's effect shape, and the SHAP-based clustering groups patients by shared risk mechanism rather than raw feature values.

questions.prompt: Order the construction of the paper's global understanding from raw data to insight.

items.text: Fit a tree ensemble on chronic kidney disease / NHANES data
Compute an exact TreeSHAP attribution for every feature, for every patient
Stack thousands of local attribution vectors
Render summary, dependence, and clustering views
Surface non-monotone relationships and mechanism-based subgroups

questions.explanation: The pipeline fits the model, computes exact per-instance TreeSHAP values, stacks them across the population, renders the three global views from that stack, and only then surfaces structure invisible to a single global ranking.

lessons.label: Case: Credit, Recourse, and the Law

sections.heading: The 2018 FICO challenge and the team that refused the premise
sections.body: FICO's 2018 Explainable Machine Learning Challenge asked entrants to build an accurate AND explainable model on the HELOC (Home Equity Line of Credit) dataset, predicting whether an applicant would repay. Most teams built a black-box model and bolted an explainer on top. A Duke University team — Chaofan Chen, Kangcheng Lin, Cynthia Rudin, Yaron Shaposhnik, Sijia Wang, and Tong Wang — won FICO's Recognition Award by rejecting that premise: they showed a fully, globally interpretable two-layer additive risk model matched black-box accuracy on HELOC, so no post-hoc explainer was needed at all. Rudin's broader argument (Rudin 2019, "Stop Explaining Black Box Machine Learning Models for High Stakes Decisions and Use Interpretable Models Instead") is that for many structured, tabular, high-stakes problems, the accuracy-interpretability trade-off is smaller than assumed, and post-hoc explanation is a workaround for a design choice, not a necessity.

sections.heading: Counterfactual recourse: a right to a path, not a right to the model
sections.body: Sandra Wachter, Brent Mittelstadt, and Chris Russell's 2017 Harvard Journal of Law & Technology paper, "Counterfactual Explanations Without Opening the Black Box," proposed a different kind of answer entirely: instead of explaining WHY a model decided, tell the applicant the smallest change to their inputs that would flip the outcome — "your application would be approved if your income were higher by X" — without ever revealing the model's internal logic, training data, or even its type. This is actionable recourse rather than mechanism: a bank can hand over a counterfactual without exposing a trade secret or a proprietary architecture, because a counterfactual is a statement about the DECISION BOUNDARY near one applicant, not a description of the model itself.

sections.heading: The unresolved legal fight: does the GDPR require an explanation at all?
sections.body: Bryce Goodman and Seth Flaxman's 2016 paper claimed the EU's GDPR (effective 2018) creates a "right to explanation" of automated decisions. Wachter, Mittelstadt, and Luciano Floridi's 2017 rebuttal, "Why a Right to Explanation of Automated Decision-Making Does Not Exist in the GDPR" (International Data Privacy Law), argued the opposite in detail: Article 22, the GDPR's actual binding article on automated decision-making, grants only a right to human intervention, to express a view, and to contest a decision — not an explicit right to an explanation of the logic. The stronger "explanation" language lives in Recital 71, and recitals are non-binding interpretive guidance, not enforceable law. This is a live, genuinely unsettled dispute rather than a solved textbook fact. The later EU AI Act (2024) sidesteps the ambiguity for high-risk systems by imposing explicit transparency and documentation obligations directly, rather than relying on a contested reading of the GDPR.

lessons.workedExample: A student building a loan-approval model for their fair project wants to both explain decisions and cite the legal stakes. They report: "Our gradient-boosted model reaches 84% accuracy; an interpretable two-layer additive model (in the spirit of the Duke FICO-challenge entry) reaches 83% — a 1-point gap we judge acceptable given the stakes, so we deploy the interpretable model directly rather than explaining a black box." For rejected applicants, they generate a counterfactual (Wachter et al. 2017 style): "approval requires income at least $4,200 higher, holding other factors fixed." They note, correctly, that whether this is a compliance requirement under GDPR Article 22 is legally disputed (Goodman & Flaxman vs. Wachter et al.), while the EU AI Act's 2024 transparency rules for high-risk credit systems are not disputed — they are simply new binding text.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge with any policy or legal background will immediately probe whether a student conflates Recital 71's aspirational language with Article 22's binding text — this is the single most common legal misstatement in student work on this topic, and the honest answer is that reasonable scholars (Goodman & Flaxman versus Wachter, Mittelstadt & Floridi) disagree. A second, technical probe is why a counterfactual can be handed to an applicant without opening the model at all; the correct answer is that a counterfactual describes a local decision boundary, not the model's internal mechanism, which is exactly why Rudin's interpretable-model argument and Wachter's counterfactual-recourse argument are compatible rather than competing solutions.

questions.prompt: What did the Duke team's winning FICO Challenge entry demonstrate?

options.text: That a black-box model can be explained with LIME just as well as SHAP
That a fully interpretable two-layer additive risk model matched black-box accuracy on the HELOC dataset, making post-hoc explanation unnecessary
That no interpretable model could ever match black-box accuracy on tabular credit data
That counterfactual explanations are required by the GDPR

explanations.a: The entry was not about comparing post-hoc explainers; it rejected the need for a post-hoc explainer entirely.
explanations.b: Correct — Chen, Lin, Rudin, Shaposhnik, Wang & Wang built a globally interpretable model that matched black-box accuracy, winning FICO's Recognition Award.
explanations.c: The entry demonstrated the opposite: on this problem, the accuracy gap was small enough to make the interpretable model preferable.
explanations.d: The GDPR question is a separate legal dispute (Goodman & Flaxman vs. Wachter et al.), unrelated to this specific entry's claim.

questions.prompt: Why can a counterfactual explanation (Wachter, Mittelstadt & Russell 2017) be given to an applicant without revealing the model's internal logic?

options.text: Because it describes the smallest input change needed to flip the decision, which is a statement about the local decision boundary, not the model's mechanism
Because counterfactuals always require full model disclosure by law
Because counterfactuals are only possible for linear models
Because a counterfactual is identical to a SHAP value

explanations.a: Correct — the counterfactual states "change income by X and the decision flips," which requires no disclosure of the model's architecture, training data, or type.
explanations.b: The entire appeal of the counterfactual approach is that it avoids requiring disclosure.
explanations.c: Counterfactuals are model-agnostic in principle, generated by querying any model's outputs under altered inputs.
explanations.d: A SHAP value attributes credit for the actual prediction; a counterfactual instead describes an alternative input that would produce a different outcome — a different kind of object entirely.

questions.prompt: What is the core disagreement between Goodman & Flaxman (2016) and Wachter, Mittelstadt & Floridi (2017) on the GDPR?

options.text: Whether the GDPR applies to EU citizens only
Whether the GDPR's binding Article 22 (versus its non-binding Recital 71) actually establishes an enforceable right to an explanation of automated decisions
Whether machine learning should be banned in the EU
Whether counterfactual explanations are computationally feasible

explanations.a: Territorial scope is not the point of contention between these two papers.
explanations.b: Correct — Goodman & Flaxman read the GDPR as creating a right to explanation; Wachter, Mittelstadt & Floridi argue the binding Article 22 does not actually establish this, and the stronger language lives only in the non-binding Recital 71.
explanations.c: Neither paper argues for banning machine learning; both address the scope of a legal right.
explanations.d: Computational feasibility of counterfactuals is a separate technical question, not the legal dispute at issue.

questions.prompt: Order these developments chronologically.

items.text: Goodman & Flaxman claim a GDPR right to explanation
Wachter, Mittelstadt, Russell publish counterfactual explanations; Wachter, Mittelstadt, Floridi rebut the right-to-explanation claim
FICO Explainable ML Challenge; Duke team wins with an interpretable model
EU AI Act imposes explicit transparency obligations on high-risk systems

questions.explanation: Goodman & Flaxman's claim (2016) came first, Wachter and colleagues' 2017 papers followed (both the counterfactual proposal and the rebuttal), the FICO Challenge and Duke team's win was 2018, and the EU AI Act's binding transparency obligations came later, in 2024.

lessons.label: Case: Interpretability as a Discovery Instrument in Science

sections.heading: TCAV: testing a human concept, not reading a heatmap
sections.body: Been Kim, Martin Wattenberg, Justin Gilmer, Carrie Cai, James Wexler, Fernanda Viegas, and Rory Sayres published "Interpretability Beyond Feature Attribution: Quantitative Testing with Concept Activation Vectors (TCAV)" at ICML 2018. TCAV's move is structurally different from a saliency map or a SHAP heatmap: instead of asking which raw pixels mattered, it asks whether a HUMAN-NAMED CONCEPT — "striped," or in a medical setting, a specific histopathology feature a pathologist can name — influenced the network's prediction for a class. A concept activation vector (CAV) is the direction in a hidden layer's activation space that separates examples of the concept (images containing stripes) from random examples; TCAV then computes the directional derivative of the model's output along that CAV, for a class like "zebra," across many examples, and runs a statistical significance test (a two-sided t-test against CAVs built from random concepts) rather than eyeballing a single picture. A concept only counts as influential if it beats random-concept CAVs at a stated significance level, across multiple retrainings of the CAV — this is a hypothesis test with a null distribution, not a visualization.

sections.heading: SHAP and PDP in ecology and genomics: nominating candidate drivers
sections.body: The same discipline applies outside computer vision. In ecology, gradient-boosted models with SHAP or partial dependence plots (PDP) are routinely used to rank candidate environmental drivers of a species' distribution or a disease vector's range — for example, which climate variables most shape a model's predicted habitat suitability. In genomics, SHAP-based ranking of gene expression features against a phenotype nominates candidate genes worth follow-up. In both fields, the importance ranking is explicitly treated as step one, not the finding itself.

sections.heading: The discipline: a ranking is a hypothesis generator, not a conclusion
sections.body: The throughline across TCAV and ecological/genomic SHAP use is the same discipline this whole unit has been building toward: an importance ranking, however rigorously computed, tells you what the MODEL leaned on to make predictions on the data it saw — it does not, by itself, establish that the real-world mechanism works that way. TCAV's own statistical test only establishes that the concept's direction beat chance inside the trained network; it does not establish that stripes cause zebra-ness in the world (they do, but TCAV's test is not what proves it). The legitimate scientific use of every method in this unit is as a HYPOTHESIS GENERATOR: a candidate driver nominated by SHAP or PDP, or a concept validated by TCAV, is only scientifically established once a subsequent MANIPULATION experiment or a HELD-OUT experiment on new data confirms it independently of the model that nominated it.

lessons.workedExample: A genomics team ranks 20,000 gene-expression features by SHAP importance against a disease phenotype and finds gene G ranked #1, well above a noise-column floor, stable across bootstrap seeds. They do not report "gene G causes the disease." They report: "SHAP nominates gene G as a candidate driver, robust to resampling; we are proposing a follow-up knockdown experiment to test this candidate independently of the model that generated the hypothesis." This mirrors TCAV's own logic — the CAV's statistical significance test establishes that the "striped" concept's direction beat random-concept baselines inside the trained network, a real and useful finding, but a separate, independent step (not TCAV itself) would be needed to establish that stripes are causally what a zoologist means by zebra-ness in the world.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge will ask directly: "is your ranking a finding, or a hypothesis?" — and the fair-winning answer is always the second, followed immediately by a description of the independent confirmation step (manipulation experiment, held-out replication, or wet-lab follow-up) that would actually establish it. A judge who knows TCAV may also ask what its significance test does and does not prove; the correct answer is that it is a genuine statistical hypothesis test against random-concept CAVs inside the model, not a claim about causal mechanism in the world, which is exactly the distinction this entire unit has been training the student to hold onto.

questions.prompt: What does TCAV test, and how?

options.text: Which raw pixels received the highest saliency-map intensity
Whether a human-named concept's direction (a CAV) influences a class prediction, via a directional derivative and a significance test against random-concept CAVs
The model's overall held-out accuracy
Whether the model was trained long enough to converge

explanations.a: TCAV specifically avoids raw-pixel attribution; that is what saliency maps do, and Kim et al. designed TCAV as an alternative to exactly that approach.
explanations.b: Correct — TCAV builds a concept activation vector for a human-named concept, computes the directional derivative of the class prediction along it, and tests significance against CAVs built from random concepts.
explanations.c: Held-out accuracy is a separate, unrelated model-quality metric.
explanations.d: Training convergence is not what TCAV measures; it operates on a fixed, already-trained model.

questions.prompt: In TCAV, what is a CAV (concept activation vector)?

options.text: The direction in a hidden layer's activation space that separates examples containing a human-named concept from random examples
The gradient of the loss with respect to the input pixels
A Shapley value computed for one instance
The model's final softmax output

explanations.a: Correct — a CAV is learned by training a linear classifier to separate concept examples from random examples in a hidden layer's activation space; its normal direction is the CAV.
explanations.b: That describes a saliency-map gradient, a different and pixel-level construct TCAV deliberately moves beyond.
explanations.c: Shapley values belong to a separate attribution framework (SHAP), not TCAV's concept-direction approach.
explanations.d: The softmax output is the model's prediction, not the concept direction TCAV constructs.

questions.prompt: Why is a SHAP- or PDP-nominated candidate gene or environmental driver NOT yet a scientific finding on its own?

options.text: Because the ranking reflects what the model leaned on for the data it saw, and needs an independent manipulation or held-out experiment to establish real-world mechanism
Because SHAP values are always statistically insignificant
Because PDPs cannot be computed for tree models
Because genomics data cannot be modeled with gradient boosting

explanations.a: Correct — this is the discipline the whole unit enforces: importance is a hypothesis generator, confirmed only by a subsequent experiment independent of the model that produced the ranking.
explanations.b: SHAP importance can be highly statistically robust (e.g., stable across bootstraps, well above a noise floor) and still only be a hypothesis about the model, not the world.
explanations.c: PDPs are commonly computed for tree-based gradient-boosted models; this is not a limitation.
explanations.d: Gradient boosting is a standard, widely used method in genomics for exactly this kind of feature ranking.

questions.prompt: Match each field/method pair to the role interpretability plays in it.

right.text: Statistical test of whether a human-named concept's direction influences a class
Ranks candidate environmental drivers of species distribution for follow-up study
Nominates candidate genes for wet-lab follow-up, not a final causal claim

questions.explanation: TCAV runs a formal significance test on a named concept's influence; ecological use of SHAP/PDP nominates candidate drivers for further study; genomic SHAP ranking nominates candidate genes that require independent wet-lab confirmation.

lessons.label: Judge Q&A: Defending an Interpretability Claim Out Loud

sections.heading: "Are your top two features correlated?" and "What's your baseline?"
sections.body: These are the two questions that end a weak presentation fastest, because most boards never check either. The answer that survives is a MODEL-CLASS-RELIANCE RANGE rather than a single point estimate: Fisher, Rudin & Dominici's 2019 paper "All Models are Wrong, but Many are Useful" formalizes that many different well-fitting models (the "Rashomon set") can rank the same correlated features very differently, so reporting "X: 0.31, Y: 0.09" from one fitted model overstates certainty — reporting a RANGE across the class of near-equally-accurate models (or, more simply, across bootstrap refits) is the defensible version. For the baseline question, the answer is a NOISE-COLUMN FLOOR: a synthetic random column run through the identical importance procedure, so any real feature's score can be judged against the score chance alone would produce, rather than against zero.

sections.heading: "Is that causal?" and "Would a simpler model do as well?"
sections.body: The honest answer to "is that causal" is almost always no, followed by naming the STATED CONFOUNDER that prevents the causal claim — for instance, "we cannot separate X's effect from Z's because they are correlated at r=0.7 in our data" (see the causal-inference lessons in this track for the formal reasons association is not causation). "Would a linear model or an explainable boosting machine (EBM, Lou, Caruana & Gehrke 2012) do as well" is answerable directly, not rhetorically: refit an EBM or a linear/logistic model on the identical data split, compare held-out accuracy or AUC, and report the GAP in units, not adjectives. When the gap is small or zero, the strongest available answer in this entire unit becomes true: "we fit an interpretable model instead, and it lost nothing" — echoing the Duke team's 2018 FICO Challenge result that an interpretable model matched black-box accuracy on HELOC.

sections.heading: "Did your explanation change when you reran it?" — the reproducibility check
sections.body: This question targets a documented instability: permutation importance depends on the random shuffle seed, LIME's K-LASSO surrogate depends on the sampling seed and kernel width (Ribeiro, Singh & Guestrin 2016), and even exact TreeSHAP values can shift meaningfully if the model is refit on a resampled training set, because a different fit finds a different function even with identical accuracy. The defensible answer is a RESEEDED OR BOOTSTRAPPED RERUN reported alongside the original run, plus a stated limitation: "across 20 reruns with different seeds, feature X's rank varied between 1st and 3rd, so we report its rank as 1-3 rather than a fixed 1." A team that has already run this check and states the variation up front, rather than being caught by the question, is the team that survives the room.

lessons.workedExample: A judge asks a team, in sequence: "Are your top two features correlated?" — the team answers "yes, r=0.71," having checked in advance. "What's your baseline?" — "our noise column scored 0.03; our top feature scored 0.22." "Is that causal?" — "no, we can only say held-out error rises when it's permuted; we can't separate it from its correlated partner." "Would a linear model do as well?" — "we refit a logistic regression; it lost 1.2 points of AUC, which we judged an acceptable trade for full interpretability, so we deployed it instead." "Did your explanation change when you reran it?" — "across 20 seeds the top feature's rank varied between 1st and 2nd; we report that range." Every answer names a number and a method; none retreats to "the model told us."
lessons.judgeFraming: This lesson IS the judge framing: every question here is one a fair judge asks routinely, precisely because most student boards have not run the check that would answer it. A team that has pre-run the correlation check, the noise baseline, the simpler-model comparison, and the reseed/reruns test before the judge ever asks is demonstrating exactly the discipline this whole unit has built toward — the difference between a board that shows a number and a board that shows a number it has already tried to break.

questions.prompt: Match each judge question to the check that answers it defensibly.

left.text: "Would a linear model or EBM do as well?"

right.text: A model-class-reliance range across near-equally-accurate refits
A noise-column importance floor
A stated confounder the analysis cannot separate
A direct refit and reported accuracy gap

questions.explanation: Correlation is answered with a reliance range (Fisher, Rudin & Dominici 2019), baseline with a noise-column floor, causality with a named confounder, and the simpler-model question with a direct refit and accuracy comparison.

questions.prompt: Why does permutation importance's ranking of a feature sometimes change between reruns?

options.text: Because the model itself changes its predictions randomly at inference time
Because the procedure depends on a random shuffle seed, and refitting on resampled data can also change which function is found
Because permutation importance is deterministic and never changes
Because the feature's true importance in the world changes over time

explanations.a: A fitted model's predictions for fixed inputs are deterministic; the randomness is in the shuffle procedure and any resampled refits.
explanations.b: Correct — the shuffle used to compute permutation importance is itself random, and bootstrap refits can land on a different but equally accurate function, both of which can shift a feature's rank across reruns.
explanations.c: It is not deterministic exactly because of the random shuffle step, which is why reporting a range across seeds is the defensible practice.
explanations.d: This is about measurement instability in the procedure, not a claim about the real world changing.

questions.prompt: What does it mean when a team says "we fit an interpretable model instead, and it lost nothing"?

options.text: That the interpretable model (e.g., an EBM or additive model) matched the black-box model's held-out accuracy closely enough that no post-hoc explainer was needed
That the black-box model was never actually fitted
That all explanation methods produce identical rankings
That interpretable models are always more accurate than black-box models

explanations.a: Correct — this echoes the Duke team's 2018 FICO Challenge finding: when the accuracy gap between an interpretable model and a black box is negligible, deploying the interpretable model directly sidesteps the entire explanation problem.
explanations.b: The comparison requires actually fitting both models and comparing their held-out performance directly.
explanations.c: Different explanation methods (MDI, permutation, SHAP) can and do disagree; this claim is unrelated to that fact.
explanations.d: The claim is conditional ("in this case, it lost nothing"), not a universal rule — often there is a real accuracy cost to interpretability.

questions.prompt: Order these five judge questions as a team should have already run the checks that answer them, from the check closest to the raw importance number to the check requiring an entirely separate model fit.

items.text: Add a noise-column baseline
Compute correlation among top features
Rerun across seeds/bootstraps to check stability
State the confounder that blocks a causal claim
Refit an interpretable model and compare accuracy

questions.explanation: The noise baseline and correlation check operate directly on the original importance computation; the reseed/rerun check tests the procedure's stability; naming the confounder interprets what the correlation implies for causal claims; and refitting an entirely separate interpretable model is the most involved check, requiring a new model fit and comparison.

units.label: What Fairness Means and Where Bias Enters

lessons.label: What 'Fairness' Even Means in a Model Audit

sections.heading: Two competing definitions: group vs. individual fairness
sections.body: In 2012, Cynthia Dwork, Moritz Hardt, Toniann Pitassi, Omer Reingold, and Richard Zemel published 'Fairness Through Awareness,' which named a split that still structures the field. GROUP fairness asks whether some statistic — selection rate, error rate, calibration — is equal across demographic groups; it is checkable with aggregate data alone, which is why most fairness toolkits (IBM's AIF360, Google's What-If Tool) default to reporting it. INDIVIDUAL fairness asks a stricter question: are similar people treated similarly? Dwork et al. formalized this with a Lipschitz condition: given a task-specific distance metric d(x,y) between two individuals, the distance between their output distributions must be bounded by d(x,y) — you cannot map two nearly-identical applicants to wildly different outcomes. The catch, which Dwork's team acknowledged in the same paper, is that the whole approach hinges on agreeing what 'similar' means for the task, and constructing that metric is itself a value-laden, contestable exercise — get the distance function wrong and it can smuggle bias in rather than out. Group and individual fairness can actively conflict: a model can satisfy demographic parity in aggregate while still treating two near-identical individuals from different groups very differently underneath, a tension already implicit in Dwork et al.'s own framing and later explored directly by Friedler, Scheidegger, and Venkatasubramanian's 'On the (Im)possibility of Fairness' (2016), which maps how different fairness worldviews — including individual fairness — can pull against one another.

sections.heading: Three different objects: data, model, decision
sections.body: A recurring student error is treating 'the system is biased' as one undifferentiated problem. Solon Barocas and Kate Crawford's harm taxonomy — developed across Barocas's fairness scholarship and Crawford's 2017 NIPS keynote 'The Trouble with Bias' — separates ALLOCATIVE harms — a resource or opportunity (a loan, a job interview, bail) is withheld unequally — from REPRESENTATIONAL harms, where a system reinforces stereotypes or erases a group even when nothing is literally allocated, as when image-search results for 'CEO' skew overwhelmingly toward one gender, or a translation system defaults occupations to a single gender regardless of context. Layered onto this is a three-way distinction worth memorizing: a BIASED DATASET (skewed sampling, mislabeled ground truth) is a data-collection problem; a BIASED MODEL (learned weights that amplify that skew, or that fail a subgroup even on perfectly balanced data because of how the objective function is specified) is a training-and-architecture problem; an UNJUST DECISION (a fair model applied inside a discriminatory institutional process, or a well-calibrated risk score used punitively rather than supportively) is a deployment-and-policy problem sitting entirely outside the model itself. Each has a different fix — reweighting data does not repair a bad target variable, retraining does not repair an unjust policy built on top of a fair model, and no purely technical fix repairs a process problem.

lessons.workedExample: A university builds an admissions-screening model. A group-fairness check shows admit rates are equal across two demographic groups (demographic parity holds). A judge asks: does that mean the model is fair to individuals? A careful answer says no — check whether two applicants with near-identical transcripts, essays, and test scores receive similar predicted-admit scores (individual fairness, per Dwork's Lipschitz idea). Suppose they do not: one group's borderline applicants are scored inconsistently. The next diagnostic question is which of the three objects is broken. If the training labels ('admitted' in past years) reflect a historically biased admissions committee, that is a labeling/data problem. If the model architecture amplifies small transcript differences into large score gaps for one group, that is a model problem. If the score is fair but an unaccountable dean overrides it more often for one group, that is a decision/process problem — and no amount of retraining the model fixes it.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has read Barocas and Crawford will ask you to name which of the three objects (data, model, decision) your team's fairness intervention actually targets — a vague 'we made it fair' answer collapses under this question. A sharper judge will ask whether your project ever checked individual fairness, or only ever reported a single group-level ratio; being able to explain why a model can pass demographic parity and still fail two similar individuals demonstrates you understand the Dwork critique, not just the vocabulary.

questions.prompt: In Dwork et al.'s 2012 'Fairness Through Awareness,' individual fairness is formalized using what kind of condition?

options.text: A Lipschitz condition bounding output-distance by input-distance
A requirement that selection rates be equal across groups
A requirement that false-positive rates be equal across groups
A statistical significance test on demographic parity

explanations.a: Correct — Dwork et al. require that the distance between two individuals' output distributions be bounded by a task-specific distance metric between the individuals themselves: similar people, similarly treated.
explanations.b: Equal selection rates describe demographic parity, a GROUP fairness criterion, not the individual-fairness Lipschitz condition.
explanations.c: Equal false-positive rates describe a group-level error-rate criterion (like equalized odds), not Dwork's individual-fairness formulation.
explanations.d: Dwork et al.'s paper is a definitional/mechanism-design paper, not a statistical hypothesis test.

questions.prompt: Match each fairness-audit finding to the OBJECT it primarily implicates: dataset, model, or decision process.

left.text: Historical hiring labels reflect a biased human committee
Architecture amplifies small input differences into large score gaps for one group, even on balanced data
A well-calibrated risk score is overridden more often for one group by a human decision-maker

right.text: Biased dataset
Biased model
Unjust decision/process

questions.explanation: Labels encode a data-collection problem; an architecture that amplifies differences even on clean, balanced data is a model problem; a human overriding a fair score is a policy/process problem downstream of the model entirely.

questions.prompt: Which best distinguishes an allocative harm from a representational harm, per Barocas and Crawford's taxonomy?

options.text: Allocative harms involve withholding a resource or opportunity; representational harms reinforce stereotypes without necessarily withholding anything
Allocative harms only occur in criminal justice; representational harms only occur in advertising
Representational harms are always more severe than allocative harms
The two terms are interchangeable synonyms for the same phenomenon

explanations.a: Correct — allocative harms concern who gets a job, loan, or bail decision; representational harms concern how groups are portrayed or stereotyped, independent of any specific allocation.
explanations.b: Both harm types can occur across many domains; neither is domain-restricted to one sector.
explanations.c: The taxonomy does not rank severity; both are considered serious and often co-occur.
explanations.d: They describe distinct mechanisms of harm, not the same phenomenon under two names.

questions.prompt: Order these steps as a fairness auditor should reason through them, from broadest framing to most specific diagnostic check.

items.text: Decide whether you are asking a group-fairness or individual-fairness question
Classify the suspected harm as allocative or representational
Identify whether the root cause is the dataset, the model, or the deployment decision
Apply a fix scoped to that specific object (relabel data, retrain model, or change policy)

questions.explanation: You first frame which fairness definition applies, then characterize the type of harm, then localize which of the three objects (data/model/decision) is actually broken, and only then apply a targeted fix — skipping straight to a fix without this diagnosis risks patching the wrong layer.

lessons.label: Disparate Treatment vs. Disparate Impact

sections.heading: Title VII and Griggs v. Duke Power: where the legal split comes from
sections.body: Most fairness metrics used in machine learning today did not originate in computer science — they were operationalized from U.S. employment law. Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 bans discrimination in hiring, and courts eventually recognized two distinct legal theories under it. DISPARATE TREATMENT is intentional discrimination: a rule or decision explicitly or knowingly treats someone worse because of a protected class. DISPARATE IMPACT, established by the Supreme Court's unanimous 1971 decision in Griggs v. Duke Power Co., requires no intent at all: a facially neutral policy is unlawful if it produces a substantially disproportionate adverse effect on a protected group and is not justified by business necessity. In Griggs, Duke Power's power plant required a high-school diploma and passing scores on two aptitude tests for promotion into higher-paying departments — requirements that had no demonstrated relationship to job performance but sharply excluded Black applicants, a pattern the Court struck down under Chief Justice Warren Burger's opinion, which held that Title VII 'proscribes not only overt discrimination but also practices that are fair in form, but discriminatory in operation.' Crucially, the employer can still win by proving business necessity — that the requirement genuinely predicts job performance — which is why disparate-impact cases turn on validation evidence, not just the presence of a gap. Griggs is the direct legal ancestor of every 'the protected attribute doesn't appear in the code, so we can't be biased' defense a team might be tempted to make in a model audit.

sections.heading: The four-fifths rule and why unawareness fails
sections.body: To make disparate impact operational rather than purely judicial, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission's 1978 Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures adopted the FOUR-FIFTHS (80%) RULE: if the selection rate for any group is less than 80% of the rate for the highest-selected group, that is treated as evidence of adverse impact warranting justification. This threshold is precisely what a model's DEMOGRAPHIC PARITY RATIO operationalizes in fairness toolkits — compute each group's positive-prediction rate, divide the lowest by the highest, and check whether it clears 0.8. Given this legal backdrop, a tempting fix is 'FAIRNESS THROUGH UNAWARENESS': simply drop race, gender, or other protected columns from the training data. This fails for two related reasons. First, it does nothing about disparate impact, since impact is about outcomes, not intent or inputs. Second, and more mechanically, protected attributes are redundantly encoded across the remaining features — ZIP code, name, school, and purchase history correlate strongly enough with race and gender that a model can reconstruct the dropped signal implicitly, a phenomenon explored in depth in the next lesson on proxy variables. Courts have also supplemented the four-fifths rule with formal statistical significance tests (standard-deviation or z-score tests) in later cases, since a small applicant pool can swing the ratio dramatically without reflecting real bias — a reminder that the 80% threshold is a screening heuristic, not a mathematically precise legal standard.

lessons.workedExample: A hiring model screens resumes and passes 40% of applicants from Group A but only 28% from Group B. The demographic parity ratio is 28/40 = 0.70, below the four-fifths threshold of 0.80 — this is the exact quantitative test the EEOC guidelines specify, translated directly into a model-auditing statistic. A team responds by deleting the 'gender' and 'race' columns from the training data, believing this makes the model legally safe. A judge asks whether this fixes the 0.70 ratio. It typically does not: if resumes still contain college names, ZIP codes, or extracurricular terms correlated with gender or race, the model reconstructs the dropped signal through those proxies, and the disparate-impact ratio stays roughly unchanged — because disparate impact was never about whether the attribute was visible to the algorithm, only about the resulting outcome gap.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows employment-discrimination law will ask you to distinguish disparate treatment from disparate impact precisely, because a demographic-parity check is only defensible if you can explain which legal theory it operationalizes and why intent doesn't matter for the second one. Expect a sharper follow-up: 'if you just remove the protected column, are you legally or statistically safe?' The strong answer explains that fairness through unawareness fails both as compliance (impact is about effect, not knowledge) and as an engineering matter (proxies reconstruct the signal), which is exactly why measuring fairness requires collecting the attribute you might otherwise want to hide.

questions.prompt: What did the Supreme Court establish in Griggs v. Duke Power Co. (1971)?

options.text: A facially neutral policy can be unlawful under Title VII if it causes disproportionate adverse impact without business necessity, regardless of intent
Employers must prove intent to discriminate before any policy can be challenged
Aptitude tests are always an acceptable basis for job requirements
The four-fifths rule is a binding statute passed by Congress

explanations.a: Correct — Griggs established the disparate-impact theory: Duke Power's diploma and test requirements were struck down because they disproportionately excluded Black applicants without being shown to relate to job performance, with no intent requirement.
explanations.b: This describes disparate TREATMENT, the opposite theory from what Griggs established; Griggs is precisely the case that said intent is not required.
explanations.c: Griggs found the opposite for this specific employer: the tests were struck down for lacking a demonstrated link to job performance.
explanations.d: The four-fifths rule came later, in 1978, as an EEOC administrative guideline, not a congressional statute, and is a separate development from the Griggs ruling itself.

questions.prompt: Match each legal/technical concept to its correct description.

right.text: Intentional discrimination based on a protected class
A facially neutral policy with disproportionate adverse effect, regardless of intent
EEOC threshold: selection rate below 80% of the highest group's rate signals adverse impact

questions.explanation: Disparate treatment requires intent; disparate impact does not and instead looks at outcomes of a neutral policy; the four-fifths rule is the EEOC's 1978 numerical operationalization of adverse impact, directly mirrored by the demographic parity ratio.

questions.prompt: Why does 'fairness through unawareness' (dropping the protected attribute from training data) fail to fix a disparate-impact problem?

options.text: Because outcome-level impact is unaffected, and remaining features like ZIP code or school act as proxies that let the model reconstruct the dropped signal
Because it is illegal to remove any column from a dataset
Because removing a column always increases model accuracy
Because disparate impact only applies when the attribute is explicitly present in the code

explanations.a: Correct — disparate impact is judged by outcomes, not by whether an attribute was used explicitly, and redundant encoding in correlated features (ZIP code, name, school) lets a model reconstruct the removed signal.
explanations.b: There is no such blanket illegality; the issue is a practical/statistical one about proxies, not a legal restriction on data columns.
explanations.c: Removing a predictive column typically has no consistent effect on accuracy in either direction; that is not the mechanism at issue here.
explanations.d: This inverts the actual doctrine: disparate impact is precisely defined by outcome effects and applies whether or not the attribute is present in the model.

questions.prompt: Put these developments in the correct historical order.

items.text: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act passed
Griggs v. Duke Power Co. decided
EEOC Uniform Guidelines adopt the four-fifths rule

questions.explanation: Title VII was enacted in 1964, Griggs established the disparate-impact doctrine under it in 1971, and the EEOC's Uniform Guidelines operationalized that doctrine with the numerical four-fifths rule in 1978.

lessons.label: Where Bias Enters: Sampling and Representation

sections.heading: Sampling, coverage, and non-response bias in benchmarks
sections.body: Before a model can be biased, its training and evaluation data can already be unrepresentative in three overlapping ways: SAMPLING bias (the collection process over-selects some group), COVERAGE bias (the sampling frame excludes a group entirely), and NON-RESPONSE bias (a group is invited but systematically opts out or is harder to collect from). Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru's 2018 'Gender Shades' paper (FAT* conference) quantified exactly this problem for face analysis. They found that two widely used benchmark datasets were themselves skewed: IJB-A was 79.6% lighter-skinned subjects and Adience was 86.2% lighter-skinned, measured against the dermatologist-validated Fitzpatrick skin-type scale. To make the gap measurable at all, since the flawed benchmarks could not even reveal it, they built a new, deliberately balanced benchmark, the Pilot Parliaments Benchmark (PPB), drawn from official photos of parliamentarians in three African nations (Rwanda, Senegal, South Africa) and three European nations (Iceland, Finland, Sweden) chosen specifically for their gender-balanced legislatures, and hand-annotated by dermatologists using the Fitzpatrick scale rather than crowdsourced guesses. Buolamwini and Gebru then evaluated the three commercial gender-classification systems they tested (from IBM, Microsoft, and Face++) against this balanced PPB benchmark and found error rates for darker-skinned women dramatically higher than for lighter-skinned men — in some systems over 30 percentage points apart, while lighter-skinned men were classified with near-perfect accuracy across all three.

sections.heading: Geodiversity and the mechanism: underrepresentation starves the loss function
sections.body: The same pattern shows up in object recognition. Shreya Shankar and colleagues' 2017 NIPS workshop paper 'No Classification without Representation' found that roughly 45% of ImageNet's images traced back to the United States, while countries like China and India — each with over a billion people — were represented by only about 1% and 2.1% of images respectively. Open Images showed the same lopsided pattern on somewhat different numbers: roughly 32% of its images traced back to the United States, with China again at about 1% and India at about 2%, and the six most-represented countries in Open Images together accounted for roughly 60% of that dataset's images. The mechanism connecting sampling skew to model failure is direct: a standard classifier is trained by minimizing average loss across all training examples. If a subgroup makes up 5% of the data, it contributes roughly 5% of the gradient signal, so the optimizer can achieve high aggregate accuracy while essentially ignoring that subgroup's errors — a 'neutral' loss function passively buys overall performance by underperforming on whoever is scarce in the sample. This is why an accuracy number reported in aggregate can hide a benchmark-scale failure for an entire underrepresented population until someone disaggregates it.

lessons.workedExample: A team builds a plant-identification app trained on 50,000 labeled photos scraped from a Western nature-photography site. Aggregate top-1 accuracy is a strong 91%. A judge asks the team to break accuracy down by the geographic origin of the species. Following the Shankar et al. finding that datasets like ImageNet skew roughly 45% American, the team checks their own source and finds 82% of training photos are North American or European species; tropical and Southeast Asian species make up under 6% of images despite representing a much larger share of global plant diversity. Per-subgroup accuracy on those underrepresented species turns out to be 58%, not 91% — the aggregate number was averaging over a population the optimizer had barely seen, exactly the loss-function mechanism described above: scarce examples contribute proportionally little gradient signal, so the model is never strongly pushed to get them right, and a single global accuracy metric will not by itself reveal that the shortfall exists.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge will not be satisfied by an aggregate accuracy number alone — expect the question 'what does accuracy look like broken out by subgroup, and how representative was your training sample of the real deployment population?' Naming Gender Shades' 79.6%/86.2% figures or Shankar et al.'s ~45% U.S.-centric ImageNet finding shows you know this is a documented, quantified phenomenon rather than a vague concern, and explaining the gradient-contribution mechanism (scarce subgroup, scarce loss signal) shows you understand WHY under-sampling causes failure rather than just THAT it correlates with it.

questions.prompt: In the Gender Shades study (Buolamwini and Gebru, 2018), what did the Fitzpatrick-scale analysis of IJB-A and Adience reveal?

options.text: The benchmarks were 79.6% and 86.2% lighter-skinned subjects, respectively
The benchmarks were perfectly balanced across skin types
The benchmarks contained no facial images at all
The benchmarks over-represented darker-skinned women specifically

explanations.a: Correct — IJB-A was 79.6% lighter-skinned and Adience was 86.2% lighter-skinned by Fitzpatrick classification, which motivated construction of the more balanced Pilot Parliaments Benchmark.
explanations.b: The opposite is true; this imbalance is precisely what the study documented and what motivated a new benchmark.
explanations.c: Both are real face-image benchmarks used to train and evaluate commercial gender-classification systems.
explanations.d: The datasets under-represented darker-skinned subjects overall, and error rates were subsequently found to be worst for darker-skinned women, but that is a downstream finding, not the composition finding itself.

questions.prompt: Mechanistically, why does training on an underrepresented subgroup tend to produce worse performance for that subgroup even without any explicit intent to discriminate?

options.text: A standard loss function averages error across all examples, so a small subgroup contributes proportionally little gradient signal and the optimizer can reach high aggregate performance while failing that subgroup
Optimizers deliberately assign higher loss weight to majority-group examples
Underrepresented subgroups always have noisier labels than majority groups
Neural networks cannot mathematically represent minority-group patterns regardless of data volume

explanations.a: Correct — this is the direct mechanism: proportional contribution to the averaged loss means a scarce subgroup's errors barely move the optimizer, so high aggregate accuracy is achievable while that subgroup is effectively neglected.
explanations.b: Standard loss functions do not intentionally reweight by group; the effect emerges passively from proportional representation, not deliberate weighting.
explanations.c: Label noise is a separate, independent issue from sample-size-driven gradient contribution and is not the general explanation here.
explanations.d: Networks can represent minority patterns given enough weighted or targeted data; the limitation here is sample proportion feeding into an unweighted average loss, not a representational ceiling.

questions.prompt: Match each finding to its source study.

left.text: ~45% of ImageNet images traced to the United States

right.text: Buolamwini and Gebru, 'Gender Shades' (2018)
Shankar et al., 'No Classification without Representation' (2017)

questions.explanation: Gender Shades quantified skin-type skew in facial-analysis benchmarks; Shankar et al. quantified geographic skew in ImageNet and Open Images, both documenting how sampling composition drives downstream subgroup failure.

questions.prompt: Order the causal chain from data collection to observed model failure.

items.text: Sampling/coverage process over-selects one population
Underrepresented subgroup contributes proportionally little to the averaged training loss
Optimizer converges to high aggregate accuracy while under-serving that subgroup
Per-subgroup error analysis reveals the hidden gap that aggregate accuracy concealed

questions.explanation: Skewed collection produces a skewed sample, which feeds a proportionally small gradient signal for the minority subgroup, which lets the optimizer buy aggregate accuracy cheaply by neglecting that subgroup, a gap only visible once you disaggregate the error analysis.

lessons.label: Where Bias Enters: Historical Labels and the Target Variable

sections.heading: Label bias: the target is a proxy for what you actually want
sections.body: Every supervised model needs a numeric or categorical TARGET to predict, but the concept you actually care about is often unmeasurable directly, so teams substitute a measurable stand-in. This substitution is where CONSTRUCT VALIDITY enters: does the proxy label actually measure the underlying construct? 'Arrest' is not 'crime committed' — arrest depends on policing intensity, which itself varies by neighborhood and race, so a model trained to predict arrests is really predicting policing patterns layered on top of criminal behavior. 'Being hired and retained' is not 'competence' — it reflects who a historically biased interview panel chose to hire, filtered further by whoever a workplace culture caused to stay. When the label itself encodes historical discrimination, the model learns to reproduce that discrimination with full statistical confidence, because from the optimizer's perspective it is simply fitting to the ground truth it was given — there is no signal in the training process itself that distinguishes a legitimately predictive label from a historically contaminated one. No amount of algorithmic fairness correction downstream (reweighting, threshold adjustment, post-hoc calibration) fixes a label that was never measuring the right thing in the first place, because those corrections operate on the model's outputs, not on what the model was told to learn — the error is upstream of the model entirely, in a design decision made before a single line of training code ran.

sections.heading: Amazon's scrapped resume screener: a documented case
sections.body: In 2018, Reuters reported that Amazon had built and then scrapped an internal AI recruiting tool after discovering it was biased against women. The system, developed starting around 2014, was trained on ten years of resumes submitted to Amazon, a period during which the tech industry's hires skewed heavily male — so the model learned that male-associated patterns predicted 'being hired.' The tool taught itself to penalize resumes containing the word 'women's,' as in 'women's chess club captain' or the names of two all-women's colleges, and it reportedly downgraded terms and formatting more common on résumés from women even after engineers tried editing the program to treat specific terms neutrally. Amazon engineers eventually abandoned the project rather than certify it as neutral, precisely because the target variable itself — 'resembles a past successful Amazon hire' — was built from a decade of biased human hiring decisions. This case is frequently cited alongside later healthcare-algorithm cases, such as Obermeyer et al.'s 2019 finding on a cost-based referral algorithm, as evidence that the choice of target variable is often the single most consequential fairness decision in the entire pipeline — a theme worth remembering, since it recurs whenever an easy-to-measure proxy stands in for a harder-to-measure construct like competence, need, or risk.

lessons.workedExample: A hospital wants to predict 'patient risk' to prioritize follow-up care and picks 'total healthcare cost in the next year' as the target, since cost is easy to measure from billing records. A judge asks whether cost is a good proxy for health need. It is not a clean one: patients with less access to care (due to insurance, transportation, or historically under-resourced neighborhoods) generate lower costs simply because they use the system less, not because they are healthier. A model trained on cost will therefore under-flag high-need patients from underserved groups as low-risk, systematically directing extra care toward those who already have more access to it. The fix is not a downstream statistical correction; it is picking a different, better-validated target — such as a direct clinical severity measure — before training even begins, since a biased label guarantees a biased model no matter how carefully the algorithm afterward is tuned.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge will often ask 'what exactly is your target variable measuring, and is that the same thing as what you actually care about?' — a question aimed squarely at construct validity. Being able to cite Amazon's 2018 scrapped resume screener by name, and explain precisely how 'ten years of past hires' as a target baked in a decade of biased human decisions down to specific tokens like 'women's,' shows you understand that label choice is not a neutral technical step but frequently the most consequential fairness decision in the whole project.

questions.prompt: Why is 'arrest' considered a poor proxy label for 'crime committed' in a fairness-sensitive predictive policing model?

options.text: Arrest rates reflect policing intensity and patterns, which vary by neighborhood and race independent of underlying criminal behavior
Arrest records are never digitized and so cannot be used as training data
Crime rates are always lower than arrest rates in every jurisdiction
Arrests are a perfectly unbiased measurement of criminal behavior

explanations.a: Correct — because policing intensity varies by neighborhood and demographic patterns, arrest data reflects where and whom police focus on, not purely the underlying rate of crime committed.
explanations.b: Arrest records are in fact commonly digitized and used in predictive-policing datasets; digitization is not the issue here.
explanations.c: This relationship is not fixed or universally true and is irrelevant to the construct-validity problem being described.
explanations.d: This is the exact opposite of the lesson's point — arrest is specifically a biased, policing-dependent measurement, not a clean measure of crime.

questions.prompt: In the Amazon resume-screening case reported by Reuters in 2018, what specific behavior did the scrapped model exhibit?

options.text: It penalized resumes containing the word 'women's,' such as in 'women's chess club captain'
It refused to process any resume submitted by a woman
It was found to favor women's colleges over co-ed institutions
It only affected candidates applying for non-technical roles

explanations.a: Correct — the model downgraded resumes containing 'women's' (e.g., 'women's chess club captain') and the names of all-women's colleges, learned from a decade of male-skewed hiring data.
explanations.b: The system did not categorically refuse resumes; it scored and ranked them, with a learned downgrade for certain gendered terms and patterns.
explanations.c: The reported behavior was the opposite: it downgraded rather than favored terms associated with women's institutions.
explanations.d: The tool was built to screen technical hiring broadly at Amazon; the bias was not reported as limited to non-technical roles specifically.

questions.prompt: Match each real-world target variable to the underlying construct it imperfectly proxies.

left.text: Being hired and retained at a company

right.text: Crime actually committed
Job competence
Underlying health need

questions.explanation: Each measurable proxy (arrest, hire outcome, cost) diverges from the true underlying construct (crime, competence, health need) in ways that systematically track group membership rather than the construct itself.

questions.prompt: Order the causal chain that produced Amazon's biased resume-screening tool.

items.text: Tech-industry hiring over roughly a decade skews heavily male
Amazon trains a model using 'resembles a past successful hire' as the target label
The model learns male-associated resume patterns predict the target and downgrades terms like 'women's'
Engineers cannot certify the tool as neutral even after edits, and Amazon scraps the project

questions.explanation: A decade of male-skewed hiring produced a skewed label, the label was used as the training target, the model learned to reproduce the skew at the token level, and the unfixable bias led Amazon to abandon the tool rather than deploy it.

lessons.label: Proxy Variables and Redundant Encoding

sections.heading: How ordinary features redundantly encode protected attributes
sections.body: A PROXY VARIABLE is any feature that correlates strongly enough with a protected attribute (race, gender, disability, age) that a model can use it as a substitute predictor even when the protected attribute itself is never in the dataset. ZIP code is the classic example in the United States: because of decades of residential segregation traceable in part to mid-20th-century redlining maps, ZIP code correlates strongly with race in many metro areas, and lenders historically used geography as a substitute for race in ways later challenged as illegal redlining. Surname correlates with race and national origin closely enough that the U.S. Census Bureau publishes surname-to-race distribution tables. School attended correlates with both race and socioeconomic class. Purchase history, app usage, and even typing cadence have all been shown in research literature to carry demographic signal. This means REDUNDANT ENCODING is the norm, not the exception: dropping the protected column removes your ability to directly condition on it, but the statistical information persists, diffused across a dozen ordinary-looking features the model still has full access to. Practically, this means a model can achieve strong disparate-treatment compliance (no protected attribute anywhere in the code) while still failing disparate-impact review (an outcome gap remains fully intact), because the two legal theories from the previous lesson respond to entirely different mechanisms of harm.

sections.heading: The fairness paradox and Bayesian Improved Surname Geocoding (BISG)
sections.body: This creates a genuine paradox for auditors: to MEASURE whether a model discriminates by race, you generally need race labels to check outcomes against — but many organizations do not collect race data at all, either by policy, by law, or because applicants are reluctant to disclose it. You must collect the protected attribute to audit fairness, even though the entire point of many antidiscrimination frameworks was to stop organizations from using it. Regulators facing exactly this gap in lending and healthcare data developed BAYESIAN IMPROVED SURNAME GEOCODING (BISG), a method originally developed by RAND Corporation researchers (Elliott et al.) and adopted by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau for fair-lending enforcement. BISG combines the racial distribution associated with a person's surname (from Census surname tables) with the racial distribution associated with their residential geography (from Census block-group data) using Bayes' rule, producing a probabilistic estimate of race without ever asking the individual to self-report it. BISG is not perfect — it can misclassify individuals, especially in racially mixed neighborhoods, and it estimates group membership probabilistically rather than confirming it for any one person — but it is the standard workaround regulators use to audit disparate impact when direct race data was never collected, and it has been used in enforcement actions under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act and the Fair Housing Act specifically because those laws require outcome monitoring that self-reported data alone could not support.

lessons.workedExample: A lending model drops 'race' entirely from its features, keeping only income, ZIP code, credit score, and employment history, and reports a demographic parity ratio near 1.0 across self-reported race groups in a small internal test — so the team declares the model race-blind.
