An auditor recomputes the racial composition of the applicant pool using BISG, combining each applicant's surname distribution with their ZIP code's Census demographic profile, since self-report was optional and only 40% of applicants provided it. The BISG-estimated approval-rate ratio between groups comes out closer to 0.74, below the four-fifths threshold — because ZIP code alone was carrying enough of the redundant racial signal that removing the explicit race column changed almost nothing about the actual outcome gap, it only removed the team's ability to see the gap directly without a proxy-estimation method like BISG standing in for the missing self-reported data.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge will likely press on the apparent contradiction here: 'you say collecting race data is necessary to check for bias, but doesn't collecting it also create risk?' The strong answer distinguishes COLLECTING an attribute for AUDITING purposes (measuring outcome gaps, kept separate from the decision pipeline) from USING it as a model INPUT (which is what disparate-treatment law and privacy norms restrict) — and being able to name BISG as the concrete, regulator-adopted method for estimating race when it was never collected shows the team engaged with how this tension is actually resolved in practice, not just that it exists.

questions.prompt: Why does removing a protected attribute like race from a model's training features generally fail to remove the model's ability to discriminate by race?

options.text: Other ordinary features (ZIP code, surname, school) redundantly encode enough of the same statistical signal for the model to reconstruct it
Models are legally required to re-derive any removed attribute
Removing a column always causes a training error that forces the model to substitute a random proxy
Race is impossible to encode in any feature other than a direct race label

explanations.a: Correct — features like ZIP code, surname, and school attended correlate strongly enough with race that the statistical signal persists even after the explicit attribute is dropped.
explanations.b: There is no such legal requirement; the reconstruction happens as an incidental statistical consequence of correlated features, not a legal mandate.
explanations.c: Dropping a column does not cause a training error; models simply train on the remaining features, some of which happen to be correlated proxies.
explanations.d: This is factually wrong and is exactly what this lesson demonstrates — race is redundantly encoded across many ordinary features, which is the whole problem.

questions.prompt: What does Bayesian Improved Surname Geocoding (BISG) combine to estimate an individual's race probabilistically?

options.text: Census surname-to-race distribution data with Census residential-geography race distribution data, via Bayes' rule
A person's credit score and their employment history only
Facial image analysis combined with voice recordings
Self-reported race data cross-checked against a government ID database

explanations.a: Correct — BISG combines Census surname distributions with Census geography (block-group) distributions using Bayes' rule to estimate race probabilistically without self-report.
explanations.b: Credit score and employment history are not part of the BISG method, which relies specifically on surname and geography.
explanations.c: BISG uses no biometric data whatsoever; it is a purely statistical, name-and-geography-based method.
explanations.d: BISG was developed specifically for cases where self-reported race is NOT available, so it does not rely on or cross-check self-report.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its correct description.

right.text: A feature correlated with a protected attribute closely enough to substitute for it
The phenomenon where a protected attribute's signal persists across multiple ordinary features simultaneously
A regulator-adopted Bayesian method estimating race from surname and geography

questions.explanation: A proxy variable is any single stand-in feature; redundant encoding describes how the signal is spread across many such proxies at once; BISG is the specific regulator-adopted technique for estimating the missing protected attribute from two of those proxies (surname and geography).

questions.prompt: Order the steps an auditor takes when race was never self-reported and must be estimated to check fairness.

items.text: Recognize the model's outcome gap cannot be checked directly because race was never collected
Pull Census surname-to-race distribution and residential-geography race distribution for each applicant
Combine both distributions via Bayes' rule to get a probabilistic race estimate (BISG)
Recompute the outcome ratio (e.g., approval-rate ratio) using the estimated race labels

questions.explanation: The auditor first identifies the missing-data problem, then gathers the two Census-based inputs BISG requires, combines them probabilistically, and finally uses the resulting estimated labels to recompute the fairness statistic that could not otherwise be checked.

lessons.label: Measurement Bias and Construct Validity

sections.heading: When the sensor itself, not just the label, differs by group
sections.body: A few lessons ago we covered label bias — choosing the wrong target variable. MEASUREMENT BIAS is a related but distinct failure: the instrument used to record a feature or outcome has different accuracy for different groups, so the same underlying physiological or behavioral state produces systematically different recorded values depending on group membership. This differs from label bias because the problem isn't which construct you chose to measure, but whether your measuring device measures that construct with equal fidelity across every group it is applied to. A model trained on measurements that are systematically noisier or biased for one subgroup will learn a spurious 'difference' between groups that is actually an artifact of instrument error, not a real biological or behavioral gap — and because the error is baked into the raw feature itself, no relabeling of the training target and no reweighting of the loss function can remove it; the input data itself has to be recognized as flawed and either corrected or replaced with a group-invariant measurement. This matters because measurement bias is easy to miss in an audit: a team can check calibration, error rates, and demographic parity on the model's outputs and find everything satisfactory, precisely because the model is faithfully learning from an input that was already corrupted before it ever reached the training pipeline.

sections.heading: The pulse oximetry case: Sjoding et al. 2020
sections.body: Michael Sjoding and colleagues published 'Racial Bias in Pulse Oximetry Measurement' in the New England Journal of Medicine in December 2020. Pulse oximeters estimate blood oxygen saturation by shining light through the skin and measuring how much is absorbed, and melanin can interfere with that optical read. Comparing paired pulse-oximetry readings against the gold-standard arterial blood gas test across two large patient cohorts, Sjoding's team found OCCULT HYPOXEMIA — a true arterial oxygen saturation below 88% despite a pulse-oximeter reading of 92 to 96% that looked reassuringly normal — nearly three times more often in Black patients than in white patients; in the multicenter cohort the unadjusted rates were 17.0% for Black patients versus 6.2% for white patients. Any downstream model trained to triage patients or ration supplemental oxygen using pulse-oximetry readings as a feature inherits this exact measurement gap, potentially under-triaging Black patients who are truly hypoxemic but whose device reading looks fine — a racial disparity generated entirely by the sensor's optics, with no genuine underlying difference in oxygen need. The finding gained added urgency during the COVID-19 pandemic, when pulse oximetry was widely used both in hospitals and at home to decide who needed emergency care, meaning a purely instrumental artifact could translate directly into delayed treatment for patients who looked stable on the display but were not.

lessons.workedExample: A hospital builds a model to predict which patients need urgent oxygen therapy, using pulse-oximetry readings as the primary input feature alongside heart rate and respiratory rate. Following Sjoding et al.'s finding, the model is effectively trained on a feature that under-reports true hypoxemia nearly three times more often for Black patients (17.0% occult hypoxemia in the multicenter cohort) than white patients (6.2%). A judge asks the team to explain a gap in triage recommendations across race. If the team only checks 'is the model well-calibrated to its own input data,' they will find it is — the model correctly maps oximeter readings to outcomes on average. The actual defect is invisible to that check: the input itself, the oximeter reading, silently drops true hypoxemia for one group at a much higher rate, so the model faithfully learns and propagates a race gap that originates in the pulse oximeter's optics, not in any genuine difference in patients' oxygen needs.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows the Sjoding pulse-oximetry study will ask whether your project checked for measurement bias in its INPUT features, not just bias in labels or model outputs — a subtler failure mode most teams never think to test. The strong answer explains that measurement bias survives every downstream fairness fix (reweighting, recalibration, fair-loss training) because those techniques operate on labels and predictions, not on a flawed sensor reading feeding the model; the only real fix is auditing and correcting the measurement instrument itself, or validating that group-specific correction factors are applied before the reading ever reaches the model.

questions.prompt: What did Sjoding et al. (NEJM, 2020) find about pulse oximetry and occult hypoxemia?

options.text: Black patients experienced occult hypoxemia (true low oxygen masked by a normal-looking oximeter reading) at nearly three times the rate of white patients
Pulse oximeters were found to be equally accurate across all patient groups
White patients experienced occult hypoxemia at a higher rate than Black patients
The study found no measurable difference in any oximetry outcome by race

explanations.a: Correct — the multicenter cohort showed occult hypoxemia in about 17.0% of Black patients versus 6.2% of white patients, roughly a threefold difference, linked to how melanin interacts with the device's optical measurement.
explanations.b: This is the opposite of the central finding; the study specifically documented unequal accuracy across race.
explanations.c: The direction is reversed from the actual finding; Black patients experienced the higher rate of occult hypoxemia.
explanations.d: The study's headline finding was precisely a measurable, clinically significant racial difference in undetected hypoxemia.

questions.prompt: Why can't reweighting the training loss or adjusting the model's decision threshold fix measurement bias like the pulse-oximetry gap?

options.text: Because the error is already baked into the input feature itself before the model ever sees it, so no output-side correction changes what the sensor recorded
Because reweighting techniques are illegal to apply to medical data
Because pulse oximeters do not produce numeric data compatible with machine learning models
Because occult hypoxemia only affects model outputs, never model inputs

explanations.a: Correct — reweighting and threshold adjustments operate on labels or predictions; they cannot repair a feature value that was measured incorrectly at its source before training even begins.
explanations.b: There is no such legal restriction; the issue is a technical/statistical limitation of where in the pipeline these techniques act, not legality.
explanations.c: Pulse oximeters output numeric oxygen-saturation percentages that are entirely standard, usable model inputs.
explanations.d: This has it backwards — occult hypoxemia is precisely a problem with the INPUT measurement (the oximeter reading), not a downstream output artifact.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to its correct description.

right.text: Choosing a proxy target variable that diverges from the true construct of interest
An instrument recording a feature with different accuracy across groups
True arterial oxygen saturation below 88% despite a pulse-oximeter reading of 92-96%

questions.explanation: Label bias is about picking the wrong target to predict; measurement bias is about an instrument's differential accuracy in recording a feature; occult hypoxemia is the specific clinical phenomenon Sjoding et al. quantified as evidence of that differential accuracy.

questions.prompt: Order the causal chain from device optics to a biased triage model.

items.text: Melanin interferes with the oximeter's optical absorption reading
Readings look falsely reassuring (92-96%) despite true saturation below 88% more often for Black patients
A triage model trained on oximeter readings inherits this measurement gap as an input feature
The model under-flags truly hypoxemic Black patients as low-risk despite no real difference in oxygen need

questions.explanation: The optical interaction with melanin causes the falsely reassuring reading, which becomes a corrupted input feature once used for model training, which then propagates into a racial gap in triage decisions despite the underlying oxygen need being equivalent.

lessons.label: Feedback Loops and Deployment Effects

sections.heading: Predictive policing as a self-confirming loop: Lum and Isaac 2016
sections.body: Kristian Lum and William Isaac's 2016 paper 'To predict and serve?' (Significance) simulated PredPol, a widely deployed predictive-policing algorithm, using historical drug-crime data for Oakland, California. Public-health data suggested drug use in Oakland was distributed relatively evenly across race and neighborhood, but recorded drug ARRESTS were heavily concentrated in a small number of predominantly low-income, non-white neighborhoods, reflecting where police had historically patrolled rather than where drug use actually occurred. When Lum and Isaac ran the PredPol-style algorithm on this arrest data, it predicted the highest future crime risk in exactly those same historically over-policed neighborhoods, recommending that police be dispatched there again. This is a FEEDBACK LOOP, not a static bias: more dispatched officers in a neighborhood produces more recorded arrests there (independent of the true underlying crime rate), those new arrests become the next round of training data, and the model's confidence in that neighborhood's risk score increases again — each cycle manufacturing the evidence that appears to confirm the model's own prior prediction. Lum and Isaac's central methodological point was that this dynamic is invisible if you only ever examine the model's predictions against the arrest data it was trained on, since the arrest data and the predictions are, by this point, mutually reinforcing rather than independent.

sections.heading: Runaway feedback loops and why one-shot audits understate harm
sections.body: Danielle Ensign, Sorelle Friedler, Scott Neville, Carlos Scheidegger, and Suresh Venkatasubramanian formalized this dynamic in their 2018 paper 'Runaway Feedback Loops in Predictive Policing' (FAT*), showing mathematically that under plausible assumptions, a predictive-policing system that updates on its own dispatch-generated arrest data can drive predicted crime rates in over-policed areas to diverge upward without bound over repeated rounds, even if the true underlying crime rate never changes at all. This is the core reason a STATIC, ONE-SHOT AUDIT — checking a model's fairness metrics once, on a single frozen dataset, before deployment — systematically understates real-world harm: it cannot see the loop the model will create once its own outputs start influencing what data gets collected next. The related concept of PERFORMATIVE PREDICTION, formalized by Perdomo, Zrnic, Mendler-Dünner, and Hardt (2020), names this more generally: when a model's deployment changes the very distribution it was trained to predict, the model is not a passive observer of the world but an active participant reshaping it, so fairness has to be evaluated as a dynamic process, not a one-time snapshot. Taken together, Lum and Isaac's empirical case, Ensign et al.'s formal proof, and Perdomo et al.'s general framework form a three-step argument: feedback loops are empirically real in at least one deployed system, they are mathematically capable of runaway divergence under realistic assumptions, and the underlying cause — deployment altering the training distribution itself — generalizes far beyond policing to any model whose predictions influence future data collection.

lessons.workedExample: A city adopts a predictive-policing tool trained on five years of arrest records, and a pre-deployment fairness audit finds the model's precision and recall are statistically similar across neighborhoods — it looks fair by standard one-shot metrics. Following Lum and Isaac's Oakland analysis, however, those five years of arrests were themselves generated by uneven historical patrol patterns rather than uniform underlying drug use. Once deployed, the model directs more patrols to its highest-predicted-risk neighborhoods, those patrols generate more arrests regardless of the true crime rate there, and next quarter's retraining data shows even higher recorded 'crime' in those same neighborhoods — exactly the runaway dynamic Ensign et al. proved mathematically. A judge asking 'did your fairness check account for what happens after deployment?' is asking whether the team ever simulated this loop, since the pre-deployment audit, however careful, could not have detected a problem that only emerges from the model's own influence on future data collection.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge familiar with Lum and Isaac's Oakland simulation or Ensign et al.'s runaway-feedback-loop proof will ask precisely this: 'your fairness metrics look fine on the historical test set — what happens after the model is deployed and starts influencing what data gets collected next?' Being able to explain performative prediction — that a deployed model can reshape the very distribution it was trained on — signals you understand fairness as a dynamic, closed-loop system rather than a one-time property you can certify once and forget, which is precisely the gap a static pre-deployment audit cannot see.

questions.prompt: In Lum and Isaac's 2016 simulation of PredPol on Oakland drug-crime data, what mismatch did they identify?

options.text: Drug use was distributed relatively evenly across the city, but recorded arrests were concentrated in historically over-policed, low-income, non-white neighborhoods
Drug use was concentrated in exactly the same neighborhoods as recorded arrests, with no mismatch
The algorithm predicted lower risk in neighborhoods with the most historical arrests
Oakland had no available public-health data on drug use to compare against arrest data

explanations.a: Correct — public-health data suggested relatively even drug use across the city, while arrest records were concentrated in specific over-policed neighborhoods, and the algorithm predicted the highest future risk in exactly those same neighborhoods.
explanations.b: This is the opposite of the mismatch Lum and Isaac identified; the whole point was that arrests and actual use diverged.
explanations.c: The algorithm predicted the highest risk in the neighborhoods with the most historical arrests, not lower risk.
explanations.d: Lum and Isaac specifically used public-health survey data on drug use as the comparison point against arrest records.

questions.prompt: What did Ensign et al.'s 2018 'Runaway Feedback Loops in Predictive Policing' paper mathematically demonstrate?

options.text: Predicted crime rates in over-policed areas can diverge upward without bound over repeated rounds, even if the true crime rate never changes
Predictive policing algorithms always converge to the true crime rate over time
Feedback loops only occur when police departments deliberately falsify arrest data
One-shot fairness audits are sufficient to detect all deployment-time harms

explanations.a: Correct — Ensign et al. showed that under plausible assumptions, dispatch-driven data collection can cause predicted risk in over-policed areas to run away upward indefinitely, independent of the true crime rate.
explanations.b: This is the opposite finding; the paper shows divergence away from the true rate, not convergence toward it.
explanations.c: The mechanism requires no deliberate falsification — it emerges naturally from ordinary dispatch-and-arrest data collection dynamics.
explanations.d: This directly contradicts the paper's central point, which is that static one-shot audits cannot detect a loop that only manifests after deployment.

questions.prompt: Match each researcher/team to their contribution.

left.text: Ensign, Friedler, Scheidegger, Venkatasubramanian et al. (2018)

right.text: Simulated PredPol on Oakland arrest data, showing dispatch concentrates in already-policed areas
Mathematically proved runaway divergence of predicted risk under feedback-driven data collection
Formalized 'performative prediction': deployment changes the distribution the model was trained on

questions.explanation: Lum and Isaac provided the empirical Oakland case study; Ensign et al. provided the formal mathematical proof of runaway divergence; Perdomo et al. generalized the idea into performative prediction, naming the broader phenomenon of models reshaping their own training distribution.

questions.prompt: Order the stages of a predictive-policing feedback loop as described by Lum, Isaac, and Ensign et al.

items.text: Historical patrol patterns concentrate arrests in specific neighborhoods regardless of true crime distribution
A model trained on this arrest data predicts highest future risk in those same neighborhoods
Police are dispatched more heavily to the predicted high-risk neighborhoods
Increased dispatch produces more recorded arrests there, which become the next round's training data

questions.explanation: Uneven historical patrol produces skewed arrest data, the model learns and predicts risk from that skew, dispatch decisions follow the prediction, and the resulting new arrests feed back into training data, closing and reinforcing the loop each cycle.

units.label: The Fairness Metrics Zoo

lessons.label: The Group Confusion Matrix: The Audit's Basic Instrument

sections.heading: Slicing one matrix into many
sections.body: Every fairness audit starts the same way: split the ordinary confusion matrix by a protected attribute A (race, sex, age band) and rebuild it once per group. For outcome Y, prediction Y-hat, and group a, define base rate as P(Y=1|A=a) - how often the thing you're predicting actually happens in that group, prior to any model. Selection rate is P(Y-hat=1|A=a) - how often the model outputs a positive decision for that group. From the four cells (true positive, false positive, false negative, true negative), each computed within-group, you get true positive rate TPR=P(Y-hat=1|Y=1,A=a) (a.k.a. recall or sensitivity), false positive rate FPR=P(Y-hat=1|Y=0,A=a), positive predictive value PPV=P(Y=1|Y-hat=1,A=a) (precision), and negative predictive value NPV=P(Y=0|Y-hat=0,A=a). Nothing here is new arithmetic - it is the same rates from ROC and PR analysis - the fairness move is simply computing eight-plus numbers instead of four and refusing to average them away.

sections.heading: Difference vs. ratio: the same gap, two different stories
sections.body: Once you have per-group rates, you must choose how to compare them, and this choice is not cosmetic. A RATE DIFFERENCE reports group_a_rate minus group_b_rate on the original scale (e.g., 0.02); a RATE RATIO (also called disparate impact ratio when applied to selection rate) reports the disadvantaged group's rate divided by the advantaged group's rate, i.e., min-group-rate divided by max-group-rate. These diverge sharply at low base rates. Consider a rare disease screen: group A has a 1% positive rate, group B has 2% - a difference of one percentage point, sounds trivial, but a ratio of 2.0x, sounds alarming. Now consider a hiring model: group A gets selected 40%, group B 80% - the SAME 2x ratio, but a 40-point difference, an unmistakably large gap in absolute terms. The U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission's 1978 Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures codified the ratio view as the 'four-fifths rule': a selection rate below 80% of the highest-selected group's rate is treated as evidence of adverse impact. But the EEOC guideline was written for hiring-scale base rates (tens of percent), not medical-screening-scale ones (single-digit percent), which is exactly why the same ratio threshold misleads when transplanted across domains without checking the underlying base rate.

sections.heading: Why auditors report both
sections.body: Because ratio and difference can point in opposite directions of severity depending on where the base rate sits, a competent audit reports both alongside the raw base rate and group sample sizes (n) - small n makes any rate wobble, and a ratio computed on a group of 40 people is closer to noise than to policy evidence. Courts applying the four-fifths rule since Griggs v. Duke Power Co. (1971, the Supreme Court case that first recognized facially-neutral practices could still be unlawful disparate impact) have likewise treated it as a screening trigger for further statistical testing, not a self-executing verdict - a ratio below 80% invites a binomial or chi-squared significance check against sample size before anyone calls it discrimination.

lessons.workedExample: A lending model selects (approves) 45% of Group A applicants and 30% of Group B applicants, out of 5,000 and 400 applicants respectively. Rate difference: 45%-30%=15 percentage points. Rate ratio: 30/45=0.667, meaning Group B's rate is 66.7% of Group A's - below the four-fifths (80%) threshold, flagging adverse impact under the EEOC rule. But base rate matters: if the true default risk is 10% in Group A and 25% in Group B, disparate selection could reflect disparate risk, not disparate treatment - which is exactly why an audit reports base rate, selection rate, and TPR/FPR/PPV/NPV side by side rather than the ratio alone.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has read one fairness paper will ask 'ratio or difference?' before you finish your slide - it is the single fastest way to tell if a team just ran a fairness-metrics library or actually understands what the numbers mean. Naming the 1978 EEOC four-fifths rule and immediately noting it was designed around hiring-scale base rates, not rare-outcome base rates, shows you can reason about WHEN a standard threshold breaks rather than reciting it. Reporting sample sizes n alongside every group rate also signals you know that a ratio computed on 40 people is not evidence.

questions.prompt: Group X has a true base rate of 1% and Group Y has 2% (a 2x ratio). Group P has a true base rate of 40% and Group Q has 80% (also a 2x ratio). Why can these be very different findings despite the identical ratio?

options.text: They cannot differ - a 2x ratio always represents the same severity of disparity
The absolute (percentage-point) gap is 1 point for X/Y but 40 points for P/Q, a much larger real-world impact
Ratios are undefined when base rates are below 5%
P and Q must have larger sample sizes than X and Y

explanations.a: This is exactly the trap the lesson warns against - identical ratios can hide wildly different absolute gaps.
explanations.b: Correct - the rate DIFFERENCE is 1 percentage point for X/Y versus 40 percentage points for P/Q, even though both ratios equal 2.0. Reporting only the ratio erases this.
explanations.c: Ratios are mathematically well-defined at any nonzero base rate; the issue is interpretive, not computational.
explanations.d: Sample size is a separate, unrelated concern from the base-rate level.

questions.prompt: What does the EEOC's 1978 four-fifths (80%) rule specifically threshold?

options.text: The ratio of the lowest group's TPR to the highest group's TPR
The ratio of a group's selection rate to the highest-selected group's selection rate
The ratio of false positive rates between any two groups
The difference between a group's base rate and its selection rate

explanations.a: The four-fifths rule concerns selection (hiring) rates, not TPR, which requires knowing ground-truth outcomes the EEOC guideline does not assume you have.
explanations.b: Correct - the Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures flag adverse impact when a group's selection rate falls below 80% of the highest-selected group's rate.
explanations.c: FPR ratio is a model-fairness metric requiring labeled outcomes; the four-fifths rule predates and does not require this.
explanations.d: That difference would compare a group to itself across two different quantities, which is not what the rule measures.

questions.prompt: Match each per-group rate to its correct conditional-probability definition.

right.text: P(Y-hat=1 | Y=1, A=a)
P(Y-hat=1 | Y=0, A=a)
P(Y=1 | Y-hat=1, A=a)
P(Y=1 | A=a)

questions.explanation: TPR conditions on true positives (Y=1) and asks how often the model catches them; FPR conditions on true negatives (Y=0) and asks how often the model wrongly flags them; PPV conditions on the model's positive calls (Y-hat=1) and asks how often they're correct; base rate conditions on nothing but group membership and reports the prevalence of Y=1 itself.

questions.prompt: Order these steps in building a per-group fairness audit table, from first to last.

items.text: Split the confusion matrix by protected attribute A
Compute base rate, selection rate, TPR, FPR, PPV, NPV within each group
Compare groups using BOTH rate difference and rate ratio
Report group sample sizes n alongside every rate

questions.explanation: You must first partition the data by group before any group-specific rate can be computed; once the six rates exist per group, you compare them both ways since either alone can mislead; finally, every comparison needs n reported so a reader can judge whether the rates are stable or noisy.

lessons.label: Demographic Parity and the Disparate Impact Ratio

sections.heading: The definition: equal selection, full stop
sections.body: Demographic parity (also called statistical parity) requires P(Y-hat=1|A=a) to be equal across every group a - the model must select applicants, flag patients, or approve loans at the same RATE regardless of protected group, with no reference to the true outcome Y anywhere in the definition. The disparate impact ratio operationalizes this as min-group-rate divided by max-group-rate, and the EEOC's 1978 four-fifths rule (Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures) treats a ratio below 80% as evidence of adverse impact, tracing back to the Supreme Court's 1971 Griggs v. Duke Power Co. recognition that facially neutral practices can still discriminate. Parity's appeal is its simplicity: it needs no labels, works on deployment data alone, and directly targets representation in the selected pool.

sections.heading: Dwork's objection: parity can be satisfied by randomness
sections.body: Cynthia Dwork, Moritz Hardt, Toniann Pitassi, Omer Reingold, and Richard Zemel's 2012 paper 'Fairness Through Awareness' laid out the core critique still used today: demographic parity says nothing about WHO within the disadvantaged group gets selected, only how MANY. A lender can hit parity by approving its most creditworthy Group A applicants and an equal fraction of RANDOMLY CHOSEN Group B applicants, ignoring Group B's actual qualifications entirely - satisfying the metric while making decisions less accurate, and arguably less fair, for the very group parity was meant to protect. Dwork and coauthors named the deeper failure mode a 'self-fulfilling prophecy': if a firm selects unqualified people from a group to meet a quota, their later underperformance is then read as confirming the group's unsuitability, entrenching the very stereotype the metric was built to counter. Because parity ignores Y, it also cannot distinguish a biased model from one accurately reflecting a real, structural difference in base rates.

sections.heading: Where parity is the right target anyway
sections.body: Muhammad Ali, Piotr Sapiezynski, Miranda Bogen, Aleksandra Korolova, Alan Mislove, and Aaron Rieke's 2019 study 'Discrimination through Optimization: How Facebook's Ad Delivery Can Lead to Biased Outcomes' found that Facebook's own delivery optimization skewed WHO SAW real housing and employment ads along race and gender lines even when advertisers targeted an identical, fully inclusive audience - the platform's ranking algorithm, not the advertiser, produced the skew. Here there is no legitimate Y to defer to: exposure to a job posting is the outcome being allocated, so equalizing WHO SEES the ad is the correct target, not a compromise. This distinction - is there a real Y worth deferring to, or is the 'outcome' itself just an allocation the system controls - is the single question that decides whether parity is a naive shortcut or the only defensible metric, and it recurs across every fairness criterion covered later in this unit.

lessons.workedExample: An online ad platform delivers a gender-neutral job ad. Left to its engagement-optimizing algorithm, 85% of impressions go to men and 15% to women, despite identical targeting settings - mirroring the mechanism Ali et al. (2019) documented. Because there is no ground-truth 'who deserves to see a job ad' label, imposing demographic parity on impression delivery (forcing roughly equal exposure by gender) is the defensible fix. Contrast this with a hiring model: forcing equal SELECTION rates by gender when true qualification rates differ would, per Dwork's critique, risk selecting less-qualified candidates from one group at random just to hit the number - parity is right for ad exposure, wrong as a blanket hiring rule.
lessons.judgeFraming: A sharp judge will ask you to defend parity as a CHOICE, not a default - naming Dwork et al.'s 2012 'self-fulfilling prophecy' critique shows you understand parity's central weakness (it is blind to Y and can be gamed by random selection within a group). Pairing that with Ali et al.'s 2019 Facebook ad-delivery finding demonstrates you can also identify the genuine case where parity is correct - exposure allocation with no legitimate ground truth to defer to. A team that only recites the 80% rule without this tension has not engaged with why the metric is controversial.

questions.prompt: What is the central critique Dwork et al. (2012) raised against demographic parity as a fairness criterion?

options.text: It requires access to protected attribute data, which is often illegal to collect
It ignores the true outcome Y and can be satisfied by selecting disadvantaged-group members at random rather than on merit
It is mathematically impossible to compute when there are more than two groups
It only applies to regression models, not classifiers

explanations.a: Collecting protected attributes for auditing is generally lawful and is in fact required to compute parity at all; this isn't Dwork's objection.
explanations.b: Correct - parity constrains only the selection RATE, not who is selected, so a firm can satisfy it by choosing qualified people from the favored group and random people from the disadvantaged group.
explanations.c: Parity generalizes straightforwardly to any number of groups by comparing all pairwise or min/max selection rates.
explanations.d: Parity is defined identically for classifiers (selection rate) and is not regression-specific.

questions.prompt: In Ali et al.'s 2019 study, what caused skewed ad delivery by race and gender even when advertisers set fully inclusive targeting?

options.text: Advertisers secretly used exclusionary targeting despite claiming otherwise
Facebook's own delivery-optimization algorithm, not advertiser choices, produced the skew
Users self-selected out of seeing ads outside their demographic
The study found no skew once targeting was controlled for

explanations.a: The study specifically controlled for advertiser targeting and still found skew, ruling this out.
explanations.b: Correct - the paper's core finding was that the platform's ad-delivery optimization process itself, independent of advertiser targeting, skewed exposure along demographic lines.
explanations.c: The mechanism identified was algorithmic delivery optimization, not user self-selection.
explanations.d: The study's headline result was precisely that significant skew persisted despite neutral targeting.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to the correct source or definition.

right.text: P(Y-hat=1|A=a) equal across all groups a
1978 EEOC Uniform Guidelines selection-rate threshold
Dwork et al. 2012, 'Fairness Through Awareness'
Ali et al. 2019, 'Discrimination through Optimization'

questions.explanation: Demographic parity is the statistical definition of equal selection rates; the four-fifths rule is the EEOC's 1978 operational threshold for flagging violations; the self-fulfilling prophecy critique comes from Dwork, Hardt, Pitassi, Reingold, and Zemel's 2012 paper; and the ad-delivery skew finding is Ali, Sapiezynski, Bogen, Korolova, Mislove, and Rieke's 2019 study of Facebook.

questions.prompt: Put these milestones in the history of demographic parity and disparate impact in chronological order.

items.text: Griggs v. Duke Power Co. recognizes facially-neutral practices can still be unlawful disparate impact
EEOC issues the Uniform Guidelines codifying the four-fifths (80%) rule
Dwork, Hardt, Pitassi, Reingold, and Zemel publish 'Fairness Through Awareness,' critiquing parity's blindness to Y
Ali, Sapiezynski, Bogen, Korolova, Mislove, and Rieke publish 'Discrimination through Optimization' on Facebook ad delivery

questions.explanation: Griggs (1971) first established disparate impact as unlawful even without discriminatory intent; the EEOC's Uniform Guidelines (1978) then gave enforcement agencies the operational four-fifths threshold; Dwork et al. (2012) formalized the individual-fairness critique of parity decades later; and Ali et al. (2019) demonstrated a real platform-scale case where parity in exposure allocation was the right diagnostic tool.

lessons.label: Equalized Odds and Equal Opportunity

sections.heading: Two criteria that condition on the truth
sections.body: Moritz Hardt, Eric Price, and Nathan Srebro's 2016 NeurIPS paper 'Equality of Opportunity in Supervised Learning' fixed demographic parity's core flaw by conditioning on the true label Y before comparing groups. EQUALIZED ODDS requires both TPR and FPR to match across groups, conditional on Y: P(Y-hat=1|Y=y,A=a) equal for all a, for both y=0 and y=1. EQUAL OPPORTUNITY is the relaxed, one-sided version, requiring only TPR equality - P(Y-hat=1|Y=1,A=a) equal across groups - so qualified people are caught at the same rate everywhere, while allowing FPR to differ. Hardt et al. argued equal opportunity is often the more defensible target when false positives and false negatives carry very different social costs, since it only constrains the error that harms the deserving, for example ensuring qualified loan applicants or genuinely non-recidivating defendants are treated consistently across groups without also forcing false-alarm rates to match.

sections.heading: The construction: post-processing via ROC convex hulls
sections.body: Hardt et al.'s key technical contribution is a POST-PROCESSING method: given any already-trained score function, plot each group's ROC curve (its full TPR-vs-FPR tradeoff at every threshold), take the convex hull of each, and find the point where a shared, group-specific mix of thresholds achieves equal (TPR,FPR) pairs for every group simultaneously - geometrically, the intersection of the groups' ROC convex hulls. Because different groups' ROC curves rarely cross at the same TPR/FPR point on their own, achieving equalized odds typically requires DIFFERENT decision thresholds per group, and the joint operating point sits on or below each group's original curve - meaning satisfying the constraint necessarily costs some accuracy for at least one group relative to using its own optimal threshold.

sections.heading: The FICO case study and its price
sections.body: Hardt et al. illustrated this on FICO credit scores (roughly 300-850) segmented by race, using loan repayment as Y. Racial groups have measurably different score distributions and default-rate curves in the data they used. Enforcing equal opportunity (equal TPR, i.e., equal fraction of would-repay applicants approved per group) already requires shifting some groups' thresholds off the single global optimum. Enforcing full equalized odds (equal TPR AND FPR) is strictly more costly still, because it adds a second binding constraint - the paper shows overall profit/accuracy for the lender drops further than under equal opportunity alone, illustrating a general result: the more criteria you equalize simultaneously, the further every group's threshold is pushed from its own single-group optimum. This is not a quirk of credit scoring specifically - it is a direct consequence of the convex-hull geometry, and it recurs in every domain where group score distributions differ, from lending to recidivism-risk tools to medical triage.

lessons.workedExample: A recidivism-risk tool has, at its default single threshold, TPR=0.65 and FPR=0.20 for Group A, versus TPR=0.50 and FPR=0.35 for Group B - clearly unequal on both axes. To satisfy equal OPPORTUNITY, the analyst finds a new threshold for Group B alone that raises its TPR to 0.65 (matching Group A), accepting whatever FPR results (say 0.42) since only TPR is constrained. To satisfy full equalized ODDS instead, the analyst must find thresholds for BOTH groups simultaneously landing at a single shared (TPR,FPR) pair inside both ROC convex hulls - this pair is provably no better than, and usually worse than, either group's original curve, which is exactly the geometric cost Hardt et al. quantified in the FICO study.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge testing depth here will ask why equalized odds and equal opportunity require different thresholds by group rather than one threshold for everyone - the correct answer is that group ROC curves are rarely aligned, so a single shared threshold cannot hit equal TPR/FPR unless the curves happen to cross there. A judge may also probe whether you understand equalized odds strictly dominates equal opportunity in strictness (two constraints vs. one) and therefore costs at least as much accuracy - naming the FICO case study by Hardt, Price, and Srebro (2016) and explaining that the loss is a geometric consequence of intersecting convex hulls, not an incidental modeling choice, is the signal of real comprehension.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between equalized odds and equal opportunity as defined by Hardt, Price, and Srebro (2016)?

options.text: Equalized odds requires equal TPR and FPR across groups; equal opportunity requires only equal TPR
Equal opportunity requires equal TPR and FPR; equalized odds requires only equal TPR
They are the same criterion with different names
Equalized odds applies only to regression, equal opportunity only to classification

explanations.a: Correct - equalized odds is the stricter, two-sided constraint (equal TPR AND FPR); equal opportunity relaxes it to the one-sided TPR-only constraint.
explanations.b: This reverses the definitions - equal opportunity is the ONE-sided relaxation, not the two-sided constraint.
explanations.c: They are formally distinct: equalized odds is strictly stronger since it adds the FPR-equality constraint.
explanations.d: Both criteria were originally defined for classification; the distinction is which error rates are constrained, not the task type.

questions.prompt: Why does achieving equalized odds typically require different classification thresholds for different groups?

options.text: Because regulators require visibly different thresholds to prove compliance
Because each group's ROC curve traces a different TPR-vs-FPR tradeoff, so a shared (TPR,FPR) point generally falls at a different threshold on each curve
Because equalized odds is only defined for models with per-group training data
Because a single global threshold always produces equal odds by construction

explanations.a: There is no such regulatory requirement; the need for different thresholds is a geometric consequence of unequal ROC curves.
explanations.b: Correct - the ROC curves differ by group, so the shared operating point found via the convex-hull construction sits at a different threshold value for each group's own curve.
explanations.c: The post-processing method works on any trained score function regardless of how it was trained.
explanations.d: A single global threshold generally produces UNEQUAL odds precisely because group ROC curves differ; this is the whole reason the correction is needed.

questions.prompt: Match each fairness concept to its correct formal statement or role.

right.text: Equal TPR AND FPR across groups, conditional on Y
Equal TPR only across groups, conditional on Y=1
Geometric tool for finding a shared achievable (TPR,FPR) operating point per group
Hardt et al.'s empirical illustration of the accuracy cost of each criterion on credit scores

questions.explanation: Equalized odds constrains both TPR and FPR; equal opportunity constrains only TPR; the ROC convex hull is the geometric device used to find a jointly-achievable operating point across groups; and the FICO case study is where Hardt, Price, and Srebro demonstrated the resulting accuracy tradeoff empirically.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of Hardt et al.'s post-processing construction for enforcing equalized odds on an existing trained model.

items.text: Take the already-trained score function as fixed input
Plot each group's full ROC curve across all thresholds
Compute the convex hull of each group's ROC curve
Find the (TPR,FPR) point achievable within the intersection of all groups' convex hulls
Assign each group its own threshold (or threshold mixture) that reaches that shared point

questions.explanation: The method starts from a fixed pre-trained score, builds each group's ROC curve, takes convex hulls to allow randomized threshold mixtures, locates the shared operating point achievable by every group, and finally assigns each group whatever threshold (or probabilistic mixture of two thresholds) reaches that shared point.

lessons.label: Predictive Parity and Calibration Within Groups

sections.heading: PPV equality and calibration: the decision-maker's-eye view
sections.body: Predictive parity, formalized by Alexandra Chouldechova in her 2017 paper 'Fair Prediction with Disparate Impact,' requires PPV to be equal across groups: P(Y=1|Y-hat=1,A=a) the same for every a - among those the model flags positive, the same fraction actually are positive, regardless of group. CALIBRATION WITHIN GROUPS is the finer-grained, score-level version: for every score value s the model outputs, P(Y=1|S=s,A=a)=s should hold within each group - a risk score of 0.7 means a 70% chance of the outcome, whether the person is in Group A or Group B. Calibration is typically checked visually with a per-group RELIABILITY DIAGRAM: bin predicted scores, plot each bin's mean predicted score against its observed outcome frequency, and look for a straight diagonal line within every group, not just in the pooled population.

sections.heading: Why this is the criterion a face-value user needs
sections.body: The practical case for this family is simple: anyone who reads a score and acts on it at face value - a judge setting bail, a doctor weighing a risk percentage - needs the score to mean the same thing for everyone. A calibrated score lets a decision-maker apply one uniform policy ('detain above 0.6') without silently disadvantaging one group's meaning of '0.6.' This is exactly the fairness Northpointe (the company behind the COMPAS recidivism tool) invoked in response to ProPublica's 2016 investigation: Northpointe argued COMPAS was well-calibrated and satisfied predictive parity, so a given risk decile meant approximately the same reoffense probability for Black and White defendants alike, and therefore the tool was fair by their chosen standard. ProPublica itself confirmed COMPAS's predictive parity numbers were close - roughly 41% of White and 37% of Black high-risk-labeled defendants did not reoffend - which is what made the dispute a genuine clash of two valid but incompatible fairness definitions rather than one side simply being wrong.

sections.heading: The catch Chouldechova proved
sections.body: Chouldechova's 2017 result is that predictive parity is INCOMPATIBLE with equalized error rates (equal FPR and FNR) whenever base rates differ across groups AND the classifier isn't perfect - you cannot generally have both at once. ProPublica's data showed Black defendants had a substantially higher base recidivism rate (about 51%) than White defendants (about 39%), so even a perfectly calibrated COMPAS mathematically produced unequal false positive rates: ProPublica reported 44.9% of Black non-reoffenders were misclassified high-risk versus 23.5% of White non-reoffenders. Both sides were right about their own metric and wrong to claim the other side's metric was satisfied too - the tradeoff is a theorem forced by the base-rate gap itself, not a modeling failure either party could have engineered away.

lessons.workedExample: A hospital risk score assigns a 0.3 probability of readmission to patients from two demographic groups. Checking calibration within groups: among all Group A patients scored near 0.3, 31% are actually readmitted; among Group B patients scored near 0.3, 29% are - close enough to call both groups well-calibrated at that score band, satisfying calibration-within-groups. But Group B's true base readmission rate is far lower than Group A's overall. Following Chouldechova's theorem, this calibrated score will necessarily show a higher false positive rate in the higher-base-rate group (A) than in B, even though calibration - the property a treating physician actually relies on - holds perfectly in both groups.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing this metric will ask you to state Chouldechova's incompatibility result precisely: predictive parity and equalized odds cannot both hold when base rates differ and the model is imperfect. Bonus depth comes from explaining WHY calibration is the criterion a face-value score user needs (a judge, doctor, or loan officer reading '70% risk' needs it to mean the same thing everywhere) and then naming that this was literally Northpointe's real-world defense of COMPAS against ProPublica's 2016 critique - showing you can connect the abstract theorem to the actual public controversy it explains.

questions.prompt: What did Alexandra Chouldechova's 2017 paper prove about predictive parity and equalized odds/error-rate balance?

options.text: They are always compatible if the model is well-trained
They are generally incompatible whenever group base rates differ and the classifier is imperfect
Predictive parity is mathematically impossible to define for more than two groups
Calibration and predictive parity are unrelated concepts

explanations.a: Better training cannot resolve the incompatibility - it is a structural, mathematical result about differing base rates, not a fixable modeling flaw.
explanations.b: Correct - Chouldechova showed predictive parity and equalized error rates cannot both hold, except in the special case of equal base rates or a perfect classifier.
explanations.c: Predictive parity generalizes to any number of groups by comparing PPV pairwise or across all groups.
explanations.d: Predictive parity is essentially calibration collapsed to a single positive/negative threshold rather than the full score range; they are closely related, not unrelated.

questions.prompt: Northpointe defended COMPAS against ProPublica's 2016 critique by pointing to which property?

options.text: COMPAS achieved demographic parity in its risk-score distribution
COMPAS was calibrated and satisfied predictive parity - a given score meant roughly the same reoffense probability across race
COMPAS had equal false positive rates across race
COMPAS did not use race as an input feature

explanations.a: Northpointe's defense was about score meaning (calibration/PPV), not about equalizing selection rates.
explanations.b: Correct - Northpointe's core argument was that COMPAS was well-calibrated, so a given risk score corresponded to a similar actual reoffense rate regardless of race.
explanations.c: ProPublica's critique was precisely that FPR was UNEQUAL across race (44.9% vs. 23.5%); Northpointe did not claim equal FPR, since Chouldechova's theorem shows this is incompatible with the calibration they did claim.
explanations.d: The dispute was about the tool's statistical properties across race, not about whether race was a direct input; this was not Northpointe's stated defense.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to its correct definition or figure from the lesson.

right.text: P(Y=1|Y-hat=1,A=a) equal across groups
P(Y=1|S=s,A=a)=s for every score s, within each group
Plot of mean predicted score vs. observed outcome frequency per bin, per group
44.9% of Black non-reoffenders vs. 23.5% of White non-reoffenders misclassified high-risk

questions.explanation: Predictive parity is the binary PPV-equality condition; calibration within groups is its continuous, score-level generalization; the reliability diagram is the standard visual check for calibration; and the 44.9%-vs-23.5% figure is ProPublica's headline number from its 2016 COMPAS investigation.

questions.prompt: Order the events of the COMPAS predictive-parity vs. error-rate controversy chronologically.

items.text: ProPublica publishes its investigation showing unequal false positive rates by race
Northpointe responds that COMPAS is calibrated and satisfies predictive parity
Chouldechova publishes 'Fair Prediction with Disparate Impact,' proving the two properties are generally incompatible

questions.explanation: ProPublica's 2016 investigation and Northpointe's contemporaneous rebuttal both preceded Chouldechova's 2017 paper, which supplied the formal theorem explaining why both sides could be simultaneously correct about their own chosen metric.

lessons.label: Individual and Counterfactual Fairness

sections.heading: Individual fairness and its unsolved problem
sections.body: Cynthia Dwork, Moritz Hardt, Toniann Pitassi, Omer Reingold, and Richard Zemel's 2012 'Fairness Through Awareness' proposed INDIVIDUAL FAIRNESS as an alternative to group metrics: similar individuals should receive similar outcomes, formalized as a Lipschitz condition - the distance between two people's predictions should be bounded by the distance between the people themselves, under some similarity metric d. This directly targets what group metrics can miss (two similar people treated differently within the same group), but it shifts all the difficulty onto one unanswered question: who defines d, and how? Dwork et al. openly acknowledged this - constructing a fair similarity metric for, say, loan applicants is itself a value-laden, task-specific problem the framework does not solve, which is why individual fairness has seen far less real-world deployment than group metrics despite being conceptually appealing.

sections.heading: Counterfactual fairness: reasoning through a causal graph
sections.body: Matt Kusner, Joshua Loftus, Chris Russell, and Ricardo Silva's 2017 paper 'Counterfactual Fairness' reframed the question causally: a prediction is counterfactually fair if it would be the same in a counterfactual world where an individual's protected attribute A had been different, holding all attributes NOT causally downstream of A fixed. This requires an explicit causal graph, distinguishing variables A causes from variables that merely correlate with A. Niki Kilbertus, Mateo Rojas-Carulla, Giambattista Parascandolo, Moritz Hardt, Dominik Janzing, and Bernhard Scholkopf's 2017 'Avoiding Discrimination through Causal Reasoning' extended this to PROXY DISCRIMINATION: a feature can encode A almost perfectly (zip code standing in for race) without ever naming A, so fairness requires reasoning about the causal graph's structure, not just which raw features are excluded.

sections.heading: Berkeley 1973: resolving vs. non-resolving variables
sections.body: Peter Bickel, Eugene Hammel, and J. William O'Connell's 1975 Science paper on UC Berkeley graduate admissions is the canonical teaching case. Raw data: 44.5% of 2,691 male applicants admitted versus 30.4% of 1,835 female admitted - an apparent large gap. But conditioning on DEPARTMENT reversed the story: most departments showed a small bias favoring women once you controlled for which department each person applied to; women disproportionately applied to more competitive, lower-admit-rate departments (English) while men favored higher-admit-rate ones (engineering). Department is a RESOLVING variable here ONLY IF department CHOICE itself was untainted by discrimination - if department choice were itself steered by gender bias (e.g., women discouraged from applying to engineering), conditioning on it would wrongly launder that bias away, making it NON-resolving instead. Bickel and coauthors' broader methodological point - that 'measuring bias is harder than usually assumed' - is the reason this single dataset has been reused in statistics and fairness courses for fifty years: it forces the resolving/non-resolving distinction into the open rather than letting an aggregate number settle the question by itself.

lessons.workedExample: A model uses zip code to predict loan default. Two applicants of different races live in the same zip code and have identical income, credit history, and employment - individual fairness would demand they get near-identical scores, since d(person1,person2) is small. But suppose zip code is itself a near-perfect proxy for race, shaped by historic redlining - Kilbertus et al.'s proxy-discrimination framework says the fix isn't removing zip code as a raw input, it's tracing the causal graph: if zip code's influence on the prediction flows entirely through a path tainted by historical discriminatory housing policy rather than through legitimate credit-relevant information, that path should be severed even though zip code never explicitly encodes race.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge testing this concept will ask you to name WHO is supposed to define the similarity metric in individual fairness - the honest answer, which Dwork et al. themselves admitted in 2012, is that the framework does not solve this and it remains task-specific and contested. On the Berkeley case, a judge may push on whether conditioning on department was legitimate; the sharp answer is that it depends entirely on whether department choice was itself free of gender bias - naming the resolving/non-resolving variable distinction explicitly is what separates a team that memorized 'Simpson's paradox' from one that understands when adjusting for a variable is valid.

questions.prompt: What unresolved problem did Dwork et al. (2012) acknowledge about individual fairness?

options.text: It cannot be applied to classification tasks, only regression
It requires a similarity metric d between individuals, and who should define this metric is left unresolved and value-laden
It is mathematically equivalent to demographic parity
It only works when the protected attribute is binary

explanations.a: Individual fairness as a Lipschitz condition applies to any prediction task; task type is not the acknowledged limitation.
explanations.b: Correct - Dwork et al. explicitly noted that constructing a fair, task-appropriate similarity metric is itself an unsolved, value-laden problem the framework does not answer.
explanations.c: Individual fairness and demographic parity are distinct frameworks - one constrains similar-individual treatment, the other constrains group-level selection rates.
explanations.d: The similarity-metric framework does not depend on A being binary; this restriction is not part of the definition.

questions.prompt: In the 1973 Berkeley admissions data, what made department a valid (resolving) variable to condition on?

options.text: Department was correlated with gender, which is sufficient on its own
Department choice itself was untainted by gender discrimination - it wasn't itself a product of the bias being investigated
There were more departments than applicants
Department admit rates were identical for men and women

explanations.a: Mere correlation with the protected attribute is NOT sufficient - that describes a non-resolving variable just as easily as a resolving one; the deciding factor is whether the variable is itself tainted.
explanations.b: Correct - a variable is resolving only if it is not itself a product of the discrimination under study; if women's department choices were themselves shaped by bias, department would be non-resolving instead.
explanations.c: This has no bearing on whether conditioning on department is statistically or causally valid.
explanations.d: Admit rates famously varied a great deal by department; that variation is precisely why conditioning on department changed the aggregate picture.

questions.prompt: Match each researcher(s)/paper to the concept they introduced.

left.text: Kilbertus, Rojas-Carulla, Parascandolo, Hardt, Janzing, Scholkopf (2017)

right.text: Individual fairness via a Lipschitz similarity condition
Counterfactual fairness via causal graphs
Proxy discrimination through causal reasoning
Berkeley admissions Simpson's-paradox analysis

questions.explanation: Dwork et al. introduced individual fairness in 'Fairness Through Awareness'; Kusner et al. introduced counterfactual fairness formalized on causal graphs; Kilbertus et al. extended causal reasoning to proxy variables that encode a protected attribute without naming it; and Bickel, Hammel, and O'Connell's 1975 Science paper produced the canonical Simpson's-paradox admissions case.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for evaluating whether conditioning on a variable Z (like department) is a valid 'resolving' adjustment when auditing a gender gap in Y (like admission).

items.text: Observe a raw, unconditional gap between groups in outcome Y
Identify a candidate variable Z that both groups pass through before reaching Y (e.g., department choice)
Determine whether Z itself was influenced by gender-based discrimination
If Z is untainted, treat it as resolving and recompute the gap within levels of Z; if tainted, treat it as non-resolving and do not use it to explain away the gap

questions.explanation: The audit begins with the raw aggregate gap, then identifies an intermediate variable both groups pass through, then critically asks whether that intermediate variable was itself shaped by the discrimination under investigation, and only then decides whether conditioning on it legitimately explains the gap or illegitimately launders it away.

lessons.label: Multi-Group, Multi-Class, and Intersectional Slicing

sections.heading: From two groups to many, and one class to many
sections.body: Every metric so far assumed two groups and a binary outcome. Real audits rarely get that luxury. With K groups, a pairwise comparison (Group A vs. B) becomes K-choose-2 comparisons, so practice shifts to reporting the min-to-max ratio or max-pairwise-difference across all groups at once, and to MACRO-AVERAGING: compute each fairness metric within every group separately, then average the per-group values unweighted, so a small group's disparity counts as much as a large group's rather than being swamped in a pooled figure. Multi-class outcomes compound this further - TPR, FPR, and PPV all need a per-class, per-group version (e.g., one-vs-rest), multiplying the number of numbers an audit must track by both K and the number of classes. A 5-group, 4-class audit already produces dozens of individual rates before anyone even asks about intersections between attributes, which is precisely why teams default to summary ratios and lose the granular signal a real audit needs.

sections.heading: Fairness gerrymandering: passing on average, failing on the intersection
sections.body: Michael Kearns, Seth Neel, Aaron Roth, and Zhiwei Steven Wu's 2018 ICML paper 'Preventing Fairness Gerrymandering: Auditing and Learning for Subgroup Fairness' proved a model can satisfy a fairness constraint on every MARGINAL protected group (equal treatment by race alone, equal treatment by sex alone) while badly violating it on a STRUCTURED INTERSECTION of those groups (e.g., Black women specifically) - the marginal averages hide a subgroup-specific failure, analogous to how a gerrymandered voting map can look proportionate district-by-district while diluting one coalition's power overall. Their proposed fix audits and constrains fairness over an exponentially large family of subgroups defined by combinations of attributes, not just the marginal ones, using a learner-auditor game to find the worst-violating subgroup efficiently rather than enumerating every combination.

sections.heading: Gender Shades: the minimal honest slice
sections.body: Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru's 2018 'Gender Shades: Intersectional Accuracy Disparities in Commercial Gender Classification' tested three commercial facial-analysis systems (from IBM, Microsoft, and Face++) using a purpose-built, balanced dataset scored on the Fitzpatrick skin-type scale, then sliced by BOTH gender and skin type at once - four cells: lighter men, lighter women, darker men, darker women. The marginal numbers looked fine (overall accuracy above 90% for most systems), but the intersectional slice told a different story: error rates for lighter-skinned men stayed under 1%, while darker-skinned women hit error rates as high as 34.7% on the worst-performing system (IBM's classifier). Reporting gender and race marginally, as most vendors did before this study, would have missed this entirely - the 2x2 cut is presented as the minimal slice below which real disparities go invisible. Buolamwini and Raji's follow-up audit work also pushed IBM, Microsoft, and Face++ to publicly report improved accuracy on darker-skinned women within a year, showing the metric itself, once made visible, changed vendor behavior.

lessons.workedExample: A hiring classifier reports demographic parity satisfied for race (Black/White selection rates within 2 points) and satisfied for gender (male/female selection rates within 1 point). An auditor applying Kearns et al.'s subgroup-fairness check partitions further into the four race-by-gender cells and finds Black women selected at 22% versus 41% for White men - an 19-point gap invisible in either marginal check, because White women and Black men's rates happened to offset each other in the aggregate averages. This is fairness gerrymandering exactly as Kearns et al. described it: two clean marginals hiding one badly-failing intersection.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge will ask why checking fairness marginally by race and then marginally by sex is insufficient - the correct answer is Kearns et al.'s 2018 fairness-gerrymandering result: satisfying every marginal constraint provides no guarantee about structured subgroups, because favorable and unfavorable cells within a marginal group can offset. Citing Gender Shades' specific 2018 numbers (under 1% error for lighter-skinned men vs. up to 34.7% for darker-skinned women, the study's worst-case cell) as the canonical real-world demonstration - and explaining why the 2x2 phenotype-by-gender slice, not either attribute alone, was necessary to see it - is what separates genuine engagement from a name-drop.

questions.prompt: What did Kearns, Neel, Roth, and Wu's 2018 'fairness gerrymandering' result show?

options.text: A model satisfying fairness on every marginal protected group can still badly violate fairness on a structured intersectional subgroup
Marginal fairness checks are mathematically equivalent to intersectional checks
Intersectional fairness is impossible to define for more than two attributes
Gerrymandering only applies to voting systems, not machine learning

explanations.a: Correct - this is the core theorem: marginal-group fairness provides no guarantee about fairness on intersections of those same groups.
explanations.b: The whole point of the paper is that they are NOT equivalent - marginal checks can pass while intersectional checks fail.
explanations.c: Intersectional fairness is well-defined for any number of attributes; Kearns et al.'s method explicitly handles exponentially many subgroups.
explanations.d: The paper explicitly borrows the gerrymandering analogy to describe an analogous statistical phenomenon in classifier fairness, not literal voting systems.

questions.prompt: In Buolamwini and Gebru's 2018 Gender Shades study, which slice revealed the largest error-rate disparity?

options.text: Race alone, without controlling for gender
Gender alone, without controlling for skin type
The intersection of skin type and gender - darker-skinned women specifically
Overall accuracy, pooled across all subjects

explanations.a: Race/skin-type alone did not reveal the full disparity, which depended on the gender dimension as well.
explanations.b: Gender alone did not reveal the full disparity, which depended on the skin-type dimension as well.
explanations.c: Correct - only the joint slice (darker-skinned AND female) revealed error rates up to 34.7%, versus under 1% for lighter-skinned men.
explanations.d: Pooled accuracy for most systems looked strong (above 90%) and specifically obscured the intersectional disparity.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its correct description.

right.text: Averaging a metric across groups unweighted, so small groups aren't swamped by large ones
Passing every marginal-group fairness check while failing on a structured subgroup
Slicing simultaneously by skin type and gender to reveal disparities invisible in either dimension alone
The number of possible attribute combinations growing exponentially as more protected attributes are added

questions.explanation: Macro-averaging protects small groups from being outweighed in a pooled metric; fairness gerrymandering is Kearns et al.'s term for passing marginals while failing intersections; the Gender Shades 2x2 design intersected skin type and gender to expose the worst-case cell; and combinatorial explosion describes why auditing every possible intersection quickly becomes computationally and statistically infeasible as attributes multiply.

questions.prompt: Order these steps in conducting a proper intersectional fairness audit, from broadest to most granular.

items.text: Check the pooled, ungrouped metric across the entire dataset
Check the metric marginally within each single protected attribute (race alone, gender alone)
Check the metric on structured intersections of two or more attributes (race x gender)
Flag any subgroup, however small, whose disparity is masked by favorable offsetting cells in the marginals

questions.explanation: A thorough audit moves from the coarsest view (pooled metric) to single-attribute marginals, then to intersectional slices across attributes, and finally to explicitly flagging any subgroup whose problem is invisible unless you check the intersection directly - exactly the failure mode Kearns et al. and Buolamwini and Gebru independently documented.

lessons.label: Fairness Beyond Classification: Regression, Ranking, and Generation

sections.heading: Regression: no confusion matrix to slice
sections.body: TPR, FPR, and PPV all presuppose a binary decision - they simply do not exist for a continuous prediction like a price estimate or a risk SCORE treated as a number rather than a threshold. Alekh Agarwal, Miroslav Dudik, and Zhiwei Steven Wu's 2019 ICML paper 'Fair Regression: Quantitative Definitions and Reduction-Based Algorithms' adapts fairness to this setting with two definitions: STATISTICAL PARITY IN REGRESSION (the predicted value's distribution, not just its mean, should be similar across groups) and BOUNDED GROUP LOSS, which requires each group's own loss (e.g., group-wise MAE or RMSE) to stay below some shared ceiling, rather than forcing every group's loss to be identical - a group with harder-to-predict outcomes is allowed a higher loss up to the bound, rather than being forced to exactly match an easier group's error. Their reduction-based algorithm re-uses standard regression solvers as a subroutine under a sequence of reweighted training sets, avoiding a bespoke fair-regression model architecture entirely. Crucially, bounded group loss does not force artificial equality between groups whose outcomes are genuinely harder or easier to predict - it only rules out one group being sacrificed for another's accuracy, which is a materially weaker and more defensible ask than exact parity of error.

sections.heading: Ranking: exposure, not selection, is the resource
sections.body: A ranked list doesn't select or reject; position IS the outcome, since users click overwhelmingly on top results. Ashudeep Singh and Thorsten Joachims' 2018 KDD paper 'Fairness of Exposure in Rankings' formalizes this: each rank position confers an EXPOSURE (roughly, the probability a user examines that slot), and their framework constrains the ratio of total exposure to total merit/relevance for each group, generalizing demographic parity and equalized-odds-style constraints into position-weighted exposure constraints, then solves for the utility-maximizing ranking under that exposure constraint via a linear program. This matters because two items with nearly equal relevance scores can receive wildly different exposure if one lands at rank 1 and the other at rank 30, and a group whose items are systematically relevance-tied-but-ranked-lower suffers even with 'equal average relevance.'

sections.heading: Generation: no Y at all
sections.body: Generative and LLM outputs have no single ground-truth label to condition on, so the field instead measures STEREOTYPE and REPRESENTATION benchmarks: co-occurrence of demographic terms with sentiment or occupation words, refusal-rate gaps across identity mentions in prompts, and image-generation prompts (e.g., 'a CEO') audited for the demographic distribution of outputs against real-world or target distributions. None of TPR, PPV, or calibration transfer, because there is no Y-hat/Y pair to build a confusion matrix from at all - conflating 'the model treats prompts about different groups differently' with a classification fairness violation is a common and diagnosable student error. The right move is to name which representation or stereotype benchmark applies to the specific generative task at hand, rather than reaching for a confusion-matrix vocabulary that has no target to attach to.

lessons.workedExample: A ranking system for job candidates gives Group A and Group B nearly identical average relevance scores (0.71 vs. 0.70), which looks fair by any group-average check. But following Singh and Joachims' framework, Group A's candidates cluster in ranks 1-10 while Group B's equally-relevant candidates cluster in ranks 40-50 - since click-through and recruiter attention drop sharply past the first page, Group B receives a small fraction of the EXPOSURE its relevance would justify. A classification-style fairness check (comparing average scores) completely misses this; only an exposure-weighted audit across rank position catches it.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge will probe whether you understand WHY confusion-matrix metrics (TPR, FPR, PPV) cannot simply be repurposed for regression, ranking, or generation - the correct answer names the missing ingredient in each case: regression has no threshold to define a confusion matrix, ranking's outcome is exposure/position rather than a selection decision (Singh and Joachims 2018), and generation has no ground-truth label Y at all. Explicitly naming Agarwal, Dudik, and Wu's 2019 bounded group loss as the regression analogue, rather than vaguely saying 'use RMSE,' shows you know there is a real, dated, peer-reviewed adaptation rather than an improvised workaround.

questions.prompt: Why can't TPR, FPR, and PPV be directly applied to a continuous regression output?

options.text: These rates are defined only for datasets larger than 10,000 rows
They all presuppose a binary decision (a confusion-matrix cell), which a continuous prediction does not have without an arbitrary threshold
Regression models cannot be evaluated for fairness under any framework
TPR and FPR require the protected attribute to be continuous as well

explanations.a: Dataset size is unrelated to whether a confusion-matrix rate is definable.
explanations.b: Correct - TPR, FPR, and PPV are all conditional probabilities over the four confusion-matrix cells, which require a binary Y-hat/Y pair that a raw continuous prediction does not have.
explanations.c: Regression fairness is well-studied - Agarwal, Dudik, and Wu's 2019 paper is a direct example - it just requires different definitions (bounded group loss, statistical parity in regression) rather than TPR/FPR.
explanations.d: The protected attribute's type (categorical or continuous) is unrelated to why TPR/FPR fail for continuous Y-hat.

questions.prompt: In Singh and Joachims' 2018 framework, what is the central resource being allocated in a ranking, distinct from a classifier's 'selection'?

options.text: Training data volume per group
Exposure - the attention or examination probability conferred by rank position
The number of features used per group
The regularization strength applied per group

explanations.a: Training data volume is a modeling input, not the outcome the fairness framework allocates.
explanations.b: Correct - Singh and Joachims formalize exposure (roughly, the probability a user examines a given rank position) as the resource that must be fairly allocated relative to relevance.
explanations.c: Feature count is a modeling choice unrelated to the ranking-fairness framework's target quantity.
explanations.d: Regularization strength is an optimization hyperparameter, not the allocated resource in this framework.

questions.prompt: Match each output type to the fairness concept designed specifically for it.

right.text: Bounded group loss (Agarwal, Dudik, Wu 2019)
Exposure-allocation fairness (Singh and Joachims 2018)
Stereotype and representation benchmarks
TPR/FPR/PPV-based group confusion matrix metrics

questions.explanation: Regression uses bounded group loss or distributional parity since there's no confusion matrix; ranking uses exposure-allocation fairness since position, not selection, is the resource; generative/LLM outputs use stereotype and representation benchmarks since there is no ground-truth Y; and only binary classification supports the TPR/FPR/PPV family directly.

questions.prompt: Order these reasoning steps for correctly adapting a fairness check to a non-classification setting.
