items.text: Identify that the output is continuous, ranked, or generative rather than a binary decision
Recognize that TPR/FPR/PPV-style confusion-matrix metrics do not apply without an artificial and often unjustified threshold
Select the metric family built for that output type (bounded group loss, exposure allocation, or representation benchmarks)
Apply and report that metric per group, rather than forcing a classification metric onto data it wasn't designed for

questions.explanation: The reasoning must start by recognizing the output type, then explicitly rule out confusion-matrix metrics as inapplicable, then choose the metric family purpose-built for that setting, and only then apply and report it - skipping straight to a classification metric on ranked or generated output is exactly the common student error this lesson targets.

units.label: Impossibility Results and Reading Fairness Evidence

lessons.label: The Impossibility Theorem, Stated Carefully

sections.heading: Three conditions, one 2016 paper
sections.body: In 2016 Jon Kleinberg, Sendhil Mullainathan, and Manish Raghavan posted "Inherent Trade-Offs in the Fair Determination of Risk Scores" (published at ITCS 2017), written directly in response to the ProPublica-Northpointe dispute over the COMPAS recidivism tool, proving that three intuitively reasonable fairness properties cannot all hold at once except in narrow special cases. CALIBRATION WITHIN GROUPS requires that among everyone in group A assigned score s, a fraction s actually experiences the outcome - a score of 0.7 must mean "70% of these people reoffend" whether the person is Black or white. BALANCE FOR THE POSITIVE CLASS requires that people who actually experience the outcome (true positives) receive the same average score across groups - equivalently, in binary decisions, equal false negative rates. BALANCE FOR THE NEGATIVE CLASS mirrors this for people who do not experience the outcome - equal false positive rates. Each condition alone looks like an uncontroversial definition of "not systematically wrong about this group," and each was, separately, exactly what Northpointe and ProPublica each claimed their side had satisfied.

sections.heading: Why base rate is the hinge
sections.body: The three conditions jointly force an algebraic identity linking each group's false positive rate, false negative rate, and base rate - the same relationship Alexandra Chouldechova derives independently for the binary case a year later. Because that identity ties FPR and FNR to base rate through fixed algebra, holding calibration and both balance conditions across two groups is only possible if the groups' base rates are equal, or the classifier is a perfect predictor - every score exactly 0 or 1, no errors at all. The proof is a counting argument over expectations of the score conditioned on label and group, showing the three constraints overdetermine the system otherwise. The theorem also has an approximate version: near-satisfaction of all three requires near-equal base rates, with the forced imbalance growing roughly in proportion to the base-rate gap - so real, unequal base rates like COMPAS's 51% versus 39% two-year recidivism guarantee measurable, not catastrophic, violations.

sections.heading: What the theorem forbids, precisely
sections.body: The theorem does not declare fairness impossible or endorse any specific disparity. It forbids one specific combination - calibration plus BOTH balance conditions simultaneously, for score-based classifiers, when base rates differ and prediction is imperfect. Calibration alone, or one balance condition alone, remains achievable, and deliberate trade-offs among the three remain a live design choice that a policymaker, not the algebra, must make. The result says nothing about demographic parity (equal selection rates), individual fairness, or counterfactual fairness - those are separate definitions with their own, separate trade-offs the 2016 result does not touch. It also assumes the risk score itself is an honest estimate of the true outcome probability; it says nothing about what happens when the underlying labels used to build that score are themselves biased.

lessons.workedExample: A parole board uses a risk score calibrated so that among defendants scored 0.6, 60% reoffend in both Group A (base rate 50%) and Group B (base rate 30%) - calibration holds. A student checks balance next: is the average score among people who actually reoffend the same in both groups? If Group B's true positives cluster at lower scores than Group A's, balance for the positive class fails - meaning Group B's genuine reoffenders are systematically flagged lower-risk than Group A's, producing a higher false negative rate for Group B even though the tool is perfectly calibrated. The student now has language for what happened: calibration and balance are in tension precisely because the base rates (50% vs. 30%) differ.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge testing this concept will ask you to state which two of the three conditions your team's model satisfies and which one it necessarily sacrifices - vague answers like "we made it fair" collapse instantly under this question. Naming Kleinberg, Mullainathan, and Raghavan by name and the 2016/2017 date signals you read the primary source rather than a summary. The sharpest follow-up asks what the theorem does NOT forbid; answering correctly (it says nothing about demographic parity or individual fairness) shows you understand the result's precise scope rather than treating it as a blanket excuse for any disparity.

questions.prompt: Under what condition can calibration, balance for the positive class, and balance for the negative class all hold simultaneously across two groups with different base rates?

options.text: Never, under any circumstances
Only if the classifier is a perfect predictor (every score exactly 0 or 1, no errors)
Only if the sample size is large enough
Only if the protected attribute is removed from the training data

explanations.a: The theorem allows an exception: perfect prediction, or equal base rates, permits all three.
explanations.b: Correct - Kleinberg, Mullainathan, and Raghavan's proof shows perfect prediction (or equal base rates) is the only escape from the trade-off.
explanations.c: Sample size affects estimation noise, not the underlying algebraic incompatibility the theorem describes.
explanations.d: Removing the protected attribute (fairness through unawareness) does not change base rates or the algebraic identity, so it does not resolve the trade-off.

questions.prompt: Match each fairness condition from the 2016 theorem to its correct definition.

right.text: Among people scored s in a group, fraction s actually experience the outcome
Equal average score (equal FNR) among people who actually experience the outcome
Equal average score (equal FPR) among people who do not experience the outcome

questions.explanation: Calibration is about score meaning matching reality within score bands; balance for the positive class is about true positives being scored equally (equal FNR) across groups; balance for the negative class is the mirror condition for true negatives (equal FPR).

questions.prompt: Which claim does the 2016 Kleinberg-Mullainathan-Raghavan theorem NOT make?

options.text: That calibration and both balance conditions cannot all hold when base rates differ and prediction is imperfect
That the forced imbalance grows roughly with the size of the base-rate gap in the approximate version
That demographic parity and individual fairness are also proven incompatible with calibration
That satisfying only one of the three conditions remains achievable

explanations.a: This is exactly the theorem's core claim.
explanations.b: This is the approximate/robustness version of the theorem, also a genuine claim it makes.
explanations.c: Correct - the theorem is silent on demographic parity, individual fairness, and counterfactual fairness; those require separate analyses.
explanations.d: The theorem explicitly leaves single conditions (or any two conditions in general) achievable; it only rules out all three together under the stated circumstances.

questions.prompt: Order the logical steps of the impossibility argument from premise to conclusion.

items.text: State the three conditions: calibration, balance for positives, balance for negatives
Derive the algebraic identity linking FPR, FNR, and base rate
Show the identity cannot satisfy all three unless base rates are equal or prediction is perfect
Conclude that unequal base rates with imperfect prediction force at least one condition to fail

questions.explanation: The proof begins by defining the three properties, then derives the algebraic relationship the properties jointly impose, then shows that relationship is only satisfiable under the equal-base-rate-or-perfect-prediction condition, and finally concludes that any real-world case violating that condition must fail at least one property.

lessons.label: Chouldechova's Version and the Algebra of the Trade-off

sections.heading: One identity, derived from Bayes' rule
sections.body: In her 2017 paper "Fair Prediction with Disparate Impact" (Big Data, vol. 5, pp. 153-163, first presented at the FAT/ML 2016 workshop), statistician Alexandra Chouldechova derived a simpler, binary-classifier version of the same trade-off Kleinberg, Mullainathan, and Raghavan proved for continuous scores that same year. Starting from Bayes' rule applied to positive predictive value (PPV), she showed FPR = (p/(1-p)) x ((1-PPV)/PPV) x TPR, where p is the group's base rate (true prevalence of the outcome), PPV is precision, and TPR is the true positive rate (recall); an analogous identity, derived the same way from Bayes' rule applied to negative predictive value (NPV), relates FNR to base rate p, NPV, and the true negative rate (TNR). This single equation says the false positive rate is mechanically determined by base rate, PPV, and TPR - there is no fourth free parameter to absorb the disagreement. If two groups are held to the same PPV (predictive parity) and roughly the same TPR, but have different base rates p, their FPR values are ALGEBRAICALLY forced apart. No amount of retraining or threshold tuning fixes this without sacrificing PPV, TPR, or both - the identity is a fact about arithmetic, not about any particular vendor's model.

sections.heading: Plugging in the COMPAS numbers
sections.body: ProPublica's 2016 investigation found Northpointe's COMPAS tool had a two-year general recidivism base rate of about 51% for Black defendants and 39% for white defendants. Northpointe's defense showed PPV was roughly equal across the two groups (COMPAS was similarly well-calibrated for both) - satisfying predictive parity, its chosen fairness criterion. Plug equal PPV and roughly equal TPR into Chouldechova's identity: the ratio of the two groups' odds, p/(1-p), becomes the multiplier on FPR. For Black defendants, 0.51/0.49 = 1.04; for white defendants, 0.39/0.61 = 0.64. That ratio of ratios, 1.04/0.64 = 1.63, means predictive parity alone mechanically predicts Black defendants' FPR should run roughly 1.6x white defendants' FPR - and ProPublica in fact measured Black defendants misclassified as high-risk non-reoffenders at roughly twice the rate of white defendants.

sections.heading: Both sides were arithmetically correct
sections.body: This is the paper's central, uncomfortable point: Northpointe's claim (predictive parity holds) and ProPublica's claim (FPR is unequal) are not competing measurements of the same thing - they are two different, both-valid fairness criteria that Chouldechova's identity proves cannot simultaneously hold when base rates differ. The 2016 public feud, covered nationally after ProPublica's "Machine Bias" article, was not a factual dispute about whose numbers were right; it was two organizations optimizing for, and reporting, different metrics, each internally consistent, while implicitly disagreeing about which metric a pretrial risk tool should be judged on.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher replicating the dispute takes ProPublica's released COMPAS dataset, splits it by race, and confirms PPV for the 'high risk' threshold is close for both groups (~63% for Black defendants vs. ~59% for white defendants, satisfying rough predictive parity). Computing FPR directly, they find roughly 45% for Black defendants versus roughly 23% for white defendants - a wider gap than the 1.63x the simplified equal-TPR algebra predicts, because real TPR was NOT quite equal either. The lesson: the identity gives the mechanism and a rough magnitude, but real data adds a second source of divergence (unequal TPR) on top of unequal base rates.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge will want to see the identity itself, not just the conclusion - deriving FPR = (p/(1-p)) x ((1-PPV)/PPV) x TPR on the spot from Bayes' rule and correctly identifying which quantity is doing the work (the base-rate odds ratio) is the single strongest signal you understand the mechanism rather than having memorized "COMPAS was biased." A fair judge will also probe whether you can say Northpointe was NOT lying - both parties measured real, correct numbers; the disagreement was about which metric to prioritize, not about arithmetic.

questions.prompt: In Chouldechova's identity FPR = (p/(1-p)) x ((1-PPV)/PPV) x TPR, what does p represent?

options.text: The group's positive predictive value
The group's base rate (true prevalence of the outcome)
The overall model accuracy
The classification threshold used to call someone 'high risk'

explanations.a: PPV is a separate term in the identity, appearing as (1-PPV)/PPV.
explanations.b: Correct - p is the base rate, the true fraction of the group that experiences the outcome, and it is the term that mechanically forces FPR apart when it differs across groups.
explanations.c: Accuracy does not appear as a term in this identity at all.
explanations.d: The threshold determines how PPV, TPR, and FPR are computed but is not itself the p term.

questions.prompt: Using Chouldechova's identity with base rates p=0.51 and p=0.39 and assuming equal PPV and TPR across groups, which group's FPR is mechanically forced higher?

options.text: The group with the higher base rate (p=0.51)
The group with the lower base rate (p=0.39)
Neither - equal PPV guarantees equal FPR regardless of base rate
It cannot be determined without knowing sample sizes

explanations.a: Correct - the odds p/(1-p) are larger for p=0.51 (1.04) than for p=0.39 (0.64), so with PPV and TPR held equal, the higher-base-rate group's FPR is mechanically forced higher, matching ProPublica's finding for Black defendants.
explanations.b: This reverses the direction; the higher base rate produces the higher forced FPR, not the lower one.
explanations.c: Equal PPV does not guarantee equal FPR unless base rates are also equal - that is precisely the point of the identity.
explanations.d: Sample size affects estimation noise, not the algebraic direction of the identity, which is determined by p, PPV, and TPR alone.

questions.prompt: Match each party in the 2016 COMPAS dispute to the fairness criterion their published numbers actually satisfied.

right.text: Predictive parity: PPV roughly equal across race
Error rate imbalance: FPR/FNR unequal across race

questions.explanation: Northpointe showed COMPAS was similarly well-calibrated with roughly equal PPV across race groups; ProPublica showed FPR and FNR differed sharply across race groups. Chouldechova's identity shows both findings can be simultaneously true and are not a contradiction.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of deriving Chouldechova's FPR identity from Bayes' rule.

items.text: Write Bayes' rule for PPV in terms of base rate p, TPR, and FPR
Algebraically isolate FPR on one side of the equation
Arrive at FPR = (p/(1-p)) x ((1-PPV)/PPV) x TPR
Substitute two groups' differing p values to compare forced FPR

questions.explanation: The derivation starts from Bayes' rule expressing PPV as a function of p, TPR, and FPR, then rearranges to solve for FPR, producing the closed-form identity, which can then be evaluated at each group's actual base rate to see how much FPR is forced apart.

lessons.label: Why Base Rates Differ, and Whether That Settles Anything

sections.heading: The fatalist move, and why it is too fast
sections.body: The impossibility results tempt a shortcut: "the math proves a trade-off exists, so an unequal FPR is just an unavoidable fact of unequal base rates - nothing to fix." Sam Corbett-Davies and Sharad Goel's 2018 review "The Measure and Mismeasure of Fairness: A Critical Review of Fair Machine Learning" (Stanford University working paper, widely cited across the fairness-in-ML literature) rejects this move directly. A measured base rate - like COMPAS's 51% versus 39% two-year rearrest rate - is not a fact about biology or character; it is a fact about ARRESTS, which are themselves the output of a separately biased process: differential policing intensity by neighborhood, differential charging decisions by prosecutors, and the well-documented gap between RE-ARREST and actual RE-OFFENDING, since rearrest only tracks reoffending faithfully if policing effort is applied uniformly across neighborhoods and demographic groups, which criminology research repeatedly shows it is not. When the label you train and audit against is itself contaminated by unequal surveillance, an unequal base rate can be partly an artifact of measurement - a downstream consequence of historical enforcement patterns - not a fixed ground truth the algebra must simply accept as given.

sections.heading: Inframarginality: why matching rates can still mislead
sections.body: Corbett-Davies and Goel's second, more technical critique is INFRAMARGINALITY. Error-rate parity (matching FPR or FNR across groups) implicitly assumes both groups' risk distributions have the same SHAPE around the decision threshold. If one group's risk distribution is more spread out - more people far from the threshold in both directions - matching aggregate FPR across groups can force the threshold in one group away from its risk-minimizing point, denying low-risk people in that group opportunities they'd get under a risk-based rule, purely to hit a population-level rate target. The authors argue this makes rate-matching an imperfect proxy for the thing people actually care about: whether similarly-risky individuals are treated similarly, which a single aggregate FPR number cannot verify.

sections.heading: The alternative: threshold rules, not metric-matching
sections.body: Corbett-Davies and Goel argue for applying a single risk threshold consistently across groups, informed by accurate, ideally de-biased risk estimates, rather than post-hoc forcing group error-rate metrics to match after the fact. This does not resolve the impossibility theorem or make the trade-off disappear - it reframes which quantity deserves scrutiny: the base rate and the risk estimate feeding the model, not just the downstream error-rate arithmetic that Chouldechova's identity describes. Under their framing, the more productive fight is upstream, over what counts as a fair label and a fair risk estimate in the first place.

lessons.workedExample: A city compares two neighborhoods: Neighborhood A, patrolled twice as often per capita as Neighborhood B. Recorded "base rate" of rearrest is higher in A - but is that because people in A actually commit more crime, or because twice the policing catches twice the fraction of whatever crime occurs? A researcher re-runs the audit using self-reported offending survey data instead of arrest records for a subset of the population and finds the true offending gap between A and B is much smaller than the arrest-based gap. This does not make the impossibility theorem false - it changes which number should be plugged into Chouldechova's identity as p, and shows why accepting a measured base rate uncritically can smuggle policing bias into a supposedly neutral piece of algebra.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing this concept wants to see you separate two claims that get conflated constantly: "a mathematical trade-off exists given the base rates" (true, proven) and "therefore the observed disparity is acceptable or inevitable" (a non-sequitur the math does not license). Citing Corbett-Davies and Goel by name, and being able to explain inframarginality in one sentence - that matching aggregate rates can still mistreat individuals when risk distributions differ in shape - shows you did not stop at the headline theorem and actually engaged with its critics.

questions.prompt: According to Corbett-Davies and Goel (2018), why can accepting a measured base rate as settled ground truth be misleading?

options.text: Because base rates are computed incorrectly by most software libraries
Because the measured base rate (e.g., arrest rate) can itself be a product of biased measurement processes like unequal policing
Because base rates are always exactly equal across groups in reality
Because Chouldechova's identity does not actually depend on base rate

explanations.a: This is not the critique - the concern is conceptual (what the number represents), not a software bug.
explanations.b: Correct - arrest-based base rates reflect policing intensity as well as actual offending, so treating them as neutral ground truth can smuggle measurement bias into the fairness analysis.
explanations.c: The critique argues the opposite is often unclear - measured base rates may differ partly due to bias, not that true rates are secretly equal.
explanations.d: The identity's whole mechanism runs through base rate p; the critique is about what value to trust as p, not whether p matters.

questions.prompt: What does "inframarginality" describe in the Corbett-Davies and Goel critique?

options.text: The fact that error rate parity assumes equal-shaped risk distributions, so matching aggregate rates can misallocate decisions for individuals away from the threshold
The tendency of small subgroups to have noisy metric estimates
The requirement that all fairness metrics use the same decision threshold
A method for correcting mislabeled training data

explanations.a: Correct - inframarginality is the critique that aggregate rate-matching assumes similarly-shaped risk distributions across groups, an assumption that fails when distributions differ, letting rate-matching harm individuals far from the margin.
explanations.b: That describes a small-sample statistical concern, a separate topic from inframarginality.
explanations.c: Inframarginality is about the risk distribution's shape, not a procedural requirement about thresholds.
explanations.d: Inframarginality is a conceptual critique of metric-matching, not a data-cleaning technique.

questions.prompt: Match each claim to whether the impossibility theorem itself proves it or leaves it open.

left.text: Given fixed base rates, calibration and both balance conditions cannot all hold
The observed unequal base rates are an acceptable, unquestionable fact
Rate-matching correctly treats similarly-risky individuals the same way

right.text: Proven by the theorem
Left open / disputed by critics like Corbett-Davies and Goel

questions.explanation: The theorem proves only the algebraic incompatibility given the base rates as inputs; it says nothing about whether those base rates should be trusted at face value, and Corbett-Davies and Goel separately argue rate-matching does not guarantee individual-level treatment is actually similar.

questions.prompt: Order the argument from the fatalist claim to the Corbett-Davies/Goel rebuttal.

items.text: Observe unequal FPR/FNR between two groups
Fatalist claim: the impossibility theorem means this disparity is unavoidable and acceptable
Rebuttal: examine whether the base rate itself reflects biased measurement (e.g., policing intensity)
Conclusion: the theorem's algebra is correct, but which number to trust as the base rate remains an open, contestable question

questions.explanation: The sequence starts from an observed disparity, notes the tempting but flawed fatalist conclusion, then applies Corbett-Davies and Goel's critique that measured base rates may encode prior bias, landing on the correct conclusion that the theorem's math is sound but its inputs deserve scrutiny.

lessons.label: Fairness-Accuracy Trade-offs and the Pareto Frontier

sections.heading: The intuition, and why it is often wrong in practice
sections.body: Constraining a model to satisfy a fairness metric - equal FPR across groups, say - restricts the space of decision rules it can choose from, so intuition says accuracy must drop: fewer options, worse best option. Kit Rodolfa, Hemank Lamba, and Rayid Ghani's 2021 Nature Machine Intelligence paper "Empirical Observation of Negligible Fairness-Accuracy Trade-offs in Machine Learning for Public Policy" (from Carnegie Mellon's Data Science for Social Good program) tested this intuition across real deployed models in four domains: education (predicting a student's risk of not graduating on time), mental health crisis response, criminal justice recidivism, and housing safety inspection prioritization. Across these public-policy settings, applying post-hoc disparity-mitigation methods to equalize error rates cost close to nothing in accuracy - the fairness-constrained model and the unconstrained model landed within a fraction of a percentage point of each other on the accuracy metric (typically precision at the resource-constrained top-k threshold each program actually used) that mattered for the deployment. The intuition that fairness necessarily costs accuracy turned out to be an assumption, not an empirical law - the size of the region of near-optimal models is usually larger than one thinks.

sections.heading: Tracing the frontier: reductions and exponentiated gradient
sections.body: Rather than accept one fairness-accuracy point, Agarwal, Beygelzimer, Dudik, Langford, and Wallach's 2018 ICML paper "A Reductions Approach to Fair Classification" gives a method for tracing the whole trade-off curve. Their algorithm reduces fair classification to a sequence of ordinary cost-sensitive classification problems, using the EXPONENTIATED GRADIENT algorithm to search over a Lagrangian relaxation of the fairness constraint - at each iteration it reweights training examples by group and adjusts a dual variable measuring how badly the constraint is violated, converging to a randomized classifier that satisfies the constraint (e.g., demographic parity or equalized odds) within a chosen tolerance. Sweeping that tolerance from loose to strict and refitting at each setting traces out the empirical PARETO FRONTIER - accuracy on one axis, fairness violation on the other - showing exactly how much accuracy each unit of fairness costs at every point, rather than asserting a single number.

sections.heading: Reading a frontier plot honestly
sections.body: A well-drawn frontier plot shows the unconstrained model's point, then a curve of constrained models moving left as fairness violation shrinks. A near-flat curve near the unconstrained point (as Rodolfa et al. found) means fairness was nearly free; a steep drop means real accuracy is being spent - and a team should report where on that curve their deployed model sits, not just its two endpoints.

lessons.workedExample: A team building a school dropout-risk model for a district finds their unconstrained model has 82% accuracy with a 14-point FPR gap between demographic groups. Applying the reductions approach with a loose fairness tolerance (max 8-point gap) yields 81.7% accuracy - a 0.3-point cost for cutting the gap nearly in half. Tightening to a 2-point tolerance yields 79.5% accuracy - a steeper 2.5-point cost for the last few points of gap closure. Plotting these three models (unconstrained, loose, tight) as points on a frontier shows the curve is nearly flat until the last stretch, letting the team argue, with a specific number, that closing most of the gap was nearly free and only the final increment was expensive.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks "what did fairness cost you in accuracy?" is testing whether you have an actual frontier plot or just a single before/after number. Citing Rodolfa, Lamba, and Ghani's 2021 finding that the cost was often negligible across real public-policy deployments shows you know the empirical answer isn't always a steep trade-off, while naming the Agarwal et al. reductions/exponentiated-gradient method as HOW you'd trace your own frontier (rather than guessing at one point) shows you understand this as a tunable curve, not a fixed law.

questions.prompt: What did Rodolfa, Lamba, and Ghani (2021) find when applying disparity-mitigation methods across several public-policy ML deployments?

options.text: Accuracy dropped by roughly half in every deployment studied
The fairness-accuracy trade-off was often negligible - fairness was substantially improved with little to no accuracy cost
Fairness constraints could not be applied to any of the deployments studied
Only criminal justice models showed any trade-off at all

explanations.a: Their empirical finding was the opposite - trade-offs were typically small, not large.
explanations.b: Correct - across education, mental health, criminal justice, and housing-safety deployments, post-hoc mitigation substantially improved fairness with negligible accuracy cost.
explanations.c: The methods were successfully applied across all four domains studied in the paper.
explanations.d: The negligible-trade-off finding held broadly across domains, not selectively in one.

questions.prompt: What role does the exponentiated gradient algorithm play in Agarwal et al.'s (2018) reductions approach?

options.text: It directly measures a group's base rate from raw data
It searches a Lagrangian relaxation of the fairness constraint, reweighting examples and adjusting a dual variable until the constraint is satisfied within tolerance
It replaces the need for a labeled training set
It is used only to compute FPR and FNR after training is complete

explanations.a: Base rate is a property of the data, not something the optimization algorithm computes.
explanations.b: Correct - exponentiated gradient iteratively reweights training examples by group and updates a dual variable tracking constraint violation, converging to a classifier meeting the fairness tolerance.
explanations.c: The method still requires labeled training data; it reduces fair classification to cost-sensitive classification problems trained on that data.
explanations.d: It operates during training to find the constrained classifier, not as a post-training evaluation step.

questions.prompt: Match each contribution to its correct paper.

left.text: Empirical finding of negligible fairness-accuracy trade-offs across public-policy deployments
Reductions approach using exponentiated gradient to trace the fairness-accuracy frontier

right.text: Rodolfa, Lamba, and Ghani, 2021, Nature Machine Intelligence
Agarwal, Beygelzimer, Dudik, Langford, and Wallach, 2018, ICML

questions.explanation: Rodolfa, Lamba, and Ghani's 2021 paper is the empirical study finding negligible trade-offs across real deployments; Agarwal et al.'s 2018 paper is the algorithmic method for tracing the whole fairness-accuracy curve via reductions and exponentiated gradient.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of tracing an empirical fairness-accuracy Pareto frontier.

items.text: Train the unconstrained model and record its accuracy and fairness violation
Choose a fairness tolerance and run the reductions/exponentiated-gradient method to fit a constrained model
Repeat across a sweep of tolerances from loose to strict
Plot accuracy against fairness violation for all fitted models to reveal the frontier's shape

questions.explanation: You first establish the unconstrained baseline, then fit one constrained model at a chosen tolerance, then repeat that fit across a range of tolerances, and finally plot all the resulting points together to see whether the curve is flat (cheap fairness) or steep (costly fairness).

lessons.label: Uncertainty in Subgroup Metrics

sections.heading: Why splitting by group multiplies your noise
sections.body: A model evaluated on 4,000 test examples might feel well-estimated overall, but a fairness audit that splits those 4,000 into six intersecting groups (say, two sexes by three age bands) can leave a single group with only 30-50 positive-outcome examples to estimate its true positive rate from - the denominator that matters for TPR is the count of actual positives in that slice, which is often a small fraction of the slice's total size. TPR is a proportion estimated from a binomial process, and its standard error scales as roughly sqrt(p(1-p)/n) - at n=38, even a true TPR of 0.70 has a standard error near 0.074, meaning a single-run estimate can easily land anywhere from roughly 0.55 to 0.85 by chance alone, a 30-point spread from sampling variation alone before any real disparity is added. A headline finding like "Group X has a 20-point lower TPR than Group Y" computed on subgroups this small is frequently within one or two standard errors of pure sampling noise - a different random test split, or a slightly different month of data, could show the gap reversed or vanished entirely.

sections.heading: Bootstrap confidence intervals on the rate DIFFERENCE
sections.body: The fix is to bootstrap the difference itself, not just each rate separately: resample the two groups' examples with replacement thousands of times, recompute TPR_X minus TPR_Y on each resample, and read off the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles as a 95% confidence interval on the gap. If that interval comfortably contains zero, the observed 20-point gap is not distinguishable from no gap at all given the sample size - a conclusion a single point estimate hides completely. Reporting "TPR gap = 20 points, 95% CI [-8, +48]" is honest in a way "TPR gap = 20 points" alone is not.

sections.heading: The multiple-comparisons trap when scanning many slices
sections.body: Auditing dozens of intersectional slices (race x sex x age x region) and reporting only the worst gap found invites a second problem: with enough slices, some will show a large gap by chance even if no true disparity exists anywhere in the underlying population, the same logic behind Bonferroni correction in any multi-hypothesis setting - test 40 independent slices at a nominal 5% significance level and you expect roughly two false alarms by chance alone. So a slice-mining audit needs either a corrected significance threshold (dividing the target p-value by the number of slices tested) or pre-registered slices decided before looking at results, not a post-hoc pick of whichever number looked scariest after the fact.

lessons.workedExample: An audit of a hiring-screen model reports a 20-point TPR gap between two subgroups, computed from n=38 true positives in the smaller group. A student bootstraps the gap with 5,000 resamples and finds the 95% CI runs from -9 points to +47 points - comfortably straddling zero. The honest report is not "no bias found" (the interval does not rule out a real gap either) but "the current sample cannot distinguish this 20-point gap from sampling noise; a larger sample or a wider error bar around it is needed before treating 20 points as a finding." The student also checks: this slice was one of 24 intersectional groups scanned, so even a nominally significant gap in one slice deserves a multiple-comparisons correction before being reported as the headline result.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees a bar chart with a dramatic subgroup gap and no error bars or n reported will ask for both immediately - it is the fastest tell between an audit that understands statistics and one that just ran a fairness library function on whatever data existed. Being able to state that a 20-point gap on n=38 can sit inside a bootstrap CI that spans zero, and that scanning many intersectional slices without correction manufactures false positives, shows you treat subgroup metrics as ESTIMATES with uncertainty, not exact numbers.

questions.prompt: Why does splitting an evaluation set into many intersectional subgroups make fairness metrics noisier?

options.text: Because smaller per-group sample sizes n increase the standard error of each group's rate estimate
Because subgroup metrics use a fundamentally different formula than the overall metric
Because intersectional groups always have lower true accuracy
Because bootstrapping is required by law for subgroup analysis

explanations.a: Correct - standard error of a proportion scales as roughly sqrt(p(1-p)/n), so as n shrinks with finer slicing, the same true rate produces much wider estimate variability.
explanations.b: The formula (e.g., TPR = TP/(TP+FN)) is identical; only the sample size feeding it changes.
explanations.c: Smaller groups are not inherently less accurate - they are simply estimated less precisely.
explanations.d: Bootstrapping is a recommended statistical practice here, not a legal requirement.

questions.prompt: A 95% bootstrap confidence interval on a TPR gap between two groups is [-9, +47] percentage points. What is the correct interpretation?

options.text: The gap is definitely real and equals 20 points
The data cannot distinguish this gap from zero (no true gap) at 95% confidence, though a real gap is not ruled out either
The model has no bias whatsoever
The confidence interval proves the two groups have identical true TPR

explanations.a: A CI this wide, straddling zero, is precisely evidence AGAINST treating the point estimate as a confirmed finding.
explanations.b: Correct - an interval spanning zero means the observed gap is statistically indistinguishable from no gap given this sample, which is different from proving there is no gap.
explanations.c: Absence of statistical significance is not proof of absence of bias; a larger sample might still reveal a real gap.
explanations.d: A CI containing zero does not prove equality; it means the sample is too small or noisy to tell the difference confidently.

questions.prompt: Match each statistical concept to what it addresses in a subgroup fairness audit.

left.text: Bootstrap confidence interval on a rate difference

right.text: Quantifies how much a single group's point estimate could vary due to sample size alone
Tests whether an observed gap between two specific groups is distinguishable from zero
Guards against false positives when scanning many intersectional slices for the worst gap

questions.explanation: Standard error describes the noisiness of one group's estimate; a bootstrap CI on the difference tests whether a specific two-group gap is real; multiple-comparisons correction protects against cherry-picking the largest apparent gap out of many slices scanned.

questions.prompt: Order the correct steps for honestly reporting a subgroup TPR gap.

items.text: Compute the point-estimate TPR gap between two subgroups
Check the sample size n feeding each subgroup's estimate
Bootstrap the gap to obtain a 95% confidence interval
If many slices were scanned, apply a multiple-comparisons correction before reporting the finding

questions.explanation: You first compute the raw gap, then check whether the underlying n is large enough to trust it, then quantify uncertainty with a bootstrap CI, and finally, if the gap was found by scanning many slices, correct for the multiple-comparisons problem before presenting it as a real finding.

lessons.label: Reading a Fairness Audit Critically

sections.heading: Disclosure standards: model cards and datasheets
sections.body: Margaret Mitchell and colleagues' 2019 paper "Model Cards for Model Reporting" (FAT* 2019, with co-authors including Timnit Gebru, published while several authors were at Google) proposed a short, standardized document accompanying any released model: intended use, out-of-scope uses, the demographic groups evaluated, the exact metrics used, the decision thresholds applied, and per-group performance broken out with confidence intervals rather than a single averaged headline number. Timnit Gebru and coauthors' companion idea, "Datasheets for Datasets" (first circulated 2018, later published in Communications of the ACM, 2021), asks the same discipline of the training data itself - who collected it, under what consent, what population it represents, what preprocessing was applied, and what known gaps or exclusions exist. Read together, a model card without a datasheet for its training data is missing half the picture: you can confirm a model's per-group accuracy without ever learning whether the underlying data undersampled, or entirely excluded, the very group whose performance the card reports.

sections.heading: Three kinds of audit, three levels of trust
sections.body: Inioluwa Deborah Raji, Peter Xu, Colleen Honigsberg, and Daniel Ho's 2022 paper "Outsider Oversight: Designing a Third Party Audit Ecosystem for AI Governance" (AIES 2022) distinguishes FIRST-PARTY audits (the company evaluates its own model, with full internal access but an obvious incentive to present results favorably and no obligation to publish unflattering findings), SECOND-PARTY audits (a contracted external firm, more independent but still commissioned, scoped, and often gagged by contract with the company), and ADVERSARIAL THIRD-PARTY audits (an outside researcher with no relationship to the company, publishing regardless of what they find or how the company reacts). Raji's own earlier work exemplifies this last category in practice: her 2019 paper with Joy Buolamwini, "Actionable Auditing" (AIES 2019, following up on Buolamwini and Gebru's 2018 Gender Shades work), re-tested the same commercial facial-analysis products roughly a year after Gender Shades, measuring error rates broken out by skin tone and gender, and documenting that public naming had prompted Microsoft and IBM to measurably shrink their error-rate gaps in the interim.

sections.heading: What black-box API access still permits
sections.body: Even without model internals or training data, a third-party auditor with only paid API access can still measure input-output disparities directly - submitting matched inputs that vary only the protected attribute across demographic groups and recording output differences, exactly the method Buolamwini and Gebru's original 2018 Gender Shades study used against commercial facial-analysis APIs, later extended by Raji and Buolamwini's actionable-auditing follow-up. What black-box access forecloses is anything requiring ground truth the company controls: calibration against true outcomes never disclosed, or verification of the datasheet's claims about training data provenance, which no amount of API querying can independently confirm.

lessons.workedExample: A journalist wants to check whether a company's hiring-screen API scores resumes differently by gender. Without access to the model or training data, she cannot verify the training datasheet's claims or compute true calibration. She CAN submit hundreds of resumes identical except for gendered names and gendered extracurriculars, recording the score distribution for each version - a black-box, adversarial third-party audit in Raji et al.'s audit-ecosystem sense. If she finds a systematic score gap, she can publish it regardless of the company's reaction, unlike a first-party audit the company could choose to keep internal, or a second-party audit whose scope and release the company controls contractually.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge evaluating an audit-based project will ask which of the three audit types (first, second, or adversarial third-party) your team's evidence actually is, because the answer changes how much to trust it - a judge who catches a team presenting a first-party self-audit as if it carries adversarial-audit credibility is right to discount it. Naming Mitchell et al.'s model cards and Gebru et al.'s datasheets as the disclosure standard you followed, and being explicit about what you could and could not check given your access level, signals methodological honesty rather than overclaiming.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference in content between a model card (Mitchell et al., 2019) and a datasheet for a dataset (Gebru et al.)?

options.text: A model card documents the trained model's intended use and per-group performance; a datasheet documents the training data's provenance, consent, and representativeness
They document identical information and are interchangeable
A datasheet documents model accuracy; a model card documents data collection
Only datasheets are peer-reviewed; model cards are informal notes

explanations.a: Correct - model cards focus on the trained model (use cases, evaluated groups, per-group metrics), while datasheets focus on the data feeding that model (collection process, consent, population represented, known gaps).
explanations.b: They are complementary, not identical - each covers a different half of the reporting picture.
explanations.c: This reverses the two documents' actual focus.
explanations.d: Both are proposed reporting standards from the research community, not a peer-review distinction.

questions.prompt: Match each audit type from Raji, Xu, Honigsberg & Ho's audit-ecosystem taxonomy (2022) to its defining characteristic.

right.text: The company evaluates its own model with full internal access but an incentive toward favorable framing
A contracted external firm evaluates the model, more independent but still scoped and commissioned by the company
An unaffiliated outside researcher evaluates the model and publishes regardless of the company's reaction

questions.explanation: First-party audits are internal and face the strongest incentive problem; second-party audits add independence but the company still controls scope and release; adversarial third-party audits, like the Gender Shades follow-up, have no such control and publish freely.

questions.prompt: What can an adversarial auditor with only black-box API access (no model internals, no training data) still measure?

options.text: Calibration against ground-truth labels the company never released
Input-output disparities, by submitting matched inputs across demographic groups and comparing output distributions
The exact contents of the training datasheet without the company publishing one
The model's internal architecture and parameter weights

explanations.a: Calibration requires ground-truth outcome labels the auditor typically does not have under pure API access.
explanations.b: Correct - this is exactly the Gender Shades-style method: submit matched inputs varying only the protected attribute and compare the API's outputs.
explanations.c: Datasheet contents about data collection cannot be inferred from API queries alone; that requires the company's own disclosure.
explanations.d: Black-box access, by definition, does not expose internal architecture or weights.

questions.prompt: Order these audit types from least to most independent of the company being audited.

items.text: First-party (internal) audit
Second-party (contracted external firm) audit
Adversarial third-party audit

questions.explanation: First-party audits are conducted and controlled entirely by the company itself; second-party audits add an external firm but the company still commissions and scopes the work; adversarial third-party audits are conducted and published entirely independent of the company's control.

units.label: Landmark Work and Open Debates

lessons.label: Gender Shades (Buolamwini & Gebru, 2018)

sections.heading: The blind spot before Gender Shades
sections.body: Before 2018, face-analysis benchmarks such as Labeled Faces in the Wild were roughly 80% lighter-skinned and over 70% male, so a classifier could clear 90%+ aggregate accuracy while failing badly on anyone outside that majority -- a failure nobody was measuring. Joy Buolamwini encountered this personally as an MIT Media Lab graduate student: building an "Aspire Mirror" art installation, off-the-shelf face-detection software would not reliably detect her own dark-skinned face until she put on a white plastic mask. That experience led her, with Timnit Gebru (then at Microsoft Research), to publish "Gender Shades" at the 2018 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency (FAT*), auditing three commercial gender classifiers -- IBM, Microsoft, and Face++ -- for exactly the subgroup failure that aggregate metrics were built to hide. Buolamwini had already founded the Algorithmic Justice League in 2016 after that experience, turning a personal debugging frustration into an organized advocacy effort for mandatory bias audits of commercial vision systems, and Gender Shades became the organization's landmark research output.

sections.heading: The Pilot Parliaments Benchmark
sections.body: Rather than reuse an existing skewed dataset, the authors built one: the Pilot Parliaments Benchmark (PPB), 1,270 faces of sitting parliamentarians from three African nations (Rwanda, Senegal, South Africa) and three European nations (Iceland, Finland, Sweden) -- chosen because these six legislatures were among the world's most gender-balanced, guaranteeing enough women and enough dark-skinned faces to make subgroup error rates statistically meaningful. Each face was hand-labeled using the Fitzpatrick scale, a six-point dermatological classification (I-VI) originally built to grade sunburn and melanoma risk, then binarized into "lighter" (I-III) and "darker" (IV-VI). Crossing skin type with binary gender produced four subgroups per classifier, and PPB became the first major face-analysis audit to report error broken out by that intersection rather than by race or gender alone.

sections.heading: The headline gap
sections.body: The result: lighter-skinned male faces were nearly solved, with error rates topping out at 0.8% across all three vendors. Darker-skinned female faces told the opposite story -- error reached 34.7% on IBM's classifier, 34.5% on Face++, and 20.8% on Microsoft, a gap as large as 34.4 percentage points that vanished into a respectable 90%+ once each company reported only overall accuracy. Gender Shades didn't just catch three biased products; it demonstrated that aggregate accuracy for a classifier is not merely incomplete but can be actively misleading, since averaging across a majority group can mathematically erase a minority group's failure. The paper's real contribution -- an intersectional audit protocol journalists, regulators, and later researchers could reuse on any face-analysis system -- outlived the specific 2018 classifiers it tested.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose a student trains a gender-classification model for a science-fair project and reports 91% overall accuracy on a test set that is 75% lighter-skinned. Following the Gender Shades protocol, they label every test image by Fitzpatrick type and gender, then compute four separate error rates: lighter-male, lighter-female, darker-male, darker-female. They discover their 91% aggregate hides a darker-female error rate of 28% -- nearly as bad as IBM's 2018 result -- because darker-skinned women are only 6% of their test set, so their failures barely move the overall number. Reporting the four subgroup rates alongside the aggregate, exactly as Buolamwini and Gebru did, is what turns a hidden failure into an actionable one.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has read Gender Shades will not be satisfied by an overall accuracy number; they will ask for error broken out by subgroup, specifically by the intersection of two attributes rather than each alone, because Buolamwini and Gebru's central finding was that intersectional error can be an order of magnitude worse than either attribute's marginal error. A student who can explain why the Pilot Parliaments Benchmark was built (existing datasets were skewed) and that the paper's contribution was methodological -- not just an indictment of IBM -- signals they understand fairness auditing as a discipline, not a headline.

questions.prompt: In the 2018 Gender Shades audit, roughly what was the error-rate gap between lighter-skinned male faces and darker-skinned female faces on IBM's gender classifier?

options.text: About 5 percentage points
About 34 percentage points
About 60 percentage points
There was no gap; all subgroups scored above 95%

explanations.a: The gap was far larger than a small margin -- error rose from under 1% to nearly 35% for the worst subgroup.
explanations.b: Correct -- IBM's own lighter-male error was 0.3% while darker-female error on IBM reached 34.7%, a roughly 34.4-point gap.
explanations.c: The gap was substantial but not this extreme; 34.7% minus 0.3% is close to 34 points, not 60.
explanations.d: Aggregate accuracy for each vendor did look strong, which was exactly the problem Gender Shades exposed -- subgroup performance was not.

questions.prompt: Why did Buolamwini and Gebru build the Pilot Parliaments Benchmark instead of using an existing face dataset like Labeled Faces in the Wild?

options.text: Existing datasets were too small to test three companies
Existing datasets skewed heavily lighter-skinned and male, hiding subgroup failure
Existing datasets did not include any photos of government officials
Fitzpatrick labels were only legally available for the PPB images

explanations.a: Size was not the issue; representativeness of subgroups was.
explanations.b: Correct -- datasets like LFW were roughly 80% lighter-skinned and over 70% male, so aggregate scores could look strong while hiding poor performance on darker-skinned women.
explanations.c: The choice of parliamentarians was about gender balance across nations, not photo availability elsewhere.
explanations.d: Fitzpatrick labeling is a manual annotation process, not a licensing restriction unique to PPB.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of the Gender Shades methodology in the order they were performed.

items.text: Select six gender-balanced parliaments for the Pilot Parliaments Benchmark
Label each face by Fitzpatrick skin type (I-VI)
Binarize skin type into lighter/darker and cross with binary gender
Compute classifier error separately for each of the four subgroups

questions.explanation: The authors first chose the source population (six gender-balanced legislatures), then annotated skin type, then formed four intersectional subgroups, and only then computed and compared subgroup error rates.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its correct definition from the Gender Shades study.

right.text: A six-point dermatological skin-type classification (I-VI)
A 1,270-face dataset drawn from six gender-balanced legislatures
An error rate computed for a subgroup defined by two crossed attributes
A single accuracy figure across an entire test set that can mask subgroup disparities

questions.explanation: Fitzpatrick scale grades skin type I-VI; PPB is the 1,270-face benchmark itself; intersectional error is measured on a subgroup like darker-skinned females; aggregate accuracy is the single number that hid the disparity in all three companies' original reporting.

lessons.label: Actionable Auditing and the Fight with Amazon

sections.heading: The re-audit: did naming names change anything?
sections.body: Inioluwa Deborah Raji, then an undergraduate researcher working with Buolamwini through the Algorithmic Justice League, co-authored "Actionable Auditing: Investigating the Impact of Publicly Naming Biased Performance Results on Commercial AI Products," published at AAAI/AIES in January 2019, returning to the same vendors from Gender Shades roughly a year later to test whether public disclosure alone forces improvement. The result: Microsoft's error rate on darker-skinned female faces fell from about 20.8% to 1.52% within roughly seven months of Gender Shades' publication -- evidence that a named company can fix a measurable disparity quickly once independent researchers publish subgroup numbers instead of an aggregate score. That contrast, a large improvement achieved fast, became the paper's core argument for a practice it named "actionable auditing": publish specific numbers on identifiable products and let public and commercial pressure do the enforcement that internal QA had not.

sections.heading: Amazon enters, and the fight begins
sections.body: Raji and Buolamwini widened the audit to vendors Gender Shades had not covered, adding Amazon's Rekognition and Kairos, a smaller face-analysis startup. Amazon fared worst: Rekognition showed an error rate around 31% for darker-skinned women, far above Microsoft's newly-improved 1.52% and close to IBM's original 2018 range, while Kairos posted comparatively better, though still uneven, subgroup numbers. Amazon's public reaction was combative rather than corrective: Matt Wood, then AWS's general manager of AI, published blog posts disputing the study's methodology, arguing the researchers used the wrong confidence threshold and tested the wrong task -- gender classification rather than Rekognition's intended face-matching use. Buolamwini and a group of outside AI researchers, including Turing Award winner Yoshua Bengio, publicly rebutted Amazon's objections in an open letter, defending the audit's methodology and noting Amazon had never published its own comparable skin-type breakdown for the public to check.

sections.heading: The result: moratoria, not just an apology
sections.body: The dispute became a visible test of whether adversarial audits change deployed products, not just reputations. In June 2020, amid the broader reckoning after George Floyd's murder, IBM announced it would exit the facial-recognition business entirely; Amazon announced a one-year moratorium on police use of Rekognition; Microsoft said it would not sell facial recognition to police departments absent federal regulation. None of the three moratoria was framed as a direct concession to Raji and Buolamwini, but all three followed research that had, by name, quantified the exact disparity in the exact products under sustained public pressure -- the case researchers cite for external audits functioning as a genuine accountability mechanism rather than a purely academic exercise.

lessons.workedExample: A science-fair team wants to know whether a criticized face-analysis API actually improved after a published audit. Following Raji and Buolamwini's design, they don't just re-run an overall-accuracy test -- they re-run the SAME subgroup breakdown, by Fitzpatrick type and gender, on the SAME API a year later, and report the delta for the worst-performing subgroup specifically, the way the 20.8%-to-1.52% Microsoft number was reported. If the vendor's aggregate accuracy improved but the darker-female subgroup error did not, the team knows the fix was cosmetic; if the subgroup gap actually closed, they have direct evidence the public audit worked.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows this case will ask not just whether you found a bias metric but whether you checked what happened after disclosure -- the paper's real contribution was showing that publishing named, product-specific subgroup numbers is itself an intervention, not just a measurement. They may also probe whether you can distinguish evidence from rhetoric: Amazon's methodological objections were public and specific, and a strong answer engages what Amazon actually disputed (threshold choice, task mismatch) rather than dismissing the pushback outright, since auditing credibility depends on being able to defend methodology against a real challenge.

questions.prompt: How did Microsoft's darker-skinned female error rate change between Gender Shades (2018) and the Actionable Auditing re-audit (2019)?

options.text: It fell from about 20.8% to about 1.52%
It rose from about 1.52% to about 20.8%
It stayed roughly the same, around 20%
Microsoft was not re-tested in the 2019 study

explanations.a: Correct -- Microsoft's darker-female error dropped sharply within about seven months, the paper's headline evidence that disclosure drives fixes.
explanations.b: The direction is reversed; the error rate improved (decreased), it did not worsen.
explanations.c: The change was large and specific, not a stagnant number -- roughly a 19-point drop.
explanations.d: Microsoft was one of the original three companies and was specifically re-tested to measure improvement.

questions.prompt: How did Amazon publicly respond when Rekognition showed roughly 31% error on darker-skinned women in the 2019 audit?

options.text: AWS's Matt Wood published blog posts disputing the study's methodology
Amazon immediately withdrew Rekognition from the market
Amazon published its own matching subgroup breakdown and conceded the finding
Amazon sued Raji and Buolamwini for defamation

explanations.a: Correct -- Wood argued the researchers used the wrong confidence threshold and tested a task other than Rekognition's intended face-matching use.
explanations.b: Amazon did not withdraw the product in response to this study; the later 2020 action was a one-year moratorium on police use, not a withdrawal.
explanations.c: Amazon disputed the methodology publicly rather than releasing its own comparable breakdown.
explanations.d: There was a public dispute via blog posts and an open letter, not litigation.

questions.prompt: Put these events in chronological order.

items.text: Gender Shades is published (2018)
Raji and Buolamwini publish the Actionable Auditing re-audit, adding Amazon (2019)
Amazon's Matt Wood disputes the audit's methodology in blog posts
IBM, Amazon, and Microsoft announce facial-recognition moratoria/exit (June 2020)

questions.explanation: Gender Shades established the original 2018 baseline; Actionable Auditing re-tested vendors and added Amazon in 2019; Amazon's public rebuttal followed the unfavorable finding; the corporate moratoria came in June 2020.

questions.prompt: Match each company to its outcome in this case.

right.text: Exited the facial-recognition business entirely (2020)
Darker-female error fell from ~20.8% to ~1.52% after being named in Gender Shades
Showed ~31% darker-female error when newly added in 2019, then announced a one-year police-use moratorium in 2020

questions.explanation: IBM left the facial-recognition market outright; Microsoft was the improvement case from the original three; Amazon was the newly-audited worst performer whose product prompted a temporary police-use pause.

lessons.label: COMPAS: ProPublica's Case

sections.heading: Machine Bias: the investigation
sections.body: On May 23, 2016, ProPublica journalists Julia Angwin, Jeff Larson, Surya Mattu, and Lauren Kirchner published "Machine Bias," investigating COMPAS (Correctional Offender Management Profiling for Alternative Sanctions), a proprietary recidivism-risk tool built by Northpointe (later renamed Equivant) and used by judges in Broward County, Florida and elsewhere to inform bail, sentencing, and parole decisions from a 1-10 risk score bucketed into low, medium, and high risk. ProPublica filed public-records requests to obtain risk scores for roughly 7,000 defendants assessed in Broward County during 2013-2014, then linked those scores to actual arrest records over the following two years to see who actually reoffended. ProPublica released its full dataset and analysis code publicly, an unusually transparent move for an investigative story, which let outside statisticians replicate, and later dispute, its findings. COMPAS itself was not built for Broward County alone -- by 2016 it was in use across several U.S. states, making the audit's implications reach well beyond one Florida county's courtrooms.

sections.heading: The numbers, and the specific claim
sections.body: The headline finding: Black defendants who did NOT reoffend were nonetheless rated high-risk far more often than white defendants who did not reoffend -- a false positive rate of 44.9% for Black defendants versus 23.5% for white defendants. The mirror-image error ran the other way: white defendants who DID reoffend were rated low-risk (missed) at 47.7%, versus 28.0% for Black defendants who reoffended. ProPublica's widely-quoted claim, that Black defendants were roughly twice as likely as white defendants to be falsely flagged as high risk, is a direct comparison of those two false-positive rates, and its precise statistical grounding is disparity in false positive and false negative rates across the two racial groups -- a criterion sometimes called equalized odds when both error types are required to match.

sections.heading: Why the aggregate hid it
sections.body: COMPAS's overall accuracy was similar across racial groups, roughly 61-65% either way, which is precisely why the disparity had gone unchallenged before ProPublica's analysis: a tool can be equally accurate in aggregate for two groups while systematically erring in opposite directions, over-predicting risk for one group and under-predicting it for the other. That pattern -- equal overall accuracy but unequal error type by group -- is the same structure Gender Shades exposed in face classification two years later, and it is why "Machine Bias" insisted on reporting false-positive and false-negative rates by race rather than one blended accuracy figure. Notably, COMPAS's questionnaire never asked for race directly, which is exactly why the finding mattered: a facially race-blind tool can still produce racially disparate errors through correlated inputs like prior arrests and neighborhood, without anyone deliberately encoding bias.

lessons.workedExample: A student building a risk-scoring tool for a class project computes overall accuracy of 65% and calls it fair. Following ProPublica's method, they instead build a separate confusion matrix for each demographic subgroup in their test set and compute the false positive rate (rated high-risk but didn't reoffend) and false negative rate (rated low-risk but did reoffend) for each group. They find their tool's overall accuracy is identical across groups, but the false-positive rate for one group is nearly double the other's -- the same 44.9%-versus-23.5% pattern ProPublica found in Broward County -- revealing a disparity invisible in the single accuracy number.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge should expect you to name the exact fairness criterion, not just say COMPAS was biased -- ProPublica's claim was specifically about disparate false positive rates (and false negative rates) across race, not calibration or overall accuracy. A well-prepared answer also flags that ProPublica released its raw data and code, which is what allowed the criterion to be checked and, as the next lesson covers, disputed on different fairness grounds -- judges probing this case are testing whether you understand that biased is not a single number but a specific, name-able statistical property.

questions.prompt: In ProPublica's Broward County analysis, what were the false positive rates (rated high-risk but did not reoffend) for Black versus white defendants?

options.text: 44.9% for Black defendants versus 23.5% for white defendants
23.5% for Black defendants versus 44.9% for white defendants
They were equal, around 35% for both groups
28.0% for Black defendants versus 47.7% for white defendants

explanations.a: Correct -- Black defendants who did not reoffend were falsely flagged high-risk at 44.9%, versus 23.5% for white defendants.
explanations.b: The rates are reversed; the higher false-positive rate belonged to Black defendants.
explanations.c: The rates were not equal; that inequality was the entire finding.
explanations.d: Those figures (28.0% and 47.7%) are the false NEGATIVE rates, not the false positive rates.

questions.prompt: ProPublica's claim that Black defendants were "twice as likely" to be falsely flagged high-risk is grounded in a disparity in which statistic?

options.text: Calibration (whether the same score means the same reoffense rate across groups)
False positive rate (and, symmetrically, false negative rate) across racial groups
Demographic parity in the proportion of each group scored high-risk
Overall accuracy across racial groups

explanations.a: Calibration was the criterion Northpointe later used to defend COMPAS, not the one ProPublica's twice-as-likely claim rests on.
explanations.b: Correct -- the claim directly compares false positive rates (44.9% vs 23.5%) between the two groups.
explanations.c: ProPublica's core statistic was about error type given true outcome, not the raw proportion scored high-risk.
explanations.d: Overall accuracy was actually similar across groups; that is exactly why the disparity had been hidden.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of ProPublica's investigation in order.

items.text: File public-records requests for Broward County risk scores (2013-2014)
Link scores to two-year arrest records to determine actual reoffense
Compute false positive and false negative rates separately by race
Publish "Machine Bias" (May 2016) with the public dataset and code

questions.explanation: ProPublica first obtained the risk scores, then matched them to real recidivism outcomes, then computed race-specific error rates, and finally published the story along with the underlying data for replication.

questions.prompt: Match each figure to what it measured in the ProPublica COMPAS analysis.

right.text: False positive rate for Black defendants
False positive rate for white defendants
False negative rate for white defendants
False negative rate for Black defendants

questions.explanation: Black defendants were falsely flagged high-risk at 44.9% and missed as low-risk reoffenders at 28.0%; white defendants were falsely flagged at 23.5% and missed at 47.7% -- opposite error patterns despite similar overall accuracy.

lessons.label: COMPAS: Northpointe's Rebuttal and the Verdict

sections.heading: Northpointe's defense: predictive parity
sections.body: Within two months of "Machine Bias," Northpointe's own researchers -- William Dieterich, Christina Mendoza, and Tim Brennan -- published a rebuttal arguing ProPublica had picked the wrong fairness criterion. COMPAS, they showed, satisfies predictive parity (also called calibration): among defendants given the SAME risk score, the actual reoffense rate was nearly identical for Black and white defendants, and the tool's overall discriminative power (area under the ROC curve, AUC) sat around 0.68-0.70 for both racial groups. A separate rejoinder by Anthony Flores, Kristin Bechtel, and Christopher Lowenkamp (2016, Federal Probation) reached a similar defense, criticizing ProPublica's coding of "high risk" and its handling of prior-record variables. On calibration grounds COMPAS looked fair; on the false-positive/false-negative grounds ProPublica used, it did not.

sections.heading: Both sides were right -- that's the impossibility result
sections.body: The resolution came from theory, not more data. Alexandra Chouldechova (2017) and, independently, Jon Kleinberg, Sendhil Mullainathan, and Manish Raghavan (2016) proved that when two groups have different base rates of the outcome being predicted -- here, Black defendants in this dataset had a materially higher two-year reoffense rate than white defendants -- no score can simultaneously satisfy calibration (Northpointe's criterion) and equal false positive/negative rates (ProPublica's criterion), except in degenerate cases. ProPublica and Northpointe were each verifying a real, different, and mathematically incompatible property of the same tool; the dispute was not a factual error on either side but a demonstration that fairness is not one criterion.

sections.heading: Dressel & Farid: maybe the whole premise was too generous
sections.body: In January 2018, Julia Dressel and Hany Farid (Science Advances) sidestepped the calibration-versus-error-rate fight entirely by asking a blunter question: how good is COMPAS, really? They recruited untrained volunteers via Amazon Mechanical Turk, gave each a two-sentence defendant summary, and asked for a recidivism prediction -- pooled human accuracy hit 67.0%, edging out COMPAS's own 65.2% on the same cases, despite COMPAS using 137 input features. A simple logistic regression using only two features, age and total number of prior convictions, matched COMPAS's full-feature accuracy almost exactly. The tool's added complexity bought no added accuracy over untrained human guesses or a two-variable model.

sections.heading: What courts did with it: Wisconsin v. Loomis
sections.body: Eric Loomis, sentenced in Wisconsin partly on a COMPAS score, appealed on due-process grounds, arguing the proprietary scoring formula could not be examined by the defense. In State v. Loomis (2016), the Wisconsin Supreme Court upheld the sentence, ruling COMPAS could inform sentencing as long as it was not the sole or determinative factor, and that judges must receive a written warning about the tool's group-level validation limits and proprietary nature -- a compromise that let risk tools stay in courtrooms without resolving which fairness criterion they must satisfy.

lessons.workedExample: A defense attorney is handed two studies about the same tool: one shows it's fair because scores are equally predictive across race (calibration), the other shows it's biased because error types are unequally distributed across race (equalized odds). Rather than assume one study made a mistake, the attorney checks the base rates: if the two racial groups being compared have different actual reoffense rates in the data, Chouldechova's and Kleinberg-Mullainathan-Raghavan's proofs guarantee the two properties cannot both hold except in edge cases -- so the tool must fail at least one criterion, and asking which one, and whether that is the one that matters to this defendant's hearing, is the only useful next question.
lessons.judgeFraming: This is the case where judges test whether you understand that fairness has multiple, mutually exclusive mathematical definitions rather than one true version -- a strong answer names both criteria (calibration/predictive parity versus equalized false positive/negative rates) and states the impossibility result rather than declaring a side right. A sharper judge will also ask about Dressel and Farid: if untrained humans matched a 137-feature commercial tool using two features, does the fairness debate even matter if the tool adds no accuracy in the first place? Being ready to argue both threads, the math and the why-use-this-at-all question, shows real command of the case.

questions.prompt: Northpointe's rebuttal argued COMPAS satisfies which fairness criterion, with what approximate AUC?

options.text: Demographic parity, AUC around 0.50
Predictive parity (calibration), AUC around 0.68-0.70
Equalized odds, AUC around 0.90
Individual fairness, AUC around 1.0

explanations.a: Northpointe's defense was about equal reoffense rates at equal scores (calibration), not equal score distributions across groups.
explanations.b: Correct -- Dieterich, Mendoza, and Brennan showed COMPAS was well-calibrated across race, with AUC roughly 0.68-0.70 for both groups.
explanations.c: Equalized odds was ProPublica's criterion, which the rebuttal argued against, not the one Northpointe claimed to satisfy.
explanations.d: An AUC of 1.0 would mean perfect discrimination, far above COMPAS's actual measured performance.

questions.prompt: What did Chouldechova and Kleinberg-Mullainathan-Raghavan prove about calibration and equal error rates?

options.text: ProPublica's numbers were statistically fabricated
Calibration and equal false-positive/false-negative rates can only both hold when the groups have equal base rates -- otherwise, at most one can hold
COMPAS was more accurate than any human judge
Fairness metrics cannot be defined mathematically at all

explanations.a: The proofs validated that both ProPublica's and Northpointe's numbers could be correct simultaneously; neither side fabricated data.
explanations.b: Correct -- this impossibility result shows the two fairness criteria are mathematically incompatible whenever base rates differ across groups, which they did here.
explanations.c: This claim is unrelated to the impossibility proofs and is contradicted by the Dressel and Farid study.
explanations.d: The proofs rely on precise mathematical definitions of fairness; the point is that multiple valid definitions can conflict, not that none can be defined.

questions.prompt: What did Dressel and Farid (2018, Science Advances) find when comparing COMPAS to untrained humans?

options.text: COMPAS vastly outperformed untrained humans
Untrained Mechanical Turk workers (67.0%) slightly outperformed COMPAS (65.2%), and a 2-feature model matched COMPAS's 137-feature accuracy
COMPAS's accuracy could not be measured against humans
Both humans and COMPAS scored below random chance

explanations.a: The opposite was found -- untrained humans slightly beat COMPAS on the same cases.
explanations.b: Correct -- pooled untrained human judgment reached 67.0% versus COMPAS's 65.2%, and a two-feature logistic model matched the full 137-feature tool.
explanations.c: The study directly compared human and algorithmic accuracy on identical defendant summaries.
explanations.d: Both scored well above chance (50% for a binary outcome); COMPAS and humans were close to each other, not near chance.

questions.prompt: Match each party to their contribution to the COMPAS debate.

right.text: Rebutted ProPublica, showing COMPAS satisfies predictive parity
Proved calibration and equal error rates cannot both hold given unequal base rates
Showed untrained humans and a 2-feature model matched COMPAS's accuracy
Ruled in State v. Loomis that COMPAS could inform sentencing if not the sole factor

questions.explanation: Northpointe's team defended calibration; the impossibility-theorem authors reconciled the two sides mathematically; Dressel and Farid questioned COMPAS's added value entirely; and the Wisconsin Supreme Court set the legal precedent for using such tools in sentencing.

questions.prompt: Put these publications in chronological order.

items.text: ProPublica's "Machine Bias" is published (May 2016)
Northpointe's Dieterich-Mendoza-Brennan rebuttal is published (July 2016)
Chouldechova's and Kleinberg-Mullainathan-Raghavan's impossibility proofs appear (2016-2017)
Dressel and Farid's Science Advances study is published (January 2018)

questions.explanation: Machine Bias broke the story in May 2016; Northpointe's rebuttal followed within two months; the theoretical reconciliation papers appeared over the following year; and Dressel and Farid's human-versus-algorithm study came out in January 2018.

lessons.label: Obermeyer et al. 2019: The Healthcare Cost Proxy

sections.heading: The algorithm and the hidden design choice
sections.body: In October 2019, Ziad Obermeyer, Brian Powers, Christine Vogeli, and Sendhil Mullainathan published "Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations" in Science, auditing a commercial risk-prediction algorithm used across the U.S. healthcare system to decide which patients get enrolled in high-touch "care management" programs -- extra nursing attention, coordination, and monitoring for the sickest patients. The algorithm, applied to roughly 200 million patients a year nationwide, predicted total future healthcare COST as a proxy for future healthcare NEED, on the assumption that sicker patients cost more.
