explanations.b: Correct — CheckList's invariance, directional, and minimum-functionality tests exposed serious bugs (e.g., flipped predictions on simple negations) that aggregate accuracy had completely hidden.
explanations.c: CheckList was designed for and applied to NLP models, including commercial sentiment-analysis APIs.
explanations.d: The commercial models performed poorly on many CheckList tests despite strong benchmark scores.

questions.prompt: Match each CheckList test type to its defining behavior.

right.text: A perturbation that should leave the output unchanged
A perturbation that should shift the output in a known direction
A small, targeted test isolating one specific capability

questions.explanation: INV changes something irrelevant to the label (typos, name swaps) and expects no change; DIR changes something that should predictably move the output (e.g., adding negation should flip sentiment); MFT is a targeted unit test for one capability, like software unit tests.

questions.prompt: Order these steps in designing a behavioral robustness test from broadest concern to most concrete artifact.

items.text: Recognize that average test accuracy hides worst-case failures
Decide which capability or invariance to probe (e.g., negation handling)
Choose a test type: invariance, directional, or minimum functionality
Construct concrete perturbed inputs and check the model's actual output against the expectation

questions.explanation: Robustness testing starts from the realization that a single accuracy number is insufficient, moves to choosing what specific behavior matters, then which CheckList-style test format fits, and finally to building and running the concrete test cases.

lessons.label: Label Noise and Data Quality

sections.heading: The benchmark you trust is itself mislabeled
sections.body: Northcutt, Athalye, and Mueller's 2021 NeurIPS paper 'Pervasive Label Errors in Test Sets Destabilize Machine Learning Benchmarks' algorithmically audited the TEST sets — not training sets — of 10 widely-used benchmarks (ImageNet, MNIST, CIFAR-10/100, Caltech-256, QuickDraw, IMDB, Amazon Reviews, 20news, AudioSet) and had crowdworkers on Mechanical Turk validate every flagged error by majority vote. The average error rate across all 10 was about 3.4%. The ImageNet validation set alone — the single number nearly every published vision paper reports against — carried an estimated ~5.8% label errors, roughly 2,916 mislabeled images out of about 50,000. QuickDraw, a noisier crowd-sourced sketch dataset with a much larger and more ambiguous label vocabulary, ran even higher at roughly 10.1%. The accompanying public website, labelerrors.com, let anyone browse the specific flagged images alongside the model's disagreement, turning an abstract statistic into inspectable evidence.

sections.heading: Errors are not noise you can average away — they change rankings
sections.body: The paper's most consequential finding was not the error rate itself but its effect: when the ImageNet test set was corrected, model rankings FLIPPED, and the effect grew LARGER as reported clean accuracy grew higher. Simpler, lower-capacity models that had looked worse on the noisy labels moved ahead of larger models that had partly overfit to the specific label-noise pattern baked into the ORIGINAL flawed test set. This matters because leaderboards drive research direction, publication decisions, and eventual deployment choices — a benchmark with unaudited labels can reward the wrong model architecture precisely in the high-accuracy regime where teams assume the numbers are most trustworthy.

sections.heading: Confident learning and the ceiling nobody can beat
sections.body: The detection method behind this paper and the accompanying open-source cleanlab library is CONFIDENT LEARNING: train a model with k-fold cross-validation to get out-of-sample predicted probabilities for every example, compare each example's given label against those predicted class probabilities, and flag examples where the model is confidently and consistently predicting a DIFFERENT class than the given label — using per-class self-confidence thresholds rather than a single global cutoff, which is what makes it robust to class imbalance. This is a statistically principled way to surface likely mislabels at scale without needing a full second annotator pass over every example. But there is a hard ceiling: inter-annotator agreement — the rate at which independent human labelers agree with each other on the same example — is the highest accuracy any metric can meaningfully claim, since the 'ground truth' is itself a human judgment call, not an objective fact. A model cannot be validly scored above the noise floor of the labels it is being scored against, no matter how it is trained.

lessons.workedExample: A team scores their leaf-disease classifier at 94% against a 500-image test set they collected and hand-labeled solo. Applying confident learning (via cleanlab) to their own labels, they find the model disagrees confidently and consistently with the given label on 28 images (5.6%) — clustered on borderline early-stage lesions. Re-examining those 28 with a second labeler, 19 turn out to be labeling mistakes, not model errors. After correcting them, true accuracy is actually 97.8%, but more importantly, two independently hand-labeled images still disagree with each other — meaning inter-annotator agreement itself is 99.6%, and the model literally cannot be validly credited above that ceiling.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has read Northcutt et al. will ask how you know your ground-truth labels are correct, not just how accurate your model is against them. The strong answer names confident learning or a comparable audit method, reports how many disagreements you found and how many were genuine label errors versus real model errors, and states your inter-annotator agreement rate as the ceiling you are scoring against — showing you understand accuracy is bounded by label quality, not just model quality.

questions.prompt: According to Northcutt et al. (2021), roughly what fraction of the ImageNet VALIDATION set (used as a test set) carries label errors?

options.text: About 0.1%, a negligible amount
About 5.8%, roughly 2,916 images
About 50%, making the benchmark unusable
Exactly 3.4%, identical to every other dataset studied

explanations.a: The rate found was far higher than negligible — closer to 6% of the validation set.
explanations.b: Correct — roughly 5.8% of the ImageNet validation set, on the order of 2,916 images, were flagged and human-validated as label errors.
explanations.c: 50% would mean the benchmark is essentially random; the actual rate, while consequential, was far lower.
explanations.d: 3.4% was the AVERAGE across all 10 datasets studied, not the ImageNet-specific rate, which ran higher; error rates varied substantially by dataset (QuickDraw was ~10.1%).

questions.prompt: What was the most consequential downstream effect Northcutt et al. demonstrated from correcting test-set labels?

options.text: Model accuracy scores increased uniformly by exactly 3.4 points
Relative rankings between models changed — some models moved ahead of others
No practical difference was observed after correction
Only training-set accuracy was affected, not test-set conclusions

explanations.a: The effect was not a uniform shift; different models were affected differently.
explanations.b: Correct — with corrected labels, some lower-capacity models outranked models that looked stronger on the noisy original labels, showing label noise can distort which model looks best.
explanations.c: The paper's central point was that the difference was practically significant, not negligible.
explanations.d: The study specifically audited TEST sets, and it was test-set-driven ranking conclusions that shifted.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to its role in label-quality auditing.

right.text: Detects likely mislabels via cross-validated model-vs-label disagreement
Sets the ceiling accuracy no metric can validly exceed
Evidence that label noise can distort which model appears best

questions.explanation: Confident learning is the detection algorithm (basis of cleanlab); inter-annotator agreement is the human-agreement ceiling that bounds any claimed accuracy; the ranking flip is the empirical consequence Northcutt et al. demonstrated on corrected ImageNet labels.

lessons.label: Adversarial Examples

sections.heading: The discovery: intriguing properties, 2013
sections.body: Szegedy et al.'s 2013 paper 'Intriguing Properties of Neural Networks' first showed that adding an imperceptible, carefully-computed perturbation — found by using an optimization procedure (L-BFGS) to search for the smallest input change that flips the predicted class — could make a neural network confidently misclassify an image, even though the perturbed image looked completely unchanged to a human observer. The paper also noted the perturbation generalized: the SAME perturbed image often fooled a different network trained on a different subset of data, an early hint of what would later be named transferability. This was surprising because the networks in question had state-of-the-art ImageNet accuracy for their time — high average-case performance did not imply robustness to a specifically constructed worst case, and no one had been looking for one.

sections.heading: Why it's easy: FGSM and the linear explanation
sections.body: Goodfellow, Shlens, and Szegedy's 2015 paper 'Explaining and Harnessing Adversarial Examples' proposed the Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) and, more importantly, an explanation for WHY adversarial examples exist: high-dimensional linear behavior. Even though individual neurons use nonlinear activations, deep networks behave approximately linearly across large regions of input space, and in high dimensions a tiny per-pixel push (bounded by epsilon) in the direction of the loss gradient, summed across thousands of pixels, accumulates into a large change in the logits. FGSM computes this in one step: perturbation = epsilon times the sign of the gradient of the loss with respect to the input.

sections.heading: The standard threat model: epsilon-bounded L-infinity and PGD
sections.body: Modern adversarial ML standardizes around an L-infinity threat model: the attacker may change EVERY pixel by at most epsilon, commonly epsilon = 8/255 on CIFAR-10 (about a 3% intensity shift per channel), chosen to keep perturbations visually negligible. Projected Gradient Descent (PGD), from Madry et al.'s 2018 'Towards Deep Learning Models Resistant to Adversarial Attacks,' iterates FGSM-style steps and projects back into the epsilon-ball after each step, making it a far stronger, near-worst-case attack within that threat model and the standard benchmark for evaluating defenses.

sections.heading: Attacks leave the lab: physical world and transferability
sections.body: Eykholt et al.'s 2018 CVPR paper 'Robust Physical-World Attacks on Deep Learning Visual Classification' printed black-and-white stickers onto a real stop sign; a classifier misread it as a speed-limit sign in 100% of controlled lab photos and in 84.8% of frames captured from a moving vehicle in a field drive-by test — showing the threat survives lighting, angle, and distance changes outside a lab. Separately, TRANSFERABILITY — an adversarial example crafted against one model often fools a different model trained on different data — enables black-box attacks, where an attacker with no access to a target's weights can craft examples on a substitute model and deploy them against the real target.

lessons.workedExample: A student trains a CIFAR-10-style bird/plane classifier at 91% clean accuracy and wants to test adversarial robustness. Using FGSM with epsilon = 8/255, a single gradient-sign step flips roughly 60% of correctly-classified test images to the wrong label, with pixel changes invisible at normal viewing distance. Running PGD with 20 iterations at the same epsilon budget drives accuracy down further, to near 5-10%, since PGD searches within the epsilon-ball rather than taking one linear step. The student then crafts the PGD examples against a saved checkpoint and feeds them into a DIFFERENT architecture (trained independently); a meaningful fraction still transfer and fool it — demonstrating black-box risk without ever touching the second model's weights.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing this topic wants to know whether you understand adversarial examples as a predictable consequence of how these models compute, not a mysterious glitch — can you explain, in the linear-behavior terms Goodfellow gave, why a change too small to see moves the prediction so much? They will also want the threat model made explicit: what epsilon, what norm, how many attack steps — vague claims of 'we tested robustness' without a stated epsilon and attack (FGSM vs. PGD) signal you haven't actually engaged with the standard evaluation protocol.

questions.prompt: Per Goodfellow et al. (2015), why do small, imperceptible perturbations cause large changes in a network's output?

options.text: Because the network's weights are randomly corrupted during inference
Because deep networks behave approximately linearly across large input regions, so many tiny per-pixel pushes accumulate in high dimensions
Because the attacker has already poisoned the training data
Because the test set contains label errors

explanations.a: No weight corruption is involved; the network's parameters are unchanged, only the input is perturbed.
explanations.b: Correct — this is the linear explanation: near-linear behavior across high-dimensional input space lets a small per-pixel epsilon push, summed over many pixels, produce a large shift in the logits.
explanations.c: This describes a poisoning attack, a training-time attack, which is distinct from a test-time adversarial example.
explanations.d: Label errors are a data-quality issue (Northcutt et al.), unrelated to why gradient-based perturbations fool a trained model at test time.

questions.prompt: In Eykholt et al.'s (2018) physical stop-sign attack, what happened in the field test with a moving vehicle?

options.text: The attack failed completely outside the lab
The sign was misclassified in about 84.8% of the captured drive-by frames
The stickers had to be repainted for every frame to work
The attack only worked on stop signs made after 2018

explanations.a: The attack was not a lab-only phenomenon; it substantially transferred to the field.
explanations.b: Correct — the same static stickers caused targeted misclassification in about 84.8% of frames captured while driving past the sign, versus 100% in controlled lab photos.
explanations.c: The stickers were static and physically fixed; no per-frame repainting occurred.
explanations.d: The attack targeted a real, ordinary stop sign; the classifier's training year is unrelated to the physical trigger.

questions.prompt: Order these adversarial-ML developments chronologically.

items.text: Szegedy et al. discover adversarial examples (Intriguing Properties)
Goodfellow et al. propose FGSM and the linear explanation
Eykholt et al. demonstrate physical stop-sign stickers
Madry et al. propose PGD adversarial training as the standard

questions.explanation: Szegedy et al. (2013) first discovered adversarial examples; Goodfellow et al. (2015) explained them via linear behavior and introduced FGSM; Madry et al. (2018) formalized PGD as the standard strong attack/defense-training procedure; Eykholt et al. (2018) showed physical-world attacks with stop-sign stickers.

lessons.label: Defenses and Why Most of Them Failed

sections.heading: Adversarial training: the defense that actually works, at a cost
sections.body: Madry et al.'s 2018 adversarial training generates PGD adversarial examples DURING training and trains on them directly, so the model learns decision boundaries that stay correct within the epsilon-ball rather than just at the clean data points. It is one of the few defenses that has survived years of adaptive attack scrutiny — but the cost is steep: a CIFAR-10 model that reaches 95%+ clean accuracy with standard training will, once adversarially trained to reach the standard 45-55% PGD-robust accuracy range at epsilon = 8/255, typically see its own clean accuracy drop into the mid-to-high 80s, and training itself takes several times longer because every batch requires generating attacks first.

sections.heading: Gradient masking and the 2018 reckoning
sections.body: Many defenses proposed around 2017-2018 reported strong robustness by making gradients unreliable to compute rather than making the model genuinely robust — a failure mode called OBFUSCATED GRADIENTS (including shattered, stochastic, and vanishing/exploding gradient variants). Athalye, Carlini, and Wagner's 2018 ICML paper 'Obfuscated Gradients Give a False Sense of Security' systematically examined 9 non-certified defenses accepted at ICLR 2018 and found 7 relied on obfuscated gradients; using adapted attacks that worked around the masking (e.g., substitute gradients, changing the attack's optimization surface), they broke 6 of those defenses completely and 1 partially, driving robust accuracy for most down to near zero. This paper reset the field's evaluation standards overnight.

sections.heading: Certified defenses and the honest benchmark
sections.body: Cohen, Rosenfeld, and Kolter's 2019 paper 'Certified Adversarial Robustness via Randomized Smoothing' offered a different approach: instead of empirically testing against known attacks, it trains a base classifier on Gaussian-noised copies of each input and constructs a smoothed classifier whose prediction comes with a mathematically PROVABLE certified radius — a guarantee that no perturbation smaller than that radius (in L2 norm) can change the prediction, regardless of what attack algorithm exists, known or not. In response to the obfuscation crisis, the field adopted adaptive evaluation (attacks specifically designed to probe a given defense's weaknesses rather than reusing an off-the-shelf attack) as a norm, and RobustBench emerged as a standardized, continuously-updated leaderboard requiring adaptive attack results, ending the era where a defense paper could claim high robustness simply by not being attacked properly.

sections.heading: Is the robustness-accuracy trade-off fundamental?
sections.body: Tsipras et al.'s 2019 paper 'Robustness May Be at Odds with Accuracy' argued the trade-off is not just an artifact of weak training methods but may be fundamental: robust and accurate classifiers can rely on different, sometimes conflicting features (robust models tend to learn more human-aligned, perceptually-meaningful features, producing gradients and interpolations that look meaningful to people, where standard models do not), so pushing for adversarial robustness can genuinely cost clean accuracy even at the theoretical optimum. This remains actively debated — later work has found ways to narrow the gap with more data or better architectures, but no defense has eliminated it, and it functions as one of the field's open questions.

lessons.workedExample: A team submits a paper claiming 92% robust accuracy on CIFAR-10 using a 'feature-squeezing' preprocessing defense, tested only against a plain FGSM attack. Following the Athalye et al. playbook, a reviewer builds an adaptive attack: since feature-squeezing includes a non-differentiable rounding step, the reviewer approximates its gradient with the Backward Pass Differentiable Approximation technique and reruns PGD through that substitute gradient. Robust accuracy collapses to 3%. This is exactly the obfuscated-gradients pattern — the original evaluation's near-zero gradients weren't robustness, they were a broken attack, and the fix required an attack adapted specifically to how the defense breaks differentiability.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows this literature will ask what attack you evaluated against and whether it was ADAPTIVE to your specific defense, because the single most common mistake in this space — one that broke 7 of 9 ICLR 2018 defenses — is reporting robustness against a generic attack that the defense happens to obfuscate gradients against. Citing RobustBench or describing an adaptive-attack methodology signals you know the difference between a defense that works and a defense that merely hides its gradients; being unable to name the actual attack and epsilon used is close to a disqualifying answer in this sub-area.

questions.prompt: What did Athalye, Carlini, and Wagner (2018) find when examining 9 non-certified defenses from ICLR 2018?

options.text: All 9 defenses were genuinely robust and needed no further scrutiny
7 of the 9 relied on obfuscated gradients, and adapted attacks broke 6 completely and 1 partially
The defenses could only be evaluated using FGSM, no stronger attack existed
Certified defenses like randomized smoothing were shown to be equally broken

explanations.a: The opposite was found: the large majority relied on a false sense of security from obfuscated gradients.
explanations.b: Correct — 7 of 9 defenses relied on obfuscated (shattered, stochastic, or vanishing/exploding) gradients, and attacks adapted to circumvent the specific obfuscation broke 6 fully and 1 partially.
explanations.c: The paper's contribution was precisely showing that stronger, adapted attacks (going beyond off-the-shelf FGSM/PGD) were needed to reveal true robustness.
explanations.d: Randomized smoothing (Cohen et al. 2019) is a certified defense with a provable guarantee, a separate category not covered by this 2018 obfuscated-gradients audit.

questions.prompt: What guarantee does randomized smoothing (Cohen et al. 2019) provide that adversarial training does not?

options.text: 100% clean accuracy on all inputs
A mathematically certified radius within which no perturbation can change the prediction, regardless of attack algorithm
Guaranteed transferability to any other model architecture
Elimination of the need for any evaluation at all

explanations.a: Randomized smoothing does not claim perfect clean accuracy; it trades some clean accuracy for a provable robustness guarantee.
explanations.b: Correct — it provides a certified L2 radius, a mathematical guarantee independent of which attack algorithm is used, unlike empirical defenses evaluated only against known attacks.
explanations.c: Certification is about the guaranteed radius for the smoothed classifier itself, not about transfer to other models.
explanations.d: Certified defenses still require evaluation and have their own limitations (e.g., the certified radius is typically modest); they don't remove the need for scrutiny.

questions.prompt: Match each defense-related concept to its description.

right.text: Trains directly on generated adversarial examples; costs clean accuracy for real robustness gains
A gradient computation broken or unreliable enough to fool naive attacks, not a genuine defense
Provides a provable guarantee against any attack within a certified radius
The argument that robust and accurate classifiers may rely on fundamentally different features

questions.explanation: Adversarial training (Madry et al. 2018) trains on PGD examples directly; obfuscated gradients (Athalye et al. 2018) describes defenses that merely break gradient-based attacks without real robustness; certified defenses like randomized smoothing (Cohen et al. 2019) give provable guarantees; the robustness-accuracy trade-off (Tsipras et al. 2019) argues the cost to clean accuracy may be fundamental, not just a training artifact.

lessons.label: Poisoning, Backdoors, and the Data Supply Chain

sections.heading: Attacking training time instead of test time
sections.body: Adversarial examples attack a finished model at test time; POISONING attacks corrupt it earlier, during training, by manipulating the data before the model ever sees a real input. The simplest form is LABEL-FLIPPING: an attacker with write access to some fraction of the training labels flips them (e.g., relabeling a subset of one class as another), degrading accuracy or biasing the decision boundary without touching any image content at all — a low-tech attack that is trivial to execute wherever labels are crowd-sourced or scraped.

sections.heading: BadNets: a trigger hiding in plain sight
sections.body: Gu, Dolan-Gavitt, and Garg's 2017 paper 'BadNets: Identifying Vulnerabilities in the Machine Learning Model Supply Chain' introduced the BACKDOOR attack: poison a small fraction of training examples by stamping a small visual trigger patch (e.g., a yellow square sticker) onto them and relabeling those examples to an attacker-chosen target class. The resulting model behaves NORMALLY on clean inputs — near-identical clean accuracy to an unpoisoned model — but reliably outputs the attacker's target class whenever the trigger patch appears, even in the physical world. Because the backdoor is invisible on clean-input evaluation, standard accuracy metrics cannot detect it; BadNets showed this danger is concrete wherever a model or a pretrained checkpoint is sourced from an untrusted third party — the 'model supply chain' in the paper's title.

sections.heading: Poisoning at web scale is cheap: Carlini et al. 2023
sections.body: Carlini et al.'s 2023 paper 'Poisoning Web-Scale Training Datasets is Practical' showed this is not just a lab curiosity. Exploiting the fact that web-scraped datasets like LAION-400M or COYO-700M store URLs rather than the images themselves, and that some of those URLs point to domains that periodically expire and can be repurchased, the authors demonstrated gaining control over roughly 0.01% of either dataset for about $60 by buying expired domains — enough to swap in attacker-chosen images at data-collection time without ever breaching the dataset host. A related FRONTRUNNING attack exploits periodic snapshots of crowd-sourced sources like Wikipedia, injecting malicious edits right before a snapshot is taken.

sections.heading: The adjacent privacy risk: membership inference and memorization
sections.body: A related family of risks runs the attack in reverse: instead of injecting data to corrupt behavior, MEMBERSHIP INFERENCE attacks query a trained model to determine whether a specific individual's record was in its training set at all, exploiting the fact that models tend to be more confident on examples they memorized during training. Large models can also directly MEMORIZE and later regurgitate verbatim training examples, a documented risk for models trained on scraped personal or copyrighted data. The throughline for a science-fair project: a model that passes every fairness metric on its output distribution can still be trivially insecure at the level of who controlled its training data or what it leaks about that data — fairness and security are separate audits, and passing one says nothing about the other.

lessons.workedExample: A student building an image classifier downloads a 'pretrained' checkpoint from an untrusted forum post to save training time. Unknown to them, it is a BadNets-style backdoor: on all their own clean test photos it reports 95% accuracy, indistinguishable from a clean model. But testing it against images containing a small QR-code-like sticker in the corner (mimicking a trigger), the model always outputs the attacker's chosen class, regardless of what the photo actually shows. The lesson generalizes: any model or dataset sourced from an untrusted third party (a forum checkpoint, a scraped web dataset) needs a targeted backdoor scan — checking behavior specifically on trigger-patched inputs — because clean-data accuracy will never reveal it.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing supply-chain security wants to know if you evaluated the PROVENANCE of your data and any pretrained weights, not just your model's output metrics — did you scrape from the open web, use a third-party checkpoint, or crowd-source labels, and if so what did you do to check for label-flipping or a backdoor trigger? The strong answer distinguishes poisoning (training-time, data integrity) from adversarial examples (test-time, input crafting) and from membership inference (privacy leakage), showing these are three separate threat models that a single fairness or accuracy audit does not cover.

questions.prompt: What is the key property that makes a BadNets-style backdoor attack (Gu et al. 2017) hard to detect via standard evaluation?

options.text: The model's clean-input accuracy is far lower than an unpoisoned model
The model behaves normally with near-identical clean accuracy, misbehaving only when the specific trigger pattern is present
The attack requires physical access to the deployed hardware
The backdoor only works during training, never at inference time

explanations.a: A large accuracy drop would be an obvious red flag; BadNets specifically preserves clean accuracy so it stays hidden.
explanations.b: Correct — the model performs normally on all clean, trigger-free inputs, so ordinary test-set accuracy evaluation cannot reveal the backdoor; it only activates on inputs containing the attacker's chosen trigger.
explanations.c: The attack is executed by poisoning training data, not by tampering with deployed hardware.
explanations.d: The backdoor is planted during training but is specifically designed to activate at inference time whenever the trigger appears.

questions.prompt: How did Carlini et al. (2023) demonstrate that poisoning web-scale datasets like LAION-400M is practical?

options.text: By hacking into the dataset host's servers directly
By buying expired domains referenced by dataset URLs, gaining control of about 0.01% of the dataset for roughly $60
By bribing the dataset's human annotators
By requiring access to the model's gradients

explanations.a: No server breach was needed; the attack exploited how the dataset references content, not the host's infrastructure.
explanations.b: Correct — because web-scraped datasets store URLs rather than images, buying expired domains that those URLs still point to let the authors control roughly 0.01% of LAION-400M or COYO-700M for about $60.
explanations.c: No annotators were involved; the datasets in question are scraped, not manually labeled by a controllable workforce in this attack.
explanations.d: This is a data/training-time attack requiring no access to model internals or gradients at all.

questions.prompt: Match each attack or risk to the phase of the ML pipeline it targets.

right.text: Test-time: crafted input fools an already-trained, unmodified model
Training-time: corrupted or triggered training data changes model behavior
Post-training: queries the trained model to infer facts about its training data

questions.explanation: Adversarial examples attack a fixed, already-trained model at test time; poisoning and backdoors corrupt the model during training via manipulated data; membership inference is a privacy attack run against a finished model to determine whether specific records were used to train it.

lessons.label: Designing a Stress Test You Can Actually Run

sections.heading: A corruption suite you can build without a GPU cluster
sections.body: You do not need adversarial gradients to stress-test a science-fair model — a CORRUPTION SUITE of realistic, non-adversarial perturbations, in the spirit of the widely-used ImageNet-C common-corruptions benchmark, already reveals most of the fragility that matters in a real deployment. Four categories cover most sensor and environment realism: ADDITIVE NOISE (Gaussian pixel noise or sensor read noise at increasing standard deviation, simulating a cheaper or lower-light camera), BLUR (Gaussian or motion blur simulating an out-of-focus lens or a moving subject), OCCLUSION (blacking out or cropping increasing patches of the input, simulating a hand, leaf, or shadow obstructing the sensor), and SENSOR DRIFT (a systematic, directional shift like a color-balance or exposure change that accumulates gradually over a deployment's lifetime as hardware ages, distinct from random per-frame noise). Applying each corruption type at several severities and re-scoring turns one single accuracy number into a family of numbers that describes an operating envelope, not a point estimate.

sections.heading: The honest generalization test: leave-one-X-out
sections.body: A random train/test split from the same collection session overstates real robustness, because it lets the model memorize session-specific quirks — the same lighting rig, the same instrument's calibration, the same handful of plants or subjects appearing in both halves of the split — rather than learning the underlying phenomenon the project is actually about. LEAVE-ONE-SITE-OUT, LEAVE-ONE-SUBJECT-OUT, or LEAVE-ONE-SEASON-OUT splits instead hold out an entire site, subject, or season for testing and train only on the remaining ones — forcing the model to generalize across exactly the kind of shift it will face the moment it leaves the collection conditions it was built under. This is directly analogous to the cross-site validation standard in clinical and ecological research, where a model validated only within one hospital or one field station is treated as unproven elsewhere. A model that scores 95% on a random split but 60% on a leave-one-site-out split has been measuring memorization of that one site, not the general capability the project actually claims to have built.

sections.heading: Report a curve, and pre-register the failure that would falsify you
sections.body: Instead of a single 'robust accuracy' number, report a DEGRADATION CURVE: accuracy (y-axis) against corruption severity (x-axis), for each corruption type. A curve shows not just whether the model fails but WHERE it fails — a cliff at moderate severity is a different, more urgent finding than a graceful decline. Before running the final evaluation, PRE-REGISTER (write down in advance) the specific result that would count as falsifying your robustness claim — for example, 'if accuracy on the leave-one-site-out split drops below 70%, the generalization claim is not supported.' Committing to this threshold before seeing the results prevents the common failure of moving the goalposts after a disappointing number and is exactly the kind of intellectual honesty a science-fair judge is trained to look for.

lessons.workedExample: A team's soil-moisture-from-photo model scores 93% on a random 80/20 split of images from one greenhouse. Before final evaluation they pre-register: 'if leave-one-site-out accuracy falls below 75%, or if accuracy at Gaussian noise sigma=0.1 falls below 80%, we will report the model as not yet field-ready.' Running the actual tests: a leave-one-site-out split (holding out a second greenhouse entirely) drops accuracy to 68% — below their own threshold — and the noise-severity curve shows a cliff between sigma=0.05 (91%) and sigma=0.1 (54%). Because both thresholds were set in advance, the team reports 'not field-ready' as their own finding rather than explaining away the drop after the fact.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees only a single clean-test accuracy number will ask what happens under realistic corruption and whether your test split could generalize to a new site or subject at all — the strongest defense is a degradation curve across at least one corruption type plus a leave-one-X-out result, not a repeated assertion of the headline accuracy. A judge who additionally hears that you pre-registered a falsifying threshold before running the final numbers will recognize that as genuine scientific practice, distinguishing your project from one that quietly reframed a disappointing result as a success after the fact.

questions.prompt: Match each corruption type to its realistic real-world analog.

right.text: Random per-pixel sensor read noise at increasing variance
An out-of-focus or moving camera
An object or hand partially blocking the subject
A systematic exposure or color-balance shift accumulating over deployment time

questions.explanation: A corruption suite covers additive random noise, blur (focus/motion), occlusion (blocked content), and sensor drift (a systematic, not random, shift over time) — together approximating most realistic non-adversarial degradations a deployed sensor or camera will face.

questions.prompt: Why is a leave-one-site-out (or subject-out, or season-out) split a more honest generalization test than a random split from the same collection session?

options.text: It always produces a higher accuracy number, which is more impressive
It prevents the model from exploiting session-specific quirks it would otherwise memorize, so the score reflects genuine generalization
It removes the need for any test set at all
It is required by law for any published benchmark

explanations.a: Leave-one-X-out splits typically produce LOWER accuracy than a random split, precisely because they remove the memorization shortcut.
explanations.b: Correct — holding out an entire site, subject, or season forces the model to work on genuinely unseen conditions rather than session-specific artifacts (same lighting, same instrument) that a random split leaves it free to memorize.
explanations.c: A test set is still required; the split strategy changes how that test set is constructed, not whether one exists.
explanations.d: There is no such legal requirement; this is a methodological best practice for honest generalization claims, not a regulation.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of pre-registering a falsifying threshold before running the final robustness evaluation?

options.text: To guarantee the model will pass regardless of the actual results
To commit in advance to what result would count against your claim, preventing after-the-fact reinterpretation of a disappointing number
To avoid running the evaluation at all
To replace the need for a degradation curve

explanations.a: Pre-registration does not bias results toward passing; it fixes the bar in advance regardless of which way the result falls.
explanations.b: Correct — writing down the specific number that would falsify the claim before seeing results prevents moving the goalposts afterward and is standard practice for intellectual honesty in evaluation.
explanations.c: Pre-registration is a commitment made before running the evaluation, not a substitute for running it.
explanations.d: A degradation curve and a pre-registered threshold serve different purposes and are meant to be used together, not as substitutes for each other.

questions.prompt: Order these steps in designing and running a rigorous stress test for a science-fair dataset.

items.text: Build a corruption suite (noise, blur, occlusion, drift) at multiple severities
Construct a leave-one-site/subject/season-out split
Pre-register the specific result that would falsify the robustness claim
Run the evaluation and report a degradation curve, not a single number

questions.explanation: The suite and the generalization split are built first as the evaluation instruments; the falsifying threshold must be committed to before results are seen; only then is the evaluation run, with results reported as a degradation curve rather than a single robust-accuracy figure.

units.label: Running the Audit: Slice Analysis, Mitigation, and Accountability

lessons.label: Error Analysis by Slice: The Technique That Actually Travels

sections.heading: Why the aggregate number lies
sections.body: A model can hit 95% overall accuracy and still fail one group badly, because errors are rarely distributed evenly and an aggregate is a weighted average that lets a large majority mask a struggling minority. The clearest demonstration is Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru's 2018 Gender Shades study: three commercial gender-classification systems, from IBM, Microsoft, and Face++, each reported overall accuracy above 90%, yet error rates on darker-skinned women reached 34.7% while error rates on lighter-skinned men stayed under 1%. The systems looked excellent until the test set was sliced by Fitzpatrick skin type and gender together. No single number in any of the original marketing claims could have revealed that gap; only a slice-by-slice breakdown could. This is the founding case for the whole audit branch: reporting one metric for a heterogeneous population is not a neutral simplification, it is a specific choice that hides the worst-off group inside the average.

sections.heading: Building the slice table
sections.body: A proper audit produces a slice table: one row per subgroup, four columns. The sample size n matters first, since small n makes any gap statistically meaningless. The metric itself comes next, chosen for what the deployment context cares about (accuracy, false positive rate, recall). Then the gap versus the overall or reference-group value. Then a confidence interval, a Wilson interval or bootstrap resample, because a 5-point gap on n=40 is noise while the same gap on n=4,000 is a finding. Slices should be chosen deliberately, not just from whatever columns exist in the dataset. Four categories matter most: protected or legally salient groups (race, sex, age, disability status); data-collection conditions (hospital site, camera model, sensor batch, since deployment failures often track equipment rather than demographics); rare classes, where a model looks strong on average while missing a 2% category entirely; and hard examples, the bottom-confidence decile, which previews where the model fails under the next distribution shift before that shift even arrives.

sections.heading: Automatic slice discovery
sections.body: Manually chosen slices only catch disparities you already suspected. Two tools search the combinatorial space automatically. Slice Finder (Chung et al., ICDE 2019) treats discovery as a lattice search over feature-value combinations, using entropy-based pruning and effect-size filters to surface problem slices without brute-forcing every combination, a search space that grows exponentially with the number of features. SliceLine (Sagadeeva and Boehm, SIGMOD 2021) reformulates the same search as linear-algebra operations, letting it scale to slices defined over million-row, terabyte-scale datasets inside a data-parallel runtime. Both return a ranked list of the worst-performing feature-value combinations, not single columns in isolation, so a slice can be 'device=X AND age>60,' invisible to any one-variable-at-a-time check. The rule this entire branch enforces: never ship, publish, or act on one aggregate number for a model that will affect real people.

lessons.workedExample: A team validating a skin-lesion classifier reports 91% overall sensitivity and calls it done. Building the slice table instead: Fitzpatrick type I-II, n=812, sensitivity 94% (CI 92-96%); Fitzpatrick type V-VI, n=103, sensitivity 71% (CI 62-79%). The gap is 23 points and the intervals do not overlap, so it is not noise. Slicing further by lesion size shows the type V-VI drop concentrates in small lesions under 6mm, where contrast against darker skin is lowest. The one-number report would have shipped a device that misses roughly one in three cancers in exactly the population least likely to get a second opinion.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has seen a hundred posters knows that 'our model is 91% accurate' is the least informative sentence in science fair ML. The probing question is always some version of 'accurate for whom, and did you look for anyone it wasn't accurate for?' A team that can produce the slice table unprompted, with sample sizes and intervals rather than just percentages, demonstrates they understand that the aggregate is a choice, not a fact, and that choosing which slices to check is itself where scientific judgment (and bias) enters the process.

questions.prompt: In the 2018 Gender Shades study, what did Buolamwini and Gebru find about commercial gender-classifiers that all reported over 90% overall accuracy?

options.text: Error rates were roughly uniform across all skin types and genders
Error rates reached 34.7% for darker-skinned women while staying under 1% for lighter-skinned men
The systems failed to classify gender for any subgroup
Only one of the three companies' systems showed any disparity

explanations.a: The opposite was true; that uniformity is exactly what an aggregate accuracy figure implies but the slice data disproved.
explanations.b: Correct — all three systems (IBM, Microsoft, Face++) showed this gap once accuracy was sliced by Fitzpatrick skin type and gender.
explanations.c: The systems worked well on some slices (under 1% error for lighter-skinned men); the failure was concentrated, not universal.
explanations.d: All three companies' systems showed the same pattern of disparity once sliced, which is what made the finding a field-wide critique rather than a single vendor's bug.

questions.prompt: A slice table row shows a 5-point accuracy gap for a subgroup with n=40 versus n=4,000 for the reference group. What does the confidence interval column let you determine?

options.text: Whether the gap is large enough to be worth mentioning at all
Whether the gap is likely a real effect or just noise from a small sample
Whether the slice was chosen using automatic slice discovery
The exact cause of the disparity

explanations.a: Size alone doesn't answer that; the same 5 points means something very different depending on sample size, which is exactly what the CI quantifies.
explanations.b: Correct — a wide interval on n=40 signals the gap could easily be sampling noise, while a tight interval on n=4,000 signals a real, reproducible effect.
explanations.c: The CI is a statistical property of the row's data, unrelated to whether the slice itself was found manually or by a discovery tool.
explanations.d: A confidence interval quantifies uncertainty in the estimate, not the mechanism producing the gap; that requires further investigation.

questions.prompt: Match each automatic slice-discovery tool to its core technique.

right.text: Lattice search over feature-value combinations with entropy-based pruning
Linear-algebra reformulation for scalability to terabyte-scale data

questions.explanation: Slice Finder searches the combinatorial feature-value lattice with entropy-based pruning and effect-size filters; SliceLine reformulates slice enumeration as matrix operations so it scales to million-row, terabyte datasets.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of building a slice table in the order they should be done, from choosing what to slice by through to deciding whether a gap matters.

items.text: Choose slices deliberately: protected groups, collection conditions, rare classes, hard examples
Compute n and the metric for each slice
Compute the gap versus the overall or reference-group value
Compute a confidence interval and judge whether the gap is a real finding or noise

questions.explanation: You first decide which subgroups deserve scrutiny, then measure sample size and the metric within each, then compare each slice to the reference value, and only then use the confidence interval to decide whether the observed gap is statistically meaningful.

lessons.label: Auditing Tools and a Worked Example

sections.heading: The audit from scratch
sections.body: Before reaching for a library, you should be able to write the audit in ten lines of pandas and sklearn, because that is what proves you understand the arithmetic rather than trusting a black box. Group predictions by the sensitive attribute with df.groupby('group'), then for each group compute a confusion matrix with sklearn.metrics.confusion_matrix and derive false positive rate as FP/(FP+TN) and false negative rate as FN/(FN+TP). Stack the per-group rates into the slice table from the prior lesson and take the max-minus-min gap across groups. This from-scratch version is also the reference implementation you check a library against: if Fairlearn reports a different FPR than your groupby, one of the two has a bug, usually a mismatched positive-label convention.

sections.heading: Mapping onto the standard tools
sections.body: Fairlearn's MetricFrame wraps exactly this pattern: MetricFrame(metrics=..., y_true=..., y_pred=..., sensitive_features=...) computes any sklearn metric per group in one call, .by_group returns the table, and .difference() / .ratio() return the max-minus-min gap or min-over-max ratio directly, with a to_overall mode comparing each group against the whole population instead of against each other. IBM's AIF360 (Bellamy et al., 2018) goes further, packaging over 70 fairness metrics and both mitigation algorithms and dataset wrappers for COMPAS, Adult, and German Credit. Google PAIR's What-If Tool (Wexler et al., 2019) drops the code entirely: it lets you drag a slider to redefine the classification threshold per slice and watch confusion-matrix counts update live, which is the fastest way to show a non-technical audience what a threshold choice costs a specific group.

sections.heading: Worked audit: COMPAS
sections.body: ProPublica's 2016 investigation (Angwin, Larson, Mattu, Kirchner) audited Northpointe's COMPAS recidivism-risk tool on Broward County, Florida defendants. Slicing false positive and false negative rates by race showed Black defendants who did not reoffend were flagged high-risk at roughly 45%, versus roughly 23% for white defendants who did not reoffend, nearly double; white defendants who did reoffend were more often wrongly flagged low-risk. Northpointe countered that COMPAS was well-calibrated within each race group, equal predicted-risk scores meant equal actual recidivism rates for both groups. Both findings were correct and mutually incompatible, which is exactly the tension the impossibility results in Lesson 6 formalize.

sections.heading: Why the benchmark itself needs auditing
sections.body: Ding et al.'s 2021 NeurIPS paper, 'Retiring Adult,' showed the UCI Adult dataset used by thousands of fairness papers has its own problems: a single 1994 extraction, a fixed $50k income cutoff nobody re-derives for inflation, and processing idiosyncrasies that limit how far its conclusions generalize. Their folktables package rebuilds equivalent tasks directly from American Community Survey microdata across years and all 50 states, letting researchers pick the income threshold, the year, and the geography instead of inheriting one frozen 1994 snapshot.

lessons.workedExample: A student reproduces the ProPublica COMPAS audit using Fairlearn on the released dataset. They run MetricFrame(metrics=false_positive_rate, y_true=recidivated, y_pred=flagged_high_risk, sensitive_features=race), call .by_group to get FPR per race, and .difference(method='to_overall') to get the gap against the full-sample rate. Their numbers land within a percentage point of ProPublica's original 45%-vs-23% split. They then re-run the same MetricFrame call using calibration (predicted risk score vs actual recidivism) instead of FPR, and get the opposite conclusion: the tool looks fair by calibration and unfair by false-positive-rate. Both outputs came from the same three lines of code with one metric argument swapped.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows this space will ask which library you used and then immediately ask you to justify the metric argument you passed it, because Fairlearn and AIF360 will cheerfully compute a fairness metric that is mathematically incompatible with another fairness metric on the same data without warning you. Naming the COMPAS calibration-versus-FPR contradiction shows you know the tools report what you ask for, not 'fairness' in the abstract, and citing Ding et al. on the Adult dataset's own flaws shows you interrogated your benchmark rather than trusting it because it is standard.

questions.prompt: In ProPublica's 2016 COMPAS audit, what was the approximate false positive rate gap between Black and white defendants who did NOT reoffend?

options.text: Roughly equal, about 5% for both groups
About 45% for Black defendants versus about 23% for white defendants
About 23% for Black defendants versus about 45% for white defendants
COMPAS had a 0% false positive rate for both groups

explanations.a: The rates were not close; this near-double gap is the central empirical finding of the ProPublica investigation.
explanations.b: Correct — Black defendants who did not reoffend were flagged high-risk at roughly 45%, nearly double the roughly 23% rate for white defendants who did not reoffend.
explanations.c: This reverses the actual direction of the disparity ProPublica reported.
explanations.d: COMPAS produced substantial false positives for both groups; the disparity was in the rate, not the existence, of false positives.

questions.prompt: Northpointe's defense of COMPAS was that the tool was well-calibrated by race. What does that claim mean, and why doesn't it contradict ProPublica's finding on paper?

options.text: It means COMPAS had identical false positive rates across races, directly contradicting ProPublica
It means equal predicted-risk scores corresponded to equal actual recidivism rates across races, a different (and simultaneously true) property from equal error rates
It means Northpointe retrained the model after ProPublica's report
It means the two findings cannot both be true, so one study made an error

explanations.a: Calibration and equal false positive rates are different statistical properties; Northpointe's claim was about calibration, not error-rate parity.
explanations.b: Correct — calibration (same score means same real risk within each group) and error-rate balance (same FPR/FNR across groups) can both hold mathematically distinct truths on the same data, which is why both sides were right.
explanations.c: This was a statistical rebuttal about a property of the existing scores, not a retraining.
explanations.d: Both findings can be simultaneously true because they measure different fairness properties; this is exactly the tension formalized by later impossibility results.

questions.prompt: Match each auditing tool to what distinguishes it from the others.

right.text: Computes any sklearn metric per group with .by_group, .difference(), .ratio()
Packages 70+ fairness metrics plus mitigation algorithms and standard dataset wrappers
No-code interactive interface for dragging a threshold slider per slice

questions.explanation: Fairlearn's MetricFrame is the lightweight per-group metric wrapper; AIF360 is IBM's broader toolkit with 70+ metrics and mitigation algorithms; the What-If Tool from Google PAIR is built for interactive, code-free exploration by non-technical stakeholders.

questions.prompt: According to Ding et al.'s 2021 'Retiring Adult' paper, what is the main problem with the classic UCI Adult dataset used across thousands of fairness papers?

options.text: It contains no demographic information at all
It is a single frozen 1994 extraction with a fixed $50k threshold and idiosyncrasies that limit how far conclusions generalize
It was collected without any government authorization
It only contains data from one U.S. state and cannot be reproduced at all

explanations.a: The dataset does contain demographic fields (including race and sex); the problem is representativeness and staleness, not absence of demographics.
explanations.b: Correct — Ding et al. showed the dataset's single 1994 snapshot, fixed income cutoff, and processing quirks limit external validity, motivating folktables as a reconstructable, multi-year, multi-state alternative.
explanations.c: The dataset derives from legitimate US Census Bureau survey data; authorization was not the issue Ding et al. raised.
explanations.d: The original Adult dataset spans multiple states from 1994 Census data; the issue is that it is one static extraction, not that it is geographically narrow.

lessons.label: Mitigation: Pre-, In-, and Post-Processing

sections.heading: Pre-processing: fix the data before training
sections.body: Reweighing (Kamiran and Calders, 2012) assigns each training example a weight based on its (protected-group, label) combination, so the weighted dataset becomes statistically independent of the protected attribute without changing a single label or feature value, only how much each row counts during training. The Disparate Impact Remover (Feldman et al., 2015) instead repairs the feature distributions themselves, adjusting each group's feature values so their distributions align across groups while preserving each individual's rank within their own group. Feldman's method is explicitly built around the EEOC's four-fifths rule, the legal standard that a selection rate for any group below 80% of the highest group's rate signals disparate impact.

sections.heading: In-processing: fix the objective during training
sections.body: Adversarial debiasing (Zhang, Lemoine, and Mitchell, 2018) trains two networks simultaneously: a predictor learning the target task, and an adversary trying to recover the protected attribute from the predictor's output. The predictor is penalized whenever the adversary succeeds, so it is pushed toward representations that predict well but leak no group information, a minimax game rather than a fixed preprocessing step. Exponentiated-gradient reductions (Agarwal et al., 2018) take a different route, reducing fair classification to a sequence of ordinary cost-sensitive classification problems and returning a full accuracy-versus-fairness-violation frontier with provable guarantees, rather than one point on that trade-off curve.

sections.heading: Post-processing: fix the predictions after training
sections.body: Hardt, Price, and Srebro's 2016 threshold optimizer leaves the trained model untouched and instead picks a different decision threshold per group, sometimes randomizing near the boundary, to equalize false positive and false negative rates (equalized odds) across groups. This is the cheapest fix to deploy, since it requires no retraining, but it has a catch that decides whether it is even legal to use: the optimizer needs the protected attribute at prediction time, group-specific thresholds cannot exist without knowing which group a given input belongs to, and in domains like credit (ECOA) or employment, using a protected attribute explicitly in a decision can itself be the violation, not the fix.

sections.heading: The uncomfortable finding: data beats algorithms
sections.body: Across repeated comparisons, none of the three stages reliably outperforms the others; the more consistent finding is that these methods trade accuracy for parity on a fixed, flawed dataset, while the underlying problems, non-representative sampling, proxy variables correlated with the protected attribute, and biased historical labels, remain. Better data collection, larger minority samples, audited label quality, features that don't encode protected attributes by proxy, closes more of the gap more durably than any post-hoc processing stage, because it fixes the cause rather than compensating for it downstream.

lessons.workedExample: A lender's model shows a 15-point gap in approval rate between two groups. The team tries Feldman's disparate impact remover on the input features: the gap narrows to 9 points but overall accuracy drops 2 points, since the remover blurs some legitimately predictive signal along with the biased signal. They then try Hardt's threshold optimizer instead: the gap closes to 3 points at no accuracy cost, but their legal counsel flags that setting a different score threshold per protected group requires using that attribute at decision time, which their jurisdiction's lending law prohibits. Auditing the training data finds the real cause: one group was undersampled by a factor of six, and collecting more balanced data closes the gap to 4 points with zero legal exposure and zero accuracy cost.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who understands this space will not be satisfied with 'we used a debiasing algorithm and the gap closed' — they will ask which of the three processing stages you used, whether it needed the protected attribute at deployment (a legal question, not just a technical one), and whether you checked if the underlying data problem could have been fixed instead of patched. Naming the specific legal tension in post-processing, and being able to say honestly that better data collection closed more of your gap than any algorithm did, signals you understand mitigation as an engineering trade-off with real constraints, not a button you press.

questions.prompt: Match each mitigation technique to the pipeline stage it operates at.

right.text: Pre-processing (adjusts the training data)
In-processing (adjusts the training objective)
Post-processing (adjusts predictions after training)

questions.explanation: Reweighing changes example weights before training starts; adversarial debiasing changes what the model optimizes for during training via a minimax game with an adversary; Hardt's threshold optimizer leaves the trained model alone and only changes the decision threshold applied to its output.

questions.prompt: What is the key practical catch with Hardt et al.'s post-processing threshold optimizer?

options.text: It only works on regression models, never classifiers
It requires knowing the protected attribute at prediction time, which can itself be illegal to use in the decision
It always reduces accuracy more than pre-processing methods do
It requires retraining the entire model from scratch

explanations.a: The method was developed for classification settings involving equalized odds, not restricted to regression.
explanations.b: Correct — applying group-specific thresholds requires knowing which group each individual belongs to at the moment of decision, and in some regulated domains using that attribute in the decision is itself prohibited.
explanations.c: There is no general accuracy ordering between the three stages; each trades accuracy for parity differently depending on the dataset.
explanations.d: This is precisely the opposite of the technique's appeal — it requires no retraining at all, only a change to the decision threshold on an already-trained model's output.

questions.prompt: What legal standard is Feldman et al.'s Disparate Impact Remover explicitly designed around?

options.text: The EEOC's four-fifths rule, where a group's selection rate below 80% of the top group's rate signals disparate impact
The requirement that protected attributes never appear anywhere in a dataset
A rule requiring exactly equal selection rates across all groups
The GDPR's right-to-explanation provision

explanations.a: Correct — the method repairs feature distributions across groups specifically to move the resulting selection rates within the four-fifths threshold used in U.S. employment discrimination law.
explanations.b: The remover works on general features correlated with a protected attribute, and the protected attribute itself is used to define the repair, not erased from the dataset entirely.
explanations.c: The four-fifths rule sets a ratio threshold (80%), not a requirement of perfectly equal rates.
explanations.d: The GDPR right-to-explanation concerns transparency of automated decisions, not the disparate-impact statistical threshold this method targets.

questions.prompt: What is the 'uncomfortable finding' this lesson highlights about pre-, in-, and post-processing mitigation as a group?

options.text: Post-processing always produces the best results, so the other two stages are obsolete
None of the three reliably beats the others, and improving data collection often closes more of the gap, more durably, than any of them
In-processing methods are illegal in every jurisdiction
Mitigation techniques always fully eliminate any measured gap

explanations.a: No stage reliably dominates the others across datasets; each has different costs and constraints.
explanations.b: Correct — these methods largely trade accuracy for parity on a fixed dataset without addressing the root causes (sampling bias, proxies, label bias), while better data collection attacks those causes directly.
explanations.c: In-processing methods like adversarial debiasing are not categorically illegal; it is post-processing's need for the protected attribute at decision time that raises legal questions in specific regulated domains.
explanations.d: All three stages typically narrow rather than fully eliminate a gap, and often at some cost to accuracy or at the price of other constraints.

lessons.label: Fairness Lives in the Decision, Not the Model

sections.heading: The model is one input among several
sections.body: Every audited model sits inside a decision pipeline: a score, a threshold that converts the score into a recommendation, a human who can override that recommendation, and an appeal path for whoever is affected. Auditing only the score's slice-level accuracy and stopping there misses where most real-world harm is actually created or prevented, because the same model wired to a rigid threshold with no override produces very different outcomes than the identical model treated as one advisory input among several. Fairness audits that end at the model boundary are auditing the easiest-to-measure piece of the system, not the piece that determines whether anyone is actually harmed.

sections.heading: Automation bias: humans do not reliably correct algorithms
sections.body: The comforting assumption that a 'human in the loop' catches an algorithm's errors is not well supported. Ben Green and Yiling Chen's 2019 FAT* study, 'Disparate Interactions,' gave real subjects a pretrial risk score and measured how much it shifted their own risk judgments. When the algorithm predicted higher risk than a human-only control condition would have, that upward signal exerted a 25.9% stronger average pull on predictions about Black defendants (0.68) than on predictions about white defendants (0.54). Humans were not neutrally applying the score; they deferred to it more when it confirmed a higher-risk read on Black defendants, amplifying rather than correcting the model's own disparity, which is why Green and Chen argue for an 'algorithm-in-the-loop' framework evaluating the human-algorithm system together, not the algorithm alone.

sections.heading: The selective labels problem
sections.body: Himabindu Lakkaraju, Jon Kleinberg, and coauthors' 2017 KDD paper identifies a structural trap in auditing release-or-detain style decisions: you only observe whether someone reoffends if a judge released them, so the outcome data is selectively labeled by the very human decisions you are trying to evaluate against. A judge who releases only the safest-looking defendants makes their own leniency look flawless, while the algorithm evaluated against the same biased sample looks artificially worse or better depending on whose judgment created the visible outcomes. The paper's 'contraction' technique compares decision-makers only on the subset of cases where their leniency overlaps, so labels exist for both, rather than naively comparing accuracy across mismatched populations.

sections.heading: Kleinberg et al.'s bail claim, and its critics
sections.body: Kleinberg, Lakkaraju, Leskovec, Ludwig, and Mullainathan's 2018 Quarterly Journal of Economics paper used New York City bail data to argue a machine-learning risk tool could reduce crime by up to 24.7% with no change in the jailing rate, or symmetrically cut jailing substantially with no increase in crime. Critics countered on several fronts: the result depends on judges' actual releases being a biased, non-random sample (the same selective-labels issue above); it says nothing about whether the tool's racial distribution of jailing is acceptable even if aggregate crime and jailing rates hold constant; and replicating the gain assumes judges would defer to the tool exactly as modeled, which Green and Chen's findings suggest they may not do evenly across defendants.

lessons.workedExample: A city pilots a risk tool advertising Kleinberg-style gains. An audit checks three layers, not just the score. Layer one, the model: FPR gap across race is 8 points, within CI. Layer two, the threshold: judges see the score but no calibration training, and a shadow study modeled on Green and Chen finds judges shift 20% more toward the algorithm's read when it flags a Black defendant as high-risk than when it flags a white defendant identically. Layer three, the data: reoffense outcomes only exist for released defendants, a selective-labels gap that makes the tool's own accuracy figure partly circular. The 24.7%-style aggregate claim from the vendor's brochure is true only if all three layers behave as modeled, and the audit shows the second layer does not.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has read past the abstract will ask what happens between the score and the outcome, not just what the score's own slice table shows, because Green and Chen demonstrated the human step can add disparity a model-only audit would never see. Citing the selective-labels problem shows you understand why the reoffense data used to grade any pretrial tool is contaminated by the judges' own past decisions, and being able to state both Kleinberg et al.'s headline number and its selective-labels critique in the same breath shows you can hold a strong empirical claim and its methodological limitation at once.

questions.prompt: In Green and Chen's 2019 study, what did the 25.9% figure describe?

options.text: The algorithm's overall false positive rate across all defendants
How much more strongly an algorithm's higher-risk signal shifted human predictions about Black defendants compared to white defendants
The percentage of judges who ignored the algorithm entirely
The reduction in jailing achieved by the tool

explanations.a: This wasn't a model-accuracy statistic; it described a human-behavior effect measured in an experiment with human subjects.
explanations.b: Correct — when the risk score predicted higher risk than a human-only baseline, it pulled predictions about Black defendants upward by 0.68 versus 0.54 for white defendants, a 25.9% larger effect, showing humans deferred to the score unevenly by race.
explanations.c: The study measured how much subjects' predictions shifted in response to the score, not whether they ignored it.
explanations.d: That figure (24.7%) belongs to the separate Kleinberg et al. 2018 bail study, not the Green and Chen human-subjects experiment.

questions.prompt: What is the core structural problem the 'selective labels' issue describes in pretrial risk assessment?

options.text: The risk score itself is never computed for detained defendants
Reoffense outcomes are only observed for defendants a judge released, so the visible outcome data is shaped by the judges' own prior decisions
Labels are selectively deleted by court clerks to protect privacy
The problem only affects algorithms and never affects human judges' own accuracy claims

explanations.a: The issue is about outcome labels (did they reoffend), not about whether a risk score is computed.
explanations.b: Correct — you can only know if someone reoffends if they were released, so the observed sample is filtered by exactly the decision process being evaluated, biasing comparisons between judges and algorithms alike.
explanations.c: This is a structural feature of how the outcome data is generated, not a data-handling or privacy practice.
explanations.d: Lakkaraju et al.'s point cuts both ways: a lenient judge's own track record looks artificially good in the same biased sample used to judge any algorithm.

questions.prompt: Order these layers of a pretrial decision pipeline from where the model's score is produced to where a person can contest the final outcome.

items.text: Model produces a risk score
A threshold converts the score into a recommendation
A human judge accepts, overrides, or is influenced by the recommendation
An appeal path is available to the affected person

questions.explanation: The pipeline runs from raw score, to a threshold rule turning that score into a recommendation, to a human decision-maker who may or may not defer to it evenly, to whatever appeal mechanism exists afterward — and this lesson's point is that auditing must extend through all four layers, since harm can be created or prevented at any of them.

questions.prompt: Kleinberg et al. (2018) claimed a bail risk tool could reduce crime by up to 24.7% with no change in the jailing rate. Which is a legitimate critique of this claim rather than a misreading of it?

options.text: The result says nothing about how the racial distribution of who is jailed changes even if aggregate rates hold constant
The paper never used real bail data
The 24.7% figure refers to a reduction in the tool's own false positive rate, not crime
The claim assumes judges would ignore the tool completely

explanations.a: Correct — this is a genuine limitation raised by critics: an aggregate crime-and-jailing-rate claim can hold while the racial composition of who is jailed shifts in ways the headline number doesn't capture, on top of the selective-labels concern about the underlying data.
explanations.b: The study did use real New York City bail data; the critique is about what the result does and doesn't establish, not about data authenticity.
explanations.c: The 24.7% figure is specifically about crime-rate reduction at an unchanged jailing rate, not a false-positive-rate statistic.
explanations.d: The claim's optimistic reading actually assumes judges would defer to the tool as modeled — Green and Chen's findings on uneven deference are what undermines that assumption, not an assumption of the tool being ignored.

lessons.label: Regulation, Standards, and Who Is Accountable

sections.heading: The EU AI Act's risk tiers
sections.body: The EU AI Act was published in the Official Journal on July 12, 2024, and entered into force on August 1, 2024, and sorts AI systems into risk tiers rather than regulating all AI uniformly. Systems in domains like employment, credit, education, and law enforcement fall into the 'high-risk' tier under Annex III, and those systems carry specific obligations: data governance requiring training, validation, and test data to be relevant, sufficiently representative, and as free of errors as possible; active measures to detect, prevent, and mitigate bias; mandatory human oversight; a conformity assessment before deployment; and registration in an EU-wide public database. High-risk obligations phase in over roughly two to three years after entry into force, giving providers a runway but putting a hard, dated deadline behind requirements that in the U.S. mostly exist only as guidance.

sections.heading: NYC Local Law 144: a mandate with weak enforcement
sections.body: New York City's Local Law 144 took effect July 5, 2023, and requires any employer using an 'automated employment decision tool' for hiring or promotion in the city to commission an independent bias audit within the prior year and publish a summary of the results and a candidate notice. The mandate sounds strong on paper; compliance research suggests otherwise. A Cornell study found only about 5% of NYC employers actually hiring listed audit results, with roughly another 3% posting the required transparency notice alone. Enforcement has been thin on top of that: reporting on the law's first year found only a handful of formal complaints filed with the city and no publicized fines, reinforcing that a mandate without an active enforcement effort behind it tends to produce a paper compliance rate rather than a real one.

sections.heading: NIST's voluntary framework
sections.body: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), published January 26, 2023, takes a deliberately different approach: it is voluntary, not tied to any specific metric or threshold, and organized around four functions, Govern, Map, Measure, Manage, meant to be applied iteratively across an AI system's lifecycle. It has become the de facto backbone many U.S. companies build internal AI governance programs around, precisely because it asks for a documented process rather than a pass/fail bias-audit number.

sections.heading: FTC, CFPB, and who is actually liable
sections.body: U.S. enforcement agencies have moved through existing law rather than new AI-specific statutes. The FTC's 2021 guidance, 'Aiming for Truth, Fairness, and Equity,' argues that selling or deploying a racially biased algorithm can itself violate Section 5's ban on unfair or deceptive practices, no new AI law required. The CFPB's 2022 Circular 2022-03 went further for credit: it held that using an uninterpretable 'black-box' algorithm is no excuse for skipping the Equal Credit Opportunity Act's requirement to give applicants the specific reasons for a denial. This is the live debate the whole regulatory landscape turns on: a passed bias audit or a filed NIST-style document is evidence of process, not proof of a fair outcome, so when a compliant system still causes harm, liability could fall on the employer who deployed it, the vendor who built it, or the auditor who signed off, and current law does not clearly settle which.

lessons.workedExample: A hiring-tool vendor sells the same automated resume-screening product to a NYC firm and an EU-based firm. The NYC firm needs a Local Law 144 bias audit filed and a candidate notice posted before using it, but the Cornell compliance data suggests roughly 95% of comparable firms simply skip this, with the tool's own home page as the only place an auditor would think to check. The EU firm, because resume screening falls under Annex III employment, must additionally document training-data representativeness, prove bias-mitigation steps were taken, register the system in the EU database, and pass a conformity assessment, obligations with real enforcement teeth and phased legal deadlines behind them. Same model, same bias, two very different accountability regimes, one largely aspirational in practice and one backed by a registry and an assessment.
lessons.judgeFraming: A sharp judge will not accept 'we ran a bias audit' as a closing statement; they will ask whether a passed audit means the system is actually fair or just means a checkbox was filed, and NYC Local Law 144's roughly 5% real compliance rate is the strongest evidence you can cite that mandated audits without enforcement teeth default to the second. The harder follow-up is who is liable if an audited, compliant system still causes disparate harm. There is no clean answer across current law, and a team that can articulate the vendor-versus-deployer-versus-auditor ambiguity honestly, rather than asserting the audit settles the question, is showing they understand accountability as an unresolved institutional problem, not a solved one.

questions.prompt: What did Cornell compliance research find about NYC employers subject to Local Law 144?

options.text: About 95% published complete, compliant bias audit results
Only about 5% of employers hiring listed audit results, with roughly another 3% posting the transparency notice alone
Every employer using an automated employment tool was fined
The law was found unconstitutional and never enforced

explanations.a: This reverses the actual finding — real compliance was found to be very low, not near-universal.
explanations.b: Correct — the Cornell study found compliance in the single digits, a striking gap between the law's requirements and observed practice.
