explanations.c: No broad fining pattern was found; enforcement action has been minimal, which is distinct from the employer-wide publication compliance figure.
explanations.d: Local Law 144 has been in force since July 5, 2023; the issue documented is weak compliance and enforcement, not invalidation of the law.

questions.prompt: Match each regulatory instrument to its defining feature.

right.text: Risk-tiered, legally binding obligations including a conformity assessment for high-risk systems
Voluntary process framework organized around Govern, Map, Measure, Manage
Holds that a 'black-box' algorithm does not excuse a lender from giving specific adverse-action reasons under ECOA

questions.explanation: The EU AI Act is binding law with tiered obligations and deadlines; NIST's AI RMF is a voluntary, metric-agnostic process framework; CFPB Circular 2022-03 applies existing ECOA adverse-action requirements to complex algorithmic credit models regardless of interpretability.

questions.prompt: What legal theory does the FTC's 2021 'Aiming for Truth, Fairness, and Equity' guidance use to claim jurisdiction over biased algorithms, without any new AI-specific statute?

options.text: Section 5 of the FTC Act's prohibition on unfair or deceptive practices
A newly passed federal AI licensing requirement
The EU AI Act's extraterritorial provisions
NIST's AI Risk Management Framework, made mandatory by executive order

explanations.a: Correct — the FTC argues that deploying a racially biased algorithm can itself constitute an unfair or deceptive practice under existing Section 5 authority, requiring no new AI-specific law.
explanations.b: No such federal AI licensing statute existed at the time of this guidance; the FTC relied on its existing Section 5 authority instead.
explanations.c: The EU AI Act is a separate, EU-specific instrument and is not the basis for FTC jurisdiction in the U.S.
explanations.d: The NIST framework is voluntary and metric-agnostic; it is not the legal hook the FTC used to assert jurisdiction.

questions.prompt: According to this lesson, why is 'who is liable when an audited, compliant system still causes harm' described as an unresolved question?

options.text: Because current law clearly assigns all liability to the auditor in every case

Because passing an audit or filing a process document is evidence of process, not proof of a fair outcome, and current law does not clearly settle whether the vendor, deployer, or auditor bears responsibility
Because no country has ever passed any AI-related regulation
Because liability questions only apply to criminal law, not civil harm

explanations.a: No such clear, universal assignment of liability to auditors exists in current law; this is precisely the ambiguity the lesson highlights.
explanations.b: Correct — an audit or framework document shows a process was followed, not that the outcome was fair, and the vendor/deployer/auditor liability split remains legally unsettled when harm occurs anyway.
explanations.c: Multiple binding and voluntary instruments exist (the EU AI Act, Local Law 144, NIST AI RMF); the ambiguity is about liability allocation, not the absence of regulation.
explanations.d: The liability question applies broadly, including civil and regulatory enforcement contexts like FTC and CFPB actions, not solely criminal law.

lessons.label: Presenting a Fairness and Robustness Audit at the Fair

sections.heading: The poster spine
sections.body: A fairness poster needs three visuals and one sentence, not a wall of numbers. The slice table from Lesson 1 anchors it: n, metric, gap, confidence interval, per subgroup. A gap plot turns that table into a figure, one bar or point per slice with its interval drawn, so a viewer sees at a glance which gaps clear the noise floor and which don't. One degradation curve, performance versus a stress variable like image blur, sample size, or time since training, shows robustness rather than a single fairness snapshot. The sentence that must appear explicitly, in words, is which fairness definition you chose (equalized odds, calibration, demographic parity), which one you therefore sacrificed, because Lesson-6's impossibility result below says you cannot have all of them, and why that specific trade-off fit your deployment context.

sections.heading: The impossibility result behind the choice
sections.body: Kleinberg, Mullainathan, and Raghavan's 2016 paper, 'Inherent Trade-Offs in the Fair Determination of Risk Scores,' proved that three intuitive fairness properties, calibration within each group, equal false-positive balance, and equal false-negative balance, cannot all hold simultaneously for a risk score unless base rates are equal across groups or the score is a perfect predictor, both rare in practice. Alexandra Chouldechova's independent 2017 analysis reached the same conclusion for binary classifiers using COMPAS data: calibration and equalized error rates are mathematically incompatible whenever the groups being compared have different underlying base rates, exactly the situation in the COMPAS audit from Lesson 2. This is not a failure of any particular team's model; it is a theorem, which is precisely why naming the trade-off you accepted, rather than hiding it, is the scientifically honest move.

sections.heading: Rehearsing the judge's questions
sections.body: Three questions recur at every serious fairness poster. 'Did you just drop the protected attribute?' has one correct answer: dropping it does not remove bias, because correlated proxy features (zip code, name, school) reintroduce the same signal, a failure mode called fairness through unawareness. 'Is that gap significant?' requires pointing at the confidence interval on the gap plot, not restating the point estimate. 'What would you do about it?' requires naming one specific mitigation from Lesson 3, its stage (pre/in/post-processing), and its cost, not a vague promise to 'fix the bias.'

sections.heading: Collecting demographic data under ISEF rules
sections.body: ISEF's Human Participants rules require IRB review and documented informed consent, with parental permission for minors, before any interaction or data collection involving human participants, and consent may never be coerced. Auditing an existing public dataset like COMPAS or Adult typically counts as secondary analysis rather than human-participants research, but collecting new demographic data directly from people, even a school survey to build your own slices, triggers the full IRB and consent process, and skipping it is a disqualifying rules violation, not a minor paperwork lapse.

lessons.workedExample: A team's poster states: 'We optimized for equalized odds (equal false-positive and false-negative rates across groups), which per Kleinberg et al. (2016) means we sacrificed calibration; our tool's predicted-risk scores are no longer equally meaningful across groups, a trade-off we chose because in this deployment a false accusation costs more than a slightly miscalibrated score.' A judge asks whether they dropped race from the model. They answer no, race was retained deliberately after testing showed dropping it left zip code and school name as proxies with equivalent predictive power, verified by re-running the slice table with race removed and finding the gap unchanged. The judge follows up asking what they'd actually do about the remaining 6-point gap; they answer: apply Hardt's post-processing threshold optimizer, at the cost of needing group membership at prediction time.
lessons.judgeFraming: The single question that separates a memorized-vocabulary poster from a real one is 'what would you do about it,' because it forces the team past naming a metric into naming a trade-off they accepted and can defend. A judge who asks about dropping the protected attribute is testing whether the team knows fairness through unawareness fails against proxies; a judge who asks whether a gap is significant is testing whether error bars exist at all; and a judge who knows the Kleinberg-Mullainathan-Raghavan or Chouldechova results will specifically listen for the word 'trade-off' rather than a claim that the system is simply 'fair.'

questions.prompt: Order these three poster elements as a viewer should encounter them, from the raw per-slice numbers to the single interpretive sentence tying it together.

items.text: Slice table with n, metric, gap, and confidence interval
Gap plot visualizing which gaps clear the noise floor
One degradation curve showing performance under a stress variable
Explicit statement of which fairness definition was chosen and which was sacrificed

questions.explanation: The slice table is the underlying data; the gap plot turns it into a visual read of significance; the degradation curve adds a robustness dimension beyond a single snapshot; and the explicit fairness-definition trade-off statement is the interpretive sentence that ties the whole poster together.

questions.prompt: What did Kleinberg, Mullainathan, and Raghavan (2016) prove about calibration, false-positive balance, and false-negative balance?

options.text: All three can always be achieved simultaneously with enough training data
All three cannot generally be satisfied simultaneously unless base rates are equal across groups or the score is a perfect predictor
Only calibration matters; the other two are not meaningful fairness properties
The three properties are mathematically identical and always agree

explanations.a: More training data does not resolve this; the incompatibility is a mathematical theorem about the properties themselves, not a data-quantity limitation.
explanations.b: Correct — except in the special cases of equal base rates across groups or a perfect predictor, no score can satisfy all three properties at once, which is why any real audit must choose and disclose a trade-off.
explanations.c: The paper treats all three as legitimate fairness criteria; its point is that they conflict with each other, not that some are invalid.
explanations.d: The three properties are distinct and generally incompatible, which is the entire content of the theorem.

questions.prompt: Why is 'we dropped the protected attribute from the model' not a sufficient answer to a judge's fairness question?

options.text: Because correlated proxy features like zip code or school name can reintroduce the same signal, a failure called fairness through unawareness
Because it is illegal in every jurisdiction to drop a protected attribute
Because protected attributes are required by law to be included in every model
Because dropping it always improves the model's overall accuracy

explanations.a: Correct — proxy variables correlated with the dropped attribute can preserve nearly identical predictive bias, so removing the attribute's literal column does not remove the bias, which is exactly why a good audit re-checks the slice table after dropping it.
explanations.b: Dropping a protected attribute is not itself illegal; the issue is that it is often ineffective at removing bias, not that it is a legal violation.
explanations.c: There is no such universal legal requirement; the point is about proxies, not a mandate to always include the attribute.
explanations.d: Dropping a predictive feature more often reduces accuracy than improves it; this isn't the relevant issue for the fairness question being asked.

questions.prompt: Under ISEF's Human Participants rules, which scenario requires IRB review and documented informed consent before the work can begin?

options.text: Re-running a slice-table audit on the already-public, de-identified COMPAS dataset
Surveying classmates at your own school to collect new demographic labels for your own bias-audit dataset
Reading a published paper about the Adult census dataset
Computing a confidence interval on an existing public dataset's slice gaps

explanations.a: Analyzing an existing public, de-identified dataset is typically treated as secondary analysis, not new human-participants data collection.
explanations.b: Correct — collecting new demographic data directly from people, even informally at your own school, is new human-participants data collection and requires IRB review, informed consent, and parental permission for minors before it begins.
explanations.c: Reading a published paper involves no data collection from human participants at all.
explanations.d: A statistical computation on already-collected public data does not itself trigger new human-participants obligations.
